media.caption: Snow at Hi Marsh, Mito (水戸 涸沼の雪 Mito hinuma no yuki)

text.headline: Snow at Hi Marsh, Mito (水戸 涸沼の雪 Mito hinuma no yuki)
text.text:
"A lone fisherman in traditional straw cape (mino) and broad basket-weave hat (kasa) is enveloped in a frigid world of icy blues and fresh falling snow. His struggle for subsistence is easily overlooked as the viewer gazes into a crystallization of winter, printed with uncanny subtlety." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Honmon Temple, Ikegami (池上本門寺)

text.headline: Honmon Temple, Ikegami (池上本門寺)
text.text:
"Faithfully rendered from a sketch the artist drew from life, the curving pine tree and its snow-laden branches seem to shimmer against the muted wintry background. Diminutive figures proceed along a well-worn path toward the temple gate. All sound seems muffled by the fresh falling snow.
"Besides his study of Western painting, Hasui also trained in traditional East Asian art. One of its concepts seemingly embodied here is the practice of subjective immersion: the artist becomes so filled with the mysterious life force of surrounding nature that it pours out as a perceptible element of the work." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Narazaki (Hasui's biographer) believes that “There are few unsuccessful snowscapes by Hasui and in this regard he equals Hiroshige (1797-1858). The treatment of the faint, distant snow-covered mountains, the centrally positioned pine, which heightens the sentiment of the piece; and the path leading to the Honmon temple in the vicinity of the Rezan bridge has the feeling of a sketch.”
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜の池畔 不忍池 Yoro no chihan Shinobazunoike)

text.headline: Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜の池畔 不忍池 Yoro no chihan Shinobazunoike)
text.text:
"Hasui was born and bred in Tokyo, and though he traveled throughout Japan to sketch and experience certain timeless, traditional aspects of the country, he frequently walked the streets of his hometown to depict both the new and the old. Here, the skyline features the built cityscape as it looked nearly a decade after the devastation of the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. Electric lights illuminate the immense Shinobazu Pond in Ueno Park, in northeast Tokyo, transformed here into a dreamlike realm where the silhouette of a couple on the promenade is nearly indistinguishable as the natural light fades." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
The wife of the publisher Doi Sadaichi, the founder of Doi Hangaten, related, "By the way, I remember a story my husband told me about Hasui. When Hasui made the drawings for the print Night at Shinobazu Pond, which Sadaichi had ordered from Hasui, it took him a long time and many attempts until we accepted the draft."
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Evening Rain in Kawarago (河原子の夜雨 Kawarago no yau)

text.headline: Evening Rain in Kawarago (河原子の夜雨 Kawarago no yau)
text.text:
"While its location on the Pacific coast made this a popular beach resort, Kawarago was originally a fishing village. Hasui has not diminished the realities of making one’s livelihood from the sea, as here the weathered houses shelter their inhabitants from the rain at night, only to see them return to their boats for the next day’s catch. The darkening sky and sheets of rain, printed here with masterful sensitivity, nearly obscure the receding figure of a man under his outstretched umbrella." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Depicting a street in Kawarago, a Japanese fishing village on the beach in Hitachi city, Ibaraki Prefecture in the northern Kanto region of Japan on a rainy evening. This print exists in two different color states - one with a blue tint and, like this collection's print, another with a green tint.

He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Supper Wagon (屋台店 Yataimise)

text.headline: Supper Wagon (屋台店 Yataimise)
text.text: "This scene is one which even today can be seen in the streets of Shinjuku in Tokyo at night. Small booths, covered only by printed cotton curtains, sell bowls of soup or noodles, often at very low prices, to passers-by.  Among the foods advertised in this keenly observed print are sushi, udon (fat noodles in soup) and meat dishes.  A woman carries her child on her back in the traditional manner.  It is difficult to reconcile this scene with a nation mobilizing for an aggressive war in 1938." - Source: The Japanese Print Since 1900: Old dreams and New Visions, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Publications Ltd, 1983, p. 106.

media.caption: Hazy Evening at Shinobazu Pond (霞む夕べ−不忍池畔 Kasumu yūbe Shinobazu chihan)

text.headline: Hazy Evening at Shinobazu Pond (霞む夕べ−不忍池畔 Kasumu yūbe Shinobazu chihan)
text.text: The last rays of the setting sun and the lamps on the edge of Ueno Park's Shinobazu Pond illuminate this quiet scene in one of the artist's best known works.

media.caption: Rain in Maekawa, Sōshū (相州前川の雨 Sōshū Maekawa no ame)

text.headline: Rain in Maekawa, Sōshū (相州前川の雨 Sōshū Maekawa no ame)
text.text:
"Hasui often depicted rural villages to capture a sense of the traditional Japanese way of life that was rapidly disappearing in the wake of industrialization and Western influence. Thatched roof houses in this old post town emit golden warmth that seems to light the way for a lone woman sheltering below her parasol. Though the road bends out of sight, and the heavy rain at dusk casts an eerie light, the dark pine boughs seem to enfold the unseen inhabitants of the village in quiet repose." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Sōshū is present-day Kanagawa Prefecture, former Sagami Province. The array of traditional thatched-roof houses along the street, the shadows of large pine trees, a person walking with an umbrella, and the straight lines of rain produce a sense of tranquility as well as the nostalgia reminiscent of some work by Utagawa Hiroshige. According to Narazaki Muneshige, Hasui's biographer, this design is "one of Hasui’s favourites. . . . The rain is created through the use of the baren (pad used to apply colour during printing.)”
Blocks, 20; superimposed printings, 25.

media.caption: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯 chanoyu)

text.headline: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯 chanoyu)
text.text:
The Japanese tea ceremony is called chanoyu or sado in Japanese and the bitter tea served is called matcha. It is basically a choreographic ritual of preparing and serving tea together with some sweets. Each movement is predefined. The whole process is not about drinking tea, it is about aesthetics. The proper performance requires a long training and the use of certain tools like chasen, a bamboo brush.
This print is likely a first edition as indicated by the date 昭和 廿九 ( Shōwa 29) on the bottom of the left margin. For a later edition of this print see IHL.1178.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Ichikawa Yaozō III as Tanabe Bunzō (複製：三代目 市川八百蔵の田辺文蔵)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Ichikawa Yaozō III as Tanabe Bunzō (複製：三代目 市川八百蔵の田辺文蔵)
text.text:
158 works and sketches survive of the Japanese artist known only by the art name Tōshūsai Sharaku. Almost all were made over a ten-month period in 1794–1795.
This collection's print is a modern reproduction by the Adachi Print Institute printed on a dark mica ground as is the original print.
"Sharaku’s skill as a portraitist lay in his ability to capture both the features and the mood of the actor in a simple, almost caricaturish, manner that conveys great emotive power. For instance, even without knowing the plot of the play, one might sense that this samurai is powerless, through his hunched shoulders, gently clasped hands inside his sleeves, slightly unkempt hair, and look of resignation. Ichikawa Yaozō III (1747–1818) played the role of a masterless samurai supporting the plot of two brothers to avenge their father in a performance of Flowering Irises: A Soga Vendetta for the Bunroku Era (Hana ayame: Bunroku Soga) that took place in the fifth month of 1794." - The Metropolitan Museum of Art https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/835960 [accessed 8-25-23]

media.caption: Reproduction of: Onoe Matsusuke as Matsushita Mikinoshin in the Play Katakiuchi noriyaibanashi (複製：尾上松助の松下酒之進・敵討乗合話)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Onoe Matsusuke as Matsushita Mikinoshin in the Play Katakiuchi noriyaibanashi (複製：尾上松助の松下酒之進・敵討乗合話)
text.text:
158 works and sketches survive of the Japanese artist known only by the art name Tōshūsai Sharaku. Almost all were made over a ten-month period in 1794–1795.
This collection's print is a modern reproduction by the Adachi Print Institute printed on a dark mica ground as is the original print.
This print portrays the actor Onoe Matsusuke as Matsushita Mikinoshin in the Play Katakiuchi noriyaibanashi performed at the Kiriza theater in Edo in May 1974.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Shinozuka Uraemon, Prologue at the Miyako Theater (複製：篠塚浦右衛門の都座口上姿)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Shinozuka Uraemon, Prologue at the Miyako Theater (複製：篠塚浦右衛門の都座口上姿)
text.text:
158 works and sketches survive of the Japanese artist known only by the art name Tōshūsai Sharaku. Almost all were made over a ten-month period in 1794–1795.
This collection's print is a modern reproduction published by the Adachi Print Institute printed on a white mica ground as is the original print.
There is controversy over whether the figure reading the announcement, often referred to as a prologue, in this print is Shinozuka Uraemon, the director of the green-room of the Miyakoza theater or Miyako Dennai II, the manager of the Miyakoza. The print may be found with either name given in the title.

media.caption: In a Kyoto Sweets Shop (京のしるこ屋 Kyo no shiruko-ya)

text.headline: In a Kyoto Sweets Shop (京のしるこ屋 Kyo no shiruko-ya)
text.text: A maiko is about to lift ohagi (a sweet made from boiled rice and red azuki beans) to her mouth, in this lovely, but seemingly empty, Kyoto sweets shop.

media.caption: Wild Geese (Gan)

text.headline: Wild Geese (Gan)
text.text: Wild geese are flying over marsh reeds in this later edition of one of the twenty-one prints designed by Shōson that were shown in the first shin hanga exhibition at the Toledo Museum of Art in 1930.

media.caption: Swallow and Wisteria

text.headline: Swallow and Wisteria
text.text: One of over fifty kachō-ga prints the artist made in the square shikishiban format. It is possible this print was published by the Daikokuya publishing house.  If so, it was likely printed c. 1930s or possibly early 1940s, after Daikokuya was taken over by S. Koizumi from the Matsuki family.  This print is stamped "MADE IN JAPAN" on the verso.

media.caption: Herons in Reeds (Ashi ni Sagi)

text.headline: Herons in Reeds (Ashi ni Sagi)
text.text: Two egrets wade at the edge of a river under a crescent moon in this later edition of one of the twenty-one prints designed by Shōson that were shown in the first shin hanga exhibition at the Toledo Museum of Art in 1930.

media.caption: Pheasant (雉)

text.headline: Pheasant (雉)
text.text: One of a large number of kachō-ga prints the artist made in the square shikishiban format.  Many were published by the Tokyo publisher Daikokuya. It is unclear exactly when Daikokuya published these prints, but it is likely they were printed c. 1930s or possibly early 1940s, after Daikokuya was taken over by S. Koizumi from the Matsuki family.  This print is stamped with the number 1 and "Made in Japan" on the verso. The date 8/19/47 is also written on the back.

media.caption: Reproduction of: The Gion Shrine in Snow (複製：祇園社雪中 Fukusei：Gionsha setchū)

text.headline: Reproduction of: The Gion Shrine in Snow (複製：祇園社雪中 Fukusei：Gionsha setchū)
text.text: "The large umbrellas and bright kimono of the Kyoto women form an eye-catching focus in the otherwise subdued scene of thickly falling snow. Through the stone 'torii' gateway on the south side of the Gion (Yasaka) Shrine can be seen the Niken-jaya (Twin teahouses)." - Source: The British Museum, Curator Comments https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_1906-1220-0-916 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Ikebana (生花)

text.headline: Ikebana (生花)
text.text: Similar in composition to the artist's print Tea Ceremony (IHL.0008 and IHL.0117), a woman, with hasami in hand, arranges flowers.

media.caption: Rainy Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜雨 不忍池 Yoru ame, Shinobazunoeki)

text.headline: Rainy Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜雨 不忍池 Yoru ame, Shinobazunoeki)
text.text:
A solitary figure walks toward Benten Temple under a steady rain. This print was issued in two color schemes, a purple-hued tint and a greyish-hued tint. The more commonly encountered hue is this print's purple-hued tint. (See IHL.1207 for the greyish-hued tint.)
Both color schemes were first issued in 1938, bearing the Watanabe type-E publishing seal used by the publisher between 1931 and 1941. This print is a later edition, c. 1946-1957, bearing the Watanabe "type-A" 6mm round seal.

media.caption: Mandarin Ducks in Pond

text.headline: Mandarin Ducks in Pond
text.text: A print after a c. 1820 painting by this Shijō school artist.

media.caption: Teranohama, Sanuki Coast (讃岐海岸寺の浜 Sanuki Kaiganji no hama)

text.headline: Teranohama, Sanuki Coast (讃岐海岸寺の浜 Sanuki Kaiganji no hama)
text.text:
"During his second sketch trip to Western Japan, Hasui visited the island of Shikoku and explored this isolated shore along the Inland Sea. While the foreground is depicted realistically to convey the contours and textures of the pines, Hasui emphasized their shadowy dark branches against the mist-enshrouded distance. Note the absence of a vanishing point, a feature of Western art; instead, Hasui opted for an atmospheric perspective in which the far-off landforms recede into a seemingly boundless, mysterious depth." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, tells us that “The pines along the coast of the Inland sea stand out for their forms, which have been shaped by the strong seawinds. A daring composition.” Sanuki province corresponds to present-day Kagawa prefecture.

He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Morning at the Arayu Spa, Shiobara (湯宿の朝 塩原新湯 Tōyado no asa Shiobara Arayu)

text.headline: Morning at the Arayu Spa, Shiobara (湯宿の朝 塩原新湯 Tōyado no asa Shiobara Arayu)
text.text:
A spring wells up along the Yumura Fault through a crevice in the granite at 98 degrees centigrade. Arayu Hot Spring produces 470 liters of hot water per minute. It is located in Shin-onsen Town, Mikata County, Hyogo Prefecture.

media.caption: Big Fire at Ryōgoku Sketched from Hama-chō (浜町より写す両国大火 Hamachō yori Utsusu Ryōgoku Taika)

text.headline: Big Fire at Ryōgoku Sketched from Hama-chō (浜町より写す両国大火 Hamachō yori Utsusu Ryōgoku Taika)
text.text:
At around 2 a.m. on January 26, 1881, fire broke out in Kanda Matsueda-cho, just one-half mile west of Kiyochika’s house near the west end of Ryogoku Bridge. Probably the work of an arsonist, the fire spread rapidly, fanned by strong seasonal winds from the northwest. Probably around daybreak, it reached the foot of Ryogoku Bridge, consuming Kiyochika’s home. The fire was then driven across the Sumida River to the Honjo area, traveling south to Fukagawa until it finally burned out in the early evening of the same day after sixteen hours of devastation. The greatest of all the many fires in Meiji Tokyo, it destroyed over 10,000 buildings.
This print was made in the 1950s by the Kyoto publisher Maria Shobo from recut woodblocks, copying the original 1881 design. Two series of Kiyochika designs, each consisting of 12 prints, were issued by the publisher. The recut prints generally, but not always, have the publisher's identifying Ma character beneath the cartouche in the print's margin. Maria Shobo was established in 1924 and continues to publish books.
This print was originally issued as part of a loosely constructed series Famous Views of Tokyo (Tokyo meisho) consisting of 93 prints issued from 1876-1881 by two publishers, Matsuki Heikichi and Fukuda Kumajirō.

media.caption: Snow Scene at Tōshōgū Shrine, Ueno (上野東照宮積雪之図 Ueno Tōshōgū sekisetsu no zu)

text.headline: Snow Scene at Tōshōgū Shrine, Ueno (上野東照宮積雪之図 Ueno Tōshōgū sekisetsu no zu)
text.text:
The Toshogu Shrine, built in remembrance of Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1627, is reached by a small path seamed by 256 stone- and bronze-lanterns. It is the historical pride of Ueno Park. Built in 1627 and remodeled 24 years later, it has hardly been touched since. It was undamaged in the battle of 1868 - an irony as the shrine is dedicated the memory of the first shogun, Tokugawa Ieyasu, who wrested power away from the Emperor and established Edo as the capital.
This print was made in the 1950s by the Kyoto publisher Maria Shobo from recut woodblocks, copying the original 1879 design. Two series of Kiyochika designs, each consisting of 12 prints were issued by the publisher. The recut prints generally, but not always, have the publisher's identifying Ma character beneath the cartouche in the print's margin. Maria Shobo was established in 1924 and continues to publish books.
This print was originally issued as part of a loosely constructed series Famous Views of Tokyo (Tokyo meisho) consisting of 93 prints issued from 1876-1881 by two publishers, Matsuki Heikichi and Fukuda Kumajirō.

media.caption: Evening Rain Yanaka Pagoda Tokyo (雨に暮るる塔   東京谷中 Amne ni kureru tō Tōkyō Yanaka)

text.headline: Evening Rain Yanaka Pagoda Tokyo (雨に暮るる塔   東京谷中 Amne ni kureru tō Tōkyō Yanaka)
text.text:
A rainy evening at Ueno Park, Tokyo, in the Yanaka district. The woman in the foreground wears a raincoat and high rain-shoes; on her arm she carries something wrapped in a furoshiki, or square of silk used by the Japanese to encase parcels of all kinds.
About 20 blocks, along about 25 superimposed printings went into making this print.
Originally part of Tennō-ji, the five-storied pagoda was built in 1644. It burned down in 1771 and was rebuilt 19 years later. This last version, built in 1791 in Japanese zelkova wood, was at almost 35 meters the tallest of its kind in the Kantō area. The five-storied pagoda had been donated in 1908 by Tennō-ji to the city of Tokyo and had been the model for Kōda Rohan's novel The Five-Storied Pagoda. It was a famous city landmark and the very symbol of the Yanaka Cemetery, but it was completely destroyed by fire at around 3 AM of July 6, 1957. The fire has been attributed to two lovers who, it is believed, committed suicide together by burning down the pagoda. It was decided not to rebuild it and leave only the five foundation stones.

media.caption: Himeji Castle, Evening (姫路城 夕 Himejijō yu)

text.headline: Himeji Castle, Evening (姫路城 夕 Himejijō yu)
text.text: This print, derived from Yoshida's 1926 print of the same title "Himeji Castle - Evening" was published in the November 1928 Enthronement Edition of The Japan Advertiser. The blocks were recut for this print and printed by the Yoshida family studio in an edition of 2000 prints. The print is described in the Japan Advertiser as follows: "The color print on the opposite page is the work of Hiroshi Yoshida, generally known as the father of modern color print work in Japan, and a recognized leader in this profession. On his three visits abroad, Mr. Yoshida received many vivid impressions of Europe and America, but it is in the Japanese Alps that he has found his greatest inspiration."

media.caption: View of the Sea at Shinagawa Bay (品川海上眺望図 Shinagawa kaijōchōbō zu)

text.headline: View of the Sea at Shinagawa Bay (品川海上眺望図 Shinagawa kaijōchōbō zu)
text.text:

The recut prints generally, but not always, have the publisher's identifying Ma character beneath the cartouche in the print's margin. media.caption: Edo River at Imai (江戸川 今井)

text.headline: Edo River at Imai (江戸川 今井)
text.text: Kasamatsu depicts what remained of the Imai ferry boat terminal in the early 1950s. The Imai river boat was used to cross Edo River until 1912 (the first year of Taishō) until Imai Bridge was built.

media.caption: The Red Gate at Tokyo University (東大赤門 Tōdai akamon)

text.headline: The Red Gate at Tokyo University (東大赤門 Tōdai akamon)
text.text: The famous Kaga Estate's Akamon 赤門, or Red Gate, on the main campus of University of Tokyo, which dates from 1827 and has been designated as an 'Important Cultural Property' by the Japanese Government.

media.caption: Snow at Heian Shrine, Kyoto (平安神宮の雪 京都 Heian jingū no yuki Kyoto)

text.headline: Snow at Heian Shrine, Kyoto (平安神宮の雪 京都 Heian jingū no yuki Kyoto)
text.text:
"At a time when the country was still marked by the ravages of war and defeat, Hasui continued to seek out scenes of continuity where only the seasons offered marks of transience. Famous landmarks, such as the Heian Shrine in Kyoto, coupled with universally understood images of temporal phenomena, like snowfall, captivated members of the Occupation forces in Japan after WWII who sought out Hasui’s prints as treasured souvenirs." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
The Heian shrine was built in 1894 to commemorate the 1100th anniversary of the founding of the city of Kyoto. It is dedicated to the emperors Kanmu (r. 781-806) in whose reign the city was established, and Komei (r. 1846-67), the last emperor in Kyoto. The large garden was principally the work of Ogawa Jihei (1860-1933), whose design was inspired by the aesthetics of the Heian period (794-1185).

He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: A Yangban (両班)

text.headline: A Yangban (両班)
text.text: According to Paul Shiota, owner of T.Z.Shiota Gallery in San Francisco, Kawase Hasui (1883-1957) and the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō (1885-1962) were commissioned by his grandfather, T.Z. Shiota (Takezō Shiota) of San Francisco, to produce a limited edition of 300 prints of this image. Approximately 200 of these prints are in circulation with the remainder being held by the Shiota family as of the year 2000. The print is an idealized portrait of a Korean gentleman-scholar created from a photograph. Paul did not know why his grandfather desired this image. His grandfather also commissioned a second print from Hasui and Watanabe of the Washington Monument.

media.caption: Senjō Cliff, Lake Towada (十和田湖 千丈幕 Tōwada-ko Senjōno maku)

text.headline: Senjō Cliff, Lake Towada (十和田湖 千丈幕 Tōwada-ko Senjōno maku)
text.text:
"Hasui began his career as a painter and his intention, even in prints, had been to depict nature as he experienced it, bringing viewers the same sense of the light and atmosphere that immersed him.
"In an interview, he described an earlier 1919 trip to this part of Aomori: 'Because the scenery of Lake Towada - a place I had wanted to visit for some years - was so sublime, I was somewhat disappointed to find that it was almost impossible to illustrate using my usual technique. However, from the moment that I saw the steep bluff called Senjō Cliff I was hypnotized as if in a dream . . . .'” - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, explains that Hasui depicted the picturesque scenery of Senjo cliff before. In this example he illustrates a foreground tree, its wizened leaves turning yellowish and falling, even though it is still early autumn. Opposite is the bizarrely shaped cliff at Senjo, hemmed with autumnal foliage. The surface of the lake is serene, the reflection of the Senjo cliff on the water, upon which a single white-sailed boat is afloat, is effective. This piece was sketched on 28 October 1932, produced in December and published in January 1933.
Blocks 20; superimposed printings, 25.

media.caption: Night at Ginza (夜の銀座 Yoru no Ginza)

text.headline: Night at Ginza (夜の銀座 Yoru no Ginza)
text.text:
Night in Ginza provides a glimpse at the Japan of the 1920s when Western dress and culture was all the rage, when young women, as seen in the foreground of the print, had bobbed hair just like the flappers in the West. These moden garu (modern girl) strolled down the avenues of the fashionable districts like the Ginza. In this print, these women contrast the kimono-clad woman who oddly enough stands with her back turned towards them. - Source: Ukiyo-e to Shin hanga - The Art of Japanese Woodblock Prints, Amy Newland and Chris Uhlenbeck, Brompton Books Corporation, 1990 p. 208, 210.
This print is a 1979 version, likely from recut blocks, of the 1929 issue of Night at Ginza for the series Shin Tokyo Hyakkei - One Hundred Views of New Tokyo and again in 1945 with re-cut blocks for the series Scenes of Lost Tokyo (Tokyo kaikō zue). See IHL.0253 for the 1945 version of this print issued as part of the portfolio Scenes of Lost Tokyo and for details on the print's subject matter.

media.caption: Near Yanagibashi (柳橋附近 Yanagibashi fukin)

text.headline: Near Yanagibashi (柳橋附近 Yanagibashi fukin)
text.text: Kasamatsu gives a view across the Kanda River as night begins to fall. A yakatabune with its distinctive red lanterns is moored along the embankment. Once lined with geisha houses, Yanagibashi, part of the Asakusabashi area of Tokyo, is today filled with wholesale stores and doll shops.

media.caption: Nihon Bridge in Snow  (雪の日本橋 Yuki no Nihon-bashi)

text.headline: Nihon Bridge in Snow  (雪の日本橋 Yuki no Nihon-bashi)
text.text: Nihon Bridge in Snow by Bannai Kōkan (1900-1963) presents the actual appearance of Nihonbashi but then hides its true face behind a blizzard. Kōkan, a painter who produced prints for the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō (1885-1962) in the 1930s, designed this scene as the first work in a proposed, but not realized, series, Fifty-three Modern Views of the Tōkaidō.  The iconic 1914 Nihonbashi Daiei Building can be seen on the right behind the bridge and streetcars.

media.caption: The Great Lantern of the Senso Temple, Asakusa (浅草觀音堂大提灯 Asakusa Kannon-dō Ō-chōchin)

text.headline: The Great Lantern of the Senso Temple, Asakusa (浅草觀音堂大提灯 Asakusa Kannon-dō Ō-chōchin)
text.text: The “Kannon Hall” is part of the Sensoji Temple in Asakusa, a fairly Bohemian district of Tokyo before the Second World War. It is famous for its huge paper lantern, of which Hiroshige had done a celebrated print in his One Hundred Views of Edo in the late 1850s. Kasamatsu’s view is similarly constructed to Hiroshige’s, but its rather pessimistic, dark atmosphere is noticeably different from the early master’s cheerful and light-filled version. As often in this artist’s work, the figures have their back to us. - Source: The Japanese Print Since 1900: Old Dreams and New Visions, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Publications, Ltd., 1983, p. 99.

media.caption: Shirahone Hotspring, Shinshū (信州白骨温泉 Shinshū Shirahone onsen)

text.headline: Shirahone Hotspring, Shinshū (信州白骨温泉 Shinshū Shirahone onsen)
text.text: This is a later, although lifetime, edition of Kasamatsu's print of these famous hot springs. The original edition used a darker green for the foliage. Shirahone Onsen (白骨温泉, literally "white bone hot spring") is a small onsen town in the Northern Japan Alps famous since the Edo period. The town is a loose collection of a dozen or so ryokan along the slopes of a steep valley, which lies near famous alpine nature spots such as Kamikochi and Norikura. Shirahone Onsen gets its name from its milky white spring water, which is nearly opaque with magnesium and calcium sediments and is believed to relieve gastrointestinal ailments.

media.caption: Starlings in Flight

text.headline: Starlings in Flight
text.text: Four gray starlings (Sturnus cineraceus) in flight during rainfall.

media.caption: Jōganden Moon – Minamoto no Tsunemoto (貞観殿の月 源経基 Jōganden no tsuki - Minamoto no Tsunemoto)

text.headline: Jōganden Moon – Minamoto no Tsunemoto (貞観殿の月 源経基 Jōganden no tsuki - Minamoto no Tsunemoto)
text.text:
Minamoto no Tsunemoto (A.D. 917- 961) was a fine poet and skilled in the martial arts. One night near Jōganden, a building in the Imperial Palace in Kyoto, he shot a demonic deer that was about to attack the Emperor.
This print is from the album issued by publisher Akiyama Buemon shortly after Yoshitoshi's death and retains its original album backing.

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, , 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: Ono no Tōfū (小野道風 )

text.headline: Ono no Tōfū (小野道風 )
text.text:
Print number 3 (三), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the calligrapher Ono no Tōfū (894-966) in front of the Daigokuden in the Heian Palace complex.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Pinecone Fish (松子魚)

text.headline: Pinecone Fish (松子魚)
text.text: This print depicting a pinecone fish was originally published in the sixth volume of Bairei's seven volume work Bairei Ekagami, originally published in 1903 by Unsōdō Publishing. This collection's print was likely removed from Unsōdō's 1982 reprinting of the book. Works from the earlier 1903, 1913 and 1942 editions can be identified by their vertical centerfold, which is lacking in the 1982 release, as it is in this collection's print. Each volume contains 15 prints.

media.caption: Damselfly

text.headline: Damselfly
text.text: This print depicting a damselfly on a branch was originally published in the sixth volume of Bairei's seven volume work Bairei Ekagami, originally published in 1903 by Unsōdō Publishing. This collection's print was likely taken from Unsōdō's 1982 reprinting of the book.  Works from the earlier publishings in 1903, 1913 and 1942 can be identified by their vertical centerfold, which is lacking in the 1982 release, as it is in this collection's print. Each volume contains 15 prints.

media.caption: The full moon coming with a challenge to flaunt its beautiful brow – Fukami Jikyū (名月や 来て見よかしの ひたい際 深見自休 Meigetsu ya kite miyo gashi no hitai giwa - Fukami Jikyū)

text.headline: The full moon coming with a challenge to flaunt its beautiful brow – Fukami Jikyū (名月や 来て見よかしの ひたい際 深見自休 Meigetsu ya kite miyo gashi no hitai giwa - Fukami Jikyū)
text.text:
This print is likely from the album containing the entire series issued by the series' publisher Akiyama Buemon shortly after Yoshitoshi's death. It portrays Fukami, a young man in full bloom, who composed the following poem implying he was as beautiful as the full moon.
"The full moon, coming with a challenge to flaunt its beautiful brow!"

media.caption: Tearing Weeds Out In Peking (北京の摘草 Pekin no tsumikusa)

text.headline: Tearing Weeds Out In Peking (北京の摘草 Pekin no tsumikusa)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In this print, two Japanese soldiers are taking a walk in occupied Beijing. They laugh as they pick sad-faced bracken and horsetail (weak Chinese soldiers) growing around Beijing Castle.

media.caption: Mice in a Trap (袋の鼠 Fukuro no nezumi)

text.headline: Mice in a Trap (袋の鼠 Fukuro no nezumi)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
Chinese warships in the form of mice or rats are fleeing into a bag from a Japanese warship in the form of a cat. When this print was issued in April 1895, China had already signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki ending the war under unfavorable terms. The bag is a gift bag (noshi) and China will have to fill it with the spoils of war.

media.caption: Asahina in the play Soga Heir (世継曽我の朝比奈 Yotsugi Soga no Asahina)

text.headline: Asahina in the play Soga Heir (世継曽我の朝比奈 Yotsugi Soga no Asahina)
text.text:
A bunraku puppet in the role ofAsahina Saburō 朝比奈三郎 in the fourth act of the play Yotsugi Soga 世継曽我 (The Soga Heir), appearing in the appendix to volume 6 of the Complete Works of Chikamatsu. .

One of 18 prints published from 1922 to 1925 as part of the celebration of the two-hundredth anniversary of the death of Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1623-1724), perhaps the greatest dramatist in the history of the Japanese theater. Each design illustrates a scene or character from one of Chikamatsu’s famous works which were compiled into 16 volumes by Chikamatsu researcher Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950). The prints were inserted into the volume containing the story they illustrated and were also separately sold.

media.caption: The Heroine Koharu in The Love Suicides of Amijima (心中天の網島の小春 Shinjū ten no amijima no Koharu)

text.headline: The Heroine Koharu in The Love Suicides of Amijima (心中天の網島の小春 Shinjū ten no amijima no Koharu)
text.text:
Usually considered Chikamatsu's masterpiece, The Love Suicides at Amijima was based on a real incident, a pair of lovers who killed themselves on the Amijima Diacho Temple grounds in Osaka on November 13, 1720. The puppet play opened January 3, 1721, not quite two months later. In Amijima, Chikamatsu goes well beyond simply staging a current event. The play explores the intricacies of a love triangle by treating the wife, Osan, as a major character. The entangling web of interactions between the wife and the courtesan, Koharu, complicates the plot and adds new depths to a familiar story (which ends in the double suicide of Koharu and her lover, Jihei.) Plays depicting love suicides became prohibited less than two years after the play's premier.
For another impression of this print which has the printer and carver names impressed on the bottom margin see ihl-1114.

media.caption: Yohei in The Oil-Hell Murder (女殺油地獄の与兵衛 Onna goroshi abura no jigoku no Yohei)

text.headline: Yohei in The Oil-Hell Murder (女殺油地獄の与兵衛 Onna goroshi abura no jigoku no Yohei)
text.text:
Yohei, a 23 year old debt-ridden oil merchant, draws his dagger to kill Okichi the wife the oil merchant Teshimaya Shichizaemon and take the money she's removed from a safe, in the third act of the The Oil-hell Murder, first performed in August 1721 on the bunraku stage.

media.caption: The Mountain Woman  in Komochi Yamanba (嫗山姥の山姥 Komochi Yamanba no Yamamba)

text.headline: The Mountain Woman  in Komochi Yamanba (嫗山姥の山姥 Komochi Yamanba no Yamamba)
text.text:
The old mountain woman, Yamauba (also read Yamanba, Onionna or Yamaonna) in Chikamatsu Monzaemon's 近松門左衛門 (1653-1724) puppet play, "Komochi Yamauba" 嫗山姥 (1712). Usen depicts Yamanba standing on the clouds to show her power.

media.caption: A Thick-Skinned Face (厚い面の皮 Atsui tsura no kawa)

text.headline: A Thick-Skinned Face (厚い面の皮 Atsui tsura no kawa)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
A Thick-Skinned Face plays on the figure of speech that in both Chinese and Japanese means an impudent person; by extension, “to peel off the skin of the face” is to put such a person to shame. In the text the war is presented as punishment for the enemy´s arrogance. The Japanese soldier depicted here shows no emotion, without mercy he is going to shave one layer after the other to punish and humiliate his Chinese counterpart. Finally, the maltreated Chinese is begging to leave one of his eyes unshaved.

media.caption: Ariko - Sink Beneath the Waves (有子)

text.headline: Ariko - Sink Beneath the Waves (有子)
text.text:
Ariko no Naishi (A.D. 829-900), a lady in waiting in the Heian court, is despondent over an unrequited love. As she prepares to jump from the boat and drown herself, she recites the following verse, "How hopeless it is; it would be better for me to sink beneath the waves; perhaps then I could see my man from Moon Capital."[1]
"This is one of the most charming designs of the series. The moon is shown only in reflection -- the printer's execution of this concept is excellent. In addition to wiping away her tears with a poignant gesture, Ariko seems also to be shading them from the brilliance of the reflected moonlight. The design was a favorite of the writer and critic Noguchi Yone; in a lecture to the London Japan Society in 1914, he described pasting an impression of this print on a screen and his pleasure whenever he looked at it.
"The black of Ariko’s robes has been burnished with a piece of ivory, giving it a shiny finish. The design on the robe is made up of large wheels and stylized vine leaves, probably morning-glories, in a colorful tie-dyed pattern. (The wheel, associated with the Buddhist concept of the Wheel of Life, was a common religious motif in Japan; as a means of transport, however, wheels were impractical and little used in Japan’s hilly countryside, where objects and people were more usually carried – during the time of Lady Ariko they were most commonly used on the oxcarts of the aristocracy.) A design of small wheels over waves was popular in the Heian period (794-1185), but the oversize wheels here seem more appropriate for a kimono pattern of the Edo period (1600-1868). Perhaps a kimono design with waves would have seemed excessive for a print where waves are the most important element of the composition. Most of the bottom half of the design is devoted to the water, which has the effect of drawing the figure downwards. The waves are choppy, blown by a cool breeze that, if we stop for a moment, we can almost feel and hear."[2]
An early, if not first, state of this print.

media.caption: Akazome Emon - The Poetess Awaiting Her Lover (赤染衛門 Akazomeemon)

text.headline: Akazome Emon - The Poetess Awaiting Her Lover (赤染衛門 Akazomeemon)
text.text:
Akazome Emon (956-1041) was a celebrated woman poet of the Heian court. After a long, sleepless night awaiting the arrival of her lover, she writes, "I wish I had gone to bed immediately; but now the night has passed and I watch the moon descend."
An early, if not first, state of this print, with heavy embossing of the white robe.

text.headline: Mount Otowa Moon - Bright God Tamura (音羽山月 田村明神 Otowayama no tuski)
text.text:
"Based on a scene from a Noh play, three itinerant priests meet a man sweeping fallen cherry petals as they visit Kiyomizu Temple in Kyoto. The man proves to be the spirit of the warrior Tamura Myojin, the deity of the mountain behind the temple."[1]

media.caption: Rising Moon Over Mount Nanping – Cao Cao (南屏山昇月 曹操 Napeizan Shogetsu - Sōsō)

text.headline: Rising Moon Over Mount Nanping – Cao Cao (南屏山昇月 曹操 Napeizan Shogetsu - Sōsō)
text.text:
On the night before the battle of Zhang Jiang, the Chinese leader Cao Cao (A.D. 155-200) called his generals to his ship for a banquet. As the moon rose, he composed the following poem to celebrate their gathering.[1]
"Cao Cao is crossing the Yangzi river on the night before the decisive Battle of the Red Cliffs. He stands in the prow of a boat at the head of 830,000 troops, in full, though anachronistic, Chinese military regalia – Yoshitoshi has captured his powerful stance very well. A following breeze stirs his robes, and mists swirl over the river. The moon rises over the distant cliffs; two crows fly overhead."[2]
An early, if not first, state of this print.

media.caption: Great Torii at Kudan (九段大鳥居 Kudan dai torii)

text.headline: Great Torii at Kudan (九段大鳥居 Kudan dai torii)
text.text:
Kawakami pictures the torii at the still controversial Yasukuni Shrine honoring Imperial Japan's war-dead. Issued in 1946, a little over a year after Japan's surrender, as part of the fifteen print series Tokyo Kaiko Zue (Scenes of Lost Tokyo), it was only the lax oversight of the print arts in general by the US Occupation censor's eye that allowed the series not only to be published but to be sold in the US military Post Exchanges.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Factory Street at Fukagawa (工場地帯 本所 Honjo kōjōchi tai)

text.headline: Factory Street at Fukagawa (工場地帯 本所 Honjo kōjōchi tai)
text.text:
Honjo, east of the Sumida River, was designated as one of Tokyo’s industrial wards during the Meiji period. Maekawa catches the bleakness of this factory area, full of smokestacks and utility poles, with overall-clad factory workers trudging up the road.
This print was originally issued in 1929 with the title Factory Streets of Honjo (Kojochitai, Honjo) as part of the series One Hundred Views of the New Tokyo (Shin Tokyo Hyakkei). The print was reissued in 1945 from newly cut blocks under the title Fakutory [sic] Street at Fukagawa for the series Tokyo kaiko zue (Scenes of Lost Tokyo). For another impression of this print see IHL.0174.

media.caption: Red Gate at Imperial University (帝大赤門 Teidai Akamon)

text.headline: Red Gate at Imperial University (帝大赤門 Teidai Akamon)
text.text:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Lost Tokyo. This print picturing the famous Red Gate entrance to Tokyo University (the first Imperial University) was one of seven new designs for the series, the other eight prints originally appearing in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This is one of six prints in Scenes of Last Tokyo which Smith points out as depicting "places with serious imperial resonances," the six being the Nijubashi Bridge at the Imperial Palace, the Akasaka Palace (residence of the Crown Prince), the Meiji Shrine, the Torii (Gateway) at Kudan, the Gate of the Imperial University (alma mater of the most senior bureaucrats of the militarist era), and the Graveyard of Sengaku-ji, burial place of Japan’s most celebrated paragons of loyalty. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p.24.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Change E Flees to the Moon (嫦娥奔月 Jōga hongetsu tsuki)

text.headline: Change E Flees to the Moon (嫦娥奔月 Jōga hongetsu tsuki)
text.text:
According to Chinese legend, the Queen Mother of the West rewarded Chang E's husband with a vial of the elixir of immortality. Chang E stole the elixir, drank it, and fled to heaven where she became the spirit of the moon.
This print is from the album containing the complete series issued by publisher Akiyama Buemon shortly after Yoshitoshi's death. It retains its original album backing.

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Sparrows and Camellia in Snow (複製：雪中椿に雀)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Sparrows and Camellia in Snow (複製：雪中椿に雀)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of a c. 1831-1833 Hiroshige print.
The poem, identified by the scholar Suzuku Juzo as the first two lines of an unsigned Chinese poem entitled “Inquiry of a Stork” by Hakurakuten (772–846), reads:
Crows and storks fight over something to eat
and sparrows over where to sleep,
You stand there all alone by the pond,
the wind blows and snow piles up."
source: Art Institute Chicago https://www.artic.edu/artworks/11039/sparrows-and-camellia-in-snow [accessed 8-17-23]
"Hiroshige, more than any other Japanese artist, is renowned for the depiction of snow, and this particular snow scene is one of the artist's supreme achievements in the genre of birds and flowers." - Source: Hiroshige Birds and Flowers, Cynthie J. Bogel, et. al., George Braziller, Inc., 1988, pl. 10.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Pheasant and Chrysanthemum (複製：菊に雉)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Pheasant and Chrysanthemum (複製：菊に雉)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of a c. 1832 Hiroshige print.
The poem reads, in translation, as:
Chrysanthemum scent -
every time a drop of dew
drips down from inside!"
source: Hiroshige Birds and Flowers, Cynthie J. Bogel, et. al., George Braziller, Inc., 1988, pl. 19.

media.caption: Reproduction of: An Egret among Rushes (複製：芦に鷺)

text.headline: Reproduction of: An Egret among Rushes (複製：芦に鷺)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of an early 1830s Hiroshige print.
"To Hillier this is 'one of the most admired of the artist's kachō-e'. This must also have been a popular print in Hiroshige's time as late impressions are known where the lines of the reeds have broken down due to excessive wear on the blocks." Source: Hiroshige Birds and Flowers, Cynthie J. Bogel, et. al., George Braziller, Inc., 1988, pl. 21.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Swallows and Peach Blossoms under a Full Moon (Fukusei: Tsukiyo momo ni tsubame)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Swallows and Peach Blossoms under a Full Moon (Fukusei: Tsukiyo momo ni tsubame)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of an early c. 1830s Hiroshige print.
The poem, in English translation, reads:
Sprint has come and all the streams
are filled with peach blossoms.
Nobody knows where Heaven is,
but all wonder.
- Source: Hiroshige Birds and Flowers, Cynthie J. Bogel, et. al., George Braziller, Inc., 1988, pl. 21.

media.caption: Reproduction of: A Pheasant and Bracken (複製：蕨に錦鶏)

text.headline: Reproduction of: A Pheasant and Bracken (複製：蕨に錦鶏)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of a mid-1830s Hiroshige print.
"The golden pheasant (kinkei) was one of the exotic birds imported to Japan by Dutch and Chinese traders who were restricted to the southern port of Nagasaki during the Edo period. Hiroshige, who created a large corpus of flower-and-bird prints (kachō-ga) in the 1830s, here presents an elegant image of the pheasant with its long tail plumage gracefully raised to follow the long, narrow format of the print. Above, a poem is inscribed:
Blundering into
a path where tasty grasses
manage to grow tall."
Source: National Museum of Asian Art https://asia.si.edu/object/S2004.3.222/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Reproduction of: A Long-Tailed Blue Bird on a Branch of Flowering Plum  (複製：梅に三光鳥)

text.headline: Reproduction of: A Long-Tailed Blue Bird on a Branch of Flowering Plum  (複製：梅に三光鳥)
text.text: A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of an early 1830s Hiroshige print picturing a magpie perched on a branch with plum blossoms. The poem in the upper right of the print reads "Hito ume dokusen tenka haru" - One solitary early plum blossom, And the whole world has spring. - Source: Hiroshige Birds and Flowers, Cynthie J. Bogel, et. al., George Braziller, Inc., 1988, pl. 16.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Peacock and Peonies (複製： 牡丹に孔雀 Fukusei：Kujaku ni botan)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Peacock and Peonies (複製： 牡丹に孔雀 Fukusei：Kujaku ni botan)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of an 1830s Hiroshige print.
The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston notes, "Chinese inscription by Yūsai (=Hiroshige) 牡丹花冨貴者也　幽斎" and the Rhode Island School of Design museum notes, "The Chinese inscription associates the peony with wealth (fu) and lofty position (ki)."

media.caption: Reproduction of: Yellow Rose and Frogs (複製：山吹に蛙 Fukusei：Yamabuki ni kairo)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Yellow Rose and Frogs (複製：山吹に蛙 Fukusei：Yamabuki ni kairo)
text.text:
A modern reproduction published by Adachi Hanga of a c. 1832 Hiroshige print.
The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston notes, Poem by Chōtei: Harusame ni/ furuku nagara mo/ yamabuki no/ mi no hitotsu dani/ naku kaeru ka na「春雨の ふる句なからも 山吹の みのひとつたに なく蛙かな　　長亭」- Source: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston https://collections.mfa.org/objects/234456 [accessed 8-25-23]

media.caption: Nenokuchi, Towada (十和田子之口)

text.headline: Nenokuchi, Towada (十和田子之口)
text.text:
"While a dramatic sunset and its reflection on Lake Towada draw the viewer’s attention back, the branch extending across the foreground with its lifelike detail and shading creates a charged dynamic. This print exemplifies the close collaboration of artist, carver and printer, each applying masterful technique to achieve results perhaps exceeding the initial sketch of the scene. As designer, Hasui produced a bold composition, reminiscent of late works by Utagawa Hiroshige, that confronts the viewer with an intricate close-up of a low-hanging branch. The block cutter faithfully reproduced the sketch by sculpting the wood surface as though wielding a brush instead of sharp edged tools, carving 20 separate blocks for this production. Then, to evoke the changes in light and movement of water, the printer applied and wiped pigments with exquisite care, using 25 superimposed printings for effects as subtle as watercolors." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, asserts that “such a daring composition is rare in Hasui’s work. A large tree cuts diagonally across the foreground plane, and the setting sun reflects brightly on Lake Towada. The distant coast and mountain are already shrouded in darkness; the clouds grow dark. Instrumental in maintaining the mood of this scene is the reflection of the red sun on the surface of the lake, and this heightens the color scheme of this relatively simple composition. In this we witness a new trend in Hasui’s work. It was sketched on 28 October 1932.”
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: The Nikko Highway (日光街道 Nikkōkaidō)

text.headline: The Nikko Highway (日光街道 Nikkōkaidō)
text.text:
The Nikkō highway or “Nikkōkaidō” was one of the five highways (gokaidō) that began from the Nihonbashi in Edo (present-day Tokyo); it ran north-south from Nihonbashi to Nikkō. The other highways were the Tokaidō, Nakasendō, Koshukaidō and Oshukaidō. The segment of the Nikkōkaidō illustrated here is in Tochigi Prefecture. The catalog from The Toledo Art Museum Show, 1936 notes "Blocks, 20; superimposed printings, 25"
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Azuma Gorge (吾妻峡 Azuma kyō)

text.headline: Azuma Gorge (吾妻峡 Azuma kyō)
text.text:
"Like the Western Impressionists, who sought out scenes of beauty and tranquility amongst periods of turmoil, Hasui depicted the autumn foliage without a hint of the struggles then engulfing the world. Instead, he offered a timeless reminder of nature’s cycle of change. Though Hasui had submitted the sketch for carving, and a few test prints were produced in 1943, wartime shortages of paper and personnel made it impossible to complete the process until two years after the war ended." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
While titled Azuma Gorge, this print may well be of Agatsuma Gorge according to Shōichirō Watanabe, the grandson of Shōzaburō Watanabe the publisher of this print, as he believes Hasui had never visited Azuma Gorge only Agatsuma Gorge. Nevertheless 吾妻峡 (Azuma Gorge) is printed in the left margin.

He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Toro, Kishū (紀州緑)

text.headline: Toro, Kishū (紀州緑)
text.text:
The Doro-kyo (Toro-kyo) Valley is situated in eastern Wakayama Prefecture at the border with Nara and Mie Prefectures. It is a collective term for the 31-kilometer-long ravines along the Kitayama-gawa River, a tributary of the Kumano-gawa River in the Yoshino-Kumano National Park. Doro-Hatcho (Toro, Kishū) is a 1.2-kilometer-long ravine that stretches from Tamaoki-guchi in Kumano-gawa Town, Wakayama to Tado in Totsukawa Village, Nara. Sheer cliffs rise on both sides offering scenic views of gigantic rocks and oddly shaped rocks.

He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Spring Dusk at the Tōshō Shrine, Ueno  (春の夕 上野東照宮 Haru no yū Ueno Tōshōgū)

text.headline: Spring Dusk at the Tōshō Shrine, Ueno  (春の夕 上野東照宮 Haru no yū Ueno Tōshōgū)
text.text:
While the print is titled Spring Dusk at the Tōshō Shrine, Ueno, Hasui presents us with a view of the Five-Story Pagoda which sits, some say forlornly, inside Ueno Zoo. In 1911 it was designated a National Important Cultural Property (Building). This pagoda was constructed as one of the temples for Tōshōgū by request of Toshikatsu Doi in 1631.

media.caption: Samburam Rock, Kūmgang Mountain (金剛山 三仙巖 Kongōsan Sansengan)

text.headline: Samburam Rock, Kūmgang Mountain (金剛山 三仙巖 Kongōsan Sansengan)
text.text:
Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, writes: "Hasui’s trip to Korea served to refresh the artist, whose art had been stagnating for sometime. The scenery and customs that Hasui witnessed in Korea marked an artistic turning point. He illustrates the bizarre shape of the Samburam rock in the Diamond mountains [Kumgangsan, in present-day Democratic People’s Republic of Korea], showcasing its imposing character. The lines of the rock are bold, the shape angular and the colour vivid."

He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Rabbits with Bush Clover Under Full Moon

text.headline: Rabbits with Bush Clover Under Full Moon
text.text: This print showing two rabbits next to a clump of bush clover with a full moon in the background may be a printer's proof, as the commonly seen version of the print has the artist's Hoson seal added along with the publisher's, Kawaguchi and Sakai, copyright information in the left margin.

media.caption: Spring Snow at Kamikochi (上高地春雪 Kamikochi Shunsetsu)

text.headline: Spring Snow at Kamikochi (上高地春雪 Kamikochi Shunsetsu)
text.text: Spring Snow on Kamikochi was completed in 1932 and is representative of the artist's realistic work done in a color tone peculiarly his own. "This vertical composition emphasizes the monumentality of the snowy mountains, while the framing trees on either side brings the viewer into the center of the composition. Itō’s use of bright, almost surreal colors and billowy clouds and snowdrifts create a dreamlike effect." - Spencer Museum of Art

media.caption: Morita Kanya XIII as Genta Kagesue in the play Genta Kandō (十三代 守田勘弥 源太景季・源太勘当)

text.headline: Morita Kanya XIII as Genta Kagesue in the play Genta Kandō (十三代 守田勘弥 源太景季・源太勘当)
text.text:
One of thirty-six prints making up the Watanabe-published series Collection of Creative Print Portraits by Shunsen (1925-1929). This print is the series installment no.28.
In the play "Genta Kandō," Genta Kagesue, played by Morita Kanya XIII (1885-1931), is ordered by his father to commit seppuku in the belief that his son has disgraced the family name because he failed to be the first to attack the enemy in battle. In reality, Genta intentionally deferred the honor to another warrior who had helped his father in the past. Genta’s mother understands this and manages to convince his son to spare his own life and to regain his honor by returning to the battlefield.

media.caption: Sakanoshita, The Kannon in the Cave, No. 49  (四十九、坂の下、 岩窟の漢音 Sakanoshita、 Gankutsu no Kannon)

text.headline: Sakanoshita, The Kannon in the Cave, No. 49  (四十九、坂の下、 岩窟の漢音 Sakanoshita、 Gankutsu no Kannon)
text.text: Depicting station 49 along the Tōkaidō Road, which connected Edo, where the shōgun resided, to Kyoto, where the emperor resided.  Hiroshige pictures three pilgrims resting enjoying the view of the waterfalls and two pilgrims along the path to the Kannon of the grotto at Sakanoshita.

media.caption: Bandō Mitsugorō as Josetsu in the play Hana to Mitsu Yuki no Shiraishi (常悦 坂東三津五郎・花三津雪端白石)

text.headline: Bandō Mitsugorō as Josetsu in the play Hana to Mitsu Yuki no Shiraishi (常悦 坂東三津五郎・花三津雪端白石)
text.text: The drama Hana to Mitsu Yuki no Shiraishi (花三津雪瑞白石), was staged in November 1834 at the Moritaza theater.  Bandō Mitsugorō IV is recorded as having played the roles of Uji Hyobunosuke and Joetsu in this play.

media.caption: Content Pages - One Hundred Aspects of the Moon (月百姿もくろく)

text.headline: Content Pages - One Hundred Aspects of the Moon (月百姿もくろく)
text.text:
A diptych print displaying the list of prints in the publisher Akiyama Buemon's bound album of all 100 prints of the series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon by the artist Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892). While Yoshitoshi designed all 100 prints in this series, the design of the table of contents is credited to a calligrapher named Sogaku, either Nagai Sogaku 永井素岳 (1852-1915) or Nashioka Sogaku 梨岡素岳 (1868-1935).

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, , 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: Illustration of the [Emperor and Empress Arriving] Opening of the Third National Industrial Exhibition (第三回博覽會開場之圖)

text.headline: Illustration of the [Emperor and Empress Arriving] Opening of the Third National Industrial Exhibition (第三回博覽會開場之圖)
text.text:
The emperor and empress are shown arriving at the Third National Industrial Exhibition in Ueno Park. The print was made in anticipation of the event as it pre-dates the April opening.
Five industrial expositions were held in Japan during the Meiji era, the first three in Ueno Park, Tokyo (1877, 1881, 1890) and the last two respectively in Kyoto (1895) and Osaka (1903). Printmakers were quick to create images of the domestic expositions to be sold as souvenirs.

media.caption: The Moon's Invention - Hōzō Temple (都幾乃発明 宝蔵院 Tsuki no hatsumei - Hōzōin)

text.headline: The Moon's Invention - Hōzō Temple (都幾乃発明 宝蔵院 Tsuki no hatsumei - Hōzōin)
text.text:
The monk In'ei (1521-1607) holding a knobbed staff gazing at the crescent moon's reflection. Yoshitoshi is suggesting that this priest was inspired to invent the formidable crescent spear by the sight of the moon bisecting his reflected staff.

media.caption: Illustration of Foreign-looking Manchurian Horsemen on an Expedition to Observe the Japanese Camp in the Distance Near Sauhoku (草河口附近日陣遠望満州騎兵異相出陣之図 Sōkakō fukin Nichijin enbō Manshū kihei isō shutsujin no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of Foreign-looking Manchurian Horsemen on an Expedition to Observe the Japanese Camp in the Distance Near Sauhoku (草河口附近日陣遠望満州騎兵異相出陣之図 Sōkakō fukin Nichijin enbō Manshū kihei isō shutsujin no zu)
text.text:
Mounted Manchurian soldiers survey the Japanese camp in this print. Near Sauhoku, the Japanese encountered a Chinese offensive of elite forces from Manchuria, whose gallantry was legendary. Until then the Chinese had been either on the defensive or in flight, as stated in a Japanese report on this unusual battle: "Up to now the enemy's customary tactic was defense. This time they pretend to take the offensive. It was bizarre. Unlike in the past, they attacked ferociously. We were outnumbered. Like an army of rats and dogs they used a hit-and-run strategy but were no match for the Japanese forces under General Tatsumi, who had a devil's wisdom and a god's bravery." - Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Okamoto, Shumpei, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p.31.
These Manchurian horsemen played both sides during the war, often working for the side that offered then the most. There was a thin line between their operating as guerrilla fighters for one side or the other and their operating as bandits (honghuzi). These bands continued operating through the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) as can be seen in this collection's print IHL.1224 "Telegraphic Record of the Russo-Japanese War: Manchurian Mounted Bandits Destroy Railroad."

media.caption: Illustration of Negotiations Between Japan and Russia (日露会見談判図 Nichiro kaiken danpan zu)

text.headline: Illustration of Negotiations Between Japan and Russia (日露会見談判図 Nichiro kaiken danpan zu)
text.text:
This print was published on February 10, 1904 the day after Japan's attack on the Russian fleet at Port Arthur and the day of the Imperial Proclamation declaring war on Russia. It illustrates one of a number of negotiating sessions, largely initiated by Japan, over the status of Manchuria and Korea prior to the start of the war.
Count Witte, who was to be the chief negotiator for Russia during the treaty conference at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, at the close of the war (won by Japan), wrote: "Not long after my return to Russia, Kurino, the Japanese minister to Russia, came to see me. In July 1903, while I was still minister of finance, he had presented a proposal to me and Count Lambsdorff that would have made a peaceful settlement of our differences possible. I favored acceptance, but to no avail, because it was sent to Viceroy Alekseev and became the subject of endless and fruitless discussion."
Of course, the scene depicted in this print may be a total or partial fiction, but the bearded Russian negotiator may be Count Witte or Baron Rosen and the mustachioed Japanese figure might well be Jutaro Komura, foreign minister, or Shin'ichiro Kurino, minister to Russia.

media.caption: Abe no Nakamaro - Kasuga Moon (阿倍仲麻呂・春日の月)

text.headline: Abe no Nakamaro - Kasuga Moon (阿倍仲麻呂・春日の月)
text.text:
The figure on the right, Abe no Nakamaro (701-770), was sent to China to study and remained there until he died. One night he composed this poem to express his homesickness for Japan - "As I look out into the vast expanse, can this be the same moon that I saw rise in Kasuga behind Mount Mikasa?" The figure to his left is presumed to be his friend Kibi no Makibi who accompanied him on this China mission, but who did get to return home in 735.
This print is from the album issued by publisher Akiyama Buemon shortly after Yoshitoshi's death and retains its original album backing. The faint diamond-shaped object to the left of the central pillar is seen on all copies of this print included in the album. The diamond-shaped object is an offset from the image of the lute on the print on the facing page.

media.caption: Illustration of a Large Intense Engagement Sino-Japanese War (日清大激戰之圖 Nisshin dai-gekisen no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of a Large Intense Engagement Sino-Japanese War (日清大激戰之圖 Nisshin dai-gekisen no zu)
text.text: The inscription in the white box to the left of the title cartouche provides a summary of action on July 29, likely making this a scene from the battle of Seonghwan (also known as the battle of Asan) in Korea, the first major land battle of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895). Chinese troops are seen fleeing the charging Japanese marines and the airborne bodies of the enemy can be seen in the bright orange explosion in this scene constructed by the artist.

media.caption: Battle Between the Japanese and Russians at Seoul: Hurrah for the Great Victory of the Great Japanese Empire (日露京城ニ撃戦ス　大日本帝国大勝利万歳 Nichiro Keijō ni gekisen su, Dai Nihon teikoku dai shōri banzai)

text.headline: Battle Between the Japanese and Russians at Seoul: Hurrah for the Great Victory of the Great Japanese Empire (日露京城ニ撃戦ス　大日本帝国大勝利万歳 Nichiro Keijō ni gekisen su, Dai Nihon teikoku dai shōri banzai)
text.text:
It is unclear which battle this print is portraying as there was no battle of Seoul per say. The Japanese so surprised the Russians by their naval attack and landing of troops at Inchon (Chemulpo) near Seoul on February 8, 1904 (Meiji 37), that they occupied Seoul the following day without much resistance. On February 10 they formally declared war on Russia, but it took the surprised Russians another week to issue their formal declaration of war.
The February publishing date of this battle scene would indicate that Kokunimasa conjured up this scene to meet the deadlines of his publisher who needed to rush into production to keep up with photographic accounts of rapidly unfolding events.

media.caption: Gravemarker Moon (卒都婆の月 Sotōba no tsuki)

text.headline: Gravemarker Moon (卒都婆の月 Sotōba no tsuki)
text.text:
The old woman seated on the fallen grave marker is the celebrated beauty and poetess Ono no Komachi (9th century). Komachi lost her beauty, position, and wealth, but after wandering destitute for many years, gained enlightenment.
An early, if not first, state of this print.

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: The Moon’s Inner Vision – Taira no Tomoume (心観月・平友梅 shinkan no tsuki・Taira no Tomoume)

text.headline: The Moon’s Inner Vision – Taira no Tomoume (心観月・平友梅 shinkan no tsuki・Taira no Tomoume)
text.text:
"Taira no Tomoume, a blind warrior, uses second sight to see his enemies and survive in battle. He carries a poem slip as a talisman. The verse reads, "From darkness I have wandered lost on to a darker path; the moon of heart is becoming clouded."
An early, if not first, state of this print.

media.caption: Inamura Promontory Moon at Daybreak (稲むらか崎の明ほのゝ月 Inamuragasaki no akebono no tsuki)

text.headline: Inamura Promontory Moon at Daybreak (稲むらか崎の明ほのゝ月 Inamuragasaki no akebono no tsuki)
text.text:
Nitta Yoshisada (1301-1338) offers his treasured sword to the sea gods and asks them for a safe passage for his army. The sea receded in answer to his prayers, enabling his soldiers to advance toward Kamakura.
An early, if not first, state of this print, with the ink used to create the sunrise and clouds partially oxidized as intended.
