Tuttle Company, 1994, p. 126.
There is an indebtedness to traditional Japanese calligraphy, in its movement, by Hara while substituting a rainbow of saturated colors for the traditional black sumi ink.
For this 1981 print, Hara presents us with a very zen-like character, the coloration of which draw us into the void.

media.caption: The Great Battle of the Ansong Ford: The Valor of Captain Matsuzaki Crossing Anjō (安城渡大激戦・松崎大尉勇猛  Anjō-watari daigekisen・Matsuzaki taii yūmō)

text.headline: The Great Battle of the Ansong Ford: The Valor of Captain Matsuzaki Crossing Anjō (安城渡大激戦・松崎大尉勇猛  Anjō-watari daigekisen・Matsuzaki taii yūmō)
text.text:
In the battle of Asan, south of Seoul, Captain Matsuzaki Naomi led his men across the deep Ansong River on July 29, 1894 to attack the enemy on the other side. He was hit, but urged his men forward, until he was killed by a second bullet. It was not the gallant officer, however, but his bugler Shirakami Genjirō, who died blowing the charge, who became the first national hero of the campaign.
Toshikata includes all the details that convey the samurai spirit of the modern warrior. Advancing under heavy fire, undaunted by personal danger, Matsuzaki charged ahead of his men. The nighttime sky, lit by a crescent moon, heightens the pathos of the hero's bravery and death. - Source: In Battle's Light: Woodblock Prints of Japan's Early Modern Wars, Elizabeth de Sabato Swinton, Worcester Art Museum, 1991, p. 74. (For a similar print by Toshikata see IHL.0530, Captain Matsuzaki Crossing the Anjō-sen.)

media.caption: Nijūbashi (二重橋)

text.headline: Nijūbashi (二重橋)
text.text:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Lost Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print was made from recut blocks. It is one of three designs contributed by Onchi to Scenes of Lost Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by him.
Nijūbashi is one of the six prints that Lawrence Smith identified from the series as depicting "places with serious imperial resonances," the six being the Nijūbashi Bridge at the Imperial Palace, the Akasaka Palace (residence of the Crown Prince), the Meiji Shrine, the Torii (Gateway) at Kudan, the Gate of the Imperial University (alma mater of the most senior bureaucrats of the militarist era), and the Graveyard of Sengaku-ji, burial place of Japan’s most celebrated paragons of loyalty the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: White Dream (白い夢 Shiroi yume)

text.headline: White Dream (白い夢 Shiroi yume)
text.text: In this print we see the influence of Ueda's teacher Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), particularly in the squiggly lines combined with textural shapes. The birds, possibly crows, add a touch of realism to the artist's dream.

media.caption: Tokyo Tower (東京タワー Tōkyō Tawaa)

text.headline: Tokyo Tower (東京タワー Tōkyō Tawaa)
text.text:
Published by the Japan Print Association (Nihon Hanga Kyokai) as part of the series One Hundred Views of Tokyo, Message to the 21st Century, the JPA began the series in 1989, commissioning 100 artists over a ten year period to create their impressions of Tokyo. In 2000, the JPA compiled the prints by all 100 artists into ten volumes. In the preface to the series, the JPA notes that the "Tokyo Hyakkei series will serve as 'a witness of time' by the artists and will consist of one hundred views by print by one hundred artists, which ultimately will take ten years in all [and] will present the changing international megalopolis Tokyo. . . . We are confident that [it] will achieve artistic and historical significance. . . ."
Commenting on the print, Takahashi states, "The ancient capital of Kyō was moved to the east in 1868, and Kyō of the east was born: Tokyo (lit. the Eastern Kyō). And now, for the purpose of leaving sights of that Tokyo behind, print artists have been asked for a work with that motif. I chose Tokyo Tower. The Tower was built likely as a symbol to uplift public sentiment after the crushing blow caused by the last war. I had a keen emotion, such as 'this again must be the authorities' adulation to the public.' That's why, though living near the Tower, I was unwilling to visit there. However, seeing today's Tokyo Tower gracefully lighten-up against the night sky, I sensed that I have gradually changed my mind. One day, seduced by the light, I visited the Tower, which absolutely enchanted me with its iron jungle and the feast of lights. Thus I made up my mind to challenge Tokyo Tower. The result is this work you see here."

media.caption: Tea House at Imadobashi - (after a design by Kiyochika)

text.headline: Tea House at Imadobashi - (after a design by Kiyochika)
text.text: A small format version of IHL.0111. The larger format print was published by the Shima Art Company which often applied the signatures of famous artists to works they did not in fact create to enhance their appeal.

media.caption: Graveyard at Sengakuji (泉岳寺墓所 Sengakuji bosho)

text.headline: Graveyard at Sengakuji (泉岳寺墓所 Sengakuji bosho)
text.text:
Azechi contribute this single print to the fifteen print 1945 series Scenes of Lost Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955).
This print picturing the graveyard where the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai are buried is one of the six prints that Lawrence Smith identified from the series as depicting "places with serious imperial resonances," the six being the Nijūbashi Bridge at the Imperial Palace, the Akasaka Palace (residence of the Crown Prince), the Meiji Shrine, the Torii (Gateway) at Kudan, the Gate of the Imperial University (alma mater of the most senior bureaucrats of the militarist era), and the Graveyard of Sengaku-ji, burial place of Japan’s most celebrated paragons of loyalty the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai.

Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Factory Street at Fukagawa (工場地帯 本所 Honjo kōjōchi tai)

text.headline: Factory Street at Fukagawa (工場地帯 本所 Honjo kōjōchi tai)
text.text:
Honjo, east of the Sumida River, was designated as one of Tokyo’s industrial wards during the Meiji period. Maekawa catches the bleakness of this factory area, full of smokestacks and utility poles, with overall-clad factory workers trudging up the road.
This print was originally issued in 1929 with the title Factory Streets of Honjo (Kojochitai, Honjo) as part of the series One Hundred Views of the New Tokyo (Shin Tokyo Hyakkei). The print was reissued in 1945 from newly cut blocks under the title Fakutory [sic] Street at Fukagawa for the series Tokyo kaiko zue (Scenes of Lost Tokyo). For another impression of this print see IHL.0056.

media.caption: Yorimasa 頼政

text.headline: Yorimasa 頼政
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 215-216) - A travelling priest stops at Uji and is admiring the view there when an old man approaches and, after telling him about various historical spots in the neighborhood, leads him to the Byōdō-in. There he shows him the patch of turf cut in the shape of a fan to commemorate the warrior Yorimasa who laid his fan down and killed himself there after being defeated in battle. Revealing that he is the spirit of the warrior, he then disappears. After the priest has prayed for the repose of his soul, Yorimasa comes to him in his true form and tells him about the battle. He asks the priest to continue to pray for him and again fades from sight.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)

text.headline: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 89) - A travelling priest stops at Akasaka in Mino Province and meets another priest who, after talking with him, gives him lodging for the night. This second priest is in reality the ghost of Kumasaka no Chôhan, a robber, and in the dream of the real priest that night the spirit appears and describers how he was killed by the young Ushikawa.

media.caption: The Uji Riverside in Kyoto (宇治川派流 Ujigawa haryu)

text.headline: The Uji Riverside in Kyoto (宇治川派流 Ujigawa haryu)
text.text: Displaying the Kyoto watercolor style of print design, Kotozuki recreates this Kyoto scene on the Uji riverside.

media.caption: Kimono design pattern, number 25 (雛形  第貮拾貮號)

text.headline: Kimono design pattern, number 25 (雛形  第貮拾貮號)
text.text: A kimono design pattern printed from a copper plate.

media.caption: Kimono design pattern, number 19 (第拾九號)

text.headline: Kimono design pattern, number 19 (第拾九號)
text.text: A kimono design pattern printed from a copper plate.

media.caption: Shinobazu Pond in Snow (Shinobazu ike sekkei)

text.headline: Shinobazu Pond in Snow (Shinobazu ike sekkei)
text.text:
Shinobazu, the pond at the southern end of Ueno Park, is shown along with the Benzaiten shrine on the island in the pond. In the background, above the trees on the hill, is the top of the famous five-storied pagoda in Ueno Park. This print, originally published in 1930 as part of the series Shin Tokyo Hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo), exists in at least two states. The print in this collection is likely the second state and may have been created from recut or retouched blocks. The original edition size for the series Shin Tokyo Hyakkei was 50 prints. This collection's print is numbered 60/100.
In 1929 Hiratsuka, along with seven other artists and the publisher Nakajima Jutaro, undertook the creation of the series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). The series goal was to depict the modern city of Tokyo that arose after the devastating 1923 earthquake.

media.caption: Stream

text.headline: Stream
text.text:
Toko Shinoda's lithographic career began in the early 1960s, when the American printer Arthur Flory visited Japan and suggested the possibilities of the medium to her.
Kihachi Kimura, artist and master printer, pulled the artist's editions for more than 25 years. He executed a few prints on stone, but the majority were printed from zinc plates. In later years, the occasional aluminum plate was used.
The paper of choice for Shindoa's lithographs was French Arches lithographic paper. Seven works were printed on silver foil paper, and on a few occasions handmade paper from Fukui Prefecture was used.
Shinoda creates the images on the plate. The printer then used this single plate to print from. A few times in her career Miss Shinoda has made two-color lithographs, wherein a separate plate is needed for each color. After the edition has been pulled, Miss Shinoda usually adds strokes of color by hand (red, green, blue, gold, or silver) [and sumi ink], thereby imparting a uniqueness to each print. - Source: Toko Shinoda, a New Appreciation by Tōkō Shinoda, Mary S. Tolman, Norman H. Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1993, p. 195.
“Lithography does not translate the history of bygone days into a print, but it is where you can contain the work of the living (moving) brush and entrust a 'prayerful spirit' to the person who brings it back to life. That spirit generates an interaction between artist and printer, and I always enjoy the ‘electric’ current bouncing back and forth between us as I work on a lithograph.” - the artist, as quoted by the Gifu Collection of Modern Arts in the exhibition Toko Shinoda and Her Lithographs 10/21/2016-12/16/2016.

media.caption: Circus No. 7 (サーカス No. 7 Saakasu No. 7)

text.headline: Circus No. 7 (サーカス No. 7 Saakasu No. 7)
text.text: Hagiwara has combined traditional woodblock techniques with a form of woodcut intaglio, which he invented, which creates lines that resemble those found in etching or drypoint. On first glance this joyous scene is very Miro-like.

media.caption: The Heroine Koman from Seki  in The Fancy Chequered Bridle of Yosaku from Tanba (丹波与作待夜の小室節の関の小萬 Tanba Yosaku matsuyo no Komurobushi no Seki no Koman)

text.headline: The Heroine Koman from Seki  in The Fancy Chequered Bridle of Yosaku from Tanba (丹波与作待夜の小室節の関の小萬 Tanba Yosaku matsuyo no Komurobushi no Seki no Koman)
text.text:
In Chikamatsu's play, "Yosaku is a samurai reduced to working as a horse driver because of his offenses in the past. He has betrayed his wife, failed to repay his master’s kindness, and abandoned his child. We learn that he gambles and has recently lost at a game in which the stake was a horse belonging to another man. In order to raise some money, Yosaku persuades the boy Sankichi to steal. When Koman, the courtesan who is Yosaku’s sweetheart, protests, Yosaku answers, 'You’re too timid. If the kid is caught, the worst he’ll get is a spanking.' Sankichi is in fact caught, and eventually condemned to be executed. Yosaku and Koman, overcome with remorse, decide they must kill themselves. On their journey to death Yosaku emerges as a tragic figure, and his transgressions, though not forgiven, seem to have made possible at last the flowering of his true nature." - sSurce: The Major Plays of Chikamatsu, translated by Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 1961, p. 22-23.

One of 18 prints published from 1922 to 1925 as part of the celebration of the two-hundredth anniversary of the death of Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1623-1724), perhaps the greatest dramatist in the history of the Japanese theater. Each design illustrates a scene or character from one of Chikamatsu’s famous works which were compiled into 16 volumes by Chikamatsu researcher Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950). The prints were inserted into the volume containing the story they illustrated and were also separately sold.

media.caption: Paper Between a Snowed Stone and Road

text.headline: Paper Between a Snowed Stone and Road
text.text: One of Ida Shōichi's (1941-2006) many prints, collages and sculptures that explore the physical space between objects that touch. Ida uses a hand-made translucent paper as his "between" and then creates his "surface" by printing a lithographic image of a road on the verso and silkscreening a stone on the print's front side. This allows a pale image, really an illusion, of the print's title to emerge on the front side of the print.

media.caption: Ueno Zoo (上野動物園 Ueno dōbutsuen)

text.headline: Ueno Zoo (上野動物園 Ueno dōbutsuen)
text.text:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Last Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print was made from recut blocks. It is one of three designs that Onchi contributed to Scenes of Last Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by him.

Ueno zoo, "Japan's oldest zoo, founded in 1882, was the site of tragedy during the war. Fearing that the wild animals might escape and cause havoc in an air raid, bears, lions, and leopards were put to death in August 1943. Later, as food supplies became increasingly scarce in Tokyo, the elephants were hidden from the public and starved to death. The zoo's facilities were in ruins because the metal in the cages and guardrails had been requisitioned for military use. It would take man years before the zoo again became a tree-sheltered park where children could view animals." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 299.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Tomonaga 朝長

text.headline: Tomonaga 朝長
text.text:
This diptych depicts a scene from the play Tomonaga attributed to the playwright Kanze Motomasa (died 1432). "At first sight the two prints have nothing in common, for they deal with different scenes of this No play. The left sheet shows the proprietress of the inn where Minamoto Tomonaga once committed suicide; in front of her a branch of a tree is lying on the ground and in the rear the outlines of a temple (the scene at Tomonaga’s grave). The right sheet shows the night scene in the inn when Tomonaga’s ghost (without a mask) has appeared and is talking about the battle, his wounds and his suicide. Next to him the proprietress of the inn."[1]

PLAY SYNOPSIS
A tragic story about the death of the eldest son of Tomonaga of Yoshitomo Minamoto. In the first scene a woman asks a priest to perform a requiem mass for sixteen-year old Tomonaga at his grave site. In the second act Tomonaga’s spirit appears and recalls the events that led to his death.
ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] “The series Nogaku hyakuban (100 No plays) by Tsukioka Kogyo (1869-1927),” Claus-Peter Schulz, Andon 67, Society for Japanese Arts, p. 32.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Island of Birds (とりの島)

text.headline: Island of Birds (とりの島)
text.text: Birds are a recurring subject in Ono's work, first appearing in the late 1950s. Lawrence Smith describes Ono's style as one which displays "restraint, sobriety and warm, rich color. . . . His work is much concerned with ordinary townscapes and unpretentious landscape, to all of which he adds the special glow of his rich oil-based pigments."

media.caption: Saint

text.headline: Saint
text.text: Is Tajima's image a luminous look into the mind of a saint? This print is typical of Tajima's work which always "seems to glow from behind, as though it incorporated a fluorescent light shielded by a mysteriously textured fabric." - Source: Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Frances Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 192.

media.caption: Work A (作品 A)

text.headline: Work A (作品 A)
text.text: One of ten prints created in 1966 making up the artist's Work series. All of these prints use a similar circular form as the dominant element.  See Work BB (IHL.0190) for another print from this series.

media.caption: Work BB (作品 BB)

text.headline: Work BB (作品 BB)
text.text: One of ten prints created in 1966 making up the artist's Work series.  All of these prints use a similar circular form as the dominant element.  See Work A (IHL.0189) for another print from this series.

media.caption: Tea Ceremony II (茶の湯 II)

text.headline: Tea Ceremony II (茶の湯 II)
text.text: One of Takahashi's two abstractions, along with Tea Ceremony (IHL.0218), depicting the tea ceremony.

media.caption: True Depiction of Citizens Greeting the Carriage of His Imperial Majesty and Commander-in-Chief upon His Return through the Triumphal Arch (大元帥陛下御還幸凱旋門御通輦市民奉迎之真圖 Daigensui heika gokan kōgaisenmon gotsūren shimin hōgei no shinzu)

text.headline: True Depiction of Citizens Greeting the Carriage of His Imperial Majesty and Commander-in-Chief upon His Return through the Triumphal Arch (大元帥陛下御還幸凱旋門御通輦市民奉迎之真圖 Daigensui heika gokan kōgaisenmon gotsūren shimin hōgei no shinzu)
text.text:
There are several other prints (see IHL.2286) that also depict this scene of Emperor Meiji's procession through the Hibiya Triumphal Arch in Tokyo after his return from Kyoto on May 30, 1895. In this print the emperor himself is not pictured.
According to Donald Keene, the emperor was not in a rush to return to Tokyo from Kyoto. "[W]hen it was announced that the imperial headquarters would move back to Tokyo on May 29, he resisted leaving, saying that some major figures in the victory over China had not yet had their triumphal return. But when the last of the heroes of the war had returned in triumph, there was no longer any excuse for remaining in Kyoto, and the emperor left for Tokyo on May 29." - Source: Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His World, 1852-1912, Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 2002, p. 508.
"He arrived at Shinbashi Station on the thirtieth, in military dress as usual, and paraded through a garishly decorated city that was packed with huge throngs of people. Tokyo’s citizens put out national flags and decorative lanterns in front of their houses and filled the streets with banners, streamers, and arches of many kinds. The most striking temporary monument for the city was a huge 'triumphal arcade,' widely touted as having no equal in any country, which was constructed at Hibiya between the official residences of the presidents of the two Diet houses. So large was this arcade - 110 meters long and 18 meters in height, with a main tower over 30 meters high and 8 meters wide – that the city government reportedly put one thousand laborers to work to widen Saiwaichō Avenue on which it was constructed. The Tokyo City Assembly also built two other great triumphal arches, one each at Shinbashi and Sakuradamon, both of which were thirty-three meters high and over three meters thick." - Source: Splendid Monarchy: Power and Pageantry in Modern Japan, T. Fujitani, University of California Press, 1998 p. 130.
On the left side of the print members of the crowd hold aloft a banner inscribed "Banzai" (literally, "Ten-thousand years.")

media.caption: Illustration of Townsmen Watching Noh on a Ceremonial Occasion Hosted by the Former Shogunate, Part 3 (旧幕府御大礼之節: 町人御能拝見之図・第三編 Kyū bakufu gotairei no setsu: chōnin onō haiken no zu・daisan hen)

text.headline: Illustration of Townsmen Watching Noh on a Ceremonial Occasion Hosted by the Former Shogunate, Part 3 (旧幕府御大礼之節: 町人御能拝見之図・第三編 Kyū bakufu gotairei no setsu: chōnin onō haiken no zu・daisan hen)
text.text:
"Chikanobu was a samurai who fought for the Tokugawa Shogunate in the civil war of 1868. He survived defeat to become a successful print designer. Alone among his fellow artists, he was familiar with the pomp and splendor of the shogunal castle in Edo and often treated it as a subject in his prints. Here, he portrays a Noh performance of Okina to which commoners are invited. The samurai watch quietly from the hall at right, while the commoners seated in the open courtyard jostle each other and shout, ignoring the performance."[1]
The purpose of these public Noh performances (machiiri nō) was to raise funds for the construction or repair of temples and shrines.

[1] Portland Art Museum, Special Exhibition NOH Dance Drama of the Samurai NOV 17, 2012 – FEB 24, 2013, wall card for the print.

media.caption: Fishing Village in the Afternoon (漁村の午后 Gyoson no gogo)

text.headline: Fishing Village in the Afternoon (漁村の午后 Gyoson no gogo)
text.text: "Kitaoka’s Fishing Village in the Afternoon is a model of layered color, technique, and meaning. Kitaoka presents his village street in the strong light of the high-noon hour. The wash of the direct light, enhanced with a sheen of luminescent mica, is beautifully accented with splashes of orange and blue in the receding background and the cuddled mass of a yellow dog in the lower right corner. Using Western perspective methods and Eastern printing expertise, the print beautifully captures an accurately observed moment. There is a timelessness to the image; the space depicted is a working man’s village, a seaside community with worn streets and lived-in houses. Portraying an identifiable setting, moment, and mood, all executed with complete artistic control and mastery, Kitaoka’s print is the paradigm of woodblock printing at its best and is a visually stunning exercise in expressive realism." - Source: Revisiting Modern Japanese Prints: Selected Works from the Richard F. Grott Family Collection, Helen M. Nagata, Helen Merritt, Northern Illinois University Art Museum, 2007, p. 24.

media.caption: Sawamura Tosshō, Bandō Sanpachi, Ichikawa Kodanji and Ichimura Kakitsu in the play Sandai Banashi Kōza no Shinsaku at the Ichimura Theater (沢村訥升、坂東三八、市川小団次、市村家橘・三題咄高座新作・市村)

text.headline: Sawamura Tosshō, Bandō Sanpachi, Ichikawa Kodanji and Ichimura Kakitsu in the play Sandai Banashi Kōza no Shinsaku at the Ichimura Theater (沢村訥升、坂東三八、市川小団次、市村家橘・三題咄高座新作・市村)
text.text:
This print shows the actors (from right to left) Sawamura Tosshō II in the role of Hiranoya Kōjirō 平野屋幸三郎, Bandō Sanpachi V in the role of Tōji's Student (Teiji) Kane 藤次弟子兼, Ichikawa Kodanji IV in the role of Wakokubashi Tōji 和国橋藤次 and Ichimura Kakitsu IV in the role of Pickpocket (Kinchakukiri) Takemon no Tora 巾着切竹門虎 in the play Sandai banashi kōza no shinsaku written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893) and performed in February 1863 at the Ichimura 市村 theatre in Edo.
Sandai banashi (also seen written as sandai hanashi) are “three-subject stories” and are considered a genre of rakugo, the traditional Japanese art of storytelling.

media.caption: Quiet Day from the magazine Han geijutsu, Vol. 1, No. 5 (版芸術１巻５号・静日)

text.headline: Quiet Day from the magazine Han geijutsu, Vol. 1, No. 5 (版芸術１巻５号・静日)
text.text: This print was created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) Han geijutsu (Print Art), Volume 5 published in August 1932 in Tokyo by Shiro to Kurosha, the company of Ryōji Chōmei (1899-1982).  The theme for Volume 5 was mountains and sea (山と海). Five hundred copies of each volume were printed and they were priced at 50 sen. "The magazines were essentially mechanically printed [the woodblock was mounted on the printing press (kikai-zuri)] with one or more hand-printed works [such as this  print, Quiet Day] usually included in each issue." - source: Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 201-202.

media.caption: Strokes 80-16

text.headline: Strokes 80-16
text.text:
Hara has been working with the theme of 'strokes' since the 1970s. The strokes have been described as paths of light, each one a range of intensities captured by Hara's magnificent technique of colour gradation. His prints, exhibiting "flat coolness and perfect evenness," at first appear to be silkscreens, but they are achieved through lithography often involving multiple printings using the artist's "special technique with a method of applying the ink with huge rollers to give his work an element of unbelievable smoothness, lushness, and control." - Sources: Contemporary Japanese Prints: Symbols of a Society in Transition, Lawrence Smith, Harper & Row Publishers, 1985, p. 28; Collecting Modern Japanese Prints, Then and Now, Mary and Norman Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1994, p. 126.
There is an indebtedness to traditional Japanese calligraphy, in its movement, by Hara while substituting a rainbow of saturated colors for the traditional black sumi ink.
For this 1980 print, Hara has softened his usual white background with the addition of a subtle cream color which allows his "strokes" to float off the page.

media.caption: Early Spring Garden

text.headline: Early Spring Garden
text.text: "Beginning in the mid-sixties, a white space appeared around the motif reminiscent of the blank areas in ink painting. In the seventies this margin was even more evident, enhancing the light, bright qualities of the print. In the seventies, this marginal space came to have more obvious structural features. First, a rigidly square geometric form emerged . . . often surrounded by empty space. These forms first appeared in the Niwa series which was based on Kyoto motif, so I would guess that the square represented a walled garden. If so, the delicate lines and planes, which cluster around the square like theatrical props, probably indicate trees, ponds, and rock formations in the garden. This Impression is reinforced by an amorphous form reminiscent of a single Chinese character made with heavy brush strokes which is placed under the square. It creates a balanced contrast with the square above it. I see it as a symbol of the living, bustling city outside the enclosed garden. This composition of a square and a ideograph was repeated in a series of prints and became a definite structural pattern in Takahashi’s work." - Source: "The World of Rikio Takahashi – The Spirit of Wood,” Masayoshi Homma, in Rikio Takahashi, The Woodblock Prints, Abe Publishing LTD. (1998) p.18-21.

media.caption: Ancient Story (昔語り)

text.headline: Ancient Story (昔語り)
text.text:
Hand applied calligraphic strokes of vermillion using cinnabar highlight this lithograph. Shinoda speaks of her fascination with vermillion in her preface to the catalog of her 2003 exhibition at the Hara Contemporary Museum of Art titled "Variations in Vermillion" in which this print was included, ending her preface with the statement, "Sumi and vermillion are the means that I have selected in the pursuit of my desire to express things that cannot be expressed through realistic depiction."
Toko Shinoda's lithographic career began in the early 1960s, when the American printer Arthur Flory visited Japan and suggested the possibilities of the medium to her.
Kihachi Kimura, artist and master printer, pulled the artist's editions for more than 25 years. He executed a few prints on stone, but the majority were printed from zinc plates. In later years, the occasional aluminum plate was used.
The paper of choice for Shindoa's lithographs was French Arches lithographic paper. Seven works were printed on silver foil paper, and on a few occasions handmade paper from Fukui Prefecture was used.
Shinoda creates the images on the plate. The printer then used this single plate to print from. A few times in her career Miss Shinoda has made two-color lithographs, wherein a separate plate is needed for each color. After the edition has been pulled, Miss Shinoda usually adds strokes of color by hand (red, green, blue, gold, or silver) [and sumi ink], thereby imparting a uniqueness to each print. - Source: Toko Shinoda, a New Appreciation by Tōkō Shinoda, Mary S. Tolman, Norman H. Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1993, p. 195.
“Lithography does not translate the history of bygone days into a print, but it is where you can contain the work of the living (moving) brush and entrust a “prayerful spirit” to the person who brings it back to life. That spirit generates an interaction between artist and printer, and I always enjoy the ‘electric’ current bouncing back and forth between us as I work on a lithograph.” - the artist as quoted by the Gifu Collection of Modern Arts in the exhibition Toko Shinoda and Her Lithographs 10/21/2016-12/16/2016.

media.caption: Early Spring (早春)

text.headline: Early Spring (早春)
text.text: This print, while similar to the print pictured in the artist's catalogue raisonné, has additional elements in the lower portion along with other variations. It is also from an edition of 50 rather than an edition of 25, as shown in the catalogue raisonné, indicating that there are two states for this print. The print in the collection of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art appears to be the same state as this collection's print.

media.caption: New Year Parade of Fire Brigades to the Capital (東京各消防出初式之図)

text.headline: New Year Parade of Fire Brigades to the Capital (東京各消防出初式之図)
text.text: A depiction of the annual New Year parade of firefighters to the Imperial Palace. Firefighters in happi coats perform acrobatic stunts on top of bamboo ladders in the inset. The same design in a smaller format was reissued by a different publisher as a book illustration in 1899.

media.caption: Nude No. 6

text.headline: Nude No. 6
text.text: One of a series of nudes by the artist, this print is a fine example of the artist's "white-line style."

media.caption: The Heroine Osan in The Almanac-Maker’s Tale (大経師昔暦のおさん Daikyōji mukashi-goyomi no Osan)

text.headline: The Heroine Osan in The Almanac-Maker’s Tale (大経師昔暦のおさん Daikyōji mukashi-goyomi no Osan)
text.text:
Picturing Osan, the unfaithful wife of a Kyoto almanac maker. The story of Osan is based upon a real life incident in which her infidelity with the clerk Moemon leads to their death by crucifixion in 1683. However, Chikamatsu's play, first performed in 1715, has a happier ending in which Osan and her lover are saved at the end of the play by the intercession of a powerful priest.

One of 18 prints published from 1922 to 1925 as part of the celebration of the two-hundredth anniversary of the death of Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1623-1724), perhaps the greatest dramatist in the history of the Japanese theater. Each design illustrates a scene or character from one of Chikamatsu’s famous works which were compiled into 16 volumes by Chikamatsu researcher Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950). The prints were inserted into the volume containing the story they illustrated and were also separately sold.

media.caption: Rō Giō 籠祇王 (Giō at the Prison)

text.headline: Rō Giō 籠祇王 (Giō at the Prison)
text.text:
This print depicts the courtesan Giō meeting with her imprisoned father in the play Rō Giō, attributed to Kanze Motomasa (d. 1432).
Play synopsis (University of Pittsburgh, ULS Digital Collections https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt%3A20091209-kogyo-0444 [accessed 8-17-23]: The famous dancer Giō visits her father in prison and performs for him and his guard. She finds outs that her father, who had himself served as a jailor, has been imprisoned for freeing an innocent man. At the end of the play, he is spared from execution by the intervention of the god Kannon.

This print is from Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints, Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Yuki 雪 (Snow)

text.headline: Yuki 雪 (Snow)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the Noh play Yuki by an unknown playwright.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 222-223.) - A priest on his way to the Tenno-ji temple is sheltering from a sudden snowstorm when a young woman appears. He learns that she is the spirit of snow and, after asking him to read a sutra for her, she dances and then fades from sight amid the swirling flakes.

media.caption: Ohara gokō 大原御幸 (Imperial Visit to Ohara)

text.headline: Ohara gokō 大原御幸 (Imperial Visit to Ohara)
text.text:
This print depicts the former Empress Kenrei who has become a nun with her two attendants, Lady Dainagon and Lady Awa, in her hut (represented by a bamboo framework) at a convent in the hills of Kyoto.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 130-131.) - An official calls a servant and orders preparations to be made for the visit of the retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa to the Jakkō-in temple at Ohara where he is going to call on the ex-Empress Kenreimon-in. She has been living there as a nun since she was saved from drowning by the Minamoto at the battle of Dan-no-ura where her young son, the Emperor Antoku, and her mother, Nii-domo, met their deaths. She is first seen setting off with a companion to gather flowers in the hills. The Emperor arrives at the temple with the Chūnagon and meets Kenreimon-in on her return. She tells him of her experience in terms of Buddhist doctrine and then describes the death of her small son before her eyes.

media.caption: Yōrō 養老 (Nurturing the Aged)

text.headline: Yōrō 養老 (Nurturing the Aged)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the Noh play Nurturing the Aged by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis (The-Noh.com website http://www.the-noh.com/en/plays/data/program_017.html [accessed 8-17-23]) - It was the time of the twenty-first Emperor Yūryaku. His majesty was informed of a rumor of a miraculous spring in Motosu of Mino Province (present-day Gifu Prefecture) and dispatched an imperial investigator to find out about it. At the site, the investigator meets an old woodcutter and his son who had found the spiritual spring. When the imperial investigator asks, they tell the story of how they found the spring and how they started to call it "Yōrō no Taki Waterfall." When the parents drank the water that his son had found, the old parents felt mentally and physically refresh and vigorous. They therefore named the fall "Yōrō (taking care of elders)." In addition, the old man points the imperial investigator to the basin of the fall, introduces historical stories related to longevity and water, and praises the medicinal benefits of the waters of the Yōrō Fall. When the investigator is pleased to be able to give a great report to His Majesty, music is heard from the sky and flowers start to fall. With these auspicious signs, a deity of a mountain, who claims to be an incarnation of Willow Bodhisattva, appears and dashingly dances to bless the peace of the world.

media.caption: Utsubozaru 靱猿 (The Monkey Skin Quiver)

text.headline: Utsubozaru 靱猿 (The Monkey Skin Quiver)
text.text:
Illustrating a scene in the kyōgen 狂言 play Utsubozaru in which a monkey dances with a lord who has just spared his life.
Compared with the sumptuous weave of the elegant noh costumes, the costumes in kyōgen are mostly dyed in light, attractive patterns.

Play synopsis (I Think I am a Verb: More Contributions to the Doctrine of Signs, Thomas Albert Sebeok, Springer-Verlag New York, LLC, 1986, p. 120.) - A Daimyo goes out hunting with his servant Taro Kaja, and on the way they meet a Monkey Trainer. The Daimyo want to borrow the Monkey’s skin to cover his quiver. The Trainer, of course, refuses so the Daimyo gets angry and threatens to kill both the Trainer and the Monkey. The Trainer finally agrees, and asks for a few minutes to say goodbye. He also says that instead of shooting the Monkey with an arrow, which would harm the skin, he will kill it himself. He starts to strike the Monkey, and the Monkey mistakes his action for a signal to perform, so it grabs the stick and uses it as an oar. The Trainer begins to cry, the Daimyo asks the reason, and the Trainer replies that he has raised and trained the Monkey from the time it was born, so it is like a son to him. The Daimyo is greatly moved, and decides not to kill either the Monkey or the Trainer. In gratitude, the Monkey performs and the Trainer sings. The Daimyo presents his fan, sword, and even his own clothes to the Monkey Trainer; then he begins to dance and perform with the Monkey, thus ending on a happy note.

media.caption: Kirokuda 木六駄 (Six Loads of Firewood)

text.headline: Kirokuda 木六駄 (Six Loads of Firewood)
text.text:
Illustrating a scene in the kyōgen 狂言 play Kirokuda (Six Loads of Firewood) in which Tarōkaja trudges through a blizzard, snow piled on his straw hat and cloak, driving six oxen carrying firewood and six others carrying charcoal over a mountain pass. The oxen are never seen in the play and the actor must be convincing in his portrayal. The stage is actually bare and the whole business is manifested through text and pantomime. This section in the play is a uniquely realistic one, and therefore considered a very difficult part in the kyōgen repertoire.
Play synopsis (Nō and Bunraku: Two Forms of Japanese Theatre, Donald Keene, Keizō Kaneko, Columbia University Press, 1990, p.91.) - A certain gentleman sends his servant Tarōkaja with six ox-loads of lumber and a cask of sake for his uncle. It is bitter cold, and Tarōkaja, stopping at an inn, drinks some of the sake to warm himself. As he gets drunk he explains to the proprietor how he plans to catch in his arms a quail, to eat with the liquor.

media.caption: Tankai 湛海

text.headline: Tankai 湛海
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Tankai concerning "the romance between the Minamoto general Kiso Yoshinaka and his concubine Tomoe, an acclaimed female warrior. Toshinaka won a great victory for the Inamoto, but later he was betrayed by others in his own clan and came under attack. Knowing that the end had come, he urged Tomoe to escape. In Tankai, the ghosts of Yoshinaka and Tomoe meet again and vow their undying love. Yoshinaka is the courtier in the background wearing the purple chōken jacket, and Tomoe the warrior carrying the halberd.

media.caption: Kōya monogurui 高野物狂 (The Madman of Mt. Kōya)

text.headline: Kōya monogurui 高野物狂 (The Madman of Mt. Kōya)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from Kōya monogurui (The Madman of Mt. Kōya), by Zeami, written before 1423.
Play synopsis (Developing Zeami: the Noh Actor's Attunement in Practice, Shelley Fenno Quinn, University of Hawaii Press, 2005, p. 301.) - Kōya monogurui is the story of a young boy who resolves to become a monk after his father dies. A family retainer who is opposed to this decision searches until he finds the boy in the company of a priest from Mount Kōya. Moved by the eloquence of the priest, the retainer gives himself up to a dance in praise of the Mount Kōya complex. He is reunited with the boy and resolves to take the tonsure and join him. In the most commonly performed version of this story, the retainer takes the boy home and he is reunited with his father.

media.caption: Congratulations on Maritime Security for All Eternity! (海上安全万代寿 Kaijō anzen bandai kotobuki)

text.headline: Congratulations on Maritime Security for All Eternity! (海上安全万代寿 Kaijō anzen bandai kotobuki)
text.text:
"In the spring of 1863, Shogun Iemochi (ruled 1858–66) was ordered to Kyoto to confer with the court on how and when the ‘foreign barbarians’ should be expelled from the country. This was the first time in more than 100 years that the shogun had been summoned by the court in this way and was a high point of influence of the ‘revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians’ (sonnō jōi) faction. Iemochi left Edo with a huge retinue on the thirteenth day of the second month, and arrived at Nijō Castle in Kyoto on the fourth day of the following month.
"Kyōsai, like most inhabitants of Edo, would have wished the shogun success in his political mission, upon which rested the future economic prosperity of the city. In the seventh month of 1863, he designed this triptych showing deities protecting the return of the Shogun to Edo in the battleship Jundō-maru, an event that had occurred the previous month." - Source: Demon of Painting: the Art of Kawanabe Kyōsai, Timothy Clark, British Museum Press, 1993, p. 114

media.caption: Novel Growth No. 2 (新しい発生 No.2)

text.headline: Novel Growth No. 2 (新しい発生 No.2)
text.text:
James Michener refers to Masaji's prints as "mysterious" in nature and divides his work into "four clear categories." Novel Growth No. 2 falls into the third category, described by Michener, as follows:
"Masaji’s third kind of print formed a radical departure and was occasioned, as such new forms ought to be, by a personal crisis within the conscience of the artist. The prints appear mostly in purple and black and always with a swarm of closely knit lines… The designs are tortured, involuted, brooding, and the mysterious colors effectively represent the spirit of the work. These are most distinguished prints, not widely favored by collectors but cherished by those who know the artist and who are concerned with the artistic problems inherent in the modern school of woodblock prints. What dark experience of the soul called forth this series I do not know, but during its issue Masaji’s son died, and the prints form a fitting memorial to this tragedy, although they were not originally called forth by it. Connoisseurs of the exquisite in art should know these prints, for they are some of the most expert issued in Japan, veritable masterpieces of printing and color. They exhibit no quick allure and one comes to them quietly after having known other prints that on the surface are much more enticing; but when one has discovered their quiet mastery one recognizes in them a milestone in contemporary Japanese woodblocks." - Source: The Modern Japanese Print - An Appreciation, James Michener, Charles E. Tuttle Co., 1968, p. 48-49.
See IHL.1231 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Tadanobu 忠信

text.headline: Tadanobu 忠信
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 214) - Escaping from the capital and the danger stemming from his brother's suspicion of him, Yoshitsune has come to Mt. Yoshino. But as Yoshimori has discovered that the soldier-priests there are unfriendly and plan to kill Yoshitsune that same night, the party flees from the mountain while Tadanobu stays behind to cover their retreat. When the attack comes at nightfall he first drives the enemy back with arrows from a tower and then, after pretending to commit suicide, jumps down into a valley behind the tower. After searching the tower in vain for his body, the soldiers find and attack him again, but once more he makes good his escape and hurries after Yoshitsune.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Koi no Omoni 恋重荷 (The Burden of Love)

text.headline: Koi no Omoni 恋重荷 (The Burden of Love)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 83-84) - A Court official announces that as an old gardener in the palace has fallen in love with a Court lady, she has had a heavy weight wrapped in brocade so that it seems light, and has said that if the gardener carries it many times around the grounds she will then let him see her again. The lady hopes that, by this means, the gardener will be led to forget her when he finds the burden too heavy to carry, but instead he is filled with a bitterness at her cruelty in setting him such as impossible task. Having failed to move the weight, he leaves with a crazed air and shortly afterwards a servant reports that he has drowned himself in the lake in the grounds. The official tells the lady what has happened and asks her to go to look at his body in the hope that the old man's bitterness of spirit will then be relieved. But the lady is unable to rise, being held down, it seems, by a weight such as that which the gardener has tried to lift. His angry ghost then appears and reviles the lady for her heartlessness, but gradually its anger abates until in the end it forgives her and promises to protect her from all harm.

media.caption: A Parody of the Final Scene in Eight Dog Chronicles (Suikoden)

text.headline: A Parody of the Final Scene in Eight Dog Chronicles (Suikoden)
text.text: This book illustration pictures a scene from what is likely a novel or play parodying the novel “The Eight Dog Chronicles.” Also known as “Tales of the Water Margin” and “108 Heroes of the Popular Suikoden,” it was completed in 1842. It was incredibly popular immediately after its publication and well into the Meiji era. This illustration shows, from right to left, the characters Yōyū, Sekishu (Yōyū’s wife) and the monk Haijokai in the final scene of the novel in which Sekishu holding a mokugyo (percussion instrument used in Buddhist prayers), kills the monk Haijokai for having an affair with Yōyū’s wife.

media.caption: Spring Night in Ginza (春の夜 銀座 Haru no Yoru, Ginza)

text.headline: Spring Night in Ginza (春の夜 銀座 Haru no Yoru, Ginza)
text.text: In the foreground is a stall selling sushi, and in the middle ground a lantern advertising the spring theater performances. The background is filled by typical between-the-wars [WWI and Pacific War] buildings of the Tokyo entertainment area. Among these inanimate features the people, in a mixture of Western and Japanese dress, seem shadowy and uncertain.  Shiro was in the 1930s very sensitive to this introverted atmosphere and has recorded it with a poetic skill which he never regained after the catastrophe of the War. - Source: Printed to Perfection: Twentieth-century Japanese Prints from the Robert O. Muller Collection, Amy Reigle Newland, et. al., Hotei Publishing, 2004, p. 113.

media.caption: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯)

text.headline: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯)
text.text:
This print is not included in the artist's catalog raisonné. For another print by Takahashi depicting the tea ceremony see Tea Ceremony II (IHL.0191).
The prominent circular form in this print made its first appearance in the artist's 1964 print, Kyoto's Mind, and appears in a number of Takahashi's prints until it is abandoned in 1966 after the Work series of prints. (See Work A and Work BB in this collection.)

media.caption: Noh Play Okina - Kanze lineage (能楽 翁 観世家 nōgaku Okina Kanze-ke)

text.headline: Noh Play Okina - Kanze lineage (能楽 翁 観世家 nōgaku Okina Kanze-ke)
text.text:
This print of a Kanze school actor in the Noh play Okina by Kondō Koichirō appeared in the last issue (#5) of Shin Nigao published in November 1915. Although the primary purpose behind the magazine was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints, five prints in the last issue of the paper portrayed individuals or characters involved in the month-long celebrations of Emperor Yoshihito's (Emperor Taishō) enthronement in November 1915. This is the only print by the artist to appear in the magazine.
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

text.headline: Yoshichō Nanako (芳町 魚子)
text.text:
This print pictures the geisha named Nanako from the Yoshichō geisha quarters of Tokyo. One of the two prints contributed by the artist to Shin Nigao.

media.caption: Descended Level 2 Stones Between Vertical and Horizon

text.headline: Descended Level 2 Stones Between Vertical and Horizon
text.text:
Ida constantly experimented with the force of gravity and its effect on media. His friend and fellow artist Robert Kushner commented, “Paper pulp was an ideal medium for his experiments. Pulp is strong and durable and yet it is able to take on three-dimensional form and hold foreign objects in its grasp, even bond with antique fabrics. In his most complex pieces all of these processes were combined [with] tour de force bravado. When these diverse materials dried, a frozen record of the convergence remained, the haunting effects of nature and the passage of time.”
One of Ida Shōichi's (1941-2006) many prints, collages and sculptures that explore the physical space between objects that touch. This work is composed of molded mud-dyed paper pulp, embedded with stones, combined with gauze and antique kimono fabric.

media.caption: Imperial Prosperity: Ceremony in the Eastern Capital (御世の栄東の粧ひ Miyo no sakae azuma no yosōi)

text.headline: Imperial Prosperity: Ceremony in the Eastern Capital (御世の栄東の粧ひ Miyo no sakae azuma no yosōi)
text.text:
Issued in the year of Crown Prince Yoshihito's wedding, this print was one of many (also see IHL.1100, "Picture of Noble's Imperial Ceremony" and IHL.1327, "Picture of Wedding Ceremony of Noble Couple") to portray the ceremonies surrounding Yoshihito's marriage to sixteen year old Kujō Sadako on May 10, 1900. The Crown Prince with his mustache and full military uniform is seen sitting [left sheet] while a lady, perhaps his bride-to-be, in Western-fashion is being presented to him. Whether this print depicts an actual event at the imperial court or was designed to promulgate the modernity of the imperial family, it is one of many prints that featured the Imperial family with the men in military attire and the women dressed in Western fashion. Prints such as this served to show that the emperor's regime was in the forefront of the modern world; that Japan was "advancing toward Civilization" and becoming "richer in all things. . . ."[1]
From the time of the decision of the prince's marriage on August 21, 1899 to the marriage ceremony itself on May 10, 1900 , a series of newly fabricated events, including the marriage ceremony itself, had been instituted by the newly formed Imperial Institutions Investigatory Bureau (teishitsu seido chōsa kyoku), which was tasked with studying European monarchy practices in order to "create a modern monarchy that they believed would represent a level of civility equal to that of the West. . . ."[2]

[1] Splendid Monarchy: Power and Pageantry in Modern Japan, T. Fujitani, University of California Press, 1998, p. 107.
[2] Ibid., p. 118.

media.caption: Welcoming the Triumphant Japanese Army Return from Asan (牙山凱旋歓迎之図 Gazan gaisen kangei no zu)

text.headline: Welcoming the Triumphant Japanese Army Return from Asan (牙山凱旋歓迎之図 Gazan gaisen kangei no zu)
text.text: A depiction of the Japanese army generals being welcomed in Seoul after their victory over the Chinese at Asan. Figures identified by labels include Brigade Commander Ōshima, Staff Officer Nagaoka, Minister Ōtori and the Korean King's Messenger Yi Yun-yong (Ri Inyo).

media.caption: Kyoto Series No. 52 Garden N (京都シリーズ NO. 52 庭 N)

text.headline: Kyoto Series No. 52 Garden N (京都シリーズ NO. 52 庭 N)
text.text:
Kyoto has been the predominant theme of Takahashi's work, the subject of sixty-three of the artists prints, spanning almost his entire career.
"Kyoto, former capital of Japan, is the focus of Takahashi's artistic inspiration, a city to which this artist remains profoundly attached. Despite its size, it has an intimacy, an accessible charm to which Takahashi has yielded completely." - Source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973, p. 148-149.

media.caption: Spring Garden (春の庭)

text.headline: Spring Garden (春の庭)
text.text: This print appears to be a different state from the impression pictured in the artist's catalog raisonné. Overall the print is in poor condition and, therefore, a poor representation of the artist's work.

media.caption: Way for Hakone (箱根路)

text.headline: Way for Hakone (箱根路)
text.text:
This print appeared in the 1960 exhibition Contemporary Japanese Woodcuts staged by the Auckland City Art Gallery. The catalog entry for this print reads, "UCHIMA ANSEI (b.1921) is an American of Japanese ancestry who was caught in Japan by the war. He has been active in organizing exhibitions of modern prints, as well as developing a style of his own."
The exhibition was the first in New Zealand devoted solely to sōsaku hanga artists and their prints.

media.caption: The Pig's Dismay (豚の当惑 Buta no tōwaku)

text.headline: The Pig's Dismay (豚の当惑 Buta no tōwaku)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
The Japanese dragonfly stands over the Chinese pig, while the three bees representing Russia, England and France buzz around China's head. By the time this print was released in December 1894, Japan was in control of Port Arthur and the Liaodong Peninsula. A few years after the war ended, Russia, England and France all obtained leases of various strategic ports from a weak China.
Depiction of Japan as a Dragonfly - Japan was not always named Japan. Japanese legend has it that an Emperor was bitten by a horsefly which, in turn, was eaten by a dragonfly. The Emperor honored the dragonfly by naming what is now Japan “Akitsushima” which, during that time, translated to “Isle of the Dragonfly”.

media.caption: These are the Pescadores (Penghu)! (是ハ澎湖島 Kore wa Hōkotō)

text.headline: These are the Pescadores (Penghu)! (是ハ澎湖島 Kore wa Hōkotō)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In the print Chinese troops fall to the ground in fear as a Japanese soldier in guise of the thunder god appears, with his drums and a lightning flash.
Although the Pescadores were garrisoned by 15 Chinese regular battalions (5,000 men) and defended by the recently-completed Hsi-tai coastal defense battery, the Japanese met very little resistance during the landing operation as the defenders were demoralized. It took the Japanese only three days to secure the islands.

media.caption: Stone Flower - White, Yellow (石の花 白黄 Ishi no hana・haku-ō)

text.headline: Stone Flower - White, Yellow (石の花 白黄 Ishi no hana・haku-ō)
text.text: The fifteen prints in this series won multiple awards at prestigious international print fairs in the 1960s, placing Hagiwara at the forefront of modern Japanese printmaking. Using his two-sided printing technique he created an almost ethereal surface on which to print these translucent petals lying on soft stone.

media.caption: Inside Asakusa Kannon Temple (浅草観世音の内堂 Asakusa Kannon-dō no naidō)

text.headline: Inside Asakusa Kannon Temple (浅草観世音の内堂 Asakusa Kannon-dō no naidō)
text.text:
Inside Asakusa Kannon Temple nicely captures the atmosphere within this venerable Tokyo landmark, where the hum of voices, clink of coins thrown into the offering box, and flutter of pigeons in the rafters reverberate off the dusty wooden floor. This cacophony is paralleled by the visual confusion of colorful kimonos, flying birds, huge lanterns, and votive paintings, all competing for space in the half-lit interior. While shin hanga prints of Tokyo usually avoid crowd scenes to find beauty in the empty stillness of the city, Narazaki’s depiction of visitors at a famous temple provides a noteworthy exception. - Source: Shin-Hanga: New Prints in Modern Japan, Kendall Brown, Hollis Goodall-Cristante, Los Angeles County Museum of Art, 1996, p. 83.
See IHL.0230a for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Turmoil at River Sanzu (三途川の大混雑 Sanzugawa no ō-konzatsu)

text.headline: Turmoil at River Sanzu (三途川の大混雑 Sanzugawa no ō-konzatsu)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
"In this print even the dead Chinese soldiers still fear the power of the Japanese Army; they try to escape as far as possible to the more 'secure' underworld. Caused by the turmoil the little boat is about to sink and so the text comments (referring to the news of Japanese victories at sea) ironically that Chinese people are used to get sunken. Furthermore there is a wordplay dealing with the similar sound of 'All good times come in threes' (Nido aru koto wa Sanzu dā) and the name of the River, Sanzu-gawa." - Source: University of Vienna website https://ukiyo-e.univie.ac.at/en/fullview.html?lang=e&docid=898 [accessed 8-17-2023]

media.caption: The Juggler of the Chinese Ball ( 支那玉遣ひ Shina tama-tsukai)

text.headline: The Juggler of the Chinese Ball ( 支那玉遣ひ Shina tama-tsukai)
text.text:

"A bearded Japanese officer is juggling with six small pig-tailed Chinese men in the form of dolls, to show how easy it is to defeat the Chinese. A young bugler provides music for the act." - Source: Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints , Lea Baten, Weatherhill, 1995, p. 118.

media.caption: Stone Flower - White (石の花・白 Ishi no hana・shiro)

text.headline: Stone Flower - White (石の花・白 Ishi no hana・shiro)
text.text: This series of 15 prints uses a technique devised by the artist in which pigment is forced through the paper from the back, effectively dying the paper and producing a textural surface on which to work.  This series is credited with enhancing “the prestige of Japan in the contemporary print world.”- Source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973, vol. I, p. 112.

media.caption: Blue Peep Show A (ブルーピープショウ A burūpipushō]

text.headline: Blue Peep Show A (ブルーピープショウ A burūpipushō]
text.text: The curvilinear forms used in Blue Peep Show A emerge in a series of prints in 1970, starting with Ocean A (artist's catalog raisonné 246) and are largely gone by 1971. Also see Seabathing (IHL.0424.)

media.caption: Musician Greenwich Village (グリニッジビレッジの音楽家)

text.headline: Musician Greenwich Village (グリニッジビレッジの音楽家)
text.text:
Created the year following Takahashi's 1963 visit to the United States, this print captures the feel of the Greenwich Village jazz scene in the early 60s. One of my favorite prints by the artist, only ten impressions were made.
It is always fascinating to look at an artist's proof print (IHL.2240) and the final edition of the print (IHL.0238). While the editioned version is of very poor quality with severe toning and horizontal and vertical "burn" marks on the paper, we can see that the biggest change from the artist proof to the editioned print was the addition of the orange markings in the lower right of the print.

media.caption: Kyoto's Voice (京都の声)

text.headline: Kyoto's Voice (京都の声)
text.text:
Kyoto has been the predominant theme of Takahashi's work. Either named or referenced in the print title, Kyoto appears in a total of sixty-three of the artists prints, spanning almost his entire career.
"Kyoto, former capital of Japan, is the focus of Takahashi's artistic inspiration, a city to which this artist remains profoundly attached. Despite its size, it has an intimacy, an accessible charm to which Takahashi has yielded completely.
"Simplicity is a keynote in Takahashi's works, yet it, too, conveys more than a mere freedom from complexity or an absence of pretentiousness. One could even go so far as to describe it as the unity of that which has no form. The lightly embossed print shown here speaks of Zen gardens under snow, glittering in the void. It is a distillation of the spirit of Kyoto, whose restraint and elegance are epitomized in its gardens." - Source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973, p. 148-149.

media.caption: Yosōi - Girl (よそおい・おんな yosōi・onna)

text.headline: Yosōi - Girl (よそおい・おんな yosōi・onna)
text.text: Hodaka's abstract design of a "made up" girl. This print is also seen titled by Hodaka as Yosōi - Woman (よそおい・おんな) or "made up woman."
