media.caption: Ducks and Withered Lotus (鴨と枯蓮 Kamo to karehasu)

text.headline: Ducks and Withered Lotus (鴨と枯蓮 Kamo to karehasu)
text.text:
This untitled print known as Ducks and Withered Lotus is a genre of print designated as a "domestic print" by Henry D. Smith. Domestic prints were similar to traditional bird and flower prints (kacho-e) but showed domestic everyday house and garden scenes. In this print Kiyochika has sought to approximate Western-style painting, eliminating the margins to approximate a canvas. (Note this collection's print has had margins added to it and it appears that the Los Angeles County Museum of Art print may also have added margins.)
While absent from both this collection's print and the print in the collection of the Chazen Museum of Art, the prints in the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art both have the publisher's name and publication date in the bottom left and center portion of the image. Kiyochika's signature is present on all prints along the lower right of the image.
Kiyochika' has made an effort to de-emphasize line in this print without abandoning the woodblock medium. It is suggested that this print was designed to compete with the new technology of color lithography. Particularly effective is the ghostly gray pattern of the decaying lotus in the background. The careful modeling of the ducks suggests that the artist had observed such birds closely and was aiming more for a scientific Audubon-like accuracy than for the elegance of the traditional bird-and-flower genre. The print is dated 1879, probably the first year in which the publisher Matsuki began issuing such prints.

media.caption: Nōgaku hyakuban zenhen morkuroku 能楽百番 前編 目録 (One Hundred Prints of Noh, first volume, table of contents)

text.headline: Nōgaku hyakuban zenhen morkuroku 能楽百番 前編 目録 (One Hundred Prints of Noh, first volume, table of contents)
text.text:
One of two woodblock prints serving as an overall index for the two bound volumes of the series Nōgaku hyakuban (One Hundred Prints of Noh) compiled and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi after the individual prints were offered for sale. This print lists the contents of Volume 1 and contains the titles of fifty prints. While Kōgyo's signature does not appear on this print, his seals appear in the lower right hand corner.

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone." - Source: The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: New Army Recruits (清国の困苦民兵 Shinkoku konku minpei)

text.headline: New Army Recruits (清国の困苦民兵 Shinkoku konku minpei)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin, a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In front of a Chinese officer holding a sword are a line of new recruits - old senile men. In the background another Chinese officer marches with various disabled recruits. While the war was over when this print was published in August 1895, it was still popular to ridicule the Chinese military.

media.caption: Thunder God and Demons

text.headline: Thunder God and Demons
text.text:
The second of nine prints from the series Comical Record of Japanese History, a parody of Hyakki Yakō (Night Parade of One Hundred Demons). The nine prints read as a scroll when placed next to each other and commemorate the Japanese military victory over China in April 1895.
The titles for the top and bottom sections of this print are given on the first print of the scroll, with the top section titled "Newly Designed Night Parade of a Hundred Demons” (Shin’an hyakki yagyô 新案百鬼夜行) and the bottom section titled "Newly Designed Night Parade of a Hundred Demons” (Shin’an hyakki yagyô 新案百鬼夜行).
"Each yōkai [demon or ghost] is designed to represent and ridicule soldiers from the Chinese army conquered in the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895), in Meiji Japan's first important military victory." - Source: Traditional Monster Imagery in Manga, Anime and Japanese Cinema, Zilia Papp, Brill, 2010, p. 90.

media.caption: Night Cherry Blossoms (夜ざくら Yozakura)

text.headline: Night Cherry Blossoms (夜ざくら Yozakura)
text.text:
This print, picturing the cherry trees at night in the Gion District of Kyoto, is the original issue (first edition) published by Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936 as part of the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. Uchida mounted these prints on a display board with Tokuriki’s authentication seal on the reverse. These square format prints on board were part of a premium set of designs originally packaged in a handmade box.
This same print, with modifications and not mounted on board, was later released as part of the series Twelve Months of Kyoto (Kyō-meisho junikagetsu).

media.caption: Gion Festival (きをん會 Gionkai)

text.headline: Gion Festival (きをん會 Gionkai)
text.text:
This print, picturing the festivities on the night before the Gion Festival in Kyoto, is the original issue (first edition) published by Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936 as part of the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. Uchida mounted these prints on a display board with Tokuriki’s authentication seal on the reverse. These square format prints on board were part of a premium set of designs originally packaged in a handmade box. For an image of the box, please see Index for the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto.
This same print, with modifications and not mounted on board, was later released as part of the series Twelve Months of Kyoto (Kyō-meisho junikagetsu).

media.caption: Daimonji (大文字)

text.headline: Daimonji (大文字)
text.text:
This print, picturing the fires lit to celebrate the end of the O-Bon festival in Kyoto, is the original issue (first edition) published by Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936 as part of the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. Uchida mounted these prints on a display board with Tokuriki’s authentication seal on the reverse. These square format prints on board were part of a premium set of designs originally packaged in a handmade box.
Uchida reissued this print after WWII as part of the series Twelve Months of Kyoto (Kyo-meisho junikagetsu).

media.caption: Niwa 80-K (庭 80-K)

text.headline: Niwa 80-K (庭 80-K)
text.text: While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa.  Also see Niwa (Sunshine), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (April) and Niwa (Winter Scenery) in this collection.

media.caption: Night at Ginza (夜の銀座 Yoru no Ginza)

text.headline: Night at Ginza (夜の銀座 Yoru no Ginza)
text.text:
"This witty hot pink and bright blue Ginza (ぎんざ, the word is written vertically along the image's right edge) is clearly the bustling place of the moga (modern girls) and mobo (modern boys). The fashionable young women promenading down the street turn their heads to observe and be observed. Kawakami creates a sense of immediacy - of the viewer being part of the crowd - with strong color and by cropping the figures in foreground and middle ground, as well as with the objects inserted along both sides of the picture surface. He is best known for including curious old foreign objects in his prints; the masked profile face seen through the rear window of the car on the left looks like a character from the Italian commedia dell'arte. The artist's consciously rough, simplified carving and his flamboyant color convey the modish modernity characteristic of the place and its habitués." - Source: Terrific Tokyo A Panorama in Prints: from the 1860s to the 1930s, Elizabeth de Sabato Swinton, Worcester Art Museum. 1998 p. 76.
See IHL.0033 to view a later reissue of the print.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Illustration of the Hard Fight at Fenghuangcheng  (鳳凰城ニ将士奮闘之図 Hōōjō ni shōshi funtō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Hard Fight at Fenghuangcheng  (鳳凰城ニ将士奮闘之図 Hōōjō ni shōshi funtō no zu)
text.text:
Perhaps more accurately titled as "Picture of the Not So Hard Fight at Fenghuangcheng," this print depicts a battle that was planned by the Japanese as a present for the emperor on his birthday, but which did not occur due to a retreat by the Chinese. Historical accuracy was not the aim of most war triptychs.
War correspondent and artist Kubota Beisen (1852-1906) reported: “Our troops were to attack Fenghuangcheng on His Majesty’s birthday, November 3. Scouts reported to General Tatsumi Naobumi that the enemy had set the citadel on fire around 5:00 PM, October 29, and fled. The enemy officers had gone to Mukden, whereas the men escaped to the coast. The following day, the Japanese entered the fort without fighting and found two hundred civilian homes burned down. Two mountain cannons, three mortars, and countless rifles and tents were left.” Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, 1894-95, Shumpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983
Other impressions of this print carry the name of another publisher 松野米治郎 (Matsuno Yunejirō) in the left margin rather than this impression's "pot-shaped" publisher seal reading 関口政治郎 (Sekiguchi Masajirō) found in the lower corner of the right sheet.

media.caption: Paper Hat, Mask, Collar, Military Decorations (紙帽子・仮面・襟・勲章)

text.headline: Paper Hat, Mask, Collar, Military Decorations (紙帽子・仮面・襟・勲章)
text.text:
Like most of Kawakami's prints, this still life of a paper hat, a mask, carnations, a starched color and two military medals is untitled. Whether this work is just an artistic exercise or poking fun at something or someone is unknown. The print is embossed and hand colored by the artist in the unique style that he started using in the 1930s. Extensive embossing (karazuri 空摺) is used throughout the design and silver metallic highlights are seen on the medals.
Another version of this print uses a different color scheme and has the artist's seal in the lower right of the image, which is not present on this print.

media.caption: Atago Kūya 愛宕空也

text.headline: Atago Kūya 愛宕空也
text.text:
The dragon king of Mount Atago creates an inexhaustible spring from which water gushes down the mountain to thank to the holy monk Kūya for helping him to find a relic of the Buddha (busshari) to relieve his pain. This print is the left half of a diptych. The right half portrays the monk Atago Kūya.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
The holy monk Kūya Shōnin (waki) climbs Mount Atago in Yamashiro Province to recite the holy texts. The mountain's Dragon God (ryūjin, shite) appears in guise of an old man, rōō. He asks for a relic of the Buddha (busshari). Three times every day Dragon Gods suffer pain because of the "Three Heats" (sannetsu). He asks for the bone of the Buddha that forms the jiku or roller of the sutra scroll, one of eight received from the Engi Emperor. Kūya opens the the scroll and is astonished to find in the roller a crystal box containing the blue bones of the Buddha. To the amazement of his companions, he gives the relics to the man, who thanks him and offer to fulfill any wish. Kūya asks for him to create an inexhaustible spring on the mountain top so that water does not need to be carried up from the valley far below. The old man vows to do this in three days, when he will appear in his real form. In the latter half of the play he returns as Dragon King (ryōō) and, as promised, creates a spring from which water gushes in waves down the mountain. (Summary by M. Watson)[1]

Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. media.caption: Illustration of the Emperor's March from the East Castle (東城御道行之図 Tōjōon (go) michiyuki no zu or Azuma jō go michiyuki no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Emperor's March from the East Castle (東城御道行之図 Tōjōon (go) michiyuki no zu or Azuma jō go michiyuki no zu)
text.text: It is April 1900 and two carriages with the Imperial Seal are departing the Imperial Palace after crossing Nijubashi, seen in the background. The occupants of the first carriage are unseen, but are assumed to be Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken. They are followed by Crown Prince Yoshito and his bride-to-be Kujō Sadako, daughter of the patriarch of one of the "five regent families" (gosekke). The procession is likely one of the pre-marriage rituals set down in one of a number of laws and regulations relating to the Imperial Household that were to govern the upcoming wedding of the Crown Prince on May 10, 1900.  It may well be that the Emperor and his entourage are heading for the Imperial Palace in Kyoto.

media.caption: Illustration of the April Negotiations (清和談判之図 Seiwa danpan no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the April Negotiations (清和談判之図 Seiwa danpan no zu)
text.text:
The title of the print makes reference to the "April negotiations," meaning the negotiations between Japan and China to conclude the Treaty of Shimonoseki ending the Sino-Japanese War.
"With the defeat of the Chinese fleet, the war was over. Li Hung-chang, the Viceroy of Tientsin, was forced to negotiate with Japanese Prime Minister Ito Hirobumi and sign the Treaty of Shimonoseki (17 April 1895). This brought Japan not only Taiwan, the Pescadores, and a foothold in South Manchuria, but also a handsome indemnity (two hundred million taels), the recognition of Korea’s independence, and most importantly, the same privileges that the Western powers were enjoying in China. Korea became a Japanese protectorate in 1905 and was annexed in 1910." - Source: "Images of the Sino-Japanese War – A Book Review," Robert Vergez, Ukiyo-e Art: A Journal of the Japan Ukiyo-e Society, No. Vol. 79, 1983, p. ii.

media.caption: Kichiemon in the role of Takechi Mitsuhide (吉右衛門 光秀)

text.headline: Kichiemon in the role of Takechi Mitsuhide (吉右衛門 光秀)
text.text:
The actor Nakamura Kichiemon I (1886-1940) in the role of Takechi Mitsuhide in the play Toki-ha Ima Kikyō no Hataage staged at the Ichimura-za, Tokyo in June 1915. One of two prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Fukusuke in the role of Yohei (福助 與兵衛)

text.headline: Fukusuke in the role of Yohei (福助 與兵衛)

text.headline: Beast (けもの)
text.text: This print was done in the middle of the artist's Primitive Energy phase when he was creating abstractions of Pre-Columbian forms.

media.caption: Ichikawa Sanshō V as a Sweetmeat Peddler in the play Uirō (五世市川三升 外郎売)

text.headline: Ichikawa Sanshō V as a Sweetmeat Peddler in the play Uirō (五世市川三升 外郎売)
text.text:
One of thirty-six prints making up the Watanabe-published series Collection of Creative Print Portraits by Shunsen (1925-1929). This print is the series installment no. 15. The character 壽 kotobuki (long life) is written on the actor's fan and refers to the medicine he is peddling.
"Ichikawa Sanshō X* appears full-figure, early in his career, in a pose established long before for the role of the fast-talking peddler. Bearing on his back a pack full of moxa – Japanese mogusa, a medicine to be burned, like incense, on the skin of the patient – Sanshō faces the audience and holds out a sample as he delivers a long sales pitch filled with puns, jokes, and other remarks."- source: Dramatic Impressions: Japanese Theatre Prints from the Gilbert Luber Collection, Chance, Frank L. & Davis, Julie Nelson, University of Pennsylvania Press, 200, p. 41.
*While the actor pictured is identified as Ichikawa Sanshō X, the Kabuki21 website (see http://www.kabuki21.com/sansho5.php [accessed 8-17-23] the Ichikawa Sanshō lineage ended with Ichikawa Sanshō V, who held the name from November 1917 until his death in February 1956.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danshirō as Sanbasō Dancer (市川段四郎 三番叟 Ichikawa Danshirō san daimei)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danshirō as Sanbasō Dancer (市川段四郎 三番叟 Ichikawa Danshirō san daimei)
text.text: Picturing the actor Ichikawa Danshirō III as a Sanbasō dancer. This print is one of 24 in the series New Portraits of Actors on the Stage, the last series Shunsen designed for the publisher Watanabe and the least critically acclaimed. Kendall Brown writes "The intense emotions and melodramatic poses found in many of these prints reveal the self-parody of Shunsen's late work, the stagnation of postwar kabuki, or perhaps both."

media.caption: Ōeyama 大江山 (Demon of Ōeyama)

text.headline: Ōeyama 大江山 (Demon of Ōeyama)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the play Ōeyama attributed to the playwright Miyamasu (15th century.)
PLAY SYNOPSIS
The great warrior Minamoto no Yorimitsu leaves the capital with many other warriors to subdue the demon Shuten dôji who lives on Mt. Ôeyama. Disguised as mountain ascetic priests they reach the mountain and seek lodgings at the demon’s residence. Since the demon has vowed never to harm a priest he, in his form as a young “wine-drinking lad,” accepts the disguised warriors and drinks wine with them. When the demon has become quite inebriated, he retires to his bedchamber. The warriors in turn attack him there, and after a frightful battle, vanquish him.

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

media.caption: Kinuta 砧 (The Fulling Block)

text.headline: Kinuta 砧 (The Fulling Block)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Kinuta by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which the wife beats the household fabrics rhythmically with a fulling block in the cool autumn evenings to pass the time in her sadness.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A man from Ashiya in Kyūshū has been in the capital for three years because of a lawsuit and therefore sends a servant, Yūgiri back to his home to assure his wife that he will return by the end of the year. The servant does her best to comfort the wife and as they beat cloth together on the fulling board, the wife wonders whether the west wind will not carry the sound through the autumn night to her husband far away in the capital. But he later sends another messenger (not represented on the stage) to say that he is unable to return that year after all. When the lady, who is even now finding the continued loneliness almost unbearable, hears this from Yūgiri, the bitter disappointment and the apparent fading of her husband's love for her drive her insane, and soon she dies. Overcome with grief when he learns of her death on his return, the husband summons up her spirit by plucking the string of a catalpa bow. The spirit of his wife reproves him for his inconstancy, but attains peace through the power of the Lotus Sutra.[1]

media.caption: Naruko in Spring (御殿場初冬 Haru no Naruko)

text.headline: Naruko in Spring (御殿場初冬 Haru no Naruko)
text.text: Mica highlights and embossing add interest to this undated abstract composition by Hagiwara, likely created very late in his career.

media.caption: Azuma Bridge (あずまばし Azumabashi)

text.headline: Azuma Bridge (あずまばし Azumabashi)
text.text:
Azumabashi 吾妻橋, built in 1887, was the first metal bridge spanning the Sumida River. It was officially dedicated and opened to the public on December 9, 1887. It served the bustling pleasure quarter of Asakusa on one side and a beer factory on the other. Kunitoshi and other artists of the period who depicted the bridge drew its vertical posts and diagonal eyebars in Western perspective, populating the walkway with ladies in bustles and the deck with top-hatted gentlemen in carriages.
For other prints depicting Azumabashi see IHL.0446, IHL.2151 and IHL.2435.

media.caption: Mekari 和布刈 (The Seaweed Gatherer)

text.headline: Mekari 和布刈 (The Seaweed Gatherer)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the play Mekari by the playwright Komparu Zenchiku (1405-c. 1470).
PLAY SYNOPSIS
On the last day of every year the priest of the Hayamoto Myōjin Shrine performed a ceremony of gathering seaweed and offering it up at the shrine. While he is preparing to do so this one year, a woman and an old fisherman appear and tell him a story of long ago. The land god Hōdemi married Princess Toyotama, daughter of the Sea God, and land and sea were as one. But when Hōdemi disobeyed her and looked at her when she was giving birth, she returned to her home in the sea and it was forever shut off from the land. Nevertheless, the priest is told, a way will be opened into the sea at the time of the ceremony so that the seaweed may be safely gathered. Then, revealing that the woman is a goddess and the old man a dragon-god, they disappear. Later the dragon-god and his daughter Toyotama come forth in their true forms. The waves recede for the priest to gather the seaweed, but once this is done they surge back again and the dragon-gods return to the depth of the sea.[1]

media.caption: View of Yomiuri Shimbun, Kyobashi Industrial Site (京橋風景読売新聞社・勧業場 Kyobashi fukei Yomiuri shinbunsha, kangyō-jō)

text.headline: View of Yomiuri Shimbun, Kyobashi Industrial Site (京橋風景読売新聞社・勧業場 Kyobashi fukei Yomiuri shinbunsha, kangyō-jō)
text.text: Scene showing the offices of Tokyo's first newspaper, the Yomiuri shimbun 読売新聞社 on Kyobashi street in the Ginza district. The founder and first president of the Yomiuri shimbun, Takashi Koyasu, was a confident of the members of the literary coterie Kenyūsha (Friends of the Inkstone) which this print's designer Takeuchi Keishū (1861-1942) belonged to.

media.caption: Bear Hunting for Gall in Kaga Province (加州熊并ニ胆ヲ取ル図 Kashū-gama narabi ni kimo o toru zu)

text.headline: Bear Hunting for Gall in Kaga Province (加州熊并ニ胆ヲ取ル図 Kashū-gama narabi ni kimo o toru zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, the Asian black bear (note the white chest mark) is being hunted for his gall. Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no kuni) was an old province in the area that is today the southern part of Ishikawa Prefecture. Ruled by the Maeda clan, the capital of Kaga was Kanazawa. Kaga bordered on Echizen, Etchū, Hida, and Noto Provinces. It was part of Hokurikudō Circuit.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1496.
The artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" or, as in the case of this print, practiced in the same manner in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

media.caption: Speculators Talking Amiably (山師の笑談 Yamashi no shōdan)

text.headline: Speculators Talking Amiably (山師の笑談 Yamashi no shōdan)
text.text:
This print is one of twelve issued as part of the second set of prints from the series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the enemy. The text on the pints was provided by the writer Nishimori Takeki (1861-1923), alias Koppi Dōjin.
Four speculators sit around a map of the Taiwanese archipelago (including the Pescadores) figuring out the riches they'd make developing Japan's newest colony.

media.caption: Hubbub in the Dragon King's Palace (竜宮の騒ぎ Ryūgū no sawagi)

text.headline: Hubbub in the Dragon King's Palace (竜宮の騒ぎ Ryūgū no sawagi)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
Kiyochika gives us a scene in the Dragon King’s palace, where a giant anchor has dropped to the seabed floor frightening him and his daughter while fish flee. The anchor is from one of the Chinese battleships sunk by the Japanese navy in the battle of the Yellow Sea.

media.caption: A Bunraku Puppet Head

text.headline: A Bunraku Puppet Head
text.text:
This collection contains two different printings of this depiction of the head of a bunraku puppet, IHL.0275 and IHL.0314. These two versions may both be artist's proofs. This print IHL.0275 carries the artist's signature written in pencil "T. Tokuriki 1962." in the lower left corner within the image. Print IHL.0314 bears the artist's signature in the lower right corner within the image.
This print was released as a numbered edition of 100 prints.

media.caption: Bird on Bamboo Branch

text.headline: Bird on Bamboo Branch
text.text: This sumi-e by Tokuriki is one of several I've seen with traditional kachō-ga motifs. Sumi-e was introduced into Japan in the 14th century by Zen Buddhist monks visiting from China.  It uses only brush-applied black ink on paper.

media.caption: Untitled Illustration for a novel or magazine

text.headline: Untitled Illustration for a novel or magazine
text.text: A priest, perhaps, bearing the characters 莱庵 on his bald head appears to have fallen asleep at his writing table. In his dream he sees a man carrying another man, perhaps injured, while a lightning storm rages. Likely an illustration (kuchi-e) for a novel or story. An unread signature appears in the bottom left corner of the image along with what is likely the artist's seal which has been obliterated by bleeding of its red ink.

media.caption: Hagiwara Taneko [dressed to perform] Gosechi no Maihime (姫舞之節五 萩原種子)

text.headline: Hagiwara Taneko [dressed to perform] Gosechi no Maihime (姫舞之節五 萩原種子)
text.text:
The court dancer Hagiwara Taneko is dressed to perform the dance Gosechi no Maihime at the coronation ceremony of the Taishō emperor. According to a newspaper report in the The Straits Times (Singapore), 28 August 1915, "In regard to the entertainments to be given on the first day of the Coronation, the ancient 'quintuple dance' known as Gosechi-no-Mai will constitute, according to the Coronation Committee the most prominent part of the programme. The origin of this dance is said to be traceable as far back as the days of Emperor Temmu (697 a.d.). The ladies who will perform the dance next November at the Coronation celebration have been selected from among the unmarried daughters of the descendants of ancient courtiers, to the number of eight, of whom three form the reserve. The ladies vary in age from 19 to 23 years, and will appear dressed in ancient costumes." One of seven prints contributed by the artist to the magazine Shin Nigao.

media.caption: Niwa - Sunshine (庭・降り注ぐ光)

text.headline: Niwa - Sunshine (庭・降り注ぐ光)
text.text: Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for Takahashi. The word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled NIWA R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa. Also see Niwa (80-K), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (April) and Niwa (Winter Scenery) in this collection.

media.caption: Kazuraki 葛城

text.headline: Kazuraki 葛城
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Kazuraki by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which an old woman gives shelter from the snow to a priest and two attendant priests, building a fire with shimoto.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
Three priests who have come to Mt. Kazuraki are given shelter from the snow by a woman. Later she asks them to pray for her to relieve her suffering, and when questioned, reveals that she is the goddess of the mountain and is being punished for having failed in her duty once in the past. Later she reappears in her true form and, having been saved from further punishment by the prayers of the priests, performs a dance for them in gratitude.[1]

media.caption: Kayoi Komachi 通小町 (The Courtship of Komachi)

text.headline: Kayoi Komachi 通小町 (The Courtship of Komachi)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the play Kayoi Komachi by the playwright Kanami (1333-1384).
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A priest who is spending the summer in the mountain village of Yase is brought wood and fruit every day by an unknown woman. When he asks who she is, he realizes from her reply that she is the ghost of Ono no Komachi, the poetess of old who was so famed for her beauty. He therefore goes to her grave and prays. At this, her spirit and that of her most ardent suitor, Fukakusa no Shōshō, appear and tell the priest of the trial Komachi set him. She promised herself to him if he came to her house every night for a hundred nights, but after braving all manner of obstacles to fulfill his task, he failed on the hundredth night.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.75-76.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Shunzei Tadanori 俊成忠度 (Shunzei and Tadanori)

text.headline: Shunzei Tadanori 俊成忠度 (Shunzei and Tadanori)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 169) - Okabe no Rokuyata, who has killed Tadanori in battle, brings Shunzei a poem which he found in Tadanori's quiver. Tadanori's ghost then appears and after complaining that Shunzei has included a poem of his in an anthology as an anonymous one, and talking of poetry in general, he speaks of the torments a warrior suffers after death.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Think Hard Before Putting Your Life of the Line (命をかけておもふ Inochi o kakete omou)

text.headline: Think Hard Before Putting Your Life of the Line (命をかけておもふ Inochi o kakete omou)
text.text:
This scene depicts a woman jumping off the terrace of Kiyomizu-dera while grasping the Japanese character for life, inochi. She has jumped due to disappointment and despair over an unhappy love affair. Perhaps she has wished for a happier conclusion to her love life before jumping as there was an Edo period tradition holding that if one were to survive jumping from the terrace of Kiyomizu Temple, one's wish would be granted.
234 jumps were recorded in the Edo period and of those, 85.4% survived. The expression "to jump off the porch at Kiyomizu" is the Japanese equivalent of the English expression "to take the plunge."
Kiyomizudera (清水寺 "PureWater Temple") was founded in 780 AD and still functions as a temple associated with the Hosso sect of Japanese Buddhism.

media.caption: Wait. Again (再び待つ)

text.headline: Wait. Again (再び待つ)
text.text: This print is a different state than the print pictured in the artist's catalog raisonné and it may well be a different print entirely, given the differences between the images.

media.caption: Comedy, Fueteiru (喜劇フェーテール Kigeki fueteiru)

text.headline: Comedy, Fueteiru (喜劇フェーテール Kigeki fueteiru)
text.text: Picturing a "shinpageki" or a New School drama in the comedy style of customs and manners in contemporary (Meiji) Japan. The database of the the National Theatre of Japan identifies the actor on the right swinging the battledore and playing the role of Fukutoku Yumesuke (the wealthy merchant Yumesuke) as Yamaguchi Sadao 山口定雄 (1861-1907), one of the first generation of shinpa actors who was trained as a kabuki onnagata. The actor in the center is identified as Shirakawa Koichi 白川広一 playing the role of nyōbō Ofuku (Ofuku, the wife).  Art historian Lynn Katsumoto comments that there is some wordplay going on here as "Fukutoku" also means fortune, or happiness, making "this duo a particularly felicitous couple. No doubt, the play plays with their happy naming and twists things up humorously."

media.caption: Zensetsū Temple, Sanshū (讃州 善通寺 Sanshū Zensetsū-ji)

text.headline: Zensetsū Temple, Sanshū (讃州 善通寺 Sanshū Zensetsū-ji)
text.text:
"The largest temple complex on the island of Shikoku, with its five-story pagoda first built in 813, the site attracts pilgrims to worship at the birthplace of Kūkai (弘法大師, 774-835), founder of Shingon esoteric Buddhism. While the towering structure is veiled in rainy mist, it stands as an unchanging icon to the spiritual foundations of Japan - there is no sign of encroaching modernity." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Like his 19th century predecessor Hiroshige, Hasui was well known for his use of atmospheric effects such as rain and mist.
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Illustration of His Majesty the Commander-in-Chief Return in Triumph to the Palace  (大元帥陛下　凱旋皇居御入城之図 Daigensui-heika gaisen kōkyo go-nyūjō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of His Majesty the Commander-in-Chief Return in Triumph to the Palace  (大元帥陛下　凱旋皇居御入城之図 Daigensui-heika gaisen kōkyo go-nyūjō no zu)
text.text: While the print is titled 大元帥陛下 凱旋皇居御入城之図, which translates to "Illustration of His Majesty the Commander-in-Chief's Triumphal Return to the Palace," the print clearly depicts a visit by Emperor Meiji and the royal family to the reconstructed (the second) Diet Building, likely in 1891. The emperor is seen stepping out of the Phoenix carriage in front of the Diet Building to be greeted by dignitaries, the crown prince (center sheet), and the Empress Shōken (right sheet). While this print does not carry either an artist's signature or seal, or a publisher's seal, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston listing for this print states "possibly by Nobukazu."  One wonders if the publisher, realizing the title and scene portrayed didn't match, decided not to apply either his seal or the artist's signature to this print.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō, Nakamura Sōjūrō and Iwai Hanshirō in the play Gempei Nunobiki no Taki (市川団十郎、中村宗十郎、岩井半四郎・ 源平布引滝)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō, Nakamura Sōjūrō and Iwai Hanshirō in the play Gempei Nunobiki no Taki (市川団十郎、中村宗十郎、岩井半四郎・ 源平布引滝)
text.text:
Gempei Nunobiki no Taki (The Genji and Heike at Nunobiki Waterfall), a five act play, was originally written for the puppet theater in 1749. It was adapted for kabuki in September 1757.
In the play, a woman is believed to have given birth to a full-grown human arm, rather than a baby. And later, when this same arm is rejoined to the woman's body from which it came, the dead woman comes back to life for a while. - source: Kabuki 21 website http://www.kabuki21.com/sanemori.php (Summary written by Watanabe Hisao and edited by Jeff Blair) [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Report of the Japanese Conquest of Port Arthur Startles Li Hung-chang (我軍旅順口占領之報ヲ聞テ李鴻章驚嘆之図 Waga gun Ryojunkō senryō no shirase o kiite Ri Kōshō kyōtan no zu)

text.headline: Report of the Japanese Conquest of Port Arthur Startles Li Hung-chang (我軍旅順口占領之報ヲ聞テ李鴻章驚嘆之図 Waga gun Ryojunkō senryō no shirase o kiite Ri Kōshō kyōtan no zu)
text.text: Within a month after landing at Chinchou, the Japanese Second Army conquered the “unconquerable” Port Arthur. The fortress fell on November 21, 1894, as Japan continued its Liaotung Peninsula operation. This print is an imaginary portrayal of the Chinese leader Li Hung-chang as he hears of the fall of his most important military base in Manchuria.

media.caption: Daimotsu, Amagasaki (尼崎大物 Amagasaki Daimotsu)

text.headline: Daimotsu, Amagasaki (尼崎大物 Amagasaki Daimotsu)
text.text:
"In this moonlit nocturne, Hasui focuses on the reflected light, the movement of water, the surface of the masonry and the wafting smoke from a flame that softly illuminates a workman’s face. The reality of smokestacks and factories appear here as an obscured background. In the decades to come, Amagasaki’s growth as an industrial port demolished locations like this, turning this harbor view into a relic of a bygone era." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, writes: "This is the Daimotsu bay made famous in the Heike monogatari (The Tale of Heike) of the early Kamakura period (1185-1333). These days there are few opportunities for a traveler to experience this area as it once was since it is now part of the harbor district in the Hanshin industrial belt. For this reason Hasui's depiction is interesting." Amagasaki is situated in Hyogo prefecture.
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Ritsuko in the role of Okon (律子 お紺)

text.headline: Ritsuko in the role of Okon (律子 お紺)
text.text:
The actress Mori Ritsuko in the role of the beautiful courtesan Okon in the play Ise Ondo Koi no Netaba 伊勢音頭恋寝刃 performed at the Imperial Theatre (帝国劇場, Teikoku Gekijō), Tokyo on July 1, 1915. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Beauty Combing Her Hair

text.headline: Beauty Combing Her Hair
text.text: One of two known bijin-ga prints designed by Oda for the publisher Ōsaka Mokuhansha. This print shows the influence of his teacher Kitano Tsunetomi (1880-1947) in composition, with the beauty shown in profile with her head bent forward to expose her sensuous neck. Her skin is pale (although somewhat darkened by the effects of age on the print) suggesting the white powder worn by geisha.

text.headline: Drawing based upon sculpture "Laocoon and His Sons" from the book Drawing based on painting style of Shōkokuji Shūbun from the book Drawing based on Western anatomical drawing showing rear facing man and skeleton from the book Kyōsai's Account of Painting, Inner Chapters, Volume 1 (暁斎画談  内篇、巻之上 Kyōsai gadan, naihen, kan no jō)
text.text:
A double-bookplate removed from the first volume of Kawanabe Kyōsai's four volume work Kyōsai Gadan. Kyōsai based this drawing on an image of the Greek marble sculpture Laocoon and His Two Sons (second century B.C. to the first century A.D.) in the Musei Vaticani, Rome, focusing on the anatomical aspects of the sculpture.
Beginning with the fourth illustration [of Kyosai gadan], Kyosai offered his readers a series of anatomy drawings showing the alignment of muscles or the underlying skeletal structure of the human body. According to Josiah Conder, Kyosai regarded with profound respect the scientific knowledge of anatomical form, perspective and sciography revealed to him in foreign works.

text.text:
A double-bookplate removed from the first volume of Kawanabe Kyōsai's four volume work Kyōsai Gadan.
This drawing from Kyōsai gadan is from the "Learning to Paint" section and displays an example of the work of Tenshō Shūbun 天章周文 (1414-1463) as redrawn by Kyōsai. The inscription along the right edge of the right page reads 相国寺ニ住ス僧周文ノ筆意 (painting of Shūbun, a monk who lives in Shokōkuji Temple)
Kyōsai Gadan "reveals how widely Kyōsai studied masterpieces from the past." It includes his copies of works by Song and Yuan dynasty painters, the great Japanese master Sesshu, generations of Kano-school artists such as Motonobu and Tan’yu, Tosa and Maruyama school painters, Ogata Korin and Tani Buncho and ukiyo-e artists such as Suzuki Harunobu, Kitagawa Utamaro and Katsushika Hokusai. - source: Suntory Museum of Art https://www.suntory.com/sma/exhibition/2019_1/display.html [accessed 3-26-2021]

media.caption: Hurrah for the Empire! Illustration of His Majesty, the Commander-in-chief, Welcoming [military officers] to the Imperial Palace with the Emperor’s Gift Cup (帝國萬歳 大元師陛下御歓迎上皇城於御盃賜圖)

text.headline: Hurrah for the Empire! Illustration of His Majesty, the Commander-in-chief, Welcoming [military officers] to the Imperial Palace with the Emperor’s Gift Cup (帝國萬歳 大元師陛下御歓迎上皇城於御盃賜圖)
text.text: The emperor, empress and crown prince are hosting a year-end celebration for the military after Japan's victory in the Sino-Japanese War which ended in April 1895. A similar, if not the same event, as in Nobukazu's print IHL.0160 depicting the emperor and empress at a military celebration. In both, Empress Haruko is in traditional rather than Western dress. The emperor and next to him the crown prince sport their military uniforms.

media.caption: Sawamura Tosshō as Tomiki Saburō, Nakamura Shikan as Hidetarō and Ōtani Tomoemon as Fyjanu Jirō in the play Sangoku Kumiage Tōrō (冨貴三郎 沢村訥升、英太郎 中村芝翫、深見次郎 大谷友右衛門 ・和漢竺爼上灯篭)

text.headline: Sawamura Tosshō as Tomiki Saburō, Nakamura Shikan as Hidetarō and Ōtani Tomoemon as Fyjanu Jirō in the play Sangoku Kumiage Tōrō (冨貴三郎 沢村訥升、英太郎 中村芝翫、深見次郎 大谷友右衛門 ・和漢竺爼上灯篭)
text.text: The three actors (R to L) Sawamura Tosshō II, Nakamura Shikan IV, and Ōtani Tomoemon V are shown dancing in lion wigs and peony (botan) hats in the play Sangoku Kumiage Tōrō at the Morita-za. Nakamura Shikan in the white wig is performing the dance with his two cubs in the red wigs. He brandishes a peony branch in what has been described as a "heaven-earth" pose. Each actor's head is adorned with a peony on top of two open fans.

media.caption: After the Bath (入浴 nyūyoku)

text.headline: After the Bath (入浴 nyūyoku)
text.text:
This print is from a series of 40 scenes documenting life inside the women quarters of the shogun's palace in Edo, prior to the Meiji Restoration in 1868. It shows a young beauty after her bath, wearing a blue and white cotton kimono, a towel on a stand next to her. An attendant offers her a cup of tea, while another turns the handle of a fan to cool her. A faint pattern of hollyhock leaves, symbol of the Tokugawa Shogunate, is printed in the background. As with other prints in this series, this print exists in at least two states.

THE INNER PRECINCTS OF CHIYODA
"Chikanobu imagines something he never saw—the inner precincts of Edo Castle, which housed the shogun’s mother, wife, and concubines. The area was off limits to all men other than the shogun himself or his young male heir."[1] "The Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku) series of 1895-1896, together with his 1897 series Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the Chiyoda Inner Palace set, Chikanobu documented various annual ceremonies in the women’s quarters, especially those at New Year’s, and seasonal activities, particularly those conducted in the palace gardens. While Chikanobu did not indicate specific events or name certain people that would link these images to a single date or time period, the scenes give an overall impression of what the shogun’s private quarters might have looked like in the mid-19th century. "Most women depicted in Chiyoda Inner Palace are portrayed as elegant dignified ideal feminine figures, showing little emotion or excitement. No one seems happy or sad, ebullient or upset. In fact, these imaginary depictions suggest a realm of tranquil harmony, without conflict or illness. Only two old women are shown, and most of the more than 150 featured figures are youthful looking, appearing to be in their 20’s or early 30’s. A few girls are present, but even they are well behaved; no babies or pregnant women are evident. There is a sense of tension among the women, though, as ritual gestures and prescribed ceremonies are carried out with great seriousness. Although some settings are animated by secondary figures (servants, actors, parade participants, etc.) or pet animals, overall the quiet rhythm of life in the Chiyoda Inner Palace is predominant and well described."[2]

[1] Portland Art Museum http://portlandartmuseum.us/mwebcgi/mweb.exe?request=record;id=46772;type=101 [accessed 8-30-23]
[2] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 169.

media.caption: A List of the House of Representatives, illustration of House of Representatives Meeting (帝國議會衆議院議員名鑑, 衆議院會議之図)

text.headline: A List of the House of Representatives, illustration of House of Representatives Meeting (帝國議會衆議院議員名鑑, 衆議院會議之図)
text.text: This print pictures the emperor and empress in bust portraits flanking the interior of the First Temporary Diet Building. The Meiji government published an imperial rescript in 1881 calling for the first session of the Imperial Diet to be convened in 1890. The first House of Representatives election was held on 1 July 1890 (Meiji 23), with 300 seats to be filled. The franchise was limited to males, with only some one percent of the total population eligible to vote.

media.caption: Atagoyama (愛宕山)

text.headline: Atagoyama (愛宕山)
text.text:
This print picturing the NHK Museum of Broadcast in Atagoyama in Tokyo, formerly the Tokyo Broadcasting Station, is one of only two prints by Sekino published by Watanabe Shōzaburō, the seminal publisher of shin hanga. While this print does not bear any Watanabe publishing seals, other impressions bear the publisher's 6mm round seal in the lower left portion of the image.
The museum is known as "the birthplace of Japanese broadcasting" and opened to the public in 1956, just after this print was published.

media.caption: Great Imperial Victory at the Fierce Battle at Pyongyang (平壌激戦 帝国大勝利)

text.headline: Great Imperial Victory at the Fierce Battle at Pyongyang (平壌激戦 帝国大勝利)
text.text:
According to accounts there was fierce fighting at Pyongyang, with the Chinese launching repeated cavalry charges, igniting prearranged blazes, and subjecting the Japanese forces to continuous fires. While the Chinese put up stiff resistance the Japanese "ripped the Chinese army to shreds" and devastated the Chinese morale. - Source: The Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895: Perceptions, Power and Primacy, S. C. M. Paine, Cambridge University Press, 2003, p. 168.
Japanese officers pictured in this print as identified in the rectangular cartouches are, from left to right: Lieutenant Colonel Fukushima 福島 中佐, Major General Oshima 大鳥 少将 and Lieutenant General Nozu (Nodzu) 野津 中将.
The Chinese officer is identified as a Qing Chinese general 清大将, but his name サボキ is unread (possibly General Sei Kinlin, who was captured at this engagement.)
While this picture shows the main protagonists in hand-to-hand combat while on horseback, it is extremely unlikely that this actually occurred. Scenes like this made the fighting easier for the public to visualize and gave them heroes to glorify.

media.caption: Illustration of the Japanese Second Army Fierce Battle at Jinzhou Castle (第二軍金州城大激戦之  Dai ni gun Kinshūjōdaigekisen no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Japanese Second Army Fierce Battle at Jinzhou Castle (第二軍金州城大激戦之  Dai ni gun Kinshūjōdaigekisen no zu)
text.text:
On September 26, 1894, the Japanese imperial headquarters had organized the Second Army. Its objective was to conquer the Chinese dockyard and arsenal of Port Arthur and then to embark on a campaign into the Peking region after winter. On October 24, while the First Army was crossing the Yalu River and entering China, the Second Army landed on on the Liaotung (Chinchou) Peninsula. By November 3, the Second Army advanced toward Chinchou, the major stronghold before Port Arthur. With a full-scale assault on November 6, the Second Army broke the stiff resistance at Chinchou, taking the fortress before noon.
Private First-Class Kubota Chuzo, a twenty-one-year-old farmer, wrote in his war diary: "Today our company had lunch in the southern section of Chinchou. Chinese corpses were piled everywhere. . . . Some enemy soldiers were found among the dead feigning death. Our litter corps found them and slashed or stabbed them to death."

media.caption: Reproduction of: Dutch Beauty with Pekinese from the portfolio Nagasaki Old Prints, Volume 1 (複製：阿蘭陀美人と狆・長崎古版画 第一集 Nagasaki kohanga dai 1 shū)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Dutch Beauty with Pekinese from the portfolio Nagasaki Old Prints, Volume 1 (複製：阿蘭陀美人と狆・長崎古版画 第一集 Nagasaki kohanga dai 1 shū)
text.text:
One of ten prints included in a portfolio of woodblock reproductions of Nagasaki-e 長崎絵, "woodblock prints, paintings, and illustrated woodblock-printed books made in the port of Nagasaki. Often serving as miyage hanga (souvenir prints: 土産版画), nagasaki-e were inexpensive mementos for merchants or scholars who traveled to Nagasaki on business. Moreover, the market for such images was large and profitable, as the Japanese were themselves endlessly curious about foreign visitors whom they were typically forbidden to meet. Nagasaki-e were sold not only in Nagasaki, but also in Edo and Osaka, and no doubt in the provinces." - Source: website of John Fiorillo's Viewing Japanese Prints https://www.viewingjapaneseprints.net/texts/topics_faq/nagasakie.html [accessed 8-25-23]
The prints in the portfolio were done under the auspices of the Nagasaki Shiritsu Hakubutsukan 長崎市立博物館 (Nagasaki Municipal Museum).

media.caption: Girl with Fan from the magazine Han geijutsu, volume 6 (版芸術　第6号)

text.headline: Girl with Fan from the magazine Han geijutsu, volume 6 (版芸術　第6号)
text.text:
This small print of nude girl holding a fan by Ryōji Chōmei (Kumata) (1899-1982) was created for his dōjin (coterie magazine) Han geijutsu (Print Art), Volume 6, published in August 1932 in Tokyo by his publishing company Shiro to Kurosha.
From four to five hundred copies of each volume of Han geijutsu were printed and each issue was priced at 50 sen. The magazine was published from April 1932 until December 1936. The printing for most of the prints was done by placing woodblocks directly in commercial printing presses, but one or more hand-printed works, such as this print, were included in each issue.
Better known as a print publisher than an artist, Ryōji was born in Okayama prefecture with the given name Kumata 熊太 which he used in association with his publishing activities. In the 1930s he published the small art magazines Shiro to kuro (White and Black), Han geijutsu (Print Art), along with others, including three devoted to folk toys. His own work often appeared in these magazines.

media.caption: Illustration of the the Army and Navy Protecting the Legations and Japanese Residents (海陸兵・公使館及ビ日本居留民保護之図 Kairikuhei kōshikan no Nihon kyoryūmin hogo no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the the Army and Navy Protecting the Legations and Japanese Residents (海陸兵・公使館及ビ日本居留民保護之図 Kairikuhei kōshikan no Nihon kyoryūmin hogo no zu)
text.text:
This print depicts the landing of Japanese troops in Incheon on June 10, 1894, prior to the official outbreak of the Sino-Japanese War on July 25th. The Japanese troops, likely parts of the Hiroshima 5th Division, were dispatched, ostensibly to protect the Japanese legation, but, in reality, as part of a troop buildup in Korea by both Japan and China.
By late July (July 23 or July 25, depending upon accounts) the First Sino-Japanese War had started. Over fifty thousand military deaths and tens of thousands of civilian deaths later, the Japanese declared victory in April 1895.
Released in July 1894, this unsigned/unsealed print was one of first of the thousands of senso-e (war prints) to “document” the Sino-Japanese War and to heroically depict the actions of the Japanese forces, to the Japanese public and Western nations.

media.caption: Four Stories, Including the Story of the Shimabara Brothel, No. 7 appearing in the Nishikie Shinbun [Kyoto]  (錦画新聞 [京都]・第七号・ 島原廓の話 など４件)

text.headline: Four Stories, Including the Story of the Shimabara Brothel, No. 7 appearing in the Nishikie Shinbun [Kyoto]  (錦画新聞 [京都]・第七号・ 島原廓の話 など４件)
text.text: This print depicting actors being arrested in a gambling den at the Shimomura brothel, was published in Kyoto long after the news nishikie boom had come and gone in 1874-1876. The cartouche reads "Nishikie shinbun" / "No. 7" / "Meiji 14-4-21" [21 April 1881].

media.caption: Police Confront Man in Black Makeup from the News Illustrated (新聞圖會 Shinbun zue)

text.headline: Police Confront Man in Black Makeup from the News Illustrated (新聞圖會 Shinbun zue)
text.text:
This news nishiki-e relates an amusing case of mistaken identity as explained in the below translation.
Translation of text on print: "A patrolman was doing his rounds at midnight in Takatsu-chō 5, 12th small ward, 2nd large ward. He saw a house whose door had been left open, so he stopped to have a look, thinking a thief might have sneaked in. Then he heard a voice, like a tiger or a wolf snoring, so he went inside. Something with a pitch black face and glittering eyes tried to grab him. Its breath was so foul that the patrolman could hardly face it. He cried out, 'Are you a fox or a tanuki? Do you not recognize a policeman?' But the black faced creature itself shouted, 'You’re a thief pretending to be a policeman.' The angry voice was using speech, so the patrolman brought his corporal to investigate. The corporal was just as astonished at the black faced creature, but when he looked closely he saw it was the master of the house. Puzzled, he asked why the man’s face was black. At last the man remembered and apologized for his rudeness. 'Last night I was invited to a drinking party at my neighbor’s house. Under the influence we painted our faces black and began playing rock-paper-scissors. I simply could not beat my opponent, and in the end my face was completely covered with soot. I came home like that, but I remember nothing more. I must have gone to sleep with the door open. All of this happened because I drank so much,' he said. The matter was let go with an apology, according to the Ōsaka News. Oh, how important it is to drink only in moderation! Self control is the key!" - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literature, University of Oregon

media.caption: The Tori-no-machi Festival at Senzoku (千束酉の町大きな唐の芋頭をかつぐ Senzoku torinomachi ōkina tōno imo gashira o katsugu)

text.headline: The Tori-no-machi Festival at Senzoku (千束酉の町大きな唐の芋頭をかつぐ Senzoku torinomachi ōkina tōno imo gashira o katsugu)
text.text: One of forty prints from the series Crazy Pictures of Famous Places in Tōkyō (Tōkyō kaika kyōga meishō) picturing "Tori no machi" (Bird Day) festivities in the Senzuko area of Tokyo, where one gives thanks for a safe year and prays for happiness in the next. The reveler in the back is holding a lucky kumade (bamboo rake) which is believed to rake in good luck.

media.caption: Woman from Ohara (大原女 Oharame)

text.headline: Woman from Ohara (大原女 Oharame)
text.text:
An "Oharame" (a woman from the town of Ohara) is seen resting. Oharame is a kind of hisame (a woman peddler) often pictured carrying firewood, charcoal or baskets of flowers bound for sale in Kyoto. Today, the Oharame is gone. However, the Ohara Tourist Information Center (Ohara Kanko Hoshokai), offers an "Oharame experience" where one can don traditional dress for a small fee. The following mid-20th century description would have been roughly contemporary with this print's publication.
"[Oharame] carry heavy loads on their heads and they have a very fine bearing. Their dress also is peculiar, as they wear narrow obi (sashes), and cover their heads with kerchiefs while over their legs and arms they wear white cotton-cloth. Parties of these naive peasant-women may frequently be seen in the streets of Kyoto, selling flowers or carrying heavy merchandise." - Source: Japan The Official Guide, Tourist Industry Bureau Ministry of Transportation (ed.), Japan Travel Bureau, 9th edition, 1962, p. 712.
This print has been attributed to both Kotozuka Eiichi (1906-1979) and his contemporary Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000), as various impressions bear different markings that can be attributed to one or the other artist. This print bears a round seal in the bottom right corner of the image that may be some variation of Kotozuka's self-printed seal "Toku kako za" and also carries the notation "PRINT T. Tokuriki", which could indicate either that he created the design or that he just did the printing with Kotozuka being responsible for the design. The two artists worked closely together, establishing the joint publishing company Koryokusha, along with the artists Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977) and Takahashi Tasaburō (1904-1977), in 1948.

media.caption: A Bunraku Puppet Head

text.headline: A Bunraku Puppet Head
text.text:
This collection contains two different printings of this depiction of the head of a bunraku puppet, IHL.0275 and IHL.0314. These two versions may both be artist's proofs. This print, IHL.0314, carries the notation written in pencil "(2.) T. Tokuriki 1962.6.8" in the lower right corner within the image. Print IHL.0275 bears the artist's signature in the lower left corner within the image.
This print was released as a numbered edition of 100 prints.

media.caption: Bunraku Puppet Head

text.headline: Bunraku Puppet Head
text.text: This print of a puppeteer's hand holding a bunraku puppet head (likely a "shako mage" used for knowing, vivacious women of middle age) is from a numbered edition of 200 prints issued by Kōrokusha 紅録社, the publishing house jointly created by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), Tokuriki Tomikichiro (1902-2000) and Kotozuka Eiichi (1906-1979).  At least two other numbered edition of this print exists, attesting to the print's popularity.

media.caption: Ichikawa Gonjūrō, Bandō Shūchō, Ichikawa Kuzō, Kataoka Gadō and Takasagoya Fukusukei in the play A Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani (市川権十郎、坂東秀調、市川九蔵、市川九蔵、熊谷陣屋、高砂屋福助・一谷嫩軍記)

text.headline: Ichikawa Gonjūrō, Bandō Shūchō, Ichikawa Kuzō, Kataoka Gadō and Takasagoya Fukusukei in the play A Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani (市川権十郎、坂東秀調、市川九蔵、市川九蔵、熊谷陣屋、高砂屋福助・一谷嫩軍記)
text.text: Picturing the "Kumagai Jin'ya" scene, the last scene in the play Ichinotani Futaba Gunki, a dramatization of the Heike Monogatari tale of the battle of Ichinotani. Pictured are the actors (right to left): Ichikawa Gonjūrō as Yoshitsune, Bandō Shūchō II as Fuji no Kata, Ichikawa Kuzō III as Kumagai Jiro Naozane, Kataoka Gadō as Midaroku and Takasagoya Fukusuke III as Sagami.

media.caption: My Town (わが街)

text.headline: My Town (わが街)
text.text: "Though the elements in Takahashi's prints seem to float in an untamed cosmos, or are simply reduced to a square or an oblong in perfect equilibrium, they fall unmistakably into place, arranged as precisely as the utensils for a formal tea ceremony. The space is so ideally formulated that no furnishings are necessary; its architecture eliminates everything but that which is aesthetically and structurally indispensable. The space itself is a product of light and shadow displayed in an 'unbalanced' tension. The search for such 'unbalanced' forms has almost become an obsession, but it is nevertheless a positive aesthetic expression. In such traditional Japanese arts as flower arranging or calligraphy, particularly in the informal styles associated with them, the consummate grace and elegance which can be achieved through the asymmetrical organization of forms in space is especially sought after. Takahashi's forms possess a freedom in space, yet are nonobstructive in their simplicity and color.  The austere sublimity of his works in the quintessence of his masterly use of asymmetry." - source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973, p. 148-149.

media.caption: Flying Angel No. 3 (天使昇天 No. 3)

text.headline: Flying Angel No. 3 (天使昇天 No. 3)
text.text: Between 1968 and 1972, Hagiwara used a brighter color palette, and the resulting prints have a new lightness. He abandoned two-sided printing which, while providing great depth to his images, kept his colors rather somber. This print, with its vivid orange highlighted with mica and playful floating forms, is a fine example of this change. To produce the etching-like lines, the artist used sharpened nails to mark the woodblock and inking techniques similar to those used in intaglio printmaking, one of many innovative woodblock techniques for which Hagiwara is famous.

media.caption: Japanese Troops Attack the Chinese Cavalry in the Vicinity of Hushan (虎山附近騎兵ヲ攻撃ス Kozan fukin kihei o kōgekisu)

text.headline: Japanese Troops Attack the Chinese Cavalry in the Vicinity of Hushan (虎山附近騎兵ヲ攻撃ス Kozan fukin kihei o kōgekisu)
text.text:
"Once the Japanese forces invaded Chinese territory, they engaged in a full-scale attack on Hushan. A severe battle began at dawn on October 25. The Japanese suffered one hundred twenty casualties, but the Chinese losses were countless. The print shows Chinese troops dropping into the swirling river as they are fired upon from both banks. It is said that corpses of Chinese soldiers and horses blocked the river. Hushan was taken by 10:30 AM, and the Chinese defense was forced further back in Manchuria to Kuliencheng. This print was issued on October 26." - Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 29.
The print in the collection of the Philadelphia Museum of Art has a preface reading 十月廿六日号外 ("October 26 extra") appearing at the top of the title cartouche, which is not present on this collection's print. To put this in context, prints of battle scenes were often issued before the actual battle took place. Upcoming battles could be gathered from news reports and other sources. Since the depiction of battle scenes was somewhat formulaic, the artist didn't need to be too concerned about depicting what actually would occur. It is likely that this collection's print without the "extra" notation was issued before the actual battle and that when the battle actually occurred on October 25th, the publisher added the "extra" notation to make it seem that the print was a true depiction of what occurred. Likely an effective advertising ploy.

media.caption: View of Nihonbashi Bridge in the Eastern Capital (東都日本橋之勝景 Tōto Nihonbashi no shōkei)

text.headline: View of Nihonbashi Bridge in the Eastern Capital (東都日本橋之勝景 Tōto Nihonbashi no shōkei)
text.text:
One of at least three triptychs designed by Sadahide depicting daimyo processions. The depiction of the cranes in this print may be reference to the procession of Lord Minamoto Yoritomo, the 12th-century military leader, who is said to have courted Buddhist favor by releasing wild cranes. Mt. Fuji rises in the background and whitewashed warehouses line the banks of the Sumida. The procession is crossing Nihonbashi and Edobashi is seen in the background.
"The Tokugawa shoguns, who in effect ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867, introduced a system whereby all daimyo were required to spend alternate years at Edo (modern-day Tokyo) in attendance on the shogun. This was known in Japanese as ‘sankin kotai’. This system maintained control over the regional daimyo, who were the appointed feudal rulers of Japan. In the Edo period they were either members of the Tokugawa family or had pledged direct allegiance to the Tokugawa shogun. The daimyo was required to maintain residential estates in Edo as well as in their regional domains. A daimyo generally travelled to the capital every other year and returned to his province after a year's service. He travelled with a retinue of 150 to 300 or more. The journeys and the upkeep of a daimyo's Edo and country estates consumed about 70 to 80 percent of his income." Source: website of Victoria and Albert Museum https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O92993/the-procession-of-the-lord-woodblock-print-utagawa-sadahide/#:~:text=The%20Tokugawa%20shoguns%2C%20who%20in,Japanese%20as%20'sankin%20kotai'. [accessed 8-27-23]

media.caption: Abstract monochrome design (untitled)

text.headline: Abstract monochrome design (untitled)
text.text: One of a number of small abstract monochrome woodblocks created by Hacker, possible done while he was stationed with the Occupation forces in Japan.

media.caption: A Lady in Waiting Hands the Noh Mask to an Actor (御能楽屋)

text.headline: A Lady in Waiting Hands the Noh Mask to an Actor (御能楽屋)
text.text:
This print is from a series of 40 scenes, published 1895-1896, documenting life inside the women quarters of the shogun's palace in Edo, prior to the Meiji Restoration in 1868. A lady in waiting hands a noh mask to an actor in the Chiyoda Palace before a performance.[1] Extensive use is made of burnishing (shomen zuri [front printing]) which leaves a reflective-polished finish on the black areas and embossing which is seen in the white areas of the lady's robes.

THE INNER PRECINCTS OF CHIYODA
"Chikanobu imagines something he never saw—the inner precincts of Edo Castle, which housed the shogun’s mother, wife, and concubines. The area was off limits to all men other than the shogun himself or his young male heir."[2] "The Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku) series of 1895-1896, together with his 1897 series Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the Chiyoda Inner Palace set, Chikanobu documented various annual ceremonies in the women’s quarters, especially those at New Year’s, and seasonal activities, particularly those conducted in the palace gardens. While Chikanobu did not indicate specific events or name certain people that would link these images to a single date or time period, the scenes give an overall impression of what the shogun’s private quarters might have looked like in the mid-19th century. "Most women depicted in Chiyoda Inner Palace are portrayed as elegant dignified ideal feminine figures, showing little emotion or excitement. No one seems happy or sad, ebullient or upset. In fact, these imaginary depictions suggest a realm of tranquil harmony, without conflict or illness. Only two old women are shown, and most of the more than 150 featured figures are youthful looking, appearing to be in their 20’s or early 30’s. A few girls are present, but even they are well behaved; no babies or pregnant women are evident. There is a sense of tension among the women, though, as ritual gestures and prescribed ceremonies are carried out with great seriousness. Although some settings are animated by secondary figures (servants, actors, parade participants, etc.) or pet animals, overall the quiet rhythm of life in the Chiyoda Inner Palace is predominant and well described."[3]

[1] The play to be performed has been identified as both Chikubushima (The God of The Island of Chikubu) and Kasuga ryujin (The Kasuma Dragon God). Both plays, I believe, use the red wig and dragon helmet.
[2] Portland Art Museum http://portlandartmuseum.us/mwebcgi/mweb.exe?request=record;id=46772;type=101 [accessed 8-30-23]
[3] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 169.

media.caption: Polishing-sand of Iga Province (伊賀国 磨砂 Iga kuni migakizuna)

text.headline: Polishing-sand of Iga Province (伊賀国 磨砂 Iga kuni migakizuna)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, workers are mining a white sand that will be be used in tooth powder, for polishing rice to make uruchi, and other applications using polishing sand. Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi, Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1488.

media.caption: Coal Mine in Iga Province (同国 [伊賀国] 石炭山之図 dōkoku sekitan yama no zu)

text.headline: Coal Mine in Iga Province (同国 [伊賀国] 石炭山之図 dōkoku sekitan yama no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting coal miners entering a mine with pickaxes (tsuruhashi) in hand and exiting the mine carrying yoked baskets (sena) of coal, this color woodblock print (nishiki-e) was one of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. As the series’ name implies, each print depicted an economic activity in a province or district of Japan. In addition, each activity was described on the print in a scroll-like cartouche.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1486. Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi,Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces. The Saruka mountains which bordered Iga were noted for their coal reserves. An 1878-1879 geological survey describes Iga coal as being "black and shining." The print's scroll mentions that the coal produced is like the color of lacquer.

media.caption: Producing Vitriol in Hyūga Province (日向緑礬製之図)

text.headline: Producing Vitriol in Hyūga Province (日向緑礬製之図)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The following description is provided in an 1878-1879 geological survey which discusses the author's tour of copper mines throughout Japan.  ".. [B]lister copper  is made with roasting in kilns and smelting in small hearths in the old Japanese style; and blue vitriol (copper sulfate) is manufactured with roasting, leaching, boiling down and crystallizing."

media.caption: Burdock Harvest in Iyo Province (伊予国牛蒡堀之図)

text.headline: Burdock Harvest in Iyo Province (伊予国牛蒡堀之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
Harvesting "Gobou" (burdock root) in Iyo (Ehime prefecture), some of which grow to about 120cm in length. It has a thin, brown root with a distinct, earthy flavor. It is used in medicine in China, but in Japan it is treated as a vegetable, and is generally cut into thin strips or shavings and soaked in vinegar to remove bitterness before cooking. It is an excellent source of dietary fiber and nutrients, and therefore aids digestion and detoxification.
For another impression of this print see IHL.0362a.

media.caption: Burdock Harvest in Iyo Province (伊予国牛蒡堀之図)

text.headline: Burdock Harvest in Iyo Province (伊予国牛蒡堀之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
Harvesting "Gobou" (burdock root) in Iyo (Ehime prefecture), some of which grow to about 120cm in length. It has a thin, brown root with a distinct, earthy flavor. It is used in medicine in China, but in Japan it is treated as a vegetable, and is generally cut into thin strips or shavings and soaked in vinegar to remove bitterness before cooking. It is an excellent source of dietary fiber and nutrients, and therefore aids digestion and detoxification.
