media.caption: Sake Shortens Life (酒で命をけづる Sake de inochi o kezuru)

text.headline: Sake Shortens Life (酒で命をけづる Sake de inochi o kezuru)
text.text: This print is the top half of number 10 in this series consisting of ten paired prints originally printed on ten oban size sheets. It tells us that alcohol consumption shortens life.

media.caption: Inner Valley at Tsukigase (月ヶ瀬奥の谷 Tsukigase Okunotani)

text.headline: Inner Valley at Tsukigase (月ヶ瀬奥の谷 Tsukigase Okunotani)
text.text:
Number 19 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
"This print depicts one of the most remote places featured in the series and a location that Kiyochika may have been unable to visit in person.
"This location is a secluded mountain valley whose fame for scenic beauty was relatively recent. . . . The plum trees at Tsukigase were made famous in Travels in Plum Valley (Baikei yuki) of 1830 by the Confucian scholar Saito Setsudo.
"The vast plum orchard that Kiyochika shows in Inner Valley at Tsukigase is located along both banks of the Naban River, the name for the Kizu River in its upper reaches in the mountains of the Kii Peninsula. Tsukigase (known locally as Tsukinose) is about ten miles due east of Nara along a stretch of the river running from east to west. Some ten thousand plum trees line both sides of the V-shaped valley for over two miles. The trees were planted in the precincts of a nearby temple in the late thirteenth century, and later propagated in great numbers as the source of a dye extracted from the plum fruits.
"The sight of the thousands of plum trees blooming in February and March is spectacular, and the white blossoms fill the valley with a heady fragrance, noted in the haiku concluding the text:
Spring in Tsukigase:
Bush warblers
Drunk with fragrance.

"Kiyochika’s print is remarkable for the coloring-or rather the absence of it. It is rendered almost completely in black sumi ink, which serves to heighten the sense of the whiteness of the blossoms; only the rushing waters of the Nabari River are shown in color, as streaks of subtle blue." Source: Kiyochika Artist of Meiji Japan, Henry D. Smith II, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, 1988, p. 108-109.
See IHL.1843 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Red Horizon A (赤い地平線 A)

text.headline: Red Horizon A (赤い地平線 A)
text.text: Gaston Petit, artist, critic and promoter of the post-war Japanese modern print movement, describes Kusaka's "point of no return" in his work, "By 1971 he reached the point of no return. With the perfect placement of the egg form, all other known references have disappeared. Of importance is the spatial tension which has a totally new reading. We cannot live and breathe in that space as we did in his former works.  Curved lines float at the horizon, suffused with lyricism."  - Source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973, p. 202-203.

media.caption: Illustration of Mitsui Group's Western-style Three Story House at Surugachō, Tokyo (東京駿河町三井組 三階家西洋形之圖  東京名所之内駿河町之圖 )

text.headline: Illustration of Mitsui Group's Western-style Three Story House at Surugachō, Tokyo (東京駿河町三井組 三階家西洋形之圖  東京名所之内駿河町之圖 )
text.text: The Mitsui Exchange Bank, with its bronze dolphin on top, was a popular building depicted in a number of woodblock prints. This print published in December of 1873, prior to the cited 1874 completion date of the building, shows the building with Mt. Fuji to its left and the First National Bank 第一銀行, with its distinctive Western-style towers, completed in 1872, in the background to its right.

media.caption: Night Trip (夜の旅)

text.headline: Night Trip (夜の旅)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally made for the 1923 cover of the musical score for Anton Rubinstein's "Wanderer's Night Song," published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha. Night Trip is a most "Munch-looking" work. Is the small figure walking down the path the wife of the elderly gentleman? Is it her "night trip" or will the old gentleman be heading off on his own trip? He looks so tired and forlorn.
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."- Source: Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: Cove of Oranges

text.headline: Cove of Oranges
text.text:
Cove of Oranges was originally created by Yumeji as an illustration for the December 1912 issue of the magazine Jogaku sekai (World of Women’s Lessons).[1] In 1963, the publisher Katō Junji issued a woodblock reproduction of the original design as part of an eight print portfolio of small woodblocks with one waka poem by Yumeji and a commentary by the publisher, titled "Yumeji Collection of Small Works, Legends of Snowy Nights, First Story."
"Cove of Oranges features the type of modern Taishō-era (1912-1926) romantic woman for which Yumeji was known: willowy with pensive large eyes suggestive of the women he had loved."[1] It "depicts a rather pensive, lithe young woman in a lighthearted, colorful style. Sitting on a grassy knoll near a water inlet with cute orange trees and what looks like a sailboat, European-style white houses, and a rising steeple in the background, the young woman looks both relaxed and uncomfortable in her kimono at the same time. The figure and setting give just enough information to capture a moment and create a mystery. Who is she? Where is she? What is she thinking? The illustrative, almost cartoonish quality of the composition combined with the small dimensions of the woodblock print creates a storybook intimacy and fantasy. Here is a charming, youthful woman dressed in traditional Japanese clothing, caught in a graceful pose outdoors as though she were sketched plein air in France. She seems to offer the perfect blend of whimsical naivete and romantic melancholy, and becomes an apt symbol for a 'modern' Taishō-era woman caught between Japanese traditions and European Jugendstil (or Art Nouveau) flair. Even the woodblock print itself seems to offer a hybrid nuance resonating as it does in technique with the ukiyo-e tradition while at the same time featuring playful, hatch-mark texturing strokes more akin to an engraving."[3]
For other prints in this portfolio see IHL.0357 and IHL.0358.

[1] Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 30.
[2] Revisiting Modern Japanese Prints: Selected Works from the Richard F. Grott Family Collection, Helen M. Nagata, Helen Merritt, Northern Illinois University Art Museum, 2007, p. 15.
[3] Ibid., p. 52.

media.caption:
Negishi Annex of the New Yoshiwara Ōguchi Brothel a scene from the play,  
A Triptych of Ueno Scenery (三幅対上野風景｜新吉原大口楼 根岸別荘の場)

text.headline:
Negishi Annex of the New Yoshiwara Ōguchi Brothel a scene from the play,  
A Triptych of Ueno Scenery (三幅対上野風景｜新吉原大口楼 根岸別荘の場)
text.text:
Starring Onoe Kikugorō V (R), Sawamura Gennosuke IV (C) and Onoe Kikusaburō V (L).
This production was a retelling of a popular 1881 kabuki play, Lost in the Clouds, the First Flowers of Ueno (天衣紛上野初花) about thieves, gamblers and a singular Yoshiwara prostitute. Starring three of the most celebrated actors of the day, Kunichika’s triptych depicts the fugitive samurai Kataoka Naojirō (right) as he bids farewell to his love, the courtesan Michitose (center). Kataoka is about to extract a letter tucked inside his kimono, explaining his long absence, while Michitose’s worry and longing are subtly represented by the strand of hair straying from her chignon. Michitose’s attendant (left) moves the story forward, alerting the couple that Kataoka must flee at once, as the police are on his trail. The background reveals allusions to winter: snow on bamboo leaves outside the window and seasonal decor in the alcove behind the lovers. - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

media.caption: Iris at Horikiri (堀切花菖蒲 Horikiri hanashobu)

text.headline: Iris at Horikiri (堀切花菖蒲 Horikiri hanashobu)
text.text:
This print depicting the Iris Garden at Horikiri, located in Katsushika-ku, Tokyo, appears to have been lacquered, displaying a yellowish discoloration and having a slick feel to it. Urushiye is the process whereby a clear lacquer is applied to a print to heighten the color-effect. The lacquer yellows over the years as it has on this print.
This print is from a loosely constructed series Famous Views of Tokyo (Tokyo meisho) consisting of 93 prints issued from 1876-1881 by two publishers, Matsuki Heikichi and Fukuda Kumajirō.

media.caption: Portrait of a kabuki actor (untitled)

text.headline: Portrait of a kabuki actor (untitled)
text.text:
This small untitled print of a kabuki actor, with a horizontal tri-fold to allow insertion into a magazine, by the Kyoto nihonga (Japanese style) artist Yoshikawa Kanpō (1894-1979) bears an untypical appearing signature for the artist. The style of the print is reminiscent of those that appeared in the short-lived 1915 magazine Shin Nigao and, confusingly, this collection's print is mounted on a page from the magazine Shin Nigao bearing the title 仁左衛門 (八郎兵衛）松田青風 (Nizaemon (Hachirōbei) Matsuda Seifū), but this print is not by Matsuda Seifū (1902-1983), nor did it appear in any of the five issues of Shin Nigao. It is possible that the actor Yoshikawa is depicting is Nakamura Ganjirō I (1860-1935), the standout actor of his day in the Kyoto theater and a subject who Yoshikawa would portray in other woodblock prints.
Merritt notes in her brief biography of the artist that he "made small hanga portraits of actors ca. 1916 to stimulate revival of hanga in Kansai."[1] This print seems to be consistent with Merritt's comment.
In addition to his painting, Yoshikawa was a print designer, a stage designer and writer. It is believed that Yoshikawa did not produce woodblock prints after 1925.[2]

[1] Guide to Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt and Nanako Yamada, University of Hawai'i Press, 1992, p. 178.
[2] Toledo Museum of Art http://emuseum.toledomuseum.org/objects/49755 [accessed 8-30-23]

media.caption: Little Pond (小さな池 Chiisa na ike)

text.headline: Little Pond (小さな池 Chiisa na ike)
text.text: Hagiwara has flattened space in depicting a partially frozen pond in winter.

media.caption: Illustration of the Genzan Soldiers Marching on Pyongyang and the Fierce Battle Between the Japanese and Chinese Troops (牙山追撃日清両軍成歓大激戦之図 Gazan tsuigeki Nisshin ryōgun Seikan daigekisen no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Genzan Soldiers Marching on Pyongyang and the Fierce Battle Between the Japanese and Chinese Troops (牙山追撃日清両軍成歓大激戦之図 Gazan tsuigeki Nisshin ryōgun Seikan daigekisen no zu)
text.text: On August 8, a battalion of infantry of the 12th Regiment (10th Brigade) had reached the port of Genzan, with a company of artillery, destination: Seoul. But having communicated with Lieutenant-General Nozu, announcing their coming, they were sent back to Sak-riong to reinforce the Battalion of the Mixed Brigade stationed there. From that moment, this united force became known as the Sak-riong Detachment, consisting of two battalions of infantry and one company of artillery.  It formed the right flank during the attack on Pyong-Yang.

media.caption: Japanese Forces Conquer Kiuliencheng (大日本大勝利九連城没落之図 Dai Nihon daishōri Kyūrenjō botsuraku no zu)

text.headline: Japanese Forces Conquer Kiuliencheng (大日本大勝利九連城没落之図 Dai Nihon daishōri Kyūrenjō botsuraku no zu)
text.text: The artist portrays a fictional battle for Kiuliencheng (Jiuliancheng) in Manchuria which was taken without opposition by the Japanese in late October 1894. While the Japanese had prepared for a fierce battle to take the Kiuliencheng citadel, the Chinese forces had withdrawn and the fortress was conquered virtually without fighting. For a second copy of this print see IHL.1358.

media.caption: Illustration of [Emperor at] National Diet Building (国会議事堂之図 Kokkai gijidōno zu)

text.headline: Illustration of [Emperor at] National Diet Building (国会議事堂之図 Kokkai gijidōno zu)
text.text: This print was issued on March 10, 1890, ten months before the opening of the First Imperial Diet Building on November 24, 1890. The artist has rendered an event, the visit of Emperor Meiji, that would not occur until later that year. He has depicted at least part of the diet building as red brick. In fact, the final design, hastily conceived as a "temporary" home for the Diet, was clad in gray-painted German clapboards and not in brick. For a more accurate depiction of the First Diet Building see the print "Illustration of the [Emperor at the] National Diet Building" (IHL.1174) by Watanabe Nobukazu (c.1872-1944) which does show the exterior clad in grey clapboard.

media.caption: Famous Places of Tokyo, Shimbashi Station (東京名所新橋ステンション Tokyo meisho Shimbashi stenshon)

text.headline: Famous Places of Tokyo, Shimbashi Station (東京名所新橋ステンション Tokyo meisho Shimbashi stenshon)
text.text:
The artist designed at least nine prints commemorating the opening of the rail line from Tokyo to Yokohama in 1872. The nine prints show either Tokyo's Shimbashi Station 新橋駅 or Yokohama Station 横浜駅 with a steam train either arriving, departing or parked. This print is from one of many different print series created by the artist titled Tokyo meisho (Famous Places of Tokyo.)
This particular Tokyo meisho series is distinguished by its Western-style red and yellow frame, an artistic device for highlighting the modernity of the subject.

media.caption: Spring (春 haru)

text.headline: Spring (春 haru)
text.text: One of a number of prints created by the artist using organic overlaid forms and colors. Particularly in his abstract woodblock prints, Shinagawa explored color attempting to achieve in his words "a living, glowing color deep in the paper, to become part of the paper.  Often the pigments should be mixed in the paper by applying one over another . . . ." - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn, Oliver Statler, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1956, p. 72.

media.caption: Benkei Bridge (弁慶橋 Benkeibashi)

text.headline: Benkei Bridge (弁慶橋 Benkeibashi)
text.text:
This was one of the seven new designs for the series Scenes of Last Tokyo (Tokyo kaiko zue).
"Sekinō had not yet moved to Tokyo when Scenes of Last [sic] Tokyo (Tokyo kaiko zue) was published, but he became involved in the postwar project after having become a member of Onchi's circle in 1939. His subject in this print is Benkei Bridge, which crosses the outer moat of Edo Castle on the north side. Named for a legendary monk-warrior of the twelfth century, it still stands today." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 300.
Benkeibashi spanned a palace moat, connecting the palace grounds to the west approach at Akasaka Mitsuke. Sadly, as with Nihonbashi, an elevated expressway (Shuto Expressway built for the 1964 Olympic Games), now almost completely obscures from aerial view the current Benkeibashi.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Reading (漢字の)

text.headline: Reading (漢字の)
text.text:
One of at least 30 prints making up the series Edo Brocades showing a young woman reading, likely a Chinese classic, while her teacher looks on. The prints from this series were bound into albums and this print retains its album backing sheet. A heavy application of silver mica was used on the shelving holding the manuscripts.
"Edo Brocades does not have any particular historical references, but presents vignettes of Edo residents (Edokko) pursuing traditional pleasures. . . . The linework in these prints is extremely fine, especially around the faces of the delicately drawn figures, although the body proportions still follow Chikanobu's 'canon of beauty.'" - Source: Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 61, 201.

media.caption: Congratulations and Long Life [Prince Yoshihito and Princess Sadako] (千代之故登富貴)

text.headline: Congratulations and Long Life [Prince Yoshihito and Princess Sadako] (千代之故登富貴)
text.text: This print depicts the 20-year-old Prince Yoshihito (the future Emperor Taishō) and 15-year-old Princess Sadako Kujō before their official marriage held on May 10, 1900. They are surrounded by auspicious symbols of good luck and longevity.

media.caption: Spring in a Mountain Village, The Time of Cherry Blossoms (山里の春―桜の頃)

text.headline: Spring in a Mountain Village, The Time of Cherry Blossoms (山里の春―桜の頃)
text.text:
This print was issued in 1963 by the publisher Katō Junji as part of the portfolio "Yumeji Collection of Small Works, Legends of Snowy Nights, First Story," consisting of eight small Yumeji woodblock prints, plus a waka poem by Yumeji. It is likely that this design was originally created during the early Taishō period as an illustration for a magazine or book.
See IHL.0344 and IHL.0358 for two other prints in this portfolio

media.caption: Serenade (セレナード)

text.headline: Serenade (セレナード)
text.text:
This print picturing a man playing a koto as a woman, arms folded, head down, stands on her balcony listening, was issued in 1963 by the publisher Katō Junji as part of the portfolio "Yumeji Collection of Small Works, Legends of Snowy Nights, First Story," consisting of eight small Yumeji woodblock prints, plus a waka poem by Yumeji. It is likely that this design was originally created during the early Taishō period as an illustration for a magazine or book.
See IHL.0344 and IHL.0357 for other prints in this portfolio.

media.caption: Yahagi Bridge at Midnight with Wild Geese Descending (矢矧橋夜半落雁)

text.headline: Yahagi Bridge at Midnight with Wild Geese Descending (矢矧橋夜半落雁)
text.text:
Ushiwakamaru (御曹子牛若丸 Onzōshi Ushiwakamaru, as written in the red cartouche to his right), the young Minamoto Yoshitsune (1159-1189), sits with a bowl demanding money to allow a group of peculiar looking bandits, led by Ise Saburo Yoshimori 伊勢三郎義盛, to pass. Ushiwaka holds the bottom of Yoshimori's Japanese long lance with his feet. Yoshimori was later to become a close personal adviser to Yoshitsune. Yoshitsune was known for having a number of followers of "low social standing" and the members of his army have been described as "guerrillas."
The website of Touken World Foundation (Token Corporation) in discussing this print states tells us that this scene is drawn from the "Taikōki," a biography of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and that this print "is not a pure depiction of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, but a 'hanji-e' (puzzle-solving picture) that includes other meanings." - Source: https://www.touken-world-ukiyo-e.jp/mushae/art0011240/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Bandō Kakitsu as Hachiman Tarō Yoshiie, Nakamura Sōjūrō as Sodehagi,  Nakamura Sōjūrō as  Abe no Sadatō, and Kawarazaki Sanshō as Abe no Munetō in the third scene of the play Ōshū Adachi-ga-Hara (八幡太郎 よし家  坂東家橘、袖萩  中村宗十郎、安倍貞任  中村宗十郎、安倍宗任  河原崎権之助・ 奥州安達原三段目)

text.headline: Bandō Kakitsu as Hachiman Tarō Yoshiie, Nakamura Sōjūrō as Sodehagi,  Nakamura Sōjūrō as  Abe no Sadatō, and Kawarazaki Sanshō as Abe no Munetō in the third scene of the play Ōshū Adachi-ga-Hara (八幡太郎 よし家  坂東家橘、袖萩  中村宗十郎、安倍貞任  中村宗十郎、安倍宗任  河原崎権之助・ 奥州安達原三段目)
text.text:
Pictured is the final scene, titled "Sodehagi Saimon", of the third act (sandanme) of the kabuki drama Ōshū Adachi-ga-Hara, which was staged in September 1873 at the Murayamaza in Tokyo.
"Abe Sadato, at center, has suddenly thrown off his disguise and revealed his true nature: his wild and disheveled character is conveyed by a wig with hair standing permanently on end. In this famous scene, Sadato is reunited with his wife Sodehagi and his brother Muneto (who is shown on the left), the only remaining members of a family that had been almost completely wiped out nine years previously. The culprit, Yoshiie, whom they have vowed to kill, is shown on the right." - Source: Walters Art Museum https://art.thewalters.org/detail/3240/adachigahara-sandanme-5/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Ichikawa Sadanji as Marubashi Chūya (丸橋忠弥  市川左團次)

text.headline: Ichikawa Sadanji as Marubashi Chūya (丸橋忠弥  市川左團次)
text.text: The actor Ichikawa Sadanji I in one of his most famous roles, that of Marubashi Chūya 丸橋忠弥 in Kawatake Shinshichi II's drama Keian Taiheiki 慶安太平記 about the Keian Uprising in 1651 which attempted to overthrow the Tokugawa Shogunate, which premiered in March 1870 at the Morita-za.

media.caption: Producing Soy Sauce and Watermelon Field in Shimōsa Province (下総国醤油製造之図・同西瓜畑之図)

text.headline: Producing Soy Sauce and Watermelon Field in Shimōsa Province (下総国醤油製造之図・同西瓜畑之図)
text.text:
Two of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
It is unusual to see an ōban-size uncut sheet on which both prints representing a single province were printed. Most of the uncut sheets would have been cut into two chuban-size sheets and most of the chuban-size sheets would eventually be bound into albums or portfolios. The cartouche for the Watermelon Field read: “Watermelons are creepers in the field, particularly rich in Katsushika and Chiba, and the fruit is like a big white gourd, but outside of this is dark green and inside is red, while some are white outside and yellow inside. They are sweet and cool down fever.” Shimōsa is still famous for producing soy sauce and for watermelon. Kikkoman, among others, continues to produce soy sauce in that area.

media.caption: Mackerel Fishing at Night in Noto Province (同 [能登] 國鯖釣之圖 dō koku [Noto] saba tsuri no zu)

text.headline: Mackerel Fishing at Night in Noto Province (同 [能登] 國鯖釣之圖 dō koku [Noto] saba tsuri no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. depicting mackerel fishing using torches, which not only attract the mackerel toward the boat but also lure smaller fish whose presence in turn is an attraction to the voracious mackerel.
As in this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.
See IHL.1500 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Catching Salmon in Echigo Province (越後国鮭洲走を捕図)

text.headline: Catching Salmon in Echigo Province (越後国鮭洲走を捕図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The print depicts men catching salmon which have become stranded on a sandbar during their autumn migration up river.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1489.
Echigo (越後国, Echigo no kuni) was an old province in north-central Japan, on the shores of the Sea of Japan. It corresponds today to Niigata Prefecture, minus the island of Sado.

media.caption: Making Camellia Oil in Izu Province (伊豆國 椿樹油取圖)

text.headline: Making Camellia Oil in Izu Province (伊豆國 椿樹油取圖)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. Camellia tree oil (tsubaki) is extracted from the seed pods of the Camellia Japonica and used as a hair conditioning treatment.
Izu Province (伊豆国 Izu-no kuni) was a province of Japan in the area of Shizuoka Prefecture. Izu bordered on Sagami and Suruga Provinces. Its abbreviated form name was Zushū (豆州). The mainland portion of Izu Province, comprising the Izu Peninsula is today the eastern portion of Shizuoka Prefecture and the Izu Islands are now part of Tokyo.

media.caption: Bleaching Fabric on the Snow in Echigo Province (越後國雪中布晒之図)

text.headline: Bleaching Fabric on the Snow in Echigo Province (越後國雪中布晒之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
The ancient technique of snow-bleaching in the final stage of the creation of Echigo-jofu (a fine-as-silk ramie weaving) is still in use today. Exposing the fabric to snow "makes use of the bleaching effect from ozone produced when snow evaporates in the sun. The wisdom of ancestors has been passed on through this method that removes excess dye, loosens snarls in the threads, and gives the cloth a light, soft finishing touch." - http://japanupclose.web-japan.org/culture/20150323_1.html [accessed 8-25-23]
For another impression of this print see IHL.1490.

media.caption: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)

text.headline: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, kuzu (Japanese arrowroot or pueraria) is being processed into starch. Kuzu root is the traditional medicine of choice for a host of digestive disorders and it is also used as a cooking starch.
See IHL.0367a and IHL.1506 for other impressions of this print.
Yamato Province (大和国, Yamato no Kuni) was a province of Japan, located in Kinai, corresponding to present-day Nara Prefecture in Honshū.

media.caption: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)

text.headline: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, kuzu (Japanese arrowroot or pueraria) is being processed into starch. Kuzu root is the traditional medicine of choice for a host of digestive disorders and it is also used as a cooking starch.
See IHL.0367 and IHL.1506 for other impressions of this print.
Yamato Province (大和国, Yamato no Kuni) was a province of Japan, located in Kinai, corresponding to present-day Nara Prefecture in Honshū.

media.caption: Wild Horse Capture in Iwaki Province (磐城国野馬捕之図)

text.headline: Wild Horse Capture in Iwaki Province (磐城国野馬捕之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
In this print spectators from neighboring villages are watching the annual wild horse roundup. "Archeological evidence suggests that horses first entered Japan from mainland Asia during the Kofun Period (250 to 552), eventually spreading to regions such as Nagano, Gunma and Fukushima." - website of the Japan Times https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/2019/07/20/general/mane-attraction-coastal-parts-fukushima-prefecture-long-standing-love-horses/#.Xn1FMohKiUk

media.caption: Iron Works in Etchu Province (越中国 鉄物細工之図 Etchū no kuni tetsumono zaiku no zu)

text.headline: Iron Works in Etchu Province (越中国 鉄物細工之図 Etchū no kuni tetsumono zaiku no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
The print's scroll reads, "Ironwork is produced in Kametani village in Shinkawa county. Workmen melt and forge iron to make hibachi, or brazier, iron kettles, hoes, sickles, etc. Buddhist altar fittings and other works produced in Takaoka are particularly good in quality, with fine carved decorations of birds, animals, and flowers. Among them, vases exhibited at the National Industrial Exposition were outstandingly exquisite and received awards."
Shinkawa county, referenced in the scroll's translation below, was a district in Etchū Province. Etchū Province (越中国 Etchū no kuni), now Toyama Prefecture, was an old province in central Honshū, on the Sea of Japan side.

media.caption: Wild Geese Hunting in Iyo Province (同國 [伊豫] 峯越鳬捕図)

text.headline: Wild Geese Hunting in Iyo Province (同國 [伊豫] 峯越鳬捕図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. Iyo Province (伊予国, Iyo-no-kuni) was an old province of Japan in the area that is today Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku. Iyo bordered on Awa, Sanuki, and Tosa Provinces. It was sometimes called Yoshū (予州).
A rough translation of the the print's cartouche tells us, "In Yoshu province in October, hunters are catching wild geese descending to the ground. They hide in holes in the ground and use ogi-shaped nets to catch the geese coming nearby."

media.caption: Charcoal Making in Izu Province (伊豆国 炭焼場之図)

text.headline: Charcoal Making in Izu Province (伊豆国 炭焼場之図)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the making of charcoal. Charcoal served as fuel and was used for both home cooking and heating (watan, made from deciduous broadleafs) and iron smelting and smithing (kotan, generally made from chestnut.)   Izu province "was a major source of fuel, particularly charcoal, for the city of Edo, but its yield also was crucial to the people in villages. . . ." - Source: Politics in the Tokugawa Bakufu, 1600-1843, Conrad D. Totman, Berkeley : University of California Press, 1989, p. 22.

media.caption: Depiction of Silkworm Culture in Iwaki Province, figure 4 (磐城国 養蚕之図　四)

text.headline: Depiction of Silkworm Culture in Iwaki Province, figure 4 (磐城国 養蚕之図　四)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
This print explains how to care for the silkworms "around the seventh or eighth day afther they hatch and start to eat the mulberry leaves. . . ." In keeping with the importance of sericulture to Japan's economy and industrialization, seven prints in the series are devoted to it. The Exposition was essentially an industrial promotion opportunity providing a meeting place for Western technologies and their Japanese counterparts. "Silk production was the first example of an industry in which European producers deliberately sought out Japanese know-how" and "the source of Japan's first export technology." - Source: "Sericulture and the Origins of Japanese Industrialization," Tessa Morris-Suzuki, appearing JSTOR, Vol. 33, No.1, January 1992, p. 1-2-103; p. 121.

media.caption: Manufacturing Bamboo Work in Suruga Province (駿河国 竹細工製ノ図)

text.headline: Manufacturing Bamboo Work in Suruga Province (駿河国 竹細工製ノ図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
Suruga craftsmen were known for the production of intriguing bamboo baskets such as insect cages and confectionery containers to sell to travelers along the Tōkaidō. They specialized in using round, often bent bamboo strips to connect round bamboo rims, forming a container.

media.caption: Catching Yellowtail in Tango Province (丹後國鰤追網之図 Tango no kuni buri ō ami no zu)

text.headline: Catching Yellowtail in Tango Province (丹後國鰤追網之図 Tango no kuni buri ō ami no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. Boatmen are herding the Yellowtail (albacore tuna, binnega maguro) into nets which are then pulled in from the shore by others who are rotating two axles of winding rollers, which were anchored on the beach.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1498.
Tango Province (丹後国, Tango no Kuni) was an old province in the area that is today northern Kyoto Prefecture facing the Sea of Japan. Tango bordered on Tajima, Tamba, and Wakasa provinces. At various times both Maizuru and Miyazu were the capital and chief town of the province.
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

media.caption: The Entrance of Asakusa Temple; Taking a Portrait of the Niō Guardians (浅草奥山花屋鋪植木家六三郎底内清人羅雪谷仮寓居之図 筑波二王尊影相之図)

text.headline: The Entrance of Asakusa Temple; Taking a Portrait of the Niō Guardians (浅草奥山花屋鋪植木家六三郎底内清人羅雪谷仮寓居之図 筑波二王尊影相之図)
text.text: In this print from the series Famous Views of Modern Tokyo, Kyōsai collaborated with an artist who signed this work 肉亭夏良写 Nikutei Karyō sha. It is believed that Nikutei Karyō was a pseudonym used by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) early on in his career. The top portion of the print by Nikutei (Kiyochika), shows an entertaining episode of a Japanese man in Chinese costume playing a traditional Chinese instrument as a gray dog dances on his hind legs to the music. The setting is the interior of a scholar's study complete with scrolls and brushes for writing and painting. In Kyōsai's contribution a photographer is positioned on a raised platform taking the portrait of one of the guardian gods, who is holding his standard ferocious pose. The photographer's assistant stands attentively on the ladder below him.  The other guardian from the pair appears captivated by the scene as he leans over the main hall with his elbows resting on the rooftop and his hands tucked under his chin.  The visitors to the temple stand under the imposing guardian looking and pointing upward under his short garment worn around his waist.  The untranslated inscriptions read, on the top portion,  浅草奥山花屋鋪植木家六三郎底内清人羅雪谷仮寓居之図 and, on the bottom portion 筑波二王尊影相之図.

media.caption: House (家 Ie)

text.headline: House (家 Ie)
text.text: Likely gouache or acrylic on a heavy paper. The paper may have first been colored with sumi, similar to how Ono treats his much thinner paper used for his prints. Tadashige also created a woodblock version of this design.

media.caption: Kototoi Bridge on the Sumida River (隅田川言問橋)

text.headline: Kototoi Bridge on the Sumida River (隅田川言問橋)
text.text: A view of Kototoibashi (言問橋) as seen from Sumida Kōen (Sumida Park). The Kototoi Bridge spans the Sumida River in the Mukojima district of Tokyo. Built in 1928, it is approximately 160 meters long and 20 meters high. Extensive reconstruction was done after WWII when the bridge was heavily damaged. A monument stands at the head of the bridge to all the fallen civilians that died in the Tokyo Air raid and resulting firestorm in 1945. Many civilians perished on this bridge.

media.caption: Distant View of Eitai Bridge (三ツ又永代橋遠景 Mitsumata Eitaibashi enkei)

text.headline: Distant View of Eitai Bridge (三ツ又永代橋遠景 Mitsumata Eitaibashi enkei)
text.text:
A view of Yeitai bashi spanning the Sumida River with Tsukuda Island in the mid-ground and a rickshaw in the foreground. There has been a bridge is this spot since 1698 when it was opened to serve as a link between the central part of Edo (modern Tokyo) to the east and the then newly developing area to the west. "Mitsumata" in the print's title references a fork in the Sumida River at its widest point between the main channel and the Hakozaki Canal.
This print is from a loosely constructed series Famous Views of Tokyo (Tokyo meisho) consisting of 93 prints issued from 1876-1881 by two publishers, Matsuki Heikichi and Fukuda Kumajirō.

media.caption: Pulling the Necks (首ツ引 Kubippiki)

text.headline: Pulling the Necks (首ツ引 Kubippiki)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
Only one Japanese soldier is playing kubippiki (neck pulling) with three Chinese rivals. Kubippiki is a Japanese game: to challenge the strength; the combatants try to pull away from each other using a looped rope around their necks. This print is a propagandistic caricature placing emphasis on the (apparent) superiority of the Japanese, as it takes only a single Japanese soldier to crane the necks of three weak enemies and give the other one a good scare.

media.caption: Hell is Booming (地獄の大繁盛 Jigoku no ōhanjō)

text.headline: Hell is Booming (地獄の大繁盛 Jigoku no ōhanjō)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin, a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
The king of the dead who passes judgment on those who have died stands behind a podium, flanked by two assistants. He looks out over a vast number of Chinese dead, drowned in battle, all of whom call themselves "Dozaemon" (drowned person), and is overwhelmed. The last sentence of the text can be read as a pun on the name Shinkoku (清国) referring to China. By using the characters 死国 (also pronounced shinkoku), China is transformed into the “land of death,” an ironic hint on the great losses on the Chinese side.

media.caption: Papermaking in Suruga Province (駿河半紙漉場ノ図)

text.headline: Papermaking in Suruga Province (駿河半紙漉場ノ図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the manufacture of hanshi, a fine washi.

MAKING THE PAPER CALLED "HANSHI"
An 1871 Account of Making Hanshi delivered to the House of Commons (Source: Parliamentary Papers (Great Britain, Parliament, House of Commons): Accounts and Papers, Volume 67, Reports on the Manufacture of Paper in Japan, Sir H. Parkes, p. 5, Harrison and Sons, 1871.)
The bucket contains warm water in which to dip the hands when cold. The box or frame used in making “sughara” (a large size of paper) is very heavy, so that men are employed in the manufacture of the latter; but women can manipulate the frames used for “hanshi.”
The “sosori” to be used is made into a large ball, from which lumps are broken off as required. These lumps are cast into what is called the “boat,” and thoroughly mixed with sell-strained “tororo” paste. It should be stirred thoroughly, and is of proper consistency when the stick makes a slight noise when passing through the pulp. If not sufficiently sticky, more “tororo” should be added, but the proportion of the ingredients can only be learned by practice.
The pulp should not cling to or wind round the stick, but should be thoroughly stirred and well mixed.
The “boat:” length 6 feet; breadth 3 feet, with a perpendicular rest for leaning the frame against it.
The false bottom is placed in the outer frame, into which a portion of the pulp is then poured. The inner frame is then fitted in to keep the false bottom steady, and a peculiar and dexterous jerk is given to the whole, which sets the paper. The frame is then leaned against the upright rest to allow the water to drain off, while another frame is prepared. By the time the second frame is ready the first may be removed. This manipulation can be performed very quickly by experts in the manufacture.

Drying the Paper
The sheet of paper is removed from the frame with a piece of bamboo…by dexterously curling the thicker end of the paper round it; the brush is taken in the right hand, and with it the paper is laid on the drying-board, … the side which adheres to the board being the face of the paper. Five sheets are placed on each side of the board, which is 6 feet long. In fine weather the paper dries quickly, and in wet weather it is sometimes dried by the heat of a fire. Each manipulator requires forty drying boards.
Cutting “Hanshi” into Proper Sizes
Between every 20 sheets two or three straws are inserted. The paper, in parcels of 100 sheets, is then placed upon a table, and a heavy ruler put on the top of it, which is kept steady with the right foot. The paper is held in the left hand, and cut off with a knife… It is then packed,… and is finally made up into bundles ready for the market.

Suruga Province (駿河国, Suruga no kuni) was an old province in the area that is today the central part of Shizuoka prefecture. Suruga bordered on Izu, Kai, Sagami, Shinano, and Tōtōmi provinces; and had access to the Pacific Ocean through Suruga Bay.

media.caption: The Fireflies of Uji River (宇治川の蛍)

text.headline: The Fireflies of Uji River (宇治川の蛍)
text.text: Originally published sometime in the 1930s, this print pictures the famous fireflies aglow in the evening along the Uji River in Yamashiro near Kyoto.  Legend has at that the fireflies are the ghosts of the Minamoto and Taira clans. Once every year on the night of the twentieth day of the fourth month, they fight a great battle on the Uji River. On that night all caged fireflies should be set free to take part in the Hotaru-Kassen, or Firefly Battle.

media.caption: Illustration of the Celebration of the Silver Wedding Anniversary (銀婚式御擧之圖 Ginkon goshiki hōshuku no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Celebration of the Silver Wedding Anniversary (銀婚式御擧之圖 Ginkon goshiki hōshuku no zu)
text.text:
A depiction of one of many ceremonies that took place on the day of the silver wedding anniversary of the emperor and empress on March 9, 1894. In this print felicitations are being read by a military official but, interestingly, Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken are off-stage, concealed by the orange curtain.
The Silver Wedding Anniversary of Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken
"The wedding anniversaries of Japanese sovereigns had never before been a matter for public rejoicing, but when the emperor was informed that it was customary for royalty in foreign countries to celebrate 'silver weddings,' he gladly gave his consent to the proposed celebrations. To make sure the proper tone for the celebration was maintained, a committee was formed to investigate foreign examples." - Source: Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His World, 1852-1912, Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 2002, p. 471.

media.caption: Sagami, Flowers of Yokoyama, Princess Terute and Oguri Hangan, No. 48 (相模、横山の花、照手姫、 小栗判官 四十八 Sagami, Yokoyama no hana, Terute-hime, Oguri Hangan・yonjūhatsu)

text.headline: Sagami, Flowers of Yokoyama, Princess Terute and Oguri Hangan, No. 48 (相模、横山の花、照手姫、 小栗判官 四十八 Sagami, Yokoyama no hana, Terute-hime, Oguri Hangan・yonjūhatsu)
text.text:
"The 17th century play Tōryū Oguri Hangan, originally by Chikamatsu Monzaemon, has taken many forms over the centuries with complex storylines added, but a popular scene is when Oguri Hangan, searching for stolen family treasures in Yokoyama, finds his beloved fiancee Princess Terute, who had been abducted, lost at sea, rescued and now worked as a maid in the house of a wealthy rice merchant. The moment of reunion is shown in this print. When the merchant's daughter (who also loves Hangan) tries to kill Terute, the merchant's wife kills her daughter, who then becomes a demon that attacks and disfigures Hangan. Terute then takes her lover to the healing waterfalls of Nachi [shown in inset], where he recovers."[1]

THE SERIES SETSUGEKKA (SNOW, MOON, FLOWERS)
"Chikanobu’s fifty-print series Setsugekka [Snow, Moon, Flowers] was published between August 1884 and April 1886. The term setsugekka / setsu getsu ka derives originally from a poem by the famous Tang-dynasty poet Bo Juyi (772-846), which was in turn included in the Heian-period anthology Wakan rōei shū:
Lute, poetry, wine – my friends
all have deserted me;
snow, moon, flowers – these seasons,
I most often think of you.
As can be seen from Bo’s usage, the phrase was a short-hand way of referring to the four seasons and their respective best features: the snow of winter, the autumn moon, and the spring cherry-blossoms."[2]

[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 107.
[2] "Setsugekka: Snow, Moon, Flowers", Joshua S. Mostow, appearing in Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 83.

media.caption: Edo, Snow on Narihira Bridge in Honjo, Courtesans of the Arimaya, Clamseller Yokichi, and Onogawa Kisaburo, Number 41 (江戸、本所業平橋の雪、有馬家奥方、蜆売与吉、小野川喜三郎・四十一 Edo、Honjo Narihirabashi no yuki、Arimaya no okata、Shijimi-uri Yokichi、Onogawa Kisaburō・yonjū ichi)

text.headline: Edo, Snow on Narihira Bridge in Honjo, Courtesans of the Arimaya, Clamseller Yokichi, and Onogawa Kisaburo, Number 41 (江戸、本所業平橋の雪、有馬家奥方、蜆売与吉、小野川喜三郎・四十一 Edo、Honjo Narihirabashi no yuki、Arimaya no okata、Shijimi-uri Yokichi、Onogawa Kisaburō・yonjū ichi)
text.text:
Both scenes in this print are from the story Arima no neko. In the bottom portion of the print, "[t]he little boy Yokichi has heard that his sister Otaki, who was sold into prostitution, has committed suicide, and he comes to the Arimaya brothel to find out more information." In the inset, "Onogawa Kisaburo fights off the monster cat, formerly the pet of Otaki," who has come to take revenge for his dead mistress.[1]

THE SERIES SETSUGEKKA (SNOW, MOON, FLOWERS)
"Chikanobu’s fifty-print series Setsugekka [Snow, Moon, Flowers] was published between August 1884 and April 1886. The term setsugekka / setsu getsu ka derives originally from a poem by the famous Tang-dynasty poet Bo Juyi (772-846), which was in turn included in the Heian-period anthology Wakan rōei shū:
Lute, poetry, wine – my friends
all have deserted me;
snow, moon, flowers – these seasons,
I most often think of you.
As can be seen from Bo’s usage, the phrase was a short-hand way of referring to the four seasons and their respective best features: the snow of winter, the autumn moon, and the spring cherry-blossoms."[2]

[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 104.
[2] "Setsugekka: Snow, Moon, Flowers", Joshua S. Mostow, appearing in Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 83

media.caption: Stone Garden of Kyoto

text.headline: Stone Garden of Kyoto
text.text:
A small print showing rock groups 2 and 4 out of 15 groups in the The Karesansui (Dry Landscape) garden at the Ryoanji temple (Temple of the Peaceful Dragon ) in Kyoto. Ryoanji is the most famous and celebrated garden in Japan. Simply composed of stone and sand, it serves as a subtle yet effective example of the dry garden type. This print is attributed to Yoshida Masaji (1917–1971) by Kanda's Gallery of Tokyo. A sticker on the back of the framed print reads:
ZEN GARDEN One of the arts that flourished under the influence of Zen philosophy was garden architecture. Although the Japanese garden was always a replica of nature in miniature, in the 14th century the size was further reduced and the trees and shrubs replaced by rocks and sand.

The stone garden of Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto, laid out in the 15th century, is the most famous for the fifteen rocks, arranged in five groups, on raked sand. The harmony in color, shape and size of the rocks makes this one of the most subtle and powerful gardens in Japan. The rocks can be interpreted as islands in a river or as high peaks soaring over clouds.
For Masaji's abstract take on Ryoan-ji see James Michener's comments on Ground No. 3 (IHL.0148).

media.caption: Clown No. 5 (道化師 No.5 Dōkeshi No. 5)

text.headline: Clown No. 5 (道化師 No.5 Dōkeshi No. 5)
text.text: Hagiwara has combined traditional woodblock techniques with a form of woodcut intaglio, which he invented, which creates lines that resemble those found in etching or drypoint. In this print we seem to be given an "exploded view" of the clown.

media.caption: Great Naval Battle of Port Arthur: A Desperate Warship Hit by One of Our Torpedoes (旅順港外大海戦・我水雷艇奮戦之図)

text.headline: Great Naval Battle of Port Arthur: A Desperate Warship Hit by One of Our Torpedoes (旅順港外大海戦・我水雷艇奮戦之図)
text.text:
Multiple Japanese torpedo boats attack the Russian fleet in Port Arthur. Searchlights pierce the sky as the Russian ships fruitlessly look for their attackers.
"On Feb. 9th and 10th the press dispatches brought sensational news regarding the attack of the Japanese torpedo boats upon the Russian naval fleet anchored in the roads just outside the entrance of Port Arthur harbor. The attack was made by the swift Japanese torpedo boats during the dark night of Monday, Feb. 8th. They fairly hugged the coast as they approached the entrance and when in close range of that part of the fleet anchored just outside the entrance to the harbor the Japs discharged several torpedoes toward their enemy's fleet. Several men-of-war, including the Cesarevitch, Retvizan and Pallada, were disabled. The crippled fighting ships of the Czar limped toward Port Arthur and almost at its very entrance were beached." - Source: Official History of the Russian-Japanese War: A Vivid Panorama of Land and Naval Battles, J. Martin Miller, 1905, p. 304-305.

media.caption: Mount Ashigara scene, an interlude entertainment (明治座中幕｜足柄山の場)

text.headline: Mount Ashigara scene, an interlude entertainment (明治座中幕｜足柄山の場)
text.text:
Starring Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (R), Ichikawa Kodanji V (C) and Ichikawa Sadanji I (L)
This scene originated in an 1804 play with the title Edo-style Autumn Maple Makeup of the Four Guardian Kings (四天王楓江戸粧), a storyline set in the military conflicts of 11th-century Japan. The drama blended history, fiction, sorcery and supernatural spectacle, keeping audiences spellbound. Mount Ashigara in Hakone rises from the mist behind three actors in a stage reinvention of a tale about Yamauba, the wild mountain-woman of legend (right) and her super-hero son, or Kaidōmaru, “Boy Wonder” – an alternate name for Kintarō, “Golden Boy” – (center), who were believed to inhabit these forests. One of the leading actors of the Meiji period appears as a character named Yamakazu (left), clutching the hilt of a sword marking him as a warrior, while his red makeup denotes strength and righteous anger. - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
The Edo-Tokyo Museum lists this play as an entr’acte or short entertainment (such as a song or dance) inserted between the acts of a play.

media.caption: Tomoakira 知章

text.headline: Tomoakira 知章
text.text:
Depicting the brave youth Tomoakira who died in place of his father, Tomomori, on the battlefield of Ichinotani. The play is classified as a shura, warrior or ghost, noh that takes its theme from the Heike monogatari.
“A son died to save his father; a father fled, leaving his son to die. Were it done by another man, I should spit in his face. But I have done it myself. What will the world call me?” - Tomomori, describing his son’s death to his brother, Munemori.

Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints issued between 1897 and 1904. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Yearning Afterward (のこるこころ)

text.headline: Yearning Afterward (のこるこころ)
text.text: A posthumous printing, printed by Yoneda Minoru in 1975, intended as a frontispiece in Onchi's print catalogue raisonné, "Onchi Koshiro hangashu" 恩地孝四郎版画集 (Prints of Onchi Koshiro), this print was originally published in 1915 in the fourth issue of the small print and poetry magazine "Tsukuhae" (Moonglow), created by Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), Shizuo Fujimori (1891-1943) and Tanaka Kyokichi (1892-1915). In 1989 the artist's son, Onchi Kunio 恩地邦郎 (1920-2001), printed another posthumous edition of this print.

media.caption: Nihonbashi (日本橋)

text.headline: Nihonbashi (日本橋)
text.text:
Hiratsuka was asked to make the first print of the Shin Tokyo Hyakkei series depicting Nihonbashi, for centuries the central point of the city from which all distances were measured. This collection's print is likely printed from the original blocks but may be a later edition, as it lacks the title, 日本橋, that appears in the right margin on other impressions identified as belonging to the Shin Tokyo Hyakkei series and the artist's identifying seal has been placed in a different location.
In 1929 Hiratsuka, along with seven other artists and the publisher Nakajima Jutaro, undertook the creation of the series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). The series goal was to depict the modern city of Tokyo that arose after the devastating 1923 earthquake.

media.caption: Stage Name Onoe Kikugorō: February 14, 1903, Dead at Sixty Years Old (芸名尾上菊五郎・ 行年六拾歳)

text.headline: Stage Name Onoe Kikugorō: February 14, 1903, Dead at Sixty Years Old (芸名尾上菊五郎・ 行年六拾歳)
text.text:
This memorial print (shini-e) issued upon the death of the actor Onoe Kikugorō V on February 18, 1903 shows the actor in costume holding a bird cage from which two birds have been released. This symbology may refer to the Buddhist release of captive animals on Buddha Day or may be a reference to the Lotus Sutra, as the call of the Japanese bush warbler (uguisu) (which looks very much like the birds in this print) is transcribed in Japanese as "Hō-hoke-kyo", a phrase from the Lotus Sutra. The print provides his date of death, his posthumous Buddhist name, stage name, secular name and age in years.
Onoe Kikugorō V belonged to the triumvirate of stars, along with Ichikawa Danjûrō IX and Ichikawa Sadanji I, who dominated the Kabuki world during the Meiji era. "It was in drama of everyday life that Kikugorō most excelled, the sentimental and realistic having the greatest appeal for him." - Source: Kabuki, the Popular Stage of Japan, Zoe Kincaid, Macmillan, 1925.

media.caption: Nakamura Shikan as Ishikawa Goemon (石川五右衛門  中村芝翫)

text.headline: Nakamura Shikan as Ishikawa Goemon (石川五右衛門  中村芝翫)
text.text: The actor Nakamura Shikan IV playing the role of the thief Ishikawa Goemon from the series Twenty-Four Favorites of New Civilization. A bird delivering a message is contrasted with the telegraph wires in the inset.

media.caption: Germination 2 (萌芽 2 hōga 2)

text.headline: Germination 2 (萌芽 2 hōga 2)
text.text: This print is one of five prints in the artist's series Germination. Each print in this series uses the similar form of egg or seed-like masses dividing. For this print, Hagiwara used the technique of forcing pigment through the paper from the back, effectively dying the paper and producing a textural surface on which to work.

media.caption: Plum, originally appearing in the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花  ・梅  Shikashū・Nihon no hana・ume)

text.headline: Plum, originally appearing in the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花  ・梅  Shikashū・Nihon no hana・ume)
text.text:
In this print by Maekawa Senpan, a branch of flowering plum sits in a teapot with the word "fuku" 福 (good fortune) painted on it. The print accompanied a poem of the same name, "Plum," by writer and poet Yonejirō Noguchi (1875-1947). "Plum" was one of three woodblock prints, along with "Rose" (see IHL.0327) by Kawanishi Hide (1894-1965) and "Thistle" (see IHL.0603) by Kawakami Sumio (1895-1972), that were tipped into the book. This collection's print is stand-alone, being either removed from the book it was tipped into or separately printed as a stand-alone print.
"Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," was edited and designed by Onchi Kōshirō, a seminal artist in the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement and pioneering book designer. Contributing twelve prints and one poem, he along with poet Inoue Yasufumi 井上康文 (1897–1973), selected the book's thirty poems by poets such as Satō Haruo (1892-1964), Kitahara Hakushū (1885-1942), Noguchi Yonejirō (1875-1947), Kaoru Maruyama (1899-1974), Tatsuji Miyoshi (1900-1964), Ryuko Kawaji (1888-1959) and Andō Ichirō (1907-1972).
When this book was published in May 1946 "much of the country, including Tokyo where it was printed, remained in ruins following the previous year’s aerial bombardments. . . . Nihon no hana demonstrated the sophisticated aesthetic sensibility of the Japanese people, while providing a hopeful image for the future rebuilding—or 're-flowering'—of the country and its people." - Source: Commentary by Alicia Volk, https://pulverer.si.edu/node/462/title/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Paradise from the portfolio The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists

text.headline: Paradise from the portfolio The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists
text.text:
"There is no nature in this landscape. Only parts of humans and of machines." - Hodaka Yoshida
This print was created in 1973 as part of a series of landscape prints portraying the devastating effects of pollution on the environment. For these prints, Hodaka cut pictures out of magazines: men and women, clothed or unclothed, pieces of fabric, junked cars, wristwatches, portable radios, paper currency, whiskey bottles, and the like. He then cut each image into a collage, with the whole appearing a bit like a landscape . . . . He then photographed the collage. A photoetched zinc plate inked with black supplied the details for the final image, while woodblocks provided the colors. - Source: "Magic, Artifact, and Art," Eugene M. Skibbe, appearing in A Japanese Legacy: Four Generations of Yoshida Family Artists, Laura W. Allen, Kendall H. Brown, Eugene M. Skibbe, et. al., The Minneapolis Institute of Arts, 2002, p.117.
This print was included in the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, published in 1973. See IHL.2269e.

media.caption: Ichikawa Sadanji as Togachi Saemon, Ichikawa Danjūrō as Benkei and Nakamura Fukusuke as Yoshitune in the play The Subscription List from the Kabuki Eighteen (歌舞伎十八番の内勧進帳・戸樫左衛門　市川左団次、弁慶　市川団十郎、義経　中村福助)

text.headline: Ichikawa Sadanji as Togachi Saemon, Ichikawa Danjūrō as Benkei and Nakamura Fukusuke as Yoshitune in the play The Subscription List from the Kabuki Eighteen (歌舞伎十八番の内勧進帳・戸樫左衛門　市川左団次、弁慶　市川団十郎、義経　中村福助)
text.text:
The three actors (R to L), Ichikawa Sadanji in the role of Togachi Saemon, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Benkei and Nakamura Fukusuke IV in the role of Yoshitsune in the play The Subscription List (Kanjinchō), performed at Tokyo's Shintomiza theatre.
In April 1887 (two months before this print was issued), in an important event for kabuki, four days of performances were arranged for the imperial family, marking the recognition of kabuki’s restored social status. The actors performed al fresco on the grounds of the residence of Foreign Minister Inoue, in Tokyo’s Azabu district. The emperor attended the first day’s performance of The Subscription List (Kanjinchō), with the actors Danjūrō IX, Ichikawa Sadanji I and Nakamura Fukusuke IV, who are pictured in this print in a performance that occurred several months later.
The Subscription List was the first of the group of plays chosen by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII as one of the Kabuki Jūhachiban ("Eighteen Favorite Kabuki Plays") which are representative of the ie no gei or "family art" of the Danjūrō acting line.
The story is set in the late 12th century. Yoshitsune is a son of Minamoto no Yoshitomo, the former head of the Minamoto clan (also called Genji clan), and he and his followers are being hunted by his brother, the Shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo, the present head of the clan. While they are fleeing in the disguise of yamabushi (Buddhist mountain priests), they come to a checkpoint at Ataka in Kaga Province. There they are harshly interrogated by Togashi Saemon no jō who is under Yoritomo's orders to arrest them. One of Yoshitsune's followers, the quick-witted Benkei, asserts that they are not Yoshitsune's party but real yamabushi, journeying around the provinces seeking donations for the rebuilding of the Tōdaiji Temple in Nara, which burned down in a battle. Challenged to prove his identity, Benkei takes out a blank scroll and says that it is a kanjinchō (subscription list formally laying out the benefits of donating to rebuilding temples) and pretends to read from it. Sparks fly from the eyes of one man to another. Benkei, anticipating that his ruse will be exposed, stares hard at his opponent. Togashi, sniffing out Benkei's deceit, unsheaths his sword. Yoshitsune, dressed as a porter but behaving as if the deception has been detected, prepares to fight.

media.caption: Kuruma-zō 車僧 (The Carriage Priest)

text.headline: Kuruma-zō 車僧 (The Carriage Priest)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 93.) - One snowy winter's day the 'carriage priest', so named because he goes everywhere in an old broken carriage, visits Saga and is there accosted by a yamabushi priest who engages him in a religious contest of words. Defeated in this, the second priest retires but returns later in his true form as a goblin. On this occasion he tries to overcome the other's holy power by his evil influence, but as this too proves to be beyond him he goes away acknowledging the superior power of the Buddhist priest.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Still Life with Crab (Kani no iru seibutsu)

text.headline: Still Life with Crab (Kani no iru seibutsu)
text.text: The black crab of the title is joined by a lobster (or shrimp) and, possibly, a squid all swimming in a sea of the artist's signature red and ochre pallet.

media.caption: Family of Thieves, No. 822 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun  (東京日々新聞・八百廿貳号・強盗夫婦)

text.headline: Family of Thieves, No. 822 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun  (東京日々新聞・八百廿貳号・強盗夫婦)
text.text:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e," in the banner held aloft by two cherubs, is the name of the newspaper who sponsored it, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞. The print is about a married couple who are professional thieves. Reversing the usual gender roles, it is the wife who breaks into houses wearing a sword and clad in a male attire. The husband keeps watch at the door, their baby strapped to his back.
Translation of text on print: "They say Liuxia Hui sees candy and thinks it’s good for nurturing children, while Dao Zhi thinks candy good for opening locked doors. This proverb means that you see things differently depending on whether you’re looking for good or evil. A sweet metaphor, but not too sweet for this couple, who extended it to cover their own matrimonial misdeeds. Thieves by night, by day they walked around peddling shiratama candy. At night the wife would disguise herself as a man and sneak into wealthy houses everywhere while her husband would hold their child and guard the door. Then they would sling their stolen clothing and goods over their shoulders and go home, talking merrily as they went. Their reversal of men’s and women’s roles inspired a theatrical adaptation, for she reminded people of no one so much as Demongod Omatsu of Kasamatsu Pass. But while Omatsu may have evaded Natsume’s gaze, these thieves could not evade the Law’s net: Heaven’s punishment came down upon them, and these days they are in jail in Tochigi, in Yashū. By Dondon, an employee of the Newspaper Bureau - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 and 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

media.caption: Twice Astonished, No. 944 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・九百四十四號・世に二度愕然)

text.headline: Twice Astonished, No. 944 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・九百四十四號・世に二度愕然)
text.text:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e," in the banner held aloft by two cherubs, is the name of the newspaper who sponsored it, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞. The print tells the story of how a rickshaw driver saved the life and money, over 1,000 yen in gold, of a merchant's agent when a robber threatened the agent and demanded his money on penalty of death on their way back to Osaka. When the agent took out the money to hand over to the robber, the quick-thinking rickshaw driver snatched the money from the agent and ran off, leaving both the robber and agent dumbfounded. Later the driver returned the money to the agent who deeply thanked him.

media.caption: The Subscription List (勧進帳 Kanjinchō)

text.headline: The Subscription List (勧進帳 Kanjinchō)
text.text:
Eight actors are depicted in the play The Subscription List (Kanjinchō), one of the masterpieces of kabuki and chosen by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII as one of the Kabuki Jūhachiban ("Eighteen Favorite Kabuki Plays"). Ichikawa Sadanji I is the actor on the far right playing the role of Togachi Saemon, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX is the actor with arm raised in the center playing the role of Benkei and Ichikawa Ebijūrō is shown playing the role of Yoshitune in the lower left of the left panel. The other actors are unread. For another print of this play by Kunichika see IHL.0398.
Play Summary: The general Minamoto no Yoshitsune has a falling out with his elder brother Yoritomo, and is forced to flee to safety in the north of Japan in disguise as a mountain priest. However, en route at the barrier gate at Ataka he is recognized by the barrier commander Togashi no Saemon. His faithful retainer Benkei distracts the guards by reading out a fake subscription scroll and then by beating his master over the head. Respecting the strength of devotion and desperation that pushed Benkei to commit such an unthinkable crime, Togashi allows the party to pass through. The Subscription List is a kabuki version of the noh play Ataka, performed on an over-sized parody of the noh stage (matsubame). - source: website of Naritaya http://www.naritaya.jp/english/compendium/18_17.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Nearby Entries in March at the Kabuki Theater (歌舞伎座三月奥行)

text.headline: Nearby Entries in March at the Kabuki Theater (歌舞伎座三月奥行)
text.text: Picturing the actors Onoe Kikugorō V as Takebe Genzo and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Matsuomaru, this print is an announcement for the play Sugawara denju tenarai kagami (Sugawara and the Secrets of Calligraphy) staged in Tokyo's Kabukiza theater in March 1899.

media.caption: Mirror of Magical Heroes (英優奇術鑑 Eiyū kijutsu kagami)

text.headline: Mirror of Magical Heroes (英優奇術鑑 Eiyū kijutsu kagami)
text.text:
A densely packed conglomeration of six magicians with their favorite conjurings.
Pictured, from left to right are:
The character 児雷也 Jiraiya [literally: child-thunder man or young thunder], played by Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川 團十郎, has conjured a giant toad allowing him to perform "toad magic." By mastering the toad's magic and with the toad by his side, Jiraiya can overcome his enemies.
The character 綱手 Tsunade [literally: rope-hand; translated as towing line], played by Suketakaya Takasuke IV 助高屋 高助, has conjured a giant snail and has mastered "snail magic."
The character 虎王丸 Tora Ōmaru [literally: tiger king-round], played by Ichikawa Sadanji 市川 左團次, has conjured a tiger.
The character 雲龍九郎 Unryūkurō [literally: cloud-dragon Kurō], played by Nakamura Shikan IV 中村 芝翫, has conjured a storm dragon.
The character 暁星五郎 Akatsuki Hoshigorō [literally: dawn-star Gorō], played by Ichikawa Kuzō III 市川 九蔵, has conjured a bat.
The character 不知火 Shiranui [literally: unknown-fire], played by Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上 菊五郎, holding a scroll of spider spells on which a spider walks.

media.caption: Shiranami Gonin Otoko (白浪五人男)

text.headline: Shiranami Gonin Otoko (白浪五人男)
text.text:
The actors, from left to right, Ichikawa Sadanji I in the role of Nangō Rikimaru (南郷力丸); Ichikawa Kuzō II* in the role of Tadanobu Rihei (忠信利平); Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Nippon Daemon (日本駄右衛門); Suketakaya Takasuke IV in the role of Akaboshi Jūzaburō (赤星十三) and Onoe Kikugoro V in the role of Benten-Kozō Kikunosuke (弁天小僧菊之助) in the play Shiranami Gonin Otoko (白浪五人男), also known as Aoto Zōshi Hana no Nishiki-e (青砥稿花紅彩画). The background writing is dialogue from the play.
The drama Aoto Zōshi Hana no Nishikie 青砥稿花紅彩画 by the playwright Kawatake Shinshichi II (1816-1893), commonly called Shiranami gonin otoko (白浪五人男, Five men of the white waves) or Benten Kozō (弁天小僧), the play's main character, is one of a number of kabuki plays based on the classic theme of "Gonin Otoko", a group of five dandy-thieves. The playwright replaced the original Ōsaka thieves Karigane Bunshichi, An no Heibei, Gokuin Sen'emon, Kaminari Shōkurō and Hotei Ichiemon with five Kamakura thieves named Nippon Daemon (modeled on the real thief Nippon Saemon, who was caught in February 1747 and executed in March), Benten Kozō Kikunosuke, Nangō Rikimaru, Tadanobu Rikei and Akaboshi Jūzaburō.
* The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University identifies this actor as Ichikawa Kuzō II <2>市川九蔵. However, Kuzō II died in 1871, making the actor likely Ichikawa Kuzō III, a stage name of Ichikawa Danzō VII which he held from the "8th lunar month of 1854 to May 1897" according to the Kabuki 21 website http://www.kabuki21.com/kuzo.php [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Izutsu 井筒, (The Well)

text.headline: Izutsu 井筒, (The Well)
text.text:
Depicting the moment in the play Izutsu by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) "when Lady Izutsu, the daughter of Ki no Aritsune and the wife of Ariwara no Narihira, appears as a ghost. Rather than wearing a traditional woman’s costume, she is wearing her husband’s headdress and noshi (a man’s imperial court kimono). Thus dressed, the ghost of Lady Izutsu moves aside the autumn grasses to look into the well, searching for her husband’s reflection."[1]
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A traveling priest comes to the Ariwara-dera and there sees a woman beside an old grave. She tells him that it is the grave of Ariwara on Narihira and that she is really the daughter of Ki no Aritsune who loved Narihira faithfully all her life. In a dream that night the priest sees the lady appear in Narihira's hat and robe. She dances and then, looking down into the well, sees what is for her the image of her lover. Dawn comes, the priest awakes and the lady has gone.[2]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[3]

[1] Scripps College website http://web-kiosk.scrippscollege.edu/Obj20843?sid=19047&x=325921 [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 63.
[3] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Showing the Flag of the Rising Sun, No. 849 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun ((東京日々新聞・八百四十九号・旭章の国旗)

text.headline: Showing the Flag of the Rising Sun, No. 849 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun ((東京日々新聞・八百四十九号・旭章の国旗)
text.text:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞. In this print, Japanese celebrate detente with China over the killings of Ryukyuan fishermen who shipwrecked on Taiwan. This print was published to celebrate the agreement signed between the governments of Japan and the Qing Dynasty of China concerning Taiwan, which a Japanese expeditionary force had partly occupied in order to punish some Taiwanese who had killed a number of shipwrecked Okinawans. The picture shows the Japanese flag raised, geisha dancing, and men toasting the end of what some Taiwanese and Chinese call the First Sino-Japanese War.
The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.
