media.caption: Minamoto no Yorimitsu, No. 27  (源頼光)

text.headline: Minamoto no Yorimitsu, No. 27  (源頼光)
text.text:
"The famous warrior Minamoto no Yorimitsu (948-1021), also known as Raikō, was devoted to the goddess Benzaiten, who appeared to him in a dream and gave him a special bow and arrow to help him in the way of the martial arts. The inset above the main panel depicts Kidōmaru in the snow wearing the skin of a bull waiting to ambush Yorimitsu. Kidōmaru will meet his fate on the receiving end of an arrow shot from the special bow."[1]

This series, consisting of 50 prints, drew its subject matter from 12th through 16th century historical epics and war chronicles. It also uses "a three part format of a large primary scene topped by a title cartouche at right and a secondary panel set into the upper left corner. This compositional arrangement encouraged a visual and intellectual conversation among the three segments, allowing subtle commentaries and inflections to be created and/or narratives to be explored."[2]

[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 126.
[2] Ibid., p. 37.

media.caption: Surrender of Goryōkaku (函館 五稜郭の降伏)

text.headline: Surrender of Goryōkaku (函館 五稜郭の降伏)
text.text:
This print is one of a number of "redemption" prints created during and immediately after Saigō Takamori's failed 1877 Satsuma Rebellion against the Meiji government. These prints sought to redeem Saigō by portraying his earlier exploits fighting to overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate and his subsequent defense of the Meiji government against continuing insurrection by rebellious samurai.
This print depicts the June 1869 surrender of the Ezo rebels at Goryōkaku, the "star fort" in Hakodate in southern Hokkaidō. The Ezo rebels were loyalists to the defeated shogunate and the last significant military threat to the Meiji imperial forces. In this scene Saigō Takamori (central figure in the center panel) is demanding (or, perhaps, accepting) the surrender of Enomoto Takeaki 榎本武揚 the leader of the short-lived Ezo Republic (seated and leaning forward in the right panel.)
Placing Saigō at the scene of the surrender is taking historical license as Saigō did not reach the rebels stronghold until after the surrender was made to Kuroda Kiyotaka 黑田 清隆, who is not shown in the print.
In addition to Saigō and Enomoto, other figures represented are Matsudaira Tarō 海軍 松平太郎, vice president of the Ezo Republic (right panel, figure in green robe); Hijikata Toshizō 土方 歳 三, vice minister of the Ezo army, (right panel, seated behind Matsudaira, and partially hidden from view); Kasuga? Zaemon 春日 左衛門, a captain in the Ezo army (right panel, seated far right in blue-gray shirt); Ootori Keisuke 大鳥圭介 Tokugawa retainer and commander-in-chief Ezo Republic (right panel into center panel, seated and leaning towards Enomoto); Beppu Shinsuke 別府 府助, an officer in the Imperial army and a loyal follower of Saigō (center panel, seated to the left of Saigō); and Arai Chokunoshin? 浅井 直之進, a follower of Saigō (left panel kneeling). The names of the remaining Saigō supporters in the left panel are currently unidentified, i.e. their names in the cartouches have not been translated. The red wigs seen in the left panel identify their wearers as imperial soldiers of the Tosa Domain.
Pictured in the background are three ships at anchor in Hakodate Bay, including the Kaiyō Maru 海陽丸 one of Japan's first modern warships and part of the flotilla that Enomoto sailed to Hakodate, and the Kasuga Maru 春日丸, both part of the imperial Japanese navy.

media.caption: Retreat of the Insurgents to the Defensive Position at Hyūga (日向険地江暴徒引退図 Hyūga no kenchi e bōto shirizoku zu)

text.headline: Retreat of the Insurgents to the Defensive Position at Hyūga (日向険地江暴徒引退図 Hyūga no kenchi e bōto shirizoku zu)
text.text:
One of approximately thirty prints by the artist portraying the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877. In this print Saigō Takamori, the rebellion's leader, is seen in the center sheet looking out to the Yatsuhiro Sea where government warships are seen. When this print was issued in May, the rebels have already suffered a major defeat at battle of Tabaruzaka Hill in northern Kagoshima and are in retreat. While the government had offered the rebellious samurai several opportunities to "repent their opposition to the Imperial authority and submit themselves to the same" and be pardoned, they fought on until their final defeat on September 24 at the Battle of Shiroyama.
As in many of the prints portraying the Rebellion the white banner carrying the slogan "Shinsei kotoku" (New Government rich in virtue) is prominently featured. The historian Mark Ravina points out that this slogan never appeared on Saigō's battle pennants, being wholly created by journalists and artists "covering" the rebellion.

media.caption: Ginza Brick Building (銀座煉瓦造 Ginza renga tsukuri)

text.headline: Ginza Brick Building (銀座煉瓦造 Ginza renga tsukuri)
text.text: The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III (1842–1894) designed at least nine different series depicting early Meiji Era Tokyo landmarks. This scene shows the headquarters of one of the many newspaper offices (possibly that of Nipposha, the publishers of the Tokyo Nichinichi Shinbun) located along the Ginza "Brick Street."  If it is the Nipposha office, it dates this print between the time Nipposha first moved its offices to Ginza in May 1874 to their move to new offices at the end of 1876 at Oharicho 1-chome 1-banchi in Kyobashi-ku.

media.caption: View from Asakusa Bridge to Yanagi Bridge (浅草橋より柳橋の景 Asakusabashi yori Yanagibashi no kei)

text.headline: View from Asakusa Bridge to Yanagi Bridge (浅草橋より柳橋の景 Asakusabashi yori Yanagibashi no kei)
text.text:
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III (1842–1894) designed at least nine different series of prints depicting Tokyo landmarks. This scene shows Asakusa Bridge in the foreground with a double-decker horse drawn omnibus on the bridge and Yanagi Bridge in the background along the Kanda River.
The numbers 一五七 (157) are shown in the left margin. It is not known what these numbers reference. Other prints in this series do not show any numbers in the left margin.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō as Minamoto no Yoritomo and and Nakamura Fukusuke as Minamoto no Yoshitsune in Kaikei genji yuki no shirahata (会稽源氏雪白旗・市川 団十郎、源兵衛佐頼朝・中村 福助、源九郎義経)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō as Minamoto no Yoritomo and and Nakamura Fukusuke as Minamoto no Yoshitsune in Kaikei genji yuki no shirahata (会稽源氏雪白旗・市川 団十郎、源兵衛佐頼朝・中村 福助、源九郎義経)
text.text: The actor Nakamura Fukusuke (IV) in the role of Minamoto no Yoshitsune (left panel) and Ichikawa Danjūrō (IX) in the role of Minamoto no Yoritomo (right panel) in the play Kaikei genji yuki no shirahata 会稽源氏雪白旗 written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893).

media.caption: Wedding Protest, No. 12 appearing in the Ōsaka Nishikiga Shinbun (大阪錦画新聞・第十二号)

text.headline: Wedding Protest, No. 12 appearing in the Ōsaka Nishikiga Shinbun (大阪錦画新聞・第十二号)
text.text:
The wedding of a 15 year old bride is protested by her ex-husband in this print appearing in the "Osaka nishikiga shinbun" (Osaka Illustrated News), which featured woodblock illustrations of stories from various newspapers. The print's text was written by 正情堂九化 (name unread).
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 and 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability. Following their introduction in Tokyo, nishiki-e shinbun made their appearance in Osaka. The Osaka issued prints differed from their Tokyo counterparts in being half-size (chūban rather than ōban size).

media.caption: Old Man Receives Award appearing in the [Osaka] Nichinichi Shinbun, No. 9 (日々新聞・第九号)

text.headline: Old Man Receives Award appearing in the [Osaka] Nichinichi Shinbun, No. 9 (日々新聞・第九号)
text.text:
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.
This print features an old farmer who has received some type of reward from the government. It is print number 9 out of a known 32 prints appearing in the Osaka-based Nichinichi Shinbun (Daily News) which illustrated stories published in other papers. The red cartouche in the upper left hand corner provides the name of the paper 日々新聞 (Daily News) and the print number 第九号 (9).
Following their introduction in Tokyo, nishiki-e shinbun made their appearance in Osaka. The Osaka issued prints differed from their Tokyo counterparts in being half-size (chūban rather than ōban size).

media.caption: Mt. Fuji Time 25

text.headline: Mt. Fuji Time 25
text.text: Takahashi has given us at least five views of Mt. Fuji in this print and, possibly, 25 if we take the print's title literally. Wonderful embossing throughout and a barely visible reflection of Fuji in the upper right of the bottom margin.

media.caption:
Uzaemon in the role of Shirai Gonpachi
(羽左衛門 白井権八)

text.headline:
Uzaemon in the role of Shirai Gonpachi
(羽左衛門 白井権八)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Uzaemon XV in the role of Shirai Gonpachi in the play Hiyokuzuka 比翼塚, staged at the Kabuki-za, Tokyo on October 3, 1915. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Building (untitled)

text.headline: Building (untitled)
text.text: Tokuriki gives us an unidentified, likely Shōwa era, building absent any human presence.

media.caption: Castle (城)

text.headline: Castle (城)
text.text:
A castle rises above the trees and hills but this scene is stolen by the intense blue sky. The artist has reused the blocks from his earlier 1967 work titled Evening Over the Castle.
Hirosaki Castle, built in 1611, is the likely model for this print.

media.caption: Pulling Pine Shoots in a Garden, with a Suspension Bridge (小松曳園生之釣橋 Komatsubiki sonō no tsuribashi)

text.headline: Pulling Pine Shoots in a Garden, with a Suspension Bridge (小松曳園生之釣橋 Komatsubiki sonō no tsuribashi)
text.text:
"This triptych was a product of two major Meiji artists, Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889), who designed the scenic imagery, and Toyohara Kunichika, who focused on the characters. The women dressed in red hakama, a style of formal, pleated trousers, seen both in the left and center sheets, are engaged in the once traditional New Year’s custom of pulling young pines. Their garments and hairstyles evoke the imperial court of a millennium earlier when the lady-in-waiting known as Murasaki Shikibu wrote Tale of Genji. The elaborately attired gentleman (right) possibly portrays the novel’s central character, Prince Genji. But there is a twist: his unusual hairstyle appeared first in illustrations for the 1830s serialized parody, Rustic Genji, Fake Murasaki (偐紫田舎源氏) designed by Utagawa Kunisada, Kunichika’s teacher. To add further humorous time warps to the depiction, the British-designed Yamazato suspension bridge of 1870 spans the background."[1]
The artists have signed the print in the areas of their contribution. Kunichika’s signature in the right panel is proceeded with the two characters 人物 (“jinbutsu”) meaning “human figure by.”
Kunichika and Kyōsai were two of the most popular woodblock print artists of the 1870s. Contemporaries, they were “well-acquainted, but at times adversarial, companions.”[2] It was not unusual for publishers to have multiple artists work on different portions of a single print, each being assigned their design strength. Kyōsai and Kunichika first collaborated in 1875 on four single sheet prints in the series Collection of Famous Views of Modern Tokyo, published by the same publisher as this triptych. See this collection's print IHL.0688 for another collaborative print by these two artist.

[1] Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
[2] "Kawanabe Kyosai and Toyohara Kunichika," by Shigeru Oikawa appearing in Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), by Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999, p. 40, 42.

media.caption: View of Yorohibashi from Edobashi (江戸ばしよりよろひ橋の景)

text.headline: View of Yorohibashi from Edobashi (江戸ばしよりよろひ橋の景)
text.text: The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III (1842–1894) designed at least nine different series of prints showing similar depictions of Tokyo landmarks. This scene shows Edobashi Bridge (江戸橋) in the foreground with the First National Bank (daiichi kokuritsu ginko 一国立銀行), constructed in 1872 by Shimizu Kisuke II, in the background (partially covered by the title cartouche.)  As in all "famous view" prints of bridges from this era there is a great deal of hustle and bustle both on and below the bridge.

media.caption: Utō 善知鳥 (Birds of Sorrow)

text.headline: Utō 善知鳥 (Birds of Sorrow)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from Utô (Birds of Sorrow), by an unknown playwright (but sometimes attributed to Zeami.)
Play synopsis (The Ohtsuki Noh Theatre Foundation website http://www.noh-kyogen.com/story/english/Uto.pdf [not accessible 8-17-23]) - A species of seabird known as utô (petrel) is said to find its young by crying out “utō” to which they reply “yasukata”. Hunters imitate this cry to catch the young. The parent birds seeing their young taken are said to weep tears of blood. A traveling priest meets the spirit of a hunter who asks him to contact his wife and child and make an offering of a hat and cloak which he used to wear. When the priest does so, the spirit appears and, now bitterly regretting having killed against Buddhist precepts, tells of his desperate misery in Hell.

Illustrations of Noh is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints issued between 1897 and 1904. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Minamoto no Yoshiie (源義家)

text.headline: Minamoto no Yoshiie (源義家)
text.text:
Print number 7 (七), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the 11th century samurai, and famed archer, Minamoto no Yoshiie on horseback noticing the activity of a flock of geese who have been disturbed by the presence of enemy troops.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Illustration of Debate Over Invading Korea (征韓議論図 Seikangiran zu)

text.headline: Illustration of Debate Over Invading Korea (征韓議論図 Seikangiran zu)
text.text:
This 1877 print depicts the 1873 seikanron debates in the Meiji government's Court Council over whether to invade Korea for ignoring the diplomatic overtures of the Meiji government and "insulting" the Japanese nation. This print is one of many issued in 1877 depicting seikanron, whose outcome led to Saigō Takamori's resignation from the government. (Saigō would go on to lead the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion against the Meiji government.)
The leaders of opposing factions, Iwakura and Saigō, are prominently shown in the center panel with their partisans shown in the side panels. The debates were fueled by political infighting and the artist Suzuki Toshimoto (active c. 1877-1890s) captures the intensity of emotions.

media.caption: Reeves's Pheasant from Bairei's Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Earth (江南雉,ヲナガキジ・楳嶺百鳥画譜 續編 地 Onagakiji・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, chi)

text.headline: Reeves's Pheasant from Bairei's Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Earth (江南雉,ヲナガキジ・楳嶺百鳥画譜 續編 地 Onagakiji・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, chi)
text.text: A pheasant is fixated on, and appears ready to attack, a snake in this 2-page print, the 17th double plate in the second volume of Bairei Hyakuchō Gafu, Zokuhen (Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing).

media.caption: Red Capped Black Crane from Bairei's Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Earth (玄鶴, クロヅル 丹鳥 タソテウ・楳嶺百鳥画譜 續編 地 Kurozuru . . . ・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, chi)

text.headline: Red Capped Black Crane from Bairei's Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Earth (玄鶴, クロヅル 丹鳥 タソテウ・楳嶺百鳥画譜 續編 地 Kurozuru . . . ・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, chi)
text.text: Red-capped black cranes and their chicks roosting under a full moon are depicted in this two-page print, the 16th double-plate in the second volume of Bairei Hyakuchō Gafu, Zokuhen (Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing).

media.caption: Monkeys Living a Quiet Life in Seclusion

text.headline: Monkeys Living a Quiet Life in Seclusion
text.text: A double bookplate, removed from an unknown picture book (gafu 画譜) attributed to the artist Imao Keinen, best known for his kachō-ga, picturing monkeys romping about in a tree. The unread title of the print (partial and unconfirmed 幽棲美術應〓) is written in seal script in the right margin.

media.caption: Leader of the Kinpeibai Quarters (金瓶梅廓魁)

text.headline: Leader of the Kinpeibai Quarters (金瓶梅廓魁)
text.text:
A male customer coyly holds a fan while a bevy of courtesans vie for his attention. His gift indicating his choice is being presented to the courtesan on the far right by the young child.
"How to account for the popularity of woodblock prints in Japan ever since their commercialization in the late 1600s? Besides the colorful graphics, the fashions and glimpses of vicarious pleasures, the pictures often held multiple layers of meaning for people to ponder and relish. Scenes that looked like one thing might be cleverly hiding historic intrigues, inside jokes, parodies and more, offering a welter of ways to construe a scene. Here, the reference is to Jinpingmei (Kinpeibai in Japanese), one of China’s Six Classic Novels. To literati, the 16th-century epic marked a new development in narrative art, but to the general reader, it was salacious erotica. In the early 19th century, a serialized version of the novel with illustrations by Kunichika’s teacher, Utagawa Kunisada, had made it widely accessible, beginning a stream of take-offs and re-imaginings, like in this triptych." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

media.caption: Drunken Husband Striking His Wife from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club)

text.headline: Drunken Husband Striking His Wife from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club)
text.text:
A frontispiece woodblock illustration appearing in an unknown issue of the literary magazine Bungei kurabu 文芸倶楽部 (Literary Club), depicting a man about to strike a woman, possibly a husband about to strike his wife in a drunken rage.

THE LITERARY MAGAZINE BUNGEI KURABU
Bungei Kurabu 文芸倶楽部 was a very popular literary magazine published from 1895-1933 by Hakubunkan. It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan. In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

media.caption: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)

text.headline: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)
text.text:
Print number 12 (十二), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Endo Morito about to cut off the head of the Kesa Gozen, the faithful young wife of a palace guard, who he has mistaken for her husband.
The blocks for this print must have been damaged or lost as subsequent editions (see IHL.0950) have a completely new design. The re-designed print kept the same print number in the series, the same publishing date and the same descriptive scroll.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Priest on a Virtuous Path and Priest on a Debauched Path (善道へ導く僧  佛道を破る僧)

text.headline: Priest on a Virtuous Path and Priest on a Debauched Path (善道へ導く僧  佛道を破る僧)
text.text:
One of twenty prints from the series Moral Lessons through Pictures of Good and Evil picturing a virtuous priest who guides people along the proper path and a debauched priest who destroys the Buddhist path by seducing a woman.
About The Series Moral Lessons through Pictures of Good and Evil
These lessons in morality were originally issued as twenty single oban-size sheets containing two paired chūban-size prints contrasting "good" behavior with "bad" behavior. Over time many of the full-size oban sheets have been cut into separate chūban size prints.
Little figures portraying good souls (zendama) and evil souls (akudama) populate each print. The faces of the zendama and akudama show variations of the characters 善 (good) and 悪 (evil). These figures originated with the author and printmaker Santō Kyōden in his 1790 book Shingaku hayasomegusa (“Learning of the Mind [or Heart] in Fast Dyes”) and they started commonly appearing in woodblock prints shortly thereafter.
Each print in the series carries the signature "ryōdōjin Yoshitoshi giga." Ryōdōjin, a person who knows both ways, suggests that the artist, perhaps like ourselves, knows both the good and evil in himself.

media.caption: Famous Soldiers of Japan (日本 武名 伝図 Nihon bumei den)

text.headline: Famous Soldiers of Japan (日本 武名 伝図 Nihon bumei den)
text.text:
In commenting on this print Roger Keyes states “Most of the aka-e, or red prints, were revolting, but the same colors could produce great beauty when the subject touched the artist’s nobler feelings. The aniline red that Yoshitoshi used for this picture of General Saigo and the other heroes of the Satsuma Rebellion is as striking and effective as the background of the Red Room of Matisse. The portraits seem quite individual and were probably recognizable likenesses. Perhaps this was one of three or four prints that the government commissioned Yoshitoshi to design for display in foreign exhibitions. The artist took these commissions very seriously and spent considerable time on their execution. Yoshitoshi’s drawing had often been tentative and broad; like Daumier, he enjoyed exaggeration and expressive distortions more than literal likeness and detailed renderings. But there was also pleasure in drawing with a finer brush and greater delicacy. The faces of the officers are quite distinct and individual, and Yoshitoshi may have drawn them from life, or from photographs."
A Few Personal Comments on Keyes' Commentary - To my eye Yoshitoshi's renderings of these 15 men are a bit stiff. In many of the portraits the heads seem stuck on to the bodies. Perhaps several carvers were involved causing this strange effect. As to the likenesses of the portraits, I've located photographs or period renderings of all the subjects and there are definite likenesses between some of the photos and Yoshitoshi's drawings.
Left sheet: Prince Arisugawa Taruhito 有栖川宮熾仁親王 (1835–1895) (center top), Kabayama Sukenori 樺山資紀 (1837-1922) (upper left), Tani Tateki 谷干城 (1837-1911) (upper right), Kawamura Sumiyoshi 川村 純義 (1836-1904) (lower left), Nozu Shizuo 野津鎮雄 (1835-1880) (lower right)
Center sheet: Saigō Takamori 西郷隆盛 (1827-1877) (seated center), Kawaji Toshiyoshi 川路 利良 (1834-1879) (upper left), Torio Koyata 鳥尾 (1847-1905) (upper right), Prince Yamagata Aritomo 山縣 有朋 (1838–1922) (lower left), Miyoshi Shigeomi 三好 重臣 (1840-1900) (lower right)
Right sheet: Prince Higashifushimi Yoshiaki 少将 東伏見宮 (1846-1903) (center), Kazukatsu? Fukuhara 福原 和勝 (1846-1877) (upper left), Yamakawa Hiroshi 山川 浩 (1845-1898) (upper right), Saigō Tsugumichi 西郷 従道 (1843–1902) (lower left), Kuroda Kiyotaka 黑田 清隆 (1840-1900) (lower right)

media.caption: The Rising Moon (月の出 Tsuki no de)

text.headline: The Rising Moon (月の出 Tsuki no de)
text.text:
One of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫 (1929-?).
This design may be after a design originally created in 1913 for a series of postcards titled Postcards by Yumeji, Series 26: Women in Four Seasons (Moonrise).
In commenting on Yumeji's women, Lawrence Smith perceives "a subtle transference of European facial expression" even when the women are placed in traditional settings as in this work.
As in this case, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

media.caption: The Living Corpse (生ける屍 Ikerushikabane)

text.headline: The Living Corpse (生ける屍 Ikerushikabane)
text.text:
This print is one of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫 (1929-?).
This print's title "The Living Corpse" references Tolstoy's play of the same name written in 1900 which tells the story of a worthless husband's failure and final sacrifice. The print is a woodblock reproduction of Yumeji's 1917-1918 painting of the same title.

media.caption: Neighbor's Dream

text.headline: Neighbor's Dream
text.text: A vibrant and sparkling waterfall of turquoise striations fractured by black and violet organic shapes. "Between 1954 and 1973, Toshi made nearly three hundred nonobjective prints . . . that signal his desire to use color, shape, line, and texture expressively to capture the nature of human experience or the human experience of nature." - Source: A Japanese Legacy: Four Generations of Yoshida Family Artists, Laura W. Allen, Kendall H. Brown, Eugene M. Skibbe, et. al., The Minneapolis Institute of Arts, 2002, p. 76.

media.caption: Illustration of Royal Visit to Ueno Park Exhibition (上野公園博覧会行幸之図 Ueno kōen hakurankai gyōkō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of Royal Visit to Ueno Park Exhibition (上野公園博覧会行幸之図 Ueno kōen hakurankai gyōkō no zu)
text.text:
The emperor, empress and young crown prince are shown arriving at the Third National Industrial Exhibition in Ueno Park, which despite attracting over 1 million visitors was considered somewhat of a failure, held against a backdrop of recession and an influenza epidemic.
Five industrial expositions were held in Japan during the Meiji era, the first three in Ueno Park, Tokyo (1877, 1881, 1890), and the last two respectively in Kyoto (1895) and Osaka (1903). Printmakers were quick to create images of the domestic expositions to be sold as souvenirs. For another print showing the royal family arriving at the exhibition see Illustration of the Emperor and Empress Arriving at the Third National Industrial Exhibition (IHL.0079).

media.caption: Picture of Pyongyang Chinese Generals Capture and Surrender (平壤陷落清將生捕の圖)

text.headline: Picture of Pyongyang Chinese Generals Capture and Surrender (平壤陷落清將生捕の圖)
text.text: This print portrays the fierce fighting to capture Pyongyang (Pingyang), Korea from the Chinese during the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) and the resulting surrender and capture of five of the Chinese commanders defending the city.  Interestingly, the Chinese Commander Tso Pao-kwei (Zuo Baogui) shown in the orange robe did not surrender and was killed in the fighting, suggesting that, as in many war prints, facts were manipulated for propaganda purposes.

media.caption: Illustration of the Occupation of the Taku Forts and the Hard Fight of Navy Lt. Colonel Hattori (服部海軍 中佐奮戦 太沽砲台 占領之図 Hattori kaigun chūsa funsen Taiko hōdai senryō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Occupation of the Taku Forts and the Hard Fight of Navy Lt. Colonel Hattori (服部海軍 中佐奮戦 太沽砲台 占領之図 Hattori kaigun chūsa funsen Taiko hōdai senryō no zu)
text.text:
This 1900 Boxer Rebellion print gives us a bird's-eye view, through the smoke of the artillery shelling, of the attack on the Chinese Taku (Dagu) Forts on June 17, 1900. Lt. Colonel Hattori of the Japanese Navy, in black uniform with raised sword, is pictured directing the attack by Japanese troops on the North-West Fort. Hattori's rank is variously given in historical documents as commander, captain and lieutenant colonel. He was to die in the assault. Stick-like figures scattered throughout the print show soldiers of the Eight Nation Alliance battling Chinese army and Boxer irregular forces.
A correspondent from the British newspaper Telegraph recounted, "The first fort was taken by the Japanese, and the second by the British, and then the Germans and Russians secured the south fort . . . . After the forts were captured they were visited by the foreign officers. They presented a ghastly sight. The forts were one mass of ruins, and rivers of blood, mutilated bodies lying everywhere. The Chinese troops fled to Tientsin."

media.caption: The Dance Michiyuki tabiji no, hanamuko, an interact in the play Kanadehon Chūshingura with the characters Koshimoto Okaru, Fukuroku and Daikoku (道行旅路の花聟・仮名手本忠臣蔵・こし元おかる、福ろく、大こく)

text.headline: The Dance Michiyuki tabiji no, hanamuko, an interact in the play Kanadehon Chūshingura with the characters Koshimoto Okaru, Fukuroku and Daikoku (道行旅路の花聟・仮名手本忠臣蔵・こし元おかる、福ろく、大こく)
text.text:
This print is the left sheet of a triptych depicting the three main characters Okaru, Kampei and Bannai in the interact hengemono (multi-role dance) Michiyuki tabiji no hanamuko. This dance was staged after Act IV, scene 2, Uramon (“The Rear Gate of the Mansion”) of the kabuki play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers.) The actors and characters pictured in this left sheet are Nakamura Fukusuke (中村 福助) as Koshimoto Okaru (こし元おかる) and, in the insets, Nakamura Fukusuke, again, as Fukuroku (福ろく), one of the Seven Lucky Gods, and Bandō Mitsugorō VI (坂東 三津五郎) as Ōkoku (大こく), another of the Seven Lucky Gods.
This michiyuki or “travel-dance” was added to the play in 1833 and is very often performed separately. The dance depicts the lovers Okaru and Kanpei journeying to the home of Okaru’s parents in the country after Hangan’s death. Kanpei was the retainer who accompanied Hangan to the shogun’s mansion and he is now guilt ridden at his failure to protect his lord. He would take his own life to atone for his sin, but Okaru persuades him to wait. The couple are waylaid by the comical Sagisaki Bannai and his foolish men. They are working for Lord Moronō but Kanpei easily defeats them and they continue on their way.
The performance date for this piece was the 13th day of the 10th month, Ansei 4 (1857) and it was staged at the Morita-za.

media.caption: The True Story of Arashi from Osaka (浪花之嵐實録噺 Naniwa no Arashi jitsuroku hanashi）

text.headline: The True Story of Arashi from Osaka (浪花之嵐實録噺 Naniwa no Arashi jitsuroku hanashi）
text.text:
This print was likely issued as a nishiki-e shinbun (newspaper woodblock print) just before the release of the actor Arashi Rikaku III (嵐璃鶴) from jail in September 1874 for the March 1871 murder, by arsenic poisoning, of the money lender Kobayashi Kinpei, the patron of Rikaku's lover, the beautiful geisha Harada Kinu 原田 絹 (also known as Harada Okinu and Yoarashi [夜嵐 night storm] Okinu.)
Of course, the newspapers had a field day with the murder which became part of the genre of dokufu, so-called “poison women” tales. This case not only generated newspaper stories and prints but also a book by the journalist and gōkan writer Okamoto Kisen, titled Night Storm Okinu’s Flowery Dream of Revenge (Yoarashi Okinu hana do ada-yume, 1878) based on a poem Harada recited before her beheading.
As the story goes, Harada conspired with Arashi Rikaku III, by whom she was five months pregnant, to kill her patron Kobayashi Kinpei. Within several months they were both arrested, tried and sentenced to death. While awaiting execution, Rikaku's sentence was commuted to three years in prison because his "crime had been deemed insufficiently serious enough to warrant capital punishment" but Okinu was told, "For having committed a capital crime a while ago your sentence is still in effect and at this time you are expected to cross the Sanzu River" (the Buddhist equivalent of crossing the River Styx.) However, the government delayed her execution to allow her to give birth.
On February 20, 1872, Okinu’s head was cut off at the Kodukahara execution grounds, and displayed in public for several days. Rikakau was released from prison in September 1874 and went back to the kabuki theater where he rebuilt his career as the actor Ichikawa Gonjurō II, dying of pneumonia in 1904.
Three akudama and a single zendama occupy the diptych representing evil and good.

media.caption: Tsukuba Mountain Seen from Sakura River at Hitachi (常陸桜川より筑波山を臨む Hitachi Sakuragawa yori Tsukubasan o nozomu)

text.headline: Tsukuba Mountain Seen from Sakura River at Hitachi (常陸桜川より筑波山を臨む Hitachi Sakuragawa yori Tsukubasan o nozomu)
text.text:
Number 20 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō xue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
Kiyochika gives us a view of the double peaks of Tsukuba-san on a windswept day. The figures are leaning into the wind as they attend to their tasks and the tree attests to the force of the wind.

media.caption: Kyōto, Imperial Palace, End (京都・大尾・内裏 Kyōto・Daibi・Dairi)

text.headline: Kyōto, Imperial Palace, End (京都・大尾・内裏 Kyōto・Daibi・Dairi)
text.text:
The last print in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Dairi, the Imperial Palace in Kyōto. The characters 大尾 (daibi), "end", appear in the right-most yellow rectangular cartouche in the bottom left of the print telling us that we've arrived, after a long journey, in Kyoto, the Imperial Capital, at the Imperial Palace.
In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.
Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

media.caption: Odawara, Sakogawa, No. 10 (小田原・酒匂川・十)

text.headline: Odawara, Sakogawa, No. 10 (小田原・酒匂川・十)
text.text:
Print number 10 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting porters carrying a trunk and a traveler crossing the Sakagawa leading into Odawara the ninth station along the Tōkaidō. Another traveler is mounting a porter on the far shore and four porters bear a traveler in a litter. Odawara was the first post station in the castle town that travelers came to when they exited Edo (modern-day Tokyo).

text.headline: Sakanoshita, Fudesute, No. 49 (坂ノ下・筆捨やま・四十九)
text.text:
Print number 49 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Fudesute peak in Sakanoshita the forty-eighth station along the Tōkaidō. Sakanoshita is located in the present-day city of Kameyama, in Mie Prefecture, Japan.
The artist provides us a view of Fudesute peak as it might be seen by travelers on the Tōkaidō but, interestingly, no travelers are seen in this print. Fudesute, means literally "to throw away the brush," as its extreme beauty and strangeness is beyond our ability to paint.

text.headline: Goyu, No. 36 (御油・夕景・三十六)
text.text:
Print number 36 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting travelers in sedge hats entering Goyu at dusk. It appears as though the travelers are hurrying away from courtesans who are seen grasping at them.
Goyu was the thirty-fifth station along the Tōkaidō. Goyu-shuku was established in 1601, at the behest of Tokugawa Ieyasu. At its most prosperous, there were four honjin (inns) in the post town, though there were never less than two at any point.

text.headline: Seki, Honjin, No. 48 (関・本陣・四十八)
text.text:
Print number 48 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Seki the forty-seventh station along the Tōkaidō. The area around Seki-juku was always a major intersection for travel. During the Edo period, it was a lively post town, because both the Isebetsu Kaidō 伊勢別街道 and the Yamato Kaidō 大和街道 intersected with the Tōkaidō here.
In this print, an arriving daimyō (seated on the litter) and his retinue are being greeted by the owner and staff of the honjin where they will spend the night. The draperies are decorated with the family crest of the arriving daimyō.

text.headline: Chiryū, Umaichi, No. 40 (地鯉鮒・馬市・四十)
text.text:
Print number 40 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting, Chiryū the thirty-ninth station along the Tōkaidō. During the Edo period, Chiryū was the westernmost post town in Mikawa Province. Three hundred and thirty kilometers from Nihonbashi, the start of the Tōkaidō, it took approximately 10 days to get there.
Chiryū-juku was well known as a horse trading town and the artist has pictured horses with their minders in a grassy field.

media.caption: Greedy Merchant, No. 7

text.headline: Greedy Merchant, No. 7
text.text: The prints in this series were issued in pairs and show comparisons between good (appropriate) behavior and bad (inappropriate) behavior. In this print which would have been the top print, if it had not been separated from its counterpart, we see a greedy merchant, abacus in hand, being encouraged by six bad souls (akudama) identified by the character 悪 (badness, vice) in the rounds of their faces. In its counterpart, the bottom print, (see IHL.0527) five good souls (zendama) identified by the character ‘zen’ 善 (goodness, virtue) are assisting the merchant in his shop.

media.caption: Solicitous Merchant, No. 7

text.headline: Solicitous Merchant, No. 7
text.text: The prints in this series were issued in pairs and show comparisons between good (appropriate) behavior and bad (inappropriate) behavior. In this print which would have been the bottom print, if it had not been separated from its counterpart, we see five good souls  (zendama) identified by the character ‘zen’ 善 (goodness, virtue) assisting a good merchant in his shop. In its counterpart of good behavior (see IHL.0526) we see a merchant displaying bad 悪 behavior.

media.caption: Illustration of the Attack on the Battery at Weihaiwei (威海衛鹿角嘴砲台攻撃之図)

text.headline: Illustration of the Attack on the Battery at Weihaiwei (威海衛鹿角嘴砲台攻撃之図)
text.text: Chinese soldiers' bodies fly as Japanese warships pound the Chinese forts defending Weihaiwei (Ikaiei in Japanese) as Japanese forces storm the battery. The naval port of Weihaiwe fell to the Japanese on February 17, 1895. The Germans had helped the Chinese Qing government build the naval base at Weihaiwei and they designed and equipped the batteries.

media.caption: Illustration of the Viewing of the Captured Chinese Warship Chinen at Yokosuka Naval Port (横須賀軍港鎮遠号観覧之図 Yokosuka gankō Chinengō kanran no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Viewing of the Captured Chinese Warship Chinen at Yokosuka Naval Port (横須賀軍港鎮遠号観覧之図 Yokosuka gankō Chinengō kanran no zu)
text.text:
The Chinese battleship Chinen 鎮遠 (Chinese: Zhenyuan 鎮遠; also romanized as Chenyuen) in its new home port at the Yokosuka navy yard in Kanagawa Prefecture after her capture following the Weihaiwei siege on February 17, 1895. The Chinen was a German-built Chinese Beiyang Fleet turret ship built with 14-inch (360 mm) thick armor and modern Krupp guns, superior to any in the Imperial Japanese Navy at the time. She would see service in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) and be scrapped in 1914.
"After the surrender at Weihaiwei, the Chenyuen [Chinen] was taken to Yokosuka, where the public was invited to see the 7,300-ton ironclad. One war reporter, Nagamatsu of the Jiji Shimpo wrote, 'Since the beginning of the war, all over Japan, men and women, young and old, have spoken of the Chinese ironclads Chenyuen and Tingyuen. Now that the Chenyuen has been captured and brought to Japan, it is understandable that everyone should want to see it. Before the public opening, Japanese naval officers constantly had to entertain visitors aboard. On August 5, the ship was opened to the public. Throngs from Tokyo and Yokohama, and even some who must travel overnight, are suddenly crowding Yokosuka. Already on the fourth, there was not a vacant room in town. Earlier, in Nagasaki, so many people visited the Chenyuen that the waterline sank one foot. Perhaps it will be worse in Yokosuka; the train between Shinbashi in downtown Tokyo and Yokosuka has been packed.'" - Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 44.

media.caption: Captain Matsuzaki Crossing the Anjō River and Advancing into the Enemy's Territory  (松嵜大尉 挺オ安城川ヲ渡リ敵中ニ進厶圖)

text.headline: Captain Matsuzaki Crossing the Anjō River and Advancing into the Enemy's Territory  (松嵜大尉 挺オ安城川ヲ渡リ敵中ニ進厶圖)
text.text: Captain Matsuzaki is captured in a similar pose in this book print (kuchi-e) as in the artist's triptych The Great Battle of the Ansong Ford: The Valor of Captain Matsuzaki Crossing Anjo (IHL.0168).

media.caption: Memoirs of Fallen Flowers, frontispiece from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 7, No.5. (落花録・文藝倶楽部 第七巻, 第五号)

text.headline: Memoirs of Fallen Flowers, frontispiece from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 7, No.5. (落花録・文藝倶楽部 第七巻, 第五号)
text.text:
This woodblock illustration (kuchi-e) portrays a young woman in her summer robe (yukata) drying herself after bathing. This print was the frontispiece for volume 7, no. 5 of the literary magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Arts Club), published in Meiji 34th year (1901) which carried, either in its entirety or a portion thereof, the novel Rakkaroku 落花録 (Memoirs of Fallen Flowers) by the writer Suiin Emi (1869-1934).

THE LITERARY MAGAZINE BUNGEI KURABU
Bungei Kurabu 文芸倶楽部 was a very popular literary magazine published from 1895-1933 by Hakubunkan. It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan. In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

media.caption: The Story of Wankyū, Vol. 2, frontispiece from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 6, No.1. (椀久物語・文藝倶楽部 第六巻, 第一号 Wankyū Monogatari dai-nibu・Bungei kurabu dai rokukan, dai ichigō)

text.headline: The Story of Wankyū, Vol. 2, frontispiece from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 6, No.1. (椀久物語・文藝倶楽部 第六巻, 第一号 Wankyū Monogatari dai-nibu・Bungei kurabu dai rokukan, dai ichigō)
text.text:
This print was the frontispiece for volume 6, no. 1 of the literary magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Arts Club), published January 1, 1900, which featured the story "Wankyū monogatari, The Story of the Dish-Potter Kyūbei," by Kōda Rohan 幸田露伴 (1867-1947). In this illustration for the story, a potter inspects a full Noborigama kiln. An inset shows an elegant bijin in the style of the Muromachi period.

"Wankyū monogatari, The Story of the Dish-Potter Kyūbei," is based on the true 17th century story of a potter and a courtesan, their love affair and involvement in trade espionage. "A Kyoto potter Kyūbei begins to seek the favors of a courtesan Matsuyama, after he learns that her father is a debt collector from the Kyushu potters' guild, whose secret of gold-painted porcelain is jealously guarded. Through the help of Matsuyama, he finally induces her unsuspecting father to confide the secret. Kyūbei succeeds in producing a new porcelain even superior to the Kyushu products, but loses his mind after Matsuyama's father is executed for revealing the trade secret inadvertently. He recovers later, eventually to settle down to a happy married life with Matsuyama." - Source: Kōda Rohan, Chieko Irie Mulhern, Twayne Publishers, 1977, p. 127.

It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan. In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

media.caption: Making Chinese Soldiers Shiver (清兵の冷かされ Shinpei no hiyakasare)

text.headline: Making Chinese Soldiers Shiver (清兵の冷かされ Shinpei no hiyakasare)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In this print Chinese soldiers are shivering before a snowman with the head of a Japanese general. The inscription explains that the generals of the Japanese army, Aritomo Yamagata 山縣有朋 and Ōyama Iwao 大山巌 both have the character "mountain" (山 yama) in their names and are therefore so immovable, impressive and insanely strong that the weak soldiers of the Qing dynasty tremble with fear. There is some wordplay going in the inscription having to do with the same Japanese characters making up the expressions "making someone cold" and "mocking someone."

media.caption: Viewing the Zhenyuan (Chin’en-gō goran)

text.headline: Viewing the Zhenyuan (Chin’en-gō goran)
text.text:
This print is one of at least thirty-four prints issued as part of the series Comical Art Exhibit of the Sino-Japanese War (Nissei sensō shōraku gakai) by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915).

This print satirizes the gawkers gathered to see the Chinese Battleship Zhenyuan [ Chinen 鎮遠] captured by the Japanese Combined Fleet during the First Sino-Japanese War Battle of Port Weihaiwei on February 17, 1895, and then towed back to Japan. Zhenyuan and her sister ship Dingyuan were built in Germany in 1882 to be the most powerful battleships in East Asia. In the foreground are a kimono-clad cat (neko) and rice paddle (shakushi) who regard the monumental ship with amazement. This print humorously represents the proverb, "neko mo shakushi mo," literally, "even the cat and the rice paddle" roughly equivalent to "every Tom, Dick and Harry." - Source:
As with his more famous comic series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs (Hyakusen hyakushō), this series parodied events of the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895 and disparaged the Chinese.

media.caption: Russo-Japanese War Pictorial part 6: Fierce Fight in the Vicinity of Pyongyang (日露戦争画報其六:平壌附近激戦 Nichiro sensōgahō roku: heijō fukin gekisen)

text.headline: Russo-Japanese War Pictorial part 6: Fierce Fight in the Vicinity of Pyongyang (日露戦争画報其六:平壌附近激戦 Nichiro sensōgahō roku: heijō fukin gekisen)
text.text:
From the print's title, it is safe to assume that it is one of a series by the artist Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) depicting battles in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905).
It is unknown what battle is depicted, but the title does tells us that this fierce battle happened in the vicinity of Pyongyang (Pingyang), possibly referring to the following incident, cited in the 1906 account of the war by Great Britain's War Office.
"As a preliminary step, however, Pingyang, the most important town in North Korea, lying one hundred and fifty miles, or twelve days’ march, north of Seoul, had been already garrisoned. On the 21st February a party of twenty Japanese infantry with a commissariat officer arrived there, and drove off a small body of Cossacks who attempted to enter the town… [A]nother company of infantry, with a commissariat officer was sent north from the capital , on the 15th, to prepare four line-of-communication posts. By means of this arrangement the cavalry of the 12th Division reached Pingyang from Seoul on the 23rd and assured the safety of the little garrison." - Source: The Russo-Japanese War, Part I, compiled by The General Staff, War Office (Great Britain), London, 1906, p. 45.

media.caption: Iwami Province: Mount Takazuno, Salt Beach (石見国・高津山汐浜  Iwami no kuni・Takazunoyama Shiohama)

text.headline: Iwami Province: Mount Takazuno, Salt Beach (石見国・高津山汐浜  Iwami no kuni・Takazunoyama Shiohama)
text.text:
Print number 47 四十七 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints. The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
This print pictures the harvesting of salt on the beach below Mount Takazuno. Hiroshige III has been inspired by (or just copied) the scene from his master Utagawa Hiroshige I's 1853 print Iwama Province, Salt Beaches at Takatsu from the series Famous Views in the Sixty Odd Provinces.
Iwami (石見国; -no kuni) was an old province of Japan in the area that is today the western part of Shimane Prefecture. Iwami bordered Aki, Bingo, Izumo, Nagato, and Suō provinces.
The price of the print in rin (rin = 0.001 yen), 定價壹弐五厘 (fixed price of 125 rin) is given beneath the date in the rectangular cartouche in the left margin.

media.caption: Capturing Falcons in Iyo Province, figure 1 (伊豫國鷹捕之図 一)

text.headline: Capturing Falcons in Iyo Province, figure 1 (伊豫國鷹捕之図 一)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the capturing of falcons using kasumi-ami in Iyo Province (伊予国, Iyo no kuni) which is now part of Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku.
Kasumi-ami 霞網 are stationary mist nets perfected for bird trapping in Japan in the late 1800s. Originally made of cotton or silk thread, modern mist nets are constructed of black nylon. Most are 6 meters long and 3 meters high. These delicate, lightweight nets, which “disappear” visually against most backgrounds, are used both with and without mechanical or live tethered lures. Mist nets are firmly suspended end-to-end from bamboo, metal, or fiberglass poles, typically in parallel or angled arrays. Nets are placed in areas that are likely to attract feeding migrants, and in many instances raptors are attracted to the nets by already-captured passerines. - Source: Migrating Raptors of the World: Their Ecology and Conservation, Keith L. Bildstein, Cornell University Press, 2006, p. 49-50.
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1508.

media.caption: Going Bankrupt (清代限りShindai kagiri)

text.headline: Going Bankrupt (清代限りShindai kagiri)

media.caption: Harvesting Lacquer in Mikawa Province (同国 [三河] 漆取之図)

text.headline: Harvesting Lacquer in Mikawa Province (同国 [三河] 漆取之図)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the tapping of lacquer 漆 trees in Mikawa Province. Mikawa Province (三河国, Mikawa no kuni) is an old province in the area that today forms the eastern half of Aichi Prefecture.

media.caption: Mandarin Orange Plantation in Kii Province (紀伊国蜜柑山畑之図)

text.headline: Mandarin Orange Plantation in Kii Province (紀伊国蜜柑山畑之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts workers harvesting mandarin oranges in a terraced grove in Kii province. Kii Province (紀伊国, Kii no Kuni), or Kishū (紀州), was a province of Japan in the part of Honshū that is today Wakayama Prefecture, as well as the southern part of Mie Prefecture. Kishū has been a major orange growing area for centuries. Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan describes a scene much as depicted in this print. "We are now in the district of Arida [in Kishū province], notable as the greatest orange-producing centre in Japan; and as we proceed, we find all the lower slopes of the wide sheltered valleys covered with orange-groves.
See IHL.1919 for the crêped version of the print.

media.caption: White Sugar Production in Sanuki Province (讃岐国白糖製造之図)

text.headline: White Sugar Production in Sanuki Province (讃岐国白糖製造之図)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts workers refining white sugar in Sanuki province. Sanuki (讃岐国,) was an old province of Japan on the island of Shikoku, with the same boundaries as modern Kagawa Prefecture. It faced the Inland Sea and bordered on Awa and Iyo Provinces. Across Naruto strait it bordered Awaji Province too. Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan, notes that "The chief production of this province of Sanuki are popularly known as ‘the three white things’ (sam-paku), viz, salt, sugar, and cotton. The sugar industry is modern, having been introduced from Satsuma only half a century ago." But he also describes scenes more like the one pictured above. "The cultivation of the rich plain includes indigo and sugar; and those curious in such matters will find establishments here and there where sugar-refining is carried on with very primitive machinery."

media.caption: Camphor Manufacture in Hyūga Province (日向国樟脳製之図)

text.headline: Camphor Manufacture in Hyūga Province (日向国樟脳製之図)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts workers preparing camphor 樟脳 in Hyūga province, an old province of Japan on the east coast of Kyūshū, corresponding to the modern Miyazaki Prefecture. Hyūga bordered on Bungo, Higo, Ōsumi, and Satsuma Provinces. Camphor was widely produced throughout Kyūshū Island.

media.caption: The Battle at Tianzhuangdai: The Gathering of Eleven Generals (田庄台之役・将校十一名 Denshōdai no yaku・shōkō jūichimei dōsho ni kai su)

text.headline: The Battle at Tianzhuangdai: The Gathering of Eleven Generals (田庄台之役・将校十一名 Denshōdai no yaku・shōkō jūichimei dōsho ni kai su)
text.text:
Nathan Chaikin comments, "one of Gekkō's masterpieces. The range of colours, totally his, the beautiful conception of the 'end of the day,' the raging fire and the tormented pine trees soon to burst into flames, the whiteness of the snow, and a certain sense of futility pervading the morning, the feeling of wastefulness of it all. Yes, a very great artist, a master . . . .
"The entire staff, an imposing one, stands still as the city is burning. Their names as they appear on the script: Yamaji, Chūjō (Lieutenant-General); Oshima Hisanao, Shōsō (Major-General); Nozu, Taishō (Marshal); Katsura, Chūjō; Nogi, Shōsō; Nishi, Shōsō; Oshima Yoshimasa, Shōsō; Oseko, Shōsō; Kuroda, Shōsō; Oku (perhaps Okuyama?), Chūjō; Ogawa, Shōsō.
"This is the end of the road for the Japanese. The Chinese retreated to North Chinchou (or Chinchow), and the country was now clear of them on both sides of the Liao river for a distance of 30 to 40 miles northeast of Yingkow (or Yingtzu), whilst on the Liaoyang road their most advanced post was north-east of Anchanchan." Source: The Sino-Japanese War, Nathan Chaikin, self-published, 1983, p. 97.

media.caption: Sino-Japanese War: Japanese Military Might Captures Pyongyang (日清戰爭・日勢平壌勝捕圖 Nisshin sensō・Nissei Heijō shōhō zu)

text.headline: Sino-Japanese War: Japanese Military Might Captures Pyongyang (日清戰爭・日勢平壌勝捕圖 Nisshin sensō・Nissei Heijō shōhō zu)
text.text:
In late July 1894, Japan began military operations in Korea against China, which had established itself as Korea's suzerain in 1860. Within a month Pyongyang was China's last position held in Korea and by September 16 they had lost this city to a Japanese assault.
"Ogata Gekko, a leading print designer and illustrator, here describes a scene in which Japanese soldiers have captured several Chinese soldiers in the foreground. One has just been pushed over the edge of the wall on the roof of a building they were defending. In the distance, a fierce battle rages, giving rise to billowing smoke and the orange streaks of gunfire." - Source: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, print label.

media.caption: Illustration of the Surrender of Port Arthur (旅順口陷落之圖 Ryojunkō kanraku no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Surrender of Port Arthur (旅順口陷落之圖 Ryojunkō kanraku no zu)
text.text:
While seventeen Chinese forts defended Port Arthur, all "heavily armed with powerful Krupp and Armstrong guns,” it took the Japanese forces under five hours to capture them.
The attack was scheduled for November 21, at 6:50 a.m., with all siege guns roaring at the same time, awakening the Chinese garrisons in the Itzu-shan Fort. At 8 a.m. the fort was in Japanese hands (2nd Infantry Sakura Brigade), unopposed; at 8:10, all three forts were taken. At 11:10, the Pine Tree Hill for fell; at 11:25 a.m. the Two Dragon Hill fort was captured; all the other forts were abandoned by their garrisons.
"With the fall of Port Arthur, the Japanese were in possession of the finest dockyards in the Far East and a splendid naval base of operation at the enemy's back doors. Japanese losses: 18 killed, 258 wounded and 8 missing. The Chinese lost over 1,000 men." - Source: The Sino-Japanese War, Nathan Chaikin, self-published, 1983, p. 82-83

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 5 (日清戦闘畫報 第五編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daigo hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 5 (日清戦闘畫報 第五編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daigo hen)
text.text: Volume 5 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895. Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 8 (日清戦闘畫報 第 八編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daihachi hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 8 (日清戦闘畫報 第 八編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daihachi hen)
text.text: Volume 8 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

media.caption: Things Suspended in the Sky (そらにかかるもの)

text.headline: Things Suspended in the Sky (そらにかかるもの)
text.text:
This print is the frontispiece in the catalogue raisonné of Onchi's prints (and some of his drawings) titled "Prints of Onchi Kōshirō," Keishosha Ltd., 1975 (a limited edition of 670 copies.) The catalogue raisonné titles the print correctly in Japanese そらにかかるもの (Things Suspended from the Sky) but then mistitles the print's English title as Shadow Falling From the Sky, a different print by Onchi.
Reprinted by Yoneda Minoru for the catalogue raisonné, likely under the auspices of the artist's family, the print originally appeared in issue III of the small print and poetry magazine "Tsukuhae" (Moonglow), a collaborative effort of Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), Shizuo Fujimori (1891-1943) and Tanaka Kyokichi (1892-1915). This image was again reprinted in 1989 by Onchi's son, Onchi Kunio 恩地邦郎 (1920-2001).

media.caption: Another Garland of Swashbuckling Heroes of the Shrimp Barbershop (又注連餝俠客之海老床 Mata shime kazari isami no ebi doko)

text.headline: Another Garland of Swashbuckling Heroes of the Shrimp Barbershop (又注連餝俠客之海老床 Mata shime kazari isami no ebi doko)
text.text:
Three actors stand in front of a barbershop’s shoji decorated with a painting of a giant shrimp (ebi). No specific play is referenced in the print, perhaps making it an advertisement for the Shrimp Barbershop. This is not as strange as it seems, as kabuki stars spent hours in the barbershop having their sakayaki (the shaved part of the forehead) looked after. Perhaps the Shrimp Barbershop business card read “Hairstylists to the Stars."
Two translations of the print's title cartouche "Mata shime kazari isami no ebi doko" (又注連餝俠客之海老床) have been suggested, "Another Story of Chivalrous Guys (otokodate) at Ebidoko Barber Shop in the New Year Season" and "Another Garland of Swashbuckling Heroes of the Shrimp Barbershop."
The actors pictured, while not named in cartouches on the print, would have been recognizable to the public by the patterns and the partial letters of their stage names visible on their garments. From left to right: Ichimura Uzaemon XIII (possibly Uzaemon XIV), according to the pattern of his clothes; Kawarazaki Gonjūrō by the half-hidden stage name on his collar and Bando Shinsui by the two kanji characters 薪水 (Shinsui) on his robe.

media.caption: Iga Province: Ueno Nagata River (伊賀国・上野 長田川 Iga no kuni・Ueno Nagatagawa)

text.headline: Iga Province: Ueno Nagata River (伊賀国・上野 長田川 Iga no kuni・Ueno Nagatagawa)
text.text:
Print number 6 六 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints. The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
This print pictures the village of Ueno 上野 and a bridge over the Nagata River 長田川. The village was located near Iga Ueno Castle, built around 1570 and known for having the highest stone wall in Japan. Hiroshige III has been inspired by (or just copied) his master Utagawa Hiroshige I's 1853 print Iga Province: Ueno from the series Famous Places in the Sixty Odd Provinces.

media.caption: Blue and white striations (fan design sample)

text.headline: Blue and white striations (fan design sample)
text.text:
Fan design samples such as this print were created as marketing tools for deluxe fan makers. While the fan design samples in this collection were likely created in the Taishō and early Shōwa eras (c. 1912-1940), fan design samples date back to the Meiji era. They showed the season's available designs, commissioned from some of the most eminent artists of the day. The designs range from Art Deco to traditional genre scenes. Once the season was over, the sample fans and books of fans were sold. Most of the samples in this collection do not carry a signature or seal and the artists will be forever unknown, but some famous names do appear on several of the prints, such as Fukuda Heihachirō 福田平八郎 (1892-1974), a nihonga painter who was awarded the Order of Culture, and Yokoyama Taikan 横山大観 (1868-1958), another famous nihonga artist and Order of Culture winner.
The shape of these prints indicate they were designs for folding fans (sensu 扇子, or ōgi 扇 as they are also known.) While often described as "woodblock prints", I believe most of these sample designs are hand painted or inked rather than printed, as on at least one sample a brush hair is embedded in the ink/paint and on several others the ink or paint has overlapped the paper edge and bled onto the back of the paper.
Some of the prints carry inventory numbers; some bear a cartouche with the word nambu (literally, "southern region" and possibly the name of a company) written in kanji 南部 or kana なんぶ, and some bear a fan-shaped cartouche with the kanji character 業 ("karma" or simply the character for "industry" or "business") inside it, possibly the trademark of another fan company.

media.caption: Mustache Shaving, Opposite Mirrors, Laughing Child, Crying Child (髭すりhigesori, 合せ鏡 awasekagami , 笑ってゐる児 warateiru ko, 泣て居る児 naiteiru ko)

text.headline: Mustache Shaving, Opposite Mirrors, Laughing Child, Crying Child (髭すりhigesori, 合せ鏡 awasekagami , 笑ってゐる児 warateiru ko, 泣て居る児 naiteiru ko)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints created by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915), each showing four faces in caricature. The first eight prints were issued in 1882 and published by Hara Taneaki under the series title Thirty-Two Faces, New Edition. The series was so popular that it led to a second series in early 1883 titled One Hundred Faces: Supplement to Thirty-Two Faces (Sanjūni sō tsuika hyakumensō), some of which were published by Hara, the remainder by Morimoto Junzaburō.
"[T]he theme of "one hundred faces" (hyakumensō) came originally from a vaudeville act of the late Edo period in which a performer imitated emotional states and social types by rapidly changing facial expression with various props." Kiyochika's prints were so popular that they "led to a staging of the series by the kabuki actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX at the Shintomiza Theater on April 23, 1883 . . . ." - Source: Kiyochika: Artist of Meiji Japan, Henry D. Smith II, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, 1988, p. 60-61.

media.caption: Illustration of Imperial Visit of Mikado Ingyō to Princess Sotoshi (允恭帝衣通姫之許ニ御幸之図 Ingyōtei Soto'ori hime no tokoro ni gyokō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of Imperial Visit of Mikado Ingyō to Princess Sotoshi (允恭帝衣通姫之許ニ御幸之図 Ingyōtei Soto'ori hime no tokoro ni gyokō no zu)
text.text:
This print depicts a night-time visit by the fifth-century Emperor Ingyō (c. 411-453) to his lover Princess Sotoshi no iratsume (aka Sotori), the younger sister of Empress Oshisaka no Ōnakatsuhime. In order not to offend the Empress, the Emperor provided a residence for Princess Sotoshi far away from the Empress, first in Fujiwara near Asuka and then in Chinu in Kawachi on the Inland Sea, and made secret visits to her. (Of course the Empress knew about the visits.)
In the eighth year, spring, the second month, he (the Emperor) went to Fujiwara and secretly observed the demeanor of Lady Sotori. That evening Lady Sotori was alone, yearning for the Emperor. Unaware that the Emperor had come, she composed a song, saying:

Tonight is the night
My young love will come to me:
Little bamboo crab
Spider’s antics make it clear.
Oh, very clear tonight!

This poem made Princess Sotori famous, and she later became a deity of poetry. - Source: A Waka Anthology: The Gem-Glistening Cup, Edwin A. Cranston, 1993, Stanford University Press, p. 85.

media.caption: Wasteful Man and Frugal Man, No. 8

text.headline: Wasteful Man and Frugal Man, No. 8
text.text: The top print shows a wasteful man being encouraged to spend his money at a geisha house, by eight bad souls (akudama) identified by the character 悪 (badness, vice) in the rounds of their faces.  In the bottom five good souls  (zendama) identified by the character ‘zen’ 善 (goodness, virtue) assist a frugal man who is eating at a small restaurant and giving alms to a beggar.

media.caption: Map of Ise Shrine Pilgrimage Route (伊勢参宮順路之図)

text.headline: Map of Ise Shrine Pilgrimage Route (伊勢参宮順路之図)
text.text:
In this 1892 woodblock printed bird's-eye view of Ise Jingū (伊勢神宮), the most important shrine in the Shintō shrine hierarchy, we see pilgrims arriving by foot, by jinrikisha, and by wagon. A network of travel agents (pilgrimage oshi), accommodations and entertainments existed to help pilgrims arrive and enjoy their visit. Printed guidebooks, route maps and various ephemera were printed and published to support the traveler.
In this map, similar to so many other shrine maps published each year, the important shrines, gates, fences (tamagaki), and landmarks in the massive Ise shrine complex and nearby areas are shown and named in the yellow and red rectangular cartouches. Being hastily and cheaply produced, it is difficult to read many of over forty identifying yellow and red cartouches. The right half of the print shows shrines and landmarks within Naikū (内宮), the Inner Shrine, official name Kōtai Jingū (皇大神宮), dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu Ōmikami, and the left half of the print shows shrines and landmarks within Gekū (外宮), the Outer Shrine, official name Toyouke Daijingū (豊受大神宮), dedicated to the goddess of grain Toyouke Okami who offers sacred food to Amaterasu. In the foreground we see the long Miyagawa Bridge (宮川橋), crowded with pilgrims, leading from Yamada Town to the shrine precincts. Pictured in the center of the print is the sacred Uji Bridge (宇治橋) over the Isuzugawa River (五十鈴川), leading to Naikū, the inner sanctum of Ise Jingū. Crossing the Uji Bridge took pilgrims from the the secular to the sacred world.
The Rising Sun (a symbol of Amaterasu), Mount Fuji, the famous Wedded Rocks of Meotoiwa in Futamiura (二見浦) and the Hinjitsukan (賓日館), built in 1887 as a rest house for important visitors to the Grand Shrine of Ise, are seen in the distance. There is no scaling to the map and the two shrine complexes are actually a few kilometers apart and the Wedded Rocks over 10 kilometers from the Inner Shrine.
Published five years before the completion of the privately owned Sangū Railway and the opening up of Yamada Station on November 11, 1897, which "brought pilgrims into Yamada from across Japan with a speed and comfort heretofore unimaginable," it is likely that the number of pilgrims visiting was still relatively low compared to pre-Meiji times. - Source: A Social History of the Ise Shrines Divine Capital, Mark Teeuwen, John Breen, Bloomsbury Publishing, 2017, p. 177.
After the arrival of the railway, maps of Ise Jingu would invariably include a depiction of a steam train.

media.caption: Evening at Sōemon-chō, Osaka (大坂宗右衛門町の夕 Ōsaka Sōemon-chō no yū)

text.headline: Evening at Sōemon-chō, Osaka (大坂宗右衛門町の夕 Ōsaka Sōemon-chō no yū)
text.text:
"Deep twilight over this central Osaka entertainment district, once bustling with hundreds of teahouses, heightens a sense of nostalgia. Sōemon-chō was known for its atmosphere of pleasure with kimono-clad geisha, good food and sake. With nightfall, strains of shamisen music and paper lanterns glowing below the eaves composed a milieu now mostly vanished. The print evokes a melancholic mood through dusky tones that reveal the shadows of two women bidding a customer farewell, while another couple quietly ambles along the road." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
According to Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, "Following WWII, the row of houses in the Sōemon district changed so much that the atmosphere and richness in sentiment as seen in this picture has long disappeared. The image recalls the jōruri [narrative musical form accompanied by the shamisen] of the playwright Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1653-1724): paper lanterns hang under the eaves, burning quietly at dusk, the shadows of the lights cast by wickets upon the street make the surrounding darkness more profound. The composition of the row houses, the couple walking together, two kamuro (attendants to a courtesan) and the shadow of the figure in the distance are exceptional. The block-cutting was done by Watanabe Tadasu." The entry from the catalog to the Toledo Art Museum Show of 1936 notes "Blocks 20; superimposed printings, 25."
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Shadow No. 11 (影法師 kagebōshi No. 11)

text.headline: Shadow No. 11 (影法師 kagebōshi No. 11)
text.text: Hagiwara created at least thirteen prints for this series, all which use the motif of a newspaper background with superimposed silhouetted figures. The figures in this print are very 70s, bell bottoms and all. The newspaper background is mirrored, leading me to wonder whether Hagiwara somehow incorporated actual newsprint into the printing block. The two prints from this series in this collection appear to be created with traditional woodblock techniques some with embossing.

media.caption: Hakone-no-Yama (箱根の山)

text.headline: Hakone-no-Yama (箱根の山)
text.text:
This song sheet for the song "Hakone-no-Yama" (Senow song sheet No. 365), arranged by the composer and conductor Yamada Kōsaku 山田耕筰 (1886-1965), with cover design (a color lithograph) by Takehisa Yumeji (1884-1934), a leading figure in the Taishō Romanticism movement, was issued in 1924 by the music publisher Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.

In 1910 the music publisher Senoo (Senow) Ongaku Shuppansha, headed by Senoo Kōjirō 妹尾幸次郎 (1891-1961), also known as Senoo Kōyō 妹尾幸陽, began issuing musical scores, the majority of them by Western composers. Over 1000 scores for classical and popular music, including children’s music, were issued, many under the titles “Senoo Gakufu” (セノオ楽譜) and “Senoo Shin-kouta" (セノオ新小唄). From 1916 until 1929, Yumeji designed over 280 covers for Senoo’s published scores and contributed the lyrics for 24 songs of his own, the most famous of which is “Evening Primrose” (Yoimachigusa), published in 1918. The scores became very popular although few people could read or play the scores. They were bought because of their cover art.
