media.caption: Watermill (水車小屋)

text.headline: Watermill (水車小屋)
text.text: This print, issued as part of the c. 1950s series Eight Views of Mount Fuji, is a re-issue of the original c. 1939-1940 print titled "Fuji from the Watermill at the Mouth of Omiya" created for the series Thirty-Six Views of Mt. Fuji. The publisher Uchida Art frequently reissued and re-packaged earlier prints of Tokuriki's, combining them into series (packaged as portfolios) with new titles and small changes to the designs.

media.caption: The Huge Win of the Armed Forces, No. 4 appearing in Kagoshima-ken ari no sonomama (鹿児島県有のそのまま・四号・はら切坂友軍大勝利)

text.headline: The Huge Win of the Armed Forces, No. 4 appearing in Kagoshima-ken ari no sonomama (鹿児島県有のそのまま・四号・はら切坂友軍大勝利)
text.text:
The fourth print in a series of twenty prints describing and depicting the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion published under the newspaper-like banner Kagoshima ken ari no sonomama, loosely translated as "Kagoshima Prefecture As It Is Now." Published in Osaka by Kanai Tokubei 金井徳兵衛, the prints, classified as nishiki-e shinbun (newspaper prints), provided short articles with accompanying simplified graphics of the Rebellion's progress, or lack thereof. All twenty prints in the series show a publication month of March or April, so the life of this "newspaper" was even shorter than the nine month rebellion. For another print published under this banner see IHL.0567
The red cartouche in the upper right hand corner reads 鹿児嶋縣 (Kagoshima-ken) 有のそのまま (Ari no sonomama) and also provides the print number in the series, 四 (4). The large print seen on the far right in the yellow scroll reads はら切坂友軍大勝利, a loose translation of which is "the huge win of the armed forces at Harakirizaka [Tawarazaka]." The red cartouches in the center of the print identify the rider on the horse as Major General Miyoshi Shigetomo, the former commander of the Osaka Brigade.
No artist's signature or seal appears on any of the twenty prints, and neither Waseda University or Kagawa University Library list the artist, but two sources, Andreas Marks on p. 190 of his book "Japanese Woodblock Prints: Artists, Publishers and Masterworks 1680-1900" and Kansai University Library attribute the prints to Hasegawa Sadanobu II (Konobu I) (1848-1940).
The entire series of twenty prints may be seen on the Waseda University Library website at http://archive.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kosho/bunko10/bunko10_08061/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Horse and Ram (午 未)

text.headline: Horse and Ram (午 未)
text.text: The actor Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 in the role of Shimo no Kunitarō とふげ下の国太郎 on the right (matched with the sign of the horse 午) and the actor Sawamura Tosshō II 沢村訥升 in the role of samurai Sanshichirō Nobutaka あしかゞ三七郎信孝 on the left (matched with the sign of the ram 未, despite the presence of a horse's snout and mouth over his shoulder.)

media.caption: American Girl, A

text.headline: American Girl, A
text.text: American Girl, A is one of at least six female semi-abstract bust prints (also American Girl B, Spanish Girl, German Girl, Parisienne and Woman in Bagdad) created in 1954 by the artist using similar broad embossed lines to bound his color areas and both break-up and define his image. American Girl A revels in red, orange hues, and blues.

media.caption: Illustration of the Capture of the Gunboat Sōkō (操江号捕獲の圖 Sōkō-gōhakaku no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Capture of the Gunboat Sōkō (操江号捕獲の圖 Sōkō-gōhakaku no zu)
text.text:
A depiction of captured Chinese sailors from the gunboat Tsao Kiang (Caojiang) which was captured off Asan, Korea by the Japanese cruiser Akitsushima on July 27, 1894 during the Battle of Pungdo, the first naval battle of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895). The sailors are likely being transferred to the Japanese dispatch vessel Yaeyama. Conflicting information exists on the history of the Tsao Kiang and also its renaming as a ship of the Japanese navy, with most sources (including the title of this print) listing its new Japanese name as "Sōkō" and at least one source listing its new name as the "Toyshina."
For another impression of this print see IHL.2429.
This set of prints by is unusal in its being published in Ōsaka rather than in Tokyo where almost all S-J War prints were published. Its publisher Ōbuchi Wataru of the publishing house Hatsubai Shinshindō was primarily a book publisher and this print was part of a twelve print gafu (picture book), a portfolio titled Sino-Japanese War Picture Book.

media.caption: Illustration of the Hospitalization of the Captured Commander Tso Pao-kwei (左寶貴生捕入院之圖)

text.headline: Illustration of the Hospitalization of the Captured Commander Tso Pao-kwei (左寶貴生捕入院之圖)
text.text:
A depiction of the wounded Chinese Commander Tso Pao-kwei and other Chinese soldiers being led into a Japanese field hospital for treatment after the fall of Pyongyang in Korea to the Japanese forces on September 16, 1894. While some accounts of the battle reported that Tso Pao-kwei had surrendered, in fact he fought bravely and died in action.
For another impression of this print see IHL.2427.
This set of prints by is unusal in its being published in Ōsaka rather than in Tokyo where almost all S-J War prints were published. Its publisher Ōbuchi Wataru of the publishing house Hatsubai Shinshindō was primarily a book publisher and this print was part of a twelve print gafu (picture book), a portfolio titled Sino-Japanese War Picture Book.

media.caption: From Kyobashi to Ginza (京橋より銀座の図)

text.headline: From Kyobashi to Ginza (京橋より銀座の図)
text.text:
This 1872 scene presents us with a view from the Kyobashi bridge looking into Ginza Street. A horse drawn carriage crosses Kyobashi bridge within its delimited zone, while pedestrians cross in their designated areas along the sides. A jinrikisha (rickshaw) awaits its turn on the far side of the bridge and a rider on horseback follows the carriage. Kyobashi bridge sat at the east end of Ginza Street and Shinbashi bridge on the west end.
After the Tsukiji area burnt to the ground in 1872, the Meiji government designated the Ginza area as model of modernization. The government planned the construction of fireproof brick buildings, and larger, better streets connecting the Shimbashi Station and the foreign concession in Tsukiji, as well as to important government buildings. Designs for the area were provided by the Irish-born architect Thomas Waters; the Bureau of Construction of the Ministry of Finance was in charge of construction. In the following year, a Western-style shopping promenade on the street from the Shinbashi bridge to the Kyōbashi bridge in the southwestern part of Chūō with two- and three-story Georgian brick buildings was completed.
"Bricktown" buildings were initially offered for sale, later they were leased, but the high rent meant that many remained unoccupied. Nevertheless, the area flourished as a symbol of "civilization and enlightenment" (bunmei kaika), thanks to the presence of newspapers and magazine companies, who led the trends of the day. The area was also known for its window displays, an example of modern marketing techniques. - Source: Wikipedia http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginza

media.caption: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)

text.headline: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Endo Morito about to mistakenly cut off the head of Kesa Gozen. The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.
The original blocks for this print (see ihl-0503 for the 1885 original issue print) were likely damaged or lost, as this 1902 print uses a new design to illustrate the story of Kesa Gozen. This new design began appearing while the earlier brocade border series was still being produced. (See ihl-0950 for the newly designed print.)

media.caption: Ono-no Tofu (小野道風)

text.headline: Ono-no Tofu (小野道風)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the calligrapher Ono no Tōfū in front of the Daigokuden in the Heian Palace complex.
The reissued series eliminated the brocade border present on the original series published between October 1885 and November 1890. For the original edition see IHL.0040.

media.caption: Satō Tsuginobu (佐藤嗣信)

text.headline: Satō Tsuginobu (佐藤嗣信)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Sato Tsuginobu on his deathbed in the arms of his commander Minamoto no Yoshitsune, for whom he sacrificed his life.
The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

media.caption: Ichimura Uzaemon XIV in the role of Tsumagasa Soyojirō (妻笠曽代次郎 市村羽左 衛門)

text.headline: Ichimura Uzaemon XIV in the role of Tsumagasa Soyojirō (妻笠曽代次郎 市村羽左 衛門)
text.text:
The actor Ichimura Uzaemon (likely Uzaemon XIV) is pictured in this 19th (十九) print in the series Kabuki Thirty-Six Poems. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University identifies the role being portrayed by Uzaemon as 妻笠曽代次郎 which can be read Tsumagasa Soyojirō.
Some prints in this series carry numbers below the cartouche containing the series name and others do not. The actors' names in this series appear in the bottom right of the open book containing, what must be, a poem.

media.caption: The Hiramatsu Restaurant in Nihonzutsumi, with the Geisha Okame of Nihonbashi (日本はし おかめ - 日本堤 平松)

text.headline: The Hiramatsu Restaurant in Nihonzutsumi, with the Geisha Okame of Nihonbashi (日本はし おかめ - 日本堤 平松)
text.text:
Picturing the geisha Okame wearing a okoso zukin, a cold weather hood, against a red brocade background, this print is from the series Thirty-Six Tokyo Restaurants which pairs famous geisha with famous Tokyo eateries. In this series, the square panel at top left shows either speciality dishes or views from the eatery. The large yellow cartouche on the right shows the series' title, name of the geisha and the restaurant's address.
In 1878 Kunichika designed another series Thirty-Six Modern Restaurants (see IHL.2186) which also paired restaurants with beautiful women. Whether the publisher or the artist received compensation for the advertising given to the restaurants portrayed is unknown, but likely.

media.caption: The Restaurant in Mukojima, with Geisha (さ〓〓於長 - 向じ満 花ぐ〓)

text.headline: The Restaurant in Mukojima, with Geisha (さ〓〓於長 - 向じ満 花ぐ〓)
text.text:
Picturing a geisha stringing a shamisen, against a red brocade background, this print is from the series Thirty-Six Tokyo Restaurants which pairs famous geisha with famous Tokyo eateries. In the series, the square panel at top left shows either speciality dishes or views from the eatery. The large yellow cartouche on the right shows the series' title, name of the geisha and the restaurant's address. The geisha's name and the name of the restaurant are unread.
In 1878 Kunichika designed another series Thirty-Six Modern Restaurants (see IHL.2186) which also paired restaurants with beautiful women. Whether the publisher or the artist received compensation for the advertising given to the restaurants portrayed is unknown, but likely.

media.caption: Horse Racing Stands at Ueno Park (上野公園競馬舎 Ueno kōen keiba-sha)

text.headline: Horse Racing Stands at Ueno Park (上野公園競馬舎 Ueno kōen keiba-sha)
text.text: One of many prints depicting the horse racing track at Ueno Park that operated from 1884 until 1892. For another prints depicting the track and a history of the racecourse see this collection's print Illustration of Horse Racing at Shinobazu Ueno (IHL.0473).

media.caption: Kanagawa in Musashi Province: Distant View of Yokohama (武蔵 神奈川 横浜眺望 Bushū Kanagawa, Yokohama enbō)

text.headline: Kanagawa in Musashi Province: Distant View of Yokohama (武蔵 神奈川 横浜眺望 Bushū Kanagawa, Yokohama enbō)
text.text:
"The title of Yoshimori’s print refers to the fifty-three stations along the Tokaido, the eastern highway linking Edo and Kyoto. Kanagawa, one of those stations, lay directly across the bay from Yokohama. From that vantage point, the prosperous town of Yokohama with its substantial Western-style buildings is illustrated in the distance.
"Dominating the scene is the figure of a woman, portrayed with studied attention to details of light and shadow that reflect the artist’s awareness of Western wood engravings or other pictorial sources. Her image may in fact be derived from a figure in the foreground of an illustration of India published in the Illustrated London News. Combining elements of traditional Japanese art with an exceptionally successful reproduction of a Western artistic model, the print presents a striking if somewhat disconcerting visual effect."[1]
In addition to Yoshimori's signature and seal appearing in the bottom panel to the left of the figure, other signatures and seals appear in the two halves of the upper panel, possibly the signatures of the calligrapher and another artist who created the inset to the left of the panel containing the calligraphy.
The calligraphy (in Chinese) reads:
The wind sends flags and sails in brocade waves/ revealing copper masts and iron hawsers/ It stops in the distance, in the inlet of the bay/ We hear news of its name and its signal fires/ and know that a steamship approaches the harbor.[2]

[1] Yokohama Prints from Nineteenth-Century Japan, Yonemura, Smithsonian Institution, 1990, p. 125.
[2] Toshidama Gallery https://www.toshidama-japanese-prints.com/item_549/Yoshimori-Painting-and-Calligraphy-from-the-53-Stations-of-the-Tokaido--Distant-View-of-Yokohama-and-Kanagawa.htm [accessed 8-28-23]

media.caption: Nakamura Tōzō in the role of Susanoo no Mikoto (中村東蔵 素盞嗚尊)

text.headline: Nakamura Tōzō in the role of Susanoo no Mikoto (中村東蔵 素盞嗚尊)
text.text:
The actor Nakamura Tōzō V in the role of Susanoo no Mikoto in the play Nippon Furisode Hajime 日本振袖始. staged at the Teikoku Gekijō, Tokyo on November 1, 1915. This print is pasted to the cover of the last issue (number 5) of the magazine. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Sugawara no Michizane (菅原道真公)

text.headline: Sugawara no Michizane (菅原道真公)
text.text:
Print number 12 (十二), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the statesman, scholar, calligrapher and poet Sugawara no Michizane (845-903) holding a signboard possibly containing a petition. In the background is a plum tree, its blossoms falling, a tree much beloved by Michizane.
This print is the second of two prints in this series by Kiyochika portraying Michizane in the same pose. The first print, a more complex composition, was published in October 1885, approximately two and a half years before the April 1889 publication of this print. The scroll-like cartouches on each print which provide the title of the print and information on the historical figure contain the same text. As with several prints in this popular series, the original blocks may have been lost or damaged, requiring the publisher to request a new design from the artist from which new blocks were carved.

This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Hanawa Hokiichi (塙保己一)

text.headline: Hanawa Hokiichi (塙保己一)
text.text:
Print number 41 (四十一 ), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, portraying the blind Scholar of National Learning (kokugakusha), Hanawa Hokiichi (1746-1821), and his students. The scene portrays a famous anecdote in which Hanawa was once reading with his students the well-known novel Genji Monogatari. The lecture room was rather small, and was provided with only one lamp, by the light of which the students were just able to see their books. But while they were busily taking notes of their master's lecture, a puff of wind suddenly blew out the lamp and left them in darkness. Hanawa, being quite unaware of this, calmly went on with his lecture; but the students, being of course unable to see to read or write, had to ask their master to stop for a few moments.
"Why, what is the matter?" inquired Hana-wa.
"It is the light, sir," they replied "The wind has blown out the light, and we can't see our books. Please wait a moment till we light the lamp again."
Hanawa smiled when he heard this, and replied, "That shows the inconvenience of having to depend on eyes; for when the light goes out, you suddenly become blind and helpless. But as for me, I'm fortunate in never having any trouble of this kind."
This scene, originally published in 1886, was recreated by the artist Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) in 1890 as a replacement for this print whose blocks were possibly lost or damaged. (See IHL.1283.) While the designs differ, the scroll-like cartouche on both prints contain exactly the same information.

media.caption: Uesugi Torachiyo (上杉虎千代)

text.headline: Uesugi Torachiyo (上杉虎千代)
text.text:
Print number 28 (廿八), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing a young Uesugi Torachiyo (born Nagao Kagetora, later name Uesugi Kenshin) instructing a young samurai in the ways of war.
This print is likely a later printing as the artist's seal, which appears on the earlier printing (see IHL.0476), is missing.

media.caption: Kai Province: Monkey Bridge (甲斐國・猿槁之圖 Kai no kuni・Saruhashi)

text.headline: Kai Province: Monkey Bridge (甲斐國・猿槁之圖 Kai no kuni・Saruhashi)
text.text:
Print number 13 十三 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints. The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
This print pictures the Monkey Bridge (Saruhashi) over the Kakegawa Gorge in modern-day Yamanashi Prefecture.
Kai Province (甲斐国, Kai no kuni), also known as Kōshū (甲州), is an old province in Japan in the area of Yamanashi Prefecture. It lies in central Honshū, west of Tokyo, in a landlocked mountainous region that includes Mount Fuji along its border with Shizuoka Prefecture.

media.caption: The Letter from New York (手紙・ニューヨークより)

text.headline: The Letter from New York (手紙・ニューヨークより)
text.text:
One of nineteen prints in Takahashi's series of prints featuring the artist's "letters" from places around the world. This series began in 1984 with the print titled The Letter and concluded in 1994 with the print The Letter (From Season). In this series, Takahashi pays homage to various cities, countries and places including Geneva, Paris, London, New York, Switzerland, Kyoto, Southern Italy, Mexico and Jerusalem.
Central Park?, skyscrapers? New York harbor? What is the almost cat-like pink figure in the middle of this print? As with many of his other prints, Takahashi employs deep embossing to bring three dimensionality to this work and "N.Y." is prominently displayed in the white oval. As with the print The Letter from Southern Italy, IHL.0587, Takahashi's abstract script flows across this print.

media.caption: The Letter from Southern Italy (手紙・南イタリアから)

text.headline: The Letter from Southern Italy (手紙・南イタリアから)
text.text:
One of nineteen prints in Takahashi's series of prints featuring the artist's "letters" from places around the world. This series began in 1984 with the print titled The Letter and concluded in 1994 with the print The Letter (From Season). In this series, Takahashi pays homage to various cities, countries and places including Geneva, Paris, London, New York, Switzerland, Kyoto, Southern Italy, Mexico and Jerusalem.
Takahashi's use of bright colors and abstracted shapes captures the sun, sky and sea of southern Italy and he writes his letter to us in an abstract script that dances across the print. As with many of his other prints, Takahashi employs deep embossing to bring three dimensionality to this work. I can't help but seeing Hokusai's great wave at the top of this print.

media.caption: Night View of Ginza Dori (銀座通夜景)

text.headline: Night View of Ginza Dori (銀座通夜景)
text.text: A night view of Ginza street in the 1880s with brightly illuminated windows and gas lights. People line the street and a horse drawn trolley and several carriages are pictured. Numerous editions of this print exist (some using recarved blocks) with varying color schemes. It is unknown whether this collection's print is an early or later edition., though it is likely not a first edition. This eidtion uses a different color scheme than other extant editions.

media.caption: Silkworm Culture [Sericulture] in Hitachi [Ibaraki] Province, figure 1 (常陸国 養蚕之図一)

text.headline: Silkworm Culture [Sericulture] in Hitachi [Ibaraki] Province, figure 1 (常陸国 養蚕之図一)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts silk industry merchants in Hitachi 常陸 province examining sheets of papers on which silk moths laid their eggs. Hitachi Province (常陸国, Hitachi no Kuni) was an old province of Japan in the area of Ibaraki Prefecture. Hitachi Province bordered on Iwashiro, Iwaki, Shimousa, and Shimotsuke Provinces.
Hitachi province was a mostly agricultural area. It "gradually became a more important production region for cocoons and raw silk, and by the early 1890s the value of the cocoons its residents produced surpassed that of raw cotton."[1]
In keeping with the importance of sericulture to Japan's economy and industrialization, seven prints in the series are devoted to it. The Exposition was essentially an industrial promotion opportunity providing a meeting place for Western technologies and their Japanese counterparts. "Silk production was the first example of an industry in which European producers deliberately sought out Japanese know-how" and "the source of Japan's first export technology."[2]

[1] Japan's Protoindustrial Elite: The Economic Foundations of the Gōnō, Edward E. Pratt, Harvard University Asia Center, 1999, p. 117.
[2] "Sericulture and the Origins of Japanese Industrialization," Tessa Morris-Suzuki, appearing JSTOR, Vol. 33, No.1, January 1992, p. 1-2-103; p. 121.

media.caption: Slate Pencil Making in Bizen Okayama (備前岡山石筆製図 Bizen Okayama sekihitsu sei zu)

text.headline: Slate Pencil Making in Bizen Okayama (備前岡山石筆製図 Bizen Okayama sekihitsu sei zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the unloading, cutting and hand carving of the limestone used to make slate pencils (kyosha). A merchant in a western-style hat is seen purchasing the pencils. After the beginning of the Meiji Era, the demand for slate pencils for use in primary schools increased.
Bizen Province (備前国, Bizen-no kuni) was a province of Japan on the Inland Sea side of Honshū, in what is today the southeastern part of Okayama Prefecture. Bizen borders Mimasaka, Harima, and Bitchū Provinces. Bizen's original center was in the modern city of Okayama. From an early time Bizen was one of Japan's main centers for sword smithing.

media.caption: The Ghost Story of Kasamori under the Moonlight (怪談月笠森 Kaidan Tsuki no Kasamori)

text.headline: The Ghost Story of Kasamori under the Moonlight (怪談月笠森 Kaidan Tsuki no Kasamori)
text.text: A triptych depicting a scene from the short play Kaidan Tsuki no Kasamori by the playwright Kawatake Mokuami 河竹黙阿弥 (1816-1893). This play was performed on June 01, 1897 as part of the Kabuki program Yumiharizuki Genke no Kaburaya, which also included the plays Kagekiyo and Gion Sairei Shinkōki. The artist, Kunimasa IV (Baidō Hōsai), was well familiar with ghosts, as Newland, in her article in Andon 89, tells us that the artist spoke of seeing apparitions. She goes on to say, "ghosts and monsters were an integral part Edo popular culture and indeed known for centuries in Japan. They were not an uncommon subject in popular oral history and literature, the theatre, in woodblock prints, and later in newspaper reports."

media.caption:
On Stage in September at the Asakusaza: A scene from The Miraculous Cripple’s Revenge 
at Hakone (浅草座九月きょうげん｜箱根霊験躄仇討)

text.headline:
On Stage in September at the Asakusaza: A scene from The Miraculous Cripple’s Revenge 
at Hakone (浅草座九月きょうげん｜箱根霊験躄仇討)
text.text:
Starring Ichikawa Kuzō III (R), Nakamura Shikan IV & Onoe Taganojō II (C) and Sawamura Tosshi VII (L)
"Revenge stories were a mainstay of the kabuki theater, fulfilling the human desire to see justice done. Often, the basic plot was a familiar one, though each season the theaters offered new elements, new twists, even new characters to tantalize fans. In this case, the play was based on vengeance for a 16th-century murder. The scene shows the wife of the hero, who had been crippled by disease, standing under the icy waters of a sacred waterfall, praying for his cure. Only later is it revealed that the faithful wife had herself been murdered, leaving her ghost to continue her ritual supplications.
"The triptych format served as an excellent device for depicting a scene on the kabuki stage, allowing stylized actor portraits (their names and roles identified in the narrow vertical cartouches) and scenery to contextualize the action. Each sheet could be sold separately. Kabuki fans collected the prints as mementos, while theater owners often co-sponsored this type of publicity to promote their productions." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

media.caption: Vegetable Market at Kanda, View 16 (神田青物市場・十六景)

text.headline: Vegetable Market at Kanda, View 16 (神田青物市場・十六景)
text.text:
The Kanda Market was completed in 1931 as part of the reconstruction of Tokyo's wholesale food markets after the 1923 earthquake. Koizumi comments “Vegetables for all of Tokyo were distributed from this place.”

Print number sixteen in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: Tōei 藤榮

text.headline: Tōei 藤榮
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 157-158) - The old mother of Saitō Tsuginobu, one of Yoshitsune's retainers who sacrificed himself for his master at the battle of Yashima, hears that Yoshitsune and his men are escaping dressed as yamabushi priests. She therefore puts up a notice offering hospitality to priests in the hope that they will call on her. They do so and after the old woman has obviously realised who they are and Tsuginobu's child has been to Yoshitsune to ask him to return his father, they admit their identity. They then describe the bravery and devotion shown in the battle by Tsuginobu and his younger brother Tadanobu. Hospitality is then provided during which the child serves them with wine just as if his father were there looking on. When Yoshtsune and his men make ready to leave, the boy pleads to be allowed to go with them, but as this is impossible, in tears he and the old lady watch the party leave.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Kasuga Ryūjin 春日龍神 (The Kasuga Dragon God)

text.headline: Kasuga Ryūjin 春日龍神 (The Kasuga Dragon God)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 74-75.) - Wishing to make a journey to China and India, Myōe Shōnin goes to take leave of the god Kasuga Myōjin. But an old man appears and says that Myōe is not to go abroad as the followers of Buddha can now find all that is necessary here in Japan. He then reveals that he is a messenger sent by the god to tell of his decision, and disappears. Later, a golden light falls all around and a dragon-god descends. He tells of the many Buddhist gods to be found at Kasuga and then has Myōe swear to give up all idea of traveling abroad.

media.caption: Kosode Soga 小袖曾我

text.headline: Kosode Soga 小袖曾我
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 85-86.) - United in their resolve to take advantage of an approaching hunting expedition to kill their father's enemy, the Soga brothers return home to take leave of their mother. But the younger one, Gorō is disowned by her for going against her wishes by abandoning the priesthood, and she refuses to forgive or even to see him. Jūrō (the older brother) then tells her that she can have no love for him either if she would send him off on the dangerous mission alone and, with these words, goes to leave. At this, however, his mother relents and, calling them both to her, pardons Gorō and gives them her blessing. Overjoyed at this, the brothers perform a dance together and then take a final farewell of their mother.

media.caption: The Teachings for Women (妹背山婦女庭訓 Imoseyama Onna Teikin)

text.headline: The Teachings for Women (妹背山婦女庭訓 Imoseyama Onna Teikin)
text.text:
Kunichika depicts the famous scene Yoshinogawa from the third act of the drama Imoseyama Onna Teikin, performed at the Shitomi-za in October 1883. In this scene the young samurai Koganosuke and the beautiful Hinadori decide that they would rather commit suicide than be separated. They exchange glances from their separate verandas on opposite sides of the Yoshino River as Hinadori's widowed mother Dazai Kōshitsu Sadaka and Koganosuke's father Daihanji Kyozumi hold sprigs of cherry blossoms, symbols of their intentions.
Kunichika's depiction of the Yoshino River replicates how the river appears in the kabuki theater through the stage device called takiguruma (waterfall wheels) in which the river painted in bright blue and white appears to be flowing out from the back of the stage toward the audience

media.caption: Shūshiki (秋色)

text.headline: Shūshiki (秋色)
text.text:
Print number 37 (卅七) in the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition portraying the thirteen year old haiku poet Shūshiki (1669-1725) walking in the rain with a palanquin carrier, accompanying her father who is inside. It is the only print in the 56 print series designed by Kunichika, most famous for his prints of the kabuki and its actors.
As the story goes, Shushiki-jo came to the attention of his Imperial Highness the Lord Abbot of Rinnoji when she wrote a haiku about the cherry blossoms and fastened it to the branch of a tree at the Ueno temple. When she went to meet the Lord Abbot, she was accompanied by her father, disguised as her servant, who wanted to see the splendor of Ueno temple. After her audience with the abbot was over her entourage set out for home. On the way a heavy rainstorm broke and feeling sorry for her poor father who had to go afoot in the drenching rain, she ordered the palanquin to stop, allowing her attendants to shelter for a while. Then she quickly doffed her outer garment and changed her clothing with that of her father, and so sent him home in her palanquin while she walked in the rain like one of her own male escorts. This affectionate act of hers as well as the fact of her haiku having won the admiration of the Lord Abbot of Ueno, made her famous overnight both as a young haiku prodigy and a filial daughter. - Source: Exploring the Japanese Ways of Life, Shunkichi Akimoto, Tokyo News Service, 1961, p. 31-32.

media.caption: Yamanōchi Kazutoyo no tsuma (山内一豊妻)

text.headline: Yamanōchi Kazutoyo no tsuma (山内一豊妻)
text.text:
Print number 29 (廿九), one of 16 contributed by Toshikata to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Yamanōchi Kazutoyo no tsuma (the wife of Yamanōchi Kazutoyo) gathering money from her mirror-table to give to her husband to buy an expensive horse. Her husband sits worrying that he cannot afford the horse and will lose the opportunity it can bring. The screen in the upper right bears the partial image of a horse.

media.caption: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)

text.headline: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the young Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟) and their mother. Five year old Juro points to five wild geese flying by to remind his younger brother Goro of their duty to avenge their murdered natural father while their mother peers fondly at them.
The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

media.caption: Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成)

text.headline: Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Fujiwara no Sanekata (藤原実方), in the black robe, glaring at the seated Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成) whose kanmuri (冠 lacquered hat) he has just knocked off. Yukinari, seated on the floor, wears a surprised look as his hand searches for his hat which now lies on the floor. While the print is titled Dainagon Yukinari, whose hat was knocked off, the incident is more associated with Fujiwara no Sanekata who was banished by the emperor to a northern province for knocking off Yukinari's hat. For the original issue of this print see IHL.1402.
The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

media.caption: Dainin Kamitsukeno Katana (大仁上毛野形名)

text.headline: Dainin Kamitsukeno Katana (大仁上毛野形名)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the shogun Kamitsukeno Katana eating while his wife serves him wine and lectures him not to disgrace his name and to defeat the rebels. One of the ladies of the court sits in the background, her hand grasping an arrow, which is a reference to Kamitsukeno's wife stringing ten bows and ordering other women to pluck the bow strings simulating a large army.
The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890. For the original edition of this print see IHL.0949.

media.caption: Thistle, originally appearing in the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花  ・薊  Shikashū・Nihon no hana・azami)

text.headline: Thistle, originally appearing in the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花  ・薊  Shikashū・Nihon no hana・azami)
text.text:
Issued as an illustration for the poem of the same name, "Thistle," by Kurahara Shinjirō (1899-1965), in the 1946 poetry and print book "Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," "Thistle" was one of three woodblock prints, along with "Rose" (see IHL.0327) by Kawanishi Hide (1894-1965) and "Plum" by Maekawa Senpan (1888-1960), that were tipped into the book. This collection's print is stand-alone, being either removed from the book it was tipped into or separately printed as a stand-alone print.
"Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," was edited and designed by Onchi Kōshirō, a seminal artist in the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement and pioneering book designer. Contributing twelve prints and one poem, he along with poet Inoue Yasufumi 井上康文 (1897–1973), selected the book's thirty poems by poets such as Satō Haruo (1892-1964), Kitahara Hakushū (1885-1942), Noguchi Yonejirō (1875-1947), Kaoru Maruyama (1899-1974), Tatsuji Miyoshi (1900-1964), Ryuko Kawaji (1888-1959) and Andō Ichirō (1907-1972).
When this book was published in May 1946 "much of the country, including Tokyo where it was printed, remained in ruins following the previous year’s aerial bombardments. . . . Nihon no hana demonstrated the sophisticated aesthetic sensibility of the Japanese people, while providing a hopeful image for the future rebuilding—or 're-flowering'—of the country and its people." - Source: Commentary by Alicia Volk, https://pulverer.si.edu/node/462/title/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Niwa - Movement B2 (庭・動 B2)

text.headline: Niwa - Movement B2 (庭・動 B2)
text.text: Warm, harmonious colors invite quiet reflection in this print, one of the artist’s best-known works. Takahashi’s careful preparation of his water-based inks allow the subtle hues to cleanly overlay one another through multiple printings of extremely thin layers of ink. While over one hundred of Takahashi’s prints bear the title Niwa, or garden, each is a new exploration in composition, color, and form.

media.caption: Akasaka Kinokuni Slope (赤坂紀ノ国坂 Akasaka Kinokuni-zaka)

text.headline: Akasaka Kinokuni Slope (赤坂紀ノ国坂 Akasaka Kinokuni-zaka)
text.text:
This print and its companion print IHL.1289 constitute a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present, which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print provides a past (古 old) view in Akasaka, depicting a busy street on the Kinokuni slope where the Edo residences of the Kishū Tokugawa family were located. It is matched with a present, c. 1894, (今 now) view (IHL.1289), depicting the Akasaka Temporary Palace (Akasaka karikōkyo), which served as the chief imperial residence during the construction of the Tokyo Imperial Palace from 1873 to 1889.
These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, that make up the series.

media.caption: Demons and Dumplings, No. 1045 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・千四拾五號)

text.headline: Demons and Dumplings, No. 1045 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・千四拾五號)
text.text:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞. This print tells the story of relatives who try to steal money from a widow by disguising themselves as demons and get their "just desserts" by eating poisoned beet jam dumplings that were given to the widow by still other relatives.
The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

media.caption: Garden in Kyoto (京の庭)

text.headline: Garden in Kyoto (京の庭)
text.text: The artist's recurring theme of Kyoto and its gardens in one of Takahashi's lovely small prints.

media.caption: Sumida River scene from The Great Thief of the Miyakodori Brothel (都鳥廓白波｜新嶋原新狂言隅田川の場)

text.headline: Sumida River scene from The Great Thief of the Miyakodori Brothel (都鳥廓白波｜新嶋原新狂言隅田川の場)
text.text:
The play is based on the real-life so-called "Yoshidaya incident" in which a boy named Umewaka Yoshida is kidnapped by a human trafficker called Shinobu no Sōta and later dies on the banks of the Sumidagawa River.
Starring Bandō Hikosaburō V (R), Sawamura Tosshō II (C) and Nakamura Kanjaku III (L)
"A real-life crime from a millennium past inspired this kabuki play, first staged in 1854. A murder, a kidnapping, false identity, and a miraculous cure are only a few of the sensational events that riveted audiences. Illustrated here is a scene in Act I when the romantic bandit, Shinobu no Sōta (right) has mistakenly killed the kidnapped boy about whom the entire intrigue has swirled. In the dark, Sōta snatches a bundle of riches off the boy and prepares to fight his rival for it. The center sheet portrays a courtesan who has just fled her brothel, though in fact she is the disguised brother of the murdered boy. The bridge in the background locates the action near the Mimeguri Shrine, not far from the licensed pleasure quarter." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

media.caption: Ueno Park, Illustration of the Japanese Red Cross Society General Meeting (上野公園日本赤十字社總會之図)

text.headline: Ueno Park, Illustration of the Japanese Red Cross Society General Meeting (上野公園日本赤十字社總會之図)
text.text: While the Japanese Red Cross Society's general meetings attracted tens of thousands of participants and would have provided an excellent opportunity to sell large numbers of prints, I have come to the conclusion that this collection's print was never released for sale, at least in this print's state which lacks a date of printing in the publisher's seal and has a strange overprinting in purple of the royal couple's likenesses. In looking at the historical records, I can find no record that the Emperor ever personally attended any meetings or celebrations of the Japanese Red Cross held in Ueno Park, although the Empress is recorded as having attended the Society's general meetings numerous times in 1889 (at the Third General Meeting), 1890 (at the Fourth General Meeting), 1892 (at the Sixth General Meeting), 1896 (at the Eighth General Meeting), 1898 (at the Ninth General Meeting) and 1901 (at the Tenth General Meeting).

media.caption: Meguro Arsenal (目くろいゑんひう蔵 Meguro Ienhyūzō)

text.headline: Meguro Arsenal (目くろいゑんひう蔵 Meguro Ienhyūzō)
text.text: A lone figure stands on a hillock overlooking the Meguro Gunpowder Factory. Mt. Fuji is seen through the smoke generated by the factory. Meguro Arsenal is one of thirty-four prints that make up the never completed series One Hundred Views of Musashi. (Musashi being the name of the province that included Edo (later named Tokyo). The series was inspired by Utagawa Hiroshige's (1797–1858) series One Hundred Views of Edo, published between 1856 and 1859.

media.caption: Hōjō Yasutoki (北條泰時)

text.headline: Hōjō Yasutoki (北條泰時)
text.text:
Print number 25 (廿五), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the armor-clad Hōjō Yasutoki 北条 泰時 (1183–1242), the third shikken (regent) of the Kamakura shogunate, being criticized by the seated Taira no Moritsuna 平の盛綱 for wasting valuable time and risking his life in coming to the aid of his younger brother Hōjō Tomotoki 北条 朝時 (1193-1245) who had come under attack. Responding Yasutoki says, “How shall it be called a small affair when my brother is in danger? If I had lost my brother, what consolation would my rank have furnished?"
Devotion to family over personal glory is only one of the reasons Yasutoki is judged by history as a paragon of warrior leadership.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1325.

This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Wheels on a Slope; Too Many Sailors Climb a Mountain (坂ニ車　船頭多くして山へ登るSaka ni kuruma, sendō ōkute yama e noboru)

text.headline: Wheels on a Slope; Too Many Sailors Climb a Mountain (坂ニ車　船頭多くして山へ登るSaka ni kuruma, sendō ōkute yama e noboru)
text.text:
Soldiers and sailors are seen trying to move a cannon up a waterfall. There is a Japanese saying "Sendō ōkute fune yama ni noboru," literally "too many boatmen will take the ship onto a mountain," or in its English proverb equivalent "too many cooks spoil the broth." Something similar applies to this scene.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

media.caption: Spleen (鬱念 Utsunen)

text.headline: Spleen (鬱念 Utsunen)
text.text: As with many of Rei's prints, the artist has presented us with a landscape "set in ambiguous space", to use Helen Merritt's words. Dark indigo vertical lines which may portray a heavy rain are interspersed with subtle light indigo and yellow-green broken lines to provide depth to the image.  Along with the celestial shapes, Rei gives us a Mt. Fuji-like image on the right and, perhaps, a cityscape along the left part of the dark indigo vertical bar that scoops under Fuji on the right. This print is an artist proof. See IHL.1267 for an editioned copy of this print.

media.caption: Momo Chidori Naruto no Shiranami (もゝちどり鳴門白浪)

text.headline: Momo Chidori Naruto no Shiranami (もゝちどり鳴門白浪)
text.text:
The play Momo Chidori Naruto no Shiranami, written by Nagawa Tokusuke I 初代 奈河篤助 (1764-1842) and Chikamatsu Tokuzō 近松徳三 (1751-1810) and performed at Osaka's Chikugo 筑後 theater in May 1875, starring the actors (from right to left): Arashi Kitsusaburō IV 四代目 嵐橋三郎 as Irumaya Kijūrō 入間屋喜十郎 , Jitsukawa Enjaku I 初代 実川延若 as the Head Clerk (Bantō) Hikoshichi 番頭彦七, and Arashi Rikan IV 四代目 嵐璃寛 as Osan おさん.

Osaka Region Prints - Kamigata-e (Osaka-e)
While Edo/Tokyo was the dominant center of woodblock print production, Osaka was an important regional production center focusing on the Osaka theater. Osaka actor prints (kamigata-e) took on a different, smaller (chūban-size) and less spectacular, appearance than those produced in Edo/Tokyo. While Edo audiences demanded their fire and brimstone, Osaka kabuki patrons craved intricate, heartrending plots.
Kawasaki Kyosen (1841-1899) the son of Yoshitaki and a print designer himself, provides a glimpse into the start of the design process in his account of the Osaka printmaking process, as follows:
"In those days, certain Osaka publishers set out to the theaters on opening day with the artists who drew actors’ likenesses. The dividers were removed from four or five boxes right in the middle of the floor section of the theater and spread with rugs. Tables were set up with brushes and paper, and all was made ready to sketch the happenings on stage. The artist sat in the middle, with the proprietor of the publishing house and his clerks alongside. Besides them, some first-class female entertainers managed the food and drink, so things were quite lively. This was a form of promotion, as much as to say that actor prints were being designed for this performance." – an account by the artist’s son, Kawasaki Kyosen (1841-1899) as translated in The Theatrical World of Osaka Prints, Roger S. Keyes and Keiko Mizushima, David R. Godine in association with Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1973 p. 318.

media.caption: Aoto Fujitsuna (青砥藤綱)

text.headline: Aoto Fujitsuna (青砥藤綱)
text.text:
Print number 19 (十九), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Aoto Fujitsuna 青砥藤綱, a councilor of the Kamakura Shogunate (1192-1333), directing the search for a few coins he has lost in the Namerigawa River. When asked we he cared about so little money he replied "It only shows that you are interested in neither public interests nor charity. If I had not looked for the 10 mon in the river, it would have been lost forever. The 50 mon that I payed for the torches profited the merchant. There was no loss at all. It was a benefit to the public, wasn't it?"
For another edition of this print see IHL.1167.

Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. media.caption: Soga Brothers New Year's Farce

text.headline: Soga Brothers New Year's Farce
text.text: It is unknown what play, plays, or scenes are being depicted in this untitled triptych issued in January 1878. The center panel presents us with Ichikawa Danjurō IX as Kudō Suketsune and Ichikawa Sadanji as (Soga no) Gorō Tokimune, characters in the Soga Brothers Revenge, a variation of which is traditionally staged in the beginning of the New Year. The left panel depicts Danjurō, again, playing a priest or monk with the  partial name Mitsume 三つ目 (literally, "third-eye") and Iwai Hanshirō VIII playing a princess, possibly named Otohime おとひめ. In the right panel we see the god of wealth, Daikokuten 大黒天, played by Onoe Kikugorō V, carrying a giant daikon 大根, played by a Bandō family actor. "Daikon yakusha" was an expression for a ham actor.

media.caption: Pilferer (小盗みする者 Konusumisuru mono)

text.headline: Pilferer (小盗みする者 Konusumisuru mono)
text.text:
From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) which show examples of children's good and bad behavior. In this print a child steals a small item from a napping vendor; an example of bad behavior that will not go unpunished by the looming figure behind the screen above and to the right of the little thief.
In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

media.caption: Hearth (いろり)

text.headline: Hearth (いろり)
text.text: A magazine and book illustrator and printmaker, the artist Hatsuyama Shigeru created a number of prints featuring children at play, including this charming image of five children gathered around a hearth. The artist uses blue ai pigment (a deep indigo color) as the background and gives us several perspectives at once. As with all of Hatsuyama's children prints the rendering of the children captures the mischievous, innocent and serious aspects of their nature.

media.caption: Night View of Shinjuku (新宿夜景 Shinjuku yakei)

text.headline: Night View of Shinjuku (新宿夜景 Shinjuku yakei)
text.text:
"Maekawa Senpan depicts his contemporary man, arms on hips, surveying this modern quarter. To the artist’s 1931 viewers [the original publication date for this image] the words 'Night at Shinjuku' meant a night on the town, with drinking and easy women. It still carried the same message in 1945 [when this collection's print was published].[1]
"As in Factory Street at Fukagawa [see IHL.0174], Maekawa re-used a design done in 1931 for the series 'One Hundred Views of New Tokyo' with new blocks, probably cut by himself. The rich dark-blue of the night sky in the original version has been replaced by grey, investing the scene with an appropriately post-war bleakness. At the time of the first series, however, Shinjuku had become known as the most go-ahead and 'modern' of Tokyo districts, and had begun its rise to rival the older centre of the city around Ginza and Marunouchi. Maekawa's cartoonist's eye seems even then to have noticed something ironically lonely about the atmosphere of a place with thousands of bars."[2][3]

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Koshiro (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan.[4]

[1] Terrific Tokyo – A Panorama in Prints from the 1860s to the 1930s, Elizabeth de Sabato Swinton, Worcester Art Museum, 1998, p. 48.
[2] Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945-1952, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 2002, p. 61.
[3] For an account of the post-earthquake rise of Shinjuku see Seidensticker, Edward, 'Tokyo Rising: The City Since the Great Earthquake', New York, 1990, pp. 50-53.
[4] Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Sumida River (Sumidagawa 隅田川)

text.headline: Sumida River (Sumidagawa 隅田川)
text.text:
A WWII era view of an industrial area along the Sumida River, softened with the presence of the kimono-clad woman with parasol on the left and the sailboats on the river. In the first half of 1942, around the time this print was produced, Japan reached the height of her power, but also suffered the first air raids on Tokyo and her first major defeats, e.g. Battle of Midway, in the latter half of the year.
This print, whose provenance is attributed to the Uchida family archives, is likely a proof print using a different color scheme as compared with the final released version of the print. This proof also omits the print's title and Tokuriki's signature that are seen on the final released version. Note that the grey border around the image is misregistered.

media.caption: Kyoto Town Hall in Snow

text.headline: Kyoto Town Hall in Snow
text.text:
A partially obscured yellow street sign provides both the speed limit and a splash of color in this atmospheric winter scene. Judging from its shape, the building in the far distance, beyond the tiny figures and cars, is Kyoto city hall. Built in 1927, this imposing building takes up one block on the corner of Kawaramachi-dōri and Oike-dōri.
This print was originally issued as part of a series titled Twelve Views of Kyoto 京都十二景.

media.caption: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)

text.headline: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)
text.text:
The redesigned version of print number 21 (廿一) in the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the young Soga Brothers and their mother. Five year old Juro points to five wild geese flying by to remind his younger brother Goro of their duty to avenge their murdered natural father while their mother peers fondly at them.
Inoue, a student of Kobayashi Kiyochika, contributed thirteen prints to this series. He was to die at the age of 25 in 1889, the year this print was issued.
The original blocks created in October 1885 for this print were likely damaged or lost. This collection contains both the original 1885 design (IHL.1352) and the revised design published in April 1889 (IHL.0622).

Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints.
