media.caption: Ushi nusubito 牛盗人 (The Cow Thief)

text.headline: Ushi nusubito 牛盗人 (The Cow Thief)
text.text:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.285-286.) - The Cow Keeper for the Emperor discovers that one of the Emperor's cows has been stolen. He puts up a sign declaring whoever will give information as to the identity or the whereabouts of the Thief will be forgiven any crime, or given anything he asks for.
Before long a Child appears, saying that he wishes to report the name and the whereabouts of the thief. He says the thief is Hyōgo Saburō who lives in the next village.
The Cow Keeper sends Tarō Kaja and Jirō Kaja to go arrest the culprit. They soon drag him in, and before long he confesses his crime. He also reveals to them the fact that the Child is his son. He curses and disowns his Child for being a traitor.
They ask him why he stole the cow, and he says it was to pay for a memorial service for his father, and goes on to recite a passage from Buddhist scripture which would seem to sanction such an action. The Cow Keeper says that no matter, the crime is still the same according to law, and Hyōgo Saburō must be put to death.
At this point the Child speaks up demanding his reward. They ask him what he wants, and he answers, 'The life of Hyōgo Saburō spared.' He goes on to explain that when he saw the sign, he decided that this was the only ways to save his Father's life. Father and Son burst into tears. The Father pleads for forgiveness from his son for his harsh words of a few minutes before. The Cow Keeper and his servants are moved by this display of the Child's love for his Father. They grant him full pardon, and Father and Son set out for home singing for joy.

media.caption: Iori no ume 庵の梅 (The Plum Blossom Hut)

text.headline: Iori no ume 庵の梅 (The Plum Blossom Hut)
text.text:
One of sixteen prints designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyogen Plays) before his death. The series was completed by his daughter Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994). In this scene the shite, an aged nun, conducts a celebration during which she drinks sake and is then asked by her women visitors to dance for them. Poems that the women have brought can be seen hanging in the branches of the plum tree.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.105-106.) - It is early spring and a group of young women come singing to the hermitage of an aged Nun to view the plum blossoms. The hermitage is a hut made of live plum trees famous for their blossoms.
The Nun apologizes because the trees are the same age she is so that the blossoms are not as plentiful and beautiful as they used to be.
The Women offer the Nun sake. They all begin drinking, singing and dancing together. They finally convince the Nun to dance for them. Before she dances, she instructs them all to take branches of the blossoms as souvenirs, but says they must pick them themselves, for her arms are too old and weak to reach that high. The Women sing the accompaniment for the Nun's dance.

media.caption: Drawbridge of Amsterdam

text.headline: Drawbridge of Amsterdam
text.text: One of the artist's sōsaku hanga prints depicting the drawbridge on Staalstraat, over Kloveniersburgwal, in the Centrum district of Amsterdam. This print exists in at least two states, one of which is a numbered edition pictured in Tokuriki's book "Wood-block Printing" and the other this collection's print, either an artist's proof or from an unnumbered edition.

media.caption: Around Ochanomizu (お茶の水附近 Ochanomizu fukin)

text.headline: Around Ochanomizu (お茶の水附近 Ochanomizu fukin)
text.text:
Picturing the Kanda River running through the Tokyo neighborhood of Ochanomizu, Kitaoka titled this print お茶の水附近 (Ochanomizu fukin), translated as "Around Ochanomizu," and dated it 1949.
The gallery label accompanying this print identifies the print as coming from the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Post-war Life and Customs." The Museum of Modern Art Tokyo titles this print in English "The Kanda River from The Face of Tokyo No. 1" and in Japanese "版画集「東京の顔 No.1」より 2.神田川" and dates it to 1950.
This collection's print and images of the 1950 dated print appear to be identical and it is possible that a second printing was done by Kitaoka to create the five-part Face of Tokyo portfolio. Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the 1950 print.
This beautifully designed and, unfortunately, overlooked series, portrays Postwar Tokyo in the social-realist style that Kitaoka embraced after the war and later rejected, telling Statler "I rebelled against their [Japan's proletarian artists] subjugation of art to politics. . . ."

media.caption: Red Memory (赤い記憶)

text.headline: Red Memory (赤い記憶)
text.text:
A full moon over rolling hills, bound by pink and black cables? (One interpretation of this work. )“Kusaka’s work is never improvised, but is the patiently elaborated expression of a simple man. His technique is totally absorbed by the discipline necessary to produce prints of great ingenuity and directness.”[1] In his smooth technique and confident abstraction he resembles others of the first post-war generation of woodblock artists such as [Akira] Kurosaki, Amano Kazumi and Amano Kunihiro.[2]

[1] Contemporary Japanese Prints, Kawakita Michiaki, Kodansha International Ltd., 1967, p. 181.
[2] Modern Japanese Prints: 1912-1989, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 1994, p. 29.

media.caption: Red Shadow 82-5  (赤い影 82-5 Akai Kage 82-5)

text.headline: Red Shadow 82-5  (赤い影 82-5 Akai Kage 82-5)
text.text: One of the artist's many prints where color and motion are the statements. Reminiscences of the akai-e of the Meiji period, when red (akai) embodied modernity and the fast pace of change.

media.caption: Amakawaya Gihei (天川屋 儀平)

text.headline: Amakawaya Gihei (天川屋 儀平)
text.text:
This print pictures the virtuous merchant Amakawaya Gihei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers, a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin), based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston identifies the actor in the role of Gihei as Kawarazaki Gonjūrō I, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.
The multi-colored cartouche gives the name of the series as Legends of the Loyal Retainers and the name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of this cartouche, in this case Amakawaya Gihei 天川屋 儀平. The background script may provide an account of Amakawaya Gihei's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.
The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.

media.caption: Ōboshi Yuranosuke (大星由良之亮)

text.headline: Ōboshi Yuranosuke (大星由良之亮)
text.text:
This print pictures the character Ōboshi Yuranosuke from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers, a.k.a. The Forty Seven Ronin), based on the Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their master. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University identifies the actor playing the role of Ōboshi Yuranosuke as Bandō Hikosaburō V [5]坂東彦三郎, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.
The multi-colored cartouche gives the name of the series as Legends of the Loyal Retainers and the name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of this cartouche, in this case Ōboshi Yuranosuke 大星由良之亮. The background script may provide an account of Yuranosuke's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.
The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.
Ōboshi Yuranosuke is the fictitious name in the play for the real-life Ōishi Kuranosuke, Lord Asano's head retainer and the head of the revenge plot to assassinate the senior bakufu protocol official, Kira Yoshinaka. It is Ōishi who took Kira's head and placed it before his master's grave at Sengakuji Temple.

media.caption: Hayano Kanpei (早野勘平)

text.headline: Hayano Kanpei (早野勘平)
text.text:
This print pictures the character Hayano Kanpei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers; a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin). The play is based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum Digital Archives Collection identifies the actor playing Hayano Kanpei as Ichimura Kakitsu IV [4]市村家橘, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.
The multi-color cartouche in the upper right corner gives the name of the series, Legends of the Loyal Retainers. The name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of the cartouche, in this case Hayano Kanpei 早野勘平. The background script may provide an account of Hayano Kanpei's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.
The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.
For another edition of this print see IHL.0927.

media.caption: Waterwheel (水車 suisha)

text.headline: Waterwheel (水車 suisha)
text.text:
One of five known prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of growing rice and its uses issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print demonstrates use of a foot-powered waterwheel to irrigate rice paddies and various rice food dishes. (For another print in this series see IHL.0633.)
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

media.caption: Rice Storage (米蔵 komegura)

text.headline: Rice Storage (米蔵 komegura)
text.text:
One of five known prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of growing rice and its uses issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print depicts a rice storage house with farmers going about their business and chickens nibbling the stray rice kernels. The top portion of the print presents various rice storage related items. (For another print in this series see IHL.0632.)
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

media.caption: Small Red Wall A

text.headline: Small Red Wall A
text.text: Layers upon layers of ink give this print a great depth as does the injection of the light turquoise on which the darker colors float.

media.caption: Act XI: The Storming of Moronao’s Mansion (十一段目 Jūichidanme)

text.headline: Act XI: The Storming of Moronao’s Mansion (十一段目 Jūichidanme)
text.text: This print pictures two maids tickling a third maid in a parody of the third scene in act XI of the play Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers).  The circular inset shows the actual scene from act XI in which the ronin, after having staged a night attack on Moronao's mansion, drag Moronao from his hiding place.

media.caption: Summer in Aizu - The Seasons: Summer (会津の夏)

text.headline: Summer in Aizu - The Seasons: Summer (会津の夏)
text.text: This untitled print depicts four people quietly going about their business in a rural village, possibly the artist's early boyhood home of Aizu, on a summer's day. When it was released as part of an offering of six Saitō prints by the Book-of-the-Month Club, it was titled "The Seasons: Summer." See IHL.0984 for another print included in the Book-of-the-Month Club set of six prints.

media.caption: Face, Male (顔、男)

text.headline: Face, Male (顔、男)
text.text: A prototypical image from the artist. This "male" face, using Kinoshita's early color scheme of orange and sumi ink, takes up almost the entire image area. While dated 1981, the blocks were likely carved earlier, possibly in the mid-1950s. Kinoshita would initially make only several prints for his "artistic satisfaction" and then make additional prints as needed. While, as in this print's case, the total edition might be shown as fifty prints, in many cases the full edition would never be completed.

media.caption: Sumida Park in Kototoi, Mukōjima, View 25 (墨田公園 向島言問・二十五景)

text.headline: Sumida Park in Kototoi, Mukōjima, View 25 (墨田公園 向島言問・二十五景)
text.text:
The artist depicts Sumida Park in the foreground with a silhouette of Kototoi Bridge, built in 1928, on the left in the background. Koizumi comments “The Takeya ferry once crossed the Sumida River from here. Now the only reminder of the former look of the old river bank is the stone lantern. Now there is a modern park along the river.”

Print number twenty-five in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: People of the Snow Country (雪国の人 yuki guni no hito )

text.headline: People of the Snow Country (雪国の人 yuki guni no hito )
text.text: Takagi's colors perfectly fit this winter scene of three figures along a pathway leading to a torii and a small shrine.  A lone bird completes the silence of this scene.

media.caption: Playing Bingo (ビンゴゲーム)

text.headline: Playing Bingo (ビンゴゲーム)
text.text:
Titled, Playing Bingo ビンゴゲーム, Kitaoka gives us a view of a crowded bingo hall in postwar Tokyo.
This print, dated 1949, was issued as part of the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Postwar Life and Customs" and subsequently included in the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio, each portfolio containing five prints, titled Print Collection, The Face of Tokyo kyo 版画集 東京の顔.
Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the print included in the later portfolio.

media.caption: Outside Shinjuku Station, the West Exit (新宿西口)

text.headline: Outside Shinjuku Station, the West Exit (新宿西口)
text.text:
Kitaoka shows us a possibly mid-day scene outside the west entrance of Tokyo's busiest railway station.
This print, dated 1949, was issued as part of the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Postwar Life and Customs," and subsequently included in the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio (each portfolio containing five prints), titled Print Collection, The Face of Tokyo kyo 版画集 東京の顔.
Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the print included in the later portfolio.

media.caption: Behind the Stage (舞台裏)

text.headline: Behind the Stage (舞台裏)
text.text:
Stagehands building a set for an unknown play.
This print, dated 1949, was issued as part of the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Postwar Life and Customs" and subsequently included in the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio (each portfolio containing five prints,) titled, Print Collection, The Face of Tokyo 版画集東京の顔 . Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the print included in the later portfolio.

media.caption: A Comparison of Actors' Wages, Tokyo (俳優 見立給金競 東京)

text.headline: A Comparison of Actors' Wages, Tokyo (俳優 見立給金競 東京)
text.text:
A depiction of eight different actors in nine roles, along with a listing of their salaries along with the names and salaries of 56 additional Tokyo-based actors. The actors' identifying crests (mon) are shown above their names. The sloppy production, stray ink marks and poor registration, along with the lack of a date of issue for this print indicate it may have been some type of proof copy. (However, the print does carry a price of six sen below the publisher's seal.)
Rankings like this were issued periodically as fans clamored to know who was on top.

media.caption: Mt. Yoshino (吉野山 Yoshinoyama)

text.headline: Mt. Yoshino (吉野山 Yoshinoyama)
text.text: Tokuriki cuts off the top part of the head of one of the Nio statues guarding the Kimpusen-ji temple on Mt. Yoshino in Nara prefecture, perhaps to draw our attention to the surrounding countryside and its cherry trees in bloom. The bottom part of the sign board on the pillar reads 金峯山寺 Kinpusen-ji Shrine. Note the votive slips pasted to the supporting timbers.

media.caption: Ichikawa Ichizō III as Nadare no Wakamatsu (なだれの若松　市川市蔵)

text.headline: Ichikawa Ichizō III as Nadare no Wakamatsu (なだれの若松　市川市蔵)
text.text: Actor Ichikawa Ichizō III as Nadare no Wakamatsu in a kabuki enactment of the novel A Present-Day Suikoden.  He wears a kimono adorned with a large shrimp and a rooster head. The series consists of 36 prints designed by Kunisada between 1861 and 1863. Suikoden (Tales of the Water Margin) is the Japanese adaptation of the 14th-century Chinese vernacular novel Shuihu zhuan, which recounts the exploits of a group of 108 robbers (or, depending upon your view, brave and righteous rebels.)

media.caption: No. 9 Good Example (善・九)

text.headline: No. 9 Good Example (善・九)
text.text:
Print number 9 (九) from the series Moral Lessons for Daughters About the Two Sides of Life, consisting of twelve ōban-size sheets, each sheet consisting of two-chūban size images, the top image displaying an example of bad behavior and the bottom half displaying good behavior. It is not unusual for the sheets to have been separated into two chūban-size prints.
In this chūban-size print (the bottom half of the ōban-size sheet) a grandmother is bathing her grandchild while the toddler's mother awaits with a robe. The father helps, as do the four good souls (zendama) dressed in white. Each zendama's face contains the character ‘zen’ 善 (goodness, virtue.)
The top print, which shows a household displaying bad behavior (not part of this collection), apparently partying when they should be attending to their children. Five bad souls (akudama) dressed in red and identified by the character 悪 (badness, vice) in the rounds of their faces, assist their bad behavior. It usually takes more akudama to foster bad behavior than zendama to encourage good behavior.

media.caption: Toy Horse

text.headline: Toy Horse
text.text: Penelope Moore, granddaughter of Hiratsuka Un'ichi, commenting on this print wrote, "This was a carousel horse outside a party goods store on Wisconsin Ave and Van Ness St." Further elaborating, Penelope remembered being with her grandfather when he sketched this print in their Washington, D.C. neighborhood. "Occasionally, when he was in a patient mood, he took my sister or me, and brought a collapsible 3-legged stool, easel, and either canvasses or sketchpads. . . . Sidwell Friends, Sullivan Toys, the Zebra Room, G.C. Murphy, Giant Foods, the Savings and Loan Bank which was recently a Starbucks, the Johnson Flower Shop . . . all of these were part of our weekly hauntings. My mother used to buy flowers at Johnson's for classes or for my grandfather to draw. There was a small old farmhouse next to the Flower Center, right across from the deep dish Chicago Pizzaria, a small shop that sold party goods, and given the absence of a sign or any palpable activity, I don't think they did much business. An old carousel horse on the porch had caught Ojichan's eye, and over a period of several hours he sketched it with gusto and it became one of my favorite woodblocks."

media.caption: Ichimura Kakitsu IV, Sawamura Tanosuke III, Nakamura Shikan IV in The Popular Children's Word Game of Continuous Phrases (流行しりとり子どももんく Ryūkō shiritori kodomo monku)

text.headline: Ichimura Kakitsu IV, Sawamura Tanosuke III, Nakamura Shikan IV in The Popular Children's Word Game of Continuous Phrases (流行しりとり子どももんく Ryūkō shiritori kodomo monku)
text.text: From right to left, the actors Ichimura Kakitsu IV 市村家橘, Sawamura Tanosuke III 沢村(澤村)田之助 and Nakamura Shikan IV 中村芝翫 engage in a contest of shiritori monku ("word game") in the play The Popular Children's Word Game of Continuous Phrases.  Shiritori monku, literally “end-taking phrase”, is a game in which the last word or syllable of a phrase is repeated as the first word or syllable of the next phrase. Even for non-readers of Japanese, you can see the repetition of the last character or characters of the previous word in the following word in the text that surrounds the actors.

media.caption: Sawamura Tosshō II as Tora Ōmaru - Tiger (虎王丸 沢村訥升 - 寅)

text.headline: Sawamura Tosshō II as Tora Ōmaru - Tiger (虎王丸 沢村訥升 - 寅)
text.text:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.

The actor Sawamura Tosshō II (1838-1886) as Tora Ōmaru, the King of the Tigers. He holds a magical scroll from which a tiger has leaped.  A faint image of the tiger remains on the scroll.

media.caption: Bandō Hikosaburō V as Inugami Hyōbu - Dragon (犬上兵部 坂東彦三郎 - 辰)

text.headline: Bandō Hikosaburō V as Inugami Hyōbu - Dragon (犬上兵部 坂東彦三郎 - 辰)
text.text:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.  

The actor Bandō Hikosabu V (1832-1877) as Inugami Hyōbu conjuring a pack of dogs that arise out of the mist. The printer has skillfully used the technique of bokashi (gradation of shade) to render the dogs and mist. The dogs are a reference to the tale of the Eight Dog Heroes in which a princess is forced to sleep with her father’s dog and gives birth to eight magical balls of light. Each of these becomes a man and they are the subject of stories of great heroism and courage, gathered together as a collection popularly called the Hakkenden.

media.caption: Bandō Hikosaburō V as Unryū Kūrō - Monkey (雲龍九郎 坂東彦三郎 - 申)

text.headline: Bandō Hikosaburō V as Unryū Kūrō - Monkey (雲龍九郎 坂東彦三郎 - 申)
text.text:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.
The actor Bandō Hikosabu V (1832-1877) as Unryū Kūrō shown reading a scroll from which he has conjured a dragon. The character is taken from the book Unryū Kurō chūtōden by Shikitei Sanba (1776-1822).

media.caption: Ichikawa Sadanji as Raigō Ajari - Rat (頼豪阿闍利 市川左団次 - 子)

text.headline: Ichikawa Sadanji as Raigō Ajari - Rat (頼豪阿闍利 市川左団次 - 子)
text.text:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.
In this print the actor Ichikawa Sadanji (1842-1904) is shown as the monk Raigō Ajari (1002-1084) grasping a sutra from which a string of rats emerge. Raigō's prayers have given Emperor Shirakawa (r. 1072-1086) an heir. He asks in return for a raised platform, like the one in the temple of the yamabushi (warrior priests) who terrorized Kyoto, but it is denied. Raigō starves himself to death and his vengeful spirit (onryō, 怨霊) changes into a thousand rats which destroy the Emperor’s sacred library. This is followed by the death of the emperor's son.

media.caption: Kinkakuji (金閣寺)

text.headline: Kinkakuji (金閣寺)
text.text:
A postcard size, unsigned print, of Kinkakuji 金閣寺 (the Golden Pavilion) in snow, after a design by the artist Kawase Hasui. (See IHL.1424 and IHL.1668 for similar designs of Kinkakuji in snow and see IHL.1538 for the original design by Hasui. Reference Hp-45 in "Kawase Hasui, The Complete Woodblock Prints, Volume 1" Hotei Publishing, 2003, p. 143.)
The publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō, became so upset by these copies of original designs by Hasui and several other artists he published that he included the following warning in his 1936 catalogue titled, " Catalogue of Wood-Cut Colour Prints of S. Watanabe, S. Watanabe, 1936" :
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.”
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. This small print pictures the O-Torii (Grand Torii Gate) at Itsukushima Shrine on the island of Itsukushima (popularly known as Miyajima.) O-Torii was designated as a National Important Cultural Property on March 29, 1952.

media.caption: Chased by the Fire, Drowned in the Water (火に追われ水に溺る Hi ni oware mizu ni oboru)

text.headline: Chased by the Fire, Drowned in the Water (火に追われ水に溺る Hi ni oware mizu ni oboru)
text.text:
One of three prints contributed by the artist Hamada Josen (1875-1928) to the series Pictures of the Taishō Earthquake, issued in 1926 three years after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. This print pictures the horror of people fleeing the firestorms that came on the heels of the earthquake, only to drowned in the hoped-for safety of the water.
This series consists of 25 prints by nine, mostly lesser-known, artists, a number of whom, including this print's creator, were students of the Nihonga artist Tomioka Eisen (1864-1905). The nine artists are Shunhan Katayama (fl. c. 1901–1926); Yawata (Yahata?) Hakuhan (1893–1957); Noguchi Kōgai (born c. 1899, active c. 1919-1930s); Igawa Sengai (1876-1961); Kiritani (Kirigaya) Senrin (1876-1932); Shibata Kōyō (fl c. 1920s); Hamada Josen (1875-1928); Kondō Shiun (fl. c. 1923– 1930s) and Unpo Takashima (fl. c. 1920s).
When this series was issued in 1926, Tokyo and its environs were already well-along in their rebuilding, which "started before the last embers were out" and was to be officially completed in 1930. - Source: Tokyo Rising: The City Since The Great Kanto Earthquake, Edward Seidensticker, Harvard University Press, 1991, p. 8.

"The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 stands in memory as one of the most terrifying calamities in Japanese history. Registering at a magnitude of 7.9, the quake struck on September 1, with its epicenter some 50 miles southwest of Tokyo, in Sagami Bay. The hour was 11:58A.M., just when households everywhere were lighting small charcoal stoves to prepare lunch. Fires broke out instantly in the densely populated cities of Tokyo and Yokohama and were spread by high winds. Since the earthquake had broken the water lines, both cities were reduced to smoldering ruins within a few hours. . . . The earthquake and its aftermath caused well over 140,000 deaths and left nearly 700,000 people homeless." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 273.

media.caption: Two Scenes from The Tale of Shiraishi  (白石 噺明神森場  吉原 大黒屋 之 場  碁太平記白石噺 Shiraishi banashi, myōjin mori ba Yoshiwara daikokuya no ba)

text.headline: Two Scenes from The Tale of Shiraishi  (白石 噺明神森場  吉原 大黒屋 之 場  碁太平記白石噺 Shiraishi banashi, myōjin mori ba Yoshiwara daikokuya no ba)
text.text:
Two scenes from the play The Tale of Shirashi. The multicolored cartouche on the left sheet of the triptych identifies the scene being portrayed as Yoshiwara daikokuya no ba 吉原大黒屋之場. The multicolored cartouche on the right sheet of the triptych identifies the scene being portrayed as myōjin mori ba 明神森場.
"In a powerful composition that slashes the triptych into two scenes, the artist evokes the suspense of a history play about an attempted coup d'etat, with numerous subplots and colorful characters. The massive hairpins of the courtesan, left, were no longer in fashion when this play was staged, but immediately brought to mind the styles and customs of an older era." - Asian Art historian Lynn Katsumoto

media.caption: Sawamura Hyakunosuki, Ichikawa Gonjūrō, Iwai Shijaku and Kataoka Gadō in the play Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety ( 沢村百之助、市川権十郎、岩井紫若、片岡 我童・本朝廿四孝 Honchō nijūshikō)

text.headline: Sawamura Hyakunosuki, Ichikawa Gonjūrō, Iwai Shijaku and Kataoka Gadō in the play Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety ( 沢村百之助、市川権十郎、岩井紫若、片岡 我童・本朝廿四孝 Honchō nijūshikō)
text.text:
Picturing from right to left the actors Sawamura Hyakunosuke 沢村百之助 as Yaegaki hime 八重垣姫 (Princess Yaegaki, Nagao Kenshin's beautiful daughter); Ichikawa Gonjūrō 市川権十郎 as Takeda Katsuyori 武田勝頼 (in love with Yaegaki); Iwai Shijaku IV 岩井紫若 as Nureginu ぬれぎ (Yaegaki’s maid) and Kataoka Gadō 片岡 我童 as Shirasuga Rokurō 白須 賀 六郎 (a retainer of Yaekagi’s father sent to kill Katsuyori) in the Jusshukō scene in the play Honchō Nijūshikō 本朝廿四孝 (Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety.)
"The widow of a murdered shogun has threatened two noble families to either find the villain, or sacrifice their sons. Plot turns and mistaken identity add chilling effect, as in this scene that foreshadows the doomed marriage of the beautiful princess, Yaegaki, far right, to the man, center, she knows only by his portrait. Yaegaki's maid appears, left, beneath the specter of a warrior sent by Yaegaki's father to kill the betrothed." - Asian Art historian Lynn Katsumoto

media.caption: New Play at the Kabuki-za (歌舞伎坐新狂言 Kabuki-za Shin Kyōgen)

text.headline: New Play at the Kabuki-za (歌舞伎坐新狂言 Kabuki-za Shin Kyōgen)
text.text:
A triptych depicting the actors Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 playing the roles of Oogosho Ieyasu 大御所家康公 (right panel) and Kasuga (Lady) Tsubone 春日局 (center panel) and Nakamura Shikan V 中村芝翫 playing the role of Kaji no Tsubone 梶の局 in the play Kasuga no Tsubone, written in 1890 by the one-time journalist and politician Fukuchi Genichirō (1841-1906).
The play was performed for the first time in 1891. Given the date of this print, May 1903, it would be one of Danjūrō IX's last stage performances before his death on September 13, 1903.

media.caption: Low Tide: Women of the Bunka Era (汐干・文化頃婦人 Shiohi・Bunka koro fujin)

text.headline: Low Tide: Women of the Bunka Era (汐干・文化頃婦人 Shiohi・Bunka koro fujin)
text.text:
One of thirty-six prints in the series Sanjūroku kasen (also transcribed as Sanjūroku kurabe) depicting a fisherwoman and a stylish geisha gathering seafood at low tide. he geisha seems to be demurely giggling at the woman struggling with the fish. Embossing is used in both the white cartouche and the fisherwoman's skirt and lacquer has been applied on the geisha's collar and obi of the fisherwoman. One of the most striking compositions in this series.
The series presents women of different classes from thirty-five different historical eras.

text.headline: Study of Gaslight and Silhouetted Figures
text.text: This Kyōsai ink and pencil on paper study of silhouetted figures and gas lamps may be a preparatory drawing for a fuller drawing, titled Customs House at Yokohama  in the collection of the Rijksmuseum voor Volkenkunde (Inventory Number : RV-3513-1347), according to Professor Matthi Forrer, curator at the National Museum of Ethnology (Museum Volkenkunde) in Leiden.

media.caption: Selling Toothpicks at Itsukushima and Hiroshima Oyster Farm (安芸国 厳島楊枝ヲ鬻図 ・安芸 広島牡蛎蓄養之図)

text.headline: Selling Toothpicks at Itsukushima and Hiroshima Oyster Farm (安芸国 厳島楊枝ヲ鬻図 ・安芸 広島牡蛎蓄養之図)
text.text:
Two of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The top print depicts the selling of souvenir toothpicks at Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima island and the bottom depicts oyster farming in Aki Province.
The top is a view from one of the "floating" buildings (Haraiden purification hall of the Marōdo auxiliary shrine) at Itsukushima Shrine. According to the Miyajima Tourist Association "the shrine was a popular landmark in Miyajima where many people came to relax and cool themselves and to buy popular souvenirs such as toothpicks, and a variety of legends and traditions have been created here." - Source: Miyajima Tourist Association http://www.miyajima.or.jp/english/spot/spot_other.html [accessed 8-26-23]
Oyster farming in Aki Province, as seen in the bottom view, began at the end of the Muromachi period around 1532-1555. Initially aquaculture methods such as stone aquaculture (Ishimaki or arranging pebbles on tidal flats, attaching oysters, and waiting for the cultivation period before harvesting it) and double cracks were used. Over the years more advanced methods became common and evolved into the hanging-type aquaculture method shown in this print. - Source: Food In Japan https://www.foodinjapan.org/chugoku/hiroshima-kaki/ [accessed 8-26-23]
Aki Province (安芸国 Aki no kuni) or Geishū (芸州) was a province in the Chūgoku Region of western Honshū, comprising the western part of what is today Hiroshima Prefecture.
This print is reduced in size by the chirimen (crêpe) process to 9 1/8 x 6 5/8 in. (23.5 x 16.8 cm) from the originally issued double-chuban size (two uncut chuban prints) of approximately 14 1/4 x 9 3/4 in. (36.2 x 23.5 cm).

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Mongaku Shōnin in the play The Austerities of Mongaku ( 市川団十郎・ 文覚上人・ 橋供養梵字文覚)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Mongaku Shōnin in the play The Austerities of Mongaku ( 市川団十郎・ 文覚上人・ 橋供養梵字文覚)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as the priest Mongaku in the play Hashi kuyō bonji no Mongaku (The Austerities of Mongaku). As in keeping with the rest of the series, extensive embossing is employed in the background along with an application of mica.

One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits. A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

media.caption: Do Not Give Money to the Indolent, No. 12

text.headline: Do Not Give Money to the Indolent, No. 12
text.text:
The top half of print number 12 (十二) from the series A Didactic Mirror of Good and Evil, consisting of twelve oban size prints. Each oban size print consists of two chuban size images, the top image displaying an example of bad behavior and the bottom half displaying good behavior. It is not unusual for the sheets to have been cut into two chuban size prints, as we see in the case of this print.
In this print a child walks toward an indolent beggar (even the akudamas are indolent!) with the intention of putting a coin in the beggar's basket. Not an activity to be encouraged.
Seven bad souls (akudama) dressed in red and identified by the character 悪 (badness, vice) in the rounds of their faces, assist the beggar's indolence. It usually takes more akudama to foster bad behavior than zendama to encourage good behavior.

media.caption: Full Moon on the Tatami Mats, Shadows of the Pine Branches - Kikaku (名月や畳の上に松の影其角 Meigetsu ya tatami no ue ni matsu no kage - Kikaku)

text.headline: Full Moon on the Tatami Mats, Shadows of the Pine Branches - Kikaku (名月や畳の上に松の影其角 Meigetsu ya tatami no ue ni matsu no kage - Kikaku)
text.text:
This picture illustrates a verse by Takarai Kikaku (1661-1707), a celebrated haiku master, that reads, "Full moon on the tatami mats; shadows of the pine branches."
"A lady looks at the shadow of pine branches thrown by a bright moon onto the straw mats of her room. That the setting is a teahouse is indicated by the furo, three-legged brazier to the left of the design, and by the rough wood pillar of the tokonoma, ceremonial alcove, to the right. But it is an unusually opulent teahouse. The screen to the left, painted in the brightly colored Rimpa style, is rather gaudy for a teahouse, and the area is large, with tatami mats extending into the foreground. It is a teahouse of the pleasure quarters, either a house where assignations are arranged, or a teahouse in a large and luxurious brothel."[1]
This print is missing the lavender color found on other impressions in the courtesan's robe and the rectangular cartouche in the upper right of the print bearing the series title has only a partial application of the light pink color normally seen in the cartouche.

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[2]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, print 5.
[2] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: Koko ga Edo ko-ude no tatehiki (慈江戸小腕達引)

text.headline: Koko ga Edo ko-ude no tatehiki (慈江戸小腕達引)
text.text:
The actors, from right to left, Ichikawa Kodanji IV (市川小団次), in the role of Ude no Kisaburo (腕ノ喜三郎 "one-arm Kisaburō"), Kataoka Jūzō (片岡十蔵) in the role of Ōtori Ippei (大鳥逸平), Ichimura Kakitsu IV (市村家橘) playing Akebono Genta (曙源太) and Ichikawa Kuzō III (市川九蔵) in the role of Maboroshi Tanizo (幻長蔵) in the kabuki play Koko ga Edo Koude no Tatehiki by Kawatake Mokuami, staged in August 1863 at the Ichimura-za (市村).
This scene is set on the Kamakura Hanamizu bridge (鎌倉花水橋, as marked on the bridge post) and we can be sure Ude no Kisaburo, the one-armed swordsman who cut his arm off at the elbow with a saw in order to earn his fencing teacher's forgiveness, is the hero.

media.caption: Auspicious Plays (ワキ狂言 Waki kyōgen)

text.headline: Auspicious Plays (ワキ狂言 Waki kyōgen)
text.text: This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts an annual waki kyogen performance starting at dawn, announced by the banging of the large drum, consisting of auspicious dances such as the Dance of the Seven Lucky Gods and the Sanboso dance.  Reference is made in the scroll to both the Ichimura-za and Nakamura-za theaters in Edo. For a later edition of this print see IHL.0612.

media.caption: Aridōshi 蟻通

text.headline: Aridōshi 蟻通
text.text:
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 134.) - In the play, the poet Ki no Tsurayuki (waki) annoys the groundskeeper (shite) by riding his horse within the precincts of the Aridōshi Shrine. Tsurayuki soothes the feelings of the shrine deity by reciting a poem he has composed, after which, at the poet’s request, the god recites some Shinto prayers.



Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Actors Bandō Takesaburō I, Bandō Shūka I, Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, Iwai Kumesaburō III and Nakamura Fukusuke I (初代坂東竹三郎、初代坂東しうか、八代目市川団十郎、三代目岩井粂三郎、初代中村福助)

text.headline: Actors Bandō Takesaburō I, Bandō Shūka I, Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, Iwai Kumesaburō III and Nakamura Fukusuke I (初代坂東竹三郎、初代坂東しうか、八代目市川団十郎、三代目岩井粂三郎、初代中村福助)
text.text:
The actors, right to left, Bandō Takesaburō I (初代 坂東竹三郎), Bandō Shūka I (初代 坂東しうか), Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII (八代目 市川団十郎), Iwai Kumesaburō III (三代目 岩井粂三郎) and Nakamura Fukusuke I (初代 中村福助) pictured against a background of wisteria. The subtle transitions of shade and color in the robes is quite impressive.
A version of this print picturing the same actors (using the same woodblocks) but with a checked fabric background can be found in the collection of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston Accession Number 11.44150a-c.

media.caption: Shizuka Gozen (静御前)

text.headline: Shizuka Gozen (静御前)
text.text:
Print number 15 (十五), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Shizuka Gozen (静御前), a famous and beautiful shirabyōshi in the days of the Heian court, dancing in front of Minamoto no Yoritomo (源頼朝) in Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū (鶴岡八幡宮) in Kamakura.
To see another edition of this print with a differently colored brocade border go to IHL.0757.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Wisteria Maiden (Fuji musume)

text.headline: Wisteria Maiden (Fuji musume)
text.text: Tokuriki's modern interpretation of traditional folk Ōtsu-e (paintings and prints), named after the town of Ōtsu where they originated in the mid-17th century. It is said that Wisteria maiden (fuji musume) adds to your amiability and helps you get a good romantic partner.

media.caption: Standard Bearer (Yarimoichi yakko)

text.headline: Standard Bearer (Yarimoichi yakko)
text.text: Tokuriki's modern interpretation of traditional folk Ōtsu-e (paintings and prints), named after the town of Ōtsu where they originated in the mid-17th century. A Standard bearer (Yarimoichi yakko) provides safety during travel.  These figures led the traveling daimyo processions, ordering all bystanders to bow down as noblemen passed with their long retinues.

media.caption: Benkei Carrying Bell (Tsurigane Benkei)

text.headline: Benkei Carrying Bell (Tsurigane Benkei)
text.text: Tokuriki's modern interpretation of traditional folk Ōtsu-e (paintings and prints), named after the town of Ōtsu where they originated in the mid-17th century. This print depicts Benkei and the Bell (Tsurigane Benkei). The story is told of how the monk-warrior Benkei took the famous bell of Mii-dera and dragged it up to the summit of mount Hiei. He struck the bell and then got angry when he heard it ringing “eeno eeno”, which means “I want to go back” in the Kansai dialect. In his anger, Benkei threw the bell down to the bottom of the valley.

media.caption: Court Noble from Bairei Drawings, 4 (公卿・楳嶺画鑑 四 (Kuge・Bairei gakan, yon)

text.headline: Court Noble from Bairei Drawings, 4 (公卿・楳嶺画鑑 四 (Kuge・Bairei gakan, yon)
text.text: Bairei depicts a Heian period (794-1185) court noble in this print, which was included in the fourth of his seven volume book of drawings titled Bairei gakan, published 18 years after the artist's death. Originally published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1903, Unsōdō republished it in 1913, 1942 and again in 1982. This collection's print was likely removed from the 1913 edition. Works from the 1913 and 1942 releases, such as this collection's print, can be identified by their vertical centerfold, which is lacking in the 1982 release. Each volume contained 15 prints.

media.caption: Bell-ring Cricket, Mt. Fuji and a Parody of Kusazuri (鈴虫, 富士, 見立草摺)

text.headline: Bell-ring Cricket, Mt. Fuji and a Parody of Kusazuri (鈴虫, 富士, 見立草摺)
text.text:
Kyōsai gives us three images in this harimaze print - Mt. Fuji, a bell-ring cricket (suzumushi - known for its unique song) on a gourd vine with a crescent moon and a comic take on the kabuki play Kusazuri. Kusazuri is a play "in which Goro and Juro try to get their revenge on Kudo Suketsune for killing their father. Goro tries to join his brother Juro on stage but Asahina tries to hold him back. Goro brakes wind, and Asahina loosens his grip." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 220.
This series, consisting of a least ten prints, using "legitimate Kano school subjects as their themes" depicted in comic situations, made Kyōsai quite popular as an ukiyo-e artist. "At the time, these harimaze prints were cut into individual scenes and the small pieces were used to repair the holes in paper sliding doors and screens. Kyosai’s humorous scenes were thus enjoyed in the everyday lives of the Japanese people." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 32-33, 220-225.

media.caption: The scene Kumagai's Battle Camp from the play A Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani ( 熊谷陣屋  一谷嫩軍記 Kumagai jin'ya Ichinotani futaba gunki)

text.headline: The scene Kumagai's Battle Camp from the play A Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani ( 熊谷陣屋  一谷嫩軍記 Kumagai jin'ya Ichinotani futaba gunki)
text.text: The Kumagai Jin'ya scene, the last scene in the play Ichinotani Futaba Gunki, a dramatization of the Heike Monogatari tale of the battle of Ichinotani. The actors (right to left): Ichikawa Kodanji 市川小團次 in the role of Yoshitsune, Iwai Komurasaki III 岩井小紫 in the role of Fuji no Kata, Nakamura Shikan IV 中村芝翫 in the role of Kumagai Jiro Naozane, Ichikawa Kuzō III 市川九蔵 in the role of Midaroku, and Bandō Shūchō II 坂東秀調 in the role of Sagami. Also see IHL.0316 picturing the same scene but showing different actors.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Higuchi Jirō Kanemitsu in the play The Secret Art of Rowing Backwards (市川団十郎・ 樋口治郎兼光・ ひらかな盛衰記)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Higuchi Jirō Kanemitsu in the play The Secret Art of Rowing Backwards (市川団十郎・ 樋口治郎兼光・ ひらかな盛衰記)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as Higuchi Jirō Kanemitsu, a personal retainer of General Yoshinaka who disguises himself as the boatman Matsuemon who has mastered the naval art of sakaro (rowing backwards) in the play The Secret Art of Rowing Backwards (Hiragana Seisuiki). Extensive shomen zuri (front printing) has been used in the black areas of Kanemitsu's clothing.

One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits. A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

media.caption: Presentation of the Emperor's Gift Cup for the Second Time to Commanders Involved in Pacifying Western Japan (西国鎮撫諸将 再度 賜天盃之図)

text.headline: Presentation of the Emperor's Gift Cup for the Second Time to Commanders Involved in Pacifying Western Japan (西国鎮撫諸将 再度 賜天盃之図)
text.text:
Military commanders are being entertained at the behest of Emperor Meiji, as a reward for their service in putting down rebellions in Western Japan. While the release of this print corresponds with the suppression of the Satsuma Rebellion, its title seems to also encompass the earlier disturbances in the Saigoku (western area) of Japan in October and November of 1876. Fourteen named senior officers in the Imperial Army are shown in the print, receiving the Emperor's Gift Cup of sake for their contributions. Note the contrast between the officer's stern expressions and those of the geisha serving them.
After the last of the rebel forces were decimated by the Imperial Army in late September 1877, the Emperor made sure to visit and congratulate both officers and soldiers.

media.caption: Evening Cool (夕涼み Yūsuzumi)

text.headline: Evening Cool (夕涼み Yūsuzumi)
text.text:
One of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫 (1929-?).
As in this case, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

media.caption: Signs of Spring Mt. Togakushi (浅春戸隠 Asai haru Togakushi)

text.headline: Signs of Spring Mt. Togakushi (浅春戸隠 Asai haru Togakushi)
text.text:
Maeda created numerous prints of Japanese mountains. In this print he has used mica highlights throughout the slopes of the mountains. In the artist's words, "A true mountaineer has to get to the top, but the finest panoramas are down in the middle heights. That's where I stop."
Togakushi along with Madarao, Myōkō, Kurohime, and Iizuna are collectively known as the Five Peaks of Northern Shinano (Hokushingogaku). They make up the border of Nagano and Niigata Prefectures.
Neither signed or sealed by the artist, this print is likely a proof.

media.caption: April Hall (奈良 四月堂 Nara Shigatsu-dō)

text.headline: April Hall (奈良 四月堂 Nara Shigatsu-dō)
text.text:
Printed during the artist's lifetime by Takahashi Studio which printed a number of Maeda's designs in the 1960s and 1970s.
April Hall (Shigatsu-dō), an Important Cultural Property, is located in the Todai Temple grounds and was built in the Edo period. It is called April Hall for the special prayer ceremony, Hokke Sanmai, held there every April.

media.caption: The Seventh Month: Suketaya Takasuke IV  in the role of Hotoke Gozen (七月 助高屋　高助 仏御前)

text.headline: The Seventh Month: Suketaya Takasuke IV  in the role of Hotoke Gozen (七月 助高屋　高助 仏御前)
text.text: One of twelve prints in a collaborative series by Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900) and Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889). Kunichika depicts the actor Suketakaya Takasuke IV (Sawamura Tossho II) in the role of Hotoke Gozen.  In the fan-shaped inset, Kyōsai depicts two nuns at a solitary mountain cottage, a reference to Hotoke Gozen, whose name means ‘nun’.

media.caption: Battles of Coxinga, Act 1 (国性爺 卷一)

text.headline: Battles of Coxinga, Act 1 (国性爺 卷一)
text.text:
Act 1 of the play the Battles of Coxinga written by Japan's great Edo-period playwright Chikamatsu Monzaemon 近松 門左衛門 (1653-1724).
The image depicts a performance given at the Kado Theater in Osaka January 1859. To the left is Jitsukawa Ensaburō 実川延三郎 as Watōnai; in the center is Arashi Kichisaburō III 嵐吉三郎 as Kanki; to the right is Bandō Hikosaburō V 坂東彦三郎 as Kinshōjō.
Synopsis of the play: "The Battles of Coxinga (Kokusenya kassen) is based on the true adventures of Coxinga/ Watonai, a warrior of Chinese and Japanese parentage, who fought for the restoration of the Ming Chinese government after its defeat in the 17th c. by Manchu invaders. In the kabuki play Watonai joined forces with Kinshojo, his Chinese step-sister, and Kanki, her husband." - Source: The Claremont Colleges Digital Library https://ccdl.claremont.edu/digital/collection/cyw/id/232 [accessed 8-27-2023]

media.caption: Captain Matsuzaki Fights Bravely in the Battle of Songhwan (成観之激戦松崎大尉奮勇ノ図 Seikan no gekisen Matsuzaki taii funyū no zu)

text.headline: Captain Matsuzaki Fights Bravely in the Battle of Songhwan (成観之激戦松崎大尉奮勇ノ図 Seikan no gekisen Matsuzaki taii funyū no zu)
text.text:
Before reaching Songhwan, the Japanese troops had to cross the deep Anson river. Forty-year-old Captain Matsuzaki Naoomi from Kumamoto on Kyushu led his men on July 29, 1894, in attacking the enemy on the other side of the river. In this print the fearless captain battles cowering Chinese soldiers. But he was ambushed from one hundred feet and was shot through the leg. Undaunted, he continued to fight gallantly with his sword. When he was struck by another bullet in the head, he is reported to have shouted, “I’ve been hit!” and to have died bravely. Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 20.
Other prints from this collection featuring the valor of Captain Matsuzaki are The Great Battle of the Ansong Ford: The Valor of Captain Matsuzaki Crossing Anjō (IHL.0168) and Captain Matsuzaki Crossing the Anjō-sen (IHL. 0530), both by Mizuno Toshikata.

media.caption: Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo (鎮西八郎源為朝)

text.headline: Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo (鎮西八郎源為朝)
text.text:
Pictured is Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo [Minamoto No Tametomo (1139-1177)] slaying a powerful konoha-tengu (Tumbling-leaf tengu), with its characteristic bright red human face, long bulbous nose, wild hair, and bulging eyes. Tametomo has cut off the tengu's head, also severing the cliff edge. Part of the tengu's severed body can be seen beneath the scroll on the right.
Tametomo was the hero of many legends, one of which has him being stopped from committing ritual suicide while at sea by a tengu sent by Emperor Sutoku.
The prints in this series were originally issued as a pair of chūban size prints on an ōban size sheet.
Yoshitoshi modeled this design after his teacher's, Utagawa Kuniyoshi (1798-1861), almost identical print created about 30 years earlier for the series Ten Famous Excellences of Tametomo (Tametomo homare no jikketsu), published by Aritaya Seiemon, c. 1848.

media.caption: Numazu: Latticework Tile Wall (沼津 なまこ壁)

text.headline: Numazu: Latticework Tile Wall (沼津 なまこ壁)
text.text:
Sekino's rendition of station number 13, Numazu, along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. This print is the 17th, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekinō created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858). Sekino's love of geometry is on show in this print with the diamond latticework, vertical slats, and the kawara (clay roofing tiles) patterns.
"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

media.caption: Strokes 93-7

text.headline: Strokes 93-7
text.text:
Hara has been working with the theme of 'strokes' since the 1970s. The strokes have been described as paths of light, each one a range of intensities captured by Hara's magnificent technique of colour gradation. His prints, exhibiting "flat coolness and perfect evenness" at first appear to be silkscreens, but they are achieved through lithography often involving multiple printings using the artist's "special technique with a method of applying the ink with huge rollers to give his work an element of unbelievable smoothness, lushness, and control." - Sources: Contemporary Japanese Prints: Symbols of a Society in Transition, Lawrence Smith, Harper & Row Publishers, 1985, p. 28; Collecting Modern Japanese Prints, Then and Now, Mary and Norman Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1994, p. 126.
There is an indebtedness to traditional Japanese calligraphy, in its movement, by Hara while substituting a rainbow of saturated colors for the traditional black sumi ink.

media.caption: Mountain and Lake (山と湖 Yama to mizuumi)

text.headline: Mountain and Lake (山と湖 Yama to mizuumi)
text.text:
One of Miyashita's post-1980s prints displaying a move back towards realism from the abstraction of his works created in the 1970s. Miyashita used a similar water and hilly shoreline motif on at least several other prints likely created around the time this collection's print was made.
The intense blues and greens are printed using water-based inks on a carved woodblock with the elevated black outlines and impressed surfaces of the buildings on the shoreline being achieved through soldering wire and bits and pieces to a zinc plate and building up the outlined areas with layers of oil-based intaglio ink.

media.caption: Autumn Moon at Tōin (洞院の秋月 Tōin no aki no tsuki)

text.headline: Autumn Moon at Tōin (洞院の秋月 Tōin no aki no tsuki)
text.text:
This print pictures Fujiwara no Yasumasa, an aristocrat of distinction, playing his flute, being stalked by the outlaw Hakamadare Yasusuke who wants to steal Yasumasa's clothing.
"Fujiwara no Yasumasa (958-1036) was a renowned musician and poet in the Heian court. One autumn night Yasumasa made his way home through the isolated Ichiharano moor. He played his flute as he sauntered along. While he believed that he was alone amidst the tall grass, a bandit lay in wait. The highwayman, Hakamadare Yasusuke (also known as Kidomaru) planned to attack the lonely traveler and steal his elegant winter robes. Yet, as the music reached Yasusuke’s ears, he found himself unable to attack. He became enchanted by the beauty of the music and followed Yasumasa all the way home. Upon reaching the courtier’s home, the flutist noticed his unintended audience and offered Yasusuke a fine gift of clothing so that he would not leave empty-handed." - Source: website of Ronin Gallery
Originally issued in April 1868, this print was posthumously reissued (a "second state") using a different color scheme and partially new blocks in April 1894. Three different versions of this reprint exist, with this collection's print being considered the second version distinguished by the orange coat worn by Yasumasa, as opposed to a blue coat in the first version. A final version, perhaps from around 1900, is without a publisher’s seal or Yoshitoshi’s signature.

media.caption: Sakaki, No. 10 (榊 第十号)

text.headline: Sakaki, No. 10 (榊 第十号)
text.text:
One of an assumed 54 prints in the series The Fifty-Four Chapters in Modern Times by Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900). Here we see Genji courting one of his lovers in front of an evergreen tree on which Genji has tied love notes in a scene from chapter 10.
"‘Genji Mania’ may have long peaked before Kunichika’s Fifty-Four Modern Feelings [a.k.a. The Fifty-Four Chapters in Modern Times] but his decision to publish the series may have been motivated as much by the publisher’s demand as by the fact that his teacher Kunisada [Utagawa Kunisada I (1786–1865)] had produced the original Rustic Genji illustrations. The title of Kunichika’s series is also a word play: the characters that can be read ‘Genji’, as in the novel, literally translate as ‘contemporary times’ (genji)." - Source: Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999, p. 20.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Daikokuya Sōroku in the play The Tale of Shiraishi, a Latter-day Taiheiki (市川団十郎 ・大黒屋惣六 ・碁太平記白石噺)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Daikokuya Sōroku in the play The Tale of Shiraishi, a Latter-day Taiheiki (市川団十郎 ・大黒屋惣六 ・碁太平記白石噺)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as the brothel proprietor Daikokuya Sōroku 大黒屋惣六 in the scene Yoshiwara Daikokuya (Yoshiwara Daikokuya no ba 吉原大黒屋之場) from the play Go Taiheiki Shiraishi Banashi (The Tale of Shiraishi, a Latter-day Taiheiki).

One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits. A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

media.caption: Dontarō 鈍太郎

text.headline: Dontarō 鈍太郎
text.text:
In this scene from the kyōgen 狂言 play Dontarō, Dontarō is carried home by his wife and mistress acting as his personal jinrikisha.
Play synopsis ("Japanese Noh and Kyogen plays: staging dichotomy," Zvika Serpera , appearing in Comparative Drama, Western Michigan University, Sept. 22, 2005.) -In the kyōgen Dontaro two women display disruptively comic selfish devotion to the same man, though the play ends in harmony. After three years in the capital, Dontaro returns home, but his ugly wife does not believe that it is really him and sends him away. His beautiful mistress reacts similarly, and he decides to become a monk. After both women, who had not previously accepted each other, understand what has happened, they search for him together, find him dressed as a monk, try to convince him to remain with them, and agree to anything he says. Dontaro uses this situation to force the two women in a comical way to accept each other; he then makes them bear him home in their joined arms as if carrying a baby, while they sing, announcing that this is the "personal jinrikisha" (teguruma) of Sir Dontaro. The play ends with a sense of agreement and intimacy among the three characters.

Illustrations of Noh is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints issued between 1897 and 1904. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Rokujizō 六地蔵 (The Six Statues)

text.headline: Rokujizō 六地蔵 (The Six Statues)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the kyōgen 狂言 play Rokujizō. For another impression of this print see IHL.0807.
Play synopsis - A countryman goes to the capital to buy six statues of the Buddhist God Jizo for a new temple. Upon reaching the city he realizes he does not know where a sculptor lives nor what one looks like. While searching in the streets, a shyster notices him and decides to trick him out of his money by posing as a master sculptor.

media.caption: Oba ga sake 伯母ヶ酒  (Auntie's Sake)

text.headline: Oba ga sake 伯母ヶ酒  (Auntie's Sake)
text.text:
In this scene from the kyōgen 狂言 play Auntie's Sake, a nephew disguised as an ogre drinks his stingy auntie's sake.
Play synopsis - The story revolves around a nephew who disguises himself as an ogre in order to steal his stingy aunt's sake. As he drinks (the actor employs a fan to mimic the use of a sake cup) he moves the mask that is his disguise to one side while ordering his aunt not to look at him. After he falls into a drunken stupor, she discovers he is her nephew and angrily chases him off.

media.caption: Sarumawashi kadode no hitofushi (猿廻しかど出の一諷)

text.headline: Sarumawashi kadode no hitofushi (猿廻しかど出の一諷)
text.text: Kunichika portrays the main characters from the play Sarumawashi Kado De no Hitofushi. "The Meiji star Onoe Kikugorō V [pictured in the brown robe] had the idea once to use a real monkey on stage when he played the role of Yojirō. The highlight of the performance was something not expected by the actor: the monkey peeing on the stage . . . to the audience's delight." - Source: Kabuki 21 website http://www.kabuki21.com/horikawa.php [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Fujidaiko 富士太鼓 (Fuji's Drum)

text.headline: Fujidaiko 富士太鼓 (Fuji's Drum)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 32) - Hearing that a drum player named Asama had been called in to play at a seven-day concert before the Emperor Hanazono, another famous player named Fuji came up to the capital too. Asama, resenting this, kills Fuji. When the official has announced this, Fuji’s wife arrives with her daughter, having been much disturbed by a dream she has had. Learning what has happened, she puts on her husband’s robes and, overcome with grief, strikes the drum which to her was the cause of her husband’s death.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Himuro 氷室 (The Cavern of Ice)

text.headline: Himuro 氷室 (The Cavern of Ice)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 55) - A Court official on his way back to the capital stops at Himuro-yama, the ‘Ice cave Mountain’, in Tango Province and there learns from an old man how the ice, which forms in sheltered spots, is preserved throughout the summer and served then to the Emperor. The old man disappears into the cave, but a little later a goddess comes and dances, and then the god appears in his true form with a gift of ice for the Emperor.

media.caption: Jinen Koji 自然居士 (Jinen the Lay Monk)

text.headline: Jinen Koji 自然居士 (Jinen the Lay Monk)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 64) - While the lay priest Jinen is preaching at the Ungo-ji temple, a young girl comes and gives him a robe as a gift. In a letter accompanying it she explains that she has sold herself to buy the robe in order to have the priest say a mass for her dead parents. As Jinen is reading this, the men who have bought the girl come and take her away. Much moved by this, the preacher hurries after them when he is told what has happened and demands that they release the girl. This they at first refuse to do, but after Jinen has entertained them with all manner of songs and dances, they agree to give the girl up.

media.caption: A True Account of the Satsuma Rebellion in Kagoshima 8 (鹿兒島縣 西南實記八 Kagoshima-ken Seinan jikki hachi)

text.headline: A True Account of the Satsuma Rebellion in Kagoshima 8 (鹿兒島縣 西南實記八 Kagoshima-ken Seinan jikki hachi)
text.text: Print number 8 in a series of woodblock prints issued as newspaper supplements providing "true accounts" of the Satsuma Rebellion (Seinan War). The red cartouche to the left of the army officer brandishing his sword calls out General Ōyama, but whether it is General Ōyama Tsunayoshi or General Ōyama Iwao, both of whom fought in the war, is unclear. The text makes reference to violent & difficult battles, the use of bamboo to hold ammunition, as well as “fire flowers.”

media.caption: Iwai Hanshirō, Ichikawa Gonjūrō and Ichikawa Danjūrō in the play Minori no aki seisho denki (岩井半四郎、 市川権十郎、市川団十郎・実成秋清正伝記)

text.headline: Iwai Hanshirō, Ichikawa Gonjūrō and Ichikawa Danjūrō in the play Minori no aki seisho denki (岩井半四郎、 市川権十郎、市川団十郎・実成秋清正伝記)
