media.caption: Hashiba Hideyoshi (羽柴秀吉)

text.headline: Hashiba Hideyoshi (羽柴秀吉)
text.text:
Print number 33 (三十三), one of 4 contributed by Yoshitoshi to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Toyotomi Hideyoshi (Hashiba Hideyoshi) seated on a tiger skin and wearing a peacock robe, discussing with a priest the terms of a truce with the rival Mōri clan.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Sketches for Artisans, Volume 4 (工業図式, 四篇 Kōgyō zushiki, yon hen)

text.headline: Sketches for Artisans, Volume 4 (工業図式, 四篇 Kōgyō zushiki, yon hen)
text.text:
Volume four of five bound volumes forming a design book for artists and craftsmen providing drawings of legendary and mythological characters, animals, flowers, Buddhist rituals, Shinto-related items, toys, landscapes, etc. Each volume contains an introduction, followed by over 30 pages of drawings and closing with a colophon.
The preface of volume 1, and possibly the other volumes, is credited to the Meiji-era writer Kanagaki Robun 假名垣 魯文 (1829-1894).

media.caption: Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu (鶴千歳曽我門松)

text.headline: Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu (鶴千歳曽我門松)
text.text: Depicting the six actors (from right to left) Ichimura Kakitsu IV 市村家橘, Ichikawa Shinsha 市川新車,  Nakamura Tsuruzō 中村鶴蔵, Bandō Hikosaburō V 坂東彦三郎, Onoe Kikujirō II 尾上菊次郎 and Sawamura Tosshō II 沢村訥升 in this Soga Brothers themed New Year's play of revenge titled Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu. For another print depicting this play see IHL.0954.

media.caption: Disquisition on the Political Affair of the Kyōwa Era (日月星享和政談 Jitsugetsusei kyōwa seidan)

text.headline: Disquisition on the Political Affair of the Kyōwa Era (日月星享和政談 Jitsugetsusei kyōwa seidan)
text.text:
While the play's title is not shown in the print, the actors (right to left), Ichikawa Sadanji, Onoe Kikugorō [V], Iwai Hanshirō [VIII] and Nakamura Nakazō [III] are portraying characters in the play Jitsugetsusei kyōwa Seidan written in 1876 by Kawatake Mokuami (Kawatake Shinshichi II, 1816–1893).
The play is based on the Kyōwa era (1801-1804) incident known as the Enmeiin Affair, in which Nichido an actor-turned-priest used a secret chamber at the Nichiren temple Enmeiin to seduce a number of leading ladies from the shogun’s house. "Nichido was first an actor but became the superior of Enmeiin, a temple of the Nichiren sect in Yanaka, and, with the aid of the priestling Ryuzen, enticed women thither, making the place a den of immorality, visited even by ladies-in-waiting at the Court. That priests should break their vows of chastity was so common that no one gave it a second thought, but when we have a man who turned priest from actor and alluring women to his temple for immoral purposes, it throws a glaring light on the moral degradation of the age." - Source: The Economic Aspects of the History of the Civilization of Japan – Volume 3, Yosaburō Takekoshi, originally 1930 and republished 2004, Routledge, p. 173.

media.caption: Moonlit Night at the Museum (博物館 月夜  Hakubutsukan tsukiyo)

text.headline: Moonlit Night at the Museum (博物館 月夜  Hakubutsukan tsukiyo)
text.text: A view of the Kyoto Imperial Museum (renamed Kyoto National Museum) on a moonlit night. A family and its dog are out for a late night walk in the snow.

media.caption: Distant View of Shijō in the Early Morning (朝方四条遠望 Asagata Shijo Enbō)

text.headline: Distant View of Shijō in the Early Morning (朝方四条遠望 Asagata Shijo Enbō)
text.text: A view of the Kanda River in the Shijō area of Kyoto in the early morning with no one about. Tea houses stretch along the river on the right and a tall modern building appears on the right beyond one of the Kandagawa's bridges.  One of Asano's sōsaku hanga works of the 1930s of views in and around Kyoto.  A second edition of this print was published in 1934.

media.caption: Nature (自然 Shizen)

text.headline: Nature (自然 Shizen)

media.caption: Nest (巣)

text.headline: Nest (巣)
text.text:
This is the only lithograph by Takahashi that I have seen, all of his other print work employs woodblock. He created it in 1965 at the legendary studios of Ken Tyler, owner of Gemini Ltd.
"Tyler established the print workshop Gemini Ltd. in 1965 and set out to work with the very best artists of his day, promising them: ‘Here is a workshop, there are no rules, no restrictions, do what you want to do.’" - Source National Gallery of Australia website http://nga.gov.au/InternationalPrints/Tyler/Default.cfm?MnuID=10 [accessed 8-17-23]
"Takahashi’s collaboration with Kenneth Tyler followed a strong tradition of artistic exchange between America and Japan in the post-war period. Titled Nest, the print in the NGA collection was produced at the Gemini workshop in 1965. It is representative of Takahashi’s typical mode of abstraction, with depth created by tonal layers and the image vaguely reminiscent of the natural forms Takahashi found so inspiring." - Source: Gwen Horsfield, 2008, National Gallery of Australia website, https://nga.gov.au/art-artists/the-kenneth-e-tyler-collection/artists/rikio-takahashi/#:~:text=Takahashi's%20collaboration%20with%20Kenneth%20Tyler,the%20Gemini%20workshop%20in%201965 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Kazusa Akushichibei in the play Kagekiyo (九世市川団十郎 上総悪七兵衛・景清)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Kazusa Akushichibei in the play Kagekiyo (九世市川団十郎 上総悪七兵衛・景清)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper right panel, playing the role of Kazusa Akushichibei 上総悪七兵衛 in the kabuki play Kagekiyo 景清. He wears "the exaggerated kumadori [stage makeup associated with the aragoto style], bushy hair and gold brocade of the 'loyal warrior'. . . ."[1] Below Danjūrō is an unidentified actor playing the role of Shigetada 重忠.
"The role of the famous Heike warrior Akushichibyoe [Akushichibei] Kagekiyo is a signature one for the Ichikawa family, and the play is part of the Kabuki Eighteen. The role was first played by Danjūrō IV, whose thin frame and long face made him unsuitable for the pure Ichikawa aragoto roles. Instead he developed his art in other directions, playing the logical and loyal heroes known as jitsugotoshi, as well as villain (katakiyaku) roles. He enjoyed huge success with the part of Kagekiyo. The part adds a new psychological dimension to aragoto, in that Kagekiyo is imprisoned by his enemies, and endures a tearful reunion with his wife and children before smashing his way out of the prison in which he is being held. The makeup he developed for the role used black lines, suggesting his evil nature. Later generations of Danjūrō continued to play the role, and it had a special significance for Danjūrō VII, who acted it to celebrate his return to Edo after seven years banishment. Perhaps we can sense a hint of pride in the way he used Kagekiyo's escape from prison to mirror his own banishment and return."[2]
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[3]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Kakoyo Akaemon in the play Nanatsumen (九世市川団十郎 賀古屋赤右衛門・七ツ面)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, playing the role of Kakoyo Akaemon, the mask maker, in the kabuki play Nanatsumen 七ツ面. Above him is the box containing the seventh mask holding a secret scroll and the actor Hakuen VII 七代目 白猿 (later known as Ichikawa Danjūrō VII).
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[1]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

media.caption: Manjū 満仲

text.headline: Manjū 満仲
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 100-101) - Tada no Manjū has sent his son Bijo to be educated in a temple. When the boy returns, Manjū is so enraged by his neglect of his studies that he goes to strike him with his sword, but his faithful retainer Nakamitsu restrains him. At this, Manjū orders him to kill Bijo himself. Unable to ignore the order altogether, and yet finding it impossible to kill his master's son, Nakamitsu finally resolves his dilemma by killing instead his own son Kōju, who himself asked to be allowed to take Bijo's place. When Manjū later regrets the hastiness which has led, he thinks, to the death of his own son, Bijo is brought back to him by a priest from the temple where Nakamitsu sent him to hide. Learning of the extent of Nakamitsu's devotion, Manjū pardons his son and then asks his retainer to perform a dance for them. This Nakamitsu does, in celebration of the reconciliation, but all the time his thoughts are on his own son whom he has sacrificed to serve his lord.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Kōtei 皇帝 (The Emperor)

text.headline: Kōtei 皇帝 (The Emperor)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 86-87) - While the Emperor Gen-sō (Hsuan Tsung) of T'ang is keeping an anxious vigil over the sick-bed of his favourite, Yō-kihi (Yang Kuei-fei), an old man comes to the palace and tells the Emperor that he is the ghost of Shō-ki (Chung K'uei), a former retainer who committed suicide when he failed in an examination. The Emperor, however, graciously appointed him posthumously to Court rank and gave him a fine burial; in return he has now come to drive the sickness away from Yō-hiki. He asks that a certain sacred mirror be placed at the head of her bed, and then disappears. When this is done, the devil who is afflicting Yō-hiki is seen in the mirror, but when the Emperor draws his sword to strike it down, it vanishes. The spirit of Shō-ki returns and succeeds in vanquishing the devil. Having this repaid his debt, Shō-ki promises the Emperor that he will become a protective deity and then disappears again like a figure in a dream.

media.caption: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)

text.headline: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 26-28) - An Imperial emissary on his way to the Great Shrines of Ise stops overnight at Saikū nearby as it happens to be the last day of winter and he hopes to see something of the votive tablets which are said to be hung up there during that particular night to foretell the fortunes of the coming year, a white one indicating sunny weather and a black one rain. He meets an old couple with such tablets who, after some discussion, agree to put up one of each kind to signify good fortune for everyone. They then disappear into the darkness after telling him that they are in fact two of the gods of Ise. In the second part Amaterasu, the Sun-goddess, appears with the goddess Uzume and the god Tajikarao and performs a dance. The three of them then depict the ancient story of Amaterasu’s withdrawal into a cave: as the world is plunged into darkness by her disappearance, the other gods dance and make merry and eventually succeed in enticing her out again by arousing her curiosity.

text.headline: Higaki 檜垣 (Cypress Fence)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 54) - A priest living in the mountains sees a very old woman come every day to draw water. Questioning her, he learns that she is the woman Higaki who long ago composed a poem on being asked for water by Fujiwara no Okinori. After asking for his prayers, the woman disappears. When she returns later, she tells the priest of her early life and performs a dance as she recalls the time when she danced for Okinori.

media.caption: Obasute 姨捨 (The Old Woman Abandoned in the Hills)

text.headline: Obasute 姨捨 (The Old Woman Abandoned in the Hills)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 128) - A man from the capital goes with two companions to view the autumn moon at a place called Obasute-yama ‘The Hill of the Old Forsaken Woman’, and there meets a woman who talks with him. Just before she disappears, she discloses that she is in fact the old woman who was left there long ago and thus gave the mountain its name. She later appears in her true form and after telling of the blessings that come with the teachings of the Buddha, dances in the moonlight.

media.caption: Kabuki Playbill for Kabuki-za featuring the play Motomezuka migawari Nitta and the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX

text.headline: Kabuki Playbill for Kabuki-za featuring the play Motomezuka migawari Nitta and the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX
text.text: The cover of this kabuki playbill (banzuke) from March 1892 features Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role oa Kusunoki, Masashige’s wife, in the play Onna Kusunoki (top inset) and the role of the pirate Kezori Kyuemon in the play Kezori Kyuemon (bottom inset.) The red cartouches using kanteiryū (the scripted kanji used for kabuki signs and advertising) provide the name of the theater, the Kabuki-za, and its location. The smaller light-colored cartouche contains the signature of the artist Utagawa Kunimasa IV, using his then current artist name Kōchōrō. The price of the playbill is marked as 8 sen.

This print, one of ninety-two full-color supplemental prints to the earlier issued six volume textbook titled Brocade Pictures of Moral Education, illustrates story number 4 in volume 4.
In October 1883 a set of ninety-two full-color oban-size prints designed by students of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi were published by Tsuji Keiji and his publishing house Fukyūsha as supplements, or accompaniments, to the six volume set of textbooks titled "Nishiki-e shūshindan" 錦絵修身談 (Brocade Prints for Moral Education), published earlier by Tsuji and illustrated by Yoshitoshi. A number of the full-color prints issued were based upon Yoshitoshi's black and white illustrations in the texts. text.headline: Chinese Ship Shop 唐船屋
text.text:
This large-format undated print, likely issued in the 1970s or 1980s by the publishing house Yūyūdō, is after a design which originally appeared in Takehisa Yumeji's 1920 book of poetry titled Yume no Furusato 夢のふるさと (Dreaming of Home), published by the Tokyo publisher Shinchōsha. The book contained 10 woodblocks and color illustrations.
The title of this print Chinese Ship Shop 唐船屋 (which can also be read as karafuneya), appearing in script to the right of the geisha, references the shop or restaurant where the geisha entertains.

media.caption: Sawamura Tosshō, Sawamura Tanosuke and Nakamura Nakazao in the dance Michiyuki chō no fubuki (沢村訥升、沢村田之助、中村仲蔵・道行蝶の吹雪)

text.headline: Sawamura Tosshō, Sawamura Tanosuke and Nakamura Nakazao in the dance Michiyuki chō no fubuki (沢村訥升、沢村田之助、中村仲蔵・道行蝶の吹雪)
text.text:
From right to left, the actors Sawamura Tosshō II as Shirakawa no Anchin 白川の安珍, Sawamura Tanosuke III as Shōji Musume Kiyohime 庄司娘清姫 and Nakamura Nakazao III as Sendo Namiroku 船頭波六 in the dance interlude Michiyuki chō no fubuki staged at the Morita-za 守田座 in January 1869. The partially seen actor in the center panel does not seem to be identified.
Michiyuki generally depict two young lovers on the way to commit suicide or two traveling characters with a romantic implication attached to their journey. Some famous michiyuki are frequently performed independently from their drama.

media.caption: Ties of Colored Threads in the Weaving Princess's Satin (織姫繻子縁色糸 Orihime no Shusu Enishi no Iroito)

text.headline: Ties of Colored Threads in the Weaving Princess's Satin (織姫繻子縁色糸 Orihime no Shusu Enishi no Iroito)
text.text: The actors, from right to left, Ichikawa Yonezō 市川米蔵 as court lady Satsuki 女官皐月, Ichikawa Sadanji II 市川左団次 as court lady Shirotaki 官女白瀧, Ichikawa Gonjūrō 市川権十郎 as Eiji Yamada Oribe 山田衛士織部 and Ichikawa Enjō 市川莚女 as court lady Minase 官女水無瀬 in Orihime no Shusu Enishi no Iroito performed at the Meiji-za in the second week of May 1894. "The title of the play involves a pun on the name of a new luxury fabric. The play itself was written to publicize this new domestic product, which was sold by the textile firm that provide the stage curtain, used as a backdrop in the theater, and as a dramatic compositional element by the artist." - Source: Asian art historian Lynn Katsumoto

media.caption: White Sake for Otafuku, No Medicine for Foolishness (おたふくに白酒  ばかにつける薬はない Otafuku ni shirozake, Baka ni tsukeru kusuri mo nai)

text.headline: White Sake for Otafuku, No Medicine for Foolishness (おたふくに白酒  ばかにつける薬はない Otafuku ni shirozake, Baka ni tsukeru kusuri mo nai)
text.text:
The second part of the print's title, "baka ni tsukeru kusuri wa nai" is a proverb meaning "there is no cure for a fool." Certainly the gentleman in the lower right is acting like a drunken fool, performing some disgusting act that provokes both consternation and hilarity. At the top of the print an otafuku (a homely woman, but also the goddess of mirth) dances and to the right of her bottles of shirozake (sweet white sake) are evident.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

media.caption: Aya no Tsuzumi 綾鼓 (Brocade Drum)

text.headline: Aya no Tsuzumi 綾鼓 (Brocade Drum)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 11) - An old gardener, who has fallen in love with a lady of the Court, is told that if he can make the sound of a drum in the grounds reach her, she will let him see her again. He gladly strikes the drum but no sound comes, for it is covered only with damask. Overcome with anger and despair, he drowns himself in the lake in the palace grounds. His angry ghost then appears and gives vent to its feelings of anger against the lady.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Nishiki-gi 錦木 (The Decorated Tree)

text.headline: Nishiki-gi 錦木 (The Decorated Tree)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 124) - In a village in Mutsu a priest meets a woman with a length of cloth over her arm and a man carrying a small, colored tree. He learns that the cloth is woven from birds' feathers and that the tree is a sign by which a man may declare his love for a woman by leaving it outside her house. She can respond by taking the tree in or refuse him by leaving it standing outside. The two take the priest to the burial mound of a man who, after leaving such trees outside a woman's house every day for three years, died from a broken heart. Then they both disappear into the mound. The priest prays there and in his dream the ghost of the man reappears and, rejoicing in the happiness that he and the woman have found, performs a dance.

text.headline: Shirahige 白鬚
text.text:

O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 162) - An Imperial envoy on a pilgrimage to the shrine of Shirahige no Myōjin meets an old fisherman there and hears from him how Mt. Hiei, with which the shrine is closely connected, first came to be a great center of Buddhism. media.caption: Shizuka Gozen (静御前)

text.headline: Shizuka Gozen (静御前)
text.text:
Print number 15 (十五), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Shizuka Gozen (静御前), a famous and beautiful shirabyōshi in the days of the Heian court, dancing in front of Minamoto no Yoritomo (源頼朝) in Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū (鶴岡八幡宮) in Kamakura.
To see another edition of this print with a differently colored brocade border go to IHL.0676.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Tanaka Tsurukichi (田中鶴吉)

text.headline: Tanaka Tsurukichi (田中鶴吉)
text.text:
Print number 48 (四十八), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the adventurer Tanaka Tsurukichi (1855-1925), known as the "Japanese Robinson Crusoe", speaking with Japanese naval officers. Tanaka traveled to the United States at an early age, possibly as young as 12, returned to Japan in 1881, and, finally, emigrated to the US in 1887. While this design was created after Tanaka's return to live in the United States, its setting appears to be on the Boshin Islands, where Tanaka established a less than successful stock farm.

media.caption: Fruitful Year at Fuji (豊年の富士 Hōnen no Fuji)

text.headline: Fruitful Year at Fuji (豊年の富士 Hōnen no Fuji)
text.text:
This 13th print in the 36 print series depicts farmers harvesting a bountiful autumn crop while Mount Fuji stands guard in all its grandeur. This print is the original issue (first edition between 1939-1940) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company as part of the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. Later editions eliminated the small telephone pole on the right side of the hill and also changed the title from 豊年の富士 to 實りの秋. To view a later edition of this image please see IHL. 0412, Fall Harvest from the series Eight Views of Fuji.

THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF 2600
Published by Uchida Bijutsu Shoshi between 1939 and 1940, this 36-print set (plus an introductory sheet and a table of contents sheet) by Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000) is a more modern take on Hokusai's (1760–1849) famous series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826-1833). Its publication was timed to coincide with nationalist celebrations in November 1940 marking Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation.
Tokuriki's series was extremely popular with domestic and foreign buyers who purchased one thousand copies within a short time after issuance. Various prints from this series were re-printed in subsequent years and subsets of the thirty-six prints were later repackaged into newly named series, such as Eight Views of Mount Fuji and Four Season of Mount Fuji, released in the 1950s. Later printings omit the information in the margin, modify Tokuriki's signature and change the seals below his signature appearing in the image area of the print.

media.caption: To と

text.headline: To と
text.text:
One of eighteen prints issued as part of the comic series "ABCs of Educational Lectures" issued between February 1897 and March 1898. This series was a collaboration between Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) and the writer Nishimori Takeki 西森武城 (1861-1913), also known as Koppi Dōjin, one of the chief comic writers for the newspaper Marumaru chinbun (Blue Pencil News of the Weird). "The conceit of this series is a spoof on the Imperial Rescript on Education (Kyōiku chokugo) issued in 1890 to boost morality by reminding people of Confucian and Shinto values." - Source: Akiko Walley, Maud I. Kerns Associate Professor of Japanese Art, History of Art and Architecture, University of Oregon.
This print represents the syllable “to” (と) with the saying, 'Tori naki sato ni kōmori,' which is roughly equivalent to 'In the Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man is King,' but more literally, 'Bats in the Land with No Birds.' It satirizes the no-good son of a wealthy provincial family returning from his 'Grand Tour' of Tokyo. The 'busker' in the original is more specifically, deroren saimon, or 'trumpet shell prayer.' The mention of 'deroren saimon' is a pun on the phrase 'hora o fuku' (to toot on one’s trumpet shell), meaning to 'boast' or 'tell tall tales.' Deroren was a type of street performance popular during the late Edo (1615-1868) and Meiji (1868-1912) periods. A performer told vendetta' stories in a distinct rhythmic phrasing, blowing the trumpet shell intermittently uttering the nonsensical word 'deroren' to retain audience’s attention." - Source: Akiko Walley, Maud I. Kerns Associate Professor of Japanese Art, History of Art and Architecture, University of Oregon.

media.caption: Crest Signboards (紋看板 Mon kanban)

text.headline: Crest Signboards (紋看板 Mon kanban)
text.text: This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print)  picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts signboards giving the names and crests of the actors who will appear at the theater that season. This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Wheel and Axle (輪軸 rinjiku)

text.headline: Wheel and Axle (輪軸 rinjiku)
text.text:
One of eight diptych prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of mechanics issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print discusses and demonstrates the principles and practical uses of the axle and wheel. (For other prints in this series see IHL.0766 and IHL.0767.)
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

media.caption: Lever (梃子 teko)

text.headline: Lever (梃子 teko)
text.text:
One of eight diptych prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of mechanics issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print discusses and demonstrates the principles and practical uses of the lever with the print on the right explaining that in raising the ladder, the closer you are to the ladder's center of gravity, the less force you will need. On the left, the diagrams explain about the lever and fulcrum and its applications. (For other prints in this series see IHL.0765 and IHL.0767.)
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

media.caption: Wedge (楔 kusabi)

text.headline: Wedge (楔 kusabi)
text.text:
One of eight diptych prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of mechanics issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print discusses and demonstrates the wedge, its principles and practical applications. The right side of the diptych relates that "a wedge is a combination of two sloping edges necessary to break wood or rock. The thinner the wedge, the less strength is needed. The thicker, the more power is required" and the left side tells us "When two large sake cups are stacked on top of each other and pressure is applied to the top, it is possible to break only the outer cup, which is also the same as the principle of a wedge." (For other prints in this series see IHL.0765 and IHL.0766.)
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

media.caption: Bandō Takesaburō, Iwai Kumesaburō and Onoe Kikujirō in the play Sekai no hana Oguri gaiden (坂東竹三郎、岩井粂三郎、尾上菊次郎・世界花小栗外伝)

text.headline: Bandō Takesaburō, Iwai Kumesaburō and Onoe Kikujirō in the play Sekai no hana Oguri gaiden (坂東竹三郎、岩井粂三郎、尾上菊次郎・世界花小栗外伝)
text.text:
From right to left, the actors Bandō Takesaburō as Oguri Sōtan (actually Kaneuji), Iwai Kumesaburō III as Manchō's daughter (musume) Okoma, and Onoe Kikujirō II As Kohagi (actually princess Terute) in the play Sekai no hana Oguri gaiden (Worldly Flowers, an Oguri Anecdote), performed at Edo's Nakamura Theatre 中村 in the 4th month of 1851. This print is part of an untitled series of horizontal actor prints, created c. 4th month of 1851 by the artist.
The shita-uri シタ売 seal is present on this collection's print indicating a print not allowed to be displayed under censorship rules and that was sold "under the counter."

media.caption: Kayano Plateau (萱野高原)

text.headline: Kayano Plateau (萱野高原)
text.text: Horses grazing on the Kayano Plateau just north of the Hakkōda Mountains of Aomori Prefecture. Sitting at an altitude of about 540 meters, it is covered with natural grass.

media.caption: At Play

text.headline: At Play
text.text: Children at play as seen through semi-transparent screens in this modern woodblock print by an unknown artist.

media.caption: Udesuke 腕助

text.headline: Udesuke 腕助
text.text:
The actor Nakayama Genjūrō II as Udesuke, who is seen twirling a slow burning matchrope, in this scene from the play Kujira Obi Nishiki no Shingata, which mixed the Tengajaya world with Ichi-no-Tani Futaba Gunki, and was performed at the Morita-za in the 4th lunar month 1867. - source: Kabuki 21 website http://www.kabuki21.com/genjuro.php [accessed 8-17-23]
The inset scene above the actor looks to be inscribed 上野 (Ueno) and, if so, is a view of Kiyomizu Kannon-do in Ueno Park.
This series matches actors portraying a specific character with famous places in Edo. It consists of at least 58 prints drawn by multiple artists, including Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900), Utagawa Kuniteru II (1830-1874) and Utagawa Yoshiiku (1833-1904) and published by Masudaya Ginjirō. Two slightly different series titles are used on the prints: 江都名所合之内 Kōto meisho awase no uchi and 江戸名所合之内 Edo meisho awase no uchi. Note that Kōto was a synonym for Edo.

media.caption: Private House in Kurashiki (倉敷の民家 Kurashiki no Minka)

text.headline: Private House in Kurashiki (倉敷の民家 Kurashiki no Minka)
text.text:
Tokuriki has given us a view from across the Kurashiki canal of an old house in the Kurashiki Bikan historical quarter. While this collection's print is unsigned and not editioned, another state of the print using brownish tints was both signed and sealed by the artist and editioned. It appears that the same blocks were used for both states of the print.
Kurashiki is located west of Okayama Prefecture's southern plains. During the Edo Period some 350 years ago, the area along the Kurashiki-gawa River was under direct control of the shogunate government and trade by boat helped the town to prosper. Clusters of of-fashioned white-walled storehouses and rows of townhouses with lattice windows line both sides of the Kurashiki River in this nationally designated Important Traditional Structures Conservation Area.

media.caption: Ikaboshi in Esashi (江差の烏賊干)

text.headline: Ikaboshi in Esashi (江差の烏賊干)
text.text:
One of twelve prints from the series Picture Notes on Native Customs of Japan depicting folk rituals from different parts of Japan. It is suggested by Lawrence Smith that the prints paid homage to the Folk Art (mingei) movement that Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), who played an unspecified role in issuing this series, was sympathetic to.
The artist comments on this work, "Esashi in Hokkaido island was famous for its folk songs - Oiwake. It was very prosperous during the Edo era but it became obsolete during the Meiji era. Because of its long history, it retained its unique customs. Squid drying was one of them."
This series of prints followed on the heels of the series Scenes of Lost Tokyo (Tokyo kaiko zue), printed in December 1945 and issued by the same publisher, Uemura Masuo of Fugaku Shuppansha. The artists of this set were Azechi Umetarō, Kawanishi Hide, Kuroki Sadao, Maeda Masao, Maekawa Senpan, Mori Dōshun, Saitō Kiyoshi, Sekino Jun'ichirō, Wakayama Yasoji, and Yamaguchii Gen.
The Editor's Statement: "Japan is now on the start-line to the new development. Getting free from militarism Japan is expected to be developed to a nation of civilization. At this time of change, it may be interesting to look back [on] the native customs and festivals as to realize the future images of Japan. These humble customs and festivals will also become the mother's milk for Japanese people to bring up the peaceful heart filled with love and piousness.
"With this purpose the present album has been compiled. The artists are the members of the Japan Artist Engraving Society and are the experts of the Contemporary Original-Engraving in Japan. Japan has been revived to the lovable Japan. We have great pleasure to send you this album at the present delightful time."
For other prints in this series see IHL.0774 and IHL.1016.

media.caption: Iwato Kagura Play (岩戸神楽)

text.headline: Iwato Kagura Play (岩戸神楽)
text.text:
One of twelve prints from the series Picture Notes on Native Customs of Japan depicting folk rituals from different parts of Japan. It is suggested by Lawrence Smith that the prints paid homage to the Folk Art (mingei) movement that Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), who played an unspecified role in issuing this series, was sympathetic to.
The artist comments, "The winter at the village in Takachiho in Hyūga Province is the merry time for the Kagura play in the evening. The religious villagers offer agricultural products to the gods. The thirty-three different kinds of dances with funny drum beats and flutes were performed in the sacred front yard of a designated house or the theater area of the shrine. This was the time when people and the gods communicated with their souls." - Kuroki Sadao

The artists for this series were Azechi Umetarō, Kawanishi Hide, Kuroki Sadao, Maeda Masao, Maekawa Senpan, Mori Dōshun, Saitō Kiyoshi, Sekino Jun'ichirō, Wakayama Yasoji, and Yamaguchi Gen. At this time of change, it may be interesting to look back [on] the native customs and festivals as to realize the future images of Japan. These humble customs and festivals will also become the mother's milk for Japanese people to bring up the peaceful heart filled with love and piousness.
"With this purpose the present album has been compiled. The artists are the members of the Japan Artist Engraving Society and are the experts of the Contemporary Original-Engraving in Japan. Japan has been revived to the lovable Japan. We have great pleasure to send you this album at the present delightful time."
For other prints in this series see IHL.1016 and IHL.0773.

media.caption: Fuji from Okitsu Beach (興津海岸の冨士 Okitsu kaigan no Fuji)

text.headline: Fuji from Okitsu Beach (興津海岸の冨士 Okitsu kaigan no Fuji)
text.text:
This 23rd print in the 36 print series depicts a lone cyclist making his way towards the end of a concrete access route to Okitsu Beach on Suruga Bay. A lone car sits at the end of the access way. Across Suruga Bay stands Mount Fuji. This print is the original issue (first edition between 1939-1940) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company as part of the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.

THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF 2600
Published by Uchida Bijutsu Shoshi between 1939 and 1940, this 36-print set (plus an introductory sheet and a table of contents sheet) by Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000) is a more modern take on Hokusai's (1760–1849) famous series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826-1833). Its publication was timed to coincide with nationalist celebrations in November 1940 marking Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation.
Tokuriki's series was extremely popular with domestic and foreign buyers who purchased one thousand copies within a short time after issuance. Various prints from this series were re-printed in subsequent years and subsets of the thirty-six prints were later repackaged into newly named series, such as Eight Views of Mount Fuji and Four Season of Mount Fuji, released in the 1950s. Later printings omit the information in the margin, modify Tokuriki's signature and change the seals below his signature appearing in the image area of the print.

media.caption: Dragon and Snake (辰 巳)

text.headline: Dragon and Snake (辰 巳)
text.text: The actor Kawarazaki Gonjūrō 河原崎権十郎 in the role of Matsunaga Daizen 松永大膳 on the right (matched with the sign of the dragon 辰) and the actor Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 in the role of Keisei (courtesan) Ayame けいせいあやめ on the left (matched with the sign of the snake 巳.)

media.caption: Mr. Saigō's Amazing Charm to Ward Off Cholera [Reliable Saigō Will Protect You Against Cholera Infection] (西郷虎狼狸予暴魔茂痢奔損 Saigō korori yobō mamori honzon)

text.headline: Mr. Saigō's Amazing Charm to Ward Off Cholera [Reliable Saigō Will Protect You Against Cholera Infection] (西郷虎狼狸予暴魔茂痢奔損 Saigō korori yobō mamori honzon)
text.text:
Saigō Takamori, the leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion (and identified in the red cartouche on his immediate left as "Saigō Takamori the head rebel" 賊魁西郷隆盛, is flanked by his lieutenants Kirino Toshiaki 桐野利秋 to his right, and Shinohara Kunimoto 篠原国幹 to his left. Saigō, who had been dead several weeks when this print was published in October 1877, is standing on a hybrid tiger/wolf/badger demon, representing the swift-killing disease cholera. Saigō is also pictured with a third arm, the meaning of which remains unclear. The imagery uses Saigō's status as an almost demigod after his death, to publicize a warning about a cholera epidemic that broke out the previous month. However, this is not one of the prints that sought to deify the rebel leader after his death, rather it uses double meanings to suggest that Saigō, and the chaos that resulted from his Rebellion, was responsible for the cholera outbreak.
The print carries a price of 1 sen 5 rin 定價一銭五厘.

media.caption: untranslated story 15, page 27 ([十五] 斉王賢女を〓（田＋狗）畝に挙ぐ [廿七丁]

text.headline: untranslated story 15, page 27 ([十五] 斉王賢女を〓（田＋狗）畝に挙ぐ [廿七丁]
text.text:
This print, one of ninety-two full-color supplemental prints to the earlier issued six volume textbook titled Brocade Pictures of Moral Education, illustrates story number 15 in volume 5.
In October 1883 a set of ninety-two full-color oban-size prints designed by students of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi were published by Tsuji Keiji and his publishing house Fukyūsha as supplements, or accompaniments, to the six volume set of textbooks titled "Nishiki-e shūshindan" 錦絵修身談 (Brocade Prints for Moral Education), published earlier by Tsuji and illustrated by Yoshitoshi. These supplemental prints illustrated the ninety-one short stories contained in the six volumes. A number of the full-color prints issued were based upon Yoshitoshi's black and white illustrations in the texts. Each of the full-color prints carries the textbook's title 錦絵修身談 and volume number across its top and the name of the story and its location in the textbook in a vertical red cartouche

media.caption: Leaping Bass, Seasons Greetings

text.headline: Leaping Bass, Seasons Greetings
text.text: Woodblock print of a bass jumping from the water, bounded on top and bottom by a brocade border to appear mounted as if it were a hanging scroll. Designed as a New Year greeting card, the printed text reads “Season’s Greetings, Kim and Masa Obata.” While often attributed to the Japanese-American painter and print designer Chiura Obata (1885-1975), whose drawings of leaping fish look similar to the leaping bass of this print, a square red seal with the letter "K" printed beneath the image of the bass, suggests that the design might be by Kim (Kimio) Obata (b. 1912), Chiura's oldest son, also an artist who was to find success in the advertising and marketing world.

media.caption: Oda Nobunaga (織田信長)

text.headline: Oda Nobunaga (織田信長)
text.text:
Print number 32 (卅二), one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Oda Nobunaga 織田信長 (1534-1582), Japanese military commander in the Azuchi-Momoyama period and one of Japan's "Three Great Unifiers." Nobunaga rides in an outlandish outfit (part of his strategy to get his enemies to underestimate him) with an attendant holding an umbrella over his head, surrounded by other attendants with his 800 troops armed with 18-foot spears and 500 arquebuses, introduced to Japan by the Portuguese, following. A disguised Saitō Dōsan 斎藤 道三 (1494–1556), his ruthless future father-in-law, is seen poking his head out of a hut, sneaking a peek at Nobunaga.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Yanaka Pagoda in Moonlight (月の八坂)

text.headline: Yanaka Pagoda in Moonlight (月の八坂)
text.text: This Unsōdō published posthumous print pictures multi-storied Yanaka Pagoda in Kyoto. The design was originally issued as part of the second series of prints in Seihō's Masterpieces (1937-1942). The style is very much that of Seihō's post-China work (after 1921), using soft washes.

media.caption: Shirakawa Village (白川村 農家)

text.headline: Shirakawa Village (白川村 農家)
text.text:
This depiction of a large farmhouse (a "gassho-zukuri" thatched roof house) in Shirakawa-mura, a reconstructed farm village in the mountains west of Tokyo was published by the now defunct Mikumo Mokuhansha in Kyoto, who specialized in creating woodblock prints from the designs of several prominent textile designer/dyers such as Minagawa Taizō (1917-2005), to whom this print is attributed, and Inagaki Nenjirō 稲垣稔次郎 (1902-1963).
This collection's print is dated 1963 and is from an edition of 300 prints. Multiple so called "limited editions" were also issued by the publisher in 1965 and 1966.

media.caption: Seiho's Guide to Drawing, Vol. 1 (栖鳳 習畫帖  第一 Seihō shūgachō)

text.headline: Seiho's Guide to Drawing, Vol. 1 (栖鳳 習畫帖  第一 Seihō shūgachō)
text.text:
Published just after Seihō's return from Europe, Seihō's Guide to Drawing was exhibited at the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition, held in St. Louis, Missouri, as part of the Japanese government's display of Books and Publications.
"Printed on deluxe paper with specially designed covers and bindings, Seihō’s Painting Instruction Album is more of a luxury object than a tool for the would-be self-taught painter. Nevertheless, the designs progress from the simplest monochrome ink sketches, in volumes 1 and 2, to more complex motifs with color, in volumes 3 and 4." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 248.
See IHL.0783 for Volume 1, IHL.0784 for Volume 2, IHL.2225 for Volume 3 and IHL.0785 for Volume 4.

media.caption: Arashiyama, Spring Scenery (嵐山春景)

text.headline: Arashiyama, Spring Scenery (嵐山春景)
text.text:
One of four prints in an untitled series with famous sites of Kyoto - Kinkakuji, Kiyomizu, Yasaka Pagoda and this print, Arashiyama. This print presents us with a view of the Togetsukyō bridge stretching across the Ōi River, with Mount Arashi in the background. Also see IHL.0787, Yasaka Pagoda, Moonlit Night.
Arashiyama (嵐山) is a pleasant, touristy district in the western outskirts of Kyoto. The area has been a popular destination since the Heian Period (794-1185), when nobles would enjoy its natural setting. Arashiyama is particularly popular during the cherry blossom and fall color seasons.
The Togetsukyō Bridge is Arashiyama's well known, central landmark.

media.caption: Yasaka Pagoda, Moonlit Night (月夜八坂塔)

text.headline: Yasaka Pagoda, Moonlit Night (月夜八坂塔)
text.text:
One of four prints in an untitled series with famous sites of Kyoto - Kinkakuji, Kiyomizu, Yasaka Pagoda and this print, Arashiyama. This print presents us with a view of Yasaka Pagoda on a moonlit night in Kyoto. Also see IHL.0786, Arashiyama, Spring Scenery.
Yasaka Pagoda is a five-story pagoda located to the west of Ninen-zaka and San'nen-zaka streets within the Hokanji temple precinct. The pagoda is 49 meters high, and is the third highest wooden building in Kyoto after Toji and Kofukuji. The temple has existed from before the transfer of the national capital to Kyoto in 794. It has been destroyed by fire and rebuilt several times with the current pagoda rebuilt in 1440 by Yoshinori Ashikaga, the 6th Shogun of Muromachi government. It is designated as an important cultural property.

media.caption: Ugetsu 雨月 (Rain and Moon)

text.headline: Ugetsu 雨月 (Rain and Moon)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 202-203) - Arriving at Sumiyoshi on a pilgrimage to the shrine there, the priest Saigyō seeks shelter in the house of an old couple. They gladly give him lodging when he succeeds in providing a beginning to the second part of a poem which the old man composed about a dispute between him and his wife:
she, liking to watch the moon,
wants the eaves of the house left unthatched
but he enjoys hearing the sound of the rain on the thatching there.
In the second part of the play, Sumiyoshi Miyōjin, the patron god of poetry, takes possession of an old keeper of the shrine to speak of poetry and dance.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Seiganji 誓願寺

text.headline: Seiganji 誓願寺
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 151) - Ippen Shōnin visits the Seigan-ji in Kyōto, and there talks with a woman about Buddhist teachings. Just before she disappears she reveals that she is the poetess Izumi Shikibu whose grave is in the temple. In the second half she appears as a goddess of song and dance and entertains the priest.

text.headline: Daibutsu Kuyō 大 佛 供養 (The Daibutsu Dedication Ceremony)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 17) - The Heike warrior Kagekiyo has come to Kyōto to pray at the Kiyomizu-dera when he hears that the Minamoto chief Yoritomo is about to hold the dedication ceremony for the giant statue of Buddha in Nara. Going there in secret, he first calls on his mother who lives nearby. Then, disguised in priestly robes, he goes to the temple itself where Yoritomo has already arrived with his men. When he tries to move close to Yoritomo to attack him, by pretending to be cleaning the place in preparation for the ceremony, an official notices that he is armed and gives the alarm as Kagekiyo disappears into the crowd. Warriors rush on him, but he drives them back and makes good his escape.

text.headline: Izutsu 井筒 (The Well)
text.text:
Play synopsis (Japan Society website http://www.japansociety.org/noh_kyogen_in_the_park_in_depth) - The noh play Izutsu is based on The Tales of Ise (Ise Monogatari), a collection of uta-monogatari (narrative stories based on poems) compiled during the mid-Heian period (the end of the 10th–11th centuries). This work is the masterpiece by Zeami written as a mugen noh (dream noh) play.

(A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 171) - A traveling priest comes to the Ariwara-dera and there sees a woman beside an old grave. She tells him that it is the grave of Ariwara on Narihira and that she is really the daughter of Ki no Aritsune who loved Narihira faithfully all her life. In a dream that night the priest sees the lady appear in Narihara's hat and robe. She dances and then, looking down into the well, sees what is for her the image of her lover. Dawn comes, the priest awakes and the lady has gone.

text.headline: Miidera 三井寺 (The Miidera Temple)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 108) - A mother whose child has disappeared makes a long pilgrimage to the Kyōmizu-dera in Kyoto and asks the goddess Kannon to help her find him again. She has a dream which is interpreted by a fortune-teller to mean that she must go to the temple called Mii-dera to meet her son again. Arriving there on the night of the full moon quite unbalanced through anxiety and grief, she rings the temple bell. The priests of the temple, who are looking after her son Semmitsu and have been viewing the moon with him, come up to reproach her. But as they talk, it is found that she is the boy's mother and the two are happily reunited.

text.headline: Kochō 胡蝶 (The Butterfly)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 81) - A priest visiting the capital is admiring some beautiful plum blossom in the rounds of a palace there, when a woman unexpectedly appears beside him. She tells the priest that she is in reality a butterfly and speaks of her regret that, although she can enjoy all the flowers that bloom in the other seasons, those of the plum which come in early spring are denied to her. She asks for the priest's prayers to help her to attain salvation and then disappears. That night, when the priest is resting beneath the tree, he sees the spirit of the butterfly perform a joyful dance because salvation has been made possible, and then watches it disappear again into the mist.

text.headline: Minazuki-Barae 水無月祓 (June Purification Rite)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 110) - A man from the capital tells how the woman he met while staying in the village of Muro no tsu was no longer living there when he returned to make her his wife. As today is the last day of the sixth month when a ceremony of purification is held, he is on his way to the shrine of Kano no Myōjin to pray that he may meet her again. He goes there with another man and after he prays a mad woman appears and dances. The man recognizes her as the woman he is seeking and after they thank the god for their good fortune, they go off happily together.

text.text:

O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 209-210) - All his life Kimmitsu has loved a work called the Ise Monogatari which deals with incidents in the life of Ariwara no Narihira. text.headline: Kiso 木曽 (Lord Kiso)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 79-80) - During his struggles with the Taira, Kiso no Yoshinaka camps in Etchu province near a shrine to Hachiman, the God of War. Pleased at this good omen, he has his amanuensis Kakumei write a petition for him and, giving him one of his arrows to take with it, sends him to present this before the god. On his return Kakumei tells Yoshinaka that the local people wish to give a feast in his honour. Kakumei dances as part of the entertainment, and then white doves are seen flying from the direction of the shrine, happy auguries of future victory.

text.headline: Ama 海人 (The Woman Diver)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 3-4) - Fujiwara Fusazaki, hearing that his mother was a fisher-girl [diver] from Shido-no-ura in Shikoku, goes there to say a mass for her soul. He arrives there and meets a woman who tells him the [following] story. Of three treasures sent from China to be deposited in the Kōfukuji temple two were safely delivered but the third, [a jewel] was seized and taken down to the Dragon Palace in the waters of the bay. The lord whose sister had become the consort of a T'ang emperor and sent the treasures to Japan, formed an alliance with a fisher-girl at Shido-no-ura and when a son was born promised to make him his heir if she would retrieve the jewel. This she did at the cost of her life. The son, the fisher-girl tells him, is the present Minister Fusazaki and she herself is the spirit of his mother. She then disappears but reappears later as a dragon-woman from the depths of the bay where she met her death, and dances as she rejoices that through the power of the Lotus Sutra she has been able to attain Buddhahood.

text.headline: Makura Jidō 枕慈童 (Jidō and the Pillow)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 98-99) - An Imperial envoy in ancient China is sent by the Emperor to trace the source of a wonderful elixir. In the hills he meets a child who tells him that it is he who makes the elixir of life by writing a magic formula on chrysanthemum leaves and floating them in the stream. The formula he obtained from an Emperor of old who had had to exile him to this place when he inadvertently stepped across his pillow. He then entertains the envoy with a dance and gives him some of the magic liquid which has preserved his youth for him over hundreds of years.

text.headline: Kogō 小督 (Lady Kogō)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 82) - A Court official announces that he has been ordered to send Nakakuni to find the Lady Kogō, the favorite of the Emperor Takakura, who has disappeared from Kyōto for fear that, since the Empress is the daughter of Taira no Kiyomori, she would incur his displeasure if she remained in the capital. As there has been word that Kogō is living near Sagano, Nakakuni goes there and is eventually led to the lady by the sound of a Japanese harp being played. He gives Kogō a letter from the Emperor and, after receiving her reply, prepares to return. But pitying Kogō in her unhappiness, he drinks some wine with her and dances in an attempt to console her. He then takes leave of the lady and sets off back to the capital.

text.headline: Shakkyō 石橋 (Stone Bridge)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 158-159) - A priest [the Monk Jakushō] goes to China to visit famous Buddhist places. One day he is about to cross a stone bridge across a ravine when a child appears. He hears from the child that since the land on the other side of the bridge is the Paradise of the deity Monju Bosatsu [Manjusri Bodhisattva], even famous priests in olden times could only cross it after long and severe religious training. Telling the priest that if he waits by the bridge he will see something wonderful, the child disappears. After a while, a lion emerges and gambols and dances among the peony flowers - the king of beast enjoying the most majestic of flowers. [Some productions use two or more lion dancers.]

text.headline: Haiyū mitate asahi shō gun'ei chū no zu (旭将軍營中図)
text.text:
The three actors (R to L) Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Tomoe gozen, Onoe Kikugorō V as Yoshinaka (named the "Asahi general" by Emperor Go-daigo), and Nakamura Fukusuke IV as Yamabuki gozen in the play Haiyū mitate Asahi shō gun'ei chū no zu.
These characters are drawn from the The Tale of the Heike (平家物語 Heike Monogatari) which includes the story of Minamoto no Yoshinaka and Tomoe gozen, the famous woman warrior of the Genpei Wars between the Taira and Minamoto clans.

media.caption: Nakamura Jyakuemon, Arashi Rikan and Arashi Kitsusaburō in A True Tale of Butterflies and Plovers (中村雀右衛門、嵐璃寛 、嵐橘三郎・蝶千鳥曽我実録  Nakamura Jyakuemon、Arashi Rikan、Arashi Kitsusaburō・Chō chidori Soga no jitsuroku)

text.headline: Nakamura Jyakuemon, Arashi Rikan and Arashi Kitsusaburō in A True Tale of Butterflies and Plovers (中村雀右衛門、嵐璃寛 、嵐橘三郎・蝶千鳥曽我実録  Nakamura Jyakuemon、Arashi Rikan、Arashi Kitsusaburō・Chō chidori Soga no jitsuroku)
text.text: The three middle panels of a pentatych depicting the actors Nakamura Jyakuemon II as Wada Yoshimori, Arashi Rikan IV as Ōiso no Tora and Arashi Kitsusaburō IV as Ōji in the play Chō chidori Soga no jitsuroku (A True Tale of Butterflies and Plovers), a tale based on the revenge of the Soga brothers, a Sogomono 曽我物.

media.caption: Chion-In Temple Black Gate Spring Scene (— 智恩院黒門 春景)

text.headline: Chion-In Temple Black Gate Spring Scene (— 智恩院黒門 春景)
text.text:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), using the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.
This print presents a view of Chion-In Temple's Black Gate (Kuromon). A fenced enclosure is seen in the lower left of the print protecting the "squash stone" (uryseki). The stone, which has a very low profile to the ground, was there before the temple was built and is connected to two legends. One is that gourds sprang from this stone, even though no one planted any seeds, and the other is that the god of Yasaka Shrine paid two visits to this stone and on the night after the second visit many gourds sprang from the stone.

media.caption: Gion Shinbashi Neighborhood (祇園新橋附近)

text.headline: Gion Shinbashi Neighborhood (祇園新橋附近)
text.text:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), using the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.
This print provides us with a view of a small bridge over the Shirakawa river in Gion Shinbashi. A kimono clad woman on the right enters the frame with umbrella in hand on this rainy day. For another impression of this print see IHL.2193.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Fuwa Banzaemon in the play Fuwa (九世市川団十郎 不破伴左衛門・不破)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Fuwa Banzaemon in the play Fuwa (九世市川団十郎 不破伴左衛門・不破)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper right panel, in the role of Fuwa Banzaemon in the kabuki play Fuwa. Pictured on the bottom wearing a sedge hat is the character Nagoya 名古屋 (Nagoya Sanza), Fuwa's rival.
"This story was first played in 1680 at the Ichimura-za in Edo with Ichikawa Danjūrō I. During the cherry blossoms season, two warriors with their faces concealed in fantastic straw hats meet in Yoshiwara, the famous red-light district in Edo. They are Fuwa Banzaemon and Nagoya Sanza. Initially, Fuwa is a nice man but in due course he forgets his wife and his friend, Nagoya and seduces his courtesan lover.
In the true style of the Kabuki Eighteen Fuwa later appeara as Shōki (a powerful man who drives away the God of Plague) and fights off the goblins who try to kill him."[1]
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1885, p. 54.
[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

media.caption: Kurama Tengu 鞍馬天狗 (The Goblin of Kurama)

text.headline: Kurama Tengu 鞍馬天狗 (The Goblin of Kurama)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the Noh play Kurama Tengu (The Goblin of Kurama), attributed to the playwright Miyamasu (15th c.), in which the goblin chief prepares to teach Ushiwaka the art of war.
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 138.) - In the play, a goblin chief (shite) tells us that he is disguised as a yambushi priest, after which he hides at the back of the stage. (The goblin chief is in fact a tengu, a type of winged mountain demon.) A priest at the Kuruma Temple (Kuramadera) (waki) receives a letter inviting him to visit the blossoms on the far side of the mountain. He goes there with the children who are studying at the temple, including Ushiwaka (kokata). The priest and children, having viewed the blossoms, prepare to return. The yamabushi priest appears, presumably to show Ushiwaka the best of the flowers, but in fact he secretly promises to teach him the art of war. In the second part of the play, he returns in the form of the goblin chief and fulfills his pledge

Illustrations of Noh is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints issued between 1897 and 1904. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Rokujizō 六地蔵 (The Six Statues)

text.headline: Rokujizō 六地蔵 (The Six Statues)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the kyōgen 狂言 play Rokujizō. For another impression of this print see IHL.0703.
Play synopsis - A countryman goes to the capital to buy six statues of the Buddhist God Jizo for a new temple. Upon reaching the city he realizes he does not know where a sculptor lives nor what one looks like. While searching in the streets, a shyster notices him and decides to trick him out of his money by posing as a master sculptor.
