media.caption: Blue and White Space, No. 366

text.headline: Blue and White Space, No. 366
text.text:
"Mr. Funasaka enjoys reducing images to their most basic components: lines, circles, dots and rectangles. The magic of Mr. Funasaka's prints lies in his ability to extract deep meaning from the simplest of images. . . ."
The colored shapes bordering the open diamond shape are likely produced with woodblock; the blue patterned areas are likely a silkscreen pattern.

media.caption: Work.At21-1969

text.headline: Work.At21-1969
text.text: An early work by Funasaka (sometimes called "The Hole Man,") featuring his punched holes through a speckled paper. In this work we see the beginnings of another signature form of the artist, a semi-organic slender vertical form with at least one straight side.

media.caption: Butterfly (蝶)

text.headline: Butterfly (蝶)
text.text: The fourth of ten prints in the first of five sets of prints comprising the series Outdoor Sketches created by the artist between 1928 and 1935.  In this print a man on a jaunty stroll tips his hat to a butterfly. Maekawa created this series of five sets (ten prints each set) of black and white linoleum cuts as, in the artist's words, prints of affection (shin'ai ban).  Each small print, its image area measuring approximately 5 x 5 in. (12.7 x 12.7 cm), depicts a figure engaged in outdoor work or recreation.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Actors Arashi Ryuzo as Ukiyo Matabei and Otani Hiroji III as Tosa no Matahei (複製：嵐竜蔵の浮世又平 三世大谷広次の土佐の又平 Fukusei：Ryūzō Arashi's Ukiyo Matahira Koji Otani III's Tosa no Matahira)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Actors Arashi Ryuzo as Ukiyo Matabei and Otani Hiroji III as Tosa no Matahei (複製：嵐竜蔵の浮世又平 三世大谷広次の土佐の又平 Fukusei：Ryūzō Arashi's Ukiyo Matahira Koji Otani III's Tosa no Matahira)
text.text:
158 works and sketches survive of the Japanese artist known only by the art name Tōshūsai Sharaku. Almost all were made over a ten-month period in 1794–1795. This modern reproduction from an unknown publisher is printed on a white mica ground, as was the original.
This print depicts the actors Ōtani Hiroji III as Tosa no Matahei and Arashi Ryūzō as and Tosa's manservant Ukiyo Matahei. Four original copies of this work are known, with one residing in the collection of the Tokyo National Museum.

media.caption: Shuto Expressway (首都高速道路)

text.headline: Shuto Expressway (首都高速道路)
text.text:
Four artists, Ino Eiji 井野英二 (b. 1949), Kamiya Kiyotaka 紙谷清貴 (b. 1951). Sugisawa Osamu 杉沢修 (b. ?) and Ōhno Takashi 大野隆司 (b. 1951) contributed to this portfolio of prints titled One Hundred Scenes in Tokyo at the End of the Century issued between 1988 and 1989. This portfolio follows in the tradition of others that have provided artist interpretations of Edo/Tokyo at various milestones, such as "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo" by Hiroshige issued between 1856 and 1858 which provided, in Henry Smith's words, "the visualization of the new national space"; "100 Views of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa Era" by Koizumi Kishio issued between 1928 and 1940 chronicling the rebuilding of Tokyo after the devastating 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake; "One Hundred Views of New Tokyo" by various artists issued between 1928 and 1932 also chronicling the rise of Tokyo after the 1923 earthquake and "Scenes of Lost Tokyo" by various artists issued in 1945, a visual argument for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan after WWII.
In this print Ohno depicts a section of the multi-level Shuto Expressway (Metropolitan Expressway) built between 1962 and 1967 to "increase traffic flow efficiency in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area." The expressway covers Nihonbashi, the iconic center of Edo and then Tokyo, but a rerouting of part of the expressway underground will allow Nihonbashi to see daylight sometime around 2040.

media.caption: Kokkai-gijidō Station on the Chiyoda Line (国会議事堂駅)

text.headline: Kokkai-gijidō Station on the Chiyoda Line (国会議事堂駅)
text.text:
Four artists, Ino Eiji 井野英二 (b. 1949), Kamiya Kiyotaka 紙谷清貴 (b. 1951). Sugisawa Osamu 杉沢修 (b. ?) and Ōhno Takashi 大野隆司 (b. 1951) contributed to this portfolio of prints titled One Hundred Scenes in Tokyo at the End of the Century issued between 1988 and 1989. This portfolio follows in the tradition of others that have provided artist interpretations of Edo/Tokyo at various milestones, such as "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo" by Hiroshige issued between 1856 and 1858 which provided, in Henry Smith's words, "the visualization of the new national space"; "100 Views of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa Era" by Koizumi Kishio issued between 1928 and 1940 chronicling the rebuilding of Tokyo after the devastating 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake (see IHL. xxxxxx); "One Hundred Views of New Tokyo" by various artists issued between 1928 and 1932 also chronicling the rise of Tokyo after the 1923 earthquake and "Scenes of Lost Tokyo" by various artists issued in 1945 a visual argument for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan after WWII.
In this print Ino depicts platform 4 at the Kokkai-gijidō Station on the Chiyoda Line, the stop that services the National Diet Building.

media.caption: Illustration of the Imperial Palace Buildings (大日本帝国造営御所之図  Dai nippon teikoku zōei gosho no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Imperial Palace Buildings (大日本帝国造営御所之図  Dai nippon teikoku zōei gosho no zu)
text.text:
An 1888 bird's eye view of the just completed Imperial Palace complex in Tokyo. The scroll on the left contains details on the complex including the intended uses of the various buildings, which are identified in the small red cartouches.
The old Edo Castle had been destroyed by fire in 1873 and for fifteen years the royal family lived in a temporary residence in the Akasaka Detached Palace. The new palace, completed in October 1888, would stand until destroyed by the air raids of WWII.

media.caption: Beautiful Riverside Village (水郷 suigō)

text.headline: Beautiful Riverside Village (水郷 suigō)
text.text:
This print of a cow grazing outside a bucolic village is one of three prints in the fourth of ten envelopes containing the prints comprising set one of Seihō's Masterpieces.

SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century."
Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.
While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

media.caption: Sumo Wrestling

text.headline: Sumo Wrestling
text.text: "The two outsize bodies are squeezed into the space, giving it energy and drama. By reducing virtually all detail to outline, the artist is able to focus our attention on the tensed toes and leg muscles, the wrestlers' arms grasping and attempting to push each other over, and the fringe and giant bow of their belts. This image is based on a woodblock print by Utagawa Kunisada (1786-1864), and as a tribute his signature is included in the bottom right-hand corner." - Source: Japanese Art in Detail, John Reeve, Harvard University Press, p. 92.

media.caption: Rainbow Night 8

text.headline: Rainbow Night 8
text.text:
Ay-O has made a number of variously titled prints, paintings and sculptures showing anatomically correct male and female figures. In this artist's proof, a vibration of color links the two figures. It is one of ten prints in the series Rainbow Night.
In discussing this series, Ay-o states, "In this series . . . I wanted to express a certain order . . . in the same way that time slowly elapses. I used cut-out dolls when I was drawing the ten prints of Rainbow night . . . . Rainbow night 8 is an angle taken from above of a man and a woman facing upward. Moreover, the form of the man and woman in Rainbow night 8 is a completely identical silhouette. Hair, breasts, and male genitals deceive the eye."

media.caption: Moon Reflection (月映)

text.headline: Moon Reflection (月映)
text.text:
Hasegawa uses the reductive woodblock technique for his work in which a single woodblock is used, rather than individual carved woodblocks, to print all the colors in a design. This usually involves 10 to 20 processes of completing the carving for one color, printing that color and then repeating this process for each color. The moon is a recurring subject for Hasegawa's work and in this work the moon's reflected light is scene in the foreground grasses.
In the words of the artist, "“From a long time past, I have been influenced by the deep spirituality of Zen. Up until now, the immense time and space of the Universe, arranged like a Buddhist Mandala, has been my theme. Going beyond that concept, my most recent images have been born from various forms of creation which can be observed in nature. Being resigned to the fact of the long history of mankind in general, I am fumbling to find the personal contribution which I can offer, in the present, and I am striving to create works with a meaningful inner spirit as well.”

media.caption: Heart Sutra (般若心経)

text.headline: Heart Sutra (般若心経)
text.text:
Ay-O has immersed the Heart Sutra among seven colors of squares. At the bottom of the print the mantra 掲諦掲諦波羅掲諦羅僧掲諦菩提莎婆呵 (gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha!) is written.
“Form is emptiness, emptiness is form,” insists the Heart Sutra, the most popular Buddhist scripture and emptiness. "Nothingness," was a major theme for the Daoist and Zen-influenced Fluxus artists [of whom Ay-O was one], permeating their work. - Source: NYU Grey Art Gallery, 2011 exhibition Fluxus and the Essential Questions of Life

media.caption: Miidera 三井寺 (The Miidera Temple)

text.headline: Miidera 三井寺 (The Miidera Temple)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Miidera, often attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which the Mother of Senmitsu rings the temple bell to gain entry.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A mother whose child has disappeared makes a long pilgrimage to the Kyōmizu-dera in Kyoto and asks the goddess Kannon to help her find him again. She has a dream which is interpreted by a fortune-teller to mean that she must go to the temple called Mii-dera to meet her son again. Arriving there on the night of the full moon quite unbalanced through anxiety and grief, she rings the temple bell. The priests of the temple, who are looking after her son Semmitsu and have been viewing the moon with him, come up to reproach her. But as they talk, it is found that she is the boy's mother and the two are happily reunited.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 108.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Hashi Benkei 橋弁慶 (Benkei on the Bridge)

text.headline: Hashi Benkei 橋弁慶 (Benkei on the Bridge)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Hashi Benkei, by an unknown playwright. In this scene a full moon illuminates the warrior-monk Benkei standing on the bridge, holding a naginata (halbert with curved, single-sided blade).

PLAY SYNOPSIS
The warrior-monk Musashibō Benkei (shite) announces his intention to go to a shrine in the capital's fifth ward late in the evening. His retainer attempts to dissuade him, saying that a youth has been attacking passerby on the Gojō Bridge at night. Benkei decides to subdue the young man and leaves. At the bridge, the youth Ushiwaka (kokata) proclaims that this is the last night that he will come to the bridge, since, in accordance with his mother's wishes, he will return to the Jurama Temple (Kurumadera) the next day to continue his studies. He waits on the bridge with a square of silk over his head and shoulders. Benkei mistakes him for a woman and walks by him. Ushiwaka then throws off the silk covering and challenges the warrior-monk. The two engage in a fierce fight and Benkei is eventually defeated. They reveal their identities, and Benkei vows to become Ushiwaka's faithful retainer.[1]

Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[br]

[1] The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 170.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Sesshōseki 殺生石 (Death Rock)

text.headline: Sesshōseki 殺生石 (Death Rock)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Sesshōseki, sometimes attributed to the playwright Sa-ami (15th c.). in which the spirit, wearing a nine-tailed fox headdress (kanmuri), stands against a dark, foreboding sky with a partially obscured moon.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
On his way from the northern provinces to the capital, the priest Gennō (waki) comes to a place called Nasuno, where there is a large rock. He is surprised when a bird flying over the rock suddenly falls dead. A local woman (shite) appears and warns him against approaching the rock, known locally as the "death rock" because it contains the evil spirit of a golden-haired fox which kills any living creature that approaches it. She explains that long ago a spirit was chased from the palace for threatening the life of the emperor and it hid in the "death rock." As Gennō prays for the spirit, the rock splits in two and the spirit emerges. It confesses that it has killed many over the years, but promises to cease forthwith.[1]

"The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Kagekiyo 景清

text.headline: Kagekiyo 景清
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Kagekiyo, sometimes attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), in which Kagekiyo, blind and old, stands alone in his hut.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
Hitomaru (tsure), the young daughter of the defeated Taira warrior Kagekiyo (shite), travels from her home in Kamakura to Kyushu to visit her father, now blind and living in exile. She has never known him. She finds an old man leading a wretched life in a humble hut, but he sends her away without revealing his identity. Hitomaru then meets a kind villager (waki) who tells her that the old man is indeed her father Kagekiyo. The villager unites father and daughter. Kagekiyo agrees to tell her the story of his last battle on the condition that she leave as soon as he finishes. He relates the tale of his last fight at the Battle of Yashima (1185), a climactic encounter between the Taira and Minamoto forces. Then, as she has promised, she leaves him in his solitude.[1]

[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Michimori 通盛

text.headline: Michimori 通盛
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Michimori, often attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which a woman and old man in a boat approach the shore. The boat, as in many Noh props, is symbolic, suggested only by an outline.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A priest visiting Naruto goes out one evening to read sutras for the souls of the Taira warriors who perished there, and meets a woman and an old man who approach the shore by boat. They tell him how Kozaisho no Tsubone, the wife of Michimori, drowned herself there at the news of her husband's death, and then disappear among the waves. The priest prays for them and after a while they reappear, Michimori being this time in his true form. The priest hears the story of the battle, and Michimori and his wife rejoice that they have been able to attain salvation together.[1]

[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Landscape Picture Album by Kubota Beisen (久保田米僊 山水画帳 Beisen sansui gachō)

text.headline: Landscape Picture Album by Kubota Beisen (久保田米僊 山水画帳 Beisen sansui gachō)
text.text:
An undated sketch album by Kubota Beisen (1852-1906) using sumi and watercolors and consisting of fourteen drawings. Twelve of the drawings are landscapes (sansui ga), one is a drawing of a bird on a plum branch (kachō-ga) and one a scene from the Japanese folktale Kachi-kachi Yama (Crackling Mountain), in which a hare smashes the boat of his rival, a tanuki (a mythical raccoon dog/badger.)
In describing Beisen's work, Henry P. Bowie, lawyer, artist, author and student of Beisen's states "Kubota was so skillful in sketching that while traveling rapidly through a country he could faithfully reproduce the salient features of an extended landscape, conformable to the general rule in sketching, that what first attracts the eye is to be painted first, all else becoming subordinate to it in the scheme."

media.caption: Tokyo Dockside (untitled)

text.headline: Tokyo Dockside (untitled)
text.text:
While primarily known for his brightly colored prints which combine woodblock and metal plate printmaking techniques, Miyashita also created a number of monochrome etchings, such as this view of old warehouses and purse seiners on an unidentified river. The print is untitled, but was auctioned under the title Tokyo Dockside. While the middle ground warehouses and fishing boats look old, the city buildings seen in the background, including one skyscraper in the distance, are modern. The work, like most of Miyashita's work is undated.
In February 12, 2014 a very similar print with minor changes to the composition and executed in color titled "テームズは London" (Thames, London) came up for auction.

media.caption: Night Under the Midnight Sun (白夜 Byakuya)

text.headline: Night Under the Midnight Sun (白夜 Byakuya)
text.text:
One of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫 (1929-?).
The original 1922 painting which this print is made after is in the collection of the Yumeji Art Museum in Okayama.
As in the case of this print, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

media.caption: Frog (蛙 Kaeru)

text.headline: Frog (蛙 Kaeru)
text.text:
One of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫 (1929-?).
The original 1930 painting titled "Frog" (蛙 Kaeru), which this print is made after, is in the collection of the Yumeji Art Museum in Okayama. As Lawrence Smith notes in "The Japanese Print Since 1900: Old Dreams and New Visions", p. 88, "This bewildering titled print is based on a hanging painting done in 1930 of which an overhanging bough of a tree has been left out. The outdoor atmosphere is therefore missing."

text.text: An evening view of the gardens of Ise inner shrine from across the Isuzu river. This print is one of two prints by Tokuriki in this collection (see IHL.0831) depicting views of Ise Jingū. media.caption: Complete Chronicle of the Subjugation of Kagoshima: Illustration of Government Forces Attacking Miyazaki (鹿兒島征討全記之内 官軍宮崎進撃之圖 Kagoshima seitō zenki no uchi Kangun Miyazaki shingeki no zu)

text.headline: Complete Chronicle of the Subjugation of Kagoshima: Illustration of Government Forces Attacking Miyazaki (鹿兒島征討全記之内 官軍宮崎進撃之圖 Kagoshima seitō zenki no uchi Kangun Miyazaki shingeki no zu)
text.text:
The Satsuma Rebellion began in late January 1877. Nine months later the rebellion had been crushed and its leader, Saigō Takamori, was dead by his own hand after being trapped by government troops and mortally wounded.
This triptych, issued in March 1878, almost six months after the end of the rebellion, depicts the rebels under the leadership of Kirino Toshiaki being attacked by government police and soldiers in a Miyazaki brothel during the final days of the rebellion. According to published accounts, after government offensives drove the rebels out of Satsuma and Higo provinces, the rebels retreated into Hiuga, eventually retreating "in small bodies to Takaoka, Miyazaki and Sadoware" with the government in hot pursuit.[1] A report of July 14, 1877 in the English language Japan Weekly Mail stated "It is now pretty clear that Saigo is at Takahara in Bungo, while Kirino and Kishima are at Miyazaki in Hiuga, making every preparation for a desperate defence."[2] In early August, Miyazaki fell to government forces and while Saigō evaded government forces for a few more weeks, he was to meet his fate on September 24, 1877 after government troops assaulted his final stronghold at Shiroyama.

[1] The Satsuma rebellion: An Episode of Modern Japanese History, Augustus Henry Mounsey, John Murray, London, 1879, p. 202.
[2] Japan Weekly Mail, Vol. 1. No. 25 July 14, 1877

media.caption: Kabayama, the Head of the Naval Commanding Staff, on board Seikyōmaru, Attacks Enemy Ship (樺山軍令部長西京丸を以って敵艦に當る Kabayama gunreibuchō Seikyōmaru o motte tekikan ni ataru)

text.headline: Kabayama, the Head of the Naval Commanding Staff, on board Seikyōmaru, Attacks Enemy Ship (樺山軍令部長西京丸を以って敵艦に當る Kabayama gunreibuchō Seikyōmaru o motte tekikan ni ataru)
text.text: Depicting one of the engagements in the September 17, 1894 Battle of the Yellow Sea (also referred to as the Battle of the Yalu River), we see Rear Admiral and chief of the navy general staff, Kabayama Sukenori, on the cruiser Saikyō-Maru directing gun fire at attacking Chinese ships.

media.caption: Man Ousts His Wife and Her Lover, No. 940 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・九百四十号)

text.headline: Man Ousts His Wife and Her Lover, No. 940 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・九百四十号)
text.text:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞. The graphic, created by Utagawa Yoshiiku (1833-1904), and the text, written by Sansantei Arindo (1832-1902), both principles in the newspaper, tells of a man who, tired of his wife's infidelities, presents his wife and her lover with gifts and sends them away.
The writer for this print is identified as Sansantei Arindo 山々亭有人, a pen name of the writer Jono Saigiku 条野採菊 (born Jono Denpei 條野伝平). Born in Edo in 1832, by his late teens he had decided to become a writer of gesaku (collective term for prose fiction during the middle to late-Edo period) stories. He published his first story in 1860, and during the 1860s first Yoshiiku, then Yoshitoshi, created illustrations for some of his books. He went on to found the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun, the Keisatsu Shinbun and the Yamato Shinbun and continued to write fiction until his death in 1902.
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

media.caption: Okina 翁 (The Old Man)

text.headline: Okina 翁 (The Old Man)
text.text:
This triptych depicts the Okina dance in the Noh play of the same name. "In the center sheet we see Okina celebrating a dance and behind him the drum and flute players. The left sheet and right sheet show the stage assistants and chorus members. In front of the chorus members, there is the box in which the Okina mask is usually stored."[1]
PLAY SYNOPSIS
Okina is a piece quite distinct in character from any other Nō play. Consisting of little more than a group of dances which are said to have been in existence in the tenth century, its history is certainly much older than that of any other Nō. Throughout its history it has had a religious significance which still exists today. With words and dances designed to win the help of the gods in obtaining peace and prosperity in the land and long life for its people, Okina is performed only at times of special celebration or commemoration.[2]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[3]

[1] “The series Nogaku hyakuban (100 No plays) by Tsukioka Kogyo (1869-1927),” Claus-Peter Schulz, Andon 67, Society for Japanese Arts, p. 31.
[2] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.132-133.
[3] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Kikujirō in the role of Hatsukiku (菊次郎 初菊)

text.headline: Kikujirō in the role of Hatsukiku (菊次郎 初菊)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikujirō III as the bride Hatsukiku in the play Ehon Taikōki 絵本大功記, staged at the Ichimura-za, Tokyo in June 1915. One of two prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Gion no Nakako (祇園の奈加子)

text.headline: Gion no Nakako (祇園の奈加子)
text.text:
This print depicting the geisha Nakako from Gion in Kyoto was one of five special prints in the last issue, number 5, of Shin Nigao published in November 1915 of famous personalities who were to be present at the enthronement of Emperor Taishō later that month. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

media.caption: The Notice Board at Yoshitsune's Cherry Tree

text.headline: The Notice Board at Yoshitsune's Cherry Tree
text.text:
This print is one of twelve in the rarely seen series Dōraku Kyōkai. It is a satire of an episode in the classic struggle between the Genji and Heike clans in medieval Japan in which Yoshitsune, the Genji clan general and superior of the warrior Kumagai, foretells that Kumagai will be faced with killing Atsumori, a young warrior of the Heike clan whose mother has previously saved Kumagai's life. Yoshitsune devises a tragic solution for Kumagai, placing a notice board near Kumigai's camp, by a cherry tree, which reads: "Here stands a rare double-flowering cherry tree from the south. If anyone cuts off a branch, his punishment, following the ancient case of the Maple Tree, shall be to cut off one finger for each branch cut. Second Month, 1184.1"
As written in Japanese, it is layered with multiple meanings. In the context of the legend, the hidden meaning is "Anyone killing a son must kill his own son" meaning Kumagai must kill his own son rather than Atsumori. This story is the basis of several famous Kabuki plays including Kumagaijinya.
Kiyochika's print shows a warrior (Kumagai?) with a surprised expression, holding onto a branch he has just broken off a cherry tree while reading the notice board message. While the notice board message remains untranslated, it appears to be a police notice prohibiting the breaking of branches from the tree.

media.caption: Hangaku-jō (阪額女)

text.headline: Hangaku-jō (阪額女)
text.text:
Print number 16 (十六), one of two designed by Chikanobu for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition (although neither his name or the titles of his two prints appear in the table of contents for the series) picturing the female warrior Hangaku of the Jō clan after her capture, being introduced to the warrior Asari Yoshitō, seated before her, whom she later marries. In 1201 Hangaku with her nephew Sukemori, raised an army to defend against her older brother Sukemoto who wanted to overthrow the Kamakura Shogunate.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Arai Hakuseki (新井白石)

text.headline: Arai Hakuseki (新井白石)
text.text:
Print number 43 (四十三), one of 16 contributed by Toshikata to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the 17th century Confucian scholar Arai Hakuseki (1657-1725) receiving the Tokugawa shogun's representatives.
Arai Hakuseki (1657-1725), born into a minor and poor samurai family, was to go on and become one of Japan's greatest Confucian scholars. As the personal adviser to the sixth Tokugawa shogun, Ienobu, and Ienobu's successor Ietsugu, he exerted considerable influence over bakufu policy. Along with instituting currency and legal reforms, he was a proponent of enhancing the status of the shogun as the national ruler.
In 1708 when the Italian missionary Father Sidotti was arrested for attempting to preach Christianity in Japan, he was sent to Edo where he was interviewed by Hakuseki, which resulted in the first written Japanese account of Europe. Hakuseki continued acquiring Western knowledge through contact with representatives of the Dutch East Asia Company and reading Chinese works about the West. He was instrumental in ending the prohibition against the study of Dutch books and other scientific and technical works. Hakuseki authored over 300 texts during his lifetime, covering history, finance, geography, painting and law.

media.caption: Kurozuka 黒塚

text.headline: Kurozuka 黒塚
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 92) - Two traveling priests are given shelter for the night in the house of a poor woman at Kurozuka in Adachigahara. When she leaves them to collect firewood, she warns them not to look into her room, but the priest's servant is unable to restrain his curiosity. The horrifying things he sees there convince the priests that they are in the house of a devil. The woman then appears as an angry demon, but is finally overcome by the power of the priests.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: River Breeze (江南風色)

text.headline: River Breeze (江南風色)
text.text:
A river breeze dries someone's laundry as a boatman guides his boat along a crowded river in this print, one of three in the third of nine envelopes containing the prints comprising set two of Seihō's Masterpieces.

SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century."
Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.
While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

media.caption: Kinsatsu 金札 (The Golden Tablet)

text.headline: Kinsatsu 金札 (The Golden Tablet)
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 77-78) - An Imperial envoy goes to the village of Fushimi in Yamashiro Province in connection with a new shrine being built there by the Emperor Kammu. While talking with an old man whom he meets there, a tablet with gold writing on it falls from the sky. Taking it up, the envoy read that the god to whom it belongs promises constant protection to the land. The old man then takes the tablet and disappears, revealing as he does so that he is the god, Amatsu Futodama. He then appears in his true form, carrying a bow and arrow with which to subdue demons and ensure the peace of the land.

media.caption: Illustration of the First Soldier on Top of Pyongyang Gate in Pyongyang (平壌玄武門兵士先登之圖 Heijō Genbumon heishi sentō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the First Soldier on Top of Pyongyang Gate in Pyongyang (平壌玄武門兵士先登之圖 Heijō Genbumon heishi sentō no zu)
text.text: Private Harada Jukichi is pictured on top of the Genbu Gate in the city walls of Pyongyang. Hailed as a hero for letting his comrades into the city, his true story is less heroic. "Pingyang (Pyongyang) was well protected by walls that had to be surmounted in order to conquer the city. Repeated frontal attacks by the Japanese failed to penetrate, even after exhausting all their ammunition. One volunteer in the Eighteenth Regiment, twenty-seven year-old Harada Jukichi of Aichi prefecture, a mild man with a wife and a daughter, saw his regiment fail three times to penetrate the fortification and fearlessly scaled the wall of Gembu Gate. Harada lowered himself into the midst of the enemy and opened the gate from within. His comrades them flooded into the enemy fort. Harada's action was considered so meritorious that he was immediately promoted to the rank of superior private. Harada received the Order of the Golden Kite for his feat, but his honor proved overwhelming. He began a life of drunken dissipation and later was employed in the theater district reenacting his deed of heroism at Gembu Gate. The military authorities are said to have rebuked him for soiling the honor of the imperial army. It is also said that the soldier who actually climbed the gate first was Matsumura Aktaro, not Harada. Since Harada had already been decorated, this embarrassing fact was silenced. Matsumura was intimidated by the authorities and did not disclose the incident but secluded himself in his father's antique shop seeking truth among the collection of antiques." - Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 24.

media.caption: March Play at the Kabuki-za (歌舞伎座・三月狂言 Kabuki-za sangatsu kyōgen)

text.headline: March Play at the Kabuki-za (歌舞伎座・三月狂言 Kabuki-za sangatsu kyōgen)
text.text: The actors from right to left, Ichikawa Shinjūrō III 市川新十郎 (1866-1929), Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 (1844-1903) and Kataoka Ichizō III 片岡市蔵 (1851-1906) in the play Zokusetsu bidan Kōmonki, staged at the Kabuki-za on March 15, 1901. While the play is not identified on the print, the title simply saying March Play at the Kabuki-za 歌舞伎座三月狂言, the Tokyo Metropolitan Library database entry for this print provides the play's name, Zokusetsu-bidan Kōmonki (The Popular and Moving Story of Kōmonki). The play tells of the adventures of the historical figure Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628-1700), a daimyo of Mito, responsible for assembling the Mitogaku scholars to compile Dai Nihon shi, a history of Japan, which is credited with the rise of nationalism in Japan.

media.caption: Soga Brothers Confrontation: A New Play at the Meiji-za (明治座新狂言・曽我対面 Meiji-za Shin Kyōgen・Soga Taimen)

text.headline: Soga Brothers Confrontation: A New Play at the Meiji-za (明治座新狂言・曽我対面 Meiji-za Shin Kyōgen・Soga Taimen)
text.text:
Five actors, from right to left, Ichikawa Enjō 市川莚女 as Keshōzaka Shōshō 化粧坂少将 (a.k.a. Oiso no Tora), Ichikawa Enshō II 市川莚舛升 as Kobayashi Asahina 小林朝比奈 (waring "monkey face" makeup), Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 as Kudō Suketsune 工藤祐経, Sawamura Tosshō III 沢村訥升 as Soga Jūrō 曾我十郎 and Ichikawa Yonezō III 市川米蔵 as Soga Gorō 曾我五郎.
"A perennial favorite, the vendetta of the Soga brothers on their father's murderer is a familiar epic, but during kabuki's heyday, playwrights added new twists each season. Recognizable by costume and makeup are the beautiful courtesan, Oiso no Tora, in flamboyant gown and hairpins; the friend, Asahina, in comic 'monkey face' makeup; the murderer Suketsune, a high-ranking official, center; and the two brothers, left. Jūrō, the eldest, restrains the younger Gorō from attacking their foe, since the moment is not yet ripe." - Lynn Katsumoto (wall card from the exhibition Kabuki: A Revolution in Color and Design.)

media.caption: Sketches of Five Actors (五人男スケッチ)

text.headline: Sketches of Five Actors (五人男スケッチ)
text.text:
Five sketches of unidentified actors. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Ōkuma Prime Minister (大隈内閣總理大臣 Ōkuma naikaku sōri daijin)

text.headline: Ōkuma Prime Minister (大隈内閣總理大臣 Ōkuma naikaku sōri daijin)
text.text:
A portrait of Prime Minister Ōkuma Shigenobu. One of five special prints in the last issue, number 5 the "coronation" issue, published in November 1915, of famous personalities who were to be present at the enthronement of Emperor Taishō later that month.

media.caption: Seikanji Utako [dressed to perform the dance] Gosechi no Maihime (清閑寺歌子 五節之舞姫)

text.headline: Seikanji Utako [dressed to perform the dance] Gosechi no Maihime (清閑寺歌子 五節之舞姫)
text.text:
The court dancer Seikanji Utako is dressed to perform the dance Gosechi no Maihime at the coronation ceremony of the Taishō emperor. According to a newspaper report in the The Straits Times (Singapore), 28 August 1915, "In regard to the entertainments to be given on the first day of the Coronation, the ancient 'quintuple dance' known as Gosechi-no-Mai will constitute, according to the Coronation Committee the most prominent part of the programme. The origin of this dance is said to be traceable as far back as the days of Emperor Temmu (697 a.d.). The ladies who will perform the dance next November at the Coronation celebration have been selected from among the unmarried daughters of the descendants of ancient courtiers, to the number of eight, of whom three form the reserve. The ladies vary in age from 19 to 23 years, and will appear dressed in ancient costumes." One of seven prints contributed by the artist to the magazine Shin Nigao.

media.caption: Young woman at art gallery (untitled)

text.headline: Young woman at art gallery (untitled)
text.text:
A young woman sits in a chair in an art gallery. Likely created as an illustration for a popular novel.
The designer of this print, Okano Sakae (1880-1942), was primarily known as an illustrator and manga artist. Okano graduated from the Western-style painting department of the Tokyo School of Fine Arts in 1902. From 1925 to 1927 he was in Europe on a research mission for the Imperial Household Agency, spending time in France and Italy.

media.caption: Woman in a garden (untitled)

text.headline: Woman in a garden (untitled)
text.text: This print was likely created as an illustration for a novel. Its designer, Watanabe Kōgai, was trained in the traditional Maruyama School of painting but would later break with it moving to a more naturalistic syle. He also worked as a lacquer artist as well as an illustrator.

media.caption: Woman with green parasol (untitled)

text.headline: Woman with green parasol (untitled)
text.text: This print was likely created as an illustration for a novel. Its designer, Sugiura Hisui (1876-1965), is known as the pioneer of commercial art in Japan, credited with establishing commercial art as an independent discipline.

media.caption: Shōchō in the role of Omatsu (松蔦 お松)

text.headline: Shōchō in the role of Omatsu (松蔦 お松)

media.caption: Gorō in the role of Kyūzaemon (五郎の久左衛門 Gorō no Kyūzaemon)

text.headline: Gorō in the role of Kyūzaemon (五郎の久左衛門 Gorō no Kyūzaemon)
text.text:
Soganoya Gorō in the role of Kyūzaemon in the play Go Taiten no On'yado 御大典の御宿 staged at the Shintomi-za, Tokyo on September 30, 1915. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

media.caption: Nakiama 泣き尼 (The Crying Nun)

text.headline: Nakiama 泣き尼 (The Crying Nun)
text.text:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.185-186.) - A Man comes in from the country in search of a Priest to bless the memorial he has built for his dead father. He stops at the first temple he comes to and presents his case. The Priest makes excuses and refuses until he finds that the Man plans to give a very large donation in return for the services.
The Priest is very poor at preaching and performing ceremonies, so he invites a Nun who is well known for bursting into tears upon the slightest provocation. He finally convinces her to come along by offering her a ten percent commission.
The Priest and the Nun go to the country with the Man. When the Priest begins his sermon, the Nun, instead of crying, immediately goes to sleep. The Priest tries in vain to wake her by coughing loudly and using the words tear (namida) and cry (naku) over and over in his sermon. The Nun finally wakes up with a start when the Priest strikes the gong indicating the end of his sermon.
On the way home, the Nun praises the Priest for his sermon and cries. Then she asks for her commission. The Priest says, "No tears, no commission." The Nun grabs hold of him, and tries to throw him down. The Priest knocks the Nun down and leaves. The Nun chases after the Priest complaining in a loud voice, very much awake at last.

media.caption: Chidori 千鳥 (Catching Plovers)

text.headline: Chidori 千鳥 (Catching Plovers)
text.text:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.42-43.) - The Master orders Tarō Kaja to go get a barrel of sake for the festival which is the next day. Tarō Kaja reminds him that he already has a big sake bill, but the Master insists that he get it somehow or other.
The Sake Shop Owner is determined not to be tricked this time. Tarō Kaja, first of all, talks him into filling the barrel by telling him that several loads of rice are on their way from his Master to pay the bill. The Owner insists that Tarō Kaja wait to leave until the rice arrives.
The Owner always enjoys hearing about Tarō Kaja's trips and adventures, so Tarō Kaja tells him about some children he saw recently catching plovers on a beach. He gets the owner to participate in the story in the form of a song and dance game. He tries to get away with the sake barrel by using it as a net, then as a plover. The Owner tires of this game soon, so Tarō Kaja begins to demonstrate horseback archery using the barrel as a target. He finally grabs the barrel and runs off. The owner curses his luck at being tricked once more and chases out after Tarō Kaja.

media.caption: Fumininai 文荷 (Two to Deliver One Letter)

text.headline: Fumininai 文荷 (Two to Deliver One Letter)
text.text:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.42-43.) - The Master calls Tarō Kaja and Jirō Kaja and says that he wants a letter delivered to a priest friend of his which says that he will go to visit him that evening. He orders Tarō Kaja to deliver the letter, but he doesn't want to go and suggests that Jirō Kaja be sent. Jirō Kaja doesn't know the way, so the Master orders them both to go.
As they go along the road, they argue about who should carry the letter. They pass it back and forth several times, all the while joking about how their Master seems to have become a religious fanatic, or perhaps it's the priest more than the religion he is interested in, etc. They soon tire of passing it back and forth, so they tie it to a pole and carry it across their shoulders singing as they go along. They become more and more curious about what the letter says. They finally open it, comment on the fact that it is written in the language a man uses when writing to his mistress, and get so excited and are having so much fun reading it that they inadvertently rip it in half. To get rid of the pieces, they begin fanning them while singing a song about a message being delivered on the wings of a breeze.
The Master, worried because they are late, goes out to look for them, and finds them fanning and singing. They try to smooth out the pieces, apologizing profusely, but the Master chases them off in a rage.

media.caption: Seihō's Painting of Vegetables (栖鳳筆野菜圖 Seihō hitsu yasai zu)

text.headline: Seihō's Painting of Vegetables (栖鳳筆野菜圖 Seihō hitsu yasai zu)
text.text:
An ink on paper scroll mounted on silk brocade with a bone roller (jikuji), picturing two small eggplants and a recently picked cucumber. On the inside of the box containing the scroll is the inscription 桂華題 (keikadai). The Japanese art historian Lynn Katsumoto explains that the word keikadai denotes, "a genre or subject matter (dai) involving plants and flowers (kei being katsura or cinnamon tree, also carries the sense of something in nature that is beautiful) and (ka being hana or flower, with the connotation of something gorgeous)."
For another hanging scroll by the artist see IHL.1025.

media.caption: Sea of Fire (火の海 Hi no umi)

text.headline: Sea of Fire (火の海 Hi no umi)
text.text:
This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, pictures the ancient fortifications along Hakata Bay erected after the first attempted Mongol invasion in 1274. The wall held back the Mongols second attack in 1281 and the invaders were ultimately defeated by a devastating typhoon which set fire to their ships. Sea of Fire refers to the raging fires in the bay. The print is from the original set of five prints issued in 1918 by Nakajima Jūtarō titled Tsukishi District which was the sixth set of prints in the ten set series Japan Scenery Prints issued between January 1917 and April 1920.
"Tsukushi is the ancient name of the area north-west of Kyushu [in the area of Chikuzen and Chikugo provinces] where Sakamoto was born. Sakamoto was rarely involved with sheet-prints, but like his colleagues on this series he had worked as a cartoonist and illustrator and had been a collaborator on the magazine Hōsun hence he was well used to graphic techniques. Indeed, his set [Tsukushi district] is the most strikingly designed in the series, combining impressionist, abstract and Expressionistic elements into a characteristically forceful blend." - Source: Modern Japanese Prints 1912-1989, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 1994, p. 42.

"The series Nihon fūkei hanga (Japan Scenery Prints) consisted of ten sets of prints, with each set composed of five small landscapes and a cover print giving the name of the series, the name and number of the set, and the name of the artist. In addition, each set was accompanied by a table of contents and colophon sheet. Specific publication dates ranging from January 1917 through April 1920 indicate that each set was issued separately. As Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958) designed the majority of prints in the series, it seems likely that Hakutei was the spearhead for the project. The artists asked Igami Bonkutsu to carve the blocks and Nakajima Jūtarō to publish the series." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 274-276.
In addition to Sakamoto Hanjirō (1882-1969), the other artists who contributed to the series were Ishii Hakutei (1182-1958), see IHL.1182 and IHL.1183, Hirafuku Hyakusui (1877-1933), Morita Tsunetomo (1881-1933), Kosugi Misei (1881-1964) and Ishii Tsuruzō (1887-1973), elder brother of Hakutei.

media.caption: Fuku no kami jōruri at the Meiji-za (明治座 上るり [浄瑠璃] 福の神)

text.headline: Fuku no kami jōruri at the Meiji-za (明治座 上るり [浄瑠璃] 福の神)
text.text: A New Year's dance performance titled Fuku no kami staged in January 1897 at the Meiji-za. Fuku no kami is better known as a Noh play in which the God of Happiness, Fuku no kami, appears to worshipers at a shrine and asks them if they know how to find happiness. When they reply, "With money," he tells them it is not money, but the way of life upon which happiness depends. He asks for wine and then dances and sings a song which tells them that the way to find happiness is to make a happy home with one's wife, get up early, and welcome guests with good wine.

media.caption: Illustration of the Great Training Maneuvers by Various Army Corps (諸隊大調錬ﾉ図 Shotai dai chōren no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Great Training Maneuvers by Various Army Corps (諸隊大調錬ﾉ図 Shotai dai chōren no zu)
text.text: This print depicts one of the recurring military training exercises to prepare the recently enlarged army. In 1882, the year previous to the release of this print, the emperor had issued the Imperial Rescript for Military Men, a code of conduct, and his Chief of the General Staff, Yamagata Aritomo informed Army Minister Oyama that the military was not meeting its conscription quotas and that the 40,000 soldiers were insufficient.

media.caption: Record and Transcript of the Korea Incident (朝鮮変報録)

text.headline: Record and Transcript of the Korea Incident (朝鮮変報録)
text.text: This print depicts the attack on the Japanese legation in Seoul, Korea on July 23, 1882 by disaffected Korean soldiers.  The right panel pictures the former regent of Korea and the father of the Korean king, the Daewongun (大院君), on horseback, leading the mutineers. The legation is shown burning in the background, while the Japanese ambassador, Hanabusa Yoshitada (identified as 英公使, "Minister Hanabusa," in the center panel) and other legation officers fight them off.  As with many battle scenes depicted in Japanese prints of the Meiji era, Chikanobu constructs this image from his imagination and news reports, and his depiction of the Daewongun actually leading the mutineers in battle is fictitious.

media.caption: Hotoke Gozen (佛御前)

text.headline: Hotoke Gozen (佛御前)
text.text:
Print number 11 (十一 ), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the court dancer Hotoke Gozen 佛御前 arriving at a mountain hut to take refuge and become a nun.
As told in The Tale of the Heike (平家物語 Heike Monogatari), an epic account of the struggle between the Taira and Minamoto clans for control of Japan at the end of the 12th century in the Genpei War (1180-1185), Hotoke Gozen, consort of Taira no Kiyomori 平清盛 (1118-1181) and a shirabyōshi 白拍子 (traditional court dancer), arrived at an isolated mountain hut made of brushwood in Sagano, built by Taira’s former consort, the court dancer Gio. The hut is occupied by Gio, her mother and younger sister who have become nuns after Gio’s expulsion by Taira from the palace to make way for Hotoke. Hotoke has come to ask Gio’s forgiveness and permission to join her as a nun. They all attained their desire for rebirth in Paradise.
Inoue was to die at the age of 25 in 1889, the year this print was issued.
For another edition of this print see IHL.0963.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Boar (亥)

text.headline: Boar (亥)
text.text:
This print, picturing a sleeping boar, the twelfth sign of the zodiac, is a later printing, likely c. 1930s-1940s, of the print contained in the earlier, 1900-1915, bound folding album Seiho's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, published by Unsōdō Publishing.

Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

media.caption: By The Lake (湖畔)

text.headline: By The Lake (湖畔)
text.text:
This print appeared in the 2005 exhibition ""Prints With/Out pressure : American relief prints from the 1940s through the 1960s" organized by the New York Public Library.

"The work of Ansei Uchima reflects a complex fusion of Western and Eastern artistic traditions. Born in California, Uchima returned to Japan at age nineteen, and after World War II studied painting and traditional Japanese printmaking. Through his job as translator for Oliver Statler, an American print collector, who was interviewing artists for a book on contemporary Japanese prints, he was introduced to the sōsaku-hanga (creative print) movement, which incorporated a Western modernist aesthetic. Like other artists in the sōsaku-hanga school, Uchima carved, inked, and printed his own wood blocks, enjoying the accidents and unexpected opportunities that arose spontaneously from interaction with the wood block. His first prints, beginning in 1957, drew from nature and the world around him. After he returned to the United States in 1959, his floating, calligraphic compositions, characteristic of sōsaku-hanga, suggested the growing influence of Abstract Expressionism. Uchima used Japanese paper made especially for him by a Japanese master papermaker and National Treasure, Ichibei Iwano." - Source: New York Public Library http://web-static.nypl.org/exhibitions/pressure/artists3.html [accessed 8-25-23]

media.caption: Shibaraku (暫)

text.headline: Shibaraku (暫)
text.text:
The artist's rendering of multiple scenes from the Kabuki play Shibaraku are presented to us like a 3-dimensional pop-up book. The Ōuchi cube appears as it does in so many of his prints. The hero Kamakura no Gongoro Kagemasa appears on the left page with the right page being composed of the female characters Katsura-no-mae and Taruha along with a Hiroshige-like mountain. Ōuchi's name in the red cartouche along with an embossed double arch complete the picture.
Ōuchi often paid homage to the great ukiyo-e print masters and here he does so again by appropriating a mountain from Utagawa Hiroshige's print The Lake at Hakone from the series Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road.

While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

text.headline: Reflection of the New Diet Building, View 45 (新議事堂の影・四十二景)
text.text:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view of the New Diet Building and its reflection prior to its completion in 1936. Koizumi comments on this print, “Late on a winter’s day the new diet building shimmers like a mirage in a golden haze.”

Print number forty-five in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: Some Sketches of the Japan-China War, Volume 1 (従征画稿  第1集)

text.headline: Some Sketches of the Japan-China War, Volume 1 (従征画稿  第1集)
text.text:
Volume 1 of four bound volumes by the artist Asai Chū (1856-1907) forming a pictorial account of the battles of Japan's Second Army on China's Liaodong Peninsula during the first Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895). Asai's sketches, created at the battle front, were done with pencil and pen and then highlighted with watercolors. They were then reproduced using full-color lithography by the publisher Shinyōdō, who included five or six color plates in each volume accompanied by a table of contents and a preface written by Asai.
Clicking on the image will allow you to view the color lithographs in the volume.

media.caption: Wind and Clear Water (水風清)

text.headline: Wind and Clear Water (水風清)
text.text:
A small bird perches on a rock in a swift flowing stream in this collotype, one of four prints in the second of ten envelopes containing the prints comprising set one of Seihō's Masterpieces. See IHL.0875 for the print showing a detail of this work.

SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century."
Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.
While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

media.caption: Wind and Clear Water - detail (水風清・部分)

media.caption: Cape Kannon (観音埼 Kannonzaki)

text.headline: Cape Kannon (観音埼 Kannonzaki)
text.text:
Number 18 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meisho zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
Kiyochika pictures a lone boat being plied off the rocky coast of Cape Kannon on the eastern edge of the Miura Peninsula along the southwest portion of Tokyo Bay. In 1812 the Tokugawa Shogunate set up a lookout here to protect Edo from Western ships. In 1868 a lighthouse was built on the cape under the direction of of the Frenchmen F. L. Verny following the requests of foreign powers under the provisions of the Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Amity and Commerce of 1858. It was the first modern lighthouse to be built in Japan, being first lit on February 11, 1869, immediately after the Meiji restoration, and during the last months of the Boshin War. It was destroyed by an earthquake in 1922. A second lighthouse was soon destroyed by the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923. The one we can see today is the third one, constructed in 1925.

media.caption: Captain Asakawa and Trooper Private Kimura (浅川大尉 二等騎兵木村源松氏 Asakawa Taii Nitō Kihei Kimura Genmatsu-shi)

text.headline: Captain Asakawa and Trooper Private Kimura (浅川大尉 二等騎兵木村源松氏 Asakawa Taii Nitō Kihei Kimura Genmatsu-shi)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty issued as part of the series Mirror of Army and Navy Heroes designed by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) and published 1895-1896 by Inoue Kichijirō. The series depicts war heroes of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) as models of behavior and self-sacrifice. "Kiyochika’s 'heroes' range from an admiral reading a newspaper to sailors helping a blinded comrade touch a cannon that has helped bring victory, and from an infantryman showing compassion to a Chinese youngster to officers and enlisted men cleaving heads and bayonetting the foe." - source: website of MIT Visualizing Cultures https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/throwing_off_asia_02/visnav_ii_f.html [accessed 8-17-23]
In this print the loyal trooper Private Kimura Gemmatsu, himself wounded, leans over his wounded commander, Captain Asakawa Toshiyasu, who grieves over his fallen horse.

media.caption: Lt. General Yamaji Motoharu (陸軍中将 山地元治君 Rikugun Chūjō Yamaji Motoharu-kun)

text.headline: Lt. General Yamaji Motoharu (陸軍中将 山地元治君 Rikugun Chūjō Yamaji Motoharu-kun)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty issued as part of the series Mirror of Army and Navy Heroes designed by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) and published 1895-1896 by Inoue Kichijirō. The series depicts war heroes of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) as models of behavior and self-sacrifice. In this print Lt. General Yamaji Motoharu, commander of the First Division of the Second Army Corps, is shown relaxing, likely after his victory at Port Arthur, while his troops celebrate.

media.caption: Butsu Sorai (物徂徠)

text.headline: Butsu Sorai (物徂徠)
text.text:
Print number 39 (三十九), one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the young Ogyū (Butsu) Sorai (1666–1728), who was to go on to become a great Confucian scholar and philosopher during his father's exile in a small village sixty miles from Edo. The exile forced Sorai to study on his own and here he is seen embracing the rural life while studying and teaching a young peasant.
Sorai may be best known for his "Essay on the Forty-Seven Samurai" in which he both lambasted the avenging 47 samurai of Chushingura fame, calling their actions "senseless," thereby offering the bakufu a way out of their dilemma on how to punish the samurai, allowing them the honorable death by seppuku.
For another edition of this print see IHL.1397.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Fukuchi Gen'ichirō (福地源一郎)

text.headline: Fukuchi Gen'ichirō (福地源一郎)
text.text:
Print number 45 (四十五), one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the journalist FukuchiGen’ichirō 福地源一郎 (1841-1906) standing on a hilltop while reporting on the government assault on rebel troops during the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. This print is the most famous in the series and is one of the two prints in the series to portray a contemporary figure.
The scroll on the print reads, in translation, "Fukuchi Gen’ichirō was born in Nagasaki in 1843 [an error for 1841]. He was very bright, and could copy characters at the age of five and read at the age of seven. He aspired from childhood to be a retainer of the shogun, and came to serve the government as a young man, traveling three times to European countries. He then withdrew from public service and launched commercial enterprises. In 1873, he became president of the Nippōsha, and at the time of the Satsuma Rebellion, he observed conditions at the front and reported them in detail before the emperor. His literary and logical skills are polished; he is a virtual wizard of the brush. He is truly one of the heroic figures of Meiji." - Source: Kiyochika Artist of Meiji Japan, Henry D. Smith II, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, 1988, p. 74-75.

text.headline: Nakamise Street Viewed from Niōmon Gate at Asakusa Kannon Temple, View 10 (浅草＝観音二王門ヨリ仲見世へ ・十景)
text.text:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view looking out from Sensō-ji's Niōmon Gate (Hōzōmon Gate) in Asakusa towards bustling Nakamise Shopping Street. Koizumi comments on this print, “The statue of the Kannon Bodhisattva survived the earthquake, but only a few of the shops on Nakamise remained.”

Print number ten in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: Gōtokuji Temple in Setagaya Ward, View 42 (世田ケ谷区・豪徳寺・四十二景)

text.headline: Gōtokuji Temple in Setagaya Ward, View 42 (世田ケ谷区・豪徳寺・四十二景)
text.text:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view of the gardens surrounding Buddha Hall on the temple grounds of Gōtokuji, the Ii Clan's family temple, where, as is noted by Koizumi, the assassinated Ii Naosuke, Tairō to the Tokugawa Shogun Tokugawa Iesada, is buried. Koizumi comments on this print, “This is the burial place of Lord Ii who was killed at Sakuradamon. It is also famous for a literal mountain of cat statues.”
