media.caption: Fan - か (ka)

text.headline: Fan - か (ka)
text.text:
From a series of at least seven prints incorporating a fan motif and a hiragana character, in this case the character "ka" か which appears right reading on the fan and in its mirror image to the left of the fan. Ōuchi has borrowed the image of the beautiful courtesan entertaining herself with calligraphy from a c. 1794 woodblock titled Portrait of Kasen of Ogiya, a Celebrated Yoshiwara Beauty by the artist Chōbunsai Eishi (1756–1829).
Other prints in this series use the characters "re" れ, "ke" け, "ri" り, "fu" ふ, "e" え and "ni" に.

While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

media.caption: Hibachi (ひばち)

text.headline: Hibachi (ひばち)
text.text:
In this silkscreen print, one of eleven in the artist's Mon Mon* portfolio, a tattooed Edo-era man, naked except for his fundoshi, sits on a hibachi with iron tongs in hand. The charcoal brazier is covered with an intricate design that includes a guardian lion dog and the legendary Phoenix.
*Mon Mon is an Osaka word for "representational or figurative tattooing." This word is also associated with the tattoos of yakuza.
"Mon Mon," The Series
"Mon Mon is Takeda's first collection of prints. In it, he used tattoos as a theme in order to push the need for color in cartoons to new limits. It was the first collection published by this artist who tried to extract art from cartoons." - statement from the artist's website
The Mon Mon series was issued both in book/portfolio form (Mon-Mon: Takeda Hideo hangashū 紋紋 武田秀雄版画集 [Tattoo: Collection of Prints by Takeda Hideo)] in a limited edition of 500 copies, in 1978 by Internal Co., Ltd. and in a limited edition of 150 stand-alone prints.
In 1976, Takeda won the Bungeishunjū Manga Award (文藝春秋漫画賞 Bungeishunjū Manga Shō) for this print series.

media.caption: Sesshōseki 殺生石 (Death Rock)

text.headline: Sesshōseki 殺生石 (Death Rock)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the Noh play Sesshōseki (Death Rock), sometimes attributed to the playwright Sa-ami (15th c.), in which the fox spirit emerges from the Death Rock.
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 118.) - On his way from the northern provinces to the capital, the priest Gennō (waki) comes to a place called Nasuno, where there is a large rock. He is surprised when a bird flying over the rock suddenly falls dead. A local woman (shite) appears and warns him against approaching the rock, known locally as the "death rock" because it contains the evil spirit of a golden-haired fox which kills any living creature that approaches it. She explains that long ago a spirit was chased from the palace for threatening the life of the emperor and it hid in the "death rock." As Gennō prays for the spirit, the rock splits in two and the spirit emerges. It confesses that it has killed many over the years, but promises to cease forthwith.
Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play, a list of the roles, and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Hanjo 班女 (The Girl Whose Lover Went Away)

text.headline: Hanjo 班女 (The Girl Whose Lover Went Away)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the Noh play Hanjo (The Girl Whose Lover Went Away), attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), in which Hanjo searches for her lover.
Play synopsis (Scripps College Ruth Chandler Williamson Gallery website https://web-kiosk.scrippscollege.edu/objects-1/info?query=mfs%20all%20%22Hanjo%22&sort=9&page=2 [accessed 8-17-23] - In this play, two lovers are forced to part. They exchange fans, representing the promise of their future reunion. Hanago soon becomes heart-stricken and can do nothing more but look longingly at the fan that her lover has left behind. Thus she is nicknamed Hanjo, a name taken from the Chinese story about Han Shoyo. According to the Chinese story, when Han Shoyo was replaced by another woman as the emperor’s favorite, she wrote a poem comparing herself to a fan: once treasured during summer, the fan is quickly abandoned in autumn. This print depicts Hanjo’s lonely, passionate, and even obsessive search for her lost love. At the end of the play, Hanjo’s lover identifies her by the fan that she has placed inside her robe and over her heart. They are once again united.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)

text.headline: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)
text.text:
Depicting the Sun goddess Amaterasu, the goddess Uzume and the god Tajikarao in the Noh play Ema (The Votive Tablets), by an unknown writer. The two votive tablets fortelling good fortune are pictured in the upper right.
Play synopsis (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 26-28.) - An Imperial emissary on his way to the Great Shrines of Ise stops overnight at Saikū nearby as it happens to be the last day of winter and he hopes to see something of the votive tablets which are said to be hung up there during that particular night to foretell the fortunes of the coming year, a white one indicating sunny weather and a black one rain. He meets an old couple with such tablets who, after some discussion, agree to put up one of each kind to signify good fortune for everyone. They then disappear into the darkness after telling him that they are in fact two of the gods of Ise. In the second part Amaterasu, the Sun-goddess, appears with the goddess Uzume and the god Tajikarao and performs a dance. The three of them then depict the ancient story of Amaterasu’s withdrawal into a cave: as the world is plunged into darkness by her disappearance, the other gods dance and make merry and eventually succeed in enticing her out again by arousing her curiosity.

media.caption: Two Turtles and a Rock (untitled)

text.headline: Two Turtles and a Rock (untitled)
text.text: One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of the 20th century. In this print a turtle suns itself on an overhanging rock, while another paddles nearby in the stream. The turtle, or tortoise (kame), living as it does to a venerable old age, has become a symbol of longevity in East Asia. It is not only highly esteemed, but even held sacred.

media.caption: Cézanne (セザンヌ)

text.headline: Cézanne (セザンヌ)
text.text: One of Ay-O's hommages to past artists, this one to Cézanne and his 1893-1894 still life Sugarbowl, Pears and Tablecloth. This artist proof was editioned under the title of Rainbow Cézanne 虹のセザンヌ. Ay-O comments, "There was a period in my youth when I, too, was 'infected by Cezanne'. Some people may not believe me, but everything that came within my vision in Japan, the scenery, people and still life, appeared to me to be exactly the same as those of Cezanne's France. Recollections of the waving trees of the forest, the apple looking as if it were made of porcelain, and the nude with a blue shadow - these are at once the heart pains of my youth. To that memory, I dedicate this piece."

media.caption: Mt. Fuji, No. 480

text.headline: Mt. Fuji, No. 480
text.text: Sixteen suns float on and behind Mt. Fuji, bathing it in shimmering (a light dusting of mica in the deep orange) sunlight. Funasaka's unique multi-color vertical forms, which appear in so many of his prints, are printed using reusable woodblock cutouts. The technique used to create the rest of the print is likely silkscreen.

media.caption: Where It All Began

text.headline: Where It All Began
text.text:
"Paul Revere, the belfry arch of the Old North Church, 'two if by sea,' the Somerset man-of-war, even the spires from the green of some Middlesex village, all appear in this work, which could possibly serve as an illustration of Longfellow’s famous poem. Miyashita works in his usual combination of woodblock and intaglio." - Source: website of University of Puget Sound, "Artwork in the Library: 7 Samurai and The Bicentennial"
Miyashita is known for combining woodblock and etching (intaglio) techniques. "Miyashita uses the Ukiyo-e woodblock technique requiring water-based inks and absorbent paper. On the same print he uses intaglio techniques demanding oil-based inks and a paper that responds sensitively to these inks, and, at the same time is strong and resilient enough to take the pressure of the etching press. Kizuki Kozo is the paper that has the necessary characteristics. It has tough fibers and accepts both water-based inks and oil-based inks. To offer the appealing characteristics of both processes, Miyashita prints color areas from woodblocks and overlays these with details and contours printed from an intaglio plate inked in black.
"By combining two techniques of vastly different origin and character, Miyashita has melded his own form of expression: bold, bright, rough-hewn, yet refined and singularly elegant in effect. The viewer's imagination may bring its own meaning to the work or the visual feast itself may be enough." -Source: Japanese Prints Today: Tradition with Innovation, Margaret K. Johnson, Dale K. Hilton, Shufunotomo Co., Ltd., 1980, p. 213-219.

media.caption: Denizen of the Lake Depths

text.headline: Denizen of the Lake Depths
text.text:
A beautiful overlay of colors make up this underwater view of a black sea creature swimming through a maze of colorful formations.
While Shinagawa worked in many medias, including metal (creating numerous mobiles) and photography, he is best known for his prints. As with many creative print (sōsaku hanga) artists of the period, he studied printmaking with Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955) and his mid-career abstract woodblock prints show the influence of his teacher in their use of simplified forms. His later works were mainly silkscreens rather than woodblock prints.

media.caption: Nostalgy (ノスタルジー)

text.headline: Nostalgy (ノスタルジー)
text.text:
One of Rei's semi-abstract landscapes created from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. In commenting on the Rei's work, Francis Blakemore notes, "The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades. The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches. It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.
"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate. The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: "Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Frances Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.)

text.headline: Lizard and Cucumber Vines
text.text:
One of twenty prints contributed by Kotozuka Eiichi (1906-1979) to the series Fifty Kinds of Flowers issued in 1935. This print, published by Unsōdō, but with woodblocks carved by the artist, show a gekko-like lizard emerging from spreading cucumber vines.
It is reported that two editions of this series were released. The first was made available by subscription and the second was released after the subscription was sold out. Also contributing to the series were Tobei Kamei and Tokuriki Tomikichirō.

media.caption: Ueno Park, Congratulatory Celebration for the Thirty-Year Festival of the Capital City (上野公園奠都三十年祭祝賀會)

text.headline: Ueno Park, Congratulatory Celebration for the Thirty-Year Festival of the Capital City (上野公園奠都三十年祭祝賀會)
text.text: On April 10, 1898 a series of celebrations, private and public, were held in Tokyo to commemorate and celebrate the thirtieth anniversary of the transfer of the capital from Japan to Tokyo. The Association for the 30th Anniversary, headed by Viscount Okabe the then Governor of Tokyo, tasked with the job of organizing and promoting the celebrations wrote, "our Tokyo now competes in its grandeur with London and Paris, the great cities of the world." The emperor and empress attended both private events in their palace and the public celebration held in Ueno Park pictured in this print.

media.caption: One Hundred Warrior Poets complete (武家百人一首 全 Buke hyakunin isshu zen)

text.headline: One Hundred Warrior Poets complete (武家百人一首 全 Buke hyakunin isshu zen)
text.text:
An 1858 version of "Buke hyakunin isshu" by the artist Utagawa Sadahide (1807-1873) and the writer Shōgetsudō Shujin (fl. 1856-1864). This 1858 version of "Buke hyakunin isshu" is prefaced with eight battle scenes (titled, Eight Scenes of Great Battles of Japan 本 朝戦場八景) each occupying a double page, all of which have taken the titles associated with the Chinese literary and artistic theme of "Eight Views."
"Buke hyakunin isshu" was originally issued in illustrated form in 1672 by the publisher Tsuruya Kiemon, with illustrations by the artist Hishikawa Moronobu (1618-1694). By signing his name to the 1672 "Buke hyakunin isshu", Moronobu became the first ukiyo-e artist to affix his name to a printed work. "Buke hyakunin isshu" is not a version of the very popular "Hyakunin isshu" (One Hundred Poets), issued six years later in illustrated form and also bearing Moronobu's name, "but an independent work bringing together one hundred poems by one hundred famous samurai," targeted at Edo's samurai class. - Source: Pictures of the Heart : The Hyakunin-isshu in Word and Image, Joshua S Mostow, University of Hawai'i Press, 1996, p. 44, 107.

media.caption: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 1 (日本歴史画報  第一號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai ichigō)

text.headline: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 1 (日本歴史画報  第一號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai ichigō)
text.text: The first of thirteen volumes published between December 1891 and June 1893 which served as a secondary school pictorial history textbook. Artists who contributed to the books included the chief editor Matsumoto Fūko 松本楓湖 (1840-1923), Takahashi Shōtei 高橋松亭 (1871-1945), the nephew of Matsumoto Fūko, Watanabe Seitei 渡邊省亭 (1851-1918), Mishima Shōsō 三島蕉窓 (1856-1928), Nagamine Shūko 永峯秀湖 (1859-1895), Ōtsuka Sōko 大塚蒼湖 (?-?), Kono Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895) and Muraoka Ōtō 村岡櫻塘 (1773-1947).

media.caption: Tokyo Imperial Hotel (東京帝国ホテル)

text.headline: Tokyo Imperial Hotel (東京帝国ホテル)
text.text:
Torn down in 1968, Frank Lloyd Wright's Imperial Hotel, completed in 1923 and located near the Imperial Palace, is shown on a rainy, but calm, day. Careful viewing of the print reveals that silver mica ink was used to create the very fine vertical striations of rain distributed throughout the image.
Wright had long been intrigued by Japanese culture (he was an avid collector of Japanese prints), so when the opportunity came to build the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, he lobbied for the project.
Commissioned in 1916, the hotel was to represent the emergence of Japan as a modern nation and symbolize Japan’s relation to the West. To that end, Wright designed the building as a hybrid of Japanese and Western architecture.

media.caption: Girl in New Year Clothes (正月娘姿)

text.headline: Girl in New Year Clothes (正月娘姿)
text.text:
This print, "published by Kyūryūdō, is faithful to the artist’s figurative style with no hint of the carver’s personal interpretation. The color, deep muted pink with gray and blue, is thick and opaque, with little of the subtle quality that we associate with moku-hanga, and suggests by its appearance that it may have been applied by stencil."[1]
Yasui designed at least sixteen woodblock prints that he then had carved and printed, under his supervision, by others. He viewed prints as "instrumental in expressing things by lines and colors."[2]

[1] Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 101.
[2] Japanese Wood-block Prints, Shizuya Fujikake, Japan Travel Bureau, 1938 revised 1949, p. 137.

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 9 (日清戦闘畫報  第 九編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daikyū hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 9 (日清戦闘畫報  第 九編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daikyū hen)
text.text: Volume 9 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895. Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (Fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

text.headline: Fruits of the Sea (海幸 umisachi)
text.text:
One of four prints in the sixth of nine envelopes containing the prints comprising set two of Seihō's Masterpieces.

SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century."
Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.
While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

media.caption: Ram (未)

text.headline: Ram (未)
text.text:
This print, picturing a woman walking through a group of sheep, is from the folding album (orihon) Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, published by Unsōdō Publishing, containing twelve prints each picturing an animal in the zodiac. This image represents the eighth animal in the set sequence of animals symbolizing the houses of the zodiac in Chinese lore, namely the rat, ox, tiger, hare, dragon, snake, horse, sheep, monkey, cock, dog and pig. Multiple editions of this print were issued by the publisher from c. 1901 into the early 1940s.

Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

media.caption: Ikina (伊企儺)

text.headline: Ikina (伊企儺)
text.text:
Print number 1 (壹), and one of 4 contributed by Yoshitoshi to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Tsuki no Kishi Ikina defying the Silla commander who has ordered him to take down his pants, point his buttocks toward Japan and shout "Japanese generals, bite my ass." Ikina's response is to shout "King of Silla, eat my ass!" shocking the Silla commander, seen on the ground, who orders Ikina's torture and death. For another impression of this print see IHL.1265.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: The Teachings of the Mother of Mencius (孟母の教)

text.headline: The Teachings of the Mother of Mencius (孟母の教)
text.text: In this print, originally created for volume one of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishiki-e shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi portrays Mencius (c. 371-289 BCE), one of the greatest Confucian philosophers of early China, and his mother at a weaving loom. A lesson about studying diligently will be forthcoming.

media.caption: The Loyalty of Pierre (ピエールの信)

text.headline: The Loyalty of Pierre (ピエールの信)
text.text: In this print, originally created for volume one of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishikie shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi portrays the Frenchman Pierre returning the money he had been trusted with by his friend. As told in print's cartouche, it seems Pierre's soldier friend had been gone many years, but although Pierre lived in poverty and could have used his friend's money for business opportunities he did not.

media.caption: Wang Lan Harmony Between Siblings (王覧の悌)

text.headline: Wang Lan Harmony Between Siblings (王覧の悌)
text.text: In this print, created for volume two of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishikie shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi depicts a young Wang Lan (206-278) protecting his older half-brother Wang Xiang (185-269) from the wrath of his mother, who favored her own son. Both brothers were to grow up and become important statesmen during the Chinese Three Kingdoms period (220-280).

media.caption: The Chastity of Shihino Shinasa (四比信紗の貞)

text.headline: The Chastity of Shihino Shinasa (四比信紗の貞)
text.text: In this print, created for volume three of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishikie shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi portrays the widow Shihino Shinasa caring for her own children along with the children of her husband's concubine without favor. After her husband's death, she vowed to remain chaste thereby fulfilling the "li" of a woman.

media.caption: Saigō Takamori (西郷隆盛)

text.headline: Saigō Takamori (西郷隆盛)
text.text: Print number 171 (第十七) in the series Personalities of Recent Times pictures the samurai Saigō Takamori (1827-1877) who fought against the shogunate to restore the emperor to power ushering in the Meiji Era (1868-1912); served as a Meiji government statesman and then resigned in 1873; lead the brief, bloody and unsuccessful 1877 Satsuma Rebellion against the Meiji government, finally committing suicide nine months after the Rebellion began, walking his dog Tsun. The scene is set in a quiet moment before the Rebellion and Saigō bears a walking stick and his hound's leash, as well as his sword.  He wears a western shirt and collar under a traditional kimono.

media.caption: Hayano Kanpei (早野勘平)

text.headline: Hayano Kanpei (早野勘平)
text.text:
This print pictures the character Hayano Kanpei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers; a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin). The play is based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum Digital Archives Collection identifies the actor playing Hayano Kanpei as Ichimura Kakitsu IV [4]市村家橘, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.
The dark yellow cartouche in the upper right corner gives the name of the series, Legends of the Loyal Retainers. The name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of the cartouche, in this case Hayano Kanpei 早野勘平. The background script may provide an account of Yuranosuke's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.
The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.
For another edition of this print see IHL.0631.

media.caption: Sakurajima in Summer (夏の桜島 九州鹿児島)

text.headline: Sakurajima in Summer (夏の桜島 九州鹿児島)
text.text: A peaceful Sakurajima, an active volcano, on a summer's day as seen from one of the villages that were gradually incorporated into Kagoshima city. Kagoshima is a city of over 600,000 today.

media.caption: Donjon of the Matsuyama Castle (天守閣 四国松山城)

text.headline: Donjon of the Matsuyama Castle (天守閣 四国松山城)
text.text: The artist's rendering of the Matsuyama Castle keep. Matsuyama Castle, in Matsuyama in Ehime prefecture, western Shikoku, was first built by Kato Yoshiaki between 1602 and 1627. (It is not to be confused with Bitchu Matsuyama Castle in Okayama prefecture.) The castle is one of Japan's twelve originally surviving castles, although it burnt down twice, once in 1642 and again in 1784, after being struck by lightning. The present structures date from 1854. The impressive, three-story central tower (or, donjon, daitenshu) is listed as an Important Cultural Property.

media.caption: Evening Glow

text.headline: Evening Glow
text.text: A stark view in early evening of Mount Fuji with bare trees in the foreground. While this collection's print appears to be hand signed by the artist, "S. Ohshiro", and is part of a numbered edition (20/100), the Los Angeles County Museum of Art version of the print, carries a stamped signature "S. Ōshiro," and is not editioned.  The LACMA print uses a brighter palette that better reflects the print's title "Evening Glow" than this collection's print.

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 4 (日清戦闘畫報 第四編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daishi hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 4 (日清戦闘畫報 第四編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daishi hen)
text.text: Volume 4 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895. Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

media.caption: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 10 (日本歴史画報  第十號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai jūgō)

text.headline: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 10 (日本歴史画報  第十號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai jūgō)
text.text: The tenth of thirteen volumes published between December 1891 and June 1893 which served as a secondary school pictorial history textbook. Artists who contributed to the books included the chief editor Matsumoto Fūko 松本楓湖 (1840-1923), Takahashi Shōtei 高橋松亭 (1871-1945), the nephew of Matsumoto Fūko, Watanabe Seitei 渡邊省亭 (1851-1918), Mishima Shōsō 三島蕉窓 (1856-1928), Nagamine Shūko 永峯秀湖 (1859-1895), Ōtsuka Sōko 大塚蒼湖 (?-?), Kono Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895) and Muraoka Ōtō 村岡櫻塘 (1773-1947).

media.caption: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 6 (日本歴史画報  第六號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai rokugō)

text.headline: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 6 (日本歴史画報  第六號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai rokugō)
text.text: The sixth of thirteen volumes published between December 1891 and June 1893 which served as a secondary school pictorial history textbook. media.caption: Ise Futami Bay (伊勢二見浦)

text.headline: Ise Futami Bay (伊勢二見浦)
text.text:
The fourth of eight prints in the series the Eight Views of Japan (Nihon hakkei) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company sometime in the 1950s. This print, depicting the "Marriage Rocks" near the town of Futami during summer at daybreak, along with the Futami Okitama Shrine, was originally published in 1941 as part of the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places.
This series reused eight previously issued images from the 1941 series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) and reissued them in a portfolio of prints titled Eight Views of Japan. The table of contents accompanying the entire series notes that the prints are "Selections from Prints of Places of Historic and Scenic Interest" (a.k.a. Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places) and that it contains "2 each of four seasons."
Meoto Iwa (夫婦岩), or the "Loved one-and-loved one Rocks" (a.k.a "Marriage Rocks"), are a couple of small rocky stacks in the sea off Futami, Mie, Japan. They are joined by a shimenawa (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers at the neighboring Futami Okitama Shrine (Futami Okitama Jinja 二見興玉神社). According to Shinto, the rocks represent the union of the creator of kami Izanagi (male divine being) and kami Izanami (female devine being). The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman. The rope, which weighs over a ton, must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small torii at its peak.
Futami Okitama Shrine is dedicated to the food goddess Miketsu. The shrine and the Marriage Rocks are near the Grand Shrine of Ise, the most important shrine in Shinto.

media.caption: Kiyomizu Temple in Kyoto (京都 清水寺)

text.headline: Kiyomizu Temple in Kyoto (京都 清水寺)
text.text:
The last of eight prints in the series The Eight Views of Japan (Nihon hakkei) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company sometime in the 1950s. This print, depicting Kiyomizu Temple and several of its associated buildings in winter snow, was originally published in 1941 as part of the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places.
This series reused eight previously issued images from the 1941 series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) and reissued them in a portfolio of prints titled Eight Views of Japan. The table of contents accompanying the entire series notes that the prints are "Selections from Prints of Places of Historic and Scenic Interest" (a.k.a. Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places) and that it contains "2 each of four seasons." This print was also reissued as part of the series Twelve Months of Scenic Views of Japan (日本勝景十二月).
Kiyomizu-dera (清水寺), known more fully as Otowa-san Kiyomizu-dera (音羽山清水寺) is an independent Buddhist temple in eastern Kyoto. The temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities) UNESCO World Heritage site.

media.caption: Cherry Blossoms of Mount Shigi (大和信貴山)

text.headline: Cherry Blossoms of Mount Shigi (大和信貴山)
text.text:
The first of eight prints in the series The Eight Views of Japan (Nihon Hakkei) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company sometime in the 1950s. This print, depicting Chogosonshi-ji Temple on a moonlit night, was originally published in 1941 as part of the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places.
This series reused eight previously issued images from the 1941 series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) and reissued them in a portfolio of prints titled Eight Views of Japan. The table of contents accompanying the entire series notes that the prints are "Selections from Prints of Places of Historic and Scenic Interest" (a.k.a. Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places) and that it contains "2 each of four seasons."
Mt. Shigi-san, 437 meters in elevation, is located at the southern end of the Ikoma Mountains lying in the northwest of Nara Prefecture. In the middle of the mountain is Chogosonshi-ji Temple, usually referred to as "Shigisan" or "Shigi-no-bishamon-san." The temple's principal deity, Vaisravana (Bishamonten in Japanese), brings good luck and protection to those who come to worship. The temple owns one of the most important illustrated handscrolls in Japanese art history, the 12th-century Shigisan Engi Emaki (Illustrated Handscroll, Legend of Mount Shigi).

media.caption: My Space and My Dimension, No. 533

text.headline: My Space and My Dimension, No. 533
text.text: Sixteen light tan circles generate a subtle glow as Funasaka's trademark multi-color vertical forms hover within their intense lacquer-black borders. Funasaka creates these vertical forms with reusable woodblock cutouts.

media.caption: Child and Dog (子供と犬)

text.headline: Child and Dog (子供と犬)
text.text: One of Azechi's many small-format prints, most designed as greeting cards. Likely printed in the 1970s by the Yokohama publisher Chikuhōdō, which still offers this design for sale, it is tipped to a 14 1/4" x 9 7/8" sheet folded into quarters with stamped information on the verso giving the name of the artist and publisher.

media.caption: Illustrations of Noh, Index, volume 3 (能楽図絵 後編上 目録 Mokuroku, kōhen jō)

text.headline: Illustrations of Noh, Index, volume 3 (能楽図絵 後編上 目録 Mokuroku, kōhen jō)
text.text:
The third of five Table of Contents prints (mokuroku) from the series Nōgakuzue (Illustrations of Noh). In the bottom right of the print is the inscription これは武蔵の国の住人 坂巻の耕漁と申者にて候 "This is by Sakamaki Kōgyō, who dwells in the Musashi Abumi region."

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Autumn play at the Kabukiza - Lord Tokihira and the Seven Laughs, Ichikawa Danjūrō (歌舞伎座秋狂言 菅原  時平公七わらひ  市川團十郎 Kabukiza Aki kyōgen Sugawara - Tokihira-kō Nanawarai, Ichikawa Danjūrō)

text.headline: Autumn play at the Kabukiza - Lord Tokihira and the Seven Laughs, Ichikawa Danjūrō (歌舞伎座秋狂言 菅原  時平公七わらひ  市川團十郎 Kabukiza Aki kyōgen Sugawara - Tokihira-kō Nanawarai, Ichikawa Danjūrō)
text.text: Kunichika portrays the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Lord Tokihira in the play "Tokihira-kō Nanawarai" (Lord Tokihira and the Seven Laughs.) The play is a rewrite of an earlier play, revised by Fukuchi Ōchi, the pseudonym of journalist, playwright and politician Fukuchi Gen'ichirō 福地 源一郎 (1841-1906), as an historical drama starring Ichikawa Danjūrō IX. The print's depicted setting fits well with the evil plan Lord Tokihira devised – to bid farewell to Sugawara Michizane who was exiled to Dazaifu. Tokihira, the one who remains behind, will break up laughing in this scene. As revised by Fukuchi, Tokihira does not hatch his evil plan to edge out the obstructing Michizane and the rewritten play failed to draw crowds.

media.caption: Collection of Ten Plays New and Old - Modoribashi (新古演劇十種之内 ・ 戻り橋 Shin koengeki jisshu no uchi・Modoribashi)

text.headline: Collection of Ten Plays New and Old - Modoribashi (新古演劇十種之内 ・ 戻り橋 Shin koengeki jisshu no uchi・Modoribashi)
text.text: Kunichika portrays Onoe Kikugorō V in the role of the demon of Mount Atago (disguised as Sayuri) in the play Modoribashi (The Bridge of Return) staged at the Ichimura-za. First staged in 1890, it is the prologue to the play Ibaraga [Ibaraki]. It describes how Watanabe no Tsuna, ordered to search for a fiend which is terrorizing the capital, meets a beautiful woman travelling alone at night. He offers to see her on her way. Reaching the Modori bridge, he looks down into the moonlit water, only to see a reflection of a horrible fiend instead of the fair face of his companion. Later he confronts her with his discovery and she assumes her true shape. A fierce fight ensues in which Watanabe cuts off the fiend’s arm, thus leading up to the events which take place in the play Ibaraga.

media.caption: Fireworks (花火)

text.headline: Fireworks (花火)
text.text: This undated and untitled print, likely issued post-WWII, is after a small woodblock print which originally appeared in Takehisa Yumeji's 1915 book of poetry titled Samisen-kusa (Shamisen Leaves), published by the Tokyo publisher Shinchōsha. The original print appeared as the last of six small woodblock prints bound into the book.

media.caption: Ugetsu 雨月 (The Moon and the Rain)

text.headline: Ugetsu 雨月 (The Moon and the Rain)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the Noh play Ugetsu by the playwright Komparu Zenchiku (1405-c. 1470).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 202-203.) - Arriving at Sumiyoshi on a pilgrimage to the shrine there, the priest Saigyō seeks shelter in the house of an old couple. They gladly give him lodging when he succeeds in providing a beginning to the second part of a poem which the old man composed about a dispute between him and his wife: she, liking to watch the moon, wants the eaves of the house left unthatched but he enjoys hearing the sound of the rain on the thatching there. In the second part of the play, Sumiyoshi Miyōjin, the patron god of poetry, takes possession of an old keeper of the shrine to speak of poetry and dance.

media.caption: Tsūen 通円 (Tsūen, The Tea Priest)

text.headline: Tsūen 通円 (Tsūen, The Tea Priest)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the kyōgen 狂言 play Tsūen, a parody of the Noh play Yorimasa.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 272.) - A Priest comes along the road to a tea house, and finds it without a priest in charge of making and serving teas. He asks the reason of a Villager who tells him that this tea house belonged to a Priest named Tsūen. It has been kept as a memorial since he died, and that today is the anniversary of his death. Then the Villager asks the Priest to pray for Tsūen’s soul. The Priest begins to pray, and the Ghost of Tsūen appears, tells the story of his life, dances, and serves the Priest tea.

media.caption: Sotoba Komachi 卒都婆小町 (Komachi on the Gravepost)

text.headline: Sotoba Komachi 卒都婆小町 (Komachi on the Gravepost)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the Noh play Sotoba Komachi, attributed to the playwright Kanami (1333-1384).

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. media.caption: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum From Heaven)

text.headline: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum From Heaven)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Tenko, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), in which Tenko's father appears before an Emperor's official to play his son's drum. For another impression of this print see IHL.1925.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 188-189.) - A boy named Tenko has a wonderful drum which had come down from Heaven, but when this was taken from him to be presented to the Emperor he drowned himself. An Imperial envoy tells this story and explains that as no one has been able to make any sound come from the drum since it was taken to the Palace, he has been sent to fetch the father of Tenko. Together they go to the Palace, and when the father strikes the drum it gives out such a miraculous sound that he is promised a rich reward and a musical performance is arranged to placate the soul of his son. When this is done, the ghost of Tenko comes and dances before them.

media.caption: Hyakuman 百万

text.headline: Hyakuman 百万
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the play Hyakuman by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443.)
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A man from Yoshino who has found a stray child takes him to pray at a temple in Saga and there sees a mad woman who prays and dances. The boy recognizes her as his mother, and when she tells the man who she is and that her son disappeared after the death of her husband, he brings them together again. She prays to give thanks for this and they joyfully takes her son home with her.[1]
ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 59.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Kosode Soga 小袖曾我

text.headline: Kosode Soga 小袖曾我
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the play Kosode Soga sometimes attributed to Miyamasu (1482-1556.)
PLAY SYNOPSIS
United in their resolve to take advantage of an approaching hunting expedition to kill their father's enemy, the Soga brothers return home to take leave of their mother. But the younger one, Gorō is disowned by her for going against her wishes by abandoning the priesthood, and she refuses to forgive or even to see him. Jūrō (the older brother) then tells her that she can have no love for him either if she would send him off on the dangerous mission alone and, with these words, goes to leave. At this, however, his mother relents and, calling them both to her, pardons Gorō and gives them her blessing. Overjoyed at this, the brothers perform a dance together and then take a final farewell of their mother.[1]
ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 85-86.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Dainin Kamitsukeno Katana (大仁上毛野形名)

text.headline: Dainin Kamitsukeno Katana (大仁上毛野形名)
text.text:
Print number 2 (二), one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing shogun Kamitsukeno Katana eating while his wife serves him wine and lectures him not to disgrace his name and to defeat the rebels. One of the ladies of the court sits in the background, her hand grasping an arrow, which is a reference to Kamitsukeno's wife stringing ten bows and ordering other women to pluck the bow strings simulating a large army.
As told in the The Nihon Shoki 日本書紀, Japan's second oldest chronicle, completed in 720: "[In 637] there was a solar eclipse. That year, the Emishi revolted and did not attend the Court. Dainin Kamitsukeno Katana was made shogun [through an imperial edict issued by Emperor Jomei (reigning 629-641)] and ordered to attack them. However, he was defeated by the Emishi and fled to his castle where he was surrounded by the rebels. His soldiers all deserted, the castle was empty and the shogun did not know what to do.
"At that time it was dusk, and he wanted to jump the wall and flee. Then Kamitsukeno Katana’s wife sighed, saying, 'How tragic, that we will be killed by the Emishi.' Then she said to her husband, ''Your ancestors crossed the blue sea, and treading 10,000 ri, pacified the governments of the countries on the water, and their powerful warrior spirit went on to future generations. Now you will stain the name of your ancestors, and you will certainly be laughed at by future generations.' Then she poured wine, and made him drink it. She then, on her own, took her husband’s sword, and strung ten bows, and ordered ten or so other women to pluck their strings. Then her husband woke up and took his weapons and advanced. The Emishi thought the army was large, and so retreated. Then the Katana's scattered soldiers again collected, and took their formations. The Emishi suffered great loss, and were completely captured." - Source: The Nihon Shoki wiki http://nihonshoki.wikidot.com/scroll-23-jomei [no longer active 8-17-23]

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)

text.headline: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)
text.text:
Print number 12 (十二), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Endo Morito about to cut off the head of the Kesa Gozen, the faithful young wife of a palace guard, who he has mistaken for her husband.
This print is a re-design of the print as originally issued. (See this collection's print IHL. 0503.) The blocks for the original design must have been damaged or lost. This re-designed print kept the same print number in the series, the same publication date, and the same descriptive scroll.

media.caption: Ōishi Yoshio (大石良雄)

text.headline: Ōishi Yoshio (大石良雄)
text.text:
Print number 40 (四十) as shown in the series' Table of Contents, although not numbered on the print. One of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Ōishi Kuranosuke Yoshio (1659-1703) leader of the 47 Ronin surrounded by female entertainers under a full moon. This scene references Ōishi's ruse of living the high life with the geisha of Kyoto, while he was plotting his revenge on Lord Kira, responsible for the death of his master Lord Asano. Ōishi's actions in avenging his master and his subsequent suicide, as ordered by the shogunate, was seen as ideal samurai behavior.
This is one of only a handful of prints depicting the historical character Ōishi Kuranosuke rather than an actor using a thinly veiled character name, e.g. Ōboshi Yuranosuke, playing Ōishi in a kabuki version of the historical incident.
This print is a re-design of the print as originally issued. (See this collection's print IHL.0503.) The blocks for the original design must have been damaged or lost. This re-designed print kept the same print number in the series, the same publication date, and the same descriptive scroll.

media.caption: Chōdensu (兆殿司)

text.headline: Chōdensu (兆殿司)
text.text:
Print number 8 (八), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Chōdensu (1352-1431), also known as Mincho 明兆, the famous 14th century ink painter and Zen priest sternly looking at his disciple Kikuchi Myōtaku (釋氏妙澤) painting a picture of the deity Fudō Myō-ō. Initially opposed to Kikuchi Myōtaku's painting, he relented when he realized Myōtaku's talent.

media.caption: Actors Iwai Shijaku, Ichikawa Komazō V and Matsumoto Kōshirō V in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki (伊達競阿國劇場・ 岩井紫若, 五代目 市川高麗蔵, 五代目 松本幸四郎)

text.headline: Actors Iwai Shijaku, Ichikawa Komazō V and Matsumoto Kōshirō V in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki (伊達競阿國劇場・ 岩井紫若, 五代目 市川高麗蔵, 五代目 松本幸四郎)
text.text:
Three sheets that may form part of a five-sheet print of actors in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki (The Date Rivalry and Okuni kabuki) by Sakurada Jisuke I (1734-1806). The left sheet in the triptych is not contiguous with the sheet to its right, although similar in design.
From right to left we see the actors Iwai Shijaku (岩井紫若) as Masaoka no Tsubone ( 政岡の局), Ichikawa Komazō V (市川高麗蔵) as Arajishi Otokonosuke (獅子男之助), and Matsumoto Kōshirō V (松本幸四郎) as Nikki Danjō (仁木弾正) in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki 伊達競阿國劇場.
The left sheet contains an inscription to the left of the actor reading 一世一代 當々 (isse ichidai, ōatari ōatari) meaning "Once in a lifetime performance, big hit, big hit!"
The play Date kurabe okuni kabuki is a derivative of the play Meiboku sendai hagi (The Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai.) Precious Incense dramatizes historical events – an attempted coup, in 1660, by retainers of the Date household and the gallant efforts of loyal retainers to thwart the coup. The scandal caused a sensation in its day. - Source: Kabuki Plays On-Stage: Villainy and Vengeance, 1773-1799, ed. James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 50.

media.caption: Actors Bandō Hikosaburō V, Ichimura Kakitsu IV and Ichikawa Danzō VI in a performance from the New Year drama Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu (鶴千歳曽我門松・五代目 坂東彦三郎, 四代目 市村家橘, 六代目 市川団蔵)

text.headline: Actors Bandō Hikosaburō V, Ichimura Kakitsu IV and Ichikawa Danzō VI in a performance from the New Year drama Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu (鶴千歳曽我門松・五代目 坂東彦三郎, 四代目 市村家橘, 六代目 市川団蔵)
text.text:
The actors Bandō Hikosaburō V (五代目 坂東彦三郎) as Ukiyo Tohai (浮世戸平), Ichimura Kakitsu IV (四代目 市村家橘) as Nozarashi Gosuke (野ざらし吾助) and Ichikawa Danzō VI (六代目 市川団蔵) as Rokuji Namuemon (六字南無右衛門) starring in a performance from the New Year's drama Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu, staged at the Ichimura-za on January 29, 1865 (1st lunar month of 1865.)
It is likely that a number of plays and dances comprised the entire performance of Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu and the Ritsumeikan Art Research Center identifies this scene as the "second prologue" (二番目序幕) of the performance.
The background text contains the actors' lines in the performance. The identity of who is speaking is shown by the use of a square (for Bandō Hikosaburō V), a circle (for Ichimura Kakitsu IV) and a triangle (for Ichikawa Danzō VI.) Note that the actors' names appearing in the upper right of the print are shown in the order they speak, not the order they appear in the triptych.

media.caption: Viewing Fireflies in the Cool of the Evening (蛍見之夕涼 Hotarubi no Yūsuzumi)

text.headline: Viewing Fireflies in the Cool of the Evening (蛍見之夕涼 Hotarubi no Yūsuzumi)
text.text: Five actors portrayed before a rimpa-stye stream enjoying the evening's delights. The names of the actors are not shown on the print, possibly due to censor rules still being enforced in 1859, but the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston which has the right panel of this triptych in its collection, identifies the two actors in the right panel as Nakamura Fukusuke I 初代中村福助 and Iwai Kumesaburō III 三代目岩井粂三郎.  It is unknown what play is depicted in this print.

media.caption: Breeze No. 2 (六月の風 Rokugatsu no kaze)

text.headline: Breeze No. 2 (六月の風 Rokugatsu no kaze)
text.text: A turquoise sky, shimmering with applied mica, provides the backdrop for Hagiwara's colorful cloth-like objects flapping in the breeze.

media.caption: Midday at the Beach (真晝の浜 Mahiru no hama)

text.headline: Midday at the Beach (真晝の浜 Mahiru no hama)
text.text: Kitaoka has captured a moment, during the heat of midday, of three villagers gathering seaweed and plants on the beach. This print has a similar feel to the languid Fishing Village in the Afternoon (IHL.0194) one of the artist's best known works created in 1967 four years after this work.

media.caption: Summer Vacation (夏休み)

text.headline: Summer Vacation (夏休み)
text.text: The sky is filled with a pale sunlight in this print titled Summer Vacation. The artist's catalogue raisonné indicates that this print appeared in a show titled "Contemporary Japanese Prints" held by The Print Club of Albany, an organization still in existence today, located in Albany, New York. It states there were two editions of this print, one in 1967 of 22 prints and one in 1966 of 50 prints (this collection's print). They note that there are color differences between the two editions.

media.caption: Lamps, jars, clock, geisha

text.headline: Lamps, jars, clock, geisha
text.text: A collector of old foreign language books, Kawakami loved depicting the objects he found in them. This print uses a number of the artist's favorite objects -  lamps, jars, a clock, and geisha. The Yokohama Museum of Art has a hand-colored version of this print.

media.caption: Kanpei's Wife, Okaru (勘平女房 おかる)

text.headline: Kanpei's Wife, Okaru (勘平女房 おかる)
text.text:
This print pictures the character Okaru, the wife of Hayano Kanpei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers, a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin), based on the Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions in the shogun's palace led to the death of their lord.
The text on the print was written by Yashima Gakutei 八島岳亭 (1786 – 1868), best-known for his surimono (privately commissioned) prints, signing as Gakutei Sadaoka 岳亭定岡文記 with a gourd-shaped seal bearing the character 島 (shima) following his signature.
The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.
"Okaru's name immediately associates her with the mistress, also named Okaru, that Kuranosuke took up residence with while living in Yamashina. However, aside from her presence at the teahouse Ichirikiya and Yuranosuke's brief feint at courting her, there are few, if any, comparisons, thematic or otherwise, to draw between the two. It is safe to say that, while the name may have been chosen for the historical resonance it brought to the text and the character, the two Okarus represent two distinctly different personas.
If Hayano Kanpei is someone who is inadvertently tempted by passion to commit a transgression against his lord, then it is Okaru who performs the role of the temptress. She is the central female character in a play that, more often than not, portrays women as nothing better than mere obstacles to samurai duty and virtue. And while it might be anachronistic and heavy-handed to judge Chūshingura as misogynistic, Okaru, through her actions and influence, without a doubt achieves much the same textual status that Eve does in the Old Testament version of Genesis." Source: Columbia University website http://www.columbia.edu/~hds2/chushinguranew/kanadehon/okaru.html [accessed 8-27-23]

media.caption: Oda Nobunaga  and Mito Rekko (Tokugawa Nariaki) of the Tokugawa Sanke (織田信長公 水戸烈公 徳川三家)

text.headline: Oda Nobunaga  and Mito Rekko (Tokugawa Nariaki) of the Tokugawa Sanke (織田信長公 水戸烈公 徳川三家)
text.text:
From a little seen series of prints pairing heroic figures from recent and past history in imaginary contests. This print pairs Oda Nobunaga 織田信長 (1534-1582), on the right, Japanese military commander in the Azuchi-Momoyama period (c. 1573 to c. 1603) and one of Japan's "Three Great Unifiers," with Mito Rekko 水戸烈公 (1800-1860; also known as Tokugawa Nariaki), on the left, father of the last Tokugawa shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu (1837-1913), and a foremost proponent of the anti-Western sonno-jōi movement.
As the sono-jōi movement weakened the Tokugawa shogunate leading to the Meiji Restoration and the end of the shogunate, I imagine the artist is depicting an angry Nobunaga castigating Nariaki for his role in this movement.
Nariaki, in an effort to strengthen Japan against the Western military threat, instituted extensive reforms in his home province of Mito, including rationalization of the taxation system, the hiring of experts in Western learning to advise him on coastal defense and battleship construction, the training of troops in Western military tactics, establishment of a state school system, combining Confucian and Shintō religious institutions, and taxation of Buddhist temples and rich samurai to fund increased military spending.[1]

[1] Japan at War: An Encyclopedia, edited by Louis G. Perez, ABC-CLIO, LLC, 2013, p. 439-440.

media.caption: Semimaru 蝉丸

text.headline: Semimaru 蝉丸
text.text:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.154-155) - On the order of the Emperor Daigo, a Court official takes Prince Semimaru, who has been blind since he was a child, to Ōsaka-yama and leaves him there with only his lute to comfort him. The Prince accepts his lot with resignation, feeling that his blindness is the result of some failure of his in a previous existence, and that the present apparent cruelty of his father is only due to a desire to help him gain a happier fate in a future life. Meanwhile, his sister Princess Sakagami has gone out of her mind and is now a wild-haired figure, wandering aimlessly from place to place. She comes one day to Ōsaka-yama and, attracted by the sound of Semimaru's lute, finds her brother again. For a while they forget their loneliness as they talk together and comfort each other, but then the Princess leaves him and continues her sad wanderings.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Hotoke Gozen (佛御前)

text.headline: Hotoke Gozen (佛御前)
text.text:
Print number 11 (十一 ), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the court dancer Hotoke Gozen 佛御前 arriving at a mountain hut to take refuge and become a nun.
As told in The Tale of the Heike (平家物語 Heike Monogatari), an epic account of the struggle between the Taira and Minamoto clans for control of Japan at the end of the 12th century in the Genpei War (1180-1185), Hotoke Gozen, consort of Taira no Kiyomori 平清盛 (1118-1181) and a shirabyōshi 白拍子 (traditional court dancer), arrived at an isolated mountain hut made of brushwood in Sagano, built by Taira’s former consort, the court dancer Gio. The hut is occupied by Gio, her mother and younger sister who have become nuns after Gio’s expulsion by Taira from the palace to make way for Hotoke. Hotoke has come to ask Gio’s forgiveness and permission to join her as a nun. They all attained their desire for rebirth in Paradise.
Inoue was to die at the age of 25 in 1889, the year this print was issued.
For another edition of this print see IHL.0866.

media.caption: Mōri Shōjumaru (毛利松寿丸)

text.headline: Mōri Shōjumaru (毛利松寿丸)
text.text:
Print number 27 (廿七), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the powerful daimyō Mōri Motonari (1497-1571) as a young boy visiting Itsukushima (Miyajima) Shrine with his maidservant, just prior to his coming of age ceremony (genpuku) in 1511. Legend has it that Shōjumaru, Motonari's childhood name, asked a young retainer accompanying him what he had wished for at the shrine. The young retainer replied that he wished for Shōjumaru to become the lord of Aki province. Shōjumaru reprimands the boy, asking why he did not wish for him to become lord of all Japan, as that is a higher goal to meet.

media.caption: Kusunoki Masashige (楠正成)

text.headline: Kusunoki Masashige (楠正成)
text.text:
Print number 21 (廿一), one of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the 14th century warrior Kusunoki Masashige (1294-1336) seated outside Shitenno-ji Temple 四天王寺 reading a scroll, likely the Miraiki みらいき, a chronicle foretelling the future and attributed to Prince Shōtoku. The Miraiki proved influential in 14th and 15th-century politics, as many of its prognostications proved true. A Buddhist monk sits beside Kusunoki and the large pine tree in the background may allude to the deposed emperor Godaigo's famous dream that foretells of his reigning again as the true emperor. After the dream Godaigo combines the character for "south" with that for "tree," producing kusunoki, or camphor tree. Kusunoki a warrior "famous as a wielder of bow and arrow," is then summoned from nearby Kawachi province. Kusunoki pledges to dedicate his life to restoring Godaigo's "imperial destiny." - source: Warriors of Japan as Portrayed in the War Tales, Paul Varley, University of Hawaii Press, 1994, p. 181-182.
The scroll makes reference to Kusunoki's lineage, stating that he is descended from the Tachibanas who are descended from the 6th century Emperor Bidatsu. Historians, however, state there is little "historical certainty" about his lineage.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Mexico City, Mexico (メキシコメキシコ市)

text.headline: Mexico City, Mexico (メキシコメキシコ市)
text.text: A view of the old Basilica de Santa Maria de Guadalupe in Mexico City from an adjoining plaza. The artist traveled to Mexico in October 1965 as part of a world tour that also would take him to the United States, Spain, Italy, Greece, and Turkey. Upon his return to Japan he began work on a series of ten prints showing views from his travels titled "Here and There in the West."  All of these prints were carved and, most likely, printed and published by the artist.

media.caption: The Farrier (蹄鐵工  其九 teitetsukō sono kyū)

text.headline: The Farrier (蹄鐵工  其九 teitetsukō sono kyū)
text.text:
A horse is prepared for shoeing in this ninth print in the series. According to The Japan Farrier Association, "Modern horseshoeing technique was introduced into Japan in 1873. The government invited a horseshoeing instructor from France to help disseminate the technique."
A translation of the commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Today all professions pursue efficiency in their method and organisation with extreme care. Although this is frequently caused by an all-consuming supply and demand relationship of contemporary life, in this profession we can still see the continuation of a more relaxed pace. The history of horseshoes is quite old, and it goes without saying that in the future, horses will likely still be running around. Until horses are no longer used to transport goods, manual crafts like these will continue to exist." - Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 24.
Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The vast majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Newspaper Photographers, Number 8  (写真班 其八 shashinhan sono hachi)

text.headline: Newspaper Photographers, Number 8  (写真班 其八 shashinhan sono hachi)
text.text:
Picturing two newspaper cameramen photographing two military officials, this print titled Newspaper Photographers was originally issued between 1939 and 1941 by Nishinomiya Shoin as the eighth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.
A translation of the commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Media reports and news are the eyes and ears of modern life, and the photographer plays a major role as the creator of the depicted records. All his efforts are devoted to the mission of capturing a given incident without missing the next one. It has been said that the best-selling photographers are brave and alert, adventurous and perseverant, and in addition they display a freshness and artistic desire in their work. By night and day, during heat and cold, by heaven and earth, be it leisure or luxury, through their pictures their world truly seems to be extraordinary."[1]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 23.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Horses in Pasture (馬三代 Uma sandai)

text.headline: Horses in Pasture (馬三代 Uma sandai)
text.text:
This untitled print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, picturing horses grazing in a pasture, is from the three print series known as Three Horse Pieces (Uma sandai), published by Mikumo Mokuhansha, first in 1951 in a limited edition of 300 and then again in 1966 as a stand-alone print in editions of 300 and 700. This print IHL.0969 is 105 in the edition of 300, published in 1966 three years before the artist's death. (Also see IHL.1205 from a later edition, using the same blocks.)
Sakamoto, a Western-style (yōga) painter, is best known for his paintings and prints of horses through. Pursuing his love of horses, he dedicated himself almost exclusively to their depiction, so much so that he “won an unenviable notoriety as a painter ‘picturing nothing but horses.’” In reply to this criticism Hanjirō wrote: "As I am painting only horses, it has been said that my production is merely repetitive. If I am laughed at for this, I am not hurt at all, bit if the meaning of such criticism is that the essence of my pictures remains somehow merely conservative, I will be dismayed indeed. I do not care if I repeat the same subject. If this repetition can endlessly improve the content of my art, then, as a painter, I am, rather, proud. I do not necessarily disregard the opinion that painters, as members of society, should take up social problems as motifs, but what matters after all is the intrinsic nature of their work. Even if a painter pictures one stone, his work, depending on his attitude, many act on contemporary society." - source: Paris in Japan: The Japanese Encounter with European Painting; Takashima, Rimer and Bolas, The Japan Foundation and Washington University, 1987, p. 228.
While the artist's painting color palette has been described as "austere," many of his prints use a lighter, pastel-like color palette.

media.caption: By now you must be near Komakata, a cuckoo calls - Takao (たか雄 君は今駒かたあたりほとゝきす Kimi wa ima/ Komakata Atari/ hototogisu - Takao)

text.headline: By now you must be near Komakata, a cuckoo calls - Takao (たか雄 君は今駒かたあたりほとゝきす Kimi wa ima/ Komakata Atari/ hototogisu - Takao)
text.text:
Often assumed to be the first print in the series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, it pictures one of the eleven famous courtesans of the Yoshiwara in the 17th and 18th centuries named Takao. It is believed Yoshitoshi's print pictures the sixth Takao, known for her poetry.

"It is early morning, and Takao's lover has recently left the pleasure quarters to return to the city. Takao hears a hototogisu, a sort of cuckoo, whose call is associated with dawn and with loneliness. Its staccato sound reminds her of the name Komakata, an area on the Sumida river a short distance south of the Yoshiwara, and she imagines her lover arriving at the boat landing in Komakata on his way home. She composes a poem, which eventually became famous. Hiroshige (1797-1858) alludes to it in a design of Komakata in his 'One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.'"[1]

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[2]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, print 1.
[2] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, , 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: A Jōruri Performance of Chūshingura, 2nd act Three Servants from the play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase (浄瑠璃忠臣蔵 二段め 三人奴・忠臣蔵形容画合 Jōruri Chūshingura Nidan me Sannin Yakko・Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase)

text.headline: A Jōruri Performance of Chūshingura, 2nd act Three Servants from the play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase (浄瑠璃忠臣蔵 二段め 三人奴・忠臣蔵形容画合 Jōruri Chūshingura Nidan me Sannin Yakko・Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase)
text.text:
This print depicts the actors (from right to left) Ichimura Kakitsu IV (四代目 市村家橘) as Momonoi's servant Kitsuhei (桃ノ井下部橘平), Bandō Hikosaburō V (五代目 坂東彦三郎) as Momonoi's servant Tsurubei (桃ノ井下部鶴平), and Sawamura Tosshō II (二代目 沢村訥升) as Momonoi's servant Kinohei (桃ノ井下部紀之平) in a performance from the 2nd act of the play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase which played at the Ichimura-za on May 7, 1865.
At the beginning of the 2nd act in Chūshingura, Momonoi Wakanosuke's servants stand outside his mansion in the garden gossiping about Moronao's humiliation of their master, essentially recounting events from the first act.
The play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), is based on the classic Kanadehon Chūshingura and had is debut in 1865 as a dance program at the Ichimura theater in Tokyo.

media.caption: Ryukyu Market (琉球の市場 Ryukyu no ichiba)

text.headline: Ryukyu Market (琉球の市場 Ryukyu no ichiba)
text.text: Primarily known as a Western-style (yōga) landscape painter, Ishikawa self-published a number of woodblock prints (possibly using the publishing name Ryokū-so Gashitsu 緑雨荘画室版), working with excellent carvers and printers to transfer his designs into prints. In addition to his best-known print series Ten Types of Female Nudes, Ishikawa published a number of landscape prints. This print shows three farmers selling their produce at an unknown location in Japan's Ryukyu Islands, the best known of which is Okinawa. Ishikawa had a fascination with native peoples which can be traced back to visits he made to Taiwan in the early 1900s.

media.caption: Sake Distillers (酒杜氏 saketoji)

text.headline: Sake Distillers (酒杜氏 saketoji)
text.text:
Five workers stir the mash during the sake fermentation process in this nineteenth print in the second series of Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 2 published by Nishinomiya Shoin between 1939 and 1941. While there is no sense of trouble brewing in this print, the Second Sino-Japanese War leading into World War II was a tough time for sake production, as the government began to tightly control distribution of rice for war efforts which led to the addition of pure alcohol and glucose to the rice mash before pressing to improve the yield. A translation of the artist's commentary accompanying this print reads, "I have been wondering for a long time about the strangeness of the fact we call the person making the sake a 'brewer'. When I looked it up in the dictionary it was described in roughly the following manner. One explanation is that 'brewer', 'master brewer', and 'sake brewer' all originate from older terms such as 'god of the sake jar'. According to other theories the person, by the name of Du Kang, preparing the sake at the court of The Yellow Emperor long ago was called a brewer. And others seem to think it was a kind of nickname. Some think that the original brewers came from Tanba, and that from this region they moved with the season to other regions. That it is a name that referred to a group of artisans who worked away from home every year to take on the whole brewing process, from washing barrels and rice to the eventual brewing of the end product."[1]
