[1] Source of translation: Translation taken from Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 59.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Landscape at Nerima Town in Itabashi Ward, View 73 (板橋区・練馬風景・七十三 景)

text.headline: Landscape at Nerima Town in Itabashi Ward, View 73 (板橋区・練馬風景・七十三 景)
text.text:
In this print, Koizumi pictures a farming couple at work pickling daikon, giant radishes. The artist comments, "Daikon of Nerima have been renowned from the time they were presented as gifts to the shogun. The priest Takuan introduced a recipe for pickling these radishes. So they became even more famous.”

Print number seventy-three in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: Shower at Nezu Gongen Shrine, View 81 (根津権現の驟雨・八十一四景)

text.headline: Shower at Nezu Gongen Shrine, View 81 (根津権現の驟雨・八十一四景)
text.text:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a truncated view of the two-story Rōmon Gate (楼門) at Nezu Gongen with the Haiden worship hall in the background. A group of children and adults seek shelter from the rain under the gate. Koizumi comments, “The patina on this National Treasure shrine is lovely but the temple surroundings seem lonely and poorly kept.”

Print number eighty-one in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: Inuhariko, Kimono, Kuma and Flying Carp

text.headline: Inuhariko, Kimono, Kuma and Flying Carp
text.text:
Four tiny prints by the artist, printed on a gummed paper with perforations between each print, and tipped into a portfolio strangely titled Loving Service Hanga Seal, published by The Central Community Chest of Japan, Inc., to familiarize foreigners with the revival of Japanese woodblock printing. Descriptions for each print are printed underneath the gummed sheet. I imagine the small prints were designed as envelope seals, given they were printed on gummed paper.

Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955) created the front and back covers of this portfolio, see IHL.1298. which contains ten perforated gummed prints by the artists Kitaoka Fumio (1918-2007), see IHL.0977, and Shinagawa Takumi (1908-2009), published by The Central Community Chest of Japan, Inc. to familiarize foreigners with the revival of Japanese woodblock printing. In addition to the two sets of gummed prints the portfolio contains an introduction to the Japanese Woodcut Print by Onchi and a historical overview of the Japanese Woodcut Print.

media.caption: Asakusa Stalls, The Palace Plaza, The Palace Moat, Kan-eiji Pagoda, The Kabuki Theater, Shinjuku Garden

text.headline: Asakusa Stalls, The Palace Plaza, The Palace Moat, Kan-eiji Pagoda, The Kabuki Theater, Shinjuku Garden
text.text:
Six tiny prints by the artist, printed on a gummed paper with perforations between each print, and tipped into a portfolio strangely titled Loving Service Hanga Seal. Descriptions for each print are printed underneath the gummed sheet.

media.caption: Zōjōji Temple in Snow (増上寺の雪 Zōjōji no yuki)

text.headline: Zōjōji Temple in Snow (増上寺の雪 Zōjōji no yuki)
text.text:
The artist gives us Zōjōji on a calm evening with gently falling snow. The temple's website provides us with the following history of Zōjōji:
"Zōjōji was founded in 1393 as an orthodox and fundamental nembutsu [literally, "buddha in mind"] seminary for Jōdō shu ["The Pure Land School"] in the Kanto (east Japan) region.
"Zōjōji was relocated to the present site in 1598 after Ieyasu Tokugawa, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, entered Edo (present-day Tokyo) in 1590 to establish his provincial government. After the start of the Edo Period when the Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan, Zōjōji became the family temple of the Tokugawa family and an unparalleled grand cathedral was built. Zōjōji also served as an administrative center to govern the religious studies and activities of Jodo shu. In those days, its precincts covered an area of 826,000 square meters which also contained 48 smaller attached temples and about 150 grammar schools. Moreover, as many as 3,000 priests and novices always resided here as students.
"Nevertheless, as the Tokugawa shogunate came to an end and the Meiji Era started, an anti-Buddhist movement got under way. The cathedral, temples and the mausoleum of the Tokugawa family were burned down by air raids during World War II. Thus, Zōjōji was profoundly affected by political and social circumstances. Today, however, its cathedral and other structures have been rebuilt, and Zōjōji continues to serve as the main temple of Jōdō shu and the central nembutsu seminary for priests and novices. Furthermore, it has endeared itself to the general public as both a grand Buddhist temple typical of the metropolis Tokyo and a hub of religious and cultural activities."
This collection's print is a posthumous printing of Kōitsu's original 1933 design published by Doi Hangaten as part of the series Tokyo Views.

media.caption: Hakone: Mt. Fuji Over the Lake (箱根 湖水富士)

text.headline: Hakone: Mt. Fuji Over the Lake (箱根 湖水富士)
text.text:
Sekino's rendition of station number 11, Hakone, along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. This print is the 53rd, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekino created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858).
There are two distinct states for this print. One, as in this collection's print, displays broad blue-gray rays from an unseen sun cutting diagonally across the upper left quarter of the print. These rays are absent in the other state of the print.
"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

media.caption: Riverside (川岸 Kawagishi)

text.headline: Riverside (川岸 Kawagishi)
text.text: One of Miyashita's etchings, done early on in his career, depicting the Tokyo waterfront region where he was born. His later prints, which he is best known for, used combined processes including metal plates, photoengraving and woodblock.

media.caption: Nagoya Castle (名古屋城)

text.headline: Nagoya Castle (名古屋城)
text.text:
Kōitsu's colorful rendering of the walls and inner moat at Nagoya Castle during the height of the spring cherry blossom season.
Nagoya Castle was constructed on the orders of Ieyasu Tokugawa to secure an important position on the Tokaido road and to ward off attacks from the direction of Osaka. Construction was completed in 1612, and the castle is typical of those built on flatlands. Until the Meiji Restoration, Nagoya Castle flourished as the castle in which the Owari lineage of the Tokugawa family, the foremost of the family’s three lineages, resided.
In May 1945, during the air raids on Nagoya in the Second World War, most of the buildings including the main and small dungeons, and the Hommaru Palace, were burned down. Fortunately, three corner towers, three gates, and most of the paintings on the sliding doors and walls in the Hommaru Palace survived the fire, and have been handed down as Important Cultural Assets. - Source: Nagoya Castle Official Website http://www.nagoyajo.city.nagoya.jp/13_english/index.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Playground 1 (遊戯場 Yūgijō 1)

text.headline: Playground 1 (遊戯場 Yūgijō 1)
text.text: "Hagiwara creates richly textured and joyfully colourful images. To do this he uses new techniques such as scratching the woodblock like an etching, and printing on the back of the paper. He has won an international reputation for his abstract prints since 1958. Choosing a theme, he then develops a series of studies: this is the first of the ‘playground’ series." -  Source: British Museum from the 2007 exhibition Japan from Prehistory to the Present

media.caption: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)

text.headline: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)

media.caption: Plowing the Rice Field in Spring (春の田んぼを耕す)

text.headline: Plowing the Rice Field in Spring (春の田んぼを耕す)
text.text: An untitled scene of a lone figure plowing a field with an ox and a primitive looking plow. Various descriptive titles have been assigned to this print, e.g. "Ploughing the Rice Field" and "Ploughing with Ox." When it was released as part of an offering of six Saitō prints by the Book-of-the-Month Club, it was titled "The Seasons: Spring." See IHL.0636 for another print included in the Book-of-the-Month Club set of six prints.

media.caption: Ginkaku-ji, Kyoto

text.headline: Ginkaku-ji, Kyoto
text.text:
Funasaka has silkscreened a monotone photograph as the background of this print to simulate a moonlight view of the Mt. Fuji-shaped Kogetsudai ("Moon-viewing platform") at Kyoto's Ginkaku-ji (Temple of the Silver Pavilion.) Superimposed on this photograph are seven of his unique brightly colored vertical forms, along with splotches of black ink. Perhaps his vibrant forms are just visitors to the temple? While the temple dates to the late 1400s, the Zen-inspired moon-viewing platform, made from sand, was added in the 1600s. On moonlit nights the Kogetsudai illuminates the Silver Pavilion.
The artist also created a diptych of this same view of Kogetsudai. Please see IHL.0987 and IHL.1049 for details on this diptych.

text.headline: M-35
text.text:
"The appeal of his work lies not only in its crafted simplicity but also in its formal purity. He manages to balance the shapes to carve out his own private space and to create tension with these elements." - Collecting Modern Japanese Prints, Then and Now, Mary and Norman Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1994, p. 83.
The prefix "M" used in the titles of many of Funasaka's works stands for 1,000, an indication that he has produced over one thousand works.

media.caption: 842 (Ginkaku-ji, Kogetsudai)

text.headline: 842 (Ginkaku-ji, Kogetsudai)
text.text: The left print of two prints forming a diptych. Each of the prints use a combination of silkscreen (from a deconstructed photograph image) for the background and woodblock for the artist's signature brightly colored vertical forms. The background image is of the Kogetsudai in the Ginkaku Temple grounds and is the same image as is used in this collection's print Ginkaku-ji Kyoto, IHL.0985.

media.caption: Charcoal Seller (炭屋 sumiya)

text.headline: Charcoal Seller (炭屋 sumiya)
text.text:
By the time this print, showing a charcoal seller cutting charcoal logs into pieces, was issued during the Pacific War, Japanese homes and small industry were demanding more and more charcoal, adding to the degradation of Japan's large forests. A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition (originally print number 14 in the second series) reads "What would be the reason for the mysterious phenomenon nowadays of the upper-class voices on the street supporting the government, while the lower-class are concentrating all their energy on rice and charcoal? And everywhere you go you hear the polite phrase 'The world has become a strange place, don't you think.' As autumn turns to winter, people's eyes are drawn more acutely to rice and charcoal with each passing day. And people go crazy over charcoal to the extent that a lump that before would have seemed completely insignificant to them, now looks like a black diamond. Some people even pine is prison because of it. Because of the current situation, almost every day new substitutes are invented and them substitutes for substitutes. . . . I wonder what on earth will happen to Japan's forests and mountains."[1]
For another impression of this print see IHL.1317.

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 54.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Kawashima Textile Mills, Hand-Woven Tapestry (綴綿手織 tsuzuri-ori teori)

text.headline: Kawashima Textile Mills, Hand-Woven Tapestry (綴綿手織 tsuzuri-ori teori)
text.text: This small print depicts weavers at Kawashima Textiles with one of their beautiful large tapestries in the background. One of twelve prints in a portfolio commissioned by the Osaka Railway Division, Japanese National Railways. The table of contents for the portfolio states "Figured Hand-Woven Brocade. Traditional Nishijin, fabric of Kyoto is gorgeous brocade hand-woven with finger-tips."

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Sōma Masakado in the kabuki play Kamahige (九世市川団十郎 相馬将門・鎌髯)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Sōma Masakado in the kabuki play Kamahige (九世市川団十郎 相馬将門・鎌髯)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, playing the role of the monk Sōma Masakado in the kabuki play Kamahige (Sickle Beard). Above him is an unidentified actor in the role of the servant Towara Tōda 俵藤太.
Kamahige "was first performed in 1774 at the Nakamura-za in Edo with Ichikawa Danjūrō IV. This drama is closely associated withh the Ennosuke and Danshirō names of the Ichikawa family.
The Shogun disguised as a traveling monk [Sōma Masakado] and a warrior dressed like a servant [Towara Tōda] appear on stage. The servant holds a sickle with which he is going to shave the monk who holds a water container. The monk tells him that he is immortal when the servant tries cut off his head. When they find out their true identities, they decide to settle their differences on the battlefield."[1]
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selections is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1985, p. 60.
[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-2023]

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Narukami Shōnin in the play Narukami (九世市川団十郎 鳴神上人・鳴神)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Narukami Shōnin in the play Narukami (九世市川団十郎 鳴神上人・鳴神)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper right panel, playing the role of Narukami Shōnin 鳴神上人 in the kabuki play Narukami 鳴神. Beneath him is an unidentified actor in the role of princess Kumo no Tamahime.
While not visible in the scanned image of this print, this print, as with others in the series, employs deluxe printing techniques, including embossing covering most of the prints background, the use of mica highlights on Taemahime's collar and a subtle pattern on Narukami's robe visible only when held up to the light at a certain angle.
The story of the play Narukami "originally came to Japan from India and after a Nō play 'Ikkaku Sennin' it was taken up for Kabuki. It is a delightful drama. The holy priest Narukami, angry that his petition to the Imperial Court has been refused, captures the dragon god of rain (ryūjin) and confines him in a rock pool beneath the waterfall which he seals off with a straw rope to indicate the sacred boundary. The country is without rain and so it is decided at the Imperial Court to send the beautiful and clever princess [Kumo no Taemahime] to Narukami. Narukami faints when the princess demonstrates how she had to lift up her skirt to get across a stream to reach her lover. When she revives him with water from her mouth, he for a moment realizes the danger. To prevent any action by him, the princess tells him that she wants to become a nun and when they are left alone she starts to complain of a violent pain. Their embrace only leads to a desire to become husband and wife which has to be celebrated with a drink of sake. Drunk, Narukami tells the princess how to release the god of rain and falls asleep. The princess hastily cuts the straw rope and her mission accomplished, departs. Narukami, in a different, spectacular wig, makeup and costume wakes up and wonders why it is raining and then gets into an uncontrollable rage and runs off after her."[1]

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Suhō Sōzu in the play Jayanagi (九世市川団十郎 須賔僧都・蛇柳)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Suhō Sōzu in the play Jayanagi (九世市川団十郎 須賔僧都・蛇柳)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, in the role of the Buddhist priest Suhō in the kabuki play Jayanagi (Snake Willow). Above his likeness is an unidentified actor in the role of the priest Kūkai 空海, who is known by his posthumous name Kōbō Daishi.
This rarely performed play was written by Kanai Sanshō and was first performed in 1763 at the Nakamura-za in Edo as the third act of the drama called 'Momochidori Ōisogayoi' with Ichikawa Danjūrō IV.
The text for this play was lost so there is little information about the plot and what information there is is not consistent. It seems that the plot revolves around Tanba no Suketarō, a village idiot, who is possessed by the angry spirit of a willow tree (possibly being the angry spirit of Kiyohime who was spurned by her lover, the Buddhist priest Suhō) on Mt. Kōya and displays vehement jealousy. The Snake Willow (Jayanagi) refers to a tree at the foot of Mount Koya that was blessed by the Buddhist saint Kūkai and said to represent a thousand year bond between men and women.

media.caption: Irokezuku sakeguse (色情氣付く酒癖)

text.headline: Irokezuku sakeguse (色情氣付く酒癖)
text.text:
This print is one of twelve prints issued as part of the comic series known as Twelve States of Mind Resulting from Drinking (Sake kigen jūnisō no uchi) by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915). "Here we see a woman (the bar’s older sister', apparently) [who] has let her clothing fall away from her body in a drunkenly suggestive manner. Her male companion, who has a sake bottle perched in front of him, looks plainly dismayed, his face conveying complete disinterest." - website of Egenolf Gallery
The text in the scroll was written by Honrai Kūjin 奔雷空人, likely a pseudonym.

media.caption: Famous Places of Tokyo, First National Bank (東京名所 第一 国立銀行 Tokyo meisho Dai-ichi Kokuritsu Ginkō)

text.headline: Famous Places of Tokyo, First National Bank (東京名所 第一 国立銀行 Tokyo meisho Dai-ichi Kokuritsu Ginkō)
text.text: The artist designed at least nine prints commemorating the Japan First National Bank built in 1872 (Meiji 5), one of the first pseudo-Western style buildings erected in Japan. This print is from one of THE many different print series created by the artist titled Tokyo meisho (Famous Places of Tokyo.) This particular Tokyo meisho series is distinguished by its Western-style red and yellow frame, an artistic device for highlighting the modernity of the subject.

media.caption: New Year Charm in the Shape of a Love Letter: Woman of the Genroku Era (懸想文・元禄頃婦人 Kesōbumi・Genroku koro fujin)

text.headline: New Year Charm in the Shape of a Love Letter: Woman of the Genroku Era (懸想文・元禄頃婦人 Kesōbumi・Genroku koro fujin)
text.text:
One of thirty-six prints in the series Sanjūroku kasen (also transcribed as Sanjūroku kurabe) depicting delivery of a love poem to a beautiful woman dressed in a Genroku Era (1688-1704) kimono with her hair in the loose style of the period. The bearer of the poem may be the woman's lover, thinly disguised with a scarf about his face, or a messenger sent by her lover.
The series presents women of different classes from thirty-five different historical eras.

media.caption: Higaki 檜垣 (Cypress Fence)

text.headline: Higaki 檜垣 (Cypress Fence)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the Noh play Higaki, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), in which the old woman Higaki tells of her early life to a priest.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 54.) - A priest living in the mountains sees a very old woman come every day to draw water. Questioning her, he learns that she is the woman Higaki who long ago composed a poem on being asked for water by Fujiwara no Okinori. After asking for his prayers, the woman disappears. When she returns later, she tells the priest of her early life and performs a dance as she recalls the time when she danced for Okinori.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Teika 定家

text.headline: Teika 定家
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the Noh play Teika, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 187-188.) - A priest visiting the capital goes into a nearby shelter to escape a sudden shower. A lady appears and tells him that the place was built by Fujiwara Teika who had a secret liaison with the Princess Shokushi. But very soon she died, and Teika's spirit turned into the vine which clings to her grave. She takes the priest to the spot and then, disclosing that she is the Princess, disappears from sight. The priest recites the Lotus Sutra, and her spirit reappears to perform a joyful dance in gratitude for having attained salvation through his prayers.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Kazuraki 葛城

text.headline: Kazuraki 葛城
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the Noh play Kazuraki, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which a yamabushi priest (note the characteristic hat) sits before an old woman transformed into a goddess.
Play synopsis: "A traveling monk leaves Mt. Haguro (in Yamagata-Prefecture) on his pilgrimage to Kazuraki-Shrine. Having arrived at Mt. Kazuraki in Yamato (in present-day Nara Prefecture), and after crossing over the peaks of mountains, he is suddenly caught in a heavy snowfall and loses his way. A local woman with a bundle of sticks on her back finds him in trouble, and feels pity for him. She offers him to stay overnight at her humble cottage down in a shadowy valley, and entertains him by building a fire with shimoto - a bundle of sticks collected in deep snow, much famed in Mt. Kazuraki. Not knowing what it is, he asks her about it. She explains, citing an old waka-poem, that the sticks bound together by a creeper reed became so famous as to be commonly associated in their minds with the mountain, and narrates tenderly of poetry and Yamato dances. At last she tells that she, the Kazuraki Goddess, was ordered by En no Gyoja to build a rock bridge from Mt. Kazuraki to Mt. Ohmine, but failed in doing so because she did not want to work during the day, hating to expose her ugly looks to the world. Thus she incurred his anger and was bound to eternal agony and suffering. She, therefore, begs him to free her from bondage.
In the stillness of night, as his clothes dry out, the monk starts his religious service. Drawn by the healing power of the religious chanting, the woman appears in the shape of the goddess, and, freed from her bonds, performs before him the Yamato dance in the snow and in the moonlight, so gracefully as if surveying the whole expanse of the Yamato field from a mountain top. As the early light of dawn approaches, however, she hides herself in a rock cave, fearing to expose her looks." - sources: Hirotakansyokai website http://hirota-kansyokai.la.coocan.jp/eibun/images/5kaiKazuraki.pdf and A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 76-77.

media.caption: Shunkan 俊寛

text.headline: Shunkan 俊寛
text.text:
In this scene from the Noh play Shunkan, Shunkan holds the boat’s rope and watches his two companions, exiled with him to the remote island of Kikaigashima, leave by boat for home after they are pardoned, but he is forced to remain in exile on the desolate island.
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 114.) - Before the story of the play unfolds, three men - the priest Shunkan (shite) and the officials Fujiwara no Naritsune (tsure), and Taira no Yasuyori (tsure) - have been exiled to the remote island of Kigaigashima beyond the southern tip of Kyushu. The men were sent away because of their plot to overthrow Taira no Kiyomori. At the beginning of the play, Naritsune and Yasuyori have returned from a mock pilgrimage around the island. Shunkan has remained behind in their miserable dwelling. Then, Kiyomori's emissary (waki) arrives by boat, bringing a pardon for two of the three men. Shunkan's joy soon turns to despair when he learns that he is the only one who will not be permitted to return to the capital. His two companions set off with heavy hearts, leaving him alone to watch their departure.

Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. media.caption: The Megumi Fire Brigade Fight (神明恵和合取組 Kami-no Megumi Wago-no Torikumi)

text.headline: The Megumi Fire Brigade Fight (神明恵和合取組 Kami-no Megumi Wago-no Torikumi)
text.text: In March 1890, the Shintomiza in Tokyo was the stage for the hit play Kami-no Megumi Wagō-no Torikumi (also called Megumi no Kenka め組の喧嘩 The Firebrigade Fight) which re-enacted the 1805 brawl between a group of drunken firefighters of the Me brigade and a group of sumo wrestlers participating in a show of strength. The fight left one firefighter dead and nearly one hundred men injured. The play, written by Takeshiba Kisuei and Kawatake Shinshichi, pupils of the great playwright Mokuami, consists of four acts. The play was written for Onoe Kigugorō V who is seen in the left panel of this collection's print playing Tatsugorō, the leader of the firefighters.

media.caption: The Teachings of Women (妹背山婦女庭訓 Imoseyama Onna Teikin)

text.headline: The Teachings of Women (妹背山婦女庭訓 Imoseyama Onna Teikin)
text.text:
This print depicts three characters in Act IV, a domestic subplot, of The Teachings of Women. From right to left, we see Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Soga no Iruka, Ichikawa Sadanji as Fukashichi, the fisherman, and, again, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Omiwa, the daughter of a sake seller. Note the fantastic dragon motif on the robe worn by Sadanji in the center panel as he strikes a mie pose.
In Act IV, Omiwa, the daughter of a sake seller, falls in love with the son of Kamatari, one of the leaders of the anti-Soga party. When he refuses to reveal his identity, she attaches a spool of thread to his cloak and follows him, winding the reel. Her lover is following an unidentified princess with the same device, and all finally find themselves at Iruka's palace. Omiwa is noticed by one of Kamatari's subjects, Kanawa Gorō, who is loitering nearby disguised as Fukashichi, the fisherman. He stabs her. As she dies, he reveals that her lover was a courtier and that she will now be helping him to overthrow Iruka. Fukashichi then mixes her blood with the blood of a black-toed deer and smears it on his magic flute, making it possible to recover a certain Sacred Sword from Iruka at last, and sap his power. - Source: The Theatrical World of Osaka Prints, Roger S. Keyes and Keiko Mizushima, David R. Godine in association with Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1973, p. 74.

media.caption: Women Weavers (織女 shokujo)

text.headline: Women Weavers (織女 shokujo)
text.text:
Two women at their looms in this second edition print by the publisher Kyoto Hanga-in of the pre-WWII design originally released by Nishinomiya Shoin in 1940 as the fifth print in series two of Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 2. The commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition reads, "The Japanese farmer from olden times has woven the cloth for his own use at home. In the leisure season for farmers, the women are busy while the men prepare firewood and charcoal. In some silk producing regions, they weave silk stuff for sale. This picture shows such a weaving scene in a farmhouse. - Painted by Sanzo Wada. Printed by KYOTO-HANGAIN CO., LTD." This post-war commentary omits the following sentence from the first edition issued during the Pacific War, "While they ply their looms their thoughts may turn to cherished ones far away and in peace of mind they may learn to appreciate more deeply the value of serenity and tranquil effort."

media.caption: Flower Vendors (花賣 hana uri)

text.headline: Flower Vendors (花賣 hana uri)
text.text:
A second edition by the publisher Kyōto Hangain of this pre-WWII design of Oharame (flower sellers from the villages of Yase and Ohara) standing on Kyōto's Sanjō bridge, originally released by Nishinomiya Shoin in June 1941 as print number twenty-one in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1.

media.caption: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)

text.headline: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)
text.text:
Children and adults gather around a storyteller dressed in an official-looking uniform. The English language commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition (originally print number 13 in the series) reads, "A Story-teller (Kamishibai) - When he finds a good place for his business on the street, he stops and makes ready the pictures illustrating his stories in the case on his bicycle. Then he calls out 'Come and look! A grand picture show you’ve never seen!' striking the wooden clappers to attract attention. Soon a crowd of children gather from all directions. The story-teller is very skilful [sic] in telling the story, immitating [sic] the voices of the various people in the story. After the story is over, he sells candies. A pictorial story-teller is a Pide-piper [sic] of Hamelin in Japan, and the children are like the rats running after the piper."
The commentary for this post-war edition leaves out the following which was included in the commentary to the first edition issued during the Pacific War. "It is indeed natural that the authorities have recently been making efforts to lead in the right direction this business [the picture card show] that may well be employed as a valuable organ to … develop their [children’s] thought."
For other impressions of this print see IHL.1542 and IHL.0983.

media.caption: Crossing Guard (踏切番 fumikiriban)

text.headline: Crossing Guard (踏切番 fumikiriban)
text.text:
A crossing guard leans against the railway gate awaiting a soon to be passing train in this eighteenth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. An unsmiling crowd of laborers, children, mothers, a salaryman, and a horse await his raising of the gate.
A translation of the original commentary in Japanese accompanying this print reads, "Among the many mechanisms that take part in the serious and extensive functions of the railway, it seems that the work of the crossing guard is the kind that is most easy-going. However, this is far from the truth. Not only does [his] flag play a vital role in safeguarding human life, but he is also the person in charge of the greatest responsibilities such as quickly managing the trains by signaling his flag up and down. Together with the sympathy I feel for his living so close to the tracks and for his selflessly submitting himself to the will of those big black monsters of trains, I do think that his job also comes with a lot of free time." - Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 33.

media.caption: Sanjō Bridge (三条大橋 Sanjō Ōhashi)

text.headline: Sanjō Bridge (三条大橋 Sanjō Ōhashi)
text.text:
Likely a self-printed and published work by Tokuriki, presenting a view from almost underneath the Sanjō Bridge, which crosses Kyoto's Kamo River, out towards the Shijō Ohashi bridge.
As with many of Tokuriki's self-printed works, this print exists in at least one other state using slightly different color shades. A a similar view of the bridge presented in a horizontal ōban format also exists. In discussing the ōban version of this print, curator George Kuwayama, notes "Tradition is strong in Tokuriki's work, and compositional analogies to Hiroshige are evident in the Sanjō Bridge. But despite his traditionalism, he is a modern print master. His palette is Fauvist and the strong, expressive lines are gouged with a knife to produce jagged contours."

media.caption: Yoshiwara Park: Army Foot Soldier Private Second Class Mr. Nakamura Fukusaburō (吉原公園 / 陸軍歩　二等卒中村福三郎君 Yoshiwara kōen / Rikugunpo nitōsotsu Nakamura Fukusaburō kun)

text.headline: Yoshiwara Park: Army Foot Soldier Private Second Class Mr. Nakamura Fukusaburō (吉原公園 / 陸軍歩　二等卒中村福三郎君 Yoshiwara kōen / Rikugunpo nitōsotsu Nakamura Fukusaburō kun)
text.text: The bravery of Private Nakamura Fukusaburō is depicted, rushing to help people trapped near Yoshiwara Pond as the firestorm that engulfed Tokyo after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake rages.

media.caption: Temporary Omnibus, in the Street of Kyobashi [sic]) (運送馬車 京橋通 Unsō basha Kyōbashi)

text.headline: Temporary Omnibus, in the Street of Kyobashi [sic]) (運送馬車 京橋通 Unsō basha Kyōbashi)
text.text:
One of six prints contributed by the Nihonga artist Isoda to the 1924 thirty-six print series Collection of Woodblock Prints of the Taishō Earthquake issued by the little-known publisher Hoshino Seki of Gahōsha who offered the prints as "a small gesture of social service."  

"The location here is Kyobashi, a central district south of Nihonbashi and north of Ginza, where Tokyo's first Western-style buildings were erected in the late nineteenth century. The district saw the first gas lit lamps, electric lights, and brick buildings during the Meiji period and remains to this day a premier business and shopping district." [The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 282.]

In 1924, the Japanese publisher Hoshino Seki [of the publishing house Gahōsha] issued a set of thirty-six prints depicting scenes from the aftermath of the September 1, 1923 great Tokyo earthquake. He commissioned six artists to each produce six designs based on eyewitness sketches and accounts, which the master carver Nagashima Kiichi and printer Tamura Tetsunosuke then translated into color woodblock prints for the portfolio.

media.caption: House of Yase Women (八瀬女の家 Yase-me no Ie)

text.headline: House of Yase Women (八瀬女の家 Yase-me no Ie)
text.text:
Picturing two traditionally dressed women in front of a home in the town of Yase near Kyoto. Women dressed as shown in the print are often referred to Oharame, Ohara being a picturesque and better known town near Yase where many women continued to wear traditional dress, even after WWII. See this collection's prints Oharame (IHL.0313) and Flower Vendors from the series Occupations of Showa Japan in Pictures, Series 1 (IHL.1003) for other depictions of Oharame.
The series Life of Kyoto consists of six chuban-sized prints depicting activities and places in and around Kyoto. The series was published by an unknown publisher identified as 宮脇美風扇版 in the rectangular cartouche in the lower right margin of each print.

media.caption: Kabuki Backstage - Ennosuke II  (歌舞伎 楽屋 - 二代猿之助)

text.headline: Kabuki Backstage - Ennosuke II  (歌舞伎 楽屋 - 二代猿之助)
text.text: The actor Ichikawa Ennosuke II 市川猿之助 (1888-1963) applying makeup in his dressing room.

media.caption: Tōbōsaku 東方朔

text.headline: Tōbōsaku 東方朔
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the Noh play Kazuraki, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which a yamabushi priest (note the characteristic hat) sits before an old woman transformed into a goddess.
Play synopsis: "A traveling monk leaves Mt. Haguro (in Yamagata-Prefecture) on his pilgrimage to Kazuraki-Shrine. Having arrived at Mt. Kazuraki in Yamato (in present-day Nara Prefecture), and after crossing over the peaks of mountains, he is suddenly caught in a heavy snowfall and loses his way. A local woman with a bundle of sticks on her back finds him in trouble, and feels pity for him. She offers him to stay overnight at her humble cottage down in a shadowy valley, and entertains him by building a fire with shimoto - a bundle of sticks collected in deep snow, much famed in Mt. Kazuraki. Not knowing what it is, he asks her about it. She explains, citing an old waka-poem, that the sticks bound together by a creeper reed became so famous as to be commonly associated in their minds with the mountain, and narrates tenderly of poetry and Yamato dances. At last she tells that she, the Kazuraki Goddess, was ordered by En no Gyoja to build a rock bridge from Mt. Kazuraki to Mt. Ohmine, but failed in doing so because she did not want to work during the day, hating to expose her ugly looks to the world. Thus she incurred his anger and was bound to eternal agony and suffering. She, therefore, begs him to free her from bondage.
In the stillness of night, as his clothes dry out, the monk starts his religious service. Drawn by the healing power of the religious chanting, the woman appears in the shape of the goddess, and, freed from her bonds, performs before him the Yamato dance in the snow and in the moonlight, so gracefully as if surveying the whole expanse of the Yamato field from a mountain top. As the early light of dawn approaches, however, she hides herself in a rock cave, fearing to expose her looks." - sources: Hirotakansyokai website http://hirota-kansyokai.la.coocan.jp/eibun/images/5kaiKazuraki.pdf [accessed 8-17-23] and A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 76-77.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 7 (日清戦闘畫 第七編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daishichi hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 7 (日清戦闘畫 第七編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daishichi hen)
text.text: Volume 7 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

media.caption: Park in Canton (廣東公園 Kōtō koen)

text.headline: Park in Canton (廣東公園 Kōtō koen)
text.text: This print was based on a sketch done by Yoshida during the last of his "three trips to China between 1939 and 1940, as a war painter for the Japanese Army. Whatever the official purpose, his personal motivation of any of his overseas trips was to sketch the places he visited." - Source: The Complete Woodblock Prints of Yoshida Hiroshi, Tadao Ogura, Abe Corporation, 1996, p. 26, 165.

media.caption: Snow at Kinkaku Temple (Kinkakuji no yuki 金閣寺の雪)

text.headline: Snow at Kinkaku Temple (Kinkakuji no yuki 金閣寺の雪)
text.text:
One of the artist's 14 prints created during his lifetime, picturing visitors on the balconies of Kinkaku temple in Kyoto during winter.
Officially named Rokuonji Temple, Kinkaku-ji (Temple of the Golden Pavilion) was originally built as a villa by Ashikaga Yoshimitsu (1358-1408). It was converted into a temple after Yoshimitsu's death. The complex, whose gardens and architecture focus around the central Golden Pavilion, is said to evoke paradise on earth and is famous both in Japan and abroad as a symbol of Kitayama culture, which was central in importing various aspects of Ming-dynasty Chinese culture into Japanese society. The temple was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.

media.caption: Hozu River in Early Summer (Shoka no Hozugawa 初夏の保津川)

text.headline: Hozu River in Early Summer (Shoka no Hozugawa 初夏の保津川)
text.text: One of the artist's 14 prints created during his lifetime, picturing an excursion boat being steered down the Hozu River rapids by three boatmen. The Hozugawa is a part of Katsura River in Kyoto Prefecture, Japan. The river begins in the mountains near Kameoka, a town northwest of Kyoto City. It snakes into the Arashiyama  section of western Kyoto before changing its name to Katsura River. Today, excursion boats continue to offer rides through the rapids.

media.caption: Gion Festival (祇園祭 Gion Matsuri)

text.headline: Gion Festival (祇園祭 Gion Matsuri)
text.text:
One of twelve prints from the series Picture Notes on Native Customs of Japan depicting folk rituals from different parts of Japan. It is suggested by Lawrence Smith that the prints paid homage to the Folk Art (mingei) movement that Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), who played an unspecified role in issuing this series, was sympathetic to.
In the artist's words, "The Gion Festival is held on July 17th and 24th in Kyoto. The musicians on the large float play elegant 'Gion-bayashi' tunes during the procession. The festival officials show their precious antiques and pictures to the spectators which is a unique custom of this festival." - Maekawa Senpan
The artists for this series were Azechi Umetarō, Kawanishi Hide, Kuroki Sadao, Maeda Masao, Maekawa Senpan, Mori Dōshun, Saitō Kiyoshi, Sekino Jun'ichirō, Wakayama Yasoji, and Yamaguchi Gen. This series followed on the heels of the series Scenes of Lost Tokyo (Tokyo kaiko zue), printed in December 1945 and issued by the same publisher, Uemura Masuo of Fugaku Shuppansha.
The Editor's Statement: "Japan is now on the start-line to the new development. Getting free from militarism Japan is expected to be developed to a nation of civilization. At this time of change, it may be interesting to look back [on] the native customs and festivals as to realize the future images of Japan. These humble customs and festivals will also become the mother's milk for Japanese people to bring up the peaceful heart filled with love and piousness.
"With this purpose the present album has been compiled. The artists are the members of the Japan Artist Engraving Society and are the experts of the Contemporary Original-Engraving in Japan. Japan has been revived to the lovable Japan. We have great pleasure to send you this album at the present delightful time."
For other prints in this series see IHL.0773 and IHL.0774.

media.caption: Portable Shrine Festival (お祭りお神輿)

text.headline: Portable Shrine Festival (お祭りお神輿)
text.text:
A dozen revelers carry a movable shrine, an omikoshi, tipping it from side to side, during a shrine festival. Omikoshi お神輿 is a portable Shinto shrine for the gods and spirits carried by the parishioners of a shrine during festivals. It is paraded around local areas and signifies the warding off of misfortune and wishing for the happiness of its people. Rocking the omikoshi invigorates the deity and enlivens the land.
While almost all of Yoshitoshi Mori's prints are stencil prints, this print appears to be at least partially created using woodblock given the baren rubbing marks on the print's verso.

media.caption: Ducks with Flowering Plum (untitled)

text.headline: Ducks with Flowering Plum (untitled)
text.text: One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of 20th century.  In this print two mandarin ducks (oshidori), which mate for life, symbolize affection, mutual consideration, and fidelity are paired with plum blossoms symbolizing prosperity and perseverance.

media.caption: Ikarikazuki 碇潜 (The Anchor Draping)

text.headline: Ikarikazuki 碇潜 (The Anchor Draping)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene inside of a shrine from the play Ikarikazuki attributed to Komparu Zenpō 金春禅鳳 (1454-?).
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A traveling priest comes to Dan-no-ura where the Taira clan were defeated in a famous sea battle with the Minamoto, and meets an old boatman who tells him of the exploits performed during the battle by Nortsune, the younger brother of Tomomori. In the second act Tomomori himself appears and describes how, when faced with defeat, Dainagon no Tsubone and Nii-dono drowned themselves, taking with them the young Emperor Antoku, and how Tomomori too threw himself into the sea, holding an anchor to weigh him down.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 60.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)

text.headline: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)
text.text:
This print, the right sheet of a triptych, depicts a scene from the play Ema by an unknown playwright.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
An Imperial emissary on his way to the Great Shrines of Ise stops overnight at Saikū nearby as it happens to be the last day of winter and he hopes to see something of the votive tablets which are said to be hung up there during that particular night to foretell the fortunes of the coming year, a white one indicating sunny weather and a black one rain. He meets an old couple with such tablets who, after some discussion, agree to put up one of each kind to signify good fortune for everyone. They then disappear into the darkness after telling him that they are in fact two of the gods of Ise. In the second part Amaterasu, the Sun-goddess, appears with the goddess Uzume and the god Tajikarao and performs a dance. The three of them then depict the ancient story of Amaterasu’s withdrawal into a cave: as the world is plunged into darkness by her disappearance, the other gods dance and make merry and eventually succeed in enticing her out again by arousing her curiosity.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 26-28.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Flag Merchants (旗屋 hataya)

text.headline: Flag Merchants (旗屋 hataya)
text.text:
Picturing an artisan painting a banner, Flag Merchants was originally issued in May 1940 by Nishinomiya Shoin as the nineteenth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. This print was not one of the prints from the series reissued after the war by Kyōto Hangain, the successor to the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin. This is not surprising, given that the depiction of nationalist sentiment, e.g. Japanese flags, was not politically acceptable after the war.

[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Soldiers, Number 13 (兵士  其十三 heishi sono jūsan)

text.headline: Soldiers, Number 13 (兵士  其十三 heishi sono jūsan)
text.text:
Picturing soldiers at rest, this print was originally issued between 1939 and 1941 by the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin. This print was not reissued after the war by Kyōto Hangain, the successor to the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin, which reprinted many prints from the two pre-war series along with issuing a new twenty-four print third series. This is not surprising, given that the depiction of patriotic sentiment, e.g. soldiers, was not politically acceptable after the War.
The original Japanese commentary accompanying the print reads, "Our soldiers, who are the ones who ought to bear the greatest responsibility in these important times, are usually trained under the simple and strict command of tradition. Therefore in the barracks they become absolutely emotionless, expressionless, and selfless. In addition, they all talk the same and move like machines. Even when they are off-duty and, for example, write letters or read magazines, the simple and concise room overflows with spirit, and you can feel a dynamic strength. In response to the many banners with 'to laugh and cry together' and 'be bright and cheerful today,' those who visit can only take their hat off to them." - Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 28.

media.caption: Women Weavers (織女 shokujo)

text.headline: Women Weavers (織女 shokujo)
text.text:
Two women at their looms in this second edition print by the publisher Kyoto Hanga-in of the pre-WWII design originally released by Nishinomiya Shoin in 1940 as the fifth print in series two of Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures.
The commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition reads, "The Japanese farmer from olden times has woven the cloth for his own use at home. In the leisure season for farmers, the women are busy while the men prepare firewood and charcoal. In some silk producing regions, they weave silk stuff for sale. This picture shows such a weaving scene in a farmhouse. - Painted by Sanzo Wada. Printed by KYOTO-HANGAIN CO., LTD"
This post-war commentary omits the following sentence from the first edition issued during the Pacific War, "While they ply their looms their thoughts may turn to cherished ones far away and in peace of mind they may learn to appreciate more deeply the value of serenity and tranquil effort."

[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Summer - Seaside No. 1 (夏 - 海辺 No. 1)

text.headline: Summer - Seaside No. 1 (夏 - 海辺 No. 1)
text.text:
Bright, primary color is rarely seen in Takahashi’s pre-1965 work, his palette being limited to the soft grays and browns associated with his chosen muse, the ancient city of Kyoto. But this print comes alive with a brilliant burst of yellow sunlight. Takahashi varied the title of this print, with some impressions titled “Summer” and others titled “Seaside”.
All of Takahashi's prints bring to mind the season, whether or not they are titled as such.

media.caption: Dried Persimmons (じろ柿 shiro kaki)

text.headline: Dried Persimmons (じろ柿 shiro kaki)
text.text: An ink on paper scroll mounted on silk brocade with a bone roller (jikuji), picturing two dried persimmons. For a print with the same subject see Dried Persimmons from the series Seihō's Masterpieces (IHL.0908).

media.caption: Matoba Beach at Takehara (Hiroshima ken) (竹原的場 [広島県])

text.headline: Matoba Beach at Takehara (Hiroshima ken) (竹原的場 [広島県])
text.text:
An unfinished state, perhaps two impressions, of Matoba Beach at Takehara (Hiroshima ken), 1948. No publisher seal, artist signature or artist seal appear on the print.
The artist's second catalog raisonne "Kawase Hasui: The Complete Woodblock Prints," p. 123 notes "Takehara, in southern Hiroshima prefecture, was an important centre for salt production during the Tokugawa period (1600-1868).

media.caption: Chūzenji, Utagahama (中禅寺 歌ヶ浜)

text.headline: Chūzenji, Utagahama (中禅寺 歌ヶ浜)
text.text:
"This is the highest altitude lake in Japan, offering an escape from the heat and humidity of summer. Two pilgrims approach the vermillion gate that marks the entrance to Chūzenji, one of the thirty-three temples dedicated to the Kannon of Mercy on the eastern Japan pilgrimage route. The day is bright and clear, yet the scene is typically timeless; nothing infringes on the natural scenery." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
A view of Utagahama on the east side of Lake Chūzenji, near Nikkō. This design was one of 111 by Hasui that were shown in the second shin hanga exhibition at the Toledo Museum of Art in 1936. The catalog entry for the 1936 show notes "Blocks, 20; superimposed printings, about 25."
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

media.caption: Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi (untitled)

text.headline: Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi (untitled)
text.text:
A very small print presenting an often seen view of Lake Kawaguchi, the largest of the Fuji Five Lakes (富士五湖, Fuji-goko), located in an arc around the northern half of Mount Fuji.
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

media.caption: Frozen River (kōru kawa 凍る河)

text.headline: Frozen River (kōru kawa 凍る河)
text.text: A bleak but beautiful view of a Hokkaido river in the dead of winter.  This print was included in an 2010 exhibition of work at the Hokkaido Museum of Modern Art, titled Art in Hokkaido: People and Nature 北海道の美術 北の自然と人々.

media.caption: Circus No. 5 (サーカス No. 5 Saakasu No. 5)

text.headline: Circus No. 5 (サーカス No. 5 Saakasu No. 5)
text.text: Print 5 in the Hagiwara's Circus series of prints created in 1968. He followed this series with the series Clowns in 1969 and the circus has been a recurring theme in the artist's work. Here the form of the clown is easily identifiable with his billowing costume.

media.caption: Kido Suikōin (木戸翠香院)

text.headline: Kido Suikōin (木戸翠香院)
text.text:
Print number 40 (四十) as shown in the series' Table of Contents, although not numbered on the print. One of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition portraying the geisha Ikumatsu (1843-1886), the future wife of Kido Kōin (1833-1877) handing food to Kido while she was hiding him in August 1864 from the pursuing special police force (shinsengumi), organized by the bakufu (military government). Kido was a leader of the Ishin shishi which sought to weaken or overthrow the shogunate, which they felt was not taking a sufficiently strong stand against the Western barbarians. It is told that Ikumatsu argued with the police and blocked their way long enough for Kido to escape. Helping him to escape to Kyoto, they both fled to the Chōshū domain. Kido was to play a major role in the overthrow of the shogunate in 1867 which brought the Emperor Meiji to power.
After the restoration of the emperor, Kido had Ikumatsu adopted into a samurai family and married her. He changed his name to Kido Takayoshi, and Ikumatsu became Kido Matsuko, later taking the name Kido Suikōin 木戸翠香院.
The scroll makes reference to Kusunoki's lineage, stating that he is descended from the Tachibanas who are descended from the 6th century Emperor Bidatsu. Historians, however, state there is little "historical certainty" about his lineage.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Murakami Yoshiteru (村上義光)

text.headline: Murakami Yoshiteru (村上義光)
text.text:
Print number 22 (廿二), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Murakami Hikoshirō Yoshiteru (村上 彦四郎 義光), a retainer of Prince Morinaga's (1308-1335), taking back his prince's Imperial banner from imperious villagers. He wears the cap of a yamabushi (fighting monk) which the Prince's party used as disguises during their flight from Kyoto to Yoshino in Yamata where the Prince intended to build a new castle outside the reach of the Regent, Hōjō Takatoki (1303-1333.)

media.caption: Katagiri Shōichi (片桐正一)

text.headline: Katagiri Shōichi (片桐正一)
text.text:
Print number 36 (卅六), one of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition.
Note: the Table of Contents title for this print is 片桐正一 (possibly read Katagiri Shōichi or Katagiri Masakazu (かたぎりまさかず) per the Ritsumeikan, Art Research Center), but the print's scroll does not reference this name.
The print pictures Katagiri Katsumoto 片桐且元 (1556-1615) on horseback with Kimura Shigenari 木村 重成 (1593-1615) by his side. Osaka Castle is seen in the background with geese flying in formation, denoting the autumn season. The date is likely the 2nd day of the 11th month, 1614 when Katagiri left the Castle after fruitless efforts to reach a compromise between the Toyotomi clan and the shogun, Tokugawa Ieyasu. The print's scroll speaks of Lady Yodo's, the mother of the young Hideyori Toyotomi (1593-c. 1615), suspicion of Katsumoto and her scheme to have him killed for suspected disloyalty. In this scene Shigenari is asking Katsumoto "what will come to be if you leave the Castle?"
Two states of this print are in this collection and at least three other states of this print are known, speaking to its, and to the entire series, popularity. IHL.1034, a later edition of this print, carries neither a print number nor a date.

media.caption: Sanjō Sanetomi (三條實美公)

text.headline: Sanjō Sanetomi (三條實美公)
text.text:
Print number 50 (五十) as shown in the series' Table of Contents, although not numbered on the print. One of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series, picturing Sanjō Sanetomi (1837-1891), a nobleman who held several important posts in Emperor Kōmei's court, prior to the Meiji Restoration, and subsequently in Emperor Meiji's government. He is shown here reprimanding a group of rebellious samurai. The scroll contains reference to several of the many government posts held by Sanetomi. The scene portrayed, while an artistic fabrication of the artist, likely references one of Sanetomi's trips to Satsuma, Chōshū, or one of the other areas of samurai rebellion, to defend the new Meiji government.

media.caption: Tomochidori (友千鳥)

text.headline: Tomochidori (友千鳥)
text.text:
Print number 40 (四十) in the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the famous rikishi (sumo) Tanikaze Kajinosuke (1750-1795) outside the home of the younger, and less accomplished, wrestler Tomochidori (b. 1756). Tomochidori, who is struggling financially, is seen feeding delicacies to his sick father, who is only seen in silhouette. His sacrifices to buy food and medicine for his father and forego his own well-being is a demonstration of shikō, or supreme filial piety. Tanikaze is reaching into the sleeve of his robe, perhaps to retrieve money to give to Tomochidori.
Kuniaki contributed a single print to this series and it is fitting that it involves sumo, as Kuniaki's most famous print is that of a sumo and he is best known for his sumo prints.
To see another edition of this print go to IHL.2254.

media.caption: Tokugawa Takechiyo (徳川竹千代)

text.headline: Tokugawa Takechiyo (徳川竹千代)
text.text:
Print number 31 (卅一), and one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, portraying ten year old Tokugawa Takechiyo (1543-1916), later to become Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate, "on the back of his retainer, seemingly directing a mock battle of children throwing stones along the banks of the Anegawa. Rocks can be seen in mid-flight. The original anecdote behind this print has the ten year old Ieyasu not directing the battle, but rather commenting on the battle, to the effect that the more organized and motivated, although smaller, group would win.
"On arriving, he said to those in attendance, 'Don’t watch the majority side. It’s best to be on the other side.'
"This was then seen as an indication of the young Ieyasu’s precocious wisdom and prowess in battle, and evidence of 'a divine gift with which Ieyasu was endowed at birth.'
"The story comes from the c. 1640 scroll titled the "Tōshō Daigongen engi". The scroll describes the origins of this “popular game” of the time and then the specific incident." - source: The Eyes of Power: Art and Early Tokugawa Authority, Karen M. Gerhart, University Of Hawai'i Press, 1999. P. 122.

media.caption: Ejiri Harbor Ship Marina (江尻港船着場 Ejiri-ko funatsukiba)

text.headline: Ejiri Harbor Ship Marina (江尻港船着場 Ejiri-ko funatsukiba)
text.text:
This 14th print in the 36 print series depicts the swimming area next to the Ejiri harbor in Shizuoka prefecture and the view out to a snowless Mount Fuji on a quiet summer day. The sign in the lower right reads 三保海水浴場行 (Miho sea bathing area). This print is the original issue (first edition between 1939-1940) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company as part of the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.

THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF 2600
Published by Uchida Bijutsu Shoshi between 1939 and 1940, this 36-print set (plus an introductory sheet and a table of contents sheet) by Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000) is a more modern take on Hokusai's (1760–1849) famous series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826-1833). Its publication was timed to coincide with nationalist celebrations in November 1940 marking Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation.
Tokuriki's series was extremely popular with domestic and foreign buyers who purchased one thousand copies within a short time after issuance. Various prints from this series were re-printed in subsequent years and subsets of the thirty-six prints were later repackaged into newly named series, such as Eight Views of Mount Fuji and Four Season of Mount Fuji, released in the 1950s. Later printings omit the information in the margin, modify Tokuriki's signature and change the seals below his signature appearing in the image area of the print.

media.caption: Komusō (虚無僧)

text.headline: Komusō (虚無僧)
text.text:
A later (post-War) re-issue by Kyōto Hangain of the pre-WWII design of two itinerant priests of the Fuke sect of Zen Buddhism originally released by Nishinomiya Shoin between 1939 and 1941 as the twentieth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1.
The commentary accompanying this post-War edition of the print reads, "The priests are playing the shakuhachi – a bamboo flute, and they beg contribution of money or rice by which they earn their living. The Fuke-sect is a Buddhist sect which originated in Japan a long time ago. In the chivalruss [sic] age, such warriors (samurais) who had to hide from the public created this sect, and built many temples where they passed their lives. This is why the Komuso wears a sword, and large head-gear to hide his face."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Picture of the October Kyōgen at the Meiji-za, Akashi's Patronage (明治座十月狂言・明石引立ノ図)

text.headline: Picture of the October Kyōgen at the Meiji-za, Akashi's Patronage (明治座十月狂言・明石引立ノ図)
text.text: A triptych issued in October 1900 depicting thirty-four actors who will be performing during the October lineup of plays at the Meiji-za 明治座 (Meiji Theater) in Tokyo. The actors, mostly part of the Ichikawa lineage, are participating in a kōjō 口上, a ceremony in which the actors present themselves to the audience. The ceremony may also include special announcements, such as an actor assuming a new stage name, or a first appearance on the stage, or memorial services.

media.caption: Miyajima in the Mist, sample print  (霧の宮島・見本 Kiri no Miyajima・mihon)

text.headline: Miyajima in the Mist, sample print  (霧の宮島・見本 Kiri no Miyajima・mihon)
text.text:
This print has the characters 見本 (sample print) written in ink within the image, clearly indicating it was not to be sold. The print pictures Miyajima Shinto shrine on Itsukushima island, located in Hiroshima bay. The shrine and its torii gate are unique for being built over water, seemingly floating in the sea during high tide.

media.caption: Sagami the Wife of Kumagai Naozane (熊谷直実の妻相模)

text.headline: Sagami the Wife of Kumagai Naozane (熊谷直実の妻相模)
text.text: The actor Ōtani Tomoemon V in the role of Sagami, the wife of  Kumagai Naozane, likely in the play Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani. This print is from the 1867 series "Parody of Thirty-Six Selected Beauties."

media.caption: China Souvenir (支那土産 Shina miyage)

text.headline: China Souvenir (支那土産 Shina miyage)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In this print we see a Chinese ship, a spoil of war, a souvenir (omiyage). On the side of the ship are written word plays for the various spoils.

media.caption: Hachinoki 鉢木 (The Dwarf Trees)

text.headline: Hachinoki 鉢木 (The Dwarf Trees)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Hachinoki by an unknown playwright in which the impoverished samurai Tsuneyo and his wife contemplate one of his beloved dwarf trees before sacrificing it.
PLAY SYNOPSIS
While travelling as an ordinary priest in order to see for himself the state of things in the country, Hōjō Tokiyori seeks shelter from a snowstorm at a poor-looking house he sees nearby. When Tsuneyo, the master of the house, returns he at first tells the priest that he must go; on to the next village since he and his wife barely have enough for their own needs, but so fierce is the storm that he then calls him back, shares with him what little food they have, and even sacrifices his last three dwarf trees by burning them to warm the guest. That night the priest learns that Tsuneyo is a warrior who fell to this wretched state after his lands were usurped and that, old and feeble though he is, he would not hesitate to answer the call of the rulers in Kamakura if the need arose. Tokiyori says nothing at the time, but after his return to Kamakura he issues a general alarm. When Tsuneyo comes, true to his word, he is summoned before the Regent and rewarded by the return of his own lands and a gift of an estate for each of the three trees which he had cherished but so ungrudgingly given up.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 45-46.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption:
Jinen Koji 自然居士
(The Lay Monk)

text.headline:
Jinen Koji 自然居士
(The Lay Monk)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Jinen Koji in which a young girl presents a robe to a priest to say prayers for her dead parents.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 64.) - While the lay priest Jinen is preaching at the Ungo-ji temple, a young girl comes and gives him a robe as a gift. In a letter accompanying it she explains that she has sold herself to buy the robe in order to have the priest say a mass for her dead parents. As Jinen is reading this, the men who have bought the girl come and take her away. Much moved by this, the preacher hurries after them and demands that they release the girl This they at first refuse to do, but after Jinen has entertained them with all manner of songs and dances, they agree to give the girl up.
For another depiction of this play see IHL.0708.
