media.caption: Miwa 三輪

text.headline: Miwa 三輪
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Miwa in which the god Miwa no Myōjin, appearing in the guise, of a woman performs an ancient dance for a priest.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 113-114.) - A woman who regularly brings aniseed water to the priest Gempin in Miwa one day asks him for a cloak to protect her from the autumn cold. This he gives her, and when he asks her where she lives, learns that her home is beside the two cryptomeria trees not far away. Shortly afterwards, a villager tells him that his cloak has been left hanging on one of the branches there. When the priest goes to see, the god Miwa no Myōjin appears in the form of a woman and tells him an ancient legend about a woman whose husband visited her only at night. Wishing to find out where he came from, she fixed the end of a length of thread to the hem of his gown and followed it after his return, only to find that it ended at the foot of the cryptomeria where they now stand. The god then performs the kind of dance that was given in the Divine Age to entice the goddess Amaterasu from the cave where she had hidden herself, and tells the priest that story.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Ominameshi 女郎花 (Maiden Flower)

text.headline: Ominameshi 女郎花 (Maiden Flower)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Ominameshi. A traveling priest is shown on stage while offstage a scene of a river with ominameshi flowers on its bank is pictured.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 133-134.) - The travelling priest comes to Otoko-yama and, seeing some yellow omina-meshi flowers blooming there, is about to break off a spray when he is stopped by an old man. He talks to the priest about the flowers and then takes him to see two mounds where a man named Yorikaze and his wife lie buried. Saying that they are connected with the omina-meshi flower, he disappears. In the second act, the spirits of Yorikaze and his wife appear and relate the story of their deaths. As a result of Yorikaze’s unkindness, the priest is told, his wife drowned herself in the river. Yorikaze buried her in a mound and from it grew omina-meshi flowers. Grief-stricken at her death, he too drowned himself and was buried in the second mound beside that of his wife.

media.caption: 841 (Ginkaku-ji, Kogetsudai)

text.headline: 841 (Ginkaku-ji, Kogetsudai)
text.text: The right print of two prints forming a diptych. Each of the prints use a combination of silkscreen (from a deconstructed photograph image) for the background and woodblock for the artist's signature brightly colored vertical forms. The background image is of the Kogetsudai in the Ginkaku Temple grounds and is the same image as that used in this collection's print Ginkaku-ji Kyoto, IHL.0985.

media.caption: Print 1 Very Popular Story

text.headline: Print 1 Very Popular Story
text.text: The first print in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk. This first print starts with an invitation, perhaps, to the EVENT and it is from this first print that the series takes its name.

media.caption: Print 36 Very Popular Story

text.headline: Print 36 Very Popular Story
text.text: Print 36 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk.

media.caption: Target (標的 Hyōteki)

text.headline: Target (標的 Hyōteki)
text.text: There's a wonderful mix of perspectives in this print achieved with single point perspective and embossing. The target set in the middle of the horizon leaps forward at us while we travel down a road toward the distant hills with blue sky beyond.

media.caption: Love and Hate

text.headline: Love and Hate
text.text:
Hodaka's semi abstract depiction of a head split by the emotions of love and hate. "Love and Hate shows the energy in emotion. The style is semi abstract, with simplicity of form and elegance in color."[1] "His idea is that, although love and hatred are two distinct concepts, sometimes they can be double faces of one entity."[2]

[1] website of Collection of Margaret and Eugene Skibbe http://www.hodakayoshidaprints.com/id2.html [website no longer active]
[2] Japanese Wood-block Prints, Shizuya Fujikake, Japan Travel Bureau, 1953, p. 187.

media.caption: Print 9 Very Popular Story

text.headline: Print 9 Very Popular Story
text.text: Print 9 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk.

media.caption: Print 15 Very Popular Story

text.headline: Print 15 Very Popular Story
text.text: Print 15 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk.

media.caption: 883 British Parliament

text.headline: 883 British Parliament
text.text: Another one of Funasaka's silkscreened images used as a backdrop for his signature brightly colored vertical forms.  This time it's the British Parliament building that he has hand pixelated as part of the print process.

media.caption: Roadside Fortune Teller (大道占師 daidō uranaishi)

text.headline: Roadside Fortune Teller (大道占師 daidō uranaishi)
text.text:
A fortune teller advises a couple in an evening divining session in this tenth print from series two of Occupations of the Shōwa Era in Pictures. This is a first edition print published by Nishinomiya Shoin.
A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this first edition print reads, "The Mainstreet Fortune Teller -for a fee of fifty sen fortunes are told in such diverse areas as marriage, occupation, lost items, missing persons, illness, and the rise and fall of the stock market, by means of reading, physiognomy, fortune telling, and onomancy. At a loss and in dire need they run to this place asking anything that is on their minds. But what are the conditions for trusting this spokesman? First, half of his hair needs to be grey, and he needs to be very old. He definitely shouldn't wear Western clothes. And even if the color is faded, a kimono with one's family crest and a hakama are considered as absolutely necessary parts of the outfit. However, wearing Chinese or Korean clothing seems to be a way to excite people's curiosity even more. What is even more interesting is that the buyer, that is, the person who seeks fortune-telling, forgets that they paid fifty sen and put themselves completely at the mercy of the fortune teller."[1]
For the post-war second edition commentary see IHL.1075.

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 50.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Extermination of the Suffering Russian Bear (苦露熊退治 Kurokuma Taiji)

text.headline: Extermination of the Suffering Russian Bear (苦露熊退治 Kurokuma Taiji)
text.text:
This print is one of eight-six prints from the third part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs which presented comic parodies of the Russian enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In this print we see Japanese soldiers chipping away at the ice surrounding the Russian Bear who has retreated north to the Arctic Ocean in order to "finish him off."

media.caption: Niwa - April (庭・4月)

text.headline: Niwa - April (庭・4月)
text.text: While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa.  Also see Niwa (Sunshine), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (Winter Scenery) and Niwa (80-K) in this collection.

media.caption: Good by[e] Winter (冬への別れ)

text.headline: Good by[e] Winter (冬への別れ)
text.text: The last bit of snow can be seen in the center of a green field with, possibly, a dark rock being heated by the sun. Deep embossing highlights this print.

media.caption: Scene at a Zen Temple (禅寺風景 Zenji fūkei)

text.headline: Scene at a Zen Temple (禅寺風景 Zenji fūkei)
text.text:
Picturing a group of monks, including two visiting monks carrying backpacks, in the courtyard of a Zen temple.
The series Life of Kyoto consists of six chuban-sized prints depicting activities and places in and around Kyoto. The series was published by an unknown publisher identified as 宮脇美風扇版 in the rectangular cartouche in the lower right margin of each print.

media.caption: Stone Lantern in Snow (雪見燈籠 yukimidōrō)

text.headline: Stone Lantern in Snow (雪見燈籠 yukimidōrō)
text.text: An untitled small print of a stone lantern covered in snow.  Unmistakably Kawanishi Hide in the lack of outlines, use of color and the soft edges of his forms, achieved with the use of a chisel, rather than carving knife, on the woodblock.

media.caption: Rice Planting (田植えTaue)

text.headline: Rice Planting (田植えTaue)
text.text: Two women planting rice in a light rain during early summer.

media.caption: The Plunder Bird (分鳥 Bundori)

text.headline: The Plunder Bird (分鳥 Bundori)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
In this print we see the "plunder bird" snatching a Chinese ship as a spoil of war.

media.caption: Sadamisaki (佐田岬)

text.headline: Sadamisaki (佐田岬)
text.text: A view of the tip of the narrow Sadamisaki Peninsula on Japan's Inland Sea which while 32 km long is never more than a few km wide. Its lighthouse, built in 1918, is one of Japan's "Fifty Famous Lighthouses" and commands one of the most spectacular views of all Japanese lighthouses. This print is one of ten from the series Here and There in Shikoku.

media.caption: Mihonoseki (美保関)

text.headline: Mihonoseki (美保関)
text.text:
A view of Mihonoseki harbor which opens up into Miho Bay and the Sea of Japan. This print is one of ten to twelve prints that Asano created from 1964 to 1965 of various scenic views in the San'in Region, encompassing the modern-day prefectures of Shimane, Tottori and the northern area of Yamaguchi. The northern areas of Hyōgo and Kyōto prefectures are sometimes included in the region as well.
Mihonoseki is located in the area at the eastern edge of the Shimane-hanto Peninsula in northeastern Shimane. While a charming fishing village today, Mihonoseki was an important trading point during the Edo period when iron, cotton and rice were shipped between Japan and the Korean peninsula.

media.caption: Tottorisakyū (鳥取砂丘)

text.headline: Tottorisakyū (鳥取砂丘)
text.text:
A view of the sand dunes at Tattori on the Sea of Japan. This print is one of ten to twelve prints that Asano created from 1964 to 1965 of various scenic views in the San'in Region, encompassing the modern-day prefectures of Shimane, Tottori and the northern area of Yamaguchi. The northern areas of Hyōgo and Kyōto prefectures are sometimes included in the region as well.
The Tottori Sand Dunes (鳥取砂丘 Tottori sakyū) are unique sand dunes located near Tottori City in Tottori Prefecture, Honshū, Japan. They are the only large dune system (over 30 km²) in Japan. The dunes were created by sediment deposits carried from the Chūgoku Mountains by the Sendai River into the Sea of Japan. Sea currents and wind help bring the sand from the bottom up onto the shore, where the wind constantly rearranges their shape. The dunes have existed for over 100,000 years, but the area of the dunes has been steadily decreasing due to a government reforestation program following World War II. Additionally, concrete barriers erected to protect the coast (the part of Sanin Kaigan National Park) from tsunamis have disrupted the currents responsible for bringing the sand to shore. In recent years authorities have adopted measures to stop the shrinkage of the dunes, partly because they attract a significant amount of tourism to the area.

media.caption: Tokugawa Yoshinobu (i徳川慶喜)

text.headline: Tokugawa Yoshinobu (i徳川慶喜)
text.text:
Print number 44 (四十四 ), and one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, portraying the last shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu (1837-1913), who surrendered power to the Imperial Court, ushering in the Meiji Restoration. This particular print in the series must have engendered strong feelings in Kiyochika, as he had served Yoshinobu for several years as a young man.
In this print, Yoshinobu is surrounded by the old (possibly a scene from The Tale of Genji to his left) and the new (a clock to his right) and books, pointing to his learning and intelligence. Yoshinobu seems to be glancing towards the window, outside of which falling leaves suggest the end of Tokugawa power.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Fujiwara no Arihira (藤原在衡)

text.headline: Fujiwara no Arihira (藤原在衡)
text.text:
Print number 9 (九), and one of 4 contributed by Yoshitoshi to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Minister of the State Fujiwara no Arihira (891-970) and his assistant, in service to Emperor Murakami 村上天皇 (926-967), making their way through a terrible rainstorm to the palace. Fujiwara was famous for never missing a day of work.

media.caption: Emperor Takakura's Palace Servants (高倉帝仕丁)

text.headline: Emperor Takakura's Palace Servants (高倉帝仕丁)
text.text:
Print number 10 (十), and one of 13 designs contributed by Inoue to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing three palace servants of the young Takakura Tennō (高倉天皇 , 1161-1181 CE) warming sake over downed maple branches from the Emperor’s special garden, “The Hill of Autumn Tints.” When a high-ranking official discovered what the servants had done, he berated them saying, “how could you dare to treat the garden that the Emperor is so fond of in such a way? You deserve to be imprisoned or banished at least, and I too may very likely incur the Imperial displeasure.” When the Emperor found out what his servants did he was not angry and only laughed, quoting the Chinese poem by Haku-raku-ten (Po-chu-i) about warming wine in the woods by burning maple-leaves. “I wonder” he said, “who can have taught it to them. Really they are quite esthetes.”

media.caption: Table or Contents or Index (目録 mokuroku) for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition

text.headline: Table or Contents or Index (目録 mokuroku) for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition
text.text:
On two scrolls, this Table of Contents (mokuroku) from the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition provides the names of the artists who contributed prints to the series, the name and address of the series' publisher and a list of all fifty prints that comprised the series as it was originally issued. One additional artist Yōshū Chikanobu (1838-1912), whose name does not appear on the Table of Contents sheet (for unknown reasons), was commissioned to create two prints and the final number of prints issued was fifty-eight rather than fifty, including three prints not listed in the Table of Contents (the two Chikanobu designs and one design by Inoue Tankei) and five modified designs of originally issued prints.
The top scroll, reading from right to left, informs us of the name of the series, Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition 教導立志基; that fifty prints make up the complete series 五十番揃; the names of the six artists contributing prints: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親, Hachisuka (Utagawa) Kuniaki II 蜂須賀国明, Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周, Inoue Tankei (Yasuji) 井上探景, Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方, Taiso (Tsukioka) Yoshitoshi 大蘇芳年 and the name of the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi 松木平吉 and, finally, the publisher's address 東京日本橋区両国吉川町二番地.
The bottom scroll is the table of contents listing the prints in the series as originally issued.

media.caption: A Gathering of Three Young Magicians (竒術揃三人童子 Kijutsu soroi sannin dōji)

text.headline: A Gathering of Three Young Magicians (竒術揃三人童子 Kijutsu soroi sannin dōji)
text.text: The three most famous actors of their time (from right to left), Ichikawa Danjūrō IX , Onoe Kikugorō V and Ichikawa Sadanji play the roles of the three young magicians Unryūkurō 雲龍九郎 (Cloud Dragon - note Danjūrō's cloud patterned garb); Tora Ōmaru 虎王丸 (Tiger Ōmaru) and Ryūō Tarō 竜王太郎 (Dragon King). It is unclear whether these actors ever appeared together in these roles as the print suggests or whether this is simply a compilation requested by the publishers.

media.caption: Record of What Was Seen and Heard on a Star-filled Moonlit Night (星月夜見聞実記 Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki)

text.headline: Record of What Was Seen and Heard on a Star-filled Moonlit Night (星月夜見聞実記 Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki)
text.text: While only the actor's names and roles are shown on this print, the Tokyo Metropolitan Library identifies the play as Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki (Record of What Was Seen and Heard on a Star-filled Moonlit Night), popularly known as Egara Mondō written by  Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893). The particular performance of the play featured in this print occurred on June 15, 1880 at the Shintomi-za (新富) and was the second play on the program (二番目) which included Mokuami's 5-act play Shimoyo no Kane Jūji no Tsujiura 霜夜鐘十字辻筮 (Crossroads at Ten Bells on a Frosty Night.) Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki is included in Ichikawa Danjūrō IX's Shin Kabuki Jūhachiban (New 18 Kabuki Plays), a list of actually 32 plays favored by the actor.

media.caption: Arashiyama in Spring (untitled)

text.headline: Arashiyama in Spring (untitled)
text.text: One of Tokuriki's half-dozen or so renderings of Togetsukyo Bridge (lit. "Moon Crossing Bridge") with Mt. Arashi (Arashiyama) in the background. This print's scene is set in the spring and Tokuriki has dotted the hillsides with cherry trees.

media.caption: Roadside Fortune Teller (大道占師 daidō uranaishi)

text.headline: Roadside Fortune Teller (大道占師 daidō uranaishi)
text.text:
A fortune teller advises a couple in an evening divining session in this tenth print from series two of Occupations of the Shōwa Era in Pictures. This is a second edition (post-war) print published by Kyoto Hanga-in. For a first (Pacific War) first IHL.1057.
The English language commentary originally accompanying this second edition print reads, "A Fortune-teller. It is very common to see one or two fortune-tellers in the precincts of a Shinto shrine or a Buddhist temple. Many people who are not well educated are apt to be enthralled by such superstition, and they consult the fortune-teller when their wish to know in regard to change of residence, marriage, loan of money, change of job, trip and in fact nearly all the matters of their daily lives. Most of the fortune-tellers open their road-side shops in the evening. Judging by his clothing, the husband seems to be a merchant, and he may have asked the fortune-teller to divine what will become of his business. The fortune-teller is trying to find the means by his divining rods. Depicted by Sanzo Wada. Printed by KYOTO-HANGA-IN"
For the original commentary accompanying the first edition print see IHL.1057.

Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Oharame's House (大原女の家 Oharame no uchi)

text.headline: Oharame's House (大原女の家 Oharame no uchi)
text.text: A scene in a typical farm house in Ohara on the outskirts of Kyoto. The women who lived in the village, known as Oharame (woman of Ohara), sold their farm products in Kyoto, travelling there by foot and cart. Wada captures a mother holding her baby and the baby's grandmother wearing the distinctive clothing of Oharame consisting of, most prominently, an indigo blue kimono (sometimes patterned, sometimes not) with a white kerchief.

media.caption: Lemon-Blue, No. 367

text.headline: Lemon-Blue, No. 367
text.text: The artist's signature lemons contained within a blue square. As with many of Funasaka's prints the use of high-gloss inks makes it radiant, something that is lost in an electronic reproduction.

media.caption: Lemon, 347

text.headline: Lemon, 347
text.text: The artist's signature lemons contained within a red rectangle which seems to recede within its black three-sided surround. A feather-like object softens the picture.

media.caption: Bon Dori (盆踊り)

text.headline: Bon Dori (盆踊り)
text.text:
Senpan's rendition of the Buddhist custom of Bon Odori (bon dance) during which one's deceased relatives are celebrated. A high wooden scaffold (yagura) is assembled especially for the festival and it is the center for the dance as well as serving as the bandstand for musicians and singers.
Writing in his seminal book Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn published in the year this print was issued, Statler comments on the artist,"People are his main interest, the ordinary people of Japan, and although he sometimes shows them at work, he likes best to catch them when they are enjoying themselves." He characterizes Bon Dori as one of his best prints. - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn, Oliver Statler, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1956, p. 47.

media.caption: Autumn Scenery at Takao (高雄秋景 Takao shūkei)

text.headline: Autumn Scenery at Takao (高雄秋景 Takao shūkei)
text.text:
One of six prints in the series Famous Places of Kyoto by the artist Nomura Yoshimitsu (1870-1958). While not the original edition of this print, it was certainly created during the artist's lifetime and likely in the late 1930s, after the completion of the second seminal exhibition of modern Japanese prints in 1936 at the Toledo Museum of Art where the original edition of the print was exhibited.
The original edition of the print was issued in a limited edition of two hundred prints and carried the Sankōkai 三光會 gourd-shaped seal under the artist's name as opposed to the 佐藤版 Satō Shō han gourd-shaped seal used on this collection's print.

media.caption: Moon at Hirosawa (広沢之月 Hirosawa no tsuki)

text.headline: Moon at Hirosawa (広沢之月 Hirosawa no tsuki)
text.text:
One of six prints in the series Famous Places of Kyoto by the artist Nomura Yoshimitsu (1870-1958). While not the original edition of this print, it was certainly created during the artist's lifetime and likely in the late 1930s, after the completion of the second seminal exhibition of modern Japanese prints in 1936 at the Toledo Museum of Art where the original edition of the print was exhibited.
The original edition of the print was issued in a limited edition of two hundred prints and carried the Sankōkai rectangular-shaped seal under the artist's name as opposed to the 佐藤版 Satō shō han square-shaped seal used on this collection's print.

media.caption: Oki Province: Takuhiyama Takibi no Yashiro (隠岐国・焚火山 焚火ノ社)

text.headline: Oki Province: Takuhiyama Takibi no Yashiro (隠岐国・焚火山 焚火ノ社)
text.text:
Print number 48 四十八 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints. The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
This print pictures the Sea of Japan off the coast of Nishinoshima Island, one of four islands making up the Oki Islands in current day Shimane Province. Takuhiyama, a 452 meter high mountain, on the island of Nishinoshima, is the highest point in the Islands and the Torch Shrine (Takibi no Yashiro), was a well-known sacred place among fishermen and sailors, who, when passing by the island would devote their prayers to the shrine's kami (deities.) The man on the boat in the print is shaking a gohei, a kind of ritual wand that along with offerings of cloth were presented to the kami by attaching them to a staff.

media.caption: Sea, Evening Calm

text.headline: Sea, Evening Calm
text.text:
An earlier print from the artist just prior to her starting her signature use of gold foil and embossing in prints. There is a range of subtle color in this print that can really only be appreciated by examining the actual print.
About this print, the artist writes:
The Ocean, with its limitless breadth and scope
Embraces all deep in its heart;
The anger, too, of the bitter and tempestuous night.
Peace descends silently in the distant horizon.
I love the Ocean
- Reika Iwami
This collection's print appeared in the Portland Art Museum for the exhibition "Joryū Hanga Kyōkai, 1956–1965 Japan’s Women Printmakers," which ran from September 24, 2020 until June 13, 2021.

media.caption: Maiko (舞子)

text.headline: Maiko (舞子)
text.text:
Wada gives us a glimpse of the famous Kyoto maiko watching and participating in a dance performance. This print is number nine in the twenty-four print post-WWII series "Occupations of Shōwa Era in Pictures, Continued" (3rd series), published from November 1954 through September 1956 by the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi, owner of Kyōto Hangain.
The English language commentary originally accompanying the print reads, in part, "'Maiko' or 'Geisha-to-be' in Gion, Kyoto, are said to be quite different from those [called Oshaku] in Tokyo and Osaka in their manners and customs. Most of Gion 'Maiko' are brought up since childhood at this Gion amusement district and their mothers also live and work in the same district. Before the war, even apprentice Maiko who entered the profession at the age of eleven or twelve had to work at the entertaining house. But now after the war, new labour regulations prohibit them to work until they reach the age of 15 or 16. [Which is still incredibly young.] They are trained strictly in such various accomplishments, as Japanese dance, signing, Shamisen musical instrument. They look innocent in appearance but they must be quite grown-up women in mind already."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Asakusa (浅草)

text.headline: Asakusa (浅草)
text.text:
In this print Ōuchi appropriates Utagawa Hiroshige's 1856 print Kinryusan Temple at Asakusa from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, to create this large format etching.

In speaking about Ōuchi's appropriation of images from famous ukiyo-e artists, the Tolmans wrote in 1982: "Ōuchi uses them to evoke the past, but it is his originality that makes them contemporary. First of all, they are not photographs but are completely redrawn by the artist, as he sees them. Secondly, he is not using a woodblock, but portrays them through the etching process in warm, soft colors - rusts, browns, gold - that give them an added poignancy." - Source: People Who Make Japanese Prints, A Personal Glimpse, Mary S. and Norman H. Tolman, Sobunsha, 1982, p. 116-117.

While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

media.caption: Between Vertical and Horizon-Descended Triangle (A)

text.headline: Between Vertical and Horizon-Descended Triangle (A)
text.text: "The something 'Between Vertical and Horizontal' is what emerges from the interaction of the forces involved. As an artist I create situations to discover my relationship to substances. The meaning of 'descended triangle' is the idea of penetrating beneath the surface, be it in a vertical or horizontal condition." - the artist Ida Shōichi

media.caption: Print 26 Very Popular Story

text.headline: Print 26 Very Popular Story
text.text: Print 26 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk.

media.caption: Windows

text.headline: Windows
text.text: An early geometric abstraction from the artist with wonderful overlays of subtle color.

media.caption: Spring

text.headline: Spring
text.text: This collection contains two almost identical prints by the artist using the same woodblocks, with minor modifications, this print titled Spring (IHL.1091), and an untitled version of the print (IHL.1985). In these prints Chizuko presents two tilting city landscapes. As compared with this print, in the untitled print Chizuko has shifted the position of the chain of heart-shaped objects to the right and darkened the background. Additional marks, most noticeable in the lower left of the image have also been made. Known for her later prints featuring myriads of butterflies, there may be one flitting about in the upper left quadrant of both these prints.

media.caption: Conversation of the Winds (風の会話 Kaze no kaiwa)

text.headline: Conversation of the Winds (風の会話 Kaze no kaiwa)
text.text:
Swirling winds come together with a face-like appearance in this abstract print.
The work of Ansei Uchima reflects a complex fusion of Western and Eastern artistic traditions. Born in California, Uchima returned to Japan at age nineteen, and after World War II studied painting and traditional Japanese printmaking. His first prints, beginning in 1957, drew from nature and the world around him. After he returned to the United States in 1959, his floating, calligraphic compositions, characteristic of sōsaku hanga, suggested the growing influence of Abstract Expressionism.

media.caption: Kasumigaseki (霞ヶ関)

text.headline: Kasumigaseki (霞ヶ関)
text.text:
The Kasumigaseki (gate of mist) district in Tokyo is the area where the Meiji government chose to build its government. In the early 1940s, when this print was created, it would have been a bustling, densely packed area, so this sparsely populated image, showing only a single building complex and two cars in the background, is a bit of a surprise even during a heavy evening snow.
This collection's print is a publisher's proof print that contains notes as to changes to be incorporated on the released print.

media.caption: Nihonbashi (日本橋)

text.headline: Nihonbashi (日本橋)
text.text:
All is quiet in a usually bustling part of Tokyo around Nihonbashi as an evening snow falls.
Nihonbashi Bridge, originally built in 1603, was the point from where all distances were marked along the Tōkaidō Road connecting Edo (now Tokyo) to the old capital of Kyoto. The current stone structure, which was rebuilt in grand Western style during the Meiji era (1868-1912), dates back to 1911. It’s now designated a national important cultural property.
Long obscured by the Metropolitan Expressway, by 2041 Nihonbashi will no longer be in the expressway's shadow when a new tunnel replaces this portion of the expressway.

media.caption: Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Nakamura Sōjūrō, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, Onoe Kikugorō V and Bandō Shiuka in the play Kumo ni magō Ueno no hatsuhana. (岩井半四郎 (八代目)、中村宗十郎、市川団十郎 (九代目)、尾上菊五郎 (五代目)、坂東志う調・天衣粉上野初花)

text.headline: Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Nakamura Sōjūrō, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, Onoe Kikugorō V and Bandō Shiuka in the play Kumo ni magō Ueno no hatsuhana. (岩井半四郎 (八代目)、中村宗十郎、市川団十郎 (九代目)、尾上菊五郎 (五代目)、坂東志う調・天衣粉上野初花)
text.text:
From right to left, the actors Iwai Hanshirō VIII 岩井半四郎 in the role of the courtesan Michitose 女房おま; Nakamura Sōjūrō 中村宗十郎 in the role of Jōshūya Sadajirō 上州屋定次郎; Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 in the role of the bogus priest Kōchiyama Sōshun 河内山宗俊; Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 as Kataoka Naojirō 片岡直次郎, nicknamed Naozamurai - the "Faithful Samurai"; and Bandō Shiuka 坂東志う調 as Masume Ofuji (reading unconfirmed) 娘おふぢ in the play Kumo ni magō Ueno no hatsuhana 天衣粉上野初花, performed at the Shintomi-za 新富 theater, Tokyo, on March 31, 1881 (Meiji 14).
"Kumo ni magō ueno no hatsuhana" is a sewamono (a play set in contemporary times) depicting the lives of six bad men. Kawatake Mokuami wrote this work while looking back with nostalgia on the Edo emotional mood which he felt was being lost after the Meiji period started.
This play became popular from its premier performance in which Ichikawa Danjūrō 9th played Kōchiyama and Onoe Kikugorō 5th played Naojirō.
Chikashige has used the Toshidama seal, denoting members of the Utagawa School, as the pattern on the red backdrop of the center sheet.

media.caption: Blue and White Space (with holes), No. 319

text.headline: Blue and White Space (with holes), No. 319
text.text: This print has a companion print without the punched holes, IHL.1097. It is possible that both prints are from the same edition of sixty prints with the artist's signature holes being added to some prints in the edition and not to others.

media.caption: Blue and White Space (without holes)

text.headline: Blue and White Space (without holes)
text.text: This print has a companion print with punched holes, IHL.1096. It is possible that both prints are from the same edition of sixty prints with the artist's signature holes being added to some prints in the edition and not to others.

media.caption: Niwa - Summer house (庭・夏の家)

text.headline: Niwa - Summer house (庭・夏の家)
text.text:
While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa. Also see Niwa (Sunshine), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (Winter Scenery), Niwa (80-K) and Niwa (April) in this collection.
Note that this collection's print from the numbered edition differs from the artist's proof (A.P.) pictured in the artist's catalogue raisonné. For the editioned print, as in this collection, Takahashi did not carry the embossing forward and simplified the bottom oblong element.

media.caption: Seashore at Midday (昼の浜)

text.headline: Seashore at Midday (昼の浜)
text.text: One of many prints picturing small boats along the shore that the artist created. For two other similar prints by the artist see IHL.1476 and IHL.1198.

media.caption: Illustration of Noble’s Imperial Ceremony (高位御大禮之図 Kōi godairei no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of Noble’s Imperial Ceremony (高位御大禮之図 Kōi godairei no zu)
text.text: Published on March 27, 1900, six weeks before the wedding ceremony of twenty-one year old Crown Prince Yoshihito to sixteen year old Kujō Sadako, daughter of Duke Michitaka Kujō, head of Kujō branch of the Fujiwara clan, this triptych portrays an unnamed ceremony being conducted at the Imperial Palace with the crown prince, his bride to be, the emperor and empress and military officials in attendance. Three court ladies are seated before the crown prince.

media.caption: Hiroshima Imperial Headquarters 廣島大本營 Hiroshima daihon'ei)

text.headline: Hiroshima Imperial Headquarters 廣島大本營 Hiroshima daihon'ei)
text.text:
Print number forty-seven (四十七, as printed in right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting an outside wall of Hiroshima Castle in the foreground with the Imperial Headquarters (daihon'ei) in the mid-ground and the castle keep in the background. Hiroshima Castle originally built in 1590 was destroyed in the atomic bombing. The keep was rebuilt in 1958.

SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.

In his commentary on the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

media.caption: Udo Shrine (鵜戸神宮 Udo jingū)

text.headline: Udo Shrine (鵜戸神宮 Udo jingū)
text.text:
Print number seven (七, as printed in right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting the Shinto shrine Udo jingū built in a cave among the cliffs of the Nichinan Coast in Miyazaki prefecture. It is the mythical birthplace of Emperor Jimmu's father and where the spirits of Jimmu and his father are enshrined.

media.caption: Kwansei Gakuin University (関西学院大学)

text.headline: Kwansei Gakuin University (関西学院大学)
text.text: View of Kwansei Gakuin University's Nishinomiya Uegahara Campus with the Chapel in the foreground right and Clock Tower in the background. The artist had a lifelong relationship with Kwansei Gakuin University with which he worked collaboratively to design a large number of promotional items.

media.caption: Illustration of the Ceremony for the Promulgation of the Constitution of Great Japan (大日本憲法発布式之圖 Dai Nippon kenpōhappushiki no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Ceremony for the Promulgation of the Constitution of Great Japan (大日本憲法発布式之圖 Dai Nippon kenpōhappushiki no zu)
text.text:
One of many prints depicting Emperor Meiji’s February 11, 1889 public pronouncement, following a private ceremony in the Palace Sanctuary, of Japan’s first constitution, which came into effect on November 29, 1890.
The artist did not attend the ceremony, which was limited to invited dignitaries, foreign and domestic, and eighteen members of the press. He created this print from the published accounts, taking a requisite amount of artistic license. While the general public were not allowed to attend the public pronouncement of the constitution, for a few sen you could choose from over a dozen different prints (all looking very similar) that made you an intimate part of these historic events.

media.caption: The Whole Nation Living in Perfect Contentment (傳聞萬民鼓腹 denbun banmin kofuku)

text.headline: The Whole Nation Living in Perfect Contentment (傳聞萬民鼓腹 denbun banmin kofuku)
text.text:
This scene depicts Empress Shōken, the Empress Dowager and their court ladies assembling pledgets (large bandages) for the Imperial troops fighting rebel samurai during the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. While this print was issued in June of 1877 when the rebels were on the run and close to defeat, the scene it depicts is set towards the end of February when the rebels were laying siege to Kumamoto Castle and its government defenders were experiencing heavy casualties. The sewing of the pledgets was one of the many charitable tasks that the Empress engaged in and was noted in an 1893 book on the historical role of Japanese women prepared for the World's Columbian Exposition, as follows: "In all these [women led educational and charitable institutions] Her Imperial Majesty, our wise and most gracious Empress, takes the lead. There has not been a notable stand taken by women that has been for the public benefit but that the Empress in the kindness of her heart has not either directly or indirectly given it her patronage.
"When the Kagoshima war broke out in 1877, she sent an immense quantity of lint pledgets of her own preparation for the use of wounded soldiers." - Source: Japan Women [The Japanese Woman's Commission for the World's Columbian Exposition], multiple unnamed Japanese women authors, A.C. McClurg & Co., 1893, p 150.

media.caption: Mount Daisen, North Wall (伯耆大山北壁 Hōki Daisen hokuheki)

text.headline: Mount Daisen, North Wall (伯耆大山北壁 Hōki Daisen hokuheki)
text.text: A depiction of the north wall of Mount Daisen, also called Hōki Daisen.

media.caption: Siblings compete in sacrificing their lives to avert danger, story 9, page 8 ([九] 兄弟死を争ふて危難を免る [八丁])

text.headline: Siblings compete in sacrificing their lives to avert danger, story 9, page 8 ([九] 兄弟死を争ふて危難を免る [八丁])
text.text:
In this print, two brothers are confronted by the robbers. Facing certain death, each brother begged the robbers to kill him and spear the other. The robbers felt compassion for their brotherly love and let them go unharmed. This print, one of ninety-two full-color supplemental prints to the earlier issued six volume textbook titled Brocade Pictures of Moral Education illustrates tory number 9 in volume 1.
In October 1883 a set of ninety-two full-color oban-size prints designed by students of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi were published by Tsuji Keiji and his publishing house Fukyūsha as supplements, or accompaniments, to the six volume set of textbooks titled ""Nishiki-e shūshindan"" 錦絵修身談 (Brocade Prints for Moral Education), published earlier by Tsuji and illustrated by Yoshitoshi. These supplemental prints illustrated the ninety-one short stories contained in the six volumes. A number of the full-color prints issued were based upon Yoshitoshi's black and white illustrations in the texts. Each of the full-color prints carries the textbook's title 錦絵修身談 and volume number across its top and the name of the story and its location in the textbook in a vertical red cartouche.

text.text:

media.caption: Crater (噴火口 Funkakō)

text.headline: Crater (噴火口 Funkakō)
text.text: Sakamoto gives us a view into the active crater of Mt. Aso, the largest active volcano in in Aso Kujū National Park in Kumamoto Prefecture, on the island of Kyūshū. This print is one of five in the series Five Views of Aso, which was first published in a limited edition of 300 in 1950 by Kuga Ichio 久我五千男 (1922-1984) of Sōjinsha, with carving and printing at Katō Hanga Kenkyūsho under the supervision of Katō Junji. The envelope in which the five prints were packaged had a small print picturing two horses grazing affixed to it (see IHL.2379) and the set of prints also contained a cover page which used the same image of two horses grazing (see IHL.2310.)

media.caption: Autumn at Lake Towada (十和田湖の秋) Towadako no aki)

text.headline: Autumn at Lake Towada (十和田湖の秋) Towadako no aki)
text.text:
A bold color statement by Yasui, considered one of Japan’s most respected Western-style (yōga) painters from the1930s through his death in 1955, demonstrating his belief that prints were an ideal vehicle for "expressing things by lines and color." - Source: Japanese Wood-block Prints, Shizuya Fujikake, Japan Travel Bureau, 1938 revised 1949, p. 137.
Yasui designed at least sixteen woodblock prints that he then had carved and printed, under his supervision, by others.

media.caption: Backlit Fuji (逆光富士)

text.headline: Backlit Fuji (逆光富士)
text.text: Not quite a "red Fuji," Miyashita gives us a view of Fuji at dusk, with the mountain taking on a deep purple hue. One of Miyashita's post-1980s prints, displaying a move back towards realism from the abstraction of his works created in the 1970s. This print is very similar to the artist's 2002 print Daybreak at Mt. Fuji featured in The Library of Congress online exhibition On the Cutting Edge, Contemporary Japanese Prints from the 50th College Women's Association of Japan Print Show. (See https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/cwaj/online/gallery3.html [accessed 8-17-23])

media.caption: Dockyard (造船所)

text.headline: Dockyard (造船所)
text.text: A ship being loaded with freight at a dockyard. One of Miyashita's post-1980s prints  displaying a move back towards realism from the abstraction of his works created in the 1970s.

media.caption: The Heroine Koharu in The Love Suicides of Amijima (心中天の網島の小春 Shinjū ten no amijima no Koharu)

text.headline: The Heroine Koharu in The Love Suicides of Amijima (心中天の網島の小春 Shinjū ten no amijima no Koharu)
text.text:
Usually considered Chikamatsu's masterpiece, The Love Suicides at Amijima was based on a real incident, a pair of lovers who killed themselves on the Amijima Diacho Temple grounds in Osaka on November 13, 1720. The puppet play opened January 3, 1721, not quite two months later. In Amijima, Chikamatsu goes well beyond simply staging a current event. The play explores the intricacies of a love triangle by treating the wife, Osan, as a major character. The entangling web of interactions between the wife and the courtesan, Koharu, complicates the plot and adds new depths to a familiar story (which ends in the double suicide of Koharu and her lover, Jihei.) Plays depicting love suicides became prohibited less than two years after the play's premier.
This print bears the printer and carver names impressed on the bottom margin. For a copy of the print without the printer and carver names see IHL.0047.

One of 18 prints published from 1922 to c. 1925 as part of the celebration of the two-hundredth anniversary of the death of Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1623-1724), perhaps the greatest dramatist in the history of the Japanese theater. Each design illustrates a scene or character from one of Chikamatsu’s famous works which were compiled into 16 volumes by Chikamatsu researcher Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950). The prints were inserted into the volume containing the story they illustrated and were also separately sold.

media.caption: Work 69.5 (作品 69.5 sakuhin 69.5)

text.headline: Work 69.5 (作品 69.5 sakuhin 69.5)
text.text: Approximately three feet high, this print by the artist that epitomizes his continuing series of prints carrying the title Work ( 作品 sakuhin) begun in the early 1960s. This series began with some reference to identifiable objects but quickly became more abstract and dynamic with use of intense primary colors. Starting around 1967 Kusaka introduced the circle form which subsequently morphed into an egg shape. This egg shape counterbalanced his straight lines and angular corners.

media.caption: Temporary Barracks at Aioichō Honjo ( 臨時 バラック 本所相生町 Rinji barakku Aioichō Honjo)

text.headline: Temporary Barracks at Aioichō Honjo ( 臨時 バラック 本所相生町 Rinji barakku Aioichō Honjo)
text.text:
One of six prints contributed by the Nihonga artist Senrin to the 1924 thirty-six print series Collection of Woodblock Prints of the Taishō Earthquake issued by the little-known publisher Hoshino Seki of Gahōsha who offered the prints as "a small gesture of social service."
"The Tokyo district of Honjo was particularly hard-hit by the firestorm that erupted after the earthquake. Senrin records that he sketched this scene three days after the disaster, when he found survivors taking shelter in scraps recovered after the ashes cooled. This displaced couple has written their name—the Yoshimuras—and address on their doorway, in pale white chalk. In the foreground, on a wooden plank, is scrawled another message: 'Searching for Yoshimura Mitsu, age 70.'" [The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 292.]
In 1924, the Japanese publisher Hoshino Seki [of the publishing house Gahōsha] issued a set of thirty-six prints depicting scenes from the aftermath of the September 1, 1923 great Tokyo earthquake. He commissioned six artists to each produce six designs based on eyewitness sketches and accounts, which the master carver Nagashima Kiichi and printer Tamura Tetsunosuke then translated into color woodblock prints for the portfolio.

media.caption: Ariadne (アリアドネ)

text.headline: Ariadne (アリアドネ)
text.text:
One of 42 prints in the artist's series Greek Mythology. Hagiwara pictures a sleeping Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, the King of Crete, suspended by a single vine. She is in her classic sleep pose of one arm raised over her head with a look or exhaustion and despair, as she has been abandoned by her lover Theseus on the island of Naxos.
The entire series was issued as a complete portfolio bound in a black woven material, imprinted in silver. Hagiwara employed both traditional Japanese woodblock technique as well as intaglio on these prints.

media.caption: Lyric: Only the Truth Shines Over (真実ひとり輝きめぐる  抒情)

text.headline: Lyric: Only the Truth Shines Over (真実ひとり輝きめぐる  抒情)
text.text:
A posthumous printing, printed by Yoneda Minoru, likely under the auspices of the artist's family. The print originally appeared in issue VI of the small print and poetry magazine Tsukuhae (Moonglow), created by Onchi Koshiro (1891-1955), Shizuo Fujimori (1891-1943) and Tanaka Kyokichi (1892-1915).
"Throughout his working life, Onchi produced many works entitled 'Lyric'. In these works he explored the characteristics of woodcut searching for a union of poetry and visual art." - Source: Art Gallery of New South Wales http://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/works/82.2000/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Takao Autumn Scenery (高雄秋色)

text.headline: Takao Autumn Scenery (高雄秋色)

media.caption: Shimabara District After the Rain (しまばらくるわ雨後 Shimabara kuruwa ugo)

text.headline: Shimabara District After the Rain (しまばらくるわ雨後 Shimabara kuruwa ugo)
text.text:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), who used the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞 starting in 1953, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.
This print depicts the main gate entrance to Shimabara, Kyoto's former red-light district, after a night rain. When this print was made Shimabara was still a licensed entertainment area. Japanese art historian Lynn Katsumoto notes: "The sign on the stand to left says 'tako' - the 'yaki' is left off, but I think that's what most people assume. Tako yaki are little bready balls with bits of octopus inside, popular street fare." A crude drawing of an octopus appears to the right on the stand's curtain. For another impression of this print see IHL.2190.

media.caption: Women Weavers (織女 shokujo)

text.headline: Women Weavers (織女 shokujo)
text.text:

The portfolio was likely first issued in the mid-1950s and the designs are replications of pre-WWII designs from the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. As the prints are a smaller format than the original releases, new blocks would have been used.
This print pictures two women weaving at home. To see the earlier and larger ōban size print, see IHL.1002.

media.caption: Semimaru 蝉丸

text.headline: Semimaru 蝉丸
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Semimaru by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which "the shite makes his entrance with his attendants and proceeds down the bridge toward the stage proper. The interior of the theater and the audience is also visible. This print is noteworthy because of the portrayal of slightly anachronistic elements: the stage attendants and audience members are depicted with antiquated Edo-period hairstyles and clothing." (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 84.)
Play synopsis ( P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.154-155.) - On the order of the Emperor Daigo, a Court official takes Prince Semimaru, who has been blind since he was a child, to Ōsaka-yama and leaves him there with only his lute to comfort him. The Prince accepts his lot with resignation, feeling that his blindness is the result of some failure of his in a previous existence, and that the present apparent cruelty of his father is only due to a desire to help him gain a happier fate in a future life. Meanwhile, his sister Princess Sakagami has gone out of her mind and is now a wild-haired figure, wandering aimlessly from place to place. She comes one day to Ōsaka-yama and, attracted by the sound of Semimaru's lute, finds her brother again. For a while they forget their loneliness as they talk together and comfort each other, but then the Princess leaves him and continues her sad wanderings.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Yorimasa 頼政

text.headline: Yorimasa 頼政
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Yorimasa by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443). The artist has set the warrior Yorimasa within a fan, referencing Yorimasa's last act of laying down his fan before committing suicide.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 215-216.) - A travelling priest stops at Uji and is admiring the view there when an old man approaches and, after telling him about various historical spots in the neighborhood, leads him to the Byōdō-in. There he shows him the patch of turf cut in the shape of a fan to commemorate the warrior Yorimasa who laid his fan down and killed himself there after being defeated in battle. Revealing that he is the spirit of the warrior, he then disappears. After the priest has prayed for the repose of his soul, Yorimasa comes to him in his true form and tells him about the battle. He asks the priest to continue to pray for him and again fades from sight.

media.caption: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)

text.headline: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Kumasaka by the playwright Zenchiku Ujinobu (1405-1468) in which the outlaw lay priest Kumasaka appears with a scarf tied around his head and a long pike over his shoulder to tell of his killing by the robber Ushikawa.

PLAY SYNOPSIS (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 95-96.) - A travelling priest stops at Akasaka in Mino Province and meets another priest who, after talking with him, gives him lodging for the night. This second priest is in reality the ghost of Kumasaka no Chôhan, a robber, and in the dream of the real priest that night the spirit appears and describes how he was killed by the young Ushikawa.

media.caption: Tamakazura 玉葛 (The Jeweled Chaplet)

text.headline: Tamakazura 玉葛 (The Jeweled Chaplet)
text.text:
In an interesting composition, Kōgyo has overlaid Tamakazura's dance over a painting of an itinerant priest.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 183.) - A priest on his way to pray at the Hade-dera comes to the Hatsuse-gawa and there meets a woman who lands from a small boat. She leads him up to two cryptomeria trees and tells him that this was where Tamakazura met the maid of her mother Yūgao when she fled from Kyūshū after refusing the attentions of a powerful warrior there. She is the spirit of Tamakazura, she adds, and then vanishes. The priest prays, and in his dream the spirit reappears to tell of her unhappiness.

media.caption: Yamamba 山姥 (The Old Woman of the Mountain)

text.headline: Yamamba 山姥 (The Old Woman of the Mountain)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Yamamba by the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443) in which the true Yamamba dances, holding a fan.
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 123.) - A dancer from the capital (tsure), famous for her performances, goes by the name of Hyakuma Yamamba because of a song she created about this mysterious woman of the mountain. While on a pilgrimage to Zenkō Temple (Zenkōji) with three fellow travelers (wakizure), she arrives at the sacred mountain of Haguro in Echigo. They ask a local person for the best route to the temple. He tells them that there are three: one upper, one lower, and a third over the mountain itself. They choose the third. On their way they meet an older woman (shite), who offers them shelter. She tells them that she is the real Yamamba, and Hyakuma asks to show her dance. As she does so, the woman says she will return when the moon is shining to demonstrate how the actual dance should be performed. Suddenly, the sky grows dark in the middle of the day. Yamamba appears in her true form and dances, unveiling the secrets of the mountain. She then disappears into the valley.

media.caption: Iwai Hanshirō, Ichikawa Danjūrō, Ichikawa Shinjūrō and Nakamura Nakazō (岩井半四郎、 市川団十郎、 市川新十郎、 中村仲蔵)

text.headline: Iwai Hanshirō, Ichikawa Danjūrō, Ichikawa Shinjūrō and Nakamura Nakazō (岩井半四郎、 市川団十郎、 市川新十郎、 中村仲蔵)
text.text: The actors, from right to left, Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, Ichikawa Shinjūrō II and Nakamura Nakazō III are depicted below extensive text. It is likely that the publication of this print coincided with the change of ownership in the Kawarazaki theater sometime in 1876 to a new group of investors who renamed the theater the Shinbori. The presence of chrysanthemums indicates that this print is marking an auspicious occasion.

media.caption: Ranking of Wages of Tokyo Actors (東京俳優給金附 Tokyo haiyū kyūkin zuke)

text.headline: Ranking of Wages of Tokyo Actors (東京俳優給金附 Tokyo haiyū kyūkin zuke)
text.text:
A depiction of nineteen actors in character, along with a listing of their salaries and the salaries of other leading Tokyo kabuki actors. The leftmost entry on the scroll running across the top of the print provides a date of Meiji 29 (1896) for the annual salaries that are given above each actor's name.
While there is some English language information available on both pre and post-Meiji salaries for kabuki actors, there seems to be little information available in English on salaries for Meiji-era kabuki actors. For the salaries shown on the print's scroll, they are likely yearly salaries as actors contracted with a theater for the entire kabuki season. On this print, the highest annual salary listed is that of Ichikawa Danjurō IX 市川団十郎 at 2,000 yen. As a point of reference, the basic starting pay of a policeman in 1881 was 72 yen per year and for an elementary school teacher in 1886, 60 yen.
In discussing actor salaries at the beginning of the 19th century, Arendie and Henk Herwig state, "[T]op actors’ annual earnings were between 1000 and 1500 ryō."[1] According to Brandon in Kabuki Plays on Stage: Villainy and Vengeance, "1000 ryō would be the equivalent of 400,000 to 800,000 American dollars today. They did have to pay for their own costly costumes, however. Popular actors received a formal salary, but they were also supported by wealthy patrons who provided extra revenue or paid for expensive costumes. In return, the patrons could expect favours such as the presence of actors at their parties or private performances. It was common practice for actors to honour their patrons with a visit during the first days of the New Year bringing gifts as tokens of gratitude."[2]

[1] Heroes of the Kabuki Stage: An Introduction to the World of Kabuki with Retellings of Famous Plays, illustrated by Woodblock Prints, Arendie Herwig and Henk J. Herwig, Hotei Publishing, 2004, p. 40.
[2] Kabuki Plays on Stage: Villainy and Vengence, 1773-1799, editors James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 288.

media.caption: Fantasy

text.headline: Fantasy
text.text: "Between 1954 and 1973, Toshi made nearly three hundred nonobjective prints . . . that signal his desire to use color, shape, line, and texture expressively to capture the nature of human experience or the human experience of nature." - Source: A Japanese Legacy: Four Generations of Yoshida Family Artists, Laura W. Allen, Kendall H. Brown, Eugene M. Skibbe, et. al., The Minneapolis Institute of Arts, 2002, p. 76.

text.text: Kōitsu's rendering of the Goju-no-To (Five-Story Pagoda) in the Nara Hōryūji temple complex on a rainy day.

media.caption: Moon at Namino (波埜の月)

text.headline: Moon at Namino (波埜の月)
text.text:
A full moon over Kujū National Park in Kumamoto Prefecture on the island of Kyūshū. The main attraction in the park in Mount Aso, a 1,592 meter (5,223 ft) active volcano, Japan's largest. The white circular ring in the distance might be a formation caused by vapors from the volcano.
The print is one of five in the series Five Views of Aso first published in a limited edition of 300 in 1950 by Kuga Ichio 久我五千男 (1922-1984) of Sōjinsha, with carving and printing at Katō Hanga Kenkyūsho under the supervision of Katō Junji. The prints in the series was reprinted a number of times, including a smaller-size version in 1962 by Kyūryūdō under a new title "Sakamoto Hanjiro gashu."

media.caption: Yoshino Tennin 吉野天人 (The Goddess at Yoshino)

text.headline: Yoshino Tennin 吉野天人 (The Goddess at Yoshino)
text.text:
The print depicts a goddess performing a dance in praise of the cherry blossoms (Gosechi).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 219.) - Some people on their way to view the cherry blossom at Yoshino meet a beautiful woman who joins them to enjoy the flowers. Before leaving she tells them that she is a goddess and that she will return later and perform an ancient dance for them. This she does, and after praising the beauties of spring, disappears on a cloud of blossoms.

media.caption: Tsuchigumo土蜘蛛 (Earth Spider)

text.headline: Tsuchigumo土蜘蛛 (Earth Spider)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Tsuchigumo in which Minamoto Raikō's retainers led by Hitorimusha rush to confront a monstrous spider in the guise of a monk who has attacked their lord.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 198-199.) - After the serving-woman has brought the sick Minamoto no Yorimitsu some medicine, a spider comes to him in the guise of a priest. But when it begins to enmesh Yorimitsu in the threads of a web, he realizes that it is some evil creature and manages to slash it with his sword. At this it vanishes but Hitori-musha, alarmed by his master's cries, hurries to the scene and after hearing what has taken place, determines to hunt out the creature. He and his men track it down by following the trail of blood to a cave and there they destroy the spider that has been the cause of Yorimitsu's illness.

media.caption: Setsubun 節分 (A Demon in Love)

text.headline: Setsubun 節分 (A Demon in Love)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the kyōgen play Setsubun, in which the demon dances and sings to win the love of the Woman.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 240.) - This Kyōgen is closely connected with the Spring holiday of the same name at which time demons and bad spirits are driven out of the house by scattering red beans in all the rooms while chanting, "In with the good, out with the evil."
A Demon has travelled all the way from Hōrai Island, and is very tired. He asks a Woman whose husband is away at the Izumo Shrine to let him rest in her house, and she, being afraid to refuse, lets him in.
The Demon tries to make love to her by singing various songs praising her beauty, etc., and he finally breaks into tears because she won't pay any attention to him. She realizes he is just like a human male, and decides to take advantage of the situation. She tricks him out of his magic straw hat and coat, and then chases him out by throwing beans at him while chanting, "In with the good, out with the evil!"

media.caption: Daihannya 大盤若 (The Buddhist Sutra and the Shintō Dance)

text.headline: Daihannya 大盤若 (The Buddhist Sutra and the Shintō Dance)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the kyōgen 狂言 play Daihannya, in which the Buddhist Priest on the left joins the Shrine Maiden in her Shintō dance.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 48.) - A Shrine Maiden of the Shintō religion appears at the Man's house to perform her monthly kagura (a Shintō dance of blessing). Before long a Buddhist Priest appears at the same Man's house to read his monthly sutras. The Man places them in separate rooms to perform their services, but before long the Priest begins to complain of the noise of the kagura bells and tells the Man to have the Shrine Maiden stop her kagura till hie is finished with his sutra reading.
The Shrine Maiden objects saying the the kagura is more important than the sutras. They argue back and forth for a time, and finally the Priest agrees to try not to pay attention to the noise.
The Priest puts his hands over his ears to keep out the noise. The Shrine Maiden comes and teases him by ringing her bells near his ears. The Priest begins to enjoy the dance and even joins in, forgetting his sutra reading even to the point of using his sutra scroll as bells in mimicking the Shrine Maiden's dance.

media.caption: Ukai 鵜飼 (The Cormorant Fisher)

text.headline: Ukai 鵜飼 (The Cormorant Fisher)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Ukai, in which cormorant fisher demonstrates to two Buddhist priests how he caught fish.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 203-204.) - When two travelling priests meet an old cormorant fisher one of them recognizes him as the man who gave him shelter two or three years ago. The old man then tells them that as he broke the strict prohibition against taking life in the nearby river by fishing there nightly with his cormorants, he has been drowned in the river as punishment. In return for the priests' promise to pray for his soul he shows them how the fishing is done and then disappears. Nichiren takes up some stones and after writing part of the Lotus Sutra on them, throws them into the river. Emma, the King of Hell, then appears and tells them that although the fisherman deserves to suffer for his sins, he will send him to Paradise because of the kindness he showed the priest.

media.caption: Shiga 志賀

text.headline: Shiga 志賀
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Shiga.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.161.) - A Court official who has come to Shiga to view the cherry blossom sees two woodcutters resting under a cherry tree with branches of the blossom added to their already heavy load of wood. Impressed by this, he speaks to them and during their talk, the old man tells of Ōtomo no Kuronushi, the poet of old who is deified and worshiped in the shrine at Shiga. He hints that he is Kuronushi and then vanishes. While the official is resting under the tree that night, he sees the god come and, rejoicing at the prosperous reign, performs a dance.

media.caption: Kusu no tsuyu 楠露 (Camphor Tree in Dew)

text.headline: Kusu no tsuyu 楠露 (Camphor Tree in Dew)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Kusu no tsuyu in which Masashige, fearing his imminent death, has his retainer read his last words of advice to his son, Masatsura. For two other impressions of this print see IHL.1896 and IHL.1923.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 95-96.) - Feeling that he will die in the coming battle with Ashikaga Takauji, Masashige calls his son Masatsura to him in the town of Sakurai and gives him his last words of advice. At the farewell party Onchi Mitsukazu dances to entertain them. Masashige then sends his faithful retainer away with his son to take him back to their home, while he himself prepares for battle.
