media.caption: Act III - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (三段目 忠臣蔵 sandanme Chūshingura)

text.headline: Act III - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (三段目 忠臣蔵 sandanme Chūshingura)
text.text:
Chūshingura Act III: Kampei confronts Bannai and his servants near the gate to the palace of Ashikaga Tadayoshi - This scene is set in the evening outside of Kamakura Castle. Kampei, behind whom stands Ōkaru by the bridge over the moat, across which rise the walls and towers of Kamakura Castle, is about to be attacked by Bannai and his men. Bannai is about to arrest Kampei and take Ōkaru, who has her orange scarf ready to strangle Bannai. The immediate aftermath of this scene, in which Bannai and his men flee Kampei, was portrayed about ten years earlier by Hiroshige II's teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige.

Utagawa Hiroshige II created this series of twelve prints under his art name (gō) Shigenobu. His teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I, created several earlier series in the horizontal ōban format depicting the acts in the play Chūshingura, one published by Izumaya Ichibei between 1835-1839 and one published by Arataya Seiemon between 1843-1847. As with Hiroshige I's series, Hiroshige II bordered the prints with the double Tomo-ye crest of Yuranosuke, the hero of the play. For several scenes, Hiroshige II borrowed heavily from his teacher as he did for this print.

media.caption: Act VIII - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (八段目 忠臣蔵 hachidanme Chūshingura)

text.headline: Act VIII - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (八段目 忠臣蔵 hachidanme Chūshingura)
text.text:
Chūshingura Act VIII: Konami's bridal journey (michiyuki travel dance) - The scene is set on the road from Edo to Kyoto. Tonase and Konami are on their way to Yamashima to find Rikiya, Yuranosuke's son and Konami's betrothed. They are resting under the shade of a large tree overlooking the seashore and admiring the fine view of Fuji with their porter sitting before them. Behind them rises the wooded island of Enoshima.
Utagawa Hiroshige II created this series of twelve prints under his art name (gō) Shigenobu. His teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I, created several earlier series in the horizontal ōban format depicting the acts in the play Chūshingura, one published by Izumaya Ichibei between 1835-1839 and one published by Arataya Seiemon between 1843-1847. As with Hiroshige I's series, Hiroshige II bordered the prints with the double Tomo-ye crest of Yuranosuke, the hero of the play. For several scenes, Hiroshige II borrowed heavily from his teacher, but for his portrayal of this act he chose to depict a different scene than his teacher, though each shows a pause in this bridal journey.

media.caption: Act XI - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (十一段目 忠臣蔵 jūichidanme Chūshingura)

text.headline: Act XI - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (十一段目 忠臣蔵 jūichidanme Chūshingura)
text.text:
Chūshingura Act XI (third episode): Moronao captured and shown Enya's suicide sword by Yuranosuke - The scene is set on a snowy night under a full moon. Moronao is discovered in his hiding-place in an outhouse used to store wood and charcoal. Yuranosuke shows him the dagger with which Enya committed suicide and invites him to do likewise, an invitation which Moronao declines.
Utagawa Hiroshige II created this series of twelve prints under his art name (gō) Shigenobu. His teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I, created several earlier series in the horizontal ōban format depicting the acts in the play Chūshingura, one published by Izumaya Ichibei between 1835-1839 and one published by Arataya Seiemon between 1843-1847. As with Hiroshige I's series, Hiroshige II bordered the prints with the double Tomo-ye crest of Yuranosuke, the hero of the play. For several scenes Hiroshige II borrowed heavily from his teacher, but for his portrayal of this act he chose to depict the moment before Moronao is seized by Yuranosuke and then killed.

media.caption: Wrapper for a set of three postcards titled Sketches of G.I. in New Japan (アメリカの兵隊さんと 新日本風景 Amerika heitaisan shin Nihon fūkei)

text.headline: Wrapper for a set of three postcards titled Sketches of G.I. in New Japan (アメリカの兵隊さんと 新日本風景 Amerika heitaisan shin Nihon fūkei)
text.text:
The wrapper for a set of three postcards created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) by unknown artists. The woodblock printed wrapper pictures a G.I. leaning against the railing on Kyoto's Sanjō Bridge. The Japanese writing on the wrapper reads 木版絵葉書 アメリカの兵隊さんと 新日本風景 和田三造 補修, which can be translated as "woodblock postcards, Scenic Views of American Soldiers in New Japan (or Sketches of G.I. in Japan), Wada Sanzō, complemented*."
Each of the three woodblock printed postcards (see IHL.1154, IHL.1155 and IHL.1156) display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war.

The meaning of the characters 補修 following Wada Sanzō's name is unclear.

media.caption: Sanjō Bridge in Kyoto (京都三條大橋 Kyoto Sanjō Ōhashi)

text.headline: Sanjō Bridge in Kyoto (京都三條大橋 Kyoto Sanjō Ōhashi)
text.text: One of three woodblock printed postcards (also see IHL.1155 and IHL.1156) packaged in a decorative envelope (see IHL.1153) which display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war. This set of postcards were created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) and the idenities of the artists whose signatures appear on the postcards are unknown. This postcard depicts three G.I.s watch two passing maiko while standing on Sanjō Bridge in Kyoto.

media.caption: Japanese Coming Home on Hakata Pier (博多港の邦人引揚げ Hakata-kō no hōjin hikiageru)

text.headline: Japanese Coming Home on Hakata Pier (博多港の邦人引揚げ Hakata-kō no hōjin hikiageru)
text.text: One of three woodblock printed postcards (also see IHL.1154 and IHL.1156) packaged in a decorative envelope (see IHL.1153) which display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war. This set of postcards were created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) and the identities of the artists whose signatures appear on the postcards are unknown. This postcard pictures civilians disembarking from the ship named the "Dockwiler" at Hakata Pier in Fukuoka. The ship is likely the Liberty Ship the S.S. John Dockweiler, launched in January 1944. Hakata was a major processing center for Japanese "displaced persons" who had been repatriated from China, Korea and other former Japanese colonies with the help of U.S. ships following Japan's defeat.

media.caption: A Snowy Sight at Hibiya Junction in Tokyo (東京日比谷交差点の雪 Tokyo Hibiya kōsaten no yuki)

text.headline: A Snowy Sight at Hibiya Junction in Tokyo (東京日比谷交差点の雪 Tokyo Hibiya kōsaten no yuki)
text.text: One of three woodblock printed postcards (also see IHL.1154 and IHL.1155) packaged in a decorative envelope (see IHL.1153) which display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war. This set of postcards were created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) and the identities of the artists whose signatures appear on the postcards are unknown. This postcard features an occupation soldier and a Japanese policeman cooperating in directing traffic at busy Hibiya Junction. They seem to be waving to each other in a comradely way, further evidence of the harmonious relations between defeated Japan and the occupation forces depicted in these postcards.

media.caption: Landscape Spring Evening (春宵 A)

text.headline: Landscape Spring Evening (春宵 A)
text.text: A semi-abstract landscape with a rising moon in a silver metallic sky. The artist has used deep embossing through the white band beneath the sky. A green field of flowers dominates the foreground. This print was exhibited at the CWAJ Twentieth Annual Print Show, October 1975 at the Tokyo American Club.

media.caption: Katsushika (葛飾)

text.headline: Katsushika (葛飾)
text.text: The artist Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki) (1871–1945) is credited with over 750 designs during his lifetime, the majority of which depicted landscapes in the shin hanga style. While he worked with at least one other publisher, most of his work was done for the publisher Watanabe  Shōzaburō, starting in 1907. In this post Great Kantō Earthquake print a fisherman, bent over with his load, carries a heavy basket after a day of fishing. A torii and shrine can be seen in the background. Titled "Katsushika" ("葛飾" above the artist's red square-shaped seal on the right side of the pirnt), Katsushika-gun (now Katsushika City) was a Tokyo ward. The river seen in the print may the Arakawa which bordered Katsushika on the west or the Edogawa bounding it on the east.

media.caption: Tsuta Onsen (蔦温泉)

text.headline: Tsuta Onsen (蔦温泉)
text.text:
From Senpan's fourth set of prints picturing Japanese onsens. This print depicts the bus or automobile stop outside of Tsuda (Tsuta) onsen with the sign reading 國鉄自動車 ったおんせん (National Railway bus stop or auto stop. Tsuda onsen). The spa-goers stand, looking perplexed, at the sign.
"Tsuta Onsen is an inn situated at the mouth of Oirase Gorge in Aomori. Records of hot spring resorts here date all the way back to the year 1147." - Source: website of Tsuta Onsen https://tsutaonsen.com/en/ [accessed 8-17-23]
ABOUT THE SERIES HOT SPRING NOTES
One of his most famous series of prints, "Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes" (Hanga yokusen fu), depicts various hot springs around Japan. It was published in five volumes of twenty prints each over an 18 year period, starting in 1941 when Maekawa was evacuated to Okayama in southwest Honshu and ending in 1959.
Merritt states that most of the prints were started during the war but could not be published until the war was over. She notes that although his countrymen are depicted at one of their favorite pastimes, spa going for rest and relaxation, "the feeling is not joyous," due to Maekawa's use of somber colors. The general demeanor of the spa goers is also somber in many of the prints.
However, writing in 1955, Oliver Statler found Senpan's spa prints "some of his pleasantest prints" and praised Senpan's "connoisseur's selection from the country's hundreds of hot spring resorts."
In 1954 the publisher Ryūseikaku 竜星閣 released a volume containing full size reproductions of the sixty woodblock prints contained in the first three volumes.
The five volumes comprising the entire series are titled are:
Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (版画 浴泉譜 Hanga yokusen fu), 1941.
More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1944.
More and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1952.
More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku yokusen fu), 1956.
More, More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku, zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1959.

media.caption: Village in snow with Mount Fuji (untitled)

text.headline: Village in snow with Mount Fuji (untitled)
text.text:
A snow covered village backed by a line of bare trees with a snow covered Fuji dominating the background.

Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) maker and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. His work also crossed over into the new print (shin hanga) genre. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own woodblock prints, such as IHL.1844, and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

media.caption: Semi Onsen (瀬見温泉)

text.headline: Semi Onsen (瀬見温泉)
text.text:
From Senpan's fourth set of prints picturing Japanese onsens. This print depicts an inn near the Semi hot springs on a winter's day. Two lonely figures sit in the inn on a bleak looking day.
The Legend of Semi Onsen
In 1187, a samurai warrior named Minamoto Yoshitsune, his companion Benkei and their party, were passing by the Semi Onsen hot springs on their way to Hiraizumi in Iwate, pursued by the forces of his brother, Yoritomo. At that time, Yoshitsune's pregnant wife, Kitanokata, suddenly began to feel labour pains, and Kamewakamaru was born.
"Benkei went down the mountain in pursuit of water for the newborn's first bath, and discovered columns of steam rising from beneath rocks. He dug down into the ground using his naginata (bladed pole weapon), and thermal waters gushed out, according to Gikeiki (The Chronicle of Yoshitsune). Since then, these top quality waters have been flowing from the spring, continuously, for over 800 years. Many historical sites and attractions in association with Yoshitsune and Benkei are lovingly preserved in Semi Onsen." - Source: website of Kansyokan Semi Onsen https://kansyokan.co.jp/en/about/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Genjō 絃上

text.headline: Genjō 絃上
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Genjō in which the sea dragon-god appears carrying a famous lute.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 41-42.) - The famous lute player Moronaga is about to sail for China for further training on the instrument in that country, when he stops for a night at Suma Bay to view the moon. He plays a piece on a lute for the old couple in whose house he is lodging, and is surprised to find them so appreciative of the music that when a shower of rain patters down on the roof they hasten to spread rush mats there to deaden the sound. He therefore asks them to play a piece, and when they play on the lute and Japanese harp their performance is so skillful that he abandons altogether his plan of going to study in China. At this, the old couple reveal that they are in fact the Emperor Murakami and his consort, the Lady Nashitsubo, and that the Emperor had played the melody on the famous lute called Genjō in the hope that after hearing it Moronaga would give up his journey abroad. They then vanish, but the Emperor reappears shortly afterwards and summons a dragon-god from the sea. He retrieves from him another famous lute, Shishi-maru, which had been seized by the dragon-god when it was on its way to Japan with Genjō, and this he presents to Moronaga.

media.caption: Pottery Works (陶藝工所)

text.headline: Pottery Works (陶藝工所)
text.text: A small print showing a potter at work from the portfolio of twelve prints titled Collection of Color-Prints with Views of Kyoto, Nara, Osaka and Kobe offered by the Osaka Railway Division, Japanese National Railways.

media.caption: Kinkakuji (Golden Pavilion) in the Snow (金閣寺雪景)

text.headline: Kinkakuji (Golden Pavilion) in the Snow (金閣寺雪景)
text.text:
A chuban size print depicting Kyoto's Golden Pavilion (Kinkakuji) during a snowfall. Five visitors, veiled by the snow, can be seen on the right.
This print is part of a set of five prints by the artist created for the famous soba shop Owariya 尾張屋 in Kyoto, which has been in business since 1465. Four of the prints depict scenic views in and around Kyoto and the fifth depicts the Owariya. Originally published in the 1930s, this set was reprinted for the celebration of the 15th generation household head of Owariya during the 1980s. The Owariya name in kana をはりや or kanji 尾張屋, within a rectangular cartouche, appears on each of the prints.

media.caption: 897 Eiffel Tower

text.headline: 897 Eiffel Tower
text.text: Another one of Funasaka's prints using a silkscreened image of an iconic building as a backdrop for his signature brightly colored vertical forms printed using woodblock technique. This time it's the Eiffel Tower that he has hand pixelated as part of the print process.
Eight of Funasaka's signature brightly colored vertical forms float over a golden grid. The background ink is laced with mica.

media.caption: Aoto Fujitsuna (青砥藤綱)

text.headline: Aoto Fujitsuna (青砥藤綱)
text.text:
Print number 19 (十九), and one of 13 designs contributed by Inoue to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Aoto Fujitsuna 青砥藤綱, a councilor of the Kamakura Shogunate (1192-1333), directing the search for a few coins he has lost in the Namerigawa River. When asked we he cared about so little money he replied "It only shows that you are interested in neither public interests nor charity. If I had not looked for the 10 mon in the river, it would have been lost forever. The 50 mon that I payed for the torches profited the merchant. There was no loss at all. It was a benefit to the public, wasn't it?"
For another edition of this print see IHL.0615.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Not Aware Man and Aware Man, No. 2

text.headline: Not Aware Man and Aware Man, No. 2
text.text:
The top print shows what appears to be a sleeping man (perhaps sleepy with too much drink), being rushed through the nighttime streets in a jinrikisha (note 人力車 jin/riki/sha on the lantern.) He is being moved ahead at great speed by both the jinrikisha drivers and a slew of bad little akudama. A wallet (kamiire) containing money (satsu), that he possibly dropped, can be seen in the lower left of the print.
The bottom print shows a man, who is carrying a box, so possibly some type of vendor, near a sake shop (note the character 酒 on the first shop on the left) whose attention is being drawn to a wallet with its contents lying on the ground by six good little zendamas. Is it his good fortune that he has found this money? Has his abstinence produced his good luck? Will he try to return the wallet to its drunken onwer

media.caption: Gathering Shellfish at Low Tide at Fukagawa Susaki (深川洲崎汐干狩)

text.headline: Gathering Shellfish at Low Tide at Fukagawa Susaki (深川洲崎汐干狩)
text.text:
Shiohigari (Shellfish gathering at low tide) a popular beach activity for the people in Edo, was an annual event in March on the beaches such as at Shinagawa, Shibaura, Fukagawa Susaki. Among all, Susaki was especially crowded with many people as a famous spot for shellfish gathering.
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III, created a number of series of prints depicting meisho (famous places or famous views) in and around the city of Tokyo/Edo. It is interesting to compare his depiction of this popular past time with his predecessors Utagawa Hiroshige I and Utagawa Hiroshige II.

media.caption: Mansei Bridge (萬世橋 Mansei bashi)

text.headline: Mansei Bridge (萬世橋 Mansei bashi)
text.text: One in a series of prints showing famous places ("prides") in and around Tokyo. The Mansei Bridge, built and destroyed a number of times, spanned the Kanda river and was one of the major gateways to Tokyo. Its current iteration is located in present day Akihabara.

media.caption: Portrait of Saigō Takamori, Former Army General Senior Grade of the Third Court Rank (西郷隆盛像旧陸軍大将正三位) Kyu Rikugun Taishō Shōsanmi Saigō Takamori zō)

text.headline: Portrait of Saigō Takamori, Former Army General Senior Grade of the Third Court Rank (西郷隆盛像旧陸軍大将正三位) Kyu Rikugun Taishō Shōsanmi Saigō Takamori zō)
text.text:
Issued in the beginning of November 1877, approximately six weeks after the end of the nine month Satsuma Rebellion and the death of its leader, Saigō Takamori, this print portrays Saigō decked out in all his military finery from the days when he was one of the most powerful men in the new Meiji government. While it was not until the end of February 1889 that Saigō, the rebel, received his official state pardon and the restoration of his imperial court rank, he and his top commanders were portrayed as heroes by printmakers and their publishers as soon as the rebellion was crushed.
Translation of text on print: "Saigō Takamori was born in Satsuma. His former name was Zenbei, and he also used the sobriquet Nanshū. He was naturally endowed with unusual talent and an imposing appearance, such that all who saw him immediately recognized him as extraordinary. Enlisting early in the royalist cause he entered the Capital of Kyoto in the Kaei era [1848-54] and became a follower of the monk Gesshō, incumbent of the Hōjōin at Kiyomizu. Favored by the noble Lord Konoe he grieved at the desuetude into which the royal house had fallen, and plotted with Ijichi Masaharu and Kaieda Nobuyoshi to do great deeds. But then the shogunate sent forces to arrest and confine these idealists. Saigō fled to Kyushu with Gesshō, meaning to return to his own holdings, but when they were prevented, they made a pact to throw themselves into the sea. They leapt into the water in each other’s arms, but others on the boat pulled them out. Saigō was revived, but Gesshō perished. Having thus been returned mysteriously to life, Saigō assumed the name Kikuchi Gengo. His domain shunned his actions and banished him to the Great Island [Amami]. He spent several years there, his aspirations becoming ever firmer even as his learning grew broader. He was pardoned in Bunkyū 3 [1863] and returned to his domain, where he changed his name to Kichinosuke and quickly rose in the domain’s government. In Keiō 1 [1865] he participated in the shogunate’s campaign against Chōshū but affected the release of imprisoned royalists in many domains. Not least of his deeds was done in the spring of Boshin [1868] when as deputee in charge of the imperial forces’ expedition to the East he took Edo Castle. Subsequently he followed the Great Governor General [Prince Arisugawa] in pacifying Hokuetsu, in which action he performed meritoriously. In further quelling brigand forces in Ezo his tactics were uniformly apt for the moment. For all of this the Court elevated him to the post of Councilor, but he refused and returned to his domain. Then on 6/2/Meiji 2 [1869] it was decreed that for his aid in the great work of Restoring the government, for seizing Edo Castle and leading the Hokuetsu expedition, and for his stalwart performance of military deeds, his leadership, and his successful and foresighted planning, all of which had brought much comfort to His Majesty, he would be rewarded with a stipend of 2000 bales of rice. In Meiji 4 [1871] he was elevated to Third Rank, First Grade, at court and made Councilor. In 4/Meiji 6 [1873] he was made Commander in Chief of the Army. In the 10th month of that year he advocated on behalf of an Imperial expedition against Korea, and when that was refused he resigned his position and returned to his home country. He also attempted to refuse all his rewards and emoluments, but the court would not allow this, and so he devoted them to the establishment of private academies in the countryside. He sent several of his students abroad to study, without requiring reimbursement. In this way the young men of the prefecture came to support him. Then in the 2nd month of this year he joined with Kirino [Toshiaki], Shinohara [Kunimoto], and others to raise a great army with himself as commander in order to make inquiries of the Government. With violence they occupied the Higo Road, and the Government moved quickly to mount an expedition against them. By land and sea, forces flying the Imperial flag advanced upon Kyushu. Battles were fought in Bungo, Higo, Satsuma, and Kumamoto. In the 9th month the rebel forces again attacked Kagoshima, but then the Imperial forces surrounded them at Shiroyama with superior numbers. At 3:00 in the morning on 9/24, they began attacking from all sides. There was no way to fend them off now, and he, along with Kirino and Murata [Sansuke], slit his belly, dying at Shiroyama. The remaining rebels were all captured, and by 7:00 that morning the rebellion had been quelled. Once he had held lofty rank and position, but in this way, having enlisted with insurrectionists, he became a traitor to the Realm." - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon

media.caption: Portrait of Kirino Toshiaki: The Former Army Major General of the Fifth Court Rank (桐野利秋像・旧陸軍少将正五位)

text.headline: Portrait of Kirino Toshiaki: The Former Army Major General of the Fifth Court Rank (桐野利秋像・旧陸軍少将正五位)
text.text: Issued in the beginning of November 1877, approximately six weeks after the end of the nine month Satsuma Rebellion and the death of its leader, Saigō Takamori, this print portrays Kirino Toshiaki, Saigō Takamori's second in command, not in his former military uniform as a Major General in the new Meiji army (as Saigō is portrayed in the print Portrait of Saigō Takamori, IHL.1171), but in his samurai regalia. This is befitting as Kirino was known as a ferocious swordsman, one of the "Four Hitokiri of the Bakumatsu" 幕末四大人斬り. Kirino was to be slain along with Saigō at the last battle of the rebellion at the end of September 1877.

media.caption: First Chanting of Noh at the New Year (御謡初 O-utai zome)

text.headline: First Chanting of Noh at the New Year (御謡初 O-utai zome)
text.text:
This print is from a series of 32 scenes documenting life for the elite during the later days of the shogunate. In this print, samurai have gathered in a large reception hall in the Chiyoda Outer Palace to hear the year's first chanting of noh at Edo Castle. The inscription in the center of the print starts off, "Every year on the evening of the third of the New Year, the first dance of the year is held in the main hall . . . ."[1] The inscription goes on to tell us that "selections were performed from Oimatsu, Takasago and other plays."[2] The different schools of noh would take turns annually to present the chants.

THE CHIYODA OUTER PALACE
The Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) series of 1897, together with Chikanobu's 1895-1896 series Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku), provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
While the Chiyoda Inner Palace series focused on women in the private quarters of the palace, Chiyoda Outer Palace focused on the society of men, centered on the shogun, inside and outside the castle. The thirty two prints (including one hexaptych) show "activities which Chikanobu may have participated in when he was part of the shogun's retinue. This set, too, while more authentic because of Chikanobu's personal experiences, is also an artistic representation, and focuses on the elite side of life in the late Edo period."[3]
The activities in the Chiyoda Outer Palace series are set both "in the more public areas and grounds of the castle and beyond the castle precincts...as far away as the shogunal mausoleum at Nikkō."[4]

[1] Princeton University Art Museum https://artmuseum.princeton.edu/collections/objects/50952 [accessed 8-30-23]
[2] The British Museum https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_1906-1220-0-1620-1-3 [accessed 8-30-23]
[3] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 170.
[4] Princeton University Art Museum https://artmuseum.princeton.edu/collections/objects/24904 [accessed 8-30-2333333]

media.caption: Illustration of the National Diet Building (國會議事堂圖 kokkai gijidō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the National Diet Building (國會議事堂圖 kokkai gijidō no zu)
text.text: On November 29, 1890 the ceremonies for the long awaited opening of the Imperial Diet took place. That morning the emperor left the palace at 10:30 and proceeded toward the House of Peers. He was accompanied by Prince Taruhito, Interior Minister Sanjo Sanetomi, Prime Minister Yamagata Aritomo, President of the Privy Council Oki Takato, and various high officials. On reaching the Diet building, the emperor was met by other dignitaries.

media.caption: Steam Train at Takanawa Seashore, Tokyo (東京高輪海岸蒸気車鉄道走行之全図 Tōkyō Takanawa kaigan jōkisha tetsudō hashiriyuki no sen zu)

text.headline: Steam Train at Takanawa Seashore, Tokyo (東京高輪海岸蒸気車鉄道走行之全図 Tōkyō Takanawa kaigan jōkisha tetsudō hashiriyuki no sen zu)
text.text: The little steam train from Shinagawa in Tokyo to Yokohama started running in the summer of 1872. This print, however, was issued sometime in 1871 and was likely based on the artist's imagination of a steam train, possibly culled from American or European illustrations. Plans for the rail line between Yokohama and Tokyo were announced in 1870 and it immediately became an emblem of civilization and enlightenment (bunmei kaika). Publishers rushed to represent this modern conveyance and dozens of prints ensued.

media.caption: Rokkasen kyōga no suminuri (六歌仙狂画墨塗)

text.headline: Rokkasen kyōga no suminuri (六歌仙狂画墨塗)
text.text: Staged in March 1880, at the Shintomiza 新富 in Tokyo, this dance play was a mitate (parody) on the theme of the Six Immortal Poets (rokkasen). Pictured in the roles of the Six Immortal Poets are the actors (from right to left), Iwai Hanshirō VIII 岩井半四郎 as the lady Ono no Komachi 小野小町, Onoe Kigugorō V 尾上菊五郎 as Hōshi [priest] Kisen 喜撰法師, Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 as the evil noble Ōtomo no Kuronushi 大伴黒主, Nakamura Sōjūrō 中村宗十郎 as Sōjō [abbot] Henjō 僧正遍昭, Ichikawa Danjūrō 市川団十郎 as the noble Bunya Yasuhide 文屋康秀 and Bandō Kakitsu 坂東家橘 as the courtier Ariwara no Narihira 在原業平.

media.caption: Bridge (橋)

text.headline: Bridge (橋)
text.text: A woodblock rendition of a 1948 oil painting by the artist. This collection's print is likely a proof print for the editioned version which was one of five prints included in the folio titled Oka Shikanosuke Woodblock Print Collection, First Series [岡鹿之助第一輯版画集 Oka Shikanosuke daiichshū hanga gashū]. The folio was issued in an edition of 150 in 1970 by the publisher Katō Hanga Kenkyūsho (Katō Print Institute).

media.caption: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯 chanoyu)

text.headline: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯 chanoyu)
text.text: The Japanese tea ceremony is called chanoyu or sado in Japanese and the bitter tea served is called matcha. It is basically a choreographic ritual of preparing and serving tea together with some sweets. Each movement is predefined. The whole process is not about drinking tea, it is about aesthetics. The proper performance requires a long training and the use of certain tools like chasen, a bamboo brush. For an earlier edition of this print see ihl-0008.

media.caption: Remaining Light at Jōshū, Minakami (残燈 上州水上 Zantō, jōshū Minakami)

text.headline: Remaining Light at Jōshū, Minakami (残燈 上州水上 Zantō, jōshū Minakami)
text.text: A later edition of a 1958 print picturing the sun setting behind the distant mountains behind the Alpine village of Minakami, a hot spring and ski resort. The Tone River, seen in the foreground, reflects the last of the sunset's glow.

media.caption: Spring Snow at Maruyama, Kyoto (春の雪 京都円山 Haru no yuki Kyoto Maruyama)

text.headline: Spring Snow at Maruyama, Kyoto (春の雪 京都円山 Haru no yuki Kyoto Maruyama)
text.text: Three woman in traditional winter clothing, geta on their feet, stroll through snow covered Maruyama Park  in early evening. This collection's print is a later edition of a much-reprinted image by Kōitsu, originally released in March 1936.

media.caption: Still Life of Crystal Vase and Rose (untitled)

text.headline: Still Life of Crystal Vase and Rose (untitled)
text.text: One of at least four similar images of a crystal vase done by the artist in various formats.  This impression from an edition of 250 prints is dated 1973, a year before the artist's death, and appears to use the same blocks as the original 1959 edition of 50 prints.

media.caption: Inbanuma, the Desolate Marsh (印旛沼、沼辺の荒涼)

text.headline: Inbanuma, the Desolate Marsh (印旛沼、沼辺の荒涼)
text.text:
This print, one of 15 contributed by Hakutei to the 50 print series Japan Scenery Prints, published by Nakajima Jūtarō, pictures a lonely fisherman's hut on Inba marsh, located in current day northeastern Chiba Prefecture on the Shimōsa Plateau about 50 km northeast of Tokyo and about 15 km west of Narita Airport.

"The series Nihon fūkei hanga (Japan Scenery Prints) consisted of ten sets of prints, with each set composed of five small landscapes and a cover print giving the name of the series, the name and number of the set, and the name of the artist. In addition, each set was accompanied by a table of contents and colophon sheet. Specific publication dates ranging from January 1917 through April 1920 indicate that each set was issued separately. As Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958) designed the majority of prints in the series, it seems likely that Hakutei was the spearhead for the project. The artists asked Igami Bonkutsu to carve the blocks and Nakajima Jūtarō to publish the series." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 274-276.
In addition to Ishii Hakutei (1182-1958), the other artists who contributed to the series were Sakamoto Hanjirō (1882-1969), see this collection's print Sea of Fire, IHL.0862 and Chikugo River, IHL.2068, Hirafuku Hyakusui (1877-1933), Morita Tsunetomo (1881-1933), Kosugi Misei (1881-1964) and Ishii Tsuruzō (1887-1973), elder brother of Hakutei.

media.caption: Daido Bay (Daidokō 大同江)

text.headline: Daido Bay (Daidokō 大同江)
text.text:
This print, one of 15 contributed by Hakutei to the 50 print series published by Nakajima Jūtarō, pictures laborers unloading what appear to be some type of tile from skiffs on the Taedong River in South Pyongan Province of North Korea.
To the left of the title, the following verse, transcribed in simplified Chinese, is inscribed:
長城一面溶々水 大野東頭點々山
长城一面溶溶水,大野东头点点山
The foot of the moss-grown old rampart/Is washed by blue streams.
Dawn is breaking over the vast fields/And the rows of mountains.
The verse is attributed to the 11th century Koryo dynasty poet Kim Hwang Won (1045-1117) who, it is said, broke his brush and cried, as words failed him to describe the beauty of the view along the Taedong River.
Japan annexed Korea in August 1910 and occupied it until 1945. Hakutei visited Korea in 1910, as did other Japanese artists, to tour the area and exhibit his work in Seoul. As was the fashion, it is likely he participated in what came to be called "sketch tours" during his travels, and that the five prints he created in this Set 8 of the series, subtitled Korea, were based upon sketches he made during his visit.
"The series Nihon fūkei hanga (Japan Scenery Prints) consisted of ten sets of prints, with each set composed of five small landscapes and a cover print giving the name of the series, the name and number of the set, and the name of the artist. In addition, each set was accompanied by a table of contents and colophon sheet. Specific publication dates ranging from January 1917 through April 1920 indicate that each set was issued separately. As Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958) designed the majority of prints in the series, it seems likely that Hakutei was the spearhead for the project. The artists asked Igami Bonkutsu to carve the blocks and Nakajima Jūtarō to publish the series." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 274-276.
In addition to Ishii Hakutei (1182-1958), the other artists who contributed to the series were Sakamoto Hanjirō (1882-1969), see this collection's print Sea of Fire, IHL.0862 and Chikugo River, IHL.2068, Hirafuku Hyakusui (1877-1933), Morita Tsunetomo (1881-1933), Kosugi Misei (1881-1964) and Ishii Tsuruzō (1887-1973), elder brother of Hakutei.

media.caption: Tug of War (つなひき Tsuna hiki)

text.headline: Tug of War (つなひき Tsuna hiki)
text.text: A smaller version, measuring 3 3/4 x 5 7/8 in. (9.4 x 14.9 cm), of a larger 1964 print by the artist, measuring 11.25 x 18.25 in. (28.6 x 46.4 cm), picturing two groups of school children at a game of tug of war. Ikeda Shūzō's best known works are those featuring children, although his later works included landscapes.

media.caption: Iwai Kumesaburō III, Ichikawa Ebizō V and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in a scene from Koi goromo karigane zome (三代目 岩井粂三郎、五代目 市川海老蔵、八代目 市川団十郎・恋衣雁金染)

text.headline: Iwai Kumesaburō III, Ichikawa Ebizō V and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in a scene from Koi goromo karigane zome (三代目 岩井粂三郎、五代目 市川海老蔵、八代目 市川団十郎・恋衣雁金染)
text.text:
The actors (right to left) Iwai Kumesaburō III as the Courtesan (Keisei) Iwasaki, Ichikawa Ebizō V as Bizen'ya Jūbei (びぜんや) and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII as Yamakawaya Gonroku (山川屋権六 ) in a scene from the Kabuki play Koi goromo Karigane zome (恋衣雁金染), staged at the Kawarazaki theater during the first month of 1852.
THE PLAY KOI GOROMO KARIGANE ZOME
The play Koi goromo Karigane zome, written by playwright Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), is based on the story Five Men of Naniwa, about five real-life outlaws who prayed on the residents of Osaka at the turn of the eighteenth century and who were eventually tried and executed in 1702.
While a number of kabuki plays had previously used the Five Men of Naniwa as the basis for their script, Koi goromo Karigane zome "added captivating new twists to the way events unfolded" and left audiences gasping as the five outlaws were executed for killing the samurai Noda Kakuzaemon. In a twist from the real story, the five outlaws are seen as heroes for killing the evil Noda and their punishment is portrayed as an injustice visited upon them by the authorities. - Source: The Merchant's Capital of Early Modern Japan, James L. MacClain and Wakita Osamu, Cornell University Press, 1999, p. 145.

media.caption: The characters Shimanuki Yoso, Akama Genzaemon and Otomi in a scene from Hana to mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku ((島ぬけ与三、赤間源左衛門、愛妾おとみ・ 花覣宿初役)

text.headline: The characters Shimanuki Yoso, Akama Genzaemon and Otomi in a scene from Hana to mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku ((島ぬけ与三、赤間源左衛門、愛妾おとみ・ 花覣宿初役)
text.text:
The actors (right to left) Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in the role of Shimanuki Yoso, Seki Sanjūrō III in the role of Akama Genzaemon and Onoe Baikō IV in the role of the prostitute Otomi 愛妾おとみ.
While only the actor's roles are provided on the print (within the orange cartouches) the website of the Tokyo Metropolitan Library provides the actor's names. The scene pictured in the print was likely from the play titled "Hanato mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku", which was part of a program of three pieces staged in the third lunar month of 1853 at Edo's Nakamura theater. The signpost in the right panel reads on its right side 大当り／＼, or "big hit, big hit!", and on its left the name of play is posted, 武覣熊ヶ谷領 (Hanato mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku).

media.caption:
The actors Ōtani Tomoemon IV, Bandō Shuka I, Nakayama Bungorō II, Bandō Kichiya and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII
(in the play Akegarasu Hana no Nureginu)

text.headline:
The actors Ōtani Tomoemon IV, Bandō Shuka I, Nakayama Bungorō II, Bandō Kichiya and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII
(in the play Akegarasu Hana no Nureginu)
text.text:
The actors (right to left) Ōtani Tomoemon IV in the role of Yamanaya Shirōbei, Bandō Shuka I in the role of the courtesan Yamanaya Urazato, Nakayama Bungorō II in the role Yaritenokaya, Bandō Kichiya in the role of Katsumi and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in the role of Kasugaya Tokijirō in the Kabuki play Akegarasu Hana no Nureginu [明烏花濡衣], staged at the Ichimura theater in Edo during the second month of 1851.
Play Synopsis: Urazato, a courtesan of the Yamana-ya, and her lover, Tokijirō, are the parents of Midori, a child maidservant at the brothel. Since a courtesan’s having a permanent lover is considered an obstacle to the business operations of the Yamana-ya, an attempt is made to separate the pair. One snowy day an employee of the brothel discovers Urazato engaged in a secret rendezvous with Tokijirō. The latter is driven away, and the courtesan is tied to a pine tree in the garden and beaten. Urazato bemoans her ills for a time and weeps. However, Tokijirō steals over the fence and rescues her; the lovers escape with Midori on her father’s back. - Source: Kabuki Encyclopedia, An English-Language Adaption of Kabuki Jiten, Samuel L. Leiter, Greenwood Press, 1979, p. 12-13.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō as Kashiwabara Koheita, Ichikawa Danjūrō as Tokugawa Ieyasu and Ichikawa Sadanji as Kakuya Shichirō in the play Matsu no sakae Chiyoda no shintoku (柏原小平太 尾上菊五郎、徳川家泰公 市川団十郎、 角屋七郎次 市川左団次 ・  松栄千代田神徳)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō as Kashiwabara Koheita, Ichikawa Danjūrō as Tokugawa Ieyasu and Ichikawa Sadanji as Kakuya Shichirō in the play Matsu no sakae Chiyoda no shintoku (柏原小平太 尾上菊五郎、徳川家泰公 市川団十郎、 角屋七郎次 市川左団次 ・  松栄千代田神徳)
text.text: The three greatest actors of the time (from right to left) Onoe Kikugorō V, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX and Ichikawa Sadanji I in the play Matsu no sakae Chiyoda no shintoku, written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1892) and staged at the Shintomi-za in June 1878. The play, which portrayed the life of first Tokugawa shogun, Tokugawa Ieyasu, was the first commercial production in the Shintomi-za and ran for forty-two days, attracting a total of 49,000 theater goers.

media.caption: Evening Sky at Suwa Shrine, Nippori (日暮里 諏方神社 Yūzora, Nippori Suwa jinja)

text.headline: Evening Sky at Suwa Shrine, Nippori (日暮里 諏方神社 Yūzora, Nippori Suwa jinja)
text.text: A later edition of the original 1932 print depicting the torii leading to Suwa Shrine (諏方神社 Suwa jinja) in the Nippori district of Tokyo. The sunset glow backlights this scene and a lone figure, a woman, perhaps with a baby on her back, is seen heading towards a shrine building.

media.caption: Yotsuya Araki Yokochō (四ツ谷荒木横町)

text.headline: Yotsuya Araki Yokochō (四ツ谷荒木横町)
text.text: One of Kōitsu's most popular designs, reprinted many times by the publisher since its original printing in January 1935. This collection's print is a posthumous edition, likely printed between 1981 and 1995. The artist presents us with two geisha bathed in the light of a teahouse in the early evening. Kōitsu's marvelous handling of light is evident in this print.

media.caption: Nezu Shrine (根津神社)

text.headline: Nezu Shrine (根津神社)
text.text:
As falling snow covers the ground, a lone woman leaves only the impression of her footsteps at Nezu Shrine, one of the oldest Shinto shrines in Tokyo, established in 1705 when the 5th shogun Tsunayoshi relocated it from Sendagi to Nezu to commemorate the adoption of Ienobu as his successor. Susanoo no Mikoto is the shrine's the guardian deity.
Originally released in December 1934, this collection's print lacks any publisher seals making its likely printing date sometime between 1960 and the early 1990s. There is at least one other state of this print.

media.caption: Tempura Chef

text.headline: Tempura Chef
text.text: One of Mori's kappizuri-e (stencil prints) depicting craftsmen at work. In this case it's a tempura chef. This print which is unsigned and uneditioned, was also issued in a numbered edition of one hundred.

media.caption: Ships at Night (untitled)

text.headline: Ships at Night (untitled)
text.text:
An unusual subject for Kōgyo. The print exists in several color variations, two of which are in this collection. Print IHL.1193 is the darkest of the color variations. It carries the "Toshihisa" seal of the artist, while other impressions of this print, including this collection's IHL.1716, do not.
"In this composition, a fire in the distance illuminates the sky and creates an effective backdrop to the three moored boats." - Source: The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 151.

media.caption: The Sakawa River and Mount Fuji  (酒匂川と富士)

text.headline: The Sakawa River and Mount Fuji  (酒匂川と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print, Fuji rises in the background as the Sakawagawa meanders between the hills and transmission lines. The stone marker in the left foreground reads "the border of Kanagawa and Shizuoka Prefectures" 神奈川縣 静岡縣 界. The foreground shows us the edge of a traditional looking village with electrical and telephone transmission lines punctuating the landscape. This combining of the traditional with the modern is one of hallmarks of this series.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: A View at the Western Suburb of the Metropolis - Rainy Season (望首都西郊・梅雨 Bo-shuto seikō・baiu)

text.headline: A View at the Western Suburb of the Metropolis - Rainy Season (望首都西郊・梅雨 Bo-shuto seikō・baiu)
text.text:
Published by the Japan Print Association (Nihon Hanga Kyokai) as part of the series One Hundred Views of Tokyo, Message to the 21st Century, the JPA began the series in 1989, commissioning 100 artists over a ten year period to create their impressions of Tokyo. In 2000, the JPA compiled the prints by all 100 artists into ten volumes. In the preface to the series, the JPA notes that the "Tokyo Hyakkei series will serve as 'a witness of time' by the artists and will consist of one hundred views by print by one hundred artists, which ultimately will take ten years in all [and] will present the changing international megalopolis Tokyo. . . . We are confident that [it] will achieve artistic and historical significance. . . ."
Commenting on the print, in which Yoshida employs both photolithography and wood block technique, she states, "Early on, the Tocho (Tokyo Metropolitan Office) was dismissed as an utter waste of tax money. But now, its 45th floor observatory seems to be popular among visitors. I have been on more than one date to that floor with my husband, Hodaka. There, on clear days, the town where I live can be seen beyond Tokyo's western suburbs of Nakano and Suginami. But because of haze, the view is often obstructed. Though most days are covered with this haze, the viewer can still readily see that Tokyo's western suburbs are packed with large and small buildings, apartments and houses. If an earthquake occurs, it is expected that this area will suffer the greatest damage."

media.caption: Outskirts of Nara (奈良郊外 Nara Kōgai)

text.headline: Outskirts of Nara (奈良郊外 Nara Kōgai)
text.text: A view of the rice fields next to Hokki-ji Temple in Ikaruga on the outskirts of Nara. Hokki-ji, a three-storied pagoda, the oldest of its kind in Japan, can be seen in the background. The reflections of the two figures on the right is seen in the flooded paddy. It seems as though Sekino has captured this scene on a moonlit night.

media.caption: The characters Yokosone Heikurō, Shimobe wataru sanpeiI, Gengō Unoki and Yokosone Heitaro in the play Ume yanagi sakigake zōshi (横曽根平九郎、下部弥三平、言号卯の木言号卯の木、横曽根平太郎 ・梅柳魁双紙)

text.headline: The characters Yokosone Heikurō, Shimobe wataru sanpeiI, Gengō Unoki and Yokosone Heitaro in the play Ume yanagi sakigake zōshi (横曽根平九郎、下部弥三平、言号卯の木言号卯の木、横曽根平太郎 ・梅柳魁双紙)
text.text: While only the actor's roles are provided on the print (within the orange cartouches) the website of the Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University provides the actor's names and the title of the play. The actors (right to left) are Nakamura Nakasuke II in the role of Yokosone Heikurō, Nakamura Fukusuke in the roll of Shimobe wataru sanpei, Nakamura Tomijūrō II in the role of Gengō Unoki and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII as Yokosone Heitaro in the play Umeyanagi sakigake zōshi 梅柳魁双紙, staged at the Ichimura theater in Edo during the third lunar month of 1854.

media.caption: Fishing Harbor at Noon (昼の漁港)

text.headline: Fishing Harbor at Noon (昼の漁港)
text.text: One of the artist's many prints picturing small boats along the shore. This print carries the number 4 on its verso, which may indicate that the print is part of an untitled series. See IHL.1476 and IHL.1099 for two other similar prints by the artist.

media.caption: Sakanoshita  (坂ノ下)

text.headline: Sakanoshita  (坂ノ下)
text.text:
Depicting the 48th of 53 stations along the Tōkaidō Road, which connected Edo (modern day Tokyo) where the shōgun resided, to Kyoto, where the emperor resided, the artist shows us two monks seated before a high ranking samurai. Off to the left we see the distinctive Mount Fudesute, which derives its odd name from an incident in which the celebrated artist Kano Motonobu [1476-1553] threw away (sute) his brushes (fude) when he could not capture the beauty of the mountain in a painting. Perhaps the monks are trying to succeed where Motonobu failed.
One of two series of chūban-size vertical prints designed by the artist, a disciple of Hiroshige I, depicting the stations along the Tōkaidō. This series, titled simply Tōkaidō Road (東海道), was published by Tsutaya Kichizō (the same publisher who published Utagawa Hiroshige I's famous "Vertical Tōkaidō" series) between the 8th month of 1863 and the 12th month of 1867, a period of over three years. It is not known why the publishing period was so extended for these prints. Hiroshige II's other series, titled Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (東海道五拾三駅), was issued by the publisher Maruya Tetsujirō in the 10th month of 1865.

media.caption: Yokkaichi (四日市)

text.headline: Yokkaichi (四日市)
text.text:

The artist presents us with a daimyō and his retainers on the coast near Yokkaichi. One of his retainers looks out to sea with a telescope and we are shown a veiled scene of a distant land.

media.caption: Hiratsuka (平塚)

text.headline: Hiratsuka (平塚)
text.text:
Depicting Hiratsuka, the 8th of 53 stations along the Tōkaidō Road connecting Edo (modern day Tokyo), where the shōgun resided, to Kyoto, where the emperor resided. "Like his master, Hiroshige II also produced popular series of prints of the fifty-three stages of the Tōkaidō highway. . . . In the equivalent print of the same place by his master Hiroshige I the scene itself is almost identical, with the round-topped Mount Kōrai dominating the middle-ground, and the snow-capped iconic Mount Fuji just peeping into view behind it." - Source: Comments of Associate Professor Alison Tokita, Monash University on the Monash University website

media.caption: Ōiso (大磯)

text.headline: Ōiso (大磯)
text.text:
Two lonely travelers on horseback cross a river flowing into Sagami Bay on their way to Ōiso, the 9th of 53 stations along the Tōkaidō Road which connected Edo (modern day Tokyo), where the shōgun resided, to Kyoto, where the emperor resided.

media.caption: Horses (馬 Ume)

text.headline: Horses (馬 Ume)
text.text:
This untitled print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, after a 1947 watercolor and 1952 oil painting of the same image, picturing horses outside of a barn, is one of three that make up the series Three Horse Pieces (Uma sandai), published by Mikumo Mokuhansha, first in 1951 in a limited edition of 300 and then again as a stand-alone print in editons of 300 and 700. This print carries no edition number and may be from a separate unnumbered edition.
Sakamoto, a Western-style (yōga) painter, is best known for his paintings and prints of horses. Pursuing his love of horses, he dedicated himself almost exclusively to their depiction, so much so that he “won an unenviable notoriety as a painter ‘picturing nothing but horses.’” In reply to this criticism Hanjirō wrote: "As I am painting only horses, it has been said that my production is merely repetitive. If I am laughed at for this, I am not hurt at all, but if the meaning of such criticism is that the essence of my pictures remains somehow merely conservative, I will be dismayed indeed. I do not care if I repeat the same subject. If this repetition can endlessly improve the content of my art, then, as a painter, I am, rather, proud. I do not necessarily disregard the opinion that painters, as members of society, should take up social problems as motifs, but what matters after all is the intrinsic nature of their work. Even if a painter pictures one stone, his work, depending on his attitude, may act on contemporary society." - source: Paris in Japan: The Japanese Encounter with European Painting; Takashima, Rimer and Bolas, The Japan Foundation and Washington University, 1987, p. 228.
While the artist's painting color palette has been described as "austere," many of his prints use a lighter, pastel-like color palette.

media.caption: Horses in Pasture (Uma sandai 馬三代)

text.headline: Horses in Pasture (Uma sandai 馬三代)
text.text:
This untitled print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, picturing horses grazing in a pasture, is from the three print series known as Three Horse Pieces (Uma sandai), published by Mikumo Mokuhansha, first in 1951 in a limited edition of 300, then again in 1966 as a stand-alone print in editions of 300 and 700 and again sometime after 1966 as an unnumbered edition. This print IHL.1204 is from the unnumbered edition which used a mica infused paper not used in the earlier editions. (Also see IHL.0969 from the first edition.)

Sakamoto, a Western-style (yōga) painter, is best known for his paintings and prints of horses through. Pursuing his love of horses, he dedicated himself almost exclusively to their depiction, so much so that he “won an unenviable notoriety as a painter ‘picturing nothing but horses.’” In reply to this criticism Hanjirō wrote: "As I am painting only horses, it has been said that my production is merely repetitive. If I am laughed at for this, I am not hurt at all, bit if the meaning of such criticism is that the essence of my pictures remains somehow merely conservative, I will be dismayed indeed. I do not care if I repeat the same subject. If this repetition can endlessly improve the content of my art, then, as a painter, I am, rather, proud. I do not necessarily disregard the opinion that painters, as members of society, should take up social problems as motifs, but what matters after all is the intrinsic nature of their work. Even if a painter pictures one stone, his work, depending on his attitude, many act on contemporary society." - Source: Paris in Japan: The Japanese Encounter with European Painting; Takashima, Rimer and Bolas, The Japan Foundation and Washington University, 1987, p. 228.

media.caption: Imamiya Street, Chōshi, at Dusk (薄暮・銚子町今宮通にて Hakubo・Chōshi machi Imamiyadōri nite)

text.headline: Imamiya Street, Chōshi, at Dusk (薄暮・銚子町今宮通にて Hakubo・Chōshi machi Imamiyadōri nite)
text.text: "This print maintains Koitsu Ishiwata's reputation gained for depicting life in Tokyo and Yokohama's streets. Choshi is a port city in the subprefecture Chiba of Tokyo and is a developing tourist destination as well as a home to many industries in Chiba. This print is a characteristic Koitsu scene at dusk in a neighborhood. The depiction of night, darkness, mist and rain became more prominent after the Meiji era because the European influence taught Japanese artists how better to construct space, depth and shadow in darker conditions. This is one of Koitsu's most well known works and is even today in high demand amongst collectors all over the world." - Source: website of the University of Alberta Art Collection https://search.museums.ualberta.ca/11-15855 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Rainy Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜雨 不忍池 Yoru ame, Shinobazunoeki)

text.headline: Rainy Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜雨 不忍池 Yoru ame, Shinobazunoeki)
text.text: A solitary figure walks toward Benten Temple under a steady rain. This print was issued in two color schemes, a more common purple-hued tint (see IHL.0019) and a greyish-hued tint as seen here. Both color schemes were first issued in 1938, as both can be found with the Watanabe type-E publishing seal used by the publisher between 1931 and 1941. This print is likely a first edition based upon the presence of the publisher's "E-type" seal in the lower right margin.

media.caption: Portrait of Kido Takayoshi with a transcript of the biographical sketch of Lord Kido Takayoshi from the Day-by-Day News (木戸孝允公略傳日々新聞ヨリ録 Kido Takayoshi-kōryakuden Nichi Nichi Shinbun yori shō)

text.headline: Portrait of Kido Takayoshi with a transcript of the biographical sketch of Lord Kido Takayoshi from the Day-by-Day News (木戸孝允公略傳日々新聞ヨリ録 Kido Takayoshi-kōryakuden Nichi Nichi Shinbun yori shō)
text.text:
A memorial portrait of the Meiji statesman Kido Takayoshi 木戸孝允 (1883-May 26, 1877), better known as Kido Kōin 木戸孝磯, published nine months after his death by Tokyo publisher Matsuki Heikichi. The print's scroll contains a short biography of Kido taken from the Tokyo newspaper Nichi nichi Shimbun.
This print is most notable for its reproducing, using both traditional and experimental woodblock techniques, the 1872 photo of Kido taken in London. Both the artist Kiyochika Kobayashi (1847-1915) and the publisher were known for their experimentation, and in this print a cross hatching (or net pattern) is used to simulate the wood engraving process that was used for mass reproduction of photographs in the days before half-tone reproduction was invented.

media.caption: The Lament of the Lord appearing in The Ladies' Graphic, Volume 1, Number 3 (おん主の嘆き・婦人グラフ 第1巻第3号 Onnushi no nageki・Fujin gahō)

text.headline: The Lament of the Lord appearing in The Ladies' Graphic, Volume 1, Number 3 (おん主の嘆き・婦人グラフ 第1巻第3号 Onnushi no nageki・Fujin gahō)
text.text: Fukiya, a painter, illustrator and poet, was strongly influenced by Takehisa Yumeji who he was introduced to in 1920 and through whose contacts he would become an illustrator for the magazine The Ladies' Graphic.

media.caption: Takino River, Ōji (王子 滝の川 Ōji Takinogawa)

text.headline: Takino River, Ōji (王子 滝の川 Ōji Takinogawa)
text.text:
One of thirty-four prints in the partially completed series One Hundred Views of Musashi. Visitors saunter along the pathway on the banks of the Takinogawa River running through Ōji during the autumn season. Their reflections, along with those of the maple trees, in the Takinogawa are masterfully created and the design of this print is quite different from the vertical format Hiroshige print of the same name from his series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.
Musashi is the name of the province in which the city of Edo (later named Tokyo) was located. It was once a vast grassy plain and perhaps the long grasses in the lower left of the print are a reference to its once wild state that would have been largely subsumed as Tokyo expanded.

media.caption: Oharame - Carrying Kindling (小原女)

text.headline: Oharame - Carrying Kindling (小原女)
text.text: Tokuriki depicts an Oharame (woman of Ohara) carrying a load of kindling on her head. For generations, the women known as Ohara-me, living in the villages of Yase and Ohara at the the foot of Mt. Hiei located in the north of Kyoto, sold bundles of kindling, flowers and charcoal in Kyoto. Today, the tradition continues as a tourist attraction. Their distinctive traditional dress consists of an indigo blue kosode, white underwear, a red and white thin obi belt, a pair of white tekko protectors, a pair of habaki leg protectors, an apron and waraji straw sandals. Her head is covered with a white tenugui towel. Also see IHL.1213 Oharame (seated).

media.caption: Oharame - Seated (小原女)

text.headline: Oharame - Seated (小原女)
text.text: Tokuriki depicts an Oharame (woman of Ohara) at rest outside a teahouse, her bundle of kindling at her feet.  For generations, the women known as Ohara-me, living in the villages of Yase and Ohara at the the foot of Mt. Hiei located in the north of Kyoto, sold bundles of kindling, flowers and charcoal in Kyoto. Today, the tradition continues as a tourist attraction. media.caption: Poppies from the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花・罌粟 Shikashū・Nihon no hana Nihon no Hana・keshi)

text.headline: Poppies from the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花・罌粟 Shikashū・Nihon no hana Nihon no Hana・keshi)
text.text:
Poppies, a collotype print of an original woodcut by Kawanishi Hide (1894-1965), appears on p. 77 of the 1946 poetry and print book "Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems." It serves as an illustration for a poem of the same name by poet and professor Andō Ichirō (1907-1972).
"Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," was edited and designed by Onchi Kōshirō, a seminal artist in the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement and pioneering book designer. Contributing twelve prints and one poem, Onchi, along with poet Inoue Yasufumi 井上康文 (1897–1973), selected the book's thirty poems by poets such as Satō Haruo (1892-1964), Kitahara Hakushū (1885-1942), Noguchi Yonejirō (1875-1947), Kaoru Maruyama (1899-1974), Tatsuji Miyoshi (1900-1964), Ryuko Kawaji (1888-1959) and Andō Ichirō (1907-1972).
When this book was published in May 1946 "much of the country, including Tokyo where it was printed, remained in ruins following the previous year’s aerial bombardments. . . . Nihon no hana demonstrated the sophisticated aesthetic sensibility of the Japanese people, while providing a hopeful image for the future rebuilding—or 're-flowering'—of the country and its people." - Source: Commentary by Alicia Volk, https://pulverer.si.edu/node/462/title/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Act VII -The Ichiriki Teahouse (七段目 Nanadanme)

text.headline: Act VII -The Ichiriki Teahouse (七段目 Nanadanme)
text.text: One of twelve prints from the series titled Pictorial Siblings to The Treasury of Royal Retainers.  The circular inset on this print depicts the actual scene from act VII of the play Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) in which Rikiya, the son of Yuranosuke, goes to the garden of the Ichiriki teahouse where his father is pretending to live a life of debauchery while he plots revenge against Moronao. Rikiya hands his father a message from Lady Kaoya telling him of Moronao's whereabouts. In the parody of this scene portrayed in the print a wad of tissues are furtively passed to a courtesan by another courtesan, pointing to a night of wild love making.  The young courtesan kneeling by the bamboo fence bites down on her head scarf indicating the passion that the night holds.

media.caption: Dampū 壇風 (The Holy Wind)

text.headline: Dampū 壇風 (The Holy Wind)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 19-21.) - While in exile on the island of Sado, Mibu no Suketomo has been placed in charge of Homma no Saburō. He has now received a strict order from the authorities in Kamakura thatSuketomoe is to be executed immediately, but just before he dies he is able to say farewell to his son Umewaka who arrives from Kyōto with the priestS otsu. Umewaka sees Homma as the cause of his father’s death and with the help of Sotsu, revenges his father by killing him. When they go to escape from the island, however, the boatman refuses to put in to shore for them to board. In answer to the priest’sprayers, a god from Kumano appears and causes a wind to blow the ship back. He then give the boat a following wind so that they are able to escape from their pursuers and return to Kyōto.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Senju 千手

text.headline: Senju 千手
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 155-156) - Shigehara, brought to Kamakura after his capture at the battle of Ichi-no-tani, has been given into the charge of Kano-no-suke Munemochi until his fate is decided. To lighten the tedium of his captivity, Senju-no mae has been sent to comfort him. When she comes on this occasion it is to tell him that even his request to be allowed to enter the priesthood has been refused. Shigehira tells of his regret at having burned the Nara temples, but Senju-no-mae entertains him with song and dance, and Shigehira himself plays a piece on his lute. Dawn comes all too soon, however, and Shigehira is taken away to face his punishment in the capital.
