"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Blockhead (木偶の坊 Dekunobō)

text.headline: Blockhead (木偶の坊 Dekunobō)
text.text:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).
"This print with the title 'pinhead' shows a wooden doll, which looks like a Chinese official. It is modeled on the military commander-in-chief of the Chinese Empire, Li Hongzhang. Next to the doll with the destroyed mouth, a Japanese soldier is also depicted. In the last line, it says 'it's a shame about the mouth', thus, the doll with the destroyed mouth points at the unfortunate loss of Port Arthur. Instead of the port of Port Arthur, the mouth of Port Arthur is mentioned again and again, this is a play with homonyms." - Source: University of Vienna website https://ukiyo-e.univie.ac.at/en/fullview.html?lang=e&docid=941 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Bandō Hikōsaburō, Sawamura Tosshō, Ichikawa Sadanji and Onoe Onoe Kikugorō in the play Hototogisu Date no kikigaki (坂東彦三郎、沢村訥升、市川左団次、尾上菊五郎・早苗鳥伊達聞書)

text.headline: Bandō Hikōsaburō, Sawamura Tosshō, Ichikawa Sadanji and Onoe Onoe Kikugorō in the play Hototogisu Date no kikigaki (坂東彦三郎、沢村訥升、市川左団次、尾上菊五郎・早苗鳥伊達聞書)
text.text: Issued as a promotion for the play Hototogisu Date no kikigaki staged at Tokyo's Shintomi theater in June 1876, this print features, from left to right, Bandō Hikosaburō V 坂東彦三郎 as Harada Kai 原田甲斐, Sawamura Tosshō  II 沢村訥升 as Itakura Naizen 板倉内膳正,  Ichikawa Sadanji I 市川左団次 as Date Aki 伊達安芸 and Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 as Kaminami Sanzaemon 神並三左衛門. The play, written in 1876 by By Kawatake Mokuami 河竹默阿彌 (1816-1893), tells the story of Harada Kai, a Date vassal, and his confederates who are plotting to usurp the power and position of the young leader of the clan, Kamechiyo.

media.caption: Illustration of Garden Cockfight (庭前闘鶏之圖)

text.headline: Illustration of Garden Cockfight (庭前闘鶏之圖)
text.text:
Young samurai, supervised by an elder, watch the beginning of a cockfight in a garden. This print is a 1898 reissue of an 1884 woodblock print of a painting made by Chikanobu for the government sponsored Second Painting Competitive Exhibition, held in April 1884. After the original painting was awarded a bronze prize and then purchased by the Imperial Household Agency, the publisher Morimoto Junzaburō (firm name Entaidō) issued a woodblock print reproduction of the painting in response to public demand.
When this collection's print was reissued fourteen years after the original print, the publisher changed the title, removed explanatory text from the left panel, removed the artist's seal below his signature and changed many of the colors used for the samurai's robes. It is not known why the publisher decided to re-issue this print in 1898.

media.caption: Captain Sakuma Raising a War Cry at the Occupation of the Pescadores (澎湖島占領佐久間大尉吶喊之図 Hōkōtō senryō Sakuma taii totsukan no zu)

text.headline: Captain Sakuma Raising a War Cry at the Occupation of the Pescadores (澎湖島占領佐久間大尉吶喊之図 Hōkōtō senryō Sakuma taii totsukan no zu)
text.text:
One of many prints, by this artist (see IHL.0690, Captain Matsuzaki Fights Bravely in the Battle of Songhwan) and other artists, that glorified the actions of particular officers or soldiers whose tales of valor were recorded by the press. In this print we see Captain Sakuma leading a bayonet-charge of his Fourth Company coming to the aid of the Japanese First and Second Companies during the afternoon of March 23, 1895. Captain Sakuma's Fourth Company, along with the First, Second and Third Companies, had been set ashore earlier in the afternoon from a detachment of transports anchored in the bay of Li-chon-chiao to capture the Kon-peh-tai fort on Pa-chau Island (modern-day Wang-an.)
As the artist was not present at the battle, he constructed this scene largely from his imagination and newspaper reports, as did almost all the artists who portrayed the war. Nine years after this print was published, the publisher of this print, Matsuno Yonejirō, reused the design to depict an engagement during the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905.) For commentary on reuse of print designs depicting the Sino-Japanese War to depict scenes from the Russo-Japanese War see the section titled "Unabashed Plagiarism" on the page for print IHL.0101, Japanese Forces Occupying Yizhou. Russian Soldiers Fleeing to the North Bank of the Yalu.

media.caption: Illustration of the Second National Industrial Exposition at Ueno Park (第二回上野内国勧業博覧会ノ図 Daini uni Ueno naikoku kangyō hakurankai no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Second National Industrial Exposition at Ueno Park (第二回上野内国勧業博覧会ノ図 Daini uni Ueno naikoku kangyō hakurankai no zu)
text.text: Another triptych by Chikanobu (also see IHL.0105) picturing the new art museum in Ueno Park design by Josiah Conder for the Second National Industrial Exhibition. In the foreground courtyard, traditionally attired court ladies mingle in front of the Shōjō Fountain designed by the Yokohama potter Makuzu Kōzan [Miyagawa Kōzan] (1842- 1916).  Whether Chikanobu was presenting the viewer with an imagined scene or if these ladies were part of the retinue of the Empress during her and the Emperor's special visit to the exhibition, is unknown.

media.caption: Telegraphic Record of the Russo-Japanese War: Manchurian Mounted Bandits Destroy Railroad (日露戦争電報実記・馬賊満州鉄道ヲ破壊ス Nichiro sensō denpōjikki・Bazoku Manshūtetsudōo hakai su)

text.headline: Telegraphic Record of the Russo-Japanese War: Manchurian Mounted Bandits Destroy Railroad (日露戦争電報実記・馬賊満州鉄道ヲ破壊ス Nichiro sensō denpōjikki・Bazoku Manshūtetsudōo hakai su)
text.text:
The Trans Siberian Railway gave Russia a huge advantage in the war, allowing Russia to send reinforcements to the war zone in a very short time. In retaliation, Japan engaged honghuzi (Manchurian bandits) to destroy the railway, as illustrated in this print.
During the decade earlier Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895), the honghuzi often attacked the Japanese. (See IHL.0081 Foreign-looking Manchurian Horsemen on an Expedition to Observe the Japanese Camp in the Distance Near Sauhoku.) During the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905), "Japanese adventurers backed by the Imperial Army contacted such gangs and led them on harassing missions behind the Russian lines, blowing up bridges and destroying railway lines in the name of the 'Righteous Army of Manchuria' (Manshū gigun).” - Source: Bandits in Republican China, Phil Billingsley, Stanford University Press, 1988, p. 216.

media.caption: Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX and Bandō Kakitsu in the play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari (岩井半四郎 (八代目)、市川団十郎 (九代目)、坂東家橘・児雷也豪傑物語)

text.headline: Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX and Bandō Kakitsu in the play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari (岩井半四郎 (八代目)、市川団十郎 (九代目)、坂東家橘・児雷也豪傑物語)
text.text:
The actors Iwai Hanshirō VIII in the role of the princess Tagoto hime 田毎姫; Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 in the role of Jiraiya 田毎姫 and Bandō Kakitsu 坂東 家橘 in the role of Takasago Yūminosuke 高砂勇美之助 in the play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari 児雷也豪傑物語 ( (The Heroic Tales of Jiraiya), performed at the Shintomi-za 新富 theater, Tokyo, in August 1881.
The play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari is drawn from an episodic illustrated novel published in multiple volumes from 1839 to 1868. The play, written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), was first performed in July 1852 at the Kawarazaki-za in Edo.
As an infant, Jiraiya’s noble family is slain by Tsukikage, lord of Echigo province and regent of the shogun who has been led astray by his adopted son Orochimaru. Tsukikage adopted Orochimaru after being saved by him from an attack by a giant snake. However, Orochimaru is possessed with the evil snake spirit and eventually kills Tsukikage and comes to rule Echigo. Jiraiya, who along with Tsunate-hime princess of another noble family killed by Tsukikage, has been saved from death by a mountain hermit who teaches them both magic – toad magic in the case of Jiraiya and slug magic in the case of Tsunate-hime. They both vow to take revenge upon Orochimaru. Capturing a magical sword they attack Orochimaru, who attempts suicide but is saved by Takasago Yūminosuke, a high ranking officer for the shogun. Yūminosuke wants to visit a harsh punishment on Orochimaru for his evil deeds, but Jiraiya and Tsunate-hime tell him that Orochimaru’s evil spirit has now been exorcised by the sword. Orochimaru departs in peace.
The character princess Tagoto is the unwilling object of Orochimaru’s affection, who wants her for his wife. - Source: website of the Japan Arts Council http://www2.ntj.jac.go.jp/unesco/kabuki/en/5/5_04_10.html [page no longer accessible 8-17-23]

media.caption: Mera Cape, Izu (妻良岬、 伊豆 Mera-misaki、Izu)

text.headline: Mera Cape, Izu (妻良岬、 伊豆 Mera-misaki、Izu)
text.text: A view of Mera Cape on the Izu Peninsula in Shizuoka Prefecture. The time of day is either sunrise or sunset and small fishing boats are on the bay. The rectangular flat object next on the far right of the print may be one of the artificial reefs built to protect the harbor. Hiratsuka was most interested in portraying the essence of objects rather than realistic renderings and he often used the color yellow for both the sea and sky in his color landscapes of the 1920s and 30s.

media.caption: Lady of the Court Junior Fifth Rank, Uematsu Michiko (從五位、植松務子)

text.headline: Lady of the Court Junior Fifth Rank, Uematsu Michiko (從五位、植松務子)
text.text: One of six prints in the series List of Musical Beauties issued in 1878. In this print the court lady (of the junior fifth rank) Uematsu Michiko plays a hichiriki 篳篥, a small double-reed instrument made out of bamboo with 7 holes on top and 2 below. Her beauty and music are compared to the brambling 獦子鳥 perched on a branch of oleander 夾竹桃 in flower.

media.caption: Lady of the Court Senior Fifth Rank, Yanagihara Naruko (正五位、柳原愛子 Shogoi-i Yanagiwara Naruko)

text.headline: Lady of the Court Senior Fifth Rank, Yanagihara Naruko (正五位、柳原愛子 Shogoi-i Yanagiwara Naruko)
text.text: One of six prints in the series List of Musical Beauties issued in 1878.  In this print the court lady (of the senior fifth rank) Yanagihara Aiko plays a shō (笙) or mouth organ. Her beauty and music are compared to a bush warbler on a Japanese flowering cherry 鶯八隔櫻.

media.caption: Shibaura (しばうら)

text.headline: Shibaura (しばうら)
text.text:
This print is likely a reprint, date unknown, of the original c. 1914-1917 issue. It is one of nine prints in the series Twelve Views of Tokyo. Picturing teahouses in the Shibaura district of Tokyo in the inset, along with a kimono-clad woman (most likely a geisha). As with other prints in the series, this print combines elements of ukiyo-e with modern realism. The series was ended before its completion due to its unpopularity.
The Shibaura district, created on reclaimed land from Tokyo Bay, was, by Ishii's day, on its way to becoming one of Tokyo's first industrial zones and losing its reputation for a place where, in the words of the novelist Osanai Kaoru, "the geisha came, the genuine sort, for delicious assignations."

media.caption: Snow Torture scene from The Pine Tree to which a Colt is Bound on Skylark Mountain (雲雀山駒絆松樹｜雪責)

text.headline: Snow Torture scene from The Pine Tree to which a Colt is Bound on Skylark Mountain (雲雀山駒絆松樹｜雪責)
text.text:
Starring Kataoka Gadō III (R), Nakamura Fukusuke IV (C) and Iwai Matsunosuke (L)
"Reminiscent of tales like Cinderella and Snow White, this play partially retold the 8th century legend of Princess Chūjō (center), daughter of a widowed nobleman whose power-hungry new wife (right) plots against her stepdaughter. The stepmother arranges for a cherished object to be hidden in the princess’s quarters, framing her for theft. When it is discovered there, she insists on punishment, ordering her servants to beat Princess Chūjō outside in the snow. That famous scene, depicted here, involves a former maid (left) fired by the stepmother for her fondness of the princess, entering the garden and preparing to toss her straw cloak to the girl. This act of kindness enrages the stepmother who moves to strike the girl with her long tobacco pipe. As the plot unfolds, other servants enter the fray, and the princess falls to the ground, feigning death. Her father appears, remorseful of his wife’s cruelty, and asks the loyal servants to carry the seemingly lifeless Chūjō to Mount Hibari for burial. Instead, they take her to a cottage in the mountains where Chūjō is eventually reunited with her father. The play was a tour-de-force for three male actors of women’s roles, onnagata." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

media.caption: Novel Growth No. 2 (新しい発生 No.2)

text.headline: Novel Growth No. 2 (新しい発生 No.2)
text.text:
James Michener refers to Masaji's prints as "mysterious" in nature and divides his work into "four clear categories." Novel Growth No. 2 falls into the third category, as described by Michener, as follows:
"Masaji’s third kind of print formed a radical departure and was occasioned, as such new forms ought to be, by a personal crisis within the conscience of the artist. The prints appear mostly in purple and black and always with a swarm of closely knit lines… The designs are tortured, involuted, brooding, and the mysterious colors effectively represent the spirit of the work. These are most distinguished prints, not widely favored by collectors but cherished by those who know the artist and who are concerned with the artistic problems inherent in the modern school of woodblock prints. What dark experience of the soul called forth this series I do not know, but during its issue Masaji’s son died, and the prints form a fitting memorial to this tragedy, although they were not originally called forth by it. Connoisseurs of the exquisite in art should know these prints, for they are some of the most expert issued in Japan, veritable masterpieces of printing and color. They exhibit no quick allure and one comes to them quietly after having known other prints that on the surface are much more enticing; but when one has discovered their quiet mastery one recognizes in them a milestone in contemporary Japanese woodblocks. - Source: The Modern Japanese Print - An Appreciation, James Michener, Charles E. Tuttle Co., 1968, p. 48-49
See IHL.0213 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Act VII (七段目 Shichidanme)

text.headline: Act VII (七段目 Shichidanme)
text.text: This print depicts a scene from Act VII of a jōruri performance of the play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase which played at the Ichimura-za on May 7, 1865. Iichimura Kakitsu IV seated on the far left and Bandō Mitsugorō VI to his right are providing a chanted narrative, accompanied by Ichikawa Shinsha on shamisen. In front of them we see Bandō Hikosaburō V as Teraoka Heiemon and his younger sister (Imōto) Okaru. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University notes 人形見ぶり for Hikosaburō's role, indicating that he is acting in a puppet-like style, using the exaggerated motions associated with puppetry.

media.caption: Sheet 1-4, Ogimachi Kanamebashi Riverside Log Landing (扇町要橋川辺丸太水揚げ  一ノ四)

text.headline: Sheet 1-4, Ogimachi Kanamebashi Riverside Log Landing (扇町要橋川辺丸太水揚げ  一ノ四)
text.text:
One of forty-eight prints included in the portfolio titled "Famous Places of Kiba," issued in 1927. The prints illustrate the customs and habits of the inhabitants, and the scenery, of the lowlands around the Sumida River estuary with particular attention being paid to activity around Fukagawa Kiba 深川木場, the home for the lumberyards servicing the city from about 1641 until the mid-1970s, located east of the Sumida River's mouth. Each print in the portfolio provides descriptive text of the scene in the margin and was originally accompanied by a sheet with further description.
This print pictures a log landing in Kiba, Fukagawa by the Kaname bridge.

media.caption: Serving Spiced Rice Wine (お流れ Onagare)

text.headline: Serving Spiced Rice Wine (お流れ Onagare)
text.text:
This print is from a series of 40 scenes, published 1895-1896, documenting life inside the women quarters of the shogun's palace in Edo, prior to the Meiji Restoration in 1868. "On the first morning of the new year, a special spiced wine (otosu) is drunk before breakfast and thought to bring good health throughout the coming year. Usually the youngest member of the family or group is served first, and in Chikanobu's print, a young woman raises a red lacquered wine cup to receive the invigorating brew from Inner Palace matron (jōrō toshiyori), while older women solemnly wait their turn in the background. The beverage is made by steeping overnight various flowers, herbs and roots in sweet rice wine (mirin). The two folding screens are painted with pine, bamboo, and plum branches (shōchikubai), the traditional evergreens and early blossoms associated with the new year."[1]

THE INNER PRECINCTS OF CHIYODA
"Chikanobu imagines something he never saw—the inner precincts of Edo Castle, which housed the shogun’s mother, wife, and concubines. The area was off limits to all men other than the shogun himself or his young male heir."[2] "The Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku) series of 1895-1896, together with his 1897 series Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the Chiyoda Inner Palace set, Chikanobu documented various annual ceremonies in the women’s quarters, especially those at New Year’s, and seasonal activities, particularly those conducted in the palace gardens. While Chikanobu did not indicate specific events or name certain people that would link these images to a single date or time period, the scenes give an overall impression of what the shogun’s private quarters might have looked like in the mid-19th century. "Most women depicted in Chiyoda Inner Palace are portrayed as elegant dignified ideal feminine figures, showing little emotion or excitement. No one seems happy or sad, ebullient or upset. In fact, these imaginary depictions suggest a realm of tranquil harmony, without conflict or illness. Only two old women are shown, and most of the more than 150 featured figures are youthful looking, appearing to be in their 20’s or early 30’s. A few girls are present, but even they are well behaved; no babies or pregnant women are evident. There is a sense of tension among the women, though, as ritual gestures and prescribed ceremonies are carried out with great seriousness. Although some settings are animated by secondary figures (servants, actors, parade participants, etc.) or pet animals, overall the quiet rhythm of life in the Chiyoda Inner Palace is predominant and well described."[3]

[1] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 172.
[2] Portland Art Museum http://portlandartmuseum.us/mwebcgi/mweb.exe?request=record;id=46772;type=101 [accessed 8-30-23]
[3] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 169.

text.headline: Chiarini's Astounding Circus (鳴響茶利音曲馬 Narihibiku Chiarini no kyokuba)
text.text: A wonderful tour de force of animals and actors playing circus performers, promoting Kawatake Mokuami's kabuki play Narihibiku Chiarini no kyokuba based upon the visit of Giuseppe Chiarini's Royal Italian Circus to Japan in the summer of 1886. This type of play, written shortly after the events it depicts, was known as ichiyazuke kyōgen (overnight pickle play.) The star of the play was Onoe Kikugorō V, playing three roles.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Musashibō Benkei in the play Kanjinchō (九世市川団十郎 武蔵坊弁慶・勧進帳)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Musashibō Benkei in the play Kanjinchō (九世市川団十郎 武蔵坊弁慶・勧進帳)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, playing the role of the warrior priest Benkei in the kabuki play Kanjinchō (The Subscription List). Above his likeness is an unidentified actor in the role of Togashi 冨樫.
"Ichikawa Danjūrō VII created this play which he based on a Nō play called 'Ataka.' It was first performed in 1840. Minamoto Yoshitsune is with his followers and his most faithful retainer Benkei, fleeing from the soldier of his nasty and insecure brother, Yoritomo. He has to pass through the Ataka barrier to reach the northern part of Japan. Togashi who was warned by Yoritomo that Yoshitsune and his party would try to get through disguised as mountain priest is immediately suspicious when they arrive. Benkei announces that they are collecting money for the restoration of the Tōdai Temple in Nara but Togashi argues that if they were real priests they would have a subscription list. Benkei immediately produces one and skillfully 'reads' it. Admiring his loyalty and presence of mind Togashi decides at this moment to let them pass through. He is by now enjoying their act and even offers to contribute to their fund. They are allowed to leave but then a guard warns Togashi that one of the priests looks like Yoshitsune. Togashi cannot ignore this and probably hopes that Benkei will save the situation. Benkei initially feebly argues that it is possible for people to look like others but then out of sheer despair strikes Yoshitsune with a wooden stick. In the end Benkei, who was treated to food and drink and performed a dance for Togashi leaves on the hanamichi quietly thanking him since he knows that Togashi will have to commit suicide."[1]
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series." - Source: website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1985, p. 14.
[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

text.headline: Takegawa 竹川

media.caption: Saburō 三郎

text.headline: Saburō 三郎
text.text:
An unidentified actor as Saburō in an unknown play. The famous view in the background inset is unidentified but might read 雲橋, Cloud Bridge. The print is numbered sixty-two (六十二) in the title cartouche.
This series matches actors portraying a specific character with famous places in Edo. It consists of at least 58 prints drawn by multiple artists, including Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900), Utagawa Kuniteru II (1830-1874) and Utagawa Yoshiiku (1833-1904) and published by Masudaya Ginjirō. Two slightly different series titles are used on the prints: 江都名所合之内 Kōto meisho awase no uchi and 江戸名所合之内 Edo meisho awase no uchi. Note that Kōto was a synonym for Edo.

media.caption: Beauty Drinking Tea

text.headline: Beauty Drinking Tea
text.text:
Amy Reigle Newland in "Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900)," offers the follow commentary on this print and the series it is part of:
"A contemporary bijin sits sipping tea in a tea house, the interior of which is rendered using single point perspective introduced to Japan by the Dutch in the 17th century and in wide use in Japan by the late 18th century. Complicated interior settings [appear in the series] Newly woven brocades: Musashi beauties (Nishiki ori Musashi no beppin) of 1883. Here Musashi is a reference to the Musashi plain, which extended across Edo (modern Tokyo). References to the Musashi plain emerged in early Japanese poetry . . . . The theme was taken up by ukiyo-e print designers, thus becoming strongly linked to Edo's cultural indentity. In Newly woven brocades half-to three-quarter length portraits of individual women from the capital are placed in both interior and exterior settings. . . ."
Newland goes on to say that the artist's rendering of beauties in this series offer a "more personalized female image more characteristic of Kunichika's age" and are a "far cry from lofty, unapproachable courtesan" of earlier times.

media.caption: Seven Variations in a Kyōka Contest in the Bunsei Era (文政狂歌合七變化)

text.headline: Seven Variations in a Kyōka Contest in the Bunsei Era (文政狂歌合七變化)
text.text:
A print designed by an unknown artist signing his name 魁州 which can be read as "Kaishū". The artist presents us with a strange assortment of Bunsei Era (1818-1830) characters engaged in writing comic tanka (kyōka) as part of a poetry contest with the theme of sake. From right to left we see a farmer, a calligrapher, the Thunder God, a child, the poet Hitomaru (one of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets), an apprentice geisha and a samurai carrying a long sword over which is slung a tsunodaru used for transporting sake.
The print references the Go Gawa (五側) poetry club, active during the Bunsei Era. Members of the club often wrote poetry on illustrated surimono, and signed their work with the Go Gawa symbol, an hourglass resembling the number five. The Go Gawa symbol appears on the sake bottles in the center panel and on the object in the farmer's left hand.

media.caption: Kabuki Playbill for Plays at the Initial Opening of the Imperial Theater: Yoritomo, Igagoe and Hagoromo (辻番付 帝国劇場初開場番付・頼朝、伊賀越、羽衣)

text.headline: Kabuki Playbill for Plays at the Initial Opening of the Imperial Theater: Yoritomo, Igagoe and Hagoromo (辻番付 帝国劇場初開場番付・頼朝、伊賀越、羽衣)
text.text:
The playbill (tsuji banzuke) from the opening performances in March 1911 at the new Imperial Theater (Teikoku gekijō). The three plays illustrated are (from right to left) Yoritomo 頼朝, Igagoe 伊賀越 and Hagoromo 羽衣. In addition to the names of the play given in the illustrations, they appear again with details of their various scenes in the rectangular box at the bottom of the print, along with the names of the cast members and their roles, and the theater name written in kanteiryū, a special calligraphy used in the Kabuki theater. Among the many cast members are the three leading actors of the Imperial Theater's in-house troupe, Onoe Baikō (尾上梅幸) VI, Ichikawa Komazō (市川高麗蔵) VIII and Sawamura Sōjūrō (沢村宗十郎) VII.
The paper used for this playbill appears to be dusted with mica.

media.caption: Illustrations of Noh, Index, volume 1 (能楽図絵 前編  目録 Mokuroku, zenpen)

text.headline: Illustrations of Noh, Index, volume 1 (能楽図絵 前編  目録 Mokuroku, zenpen)
text.text:
The first of five Table of Content prints (mokuroku) from the series Nōgakuzue (Illustrations of Noh).

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Ikina (伊企儺)

text.headline: Ikina (伊企儺)
text.text:
Print number 1 (壹), and one of 4 designs contributed by Yoshitoshi to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Tsuki no Kishi Ikina defying the Silla commander who has ordered him to take down his pants, point his buttocks toward Japan and shout "Japanese generals, bite my ass." Ikina's response is to shout "King of Silla, eat my ass!" shocking the Silla commander, seen on the ground, who orders Ikina's torture and death. For a "deluxe" impression of this print see IHL.1921.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as the Englishman Spencer and Onoe Ushinosuke II as Spencer in the distance [inset] in the play Riding the Famous Hot-Air Balloon (英人スペンサー 尾上菊五郎・遠見 尾上丑之助・風船乗評判高楼)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as the Englishman Spencer and Onoe Ushinosuke II as Spencer in the distance [inset] in the play Riding the Famous Hot-Air Balloon (英人スペンサー 尾上菊五郎・遠見 尾上丑之助・風船乗評判高楼)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the English balloonist Percival Spencer (1864-1913) in the dance play Riding the Famous Hot-Air Balloon (Fūsen Nori Uwasa Takadono), staged as the final piece (ōgiri) on the January 1891 bill at the Kabuki-za. The inset in the top left shows the actor Onoe Ushinosuke II, the five year old son of Onoe Kikugorō V, playing the tōmi, airborne version of the balloonist.[1]
"In the play Kikugorō addressed the audience in English while suspended from the theatre’s rigging: 'Ladies and gentlemen. I have been up three thousand feet. Looking down, I was pleased to see you in this Kabuki-za. Thanks [sic] you. Ladies and gentlemen, with all my heart, I thank you.' The play was enthusiastically received during thirty-three-day run."[2]
The play, written by Kawatake Mokuami ( (1816-1893), was based upon the balloon ascent, and descent by parachute, in Ueno Park by the English balloonist Percival Spencer in November 1891.

In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

[1] Tōmi 遠見 ("Distant View") - a kabuki convention meaning both a painted background showing a perspective vista and a way of indicating distant characters by having child actors placed upstage and dressed in exactly the same costumes as the adult players as if the latter were being seen from far away. - Source: New Kabuki Encyclopedia: A Revised Adaptation of Kabuki Jiten, Samuel Leiter, Greenwood Press, 1997, p. 655.
[2] Kabuki Plays on Stage: Restoration and Reform, 1872-1905, ed., James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 17-18.

media.caption: Spleen (鬱念 Utsunen)

text.headline: Spleen (鬱念 Utsunen)
text.text: As with many of Rei's prints, the artist has presented us with a landscape "set in ambiguous space", to use Helen Merritt's words. Dark indigo vertical lines which may portray a heavy rain are interspersed with subtle light indigo and yellow-green broken lines to provide depth to the image.  Along with the celestial shapes, Rei gives us a Mt. Fuji-like image on the right and, perhaps, a cityscape along the left part of the dark indigo vertical bar that scoops under Fuji on the right. (See IHL.0613 for an artist's proof of this print.)

media.caption: Distant Home (遠い里 Tōi sato)

text.headline: Distant Home (遠い里 Tōi sato)
text.text: A small semi-abstract work in bold colors in which we can make out a figure on the right and, perhaps, a boat on the bottom. A frequent traveler, as were all the Yoshida family artists, perhaps this print is a longing to be back in Tokyo while on one of his many sojourns.

media.caption: Miniprint Y (ミニプリント Y)

text.headline: Miniprint Y (ミニプリント Y)
text.text:
Miyashita created a number of undated small prints that he denoted as "Miniprint" or "Mini Print" in their titles. On some of these "miniprints" he also added ミニプリント (minipurinto) in katakana. The paper size of these prints is approximately 7 x 5 in. (17.8 x 12.7 cm) with the image area encompassing only a small portion of the paper. (Also see IHL.1270 and IHL.1271)
In this print, Miniprint Y, Miyashita has perhaps given us a "postcard" of one of his travels, as we see a sign for Rome and, possibly, Athens. As with most of his prints, the deeply deeply saturated colors immediately catch our eye and we are drawn into the image by his reverse embossing achieved through intaglio printing.

media.caption: Index, The Kabuki Eighteen (歌舞伎十八番・目録)

text.headline: Index, The Kabuki Eighteen (歌舞伎十八番・目録)
text.text:
The title page and index (mokuroku 目録) for the series The Kabuki Eighteen.
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. The eighteen plays are 不破 (Fuwa), 矢の根 (Yanone), 鳴神 (Narukami), 関羽 (Kan'u), 不動 (Fūdō), 七ツ面　(Nanatsumen), 嫐 (Uwanari), 毛抜 (Kenuki), 押戻し (Oshimodoshi), 景清 (Kagekiyo), 象引 (Zohiki), 鎌髭 (Kamahige), 助六 (Sukeroku), 解脱 (Gedatsu), 暫 (Shibaraku), 蛇柳 (Jayanagi), 外郎 (Uirō Uri) and 勧進帳 (Kanjinchō). In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[1]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

media.caption: Sawamura Tosshō II as Kōbō Daishi, Kawarazaki Gonjūrō as Fudō Myōō and Nakamura Shikan IV as Daikoku in the play Kaihi sandai banashi (沢村訥升 (二代目) 弘法大師、河原崎権十郎 不動明王、中村芝翫 (四代目) 大黒天・開扉三題はなし)

text.headline: Sawamura Tosshō II as Kōbō Daishi, Kawarazaki Gonjūrō as Fudō Myōō and Nakamura Shikan IV as Daikoku in the play Kaihi sandai banashi (沢村訥升 (二代目) 弘法大師、河原崎権十郎 不動明王、中村芝翫 (四代目) 大黒天・開扉三題はなし)
text.text:
A comic performance authored by the famous rakugo storyteller of the time, Ryūtei Enshi 柳亭燕枝 (1838-1900). Given the red banner displaying the characters 成田山 (Narita-san) held by one of the spectators, as seen on the far right of the right sheet, it is likely that this play is being staged at or near Narita-san temple (the head temple of the Chisan sect of Shingon Buddhism) in Fukagawa, where the deity, the Wrathful Bright King Fudō Myōō, is worshipped. The timing of this performance was likely coincident with one of the periodic public displays (unveilings) of sacred objects (kaichō) held by Narita-san and other temples to raise funds.
The right sheet of this print shows Sawamura Tosshō II in the role of the monk/spiritual leader Kōbō Daishi, founder of Shingon Buddhism, who is said to have carved an image of Fudō Myōō while in China in the early 800s which he used to pacify the waves in a great storm.
The center sheet shows Kawarazaki Gonjūrō, who will take the name of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in 1884, as the deity Fudō Myōō surrounded by flames representing the burning of anger and passion to purify the mind.
The left sheet shows Daikoku, the god of good fortune, whose presence may relate to the fund raising aspect of the kaichō.
The three figures are matched with three low-city districts in early Tokyo, renowned for working-class entertainment and commerce: god of good fortune Daikoku is matched with Asakusa; the Fudō Myōō of the Narita-san temple complex is matched with Fukagawa; and the monk/spiritual leader Kōbō Daishi is matched with Ryōgoku.

media.caption: Nakamura Shikan, Sukedakaya Takasuki, Ichikawa Danjūrō and Bandō Kakitsu in the play Sukeroku, Flower of Edo (中村芝翫、助高屋高助、市川団十郎、坂東家橘・助六由縁江戸桜)

text.headline: Nakamura Shikan, Sukedakaya Takasuki, Ichikawa Danjūrō and Bandō Kakitsu in the play Sukeroku, Flower of Edo (中村芝翫、助高屋高助、市川団十郎、坂東家橘・助六由縁江戸桜)
text.text: "A new Tokyo theater wecomed Meiji audiences with an updated version of the classic blockbuster about Sukeroku, the samurai-turned-street-fighter (otokodate) who stands up for the little guy, played by Ichikawa Danjūrō IX. He appears, left, with his characteristic purple head wrap, beside his brother, played by Bandō Kakitsu. In the center is the courtesan Agemaki, played by Sukedakaya Takasuke IV, Skukeroku's lover, garbed in magnificence, all of them fending off the evil Ikyū played by Nakamura Shikan IV, who bears the sword that was stolen from Sukeroku." - Source: wallcard from the exhibition "Kabuki: A Revolution in Color and Design," Portland Japanese Garden, July 29-September 3, 2017.

media.caption: The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest (西南雲晴朝東風 Okige no kumo harau asa kochi)

text.headline: The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest (西南雲晴朝東風 Okige no kumo harau asa kochi)
text.text: From right to left, the actors Iwai Hanshirō VIII 岩井半四郎 as Aki the mistress of Kishino Toshiaki 岸野の妾おあき (the mistress of Kirino Toshiaki in real life); Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 as Saijō Takamori 西條高盛 (Saigō Takamori in real life) and Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 as Hyakushō Sakuzō 百姓作蔵 in the play Okige no kumo harau asagochi (The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest), written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), produced by Morita Kanya (1846-1897) and performed at Morita's Shitomi Theater beginning in February 1878. The background text is dialogue between Danjūrō's character and Sadanji's character. The play dramatized the recently ended Satsuma Rebellion which pitted rebellious samurai mainly from the Southwest (Satsuma and Chōshū provinces) under the leadership of Saigō Takamori against the vastly superior forces of the new Meiji government. The use of contemporary subject matter, the graphic depiction of the battle scenes (which used fireworks onstage), and the popular sympathy for the defeated hero Saigō Takamori all contributed to the enormous success of the play which ran for eighty days.

media.caption: Bronze Statue of Saigō in Ueno Park (上野 公園 西郷銅像 Ueno Kōen Saigō dōzō)

text.headline: Bronze Statue of Saigō in Ueno Park (上野 公園 西郷銅像 Ueno Kōen Saigō dōzō)
text.text:
A spring day in Ueno Park with the cherry trees in bloom and strollers lingering by the recently erected bronze statue of Saigō Takamori, a leader in both the 1867 Meiji Reformation that overthrew the shogun, restoring the emperor and bringing a modern government into power, and the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion which sought to overthrow that same government.
Sitting on a rise near the main entrance to the park, the statue was designed by Takamura Kōun (1852-1934) and unveiled on December 18, 1898. Oriented so that it faces Edo Palace, it promotes Saigō in his earlier role as the hero of the Restoration who led the imperial army in its takeover of Edo Castle, not as the disgruntled leader of samurai interests who had been forsaken by the Tokyo regime. The statue pictures Saigō in informal attire with his dog and conjures the earlier military leader, diplomat and humanist who cherished slogan was 'Revere Heaven, love mankind' and whose spiritual and physical magnanimity earned him the epithet 'Saigo the Great' and the adoration of an entire nation.

media.caption: Kinryūzan Kaminarimon (金竜山風雷門)

text.headline: Kinryūzan Kaminarimon (金竜山風雷門)
text.text: Asakusa Kannon is the popular name of the temple more properly known as Kinryūzan Sensō-ji, dating back to 628. This print pictures the temple's Furai-mon (Wind and Thunder Gate) with its huge lantern reading 志ん橋 Shinbashi (an area in Edo whose constituents contributed funds for the lantern.) This print is marked 古 "old" in the upper right-hand margin, indicating it is a view from the past. It was originally issued as the top half of an ōban size sheet, with the bottom sheet showing a "present" view of the temple grounds. It is one of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, that make up the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present.

media.caption: Yoroi Ferry at Koami-chō (よろひのわたし小阿ミ町  Yoroi no watashi Koamichō)

text.headline: Yoroi Ferry at Koami-chō (よろひのわたし小阿ミ町  Yoroi no watashi Koamichō)
text.text:
This print and its companion print IHL.1290 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. Both prints are views within Nihonbashi, the most densely populated area of Tokyo. This print provides a past (古 old) view of the Yoroi Ferry, which carried passengers across the Nihonbashi canal to at Kabuto-chō to Koami-chō, Tokyo’s mercantile quarter of Nihonbashi, an area filled with warehouses stocked with rice, soy, and oil. It is matched with a present (今 now) view on print IHL.1290, depicting the Yoroi Bridge, built in 1873, that replaced the Yoroi Ferry. In the present view, a gentleman in modern Western-style dress carrying a walking stick is seen in the foreground. Interesting and confusing is how the Yoroi Bridge, built as a Western-style iron bridge, is depicted, showing no modern elements of steel construction.
These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, that make up the series.

media.caption: Ōji Paper Company Viewed from Asukayama Park (飛鳥山公園地王子製紙会社 Asukayama kōenchi Ōji seishi kaisha)

text.headline: Ōji Paper Company Viewed from Asukayama Park (飛鳥山公園地王子製紙会社 Asukayama kōenchi Ōji seishi kaisha)
text.text:
This print and its companion print IHL.1291 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print (IHL.1285) presents a present (今 "now") view of Asukayama Park where a group of men gaze out to the Ōji Paper Company founded in 1873 by the industrialist Shibusawa Eiichi (渋沢 栄一, 1840–1931). Its companion print (IHL.1291) presents an old (古) view of Asukayama Park, where women are playing kawarake-nage (throwing unglazed or sun-dried earthenware from a high place with prayers for warding off evil and enjoying watching them flying in the wind).
These past and present views were originally printed together as one oban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut oban-size sheets, in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present. Many of the views are similar to those found in Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei).

media.caption: From Science and Experience: Essential Medicines for Health (學理と經驗とにより・配劑せられたる衛生の要藥)

text.headline: From Science and Experience: Essential Medicines for Health (學理と經驗とにより・配劑せられたる衛生の要藥)
text.text:
A Taishō era (1912-1936) woodblock printed advertisement (hikifuda) for "medicines for health, based on science and experience." Displayed in the top center of the print is a trademark seemingly made up of the characters 井本 ("Imoto" or "Inomoto"), possibly the trademark of the manufacturer of the five medicines being advertised or a trademark associated with the named pharmacy 磯矢榮壽軒薬房 (possibly reading "Isoya Eijuken pharmacy") located in 伊賀玉瀧 (Tamataki Iga-shi), as printed in the top left corner within the image. The five medicines listed beneath the trademark are,
ヘブリン丸 Heburingan (a cold medicine in pill form)
ヒスミシト丸 (くだりとめ) (possibly an anti-diarrheal in pill form)
五龍圎 (かんぐすり) (possibly a nerve medicine)
胃痛散 (ぬびやりのく〓) (a stomach care powder, also known in Chinese as wèi tòng powder)
腹痛丸 (〓らぐすり) (a stomach ache pill).
In this print, a group of rugged boys are engaged in a strenuous physical activity, which is supplemented with dialogue between the boys. The boy wearing the shirt with the trademark stands his ground against the "frontal attack" of his opponents, while calling the two boys on the left "scaredy-cats." His opponents are in awe telling our boy hero, "your legs are like stone." An interesting choice of illustration to advertise the efficacy of the medicines being sold, cold and stomach medications, but consistent with the statement appearing in the left margin, "The effectiveness of a product depends on the individual's attention to personal health and quality of life."
Building brand and trust for patent medicines was important in an industry that competed not only with other patent medicine companies but with drug companies providing western and scientifically developed products. This collection's print contains the following assurances from the chief pharmacist 擔當薬製師:
Each product is made from the finest raw materials.
Each product is made to the highest standards of quality.
Our products are the most effective and ready-to-use medicine available.
The best medicines for health and to lose weight.
I hope it will be the best medicine for you.

media.caption: Kawarasaki Kunitarō as Ōkaru (河原崎国太郎 おかる)

text.headline: Kawarasaki Kunitarō as Ōkaru (河原崎国太郎 おかる)
text.text: One of a series of prints highlighting individual actors in their roles in the July 1866 performance of the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (variously translated as The Treasury of Loyal Retainers or Revenge of the 47 Ronin or The Revenge of the 47 Loyal Samurai) at the Ichimura-za. This print features the actor Kawarazaki Kunitarō I ( 河原崎国太郎 1849-1867) in the role of Okaru おかる in Act VI of the play.

media.caption: Angry Sumo Fan Demands Refund, No. 1050 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・千五拾號)

text.headline: Angry Sumo Fan Demands Refund, No. 1050 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・千五拾號)
text.text:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞. This print tells the story of an angry sumo fan, a Mr. Yamada, attending a sumo match near Hamamatsu station in Tōtōmi Province, who argues with the promoter about a refund of his ticket fee, as the rain has interfered with part of the wrestling match. At one point he jumps into the ring and tears down a curtain and creates quite a commotion. As we can see from the graphic, the promoter is in some pain from returning Mr. Yamada's fee.
The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

media.caption: Akasaka Temporary Place (Akasaka karikōkyo 赤坂仮皇居)

text.headline: Kawarake-nage at Asukayama Park (飛鳥山かわらけなげ Asukayama kawarake-nage)
text.text:
This print and its companion print IHL.1285 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. media.caption: Toyotomi Hideyasu (織田信長)

text.headline: Toyotomi Hideyasu (織田信長)
text.text:
Print number 34 (三十四), and one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, portraying Toyotomi Hideyasu 織田信長 (1574-1607), (adopted son of Toyotomi Hideyoshi), shedding tears at the performance of the dancer Okuni 阿国 in Fushimi 伏見 Castle. While there is historical evidence for Okuni's performance at Fushimi, whether Hideyasu was actually moved to tears is unknown.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Takayama Hikokurō (高山彦九郎)

text.headline: Takayama Hikokurō (高山彦九郎)
text.text:
Print number 45 (四十五) as shown in the series' Table of Contents, although not numbered on the print. One of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series. This print pictures Takayama Hikokurō (1747-1793) one of the "three eccentrics of the Kansei era" and a fierce proponent of reverence for, and loyalty to, the emperor. In this scene he angrily tosses aside a book about shogun Ashikaga Takauji's usurpation of imperial authority. Ashikaga defeated the Imperial Court in 1336 and established the Ashikaga Shogunate that ruled japan from 1336 to 1573.

media.caption: Akazome Emon (赤染衛門)

text.headline: Akazome Emon (赤染衛門)
text.text:
Print number 6 (六), and one of 13 designs contributed by Inoue to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the poetess Akazome Emon (赤染衛門 956–1041) leaving Sumiyoshi Shrine after offering her life for the life of her ill son. The story is told in the Konjaku Monogatarishū (今昔物語集 Anthology of Tales from the Past), a collection of over one thousand tales written during the late Heian period (794-1185), as follows: Ōe no Takachika, 大江の挙周 (c. 977-1046) the son of the 11th century poetess Akazome Emon fell seriously ill after he became Governor of Izumi. Akazome Emon, much aggrieved, dedicated a sacred staff with a poem offering her life for her son’s to Sumiyoshi Shrine. The poem read:
The life I pray
Be taken in place of his
I do not begrudge;
But on the parting
Is so bitter!

That night in a dream she saw a white-haired old man take the poem. Takachika recovered completely.
Inoue, a student of Kobayashi Kiyochika, contributed thirteen prints to this series. He was to die at the age of 25 in 1889, three years after this print was issued.

media.caption: Hanawa Hokiichi (塙保己一)

text.headline: Hanawa Hokiichi (塙保己一)
text.text:
This unnumbered print was issued in November 1890 as a replacement for the Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) print of the same subject issued in January 1886. It is likely that the blocks for the Kiyochika print were damaged or lost and that Toshikata was asked to provide a new design on the same subject.
Toshikata's print portrays the same anecdote about Hanawa Hokiichi (1746-1821), the blind Scholar of National Learning (kokugakusha) and his students, as Kiyochika's print in which Hanawa was once reading with his students the well-known novel Genji Monogatari. The lecture room was rather small, and was provided with only one lamp, by the light of which the students were just able to see their books. But while they were busily taking notes of their master's lecture, a puff of wind suddenly blew out the lamp and left them in darkness. Hanawa, being quite unaware of this, calmly went on with his lecture; but the students, being of course unable to see to read or write, had to ask their master to stop for a few moments.
"Why, what is the matter?" inquired Hana-wa.
"It is the light, sir," they replied "The wind has blown out the light, and we can't see our books. Please wait a moment till we light the lamp again."
Hanawa smiled when he heard this, and replied, "That shows the inconvenience of having to depend on eyes; for when the light goes out, you suddenly become blind and helpless. But as for me, I'm fortunate in never having any trouble of this kind."
This scene, originally published in 1886, was recreated by the artist Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) in 1890 as a replacement for this print whose blocks were possibly lost or damaged. (See IHL.1283.) While the designs differ, the scroll-like cartouche on both prints contain exactly the same information.

media.caption: Maiko (舞妓)

text.headline: Maiko (舞妓)
text.text: The artist pictures this maiko with a beautiful chrysanthemum (kiku) kanzashi (hair ornament) associated with the month of October.

media.caption: Loving Service Hanga Seal (portfolio folder)

text.headline: Loving Service Hanga Seal (portfolio folder)
text.text:
Onchi designed the folder for this portfolio titled, a bit strangely, "Loving Service Seal HANGA." Published by The Central Community Chest of Japan, Inc. to familiarize foreigners with the revival of Japanese woodblock printing, the portfolio contains ten very small perforated gummed woodblock prints by the artists Kitaoka Fumio (1918-2007). see IHL.0977, and Shinagawa Takumi (1908-2009), see IHL.0976. The folder itself, has two woodblock printed images on it designed by Onchi. On the front is a view of a snow covered Mount Fuji, with the portfolio's title above it, and on the back is an image of a young girl holding a snow rabbit (yuki usagi). In addition to the two sets of gummed prints, the portfolio contains an introduction by Onchi to the "Japanese woodcut print" and its "recent trends," by which Onchi means the "creative print" (sōsaku hanga) movement and a brief historical and process overview of the "Japanese woodcut print" by the publisher.
The cover prints by Onchi, which are not listed in the catalog raisonné of his prints, "Prints of Onchi Koshiro," Keishosha, 1975, were two of his last works. The notes in the portfolio state that the prints were "done by an expert printer under strict supervision of the artist, because larger number of prints are required than usual."

Portfolio Notes "JAPANESE WOODCUT PRINT" by Kōshirō Onchi
Though it has been much accepted and widely admired by the art connoisseurs of the world, particularly after the introduction of "ukiyo-e" prints, the art of woodcut print declined in popularity in face of the modern technology of mechanical printing toward the end of the Meiji era (1868-1912). In the 1910's, however, the art revived, but not so much as a means of reproduction as for its art's sake. Now under the influence of the Western art as well, the artist does the entire work from initial stage of cutting to the final printing.
The SEAL is a further attempt to present the recent trend of the school through works of the leading artists in its miniature form - something entirely different from the traditional large-sized prints.
- August, 1953 - Kōshirō Onchi (Note: Mr. Koshiro Onchi is one of the foremost modern woodcut print artists in Japan - Editor)

media.caption: Timepiece and Lamp (時計とラシプ Tokei to ranpu)

text.headline: Timepiece and Lamp (時計とラシプ Tokei to ranpu)
text.text:
One of three prints commissioned from the artist by Hotta Watchmakers (Hotta Corporation) to commemorate the 95th anniversary of their watch shop. (Also see IHL.2066.) The print was published in collaboration with the Kokugakai (National Picture Association).
Carved and printed by Kawakami, this print was printed on paper made by Ichibei Iwano VIII, a Living National Treasure (Preserver of Important Intangible Cultural Properties) of Japan.
Ryohei Hotta (1913-1989), ex-president of the Hotta Corporation, was a collector of timepiece ephemera who donated his collection, the "Hotta Collection", to the National Diet Library in 1987. Included in the collection is a privately printed 1971 catalog of colored woodblock prints on watches and calendars titled "Tokei to koyomi no nishikie mokuroku." For a second impression of this print see IHL.2056.

media.caption: Satō Tsuginobu (佐藤嗣信)

text.headline: Satō Tsuginobu (佐藤嗣信)
text.text:
Print number 14 (十四), and one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, portraying Sato Tsuginobu on his deathbed in the arms of his lord Minamoto no Yoshitsune, for whom he sacrificed his life.
The death of Satō Tsuginobu is told in the Heike Monogatari, an epic work that chronicles the Genpei War 源平合戦 (1180-1185), a conflict between the Taira and Minamoto clans during the late-Heian period of Japan which resulted in the fall of the Taira and the establishment of the Kamakura shogunate under Minamoto Yoritomo in 1192. "Felled by an arrow while shielding his lord Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Tsuginobu is carried to the rear where he dies holding Yoshitsune's hand. As recorded in the Heike Monogatari, his last words are I regret that I must die without seeing my lord rise to fame in the world. Apart from that, he who wields bow and arrow must expect to meet his end before an enemy's shaft. It is an honor for this existence and memory for the next that the war tales of future generations will record that 'In the war between the Minamoto and Taira, Satō no Saturōbyōe Tsuginobu gave his life for his lord on the beach at Yashima in Sanuki province" - source: Warriors of Japan as Portrayed in the War Tales, Paul Varley, University of Hawaii Press, 1994, p. 138-139.
