media.caption: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)

text.headline: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)
text.text:
Print number 21 (廿一), and one of 13 designs contributed by Inoue to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the young Soga Brothers and their mother. Five year old Juro points to five wild geese flying by to remind his younger brother Goro of their duty to avenge their murdered natural father while their mother peers fondly at them.
The blocks for this print created in October 1885 were likely damaged or lost and in April 1889 a revised design was made by Inoue. This collection contains both the original 1885 design (IHL.1352) and the revised design published in April 1889 (IHL.0622).

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Distant View of Izumo Fuji (出雲富士遠望)

text.headline: Distant View of Izumo Fuji (出雲富士遠望)
text.text:
One of three designs for a series of prints titled "Sights of Matsue." This print is titled "Distant View of Mt Fuji of Izumo" in the bottom margin. The print gives us a view of Mount Daisan, also called Izumo Fuji, from Matsue City, about 50 km west of the mountain.
The publisher's name 内田美術書肆納 (Uchida Fine Art Store) appears in the left margin and the print's two rectangular cartouches in the bottom right of the image are blank, indicating the print is a proof or trial print. In the production version of this print the two cartouches contain the following text: 松江日本画文化研究所版 Matsue Nihon ga bunka kenkyujo (Matsue Japanese Painting Culture Research Institute Edition) and 松江名所 出雲富士 Matsue meisho, Izumo Fuji embo (Sights of Matsue, Distant View of Izumo Fuji).
The other two extant prints from this series, are titled "Moonlight of Lake Shinti" (Lake Shishido) and "Scenery of Snon [sic] Castle of Matsue." All three prints are attributed to the artist Asada Benji 麻田辨次 (1900-1984), a Kyoto-based print artist and nihonga (Japanese style) painter.
While not dated, the English titles in the bottom margin, indicate these prints were a post-WWII issue, targeted at an American audience.
Matsue bills itself as "As an International City of Culture and Tourism. Matsue is a place visitors come to find Japanese culture as they’ve always dreamed of encountering it." - Source: Matsue City Official Travel Guide https://www.visit-matsue.com/more/culture [accessed 2-27-24]

media.caption: Fishermen (漁師 ryōshi)

text.headline: Fishermen (漁師 ryōshi)
text.text:
Three fishermen look out to sea on what might be the day before the New Year. This print was originally issued in 1940 by the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin as the fifteenth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1.
A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "When I was drunk on New Year's sake, I unsteadily put on my shoes and went to the beach alone. Today is the spring of the 2600th Year of Imperial Rule (1940). Outside the cape that protrudes beyond the shore on which the sun shines warmly, there is no smoke or clouds of the boats going off into the distant haze on the boundless open sea. Among the group of friends talking between the landed boats about the same unchanging topics with the same unchanging faces, and some already have grandchildren. These days, quilted coats and festive dresses have become a rare sight. Their place has been taken by convenient wood sweaters. Boats, too, have been replaced by motorboats."[1]

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: The Old Story of Sanshō Dayū, (昔談柄三升太夫 Mukashi-banashi Sanshō Dayū)

text.headline: The Old Story of Sanshō Dayū, (昔談柄三升太夫 Mukashi-banashi Sanshō Dayū)
text.text: The highlight of this performance involving kidnap, slavery, revenge and redemption, is the afflicted Osan turning into a fowl, as she is depicted in the left sheet, in the play The Old Story of Sanshō Dayū, as performed at the Kawarazaki theater in the 4th month of 1852. Osan will soon chew the ropes from Kanamenosuke (right sheet), with whom she is in love, and then kill herself. The evil Sanshō Dayū, in the center sheet, looks on.

media.caption: A Great Victory of Our Forces at Kiuliencheng (九連城ニ於テ我軍大勝利)

text.headline: A Great Victory of Our Forces at Kiuliencheng (九連城ニ於テ我軍大勝利)
text.text: The artist has taken some liberties with this scene in portraying a bigger battle than actually occurred as the Chinese troops had previously withdrawn from Kiuliencheng and the fortress was conquered virtually without fighting.

media.caption: A Great Victory of Our Fleet: An Enemy Ship was Attacked and Sunk on the Open Sea off of Haiyang Island (我艦隊大勝利 海洋嶋沖ニ敵艦ヲ撃沈ム Waga kantai daishori ・ Kaiyoto oki ni tekikan o uchishizumu)

text.headline: A Great Victory of Our Fleet: An Enemy Ship was Attacked and Sunk on the Open Sea off of Haiyang Island (我艦隊大勝利 海洋嶋沖ニ敵艦ヲ撃沈ム Waga kantai daishori ・ Kaiyoto oki ni tekikan o uchishizumu)
text.text:
This print depicts the first great naval battle of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) on September 17, 1894 near the islands of Haiyang and Zhangzi, off the coast of the Liaodong Peninsula, midway between Port Arthur and the mouth of the Yalu River. It pitted the Chinese fleet of larger but older ships against newly built and more maneuverable Japanese ships. The Chinese fleet was led by Admiral Ding Ruchang who was injured by his own ship's gunfire early in the battle and the Japanese fleet was led by Admiral Itō Yūkō. Two Chinese ships were sunk in the engagement and the remainder of Chinese ships fled. There was also extensive fire damage to Chinese and some Japanese ships. The New York Times headlines of this battle ran "China's Waterloo in Corea" and "Japan's Great Naval Victory."
The artist, who did not witness the battle, must have reconstructed it from newspaper accounts. One error of fact appears on the print. The Chinese ship the Lai-yuen [Laiyuan], shown sinking at the bottom of the center panel, did not, in fact, sink at the battle. It was its sister-ship, the King-yuen, that was sunk.

media.caption: Japanese Forces Conquer Kiuliencheng (大日本大勝利九連城没落之図 Dai Nihon daishōri Kyūrenjō botsuraku no zu)

text.headline: Japanese Forces Conquer Kiuliencheng (大日本大勝利九連城没落之図 Dai Nihon daishōri Kyūrenjō botsuraku no zu)
text.text: The artist portrays a fictional battle for Kiuliencheng (Jiuliancheng) in Manchuria which was taken without opposition by the Japanese in late October 1894. While the Japanese had prepared for a fierce battle to take the Kiuliencheng citadel, the Chinese forces had withdrawn and the fortress was conquered virtually without fighting. For a second copy of this print see IHL.0350.

media.caption: Yu-no-hama Onsen (湯野浜温泉)

text.headline: Yu-no-hama Onsen (湯野浜温泉)
text.text:
From Senpan's fourth set of prints picturing Japanese onsens. This print depicts a gentleman in a trench coat sitting with two traditionally dressed women on the rocks overlooking the Yu-no-hama hot springs resort along the coast of Yamagata. To quote from a current-day advertisement about these hot springs:
"Warming yourself up with a soak in this hot spring after swimming in the ocean and playing water sports on a beach of white sand and clear blue skies is a truly unique experience. Because this hot spring is along the ocean, the seafood is exquisite. After you’re done enjoying the hot spring, you can have a romantic evening eating delicious seafood while watching the sun set into the ocean."
ABOUT THE SERIES HOT SPRING NOTES
One of his most famous series of prints, "Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes" (Hanga yokusen fu), depicts various hot springs around Japan. It was published in five volumes of twenty prints each over an 18 year period, starting in 1941 when Maekawa was evacuated to Okayama in southwest Honshu and ending in 1959.
Merritt states that most of the prints were started during the war but could not be published until the war was over. She notes that although his countrymen are depicted at one of their favorite pastimes, spa going for rest and relaxation, "the feeling is not joyous," due to Maekawa's use of somber colors. The general demeanor of the spa goers is also somber in many of the prints.
However, writing in 1955, Oliver Statler found Senpan's spa prints "some of his pleasantest prints" and praised Senpan's "connoisseur's selection from the country's hundreds of hot spring resorts."
In 1954 the publisher Ryūseikaku 竜星閣 released a volume containing full size reproductions of the sixty woodblock prints contained in the first three volumes.
The five volumes comprising the entire series are titled are:
Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (版画 浴泉譜 Hanga yokusen fu), 1941.
More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1944.
More and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1952.
More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku yokusen fu), 1956.
More, More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku, zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1959.

media.caption: Totems

text.headline: Totems
text.text:
One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945.
Five wood totems, jangseung in Korean, which serve as village guardians and are traditionally placed at the edges of villages to mark village boundaries, stand along the edge of a road as children play and villagers pass by. The left totem reads 天下大將軍 "Great General of All Under Heaven" and the totem to its right reads 地下女將軍 "Female General of the Underworld."

media.caption: Castle Gate

text.headline: Castle Gate
text.text:
One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945.
This print may be a depiction of Pyongyang's Taedongmun Street with Taedongmun Gate, built in mid-6th century, dominating the background.

media.caption: Asaki Haru (浅き春)

text.headline: Asaki Haru (浅き春)
text.text: This small print titled Asaki Haru after the poem it illustrated was most likely produced by the Katō Print Institute under the supervision of the Yumeji Art Museum.  It is a reproduction of an earlier 1919 work by the artist.

media.caption: Mt. Fuji from the Pass (峠の富士 Tōge no Fuji)

text.headline: Mt. Fuji from the Pass (峠の富士 Tōge no Fuji)
text.text:
This collection's print by an unknown artist, issued by an unknown publisher, is instructive as an example of the copying, i.e., plagiarizing, of shin hanga designs, by unscrupulous publishers, to satisfy the demand in the United States and Europe for inexpensive shin hanga prints. This collection's print is actually a simplified copy of a previous print, c. mid-1930s, which copied the design of a 1932 print by the prolific shin hanga artist Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki), published by the well-known publisher of shin hanga prints Watanabe Shōzaburō. All three prints are shown to the left, but note that only IHL.1363 is part of this collection.

The copying of designs without authorization became troublesome enough that Watanabe printed the following notice on page 123 in his 1936 catalogue:
About "Copyright"
"At the same time an artist draws a certain atmosphere, there are created copyright and right of personality as in the case of an author. The right of personality should not be infringed by other people and is not transferrable. It lasts as long as an artist lives, while the copyright is a transferable property.
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.
"As said above, the copyright is well protected with the right of the artist's personality according to the copyright law."

media.caption: Noh mask, Onna : Manbi (能面 女 : 万媚)

text.headline: Noh mask, Onna : Manbi (能面 女 : 万媚)
text.text: A depiction by an unidentified artist of what appears to be a onna manbi mask used in the Noh theater to represent a "a mysteriously beautiful young woman. The name manbi, or '10,000 coquetries,' derives from the phrase 'winning over 100 coquetries.' The manbi mask is typically used to represent a demon that has transformed into a beautiful woman." - Source: website of the-Noh.com https://www.the-noh.com/sub/jp/index.php?mode=db&action=e_view_detail&data_id=77&class_id=1 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Gojō Bridge (五條橋) - untitled

text.headline: Gojō Bridge (五條橋) - untitled
text.text: Little is known about the production of woodblock prints from Miyake's drawings and paintings, although it is likely he worked closely with the carver and printer who executed the finished prints. This small print with an impressionistic take on Gojō-bashi over the Horikawa River in Nagoya may have appeared in one of the many magazines of the period or as an illustration for a novel.

media.caption: Canal (untitled)

text.headline: Canal (untitled)
text.text: Little is known about the production of woodblock prints from Miyake's drawings, although it is likely he worked closely with the carver and printer who executed the finished prints. This small untitled print may have appeared in one of the many journals of the period or as an illustration for a novel. Whether this impressionistic view of a canal and what may be a farmhouse in the distance is a scene from Europe or from the artist's native Japan is unknown.

media.caption: Venice

text.headline: Venice
text.text: Little is known about the production of woodblock prints from Miyake's drawings, although it is likely he worked closely with the carver and printer who executed the finished prints. This small print, titled Venice, may have appeared in one of the many journals of the period or as illustrations for a novel. Miyake made at least two trips to Europe which included some time in southern Italy and in 1911 his European painting tour book, Ōhshū Ryokō e Angya, was published.

media.caption: Autumn (秋 Aki)

text.headline: Autumn (秋 Aki)
text.text:
A courtesan holds a cup of sake with the character 亀 "heavy drinker" denoting the courtesan's name, her habits or the artist's admitted love of the drink. And, the artist comments, "Liquor. I like it. I like the atmosphere of drinking parties more than the liquor itself. The refreshing Australian beer in Sydney. Wine at a party in Melbourne. A whisky and water at a back-street bar in Kawasaki, etc. etc." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 103

While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

media.caption: Crane (鶴 Tsuru)

text.headline: Crane (鶴 Tsuru)
text.text:
The artist comments, "The decorative standard borne by the fireman is called 'matoi'. In the age of chronic civil strife in Japan, from about the middle of the 15th century to the middle of the 16th century, warriors stripped off an enemy's clothes and made it their mark. During the Edo Period 'matoi' became the sign of a team of firemen. It developed into a battle flag in recent times." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 102.

His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

media.caption: Sumizō in the role of Hōkaibō (壽美蔵 法界坊)

text.headline: Sumizō in the role of Hōkaibō (壽美蔵 法界坊)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Sumizō VI in the role of Hōkaibō in the play Hōkaibō 法界坊, staged at the Meiji-za, Tokyo on July 3, 1915. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Kiyoko in the role of Akagashi Mitsue (京子 赤樫満枝)

text.headline: Kiyoko in the role of Akagashi Mitsue (京子 赤樫満枝)
text.text:
The actress Shimoyama Kyōko*下山京子 as Akagashi Mitsue in the play Konjiki Yasha 金色夜叉, staged at the Engi-za, Tokyo on July 1, 1915. (* the actress in this print is most likely Hisamatsu Kyōko, born 1886 and active in the Shin kokugeki (New Theater) movement, rather than Shimoyama Kiyoko who was a pioneering female journalist of the period, not an actress.)
One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

media.caption: A Record of Modern Events, volume 1 (近世紀聞 巻之一 Kinsei kibun, maki no ichi)

text.headline: A Record of Modern Events, volume 1 (近世紀聞 巻之一 Kinsei kibun, maki no ichi)
text.text: Volume 1 of 12 volumes of a history jitsuroku (歴史実録) co-authored by Jōno Arindō and Somezaki Nobufusa, also known as Tamenaga Shunsui II, published from 1874 to 1882. It took its material from official government proclamations, newspaper reports, and gossip and rumor to create modern histories of Japan in a familiar gesaku form, adopting the language and published format of popular Edo period fictional genres.

media.caption: Gion District (祇園まち Gion machi)

text.headline: Gion District (祇園まち Gion machi)
text.text:
Standing outside the gate of the Ichiriki teahouse, young Rikiya, son of Yuranosuke, the leader of the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai, looks warily around. He has a secret letter for his father with the details of their plot to kill Lord Moronao who they blame for their master's death. This scene is from ACT VII, "The Ichiriki Teahouse," in the play "Revenge of the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai" (Kanadehon Chūshingura). The full moon will light the way for the Loyal Samurai's subsequent attack on Moronao's mansion and his beheading.
This collection's print is from a bound album, created by the publisher, of the entire series of one hundred prints.

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as Torii Tsuneemon and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Okudaira Heihachirō in the play Go fūdoki kabuki no hon'yomi (鳥井弥左衛門 尾上菊五郎・奥平平八郎 市川団十郎・後風土記劇本読)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Torii Tsuneemon and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Okudaira Heihachirō in the play Go fūdoki kabuki no hon'yomi (鳥井弥左衛門 尾上菊五郎・奥平平八郎 市川団十郎・後風土記劇本読)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the faithful messenger Torii Tsuneemon passing through a moat strung with ropes of warning bells on his return to Mikawa, in the play Go fūdoki kabuki no hon'yomi (Reading a Play on the History of the Region.) The inset in the top left shows the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Okudaira Heihachirō.

In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

media.caption: Stone Bodhisattva at Datong (Yungang), China (大同雲崗石佛)

text.headline: Stone Bodhisattva at Datong (Yungang), China (大同雲崗石佛)
text.text: The artist's depiction of a stone statue of the Buddha in meditation from the famous Yungang caves in Datong, China, which the artist must have visited during his 1943 stint teaching print classes in Japanese-occupied Beijing.

media.caption: Nakamura Tokizō as Danshichi Shima no Okaji (中村時蔵の団七縞お梶)

text.headline: Nakamura Tokizō as Danshichi Shima no Okaji (中村時蔵の団七縞お梶)
text.text:
Depicting the actor Nakamura Tokizō III as Danshichi Shima no Okaji in the play Shinzō Tsurifune Kidan.

The Play Shinzō Tsurifune Kidan
A play centering on the conflict between a greedy mother and an upright daughter. The evil old father-in-law Giheiji has conspired with the enemies of the young nobleman whom the hero Danshichi, his son-in-law, is trying to protect and kidnaps his lover Kotoura to take her to a rival. When Danshichi confronts him about this, the father-in-law accuses him of the expenses he had to make for his daughter and grandson during Danshichi's temporary absence, when it was actually Danshichi's job as a husband and father to support them. Danshichi offers him money to compensate him, and the old man pretends to be very generous in accepting it. But when Danshichi cannot pay him off immediately, Giheiji scolds him and arrogantly makes fun of him: as a father-in-law he is a person of respect from whom Danshichi has to take verbal abuse and beatings without complaining. However, the insults become too much for Danshichi, and he hits Giheiji with his sword. At first the injury is only minor, but when Giheiji starts screaming "Patricide, patricide," Danshichi has no choice but to kill the old man and thereby seal his own fate.

media.caption: Ichikawa Somegorō, et al., in Ichiriki Kajiwara at the Mitsukoshi Theater

text.headline: Ichikawa Somegorō, et al., in Ichiriki Kajiwara at the Mitsukoshi Theater
text.text:
This print depicts a scene in act III from the play Kajiwara Heiza Homare no Ishikiri, in which the hero, Kajiwara Kagetoki, seated center, inspects a precious sword that has been offered for sale. The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in February 1949. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.
The inscriptions on the print provide the name of the play 石切梶原 (Ichiriki Kajiwara), the location of the scene 八幡宮社頭 (the front of the Hachiman Shrine) and the names of the five actors seated in the foreground, from right to left, as follows: Bandō Keizō 坂東慶三 (初代) in the role of Matano Gorō Kagehisa 俣野五郎景久; Ichikawa Danzō VIII 市川團蔵 (8代目) as Ōba Saburō Kagechika 大庭三郎景親; Ichikawa Somegorō V 市川染五郎 (5代目) as Kajiwara Heizō Kagetoki 梶原平三景時; Nakamura Kichinojō 中村吉之丞 (初代) as Aogaishi Rokurōdayū 青貝師六郎太夫; Nakamura Matagorō 中村又五郎 (2代目) as Musume Kozue 娘梢.
Sasajima has hand-applied ink on the verso of this print to provide a subtle coloring when viewed from the front, a technique he learned from the artist Munakata Shikō 棟方志功 (1903-1975).

media.caption: Sawamura Sōjūrō VII and Nakamura Shikaku II in Wakaki no Adanagusa at the Mitsukoshi Theater

text.headline: Sawamura Sōjūrō VII and Nakamura Shikaku II in Wakaki no Adanagusa at the Mitsukoshi Theater
text.text:
This print depicts the actor Sawamura Sōjūrō VII (1875-1949) in the role of Ranchō in the play Wakaki no Adanagusa, a dramatic version of a shinnai bushi musical number Ranchō. The circular inset depicts the actor Nakamura Shikaku II (1900-1981) in the role of Konoito.
The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in October 1948. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.
The inscription along the left edge reads らんてふ (Ranchō) followed by 宗十郎 Sōjūrō (Sawamura Sōjūrō VII). The inscription in the inset reads 此糸 (Konoito) and beneath it しかく (Kiya) [as in Konoito of the Wakakiya] and 木屋 Shikaku (Nakamura Shikaku II).

media.caption: Nakamura Moshiho IV as Sodehagi in Sodehagi Saimon at the Mitsukoshi Theater

text.headline: Nakamura Moshiho IV as Sodehagi in Sodehagi Saimon at the Mitsukoshi Theater
text.text:
This print depicts the blind beggar Sodehagi in act III, Sodehagi saemon, from the kabuki drama Ōshū Adachi-ga-Hara. The role of Sodehagi is played by the actor Nakamura Moshiho IV 中村もしほ(4代目).
The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in February 1949. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.
The inscriptions on the print provide the name of the play 袖萩 (Sodehagi), and the name of the actor depicted, もしほ (Moshiho).

media.caption: Nakamura Moshio IV and Sawamura Tosshō IV in Onna Goroshi Abura no Jigoku at the Mitsukoshi Theater

text.headline: Nakamura Moshio IV and Sawamura Tosshō IV in Onna Goroshi Abura no Jigoku at the Mitsukoshi Theater
text.text:
This print depicts a scene in the third act from the play Onna Goroshi Abura no Jigyoku, in which Kawachiya Yohei, played by Nakamura Moshio IV (1909-1988), is about to slay Okichi, the wife of the proprietor of the Teshimaya oil store, played by Sawamura Tosshō IV (1908-1975). The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in February 1949. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.
Sasajima has hand-applied ink on the verso of this print to provide a subtle coloring when viewed from the front, a technique he learned from the artist Munakata Shikō 棟方志功 (1903-1975).

media.caption: Kataoka Roen V as Yaoya Oshichi in Date musume koi no hikanoko at the Mitsukoshi Theater

text.headline: Kataoka Roen V as Yaoya Oshichi in Date musume koi no hikanoko at the Mitsukoshi Theater
text.text:
This print depicts Yaoya Oshichi ("the greengrocer's daughter"), played Kataoka Roen V (1910-1993) in act VI, Yaoya, from the kabuki drama Date musume koi no hikanoko.
The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in October 1948. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.
The inscriptions on the print provide the actor's name 芦燕 (Roen) and the character played 八百屋お七 (Yaoya Oshichi).

media.caption: Ichikawa Omezō IV as Hayase Iori in Katakiuchi tengajaya mura at the Mitsukoshi Theater

text.headline: Ichikawa Omezō IV as Hayase Iori in Katakiuchi tengajaya mura at the Mitsukoshi Theater
text.text:
This print depicts the actor Ichikawa Omezō IV (1898-1969) in the role of Hayase Iori in the play Katakiuchi tengajaya mura, a classic tale of revenge, at the Mitsukoshi Theater in September 1948.
The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in September 1948. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.
The inscription in the cartouche reads 伊織 (Iori) and the kana below reads おめぞう (Omezō).

media.caption: Mitsukoshi Kabuki Hanga, Works of Sasajima Kihei, September 1948 (三越歌舞伎版画 昭和二十三年 九月 笹島喜平作)

text.headline: Mitsukoshi Kabuki Hanga, Works of Sasajima Kihei, September 1948 (三越歌舞伎版画 昭和二十三年 九月 笹島喜平作)
text.text:
Likely the introductory print for the series of prints Sasajima created for the 1948-1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater. The inscription in the top cartouche reads Mitsukoshi Kabuki hanga and in the left cartouche is written 昭和二十三年 九月 (September 1948) followed by 笹島喜平作 (works of Sasajima Kihei) .The actor pictured is not identified in the print, nor is the character he is playing.
Sasajima has hand-applied ink on the verso of this print to provide a subtle coloring when viewed from the front, a technique he learned from the artist Munakata Shikō 棟方志功 (1903-1975).

media.caption: Three Dance Performances at the Mitsukoshi Gekijō: Onoe Shōroku II in Sarutori, Ichikawa Omezō IV in Tonbi Yakko, Onoe Baikō VII in Karigane

text.headline: Three Dance Performances at the Mitsukoshi Gekijō: Onoe Shōroku II in Sarutori, Ichikawa Omezō IV in Tonbi Yakko, Onoe Baikō VII in Karigane
text.text: This print portrays three actors in three dance performances, performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in September 1948.  The actors and their roles are as follows: Onoe Shōroku II 二代目 尾上松緑  (1913-1989) as Tobi no mono 鳶のもの in Sarutori さる酉 ; Ichikawa Omezō IV 四代目 市川男女蔵 (1898-1969) as Yatsutaki taira 奴瀧平 in Tonbi Yakko とんび奴; Onoe Baikō VII 七代目 尾上梅幸 (1915-1995) as Benten Oteru 弁天おてる in Karigane 雁がね.

media.caption: A Sweet Pastry into the Open Mouth. Love Makes No Distinction Between High and Low; The Famous Holy Man of Shiga Temple (あいた口へおはき  恋に上下のへだてなし  志賀寺之名高キ上人 Aito kuchi e ohagi. Koi ni ueshita no hedate nashi, Shigadera no nadakaki shōnin)

text.headline: A Sweet Pastry into the Open Mouth. Love Makes No Distinction Between High and Low; The Famous Holy Man of Shiga Temple (あいた口へおはき  恋に上下のへだてなし  志賀寺之名高キ上人 Aito kuchi e ohagi. Koi ni ueshita no hedate nashi, Shigadera no nadakaki shōnin)
text.text:
Kyōsai pairs the proverb "A sweet pastry [bean-jam rice cake] into an open mouth," (meaning, an unexpected windfall) with the ancient story of the infatuation of the holy man of Shiga Temple for the Empress Somedomo. In the bottom scene of the print, we see the holy man grasping the hand of the empress while several onlookers giggle. In the story the holy man from the Shiga temple grasped the hands of the Empress Mother (Empress Somedomo) and recited the poem on the Jeweled Broom to liberate himself from obsessive thoughts and worldly desires. In the end he was unable to endure such passion and turned into a blue ghost.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

media.caption: The Complete Sixteen Divine Generals of the Tokugawa (徳川英勇揃 十六將之圖)

text.headline: The Complete Sixteen Divine Generals of the Tokugawa (徳川英勇揃 十六將之圖)
text.text: The artist portrays the Sixteen Divine Generals serving Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616) founder and first shogun of the Tokugawa shogunate of Japan, which ruled Japan until the Meiji Restoration of 1867. It is interesting to ponder why this subject was depicted in 1874, seven years after the emperor was restored to power. 1873 and the beginning of 1874 were rough times for the new Meiji emperor and government, with open revolts by both the masses (over misinterpreted conscription laws and demands for tax reduction) and disaffected samurai, a handful of whom tried to assassinate the Minister of the Right, Iwakura Tomomi (1825-1883), on January 13, 1874.  Perhaps this reminder of the loyalty of these generals to the first shogun was to be a lesson in showing loyalty to the young emperor?

media.caption: The Old Capital in Late Fall (古都晩秋 Koto banshū)

text.headline: The Old Capital in Late Fall (古都晩秋 Koto banshū)
text.text:
Depicting the five-story pagoda at Tōji (East Temple) in Kyoto on a late autumn day.
Toji Temple (東寺, Tōji), literally "East Temple", was founded at the beginning of the Heian Period just after the capital was moved to Kyoto in the late 700s. The large temple, together with its now defunct sister temple Saiji ("West Temple"), flanked the south entrance to the city and served as the capital's guardian temples. Toji Temple is one of Kyoto's many UNESCO world heritage sites.
Across from the Kondo (the temple's main hall and largest building) and Kodo (a lecture hall) stands Tōji's five storied pagoda, which was originally erected by Kobo Daishi in 826. It stands 57 meters tall, making it the tallest pagoda in Japan, and has become a symbol of both the temple and Kyoto as it can be seen from many places across the city. The ground floor of the pagoda is irregularly opened to the public and houses four smaller Buddha statues. - Source: website of japan-guidel.com http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3919.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Fuji (Lake Ashi) B (富士 [芦ノ湖] B Fuji Ashi no ko B)

text.headline: Fuji (Lake Ashi) B (富士 [芦ノ湖] B Fuji Ashi no ko B)
text.text: Depicting Mount Fuji as seen from across Lake Ashi, this is one of at least fifteen views of Mount Fuji created by Sasajima. Sasajima used his "takuzuri" process, forcing damp paper into the grooves of a carved woodblock with a press, to give this print a dynamic three-dimensional effect. He has hand-applied black ink directly on the raised areas of the print.

media.caption: Kami Harbor, Distant View of Genkai Sea (神湊 玄海灘を遠望 Kami no minato, Genkai nada oenbō)

text.headline: Kami Harbor, Distant View of Genkai Sea (神湊 玄海灘を遠望 Kami no minato, Genkai nada oenbō)
text.text: This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, depicts Kami Harbor in Kōnominato in Fukuoka Prefecture. On the right we see what is  likely Kusasaki, with Katsu Island, seen center, and Jinoshima Island, seen left in the far background. This print is from the 1970 set of reissued prints titled Five Scenes of Tsukushi by the publisher Katō Junji.  This set was originally issued in 1918 as part six of the six set series titled Japan Scenery Prints by the publisher Nakajima Jūtarō. New printing blocks were very carefully recarved for this reissue, resulting in prints that closely match the 1918 releases.

media.caption: Sea of Fire, View from Offshore (火の海 沖の端より望む Hi no umi Oki no hata yori nozumo)

text.headline: Sea of Fire, View from Offshore (火の海 沖の端より望む Hi no umi Oki no hata yori nozumo)
text.text: This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, picturing the ancient fortifications along Hakata Bay, is a 1970 reissue of a print originally released in 1918. (See IHL.0862 for the original 1918 print.)  Originally the print was published by Nakajima Jūtarō and the Japan Scenery Prints Association as part of the set of five prints titled Tsukishi District which was part of the ten set series titled Japan Scenery Prints. In 1970, the publisher Katō Junji reissued the five scenes of Tsukushi under the title Five Scenes of Tsukushi (筑紫五景 Tsukushi Gokei.)  New printing blocks were very carefully recarved for this reissue, resulting in prints that closely match the 1918 releases.

media.caption: Enoki Temple Shrine, View from the Direction of Tofurō (榎寺神社 都府樓方面よ Enokidera jinja Tofurō hōmen yori nozomu)

text.headline: Enoki Temple Shrine, View from the Direction of Tofurō (榎寺神社 都府樓方面よ Enokidera jinja Tofurō hōmen yori nozomu)
text.text:
This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, presents the view from the Tofurō Ruins in Dazaifu looking out to the wooded area where Enoki Shrine is located. Dazaifu is where Sugawara Michizane (845-903), poet, scholar and statesman of the mid-Heian period, whose spirit is worshiped as a god of thunder, passed away while in exile.
This print is from the 1970 set of five prints titled Five Scenes of Tsukushi by the publisher Katō Junji. The five prints are re-issues (using newly cut blocks) of the original 1918 prints issued as set six of the ten set series titled Japan Scenery Prints published by Nakajima Jūtarō. The new printing blocks were very carefully recarved for this reissue, resulting in prints that closely match the 1918 releases.

media.caption: Boxers, Number 3 (拳闘家 其三 kentōka sono san)

text.headline: Boxers, Number 3 (拳闘家 其三 kentōka sono san)
text.text:
This first edition 1939 print, issued as the Japanese were ruthlessly continuing their colonization of Asia, depicts two fighters slugging it out in a boxing match. Boxing in Japan is traced back to Commodore Perry's second visit to Japan and shipboard boxing matches.
The commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Boxing the sport in which men of equal weight contend in skill and strength, reached its full development in America, and having been introduced into Japan in recent years has made great progress here too. Consequently the number of professional Japanese boxers has gradually increased. Battle of human bodies staged in the blue glare of flood lights under a summer evening sky have a great fascination for the young men and women of Japanese cities. The fighting spirit - no, the killing spirit - of men covered with blood still trying to knock out their opponents might even be called brutal and makes one feel that for the Japanese nature, which ordinarily strives to make fine arts of courtesy and rules even in the coarsest moods and at the most critical moments, this sport may be a little excessively gruesome."
Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as Masaoka supported by Onoe Iwagorō as Senmatsu and Ichikawa Botan as Tsurikyō in the play Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai (政岡尾上菊五郎・鶴千代丸 市川ぼたん・千松 尾上きく・伽羅先代萩)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Masaoka supported by Onoe Iwagorō as Senmatsu and Ichikawa Botan as Tsurikyō in the play Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai (政岡尾上菊五郎・鶴千代丸 市川ぼたん・千松 尾上きく・伽羅先代萩)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the nursemaid Masaoka 政岡 in the play Meiboku Sendai Hagi (Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai). The inset in the top right shows the actors Onoe Kiku [Onoe Iwagorō 尾上岩五郎 ] as Masaoka's own son Senmatsu 千松 and Ichikawa Botan 市川ぼたん [Ichikawa Sadanji II] as the young lord Tsurikyō, Masaoka's charge.

n 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

media.caption: By now you must be near Komakata, a cuckoo calls - Takao (たか雄 君は今駒かたあたりほとゝきす Kimi wa ima/ Komakata Atari/ hototogisu - Takao)

text.headline: By now you must be near Komakata, a cuckoo calls - Takao (たか雄 君は今駒かたあたりほとゝきす Kimi wa ima/ Komakata Atari/ hototogisu - Takao)
text.text:
Often assumed to be the first print in the series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, it pictures Takao, one of the eleven famous courtesans of the Yoshiwara in the 17th and 18th centuries. It is believed Yoshitoshi's print pictures the sixth Takao, known for her poetry.
This print is a modern re-issue of the original 1885 print [see IHL.0970], created from re-cut blocks. It is part of a portfolio of 15 designs from the series issued by the woodblock department 版画部 of the publishing company Nihon Bijutsu Gakai 日本美術画会 and overseen by Japanese art historian and one-time president of the Japan Ukiyo-e Society Yamaguchi Keizaburō 山口桂三郎 (1928-2012) who also provided a commentary for each print. For the original print see IHL.0970.

media.caption: Butsu Sorai (物徂徠)

text.headline: Butsu Sorai (物徂徠)
text.text:
Print number 39 (三十九), one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the young Ogyū (Butsu) Sorai (1666–1728), who was to go on to become a great Confucian scholar and philosopher during his father's exile in a small village sixty miles from Edo. The exile forced Sorai to study on his own and here he is seen embracing the rural life while studying and teaching a young peasant.
Sorai may be best known for his "Essay on the Forty-Seven Samurai" in which he both lambasted the avenging 47 samurai of Chushingura fame, calling their actions "senseless," thereby offering the bakufu a way out of their dilemma on how to punish the samurai, allowing them the honorable death by seppuku.
For another edition of this print see IHL.0880.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Takemitsu Kikuchi (菊地武光)

text.headline: Takemitsu Kikuchi (菊地武光)
text.text:
Print number 25 (廿五), one of 20 designs contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Kikuchi Takemitsu 菊池武光 (1319-1373), a loyal supporter of imperial rule and a military leader of forces loyal to the Southern Dynasty (once led by the Emperor Godaigo), standing over the body of his enemy (likely that of Naosuke Shōni of the Northern Dynasty, loyal to the Ashikaga shogunate.) It is 1359 and the forces of the Southern Dynasty, led by Emperor Godaigo's son Prince Kanenaga 懐良親王 (1329-1383), have defeated the forces of the Northern Dynasty in the Battle of the Chikugo River 筑後川の戦い.

media.caption: Takasugi Shinsaku (高杉晋作)

text.headline: Takasugi Shinsaku (高杉晋作)
text.text:
Print number 44 (四十四) as shown in the series' Table of Contents, although not numbered on the print. One of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series. This print pictures the arrival in February 1864 of the exiled Chōshū rebel, and later hero of the Meiji Revolution, Takasugi Shinsaku 高杉晋作 (September 1839–May 1867), at the home of the rebel sympathizer, the poetess Nomura Bōtō. For aiding Takasugi, Nomura would herself be sent into exile by the bakufu.

media.caption: Sano Tsuneyo (佐野常世)

text.headline: Sano Tsuneyo (佐野常世)
text.text:
Print number 18 (十八) as shown in the series' Table of Contents, although not numbered on the print. One of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series. This print pictures the thirteenth-century dispossessed and impoverished daimyō Sano Genzaemon Tsuneyo burning his cherished bonsai to provide warmth to a an itinerant priest, who turns out to be the regent Hōjō Tokiyori (1226-1263) who returns Tsuneyo's stolen lands to him.

media.caption: Koshikibu no Naishi (小式部内侍)

text.headline: Koshikibu no Naishi (小式部内侍)
text.text:
Print number 5 (五), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the young poetess Koshikibu no Naishi tugging at the robe of Middle Counselor Fujiwara no Sadayori, who had come to her room to tease her about being chosen to participate in a poetry contest.
For another impression of this print see IHL.0759.

media.caption: Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成)

text.headline: Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成)
text.text:
Print number 4 (四), and one of 13 designs contributed by Inoue to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Fujiwara no Sanekata 藤原実方, in the black robe, glaring at the seated Dainagon Yukinari 大納言行成 whose kanmuri 冠 (lacquered hat) he has just knocked off. Yukinari, seated on the floor, wears a surprised look as his hand searches for his hat which now lies on the floor.
While the print is known by the title Dainagon Yukinari, whose hat was knocked off, the incident is more associated with Fujiwara no Sanekata who was banished by the emperor to a northern province for this act.

media.caption: Kojima Takanori (児島高徳)

text.headline: Kojima Takanori (児島高徳)
text.text:
Print number 24 (廿四), one of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the fourteenth-century daimyō Kojima Takanori 児島高徳 kneeling before the cherry tree upon which he has carved a poem to his exiled emperor Go Daigo (r. 1318-1330). The poem is meant to be seen by Go Daigo on his way into exile on one of the Oki Islands in Bizen Province.
In 1331, Emperor Go-Daigo (1288-1339) was deposed and sent into exile by the Hōjō family. Takanori, a loyal supporter of the Emperor, disguised himself as a peasant and tracked the Emperor to the small inn on the border of Bizen province. As a message to the Emperor, Takanori rips a patch of bark off the cherry tree and writes a classical Chinese poem of loyalty, recounting how the King of Yue was saved by his loyal retainer, Huan Lei. Although the Emperor was heartened by the poem, it was two more years before he was reinstated.

media.caption: Kisshōten V (吉祥天 V)

text.headline: Kisshōten V (吉祥天 V)
text.text:
Depicting the Buddhist goddess Kisshōten, goddess of fertility, wealth, and beauty. In her left hand she holds the "wish-granting jewel" while her right hand is held in the position of the Karana Mudra to expel demons.
This is one of over a dozen prints depicting this goddess designed by Sasajima. Sasajima used his "takuzuri" process, forcing damp paper into the grooves of a carved woodblock with a press, to give this print a dynamic three-dimensional effect. He has hand-applied black ink directly on the raised areas of the print.

media.caption: Taking Refuge on the Tracks (線路の避難 Senro no hinan)

text.headline: Taking Refuge on the Tracks (線路の避難 Senro no hinan)
text.text:
One of three prints (also see IHL.1406) contributed by the artist Igawa Sengai (1876-1961) to the series Pictures of Taishō Earthquake, issued in 1926 three years after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. This print pictures a family sitting on the streetcar tracks gazing at the city in ruins while fires smolder and refugees flee with their belongings. They are well dressed and without the backdrop of devastation it would look like a picnic.
The series consists of 25 prints by nine, mostly lesser-known, artists, a number of whom, including this print's creator, were students of the Nihonga artist Tomioka Eisen (1864-1905). The nine artists are Katayama Shunhan (fl. c. 1901–1926); Hakuhan Yawata (1893–1957); Noguchi Kōgai (born c. 1899, active c. 1919-1930s); Igawa Sengai (1876-1961); Kirigaya (Kiriya) Senrin (1877–1932); Shibata Kōyō (fl c. 1920s); Hamada Josen (1875-1928); Kondō Shiun (fl. c. 1915–1940) and Takashima Unpō (1894-1987).
"The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 stands in memory as one of the most terrifying calamities in Japanese history. Registering at a magnitude of 7.9, the quake struck on September 1, with its epicenter some 50 miles southwest of Tokyo, in Sagami Bay. The hour was 11:58A.M., just when households everywhere were lighting small charcoal stoves to prepare lunch. Fires broke out instantly in the densely populated cities of Tokyo and Yokohama and were spread by high winds. Since the earthquake had broken the water lines, both cities were reduced to smoldering ruins within a few hours. . . . The earthquake and its aftermath caused well over 140,000 deaths and left nearly 700,000 people homeless." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 273.

media.caption: Disaster in the Red-Light District (花柳の難 Karyū no nan)

text.headline: Disaster in the Red-Light District (花柳の難 Karyū no nan)
text.text:
One of three prints (also see IHL.1405) contributed by the artist Igawa Sengai (1876-1961) to the series Pictures of Taishō Earthquake, issued in 1926 three years after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. This print pictures one of the horrific firestorms (fire tornadoes) that came in the aftermath of the earthquake. Sengai portrays three geisha being swept in the spinning fire tornado in the Yanagibashi district. The worst of the firestorms immolated "44,000 people who had sought refuge near Tokyo’s Sumida River in the first few hours, only to be immolated by a freak pillar of fire known as a 'dragon twist'”.
In his recollections of the fires, playwright and theater historian Kawatake Shigetoshi (1889-1967) describes "scenes of frenzied panic and terror." Fleeing his home in Honjo in eastern Tokyo, he recalls looking north to a "blazing inferno." He writes, "I was speechless, watching the whirlpools of fire and the undulating waves of flames. It was utterly beyond description." Kawatake's son perished in the disaster.
The series consists of 25 prints by nine, mostly lesser-known, artists, a number of whom, including this print's creator, were students of the Nihonga artist Tomioka Eisen (1864-1905). The nine artists are Katayama Shunhan (fl. c. 1901–1926); Hakuhan Yawata (1893–1957); Noguchi Kōgai (born c. 1899, active c. 1919-1930s); Igawa Sengai (1876-1961); Kirigaya (Kiriya) Senrin (1877–1932); Shibata Kōyō (fl c. 1920s); Hamada Josen (1875-1928); Kondō Shiun (fl. c. 1915–1940) and Takashima Unpō (1894-1987).
"The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 stands in memory as one of the most terrifying calamities in Japanese history. Registering at a magnitude of 7.9, the quake struck on September 1, with its epicenter some 50 miles southwest of Tokyo, in Sagami Bay. The hour was 11:58A.M., just when households everywhere were lighting small charcoal stoves to prepare lunch. Fires broke out instantly in the densely populated cities of Tokyo and Yokohama and were spread by high winds. Since the earthquake had broken the water lines, both cities were reduced to smoldering ruins within a few hours. . . . The earthquake and its aftermath caused well over 140,000 deaths and left nearly 700,000 people homeless." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 273.

media.caption: Pacific Saury and Eggplant (さんまと茄子 Sanma to Nasu)

text.headline: Pacific Saury and Eggplant (さんまと茄子 Sanma to Nasu)
text.text: Three Pacific Saury (literally "autumn night fish" 秋刀魚) occupy this still life with a single small eggplant.

media.caption: Castle (城 Shiro)

text.headline: Castle (城 Shiro)
text.text: An unidentified castle rises up above a stand of bare trees. Stands of bare trees appear often in the artist's work.

media.caption: Boundary, special appendix to the magazine Hanga Geijutsu, Volume 18 (版画藝術 第18号 境界)

text.headline: Boundary, special appendix to the magazine Hanga Geijutsu, Volume 18 (版画藝術 第18号 境界)
text.text:
An abstract design created as a "special appendix" to Volume 18 of the magazine Hanga Geijutsu 版画藝術 (Print Arts) issued in the summer of 1977. The print was bound into the magazine along with a protective translucent cover sheet containing the print details. The magazine notes, "This original woodcut is found at the beginning of each copy of this quarterly. Kenji Kusaka cut the blocks for four woodcuts, printed 8575 in all, signed and numbered respectively."
Hanga Geijutsu has been published continuously since 1973 and, according to its publisher is, "the only art magazine in Japan that specializes in print art."

text.headline: S. Watanabe Woodcut Print Shop
text.text: Likely a promotional print issued by the S. Watanabe Woodcut Print Shop.

media.caption: Dake Onsen (嶽温泉)

text.headline: Dake Onsen (嶽温泉)
text.text:
From Senpan's fifth and last set of prints picturing Japanese onsen. This print depicts a gentlemen's bath at Dake hot springs in Aomori Prefecture, Tohoku Region, Honshu Island.
"Hot Spring Notes" is one of Maekawa's most famous series of prints. Depicting various hot springs around Japan, it was published in five volumes of twenty prints each, with each print having an accompanying commentary sheet, over an 18 year period, starting in 1941 when Maekawa was evacuated to Okayama in southwest Honshu and ending in 1959.
The five volumes comprising the entire series are titled as follows:
Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (版画 浴泉譜 Hanga yokusen fu), 1941.
More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1944.
More and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1952.
More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku yokusen fu), 1956.
More, More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku, zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1959.

media.caption: Ishizuchi Plateau (石鎚高原)

text.headline: Ishizuchi Plateau (石鎚高原)
text.text:
Kitaoka's rendering of the Ishizuchi plateau with Mt. Ishizuchi, western Japan's highest peak, in the background.
East of the city of Matsuyama is Mt. Ishizuchi ("Stone Hammer"), at 6,502 feet. It is the tallest peak in western Japan and one of Japan's Seven Holy Mountains, where kami alight to restore vitality to the land. It is said to protect the city of Saijo to its northeast from typhoons. Dedicated to gongen (deities with both Shinto and Buddhist forms), Mt. Ishizuchi is a pilgrimage site during the summer climbing season.

media.caption: Komoro Castle and Mount Asayama (小諸城と浅間山 Komoro-jō to Asamayama)

text.headline: Komoro Castle and Mount Asayama (小諸城と浅間山 Komoro-jō to Asamayama)
text.text:
The San-no-mon Gate at Komoro Castle (Komoro-jō), designated an Important Cultural Property by the Japanese government, is depicted with the city of Komoro sitting beyond the gate with the active volcano Mount Asama in the background. As with all Miyata's prints, this print's beauty is in its abstracted simplicity. This print is number 3 in the third volume of prints titled Shinshū from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.

Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

media.caption: Tenryū Gorge (天龍峡 Tenryūkyō)

text.headline: Tenryū Gorge (天龍峡 Tenryūkyō)
text.text:
The Tenryū Gorge, located near the center of the Tenryū River watershed where the river passes through narrow and deep gorges, is the subject of many artists. Miyata pictures the gorge in autumn. On the right we see the Ryukyo-tei Hotel, perched on the steep cliffs and further along the river the old bridge (subsequently made obsolete by the 492 highway bridge, but still remaining in place). This print is number 18 in the third volume of prints titled Shinshū from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.

media.caption: Red Cow at the Seashore (海岸の赤牛)

text.headline: Red Cow at the Seashore (海岸の赤牛)
text.text:
This charming large print of farmer and his daughter tending to a red cow aptly demonstrates Merritt's comment on Senpan: "His prints are refreshing and seemingly naive. His innate feelings, transformed into cheerful colors and gay patterns, created a unique and personal record of the Japan he loved." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 222.
A later posthumous 1961 impression of this print is known.

media.caption: Himeji Castle (姫路城 Himejijō)

text.headline: Himeji Castle (姫路城 Himejijō)
text.text:
View of Himeji Castle with cherry trees in bloom.
Originally built in 1346, Himeji Castle was built for warfare. The walls contain geometrically shaped sama, openings through which archers and gunners shot at attacking troops and ishiotoshi, an opening through which stones or boiling water were dumped on enemy soldiers scaling the wall.
Throughout its history it was owned by thirteen warrior families, including Hashiba (Toyotomi) Hideyoshi, the commoner who rose to become the de facto military dictator of Japan during the Sengoku-jidai (Civil War Era). Lord Hideyoshi reconstructed the castle as a three storied structure in 1581. In 1601, Ikeda Terumasa, son-in-law of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogun who defeated the Hideyoshi family, transformed the castle into its present five tiered configuration with three smaller donjons. The castle was designated at UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.

media.caption: Lake Haruna in Autumn (榛名湖の秋)

text.headline: Lake Haruna in Autumn (榛名湖の秋)
text.text:
This colorful small print presents us with a view of the boathouse on Lake Haruna, a crater lake sitting on top of Mount Haruna. Maekawa has chosen to give us only a partial view of Mount Haruna Fuji, a lava dome shaped like Mt. Fuji that arises out of the lake. This print was included in the second of two portfolios of twelve prints each published by Hanga kanshōkai, titled Hanga kanshōkai sakuhin-shū.

COLLECTION OF WORKS BY THE WOODBLOCK PRINT APPRECIATION SOCIETY
The two volumes of Hanga kanshōkai sakuhin-shū (Collection of Works by the Woodblock Print Appreciation Society), were published by Hanga kanshōkai, a creation of the Yokohama publisher and gallery Chikuhōdō (竹芳洞 or 竹芳堂). The two portfolios were initially issued in 1959 or 1960 in an edition of 700 for volume 1 (上) and 500 copies for volume 2 (下) and reissued at least once in 1980 in an edition of 200. This collection's print is from the first edition.

media.caption: Clear Sky After the Snow (雪霽れ) from the magazine HANGA (Prints), Volume 14

text.headline: Clear Sky After the Snow (雪霽れ) from the magazine HANGA (Prints), Volume 14
text.text:
This calm landscape print was created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) HANGA (Print Art), Volume 14, issued in 1928 by the publisher Hanga no Ie.
Published by Hanga-no-Ie in Kobe under the direction of Yamaguchi Isayoshi, HANGA made its appearance in February 1924 and sold to subscribers for 80 sen each. Sixteen quarterly issues (numbers 9 and 10 combined) were published until April 1930. Merritt estimates that there were no more than 300 subscribers. As announced in its table of contents, the purpose of the magazine was "to publish, exhibit, and encourage appreciation of sōsaku hanga."

media.caption: Kyoto Maruyama (京都丸山)

text.headline: Kyoto Maruyama (京都丸山)
text.text:
A postcard-size print picturing the pond in a snow covered Maruyama Park. The publisher of this print was Yokohama-based Hideo Takemura (H. Takemura & Co.) who targeted his work at a Western audience, specializing in, as printed on his business card, Christmas Cards, Japanese Old Colour Prints, Famous Modern Colour Prints and Water Colors.
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

media.caption: City in the Rain (町の雨 Machi no ame)

text.headline: City in the Rain (町の雨 Machi no ame)
text.text:
Issued by an unknown publisher, this print is a near exact copy of a small format print by Kawase Hasui, the most famous of shin hanga landscape artists, titled "City in the Rain," originally published c. 1930s by Watanabe Shōzaburō, the best known publisher, and pioneer, of shin hanga prints. The unknown designer of this collection's print, simply horizontally flipped the original design an added a few minor changes, as shown on the left.
Watanabe became so upset by these copies of original designs by Hasui and several other artists he published that he included the following warning in his 1936 catalogue, "Catalogue of Wood-Cut Colour Prints of S. Watanabe, S. Watanabe, 1936.":
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.”

media.caption: Edo in Spring (江戸の春 Edo no Haru)

text.headline: Edo in Spring (江戸の春 Edo no Haru)
text.text:
No information is available on the artist Inagaki Kadō who designed this Hiroshige-like print of two boys flying a kite near a fire watchtower in Edo with Mount Fuji in the background. The characters 立月 on the kite tell us the time is the first lunar month of the year. Inagaki's extant work consists of a number of prints related to the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War and various senjafuda (votive prints).

media.caption: Jinzhou Castle After Occupation (占領後の金州城内)

text.headline: Jinzhou Castle After Occupation (占領後の金州城内)
text.text:
From the printed title below the image we know this is a view of Jinzhou Castle after it was occupied by the Japanese. As Jinzhou was fought over and then occupied by the Japanese in both the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) and the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) this scene could have been from either war. However, given the artist's 1874 birth date, it is more likely a scene from the Russo-Japanese War. Jinzhou was taken by the Japanese from the Russians on May 26, 1904. I can find no information on the artist having been to the front in either of these wars.
It is difficult to tell whether this print is a woodblock or a lithograph. The artist worked in both mediums.

media.caption: Idaten (韋駄天)

text.headline: Idaten (韋駄天)
text.text:
In this print Sasajima depicts the Buddhist deity Idaten (the Indian deity Skanda) who is "faster than the wind."
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with Sasajima's original printing of the work, Yoneda has used the technique of "back coloring" 裏彩色 in his reproduction.

media.caption: Pontochō Through Street 2 (先斗町通りぬけ II)

text.headline: Pontochō Through Street 2 (先斗町通りぬけ II)
text.text: An early morning view of Pontochō alleyway connecting Shijō and Sanjō streets in Kyoto, famous for its shops and restaurants. The street is empty except for a lone geisha. Konishi created two editions of this print, a "private printing" (shikaban) of 200 impressions and this collection's print of 500 impressions, which carries the suffix II after its title.

media.caption: Sukeroku (助六)

text.headline: Sukeroku (助六)
text.text:
Picturing the kumadori makeup for the kabuki character Sukeroku, this print is one of ten in the second set (or "collection") that the publisher Hangakai hanmoto intended to issue in monthly installments for ten months, making for a total of one hundred prints when complete.
Kumadori is the stylized exaggerated makeup used in the kabuki theater particularly when performing in the bold and bombastic aragoto style. Kumadori makeup generally consists of brightly colored stripes or patterns over a white foundation, the colors and patterns symbolizing aspects of the actor's character. The three basic colors, other than black, are red (denoting a hero), blue (denoting an evil character) and brown (denoting a supernatural character).

media.caption:
Reproduction of: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge at Atake,
No. 58, after Hiroshige (複製：大はしあたけの夕立・ 広重後 Fukusei：Ōhashi Atake no yūdachi・Hiroshige no ato)

text.headline:
Reproduction of: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge at Atake,
No. 58, after Hiroshige (複製：大はしあたけの夕立・ 広重後 Fukusei：Ōhashi Atake no yūdachi・Hiroshige no ato)
text.text:
An undated (c. 1930s) small format reproduction after Hiroshige's 1857 Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge at Atake, No. 58 from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. The original print has been called the "undisputed masterpiece" of the series.
The publisher of this print was Yokohama-based Hideo Takemura (H. Takemura & Co.) who targeted his work at a Western audience, specializing in, as printed on his business card, Christmas Cards, Japanese Old Colour Prints, Famous Modern Colour Prints and Water Colors.
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

text.text:
An undated (c. 1930s) small format reproduction loosely based on Hiroshige's The Monkey Bridge in Kai Province, originally issued between 1840 and 1842 and designed as part of a four panel harimaze print. media.caption: After: Shrine by the River by Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki)

text.headline: After: Shrine by the River by Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki)
text.text:
After Shōtei's small format print Shrine by the River originally published by Watanabe Shōzaburō (1885-1962) in 1936. The unidentified artist who created this collection's print, published by an unnamed publisher, has taken the background from Shōtei's print and substituted a new foreground. Watanabe became so concerned about Shōtei's designs being copied that he put the following notice into his 1936 catalogue:
About "Copyright"
"At the same time an artist draws a certain atmosphere, there are created copyright and right of personality as in the case of an author. The right of personality should not be infringed by other people and is not transferrable. It lasts as long as an artist lives, while the copyright is a transferable property.
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.
"As said above, the copyright is well protected with the right of the artist's personality according to the copyright law."

text.headline: Tenmangū 天満宮
text.text: A print with a portion of its right side and bottom trimmed. A torii reads 天満宮 (Tenman-gū) and the inscription in the lower left partially reads 神社  (Shinto shrine). Tenman-gū enshrines Sugawara no Michizane 菅原道真 (845-903), scholar, poet and politician as Tenjin. There are about 14 thousand Tenman-gū in Japan and it is unknown which of these shrines is being portrayed.

The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints).

media.caption: Village houses in snow (untitled)

text.headline: Village houses in snow (untitled)
