media.caption: The Port Arthur Surrender - Illustration of the Second Meeting Between General Nogi and General Stoessel to Review Prisoners of War (旅順降服・乃木大將トステツセル将軍ノ會見并二捕虜檢閲之図)

text.headline: The Port Arthur Surrender - Illustration of the Second Meeting Between General Nogi and General Stoessel to Review Prisoners of War (旅順降服・乃木大將トステツセル将軍ノ會見并二捕虜檢閲之図)
text.text: Using the signature Ryūa, as he did for all of his Russo-Japanese War triptychs, Kokunimasa gives us a view of the second meeting between Japanese General Count Nogi Maresuke (乃木 希典), (1849–1912) and the Russian Major-General Baron Anatoly Mikhailyovich Stoessel (1848–1915) on January 7, to discuss the conditions for the transfer of prisoners. In the left sheet we see captured Russian soldiers being led by Japanese officers bearing the Imperial Russian flag as a sign of respect for their vanquished foe.

media.caption: Making Sanbon Sugar [Highly Refined Sugar] in Sanuki Province (同 [讃岐国] 三盆糖製造之図  Dō sanbontō seizō no zu)

text.headline: Making Sanbon Sugar [Highly Refined Sugar] in Sanuki Province (同 [讃岐国] 三盆糖製造之図  Dō sanbontō seizō no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of sanbon (highly refined sugar) in Sanuki Province, present day Kagawa Prefecture.
Sanuki (讃岐国) was an old province of Japan on the island of Shikoku, with the same boundaries as modern Kagawa Prefecture. It faced the Inland Sea and bordered on Awa and Iyo Provinces. Across Naruto strait it bordered Awaji Province too.
Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan, notes that "The chief production of this province of Sanuki are popularly known as ‘the three white things’ (sam-paku), viz, salt, sugar, and cotton. The sugar industry is modern, having been introduced from Satsuma only half a century ago."

media.caption: Niwa - Birth of the Season (庭・季節の誕生)

text.headline: Niwa - Birth of the Season (庭・季節の誕生)
text.text:
This print Niwa (Birth of the season), along with Niwa (Andante), was one of the first two prints of the artist's acquired by the British Museum. Lawrence Smith describes the print as having "sober tonalities."
While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa. Also see Niwa (80-K), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (April) and Niwa (Winter Scenery), Niwa (Summer house) and Niwa (Sunshine) in this collection.

media.caption: I Love You (Love Letters)

text.headline: I Love You (Love Letters)
text.text: I Love You (Love Letters), a silkscreen print with an edition size of 11,111 prints, was the result of discussions between Ay-O, Tokuzo Okabe (founder of the first silkscreen printing studio in Japan), gallery owner Fujio Watanuki and others about expanding the appeal of prints to a wider audience and, particularly, a younger audience. Ay-O suggested adapting his 1973 lithograph Love Letter for this purpose and in 1974 a full run of 11,111 prints was completed.

media.caption: Shinshū Matsushiro-chō  (信州松代町)

text.headline: Shinshū Matsushiro-chō  (信州松代町)
text.text: Two travelers walking through the town of Matsushiro-chō in Shinshū (modern-day Nagano Prefecture.) This print along with another print by the artist, Mitarai Inland Sea Port (Shimozima Ōsaki) 瀬戸内海御手洗港 (大崎下島), were bundled, each in its own separate folder, with the artist's book titled "Kaidō kōryo, Sekino Jun'ichirō gabunshū" (Travels Along Highways: Illustrations and Text by Sekino Jun'ichirō), published by Bijutsu Shuppansha in 1983.

media.caption: Lathe Operator (旋盤工 senbankō)

text.headline: Lathe Operator (旋盤工 senbankō)
text.text:
Five male machinists at work on their lathes in this sixteenth print from the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. This print is one of a small number of prints in the series depicting modern industry in Japan.
A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "A machine is formed by a collection of parts. The more complex the individual parts are, the more sophisticated the machine and its function. Nowadays, compared to a carpenter and a potter, the machinist has already become a major occupation. As a major role in heavy industry, light industry, and precision machinery industry, everyone agrees that this profession is a vital cornerstone. There is no doubt that this profession, which requires extraordinary skill instead of manpower, is extremely popular in today's world."[1]

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Shoe Shiners (靴みがき kutsumigaki)

text.headline: Shoe Shiners (靴みがき kutsumigaki)
text.text:
Wada presents us with his rendition of shoe shiners at work in a park-like setting on a sunny day in this 4th print in the twenty-four print post-WWII series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Continued" (3rd series). The happy picture that Wada presents us with is a much prettier picture than reality. Finding work in the aftermath of the war was tough, especially for veterans many of whom were forced to take this type of labor to survive. Disadvantaged boys also worked shining shoes to survive.
The English language commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "'Shoe-Shine' became so popular in Japan after the war, that the 'shoe-shine boy' became the title of a hit song. Shoe-shine seems now to have become a legal occupation for men, and is a business conducted on the streets of Japan. Originally most Japanese thought it was rather a luxurious service, and a waste of money and time. After the war many people began to wear well-polished shoes as they came to afford well pressed white shirts. I am told that Spain is famous for this skill, and there are many shoe-shiners in its big cities, but this does not mean that all Spanish men are beaus. It seems to me that this profession may be considered as one of the solutions for unemployment. [I do not have much interest in this, so I am not very sure, but it seems.] Shoe-shiners are making their own efforts to make all shoes shine beautifully. Some of them have actually achieved a technique like a craftsman."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

media.caption: White Fishing Boat (白い漁船)

text.headline: White Fishing Boat (白い漁船)
text.text: Another of the artist's many prints picturing small boats along the shore.  For two similar prints by the artist see IHL.1099 and IHL.1198.

media.caption: Gorō (五郎)

text.headline: Gorō (五郎)
text.text: One of several stencil prints created by Mori Yoshitoshi portraying a kabuki actor in the role of Gorō who along with his older brother Jurō sought revenge for the death of their father. The story of the Soga brothers' revenge was originally told in the 12th century "Soga monogatari" 曽我物語.

media.caption: Catching Sea Otter in Chishima Province (千島国 海獺採之図 Chishima no kuni rakko to no zu)

text.headline: Catching Sea Otter in Chishima Province (千島国 海獺採之図 Chishima no kuni rakko to no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It portrays Ainu hunters chasing and harpooning sea otters. In the background we see foreign ships who contributed to the near decimation of the sea otter population in the Kuril Islands (Chishima.)
Records of the Ainu hunting sea otters go back to the 1500s. Traditionally the Ainu hunted sea otters with bow and arrow, leister, and harpoon. Starting in the 1870s, at about the time this print was published, it was reported that most of the hunting was being done by foreign vessels and by 1897 a British sea captain reported that “sea-otter hunting on the Kurils are practically no longer worth considering…” due to their declining numbers. - Source: Notes on the Kuril Islands, Captain H. J. Snow, John Murray, 1897, p. 88.

media.caption: Shipping Ice from Hakodate, Hokkaidō (北海道函館氷輸出之図 Hokkaidō Hakodate kōri yushutsu no zu)

text.headline: Shipping Ice from Hakodate, Hokkaidō (北海道函館氷輸出之図 Hokkaidō Hakodate kōri yushutsu no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.  It portrays people in Western-style garments cutting ice from the moat around Goryōkaku fort near Hakodate on the island of Hokkaidō, from where it was shipped, insulated with sawdust, to Yokohama, Tokyo and other southern destinations.  The ice would be held in storage until the summer months when it would fetch the highest prices. Production and transportation of natural water ice first succeeded in 1869.
Hakodate, located on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaidō, developed as a port town for trade with foreign countries at the end of the 19th century. From December 4, 1868 to June 27, 1869 the Goryōkaku fort was the site of the Battle of Hakodate fought between the remnants of the Tokugawa shogunate army, consolidated into the armed forces of the rebel Ezo Republic, and the armies of the newly formed Imperial government. This was the final battle in the Boshin War.

media.caption: Digging Kudzu [Pueraria] Root in Yamato Province (大和国 葛根堀図 Yamato no kuni kakkon hori zu)

text.headline: Digging Kudzu [Pueraria] Root in Yamato Province (大和国 葛根堀図 Yamato no kuni kakkon hori zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the harvesting of kudzu (Japanese arrowroot or pueraria) root its being processed into powder. Yamato Province (大和国,Yamato no Kuni) was a province of Japan, located in Kinai, corresponding to present-day Nara Prefecture in Honshū.
"Young shoots from this abundant plant are boiled in an iron kettle in pieces 1 m. long, and then submitted to longer soaking in running water, till their bast becomes loose, when it is stripped off by hand. To bleach, soften, and divide its fibres, it is pounded and treated with water, and otherwise manipulated. When finished, the fibres are tolerably firm and white, like hemp-bast. They are used for the woof of several kinds of cloth, but only to a very limited extent." - Source: The Industries of Japan: Together with an Account of its Agriculture, Forestry, Arts and Commerce, Johannes Justus Rein, A. C. Armstrong & Son, 1889, p. 169.
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

media.caption: Producing Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 2 (山城国 宇治茶製之図 二  Yamashiro no kuni Uji cha sei no zu ni)

text.headline: Producing Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 2 (山城国 宇治茶製之図 二  Yamashiro no kuni Uji cha sei no zu ni)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women and men sorting, sifting, steaming, drying, and packaging tea in Uji in Yamashiro Province. The Uji district was famed for its tea plantations and its high-quality tea which was unequaled in Japan. Historically, "the Uji powdered-tea industry was so important that it received bakufu protection, and farmers had to sell their tea through designated channels. [Uji farmers excelled] in the processing of green tea,especially as a result of innovations developed in the 1730’s. Instead of kettle-firing, they steamed theleaves and then rolled rubbed them over a hearth. This process produced a flavorful tea highly prized in central markets. [This superior tea] "became especially important with the opening of the ports in 1859, when tea became one of the country's leading export items. From 1859 to 1867 tea exports increased over eighteen-fold,with more than 7 million pounds being exported in 1867 alone." - Source: Japan's Protoindustrial Elite: The Economic Foundations of the Gōnō, Edward E Prat, Cambridge: Harvard Univ. Asia Center, 1999. p. 52.
For Figure 1 "Picking Uji Tea" see IHL.1495.

media.caption: Abalone Divers in Ise Province (伊勢国 鮑採之図 Ise no kuni awabi tori no zu)

text.headline: Abalone Divers in Ise Province (伊勢国 鮑採之図 Ise no kuni awabi tori no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women divers (ana) bringing abalone (awabi) up to waiting boats in Ise Bay. Cave ruins containing tools the divers used for peeling abalone from the sea bed go back 3,000 years and there are written records of women divers dating to the year 927.
As in this design, the artist based many of his designs on designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

media.caption: Ennosuke in the role of the Exiled King and Tōzō in the role of the Warrior Priest Kōku (猿之助 流離王 東蔵 好苦梵士)

text.headline: Ennosuke in the role of the Exiled King and Tōzō in the role of the Warrior Priest Kōku (猿之助 流離王 東蔵 好苦梵士)
text.text:
The actors Ichikawa Ennosuke II in the role of the exiled king and Nakamura Tōzō II as the warrior priest Kōku in the play Washimo Shiranai わしも知らない staged at tje Gekijō, Tokyo on June 28, 1915. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Along the River (川沿ひ)

text.headline: Along the River (川沿ひ)
text.text: A large woodblock print tipped to a backing sheet depicting two women washing clothes along a riverbank below village houses perched above a steep enbankment. No biographical information is available on this artist who, auction records show, created both woodblock prints and watercolors of landscapes.

media.caption: Fishing for Flatfish in Wakasa Province (若狭国 鰈を取図 Wakasa no kuni karei oto zu)

text.headline: Fishing for Flatfish in Wakasa Province (若狭国 鰈を取図 Wakasa no kuni karei oto zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting fishermen netting flatfish in Wakasa Bay.
Wakasa was famous for the flatfish caught in their offshore waters which were considered a winter delicacy. Wakasa flatfish were often steamed in salt water and then dried, as shown in the print Steaming Flatfish in Wakasa Province (IHL.1487).
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

media.caption: Coal Mine in Iga Province (同国 [伊賀国] 石炭山之図 dōkoku sekitan yama no zu)

text.headline: Coal Mine in Iga Province (同国 [伊賀国] 石炭山之図 dōkoku sekitan yama no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting coal miners entering a mine with pickaxes (tsuruhashi) in hand and exiting the mine carrying yoked baskets (sena) of coal, this color woodblock print (nishiki-e) was one of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. As the series’ name implies, each print depicted an economic activity in a province or district of Japan. In addition, each activity was described on the print in a scroll-like cartouche.
For another impression of this print see IHL.0324.
Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi,Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces. The Saruka mountains which bordered Iga were noted for their coal reserves. An 1878-1879 geological survey describes Iga coal as being "black and shining." The print's scroll mentions that the coal produced is like the color of lacquer.

media.caption: Making Steamed Flatfish in Wakasa Province (同[若狭]蒸鰈製造之図 Dō [Wakasa] mushi karei seizō no zu)

text.headline: Making Steamed Flatfish in Wakasa Province (同[若狭]蒸鰈製造之図 Dō [Wakasa] mushi karei seizō no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the steaming and drying of flatfish to make mushi-garei.
Wakasa was famous for the flatfish (karei) caught in their offshore waters which were considered a winter delicacy. Wakasa flatfish were often steamed in salt water and then dried, as shown in this print. The mushi-garei from Wakasa were considered the best and known to be offered as gifts to the imperial family.

media.caption: Polishing-sand of Iga Province (伊賀国 磨砂 Iga kuni migakizuna)

text.headline: Polishing-sand of Iga Province (伊賀国 磨砂 Iga kuni migakizuna)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, workers are mining a white sand that will be be used in tooth powder, for polishing rice to make uruchi, and other applications using polishing sand. Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi, Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces.
For another impression of this print see IHL.0323.

media.caption: Catching Salmon in Echigo Province (越後国 鮭洲走を捕図)

text.headline: Catching Salmon in Echigo Province (越後国 鮭洲走を捕図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The print depicts men catching salmon which have become stranded on a sandbar during their autumn migration up river.
For another impression of this print see IHL.0364.
Echigo (越後国, Echigo no kuni) was an old province in north-central Japan, on the shores of the Sea of Japan. It corresponds today to Niigata Prefecture, minus the island of Sado.

media.caption: Bleaching Fabric on the Snow in Echigo Province (越後國雪中布晒之図)

text.headline: Bleaching Fabric on the Snow in Echigo Province (越後國雪中布晒之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.
The ancient technique of snow-bleaching in the final stage of the creation of Echigo-jofu (a fine-as-silk ramie weaving) is still in use today. Exposing the fabric to snow "makes use of the bleaching effect from ozone produced when snow evaporates in the sun. The wisdom of ancestors has been passed on through this method that removes excess dye, loosens snarls in the threads, and gives the cloth a light, soft finishing touch." - http://japanupclose.web-japan.org/culture/20150323_1.html [accessed 8-25-23]
For another impression of this print see IHL.0366.

media.caption: Making Willow Baskets in Tajima Province (但馬国 柳行李製図)

text.headline: Making Willow Baskets in Tajima Province (但馬国 柳行李製図)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting a group of men and one woman making yanagigōri (wicker trunks). The trunks and baskets made in Tajima were especially beautiful and were "sent to the baths at Arima, and further still to Kobe, and also exported." - Source: The Industries of Japan: Together with an Account of its Agriculture, Forestry, Arts and Commerce, J. J. Rein, A. C. Armstrong and Son, 1889, p. 173.

media.caption: Fishing for Bonito in Tosa Province (土佐国 鰹釣之図 Tosa no kuni katsuo tsuri no zu)

text.headline: Fishing for Bonito in Tosa Province (土佐国 鰹釣之図 Tosa no kuni katsuo tsuri no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting fishermen throwing their catch of bonito up on the shore to a group of men and women waiting to clean them.
"Bonito is arguably the most favored fish among the people in Japan. Hatsu-gatsuo, the first bonito of the season, becomes available in early summer and was a highly prized delicacy in the capital city of Edo in the 19th century. Bonito fishermen traditionally used fishing poles rather than nets in order to minimize the damage and stress on the fish, believing that this would enhance their flavor." - website of Minneapolis Institute of Art http://collections.artsmia.org/art/61327/bonito-fishing-on-the-ocean-tosa-province-utagawa-hiroshige[accessed 8-25-23]
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

media.caption: Picking Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 1 (山城国 宇治茶摘図 一  Yamashiro no kuni Uji chatsumi zu ichi)

text.headline: Picking Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 1 (山城国 宇治茶摘図 一  Yamashiro no kuni Uji chatsumi zu ichi)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women and children picking tea in Uji, Yamashiro Province. The Uji district was famed for its tea plantations and its high-quality tea. Historically, the "Uji powdered-tea industry was so important that it received bakufu protection, and farmers had to sell their tea through designated channels. Unlike farmers in other parts of the country, who cultivated tea on the footpaths between fields or on mountain slopes, Uji farmers grew their plants in groves. To produce a high-quality product, they latticed over their groves for superior grades of tea with straw or reed to protect the plants from the elements until the buds appeared." - Source: Japan's Protoindustrial Elite: The Economic Foundations of the Gōnō, Edward E Prat, Cambridge: Harvard Univ. Asia Center, 1999. p. 52
Also see IHL.1481 Producing Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 2.

media.caption: Bear Hunting for Gall in Kaga Province (加州熊并ニ胆ヲ取ル図 Kashū-gama narabi ni kimo o toru zu)

In this print, the Asian black bear (note the white chest mark) is being hunted for his gall. Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no kuni) was an old province in the area that is today the southern part of Ishikawa Prefecture. Ruled by the Maeda clan, the capital of Kaga was Kanazawa. Kaga bordered on Echizen, Etchū, Hida, and Noto Provinces. It was part of Hokurikudō Circuit.
For another impression of this print see IHL.0272.

media.caption: Cultivating Wild Silkworms in Tajima Province (同国 [但馬国] 野蚕(蠶)養之図 dōkoku [Tajima no kuni] yasan yō no zu)

text.headline: Cultivating Wild Silkworms in Tajima Province (同国 [但馬国] 野蚕(蠶)養之図 dōkoku [Tajima no kuni] yasan yō no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the tending of mulberry trees and silkworm cocoons. When this print was issued in 1877 silk was Japan's leading export and by 1909 Japan surpassed China as the world's number one silk producer.
In keeping with the importance of sericulture to Japan's economy and industrialization, seven prints in the series are devoted to it. The Exposition was essentially an industrial promotion opportunity providing a meeting place for Western technologies and their Japanese counterparts." "Silk production was the first example of an industry in which European producers deliberately sought out Japanese know-how" and "the source of Japan's first export technology." - Source: "Sericulture and the Origins of Japanese Industrialization", Tessa Morris-Suzuki, appearing JSTOR, Vol. 33, No.1, January 1992, p. 1-2-103; p. 121.

media.caption: Making Sōmen in Noto Province (能登 素麺製造ノ図 Noto sōmen seizō no zu)

text.headline: Making Sōmen in Noto Province (能登 素麺製造ノ図 Noto sōmen seizō no zu)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of sōmen, very thin, white Japanese noodles made of wheat flour.
Sōmen was introduced to Japan from China during the Kamakura period (1185-1333) and were originally made at Zen monasteries. In the mid-1400s "sōmen production requiring certain techniques and skill and a wide space, transferred from Zen monasteries to other artisans, marking the birth of the sōmen industry." - website of Kikkoman Company https://www.kikkoman.com/jp/kiifc/foodculture/pdf_17/e_001_004.pdf [accessed 8-25-23]

media.caption: Watōnai, Master of Papier Mache (和藤内　はりこの名人 Watōnai hariko no meijin)

text.headline: Watōnai, Master of Papier Mache (和藤内　はりこの名人 Watōnai hariko no meijin)
text.text:
In this print Kyōsai portrays the fierce warrior Watōnai (Coxinga) as a maker of paper mache daruma dolls. Watōnai is staring at paper mache tigers (tora), alluding to the play The Battles of Coxinga in which Watōnai vanquishes the fierce tiger.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

media.caption: Putting Her Husband Under Her Behind; Plastering Mud on Her Husband's Face (亭主を尻に敷く　亭主の顔へ泥を塗る Teishū o shiri ni shiku Teishū no kao e doro o nuru)

text.headline: Putting Her Husband Under Her Behind; Plastering Mud on Her Husband's Face (亭主を尻に敷く　亭主の顔へ泥を塗る Teishū o shiri ni shiku Teishū no kao e doro o nuru)
text.text:
In both the top and bottom scenes Kyōsai portrays a husband dominated by his wife. In the top scene, a wife sits on her husband smoking a pipe, while her husband holds a tabakobon (tobacco tray) for her comfort. The smoke from her pipe is spelling out the words noroma-yarō (のろま やろう), meaning "slow-witted man." To their left, their little girl, dressed in rags, is tracing out in the air (as children often due when learning new words) the characters from the pipe and learning from the bad example her parents are setting. In the bottom print, a wife is putting mud on her husband's face to keep him from seeing her lover hiding behind a hanging kimono, to whom she hands a love letter.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

Tango Province (丹後国, Tango no Kuni) was an old province in the area that is today northern Kyoto Prefecture facing the Sea of Japan. Tango bordered on Tajima, Tamba, and Wakasa provinces. At various times both Maizuru and Miyazu were the capital and chief town of the province.

media.caption: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)

text.headline: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, kuzu (Japanese arrowroot or pueraria) is being processed into starch. Kuzu root is the traditional medicine of choice for a host of digestive disorders and it is also used as a cooking starch. Yamato Province (大和国, Yamato no Kuni) was a province of Japan, located in Kinai, corresponding to present-day Nara Prefecture in Honshū.

media.caption: Crane Hawk [falconry] in Iyo Province, figure 2 (伊予国 鶴鷹之図二 Iyo no kuni kaku yō no zu ni)

text.headline: Crane Hawk [falconry] in Iyo Province, figure 2 (伊予国 鶴鷹之図二 Iyo no kuni kaku yō no zu ni)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the capturing of a "crane hawk" using a tame crane hawk and a bird on a lure in Iyo Province. While the title of this print, shown in the leftmost red part of the scroll, does not give the location, the scroll itself tells us that the scene is taking place in Iyo (伊豫) which is now part of Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku in Southeast Japan. The small yellow cartouche informs us that the bird resting on the falconer's gloved hand is tame.

media.caption: Capturing Falcons in Iyo Province, figure 1 (伊豫國鷹捕之図 一)

text.headline: Capturing Falcons in Iyo Province, figure 1 (伊豫國鷹捕之図 一)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the capturing of falcons using kasumi-ami in Iyo Province (伊予国, Iyo no kuni) which is now part of Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku.
Kasumi-ami 霞網 are stationary mist nets perfected for bird trapping in Japan in the late 1800s. Originally made of cotton or silk thread, modern mist nets are constructed of black nylon. Most are 6 meters long and 3 meters high. These delicate, lightweight nets, which “disappear” visually against most backgrounds, are used both with and without mechanical or live tethered lures. Mist nets are firmly suspended end-to-end from bamboo, metal, or fiberglass poles, typically in parallel or angled arrays. Nets are placed in areas that are likely to attract feeding migrants, and in many instances raptors are attracted to the nets by already-captured passerines. - Source: Migrating Raptors of the World: Their Ecology and Conservation, Keith L. Bildstein, Cornell University Press, 2006, p. 49-50.
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. media.caption: Making Dried Bonito Flakes in Tosa Province (同 [土佐国] 鰹節を製ス図 Dō katsuobushi o seisu zu)

text.headline: Making Dried Bonito Flakes in Tosa Province (同 [土佐国] 鰹節を製ス図 Dō katsuobushi o seisu zu)
text.text: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes, a staple of Japanese cookery) are being processed. Tosa Province (土佐国 Tosa no kuni) is a former province of Japan in the area that is today Kōchi Prefecture on Shikoku. Tosa was bordered by Iyo and Awa Provinces. It was sometimes called Doshū (土州). "The waters of the bay [Tosa Bay] made possible a flourishing fishing industry, and dried bonito (katsuobushi) from Tosa found its way from the fishing villages, via the proper guild channels, to the markets of Osaka and Edo." - Source: Sakamoto Ryoma and the Meiji Restoration, Marius B. Jansen, Princeton University Press, 1961, p. 23.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Teruhi no Miko in the play Uwanari (九世 市川団十郎 照日の神子・嫐)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Teruhi no Miko in the play Uwanari (九世 市川団十郎 照日の神子・嫐)
text.text:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper left panel, playing the role of Teruhi no Miko in the kabuki play Uwanari. He wears a white hannya mask, denoting a vengeful female spirit of aristocratic background. Below Danjūrō is an unidentified actor playing the role of Kishō 吉聖.
The play Uwanari is variously translated as “The Mistress,” “The Second Wife,"“Jealousy,” and “Ambush of the Second Wife.” Uwanari was originally staged in 1699. While the original script has been lost, the play was re-written and re-staged in 1936.
Uwanari, which means “second wife” and “jealousy”, is a torrid tale of jealousy, hate, and love. In it, a man divorces his wife and marries another woman. But while the newlyweds enjoy marital bliss, the jilted wife fumes, and plots her revenge on her ex-husband and the woman who replaced her. Passions will flare and dark schemes will bloom in this in riveting play, all told through impassioned dance.[1]
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

[1] https://metropolitant.com/2015/06/22/ebizo-ichikawa-xi-returns-to-singapore-with-japan-theatre-2015/ [accessed 8-23-23]
[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

media.caption: Sado Traveler's Journal (佐渡紀行 Sado kikō)

text.headline: Sado Traveler's Journal (佐渡紀行 Sado kikō)
text.text:
Miyashita's limited edition book, published in 1999, of essays and prints about Sado Island 佐渡島 in the Sea of Japan off the coast of Niigita Prefecture. Bound into the book are four multi-color prints, woodblocks and combinations of woodblock and intaglio techniques, and six copperplate engravings. The heavy-weight paper used in the book was made by Yamada Shōkai located in the Higashichichibu Washi Center, Higashichichibu. In 2014, along with the neighboring village of Ogawa, Higashichichibu received UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Status for keeping the ancient traditions of Japanese paper making alive and flourishing.

media.caption: Cormorant Fishing on the Nagara River in Gifu Prefecture Scene 2 (岐阜長良川鵜飼 その二 Gifu Nagaragawa ukai sono ni)

text.headline: Cormorant Fishing on the Nagara River in Gifu Prefecture Scene 2 (岐阜長良川鵜飼 その二 Gifu Nagaragawa ukai sono ni)
text.text: One of two prints designed by the artist depicting the ancient art of cormorant fishing on the Nagara River in Gifu Prefecture.

media.caption: Bunraku Samurai

text.headline: Bunraku Samurai
text.text: In a January 2023 email in response to collector Jon Lipka's inquiry about this little known series of bunraku prints, Koko Nakayama of the Adachi Institute of Woodcut Prints wrote, "Adachi produced the Bunraku series of Kiyoshi Saito around the 50s (late Showa 20s). And the red small stamp on the back is ours. It was commission work just for the production, so we did not sell them. They were printed on the dyed in black non washi paper. It is quite an unusual production method for us, but it seems that we were asked to try it that way. Instead of printing with watercolors and letting them soak in the fibers of the washi paper, only this series was printed to let the colors sit on the paper with different types of paints, which creates the thick texture of the print as you mentioned. The black area we see underneath the other colors is the color of the dyed paper. It was ordered by either artist, Kiyoshi Saito or his publisher. After this series, we produced the other series (Children), but they were printed with a standard ukiyo-e style woodcut printing method."

media.caption: Illustration of The Imperial Assembly of the House of Peers (帝国議会貴族院之図 Teikoku gikai kizokuin no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of The Imperial Assembly of the House of Peers (帝国議会貴族院之図 Teikoku gikai kizokuin no zu)
text.text: Picturing a meeting of the Imperial Diet's House of Peers, the upper house of the Imperial Diet consisting of appointed high-ranking nobles, this print was published in September 1890, two months before the actual first meeting of the House of Peers (貴族院 Kizoku-in) on November 29, 1890. This type of portrayal of future events was not unusual, as the Meiji government encouraged publishers to inform the public of new institutions.

media.caption: Rat and Radish (untitled)

text.headline: Rat and Radish (untitled)
text.text: A small rat (nezumi) nibbles on a bright red radish. One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of last century. Multiple editions of this print exist. See IHL. 2141 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Seto Inland Sea, Tomonotsu (瀬戸内海 鞆之津 Setonaikai Tomonotsu)

text.headline: Seto Inland Sea, Tomonotsu (瀬戸内海 鞆之津 Setonaikai Tomonotsu)
text.text: The harbor at Tomonotsu in the waning glow of sunset. This image, originally published in the summer of 1940, is one of the artist's most famous and was reprinted numerous times by the publisher, Watanabe Shōzaburō, including one edition using re-carved blocks. This collection's print bears Watanabe's round 7mm seal indicating a later edition. The paper type, the coloration of the print and the presence of the date in the left-hand margin point to a mid-1950s to mid-1960s impression.

media.caption: The Woodcutter from Mino (美濃樵夫 Mino no kikori)

text.headline: The Woodcutter from Mino (美濃樵夫 Mino no kikori)
text.text:
One of two known prints in the series Selections from Japanese History, issued by the little-known publisher Yazawa Hisakichi 矢沢久吉. This triptych pictures the tale of a woodcutter from Mino whose filial piety brought about a visit by the Empress Gensho 元正天皇 (reign 715-724). On the left we see the woodcutter and his father in front of Yōrō Falls paying reverence to the Empress in her palanquin who has come to see the reported miracle of the falls' water turning into sake.
As told in the Zenken kojitsu 前賢故実, during the 8th century a poor woodcutter went to the forest for firewood to warm his sick father. While searching, he came upon a waterfall whose water magically turned into sake. Filling his gourd he returns home to his ailing father who drinks the sake and miraculously recovers.
Hearing about this miracle, Empress Gensho visited the waterfall herself and determined that the miracle was a reward for the filial piety of the woodcutter. In honor of this miracle the Empress renamed the year of her reign "Yōrō", for the location of the waterfall.

media.caption: The Courtesan of Eguchi; A Lotus in the Mud (江口ノ遊君 江口里 でい中乃蓮 Eguchi no yūkun, Eguchi no sato, Deichū no hasu)

text.headline: The Courtesan of Eguchi; A Lotus in the Mud (江口ノ遊君 江口里 でい中乃蓮 Eguchi no yūkun, Eguchi no sato, Deichū no hasu)
text.text:
The top portion of the print parodies the tale in which the bodhisattva Samantabhadra (Fugen), the protector of the Lotus Sutra, takes the guise of the courtesan Eguchi and offers shelter to a travelling monk. The bottom portion of the print, showing a lotus coming out of the mouth of courtesan, parodies the saying "a lotus in the mud", meaning that although the lotus grows in the mud, it is pure, the quintessential flower for Buddhists, as is the courtesan who tries to keep her heart pure although she is in a house of prostitution.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

media.caption: Distant View of Snow and Komagatake (雪の駒ヶ岳遠望 Yuki no Komagatake enbō)

text.headline: Distant View of Snow and Komagatake (雪の駒ヶ岳遠望 Yuki no Komagatake enbō)
text.text: A horse-pulled sled and its driver pause to look out at Lake Onuma on Hokkaidō with Komagatake, an active volcano, in the background.

media.caption: Children Blowing up the Belly of Hotei and Painting It Like a Candy (漢子以布袋腹擬吃飴)

text.headline: Children Blowing up the Belly of Hotei and Painting It Like a Candy (漢子以布袋腹擬吃飴)
text.text:
In this print a raucous group of children are painting the belly of Hotei, the god of happiness. It is one of forty prints (chūban size) which make up the series Sketches by Yoshitoshi (Yoshitoshi ryakuga). The series consists of forty humorous subjects originally printed in pairs on an ōban size sheet.
Lea Baten in Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints provides us with the following description of this print:
"[C]hildren painting Hotei’s belly to look like a giant mochi cake. Hotei, one of the seven gods of good luck, is the Japanese god of happiness, for in his huge sack he carries toys and treasures for the flocks of children who swarm around him everywhere. He is very tolerant and allows the boisterous bevy many liberties, while pondering sleepily and not too seriously on the deterioration of today’s morals. Here, after having received paint and paintbrush, a mischievous youngster is trying out his artistic talents on Hotei’s immense hairy stomach to the joy of the others who are accompanying his efforts with jumping, laughter, and brandishing toys. A plum blossom and a pine needle adorn the patient Hotei’s grotesque belly, which is being blown up through a natural channel, to put it euphemistically, by a daring juvenile delinquent with a long bamboo pipe." - Source: Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints, Lea Baten,Weatherhill, 1995, p. 110-112.

media.caption: Raikō (Yorimitsu) Enters the Treasure Mountain (頼光宝之山入Yorimitsu takara no yama ni iru)

text.headline: Raikō (Yorimitsu) Enters the Treasure Mountain (頼光宝之山入Yorimitsu takara no yama ni iru)
text.text: In this print Minamoto no Yorimitsu, also known as Minamoto no Raikō, in full armor prepares to lop off the head of the drunken ogre (oni) Shutendōji 酒呑童子 (literally, "drunken child"). Shutendōji, who can change form, here seen in the guise of a giant child, has fallen asleep on an armrest held up by coral legs. An overturned sake bowl (sakazuki) and a ladle lie in front attest to his being drunk and various treasures (takaramono) are scattered about. This print is one of forty prints (chūban size) which make up the series Sketches by Yoshitoshi (Yoshitoshi ryakuga). The series consists of forty humorous subjects originally printed in pairs on an ōban size sheet.

media.caption: Lamps and Pots (洋燈とつぼ)

text.headline: Lamps and Pots (洋燈とつぼ)
text.text: A collector of old foreign language books, Kawakami loved depicting the objects he found in them. This 1955 print uses two of the artist's favorite objects -  lamps and a jar. In addition to numerous prints depicting these objects, Kawakami devoted an entire book to the lamp titled "ranpu" (ランプ)

media.caption: Apricot in the Night, Nap, Dance of the Three-legged Kettle (夜の梅, 居眠り, 鼎踊り)

text.headline: Apricot in the Night, Nap, Dance of the Three-legged Kettle (夜の梅, 居眠り, 鼎踊り)
text.text:
Kyōsai gives us two comic scenes and one image of an apricot tree (in the stone-rubbing style) in this harimaze print. The two comic scenes show us a drunken folk dance and a napping scholar being teased by two courtesans hiding behind a curtain.
This series, consisting of a least ten prints, using "legitimate Kano school subjects as their themes" depicted in comic situations, made Kyōsai quite popular as an ukiyo-e artist. "At the time, these harimaze prints were cut into individual scenes and the small pieces were used to repair the holes in paper sliding doors and screens. Kyosai’s humorous scenes were thus enjoyed in the everyday lives of the Japanese people." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 32-33, 220-225.

media.caption: Egret, Ofuku, Coiffeur, Holes in Their Abdomen (連封一品, お福, 髪結い, 胴に穴あき)

text.headline: Egret, Ofuku, Coiffeur, Holes in Their Abdomen (連封一品, お福, 髪結い, 胴に穴あき)
text.text:
The three multi-color panels of the print are referred to as Ofuku (goddess of mirth who at the time of creation with her boisterous dance brought the sun goddess Amaterasu from her dark cave, bringing sunshine to the world), Holes in Their Abdomen and Coiffeur. The upper right panel depicting a crane and lotus bears the kanji characters 連封一品. The pairing of a crane (yipin niao) and lotus (lianhua) is a rebus for lianfeng yipin (may you continuously be promoted to the first rank).
This series, consisting of a least ten prints, using "legitimate Kano school subjects as their themes" depicted in comic situations, made Kyōsai quite popular as an ukiyo-e artist. "At the time, these harimaze prints were cut into individual scenes and the small pieces were used to repair the holes in paper sliding doors and screens. Kyosai’s humorous scenes were thus enjoyed in the everyday lives of the Japanese people." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 32-33, 220-225.

media.caption: Wind God (風神 Fūjin)

text.headline: Wind God (風神 Fūjin)
text.text:
Picturing the Shinto god of the wind Fūjin, one of the oldest Shinto gods, Fūjin was present at the creation of the world when he first let the winds out of his bag, clearing the morning mists and filling the space between heaven and earth allowing the sun to shine. He is portrayed as a terrifying dark demon carrying a large bag of winds on his shoulders. Fūjin is often seen paired with Raijin, the thunder god.
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. The printer, Yoneda Minoru, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique, employed on the original print, of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance.

media.caption: Stone Path (石径)

text.headline: Stone Path (石径)
text.text:
Picturing a pathway through the trees to what is likely a temple building, the printer, Yoneda Minoru, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance. For this print, he appears to have used a dyed kozo paper.
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru.

media.caption: Bunraku Theater Stage Set for Sugawara and the Secrets of Calligraphy (文楽人形、舞台図、菅原伝授手習鑑 Bunraku ningyō butaizu Sugawara denju tenarai kagami)

text.headline: Bunraku Theater Stage Set for Sugawara and the Secrets of Calligraphy (文楽人形、舞台図、菅原伝授手習鑑 Bunraku ningyō butaizu Sugawara denju tenarai kagami)
text.text:
An illustration of the stage set for the opening scene of Act III “Tearing the Carriage Apart” in the play Sugawara Denju Tenarai Kagami [Sugawara and the Secrets of Calligraphy]. In this set an ox drawn carriage sits in front of Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto. Sakuramaru and Umeōmaru will battle their blood triplet brother Matsuōmaru over control of the carriage carrying Great Minister Shihei and the carriage and its axle will be reduced to mangled splinters.
The play is one of the “Three Masterpieces” of the puppet theater along with Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura and Kanadehon Chūshingura. It was written in 1746 by Namiki Sōsuke (Senryū) (1695-1751), Miyoshi Shōraku(1696-1772) and Takeda Koizumo (Izumo II) (1691–1756).
A later edition, post-WWII, print by Uchida Publishing issued without the tissue overlay present in the original edition.
The Illustrated Collection of Famous Japanese Puppets of the Osaka Bunrakuza
The Illustrated Collection of Famous Japanese Puppets of the Osaka Bunrakuza consists of twelve sets of prints each set depicting a specific play in the bunraku repertory. Each set contains a stage set for the specific play along with three prints of puppet characters appearing in the play and an explanatory sheet, for a total of forty-eight color woodblock prints and twelve monochrome explanatory sheets. All of the plays pictured were performed at the Bunraku Theater (Bunraku-za) located within the Goryō Shrine compound in Osaka. The Goryō Bunraku-za burned down in November 1926 after what has been described as "an extremely difficult managerial era" and "lost interest" by the public in the late Taishō era. It is unknown what role, if any, the management of the Goryō Bunraku-za may have played in the formulation and issuance of this print series in their efforts to revitalize the theater.

media.caption: Dutch Lantern (蘭燈 Rantō)

text.headline: Dutch Lantern (蘭燈 Rantō)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally made for the 1917 cover of the musical score for Matoori Nagayo's "Rantō Kōta" (Song of the Lantern), published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"This woodblock print exemplifies Yumeji's lifelong interest in the exotic and foreign, as manifest in the recurring imagery of port cities. Here, a woman dressed in a vivid red kimono with shibari-dyed patterns and floral motifs casually plays a shamisen. A large paper lantern hangs behind here, with a view of the bay in the distance."[1]
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."[2]

[1]Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 15.
[2]Ibid., p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: The Old Refrain (古歌の思出 Koka no omoide)

text.headline: The Old Refrain (古歌の思出 Koka no omoide)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally made for the 1924 cover of the musical score "The Old Refrain" by the Austrian composer Fritz Kreisler (1875-1962) published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."- Source: Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: Maiko [3] (舞妓 [三])

text.headline: Maiko [3] (舞妓 [三])
text.text:
One of at least fifteen prints from Saitō that depict maiko (Kyoto apprentice geisha) in various poses and from various angles. The first maiko print appeared in 1959 and they continued into the 1960s and, possibly, into the early 1970s. This print is from an unnumbered (open) edition and is not dated, but is likely from the late 1960s or early 1970s. The print is also seen with the artist's signature in white ink rather than black ink, as on this collection's print.
As with many of his prints, Saitō makes brilliant use of the natural grain of the woodblock. Melanie C. Gibb comments on Saitō's use of woodblock grain in the catalog of the exhibition Revisiting Modern Japanese Prints" as follows:
"He often began the carving process with a solid piece of katsura or plywood while later executing large areas of his designs with mokumezuri, or grain printing. This natural texture, exposed by scouring out the soft surface of the grain, is beautifully applied in the print Maiko, as seen in the large flat area of obi fabric which beautifully undulates against the curvilinear form of the geisha-in-training."

media.caption: Otonashi River at Ōji, No. 36 (王子音無川・三十六 Ōji Otonashigawa・sanjū roku)

text.headline: Otonashi River at Ōji, No. 36 (王子音無川・三十六 Ōji Otonashigawa・sanjū roku)
text.text:
This view of a dam, built in 1657, along the Otonashi River borrows heavily from the more famous print by Utagawa Hiroshige I issued in 1857 by the same publisher as part of the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei). The dam was popularly referred to at the "Great Waterfall."
By the 1960's the Otonashi River had been reduced to a concrete channel, but in 1985 a three year construction plan was begun to revive and beautify the 100 meter length of the river. Otonashi Shinsui Park was opened in 1988.

media.caption: Series "Kyoto" No. 22 (シリーズ京都 No. 22)

text.headline: Series "Kyoto" No. 22 (シリーズ京都 No. 22)
text.text: It is generally assumed, whether or not the artist has used the Japanese words "Niwa" (Garden) or "Kyoto" as part of a print's title, that the print portrays a Japanese garden.  Whether this print Series Kyoto No. 22 portrays the abstracted elements of a Japanese garden, e.g. rocks, water, trees, moss, plants, buildings, gates, lanterns and fences or the abstracted elements of a Kyoto city scene, the artist's forms and layers of color are left to the viewer to interpret.

media.caption: Reproduction of: A Bijin Writing Poem Slips for the Tanabata Festival  (複製：円窓七夕短冊かき美人)

text.headline: Reproduction of: A Bijin Writing Poem Slips for the Tanabata Festival  (複製：円窓七夕短冊かき美人)
text.text:
A small format reproduction, date unknown, after Suzuki Harunobu's "A Bijin Writing Poem Slips for the Tanabata Festival" (Round Window), originally published between 1750 and 1770. A courtesan is writing poem slips for the Tanabata (Star) festival, held on the 7th day of the 7th month.
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publisher's who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

media.caption: [After the print] Two Geisha and Porter in Wind and Rain at Night, from Vol. 2 of the book Flowers of the Four Seasons (絵本四季花　下　風雨の中を歩む芸者と箱屋 Ehon shiki no hana)

text.headline: [After the print] Two Geisha and Porter in Wind and Rain at Night, from Vol. 2 of the book Flowers of the Four Seasons (絵本四季花　下　風雨の中を歩む芸者と箱屋 Ehon shiki no hana)
text.text:
A small format woodblock reproduction, mounted on a greeting card, after Kitagawa Utamaro's 1801 nighttime depiction of two geisha and a porter in the driving wind and rain. There are many small woodblock reproductions derived from Utagawa's original print which can be seen in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. The original design was modified at some point, likely in early to mid 20th century, to add Utamaro's signature in the lower right corner of the image, which is not present on the original print, and to make color and other changes to the design. The earliest known small reproduction, similar to this collection's print, was shown in the catalog of the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō in 1938.

media.caption: Konjiki Pagoda (平泉金色堂)

text.headline: Konjiki Pagoda (平泉金色堂)
text.text:
A small format unsigned print very similar to a design created by Kawase Hasui for the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. Konjiki-dō (Golden Hall) is part of the Chūson-ji Temple complex. (Reference Hp-47 in "Kawase Hasui, The Complete Woodblock Prints, Volume 1" Hotei Publishing, 2003, p. 143.) See IHL.0654 for another similar design of Konjiki-dō by another unknown artist.

The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

text.headline: Peacock and Cherry Blossom
text.text: This print picturing a peacock and peahen on cherry tree branch was tipped into the 1936 Watanabe sales catalog, Catalogue of Wood-cut Color Prints, of S. Watanabe, p. 39.  On p. 36 of that catalog the print is titled "Peacock and cherry blossom." Postcard size prints were first offered by Watanabe in his 1931 sales catalog.

media.caption: Kyoto Kinkakuji (京都金閣寺)

text.headline: Kyoto Kinkakuji (京都金閣寺)
text.text:
One of at least 83 small format prints, often referred to as "postcard size" prints, designed by Hasui for the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō (1885-1962). This image of Kyoto's Golden Pavilion (Kinkakuji) in snow has been often reproduced by other publishers without credit to the artist. (See IHL.0653, IHL.1424 and IHL.1668 for examples of prints very similar in design to Hasui's.) The publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō became so upset by these copies of original designs by Hasui and several other artists he published that he included the following warning in his 1936 catalogue titled, " Catalogue of Wood-Cut Colour Prints of S. Watanabe, S. Watanabe, 1936" :
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.”
This collection's print was originally tipped into the 1936 Watanabe sales catalog titled Catalogue of Wood-cut Color Prints, of S. Watanabe, p. 41, catalogue No. 896, and then removed. On p. 38 of that catalog the print is titled as "Snow scenery at Kinkakuji (Golden Temple)." Postcard size prints were first offered in Watanabe's 1931 sales catalog.
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

text.headline: Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Volume 2 (錦絵修身談 巻二 Nishiki-e Shūshindan kanni)
text.text:
Volume two of a six volume set of moral instruction textbooks designed for young children. Each volume contains from one to three color woodblock prints by one of the most popular artists of the time Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), who also designed the black and white illustrations that accompanied the short stories written by Yamana Tomesaburō, based upon the morally illustrative actions of adults and children from Japan, China and the West.
This volume contains three color woodblock prints by Yoshitoshi titled The Loyalty of Kusunoki Masashige 楠正成の忠 (IHL.1539a), Wang Lan Harmony Between Siblings 王覧の悌 (IHL.1539b) and The Benevolence of Harry Lane エリーレーンの仁 (IHL.1539c) along with fifteen short stories and eight black and white illustrations.

media.caption: The Loyalty of Kusunoki Masashige (楠正成の忠)

text.headline: The Loyalty of Kusunoki Masashige (楠正成の忠)
text.text:
In this print, one of three color prints in Volume 2 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays Kusonoki's parting speech to his son at Sakura Station on his way to the Battle of Minatogawa, telling his eleven year old son Masatsura "I feel this is the last time I will see your face in this life." He orders him to return home to Kawachi to continue the family line and to support the emperor until death, ending by saying "This will be your most important filial duty to me." For the other two color prints in this volume see IHL.1539b and IHL.1539c.

text.headline: Wang Lan Harmony Between Siblings (王覧の悌)
text.text:
In this print, one of three color prints in Volume 2 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays a young Wang Lan (206-278) protecting his older half-brother Wang Xiang (185-269) from the wrath of his mother, who favored her own son. Both brothers were to grow up and become important statesmen during the Chinese Three Kingdoms period (220-280). For the other two color prints in this volume see IHL.1539a and IHL.1539c.

text.headline: The Chastity of Shihino Shinasa (四比信紗の貞)
text.text:
In this print, one of two color prints in Volume 3 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the widow Shihino Shinasa caring for her own children along with the children of her husband's concubine without favor. After her husband's death, she vowed to remain chaste thereby fulfilling the "li" of a woman. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1540b.

text.headline: The Decorum of Gekiketsu (郤缼の禮)
text.text:
In this print, one two color prints in Volume 3 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the minister of state during China's Spring and Autumn Era (770-476 BC) as he observes the poor farmer Xi Que (Gekiketsu in Japanese) and his wife treating each other with great respect, as if they were each other's guest. When the minister told the king, the king appointed Xi Que to an important position in the state of Jin. Xi Que would go on to successively higher positions. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1540a.

media.caption: The Frugality of Kuroda Josui (黒田如水の倹)

text.headline: The Frugality of Kuroda Josui (黒田如水の倹)
text.text:
In this print, one two color prints in Volume 4 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the samurai and Christian convert Kuroda Jusoi (1546-1604) who was known for his frugality and his generosity. Here he has instructed his servant to remove the flesh from some tai he had been sent as a present and make soup of the bones for he and his guests, who had borrowed money from him. His guests seeing this severe economy worried that they would be charged high interest on their loan but Kuroda would not even take the principal. The print's large cartouche provides an explanation suitable for a child of elementary school age to understand. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1541b.

text.headline: The Wisdom of Gassendi (ガセンヂの智)
text.text:
In this print, one two color prints in Volume 4 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the French astronomer, mathematician, philosopher and priest Pierre Gassendi (1592-1655) as a child proving to his friends that the moon remains stationary while the clouds move. The print's large cartouche provides an explanation suitable for a child of elementary school age to understand. For a later edition of this print, issued as a single-sheet stand-alone print see IHL.1304. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1541a.
