media.caption: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)

text.headline: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)
text.text:
Children and adults gather around a storyteller dressed in an official-looking uniform.
The commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition (originally print number 13 in the series) reads "A Story-teller (Kamishibai) - When he finds a good place for his business on the street, he stops and makes ready the pictures illustrating his stories in the case on his bicycle. The he calls out 'Come and look! A grand picture show you’ve never seen!' striking the wooden clappers to attract attention. Soon a crowd of children gather from all directions. The story-teller is very skilful [sic] in telling the story, imitating [sic] the voices of the various people in the story. After the story is over, he sells candies. A pictorial story-teller is a Pied-piper [sic] of Hamelin in Japan, and the children are like the rats running after the piper."
The commentary for this post-war edition leaves out the following which was included in the commentary to the first edition issued during the Pacific War. "It is indeed natural that the authorities have recently been making efforts to lead in the right direction this business [the picture card show] that may well be employed as a valuable organ to … develop their [children’s] thought."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Sponsored by the Votive Women's Association, print 18, Lake Hamana and  Futaminoura (納札 婦人會 催主, 十八・濱各湖・二見浦)

text.headline: Sponsored by the Votive Women's Association, print 18, Lake Hamana and  Futaminoura (納札 婦人會 催主, 十八・濱各湖・二見浦)
text.text:
One of a set of at least eighteen votive prints (nōsatsu 納札 or senjafuda 千社札) picturing various scenic places designed by the painter Takeda Keihō, a student of the Meiji era nihonga painter and woodblock designer Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) for an unknown women's votive association. Over the years votive temple offerings evolved from small wood plaques, to small paper slips bearing the names of pilgrims, attached by pilgrims to Buddhist and Shinto shrine buildings, to woodblock printed designs called kōkanfuda (交換札), to be shared among members of votive associations (nōsatsukai) at nōsatsu exchange meetings. The various motifs of kōkanfuda were inspired by nishiki-e themes: kabuki actors, famous landscapes, scenes from popular literature, and legendary and mythical figures.
This print provides views of Lake Hamana and Meoto Iwa (Wedded Rocks) at Futaminoura.

media.caption: Flowers (花)

text.headline: Flowers (花)
text.text:
Picturing a vase with flowers and two stemmed fruit on the side. This is one of the few still lifes created by Sasajima.
Sasajima used his "takuzuri" process, forcing damp paper into the grooves of a carved woodblock with a press, to give this print a dynamic three-dimensional effect. He has hand-applied black ink directly on the raised areas of the print.

media.caption: Even Reaching the Top, the Sky is Still Higher

text.headline: Even Reaching the Top, the Sky is Still Higher
text.text:
This print is one of at least forty prints created by the painter/manga artist Kondō Kōichiro 近藤浩一路 (1884–1962) and the poet/journalist Inoue Kenkabō 井上剣花坊 (1870-1934) in 1930, which pair a senryū (short humorous verse), almost all of which were written by Kenkabō, with an illustration by Kondō.
In this print the senryū reads 絶頂へ 來 ても まだ〱 高い空 - "Even reaching the top/summit, the sky is still higher" - and the illustration pictures a self-satisfied climber on a mountain's summit.
All the titles assigned to prints in this series are more-or-less descriptive of the images, enhanced, on occasion, by isolated words translated from the senryū on the print. They are in no way translations of the senryū, which are extremely difficult to translate.

text.headline: Senior Officer Gives Subordinate a Tongue Lashing for Wearing the Wrong Uniform
text.text:
This print is one of at least forty prints created by the painter/manga artist Kondō Kōichiro 近藤浩一路 (1884–1962) and the poet/journalist Inoue Kenkabō 井上剣花坊 (1870-1934) in 1930, which pair a senryū (short humorous verse), almost all of which were written by Kenkabō, with an illustration by Kondō.
In this print the senryū partially reads 鎧着て交番へ来る… and the illustration pictures a senior officer reprimanding a soldier for wearing the wrong uniform.
All the titles assigned to prints in this series are more-or-less descriptive of the images, enhanced, on occasion, by isolated words translated from the senryū on the print. They are in no way translations of the senryū, which are extremely difficult to translate.

media.caption: Asakusa Kinryūzan (浅草金龍山 )

text.headline: Asakusa Kinryūzan (浅草金龍山 )
text.text: Kunitoshi did a number of quick sketches for a few Meiji-era publishers which were turned into sloppily produced prints, including this print. This print pictures part of the grounds of Kinryūzan Sensoji Temple, which dates back to 628, including the Five-Storied Pagoda (Gojūnotō) first built in 942, Hozomon Gate to its right and Hondō, the main hall, on the left in the foreground. The area around the temple was filled with shops and was a popular entertainment center, as it is today.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as Shinohara Kunimoto and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Saigō Takamori in the play Mikawa gofūdo-ki (篠原国幹尾上菊五郎・西郷隆盛 市川 團十郎・三河後風土記)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Shinohara Kunimoto and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Saigō Takamori in the play Mikawa gofūdo-ki (篠原国幹尾上菊五郎・西郷隆盛 市川 團十郎・三河後風土記)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the pro-government soldier Shinohara Kunimoto (1836-1877) and, in the top inset, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Saigō Takamori, the leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion, in the play The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest (Okige no Kumo Harau Asagochi) performed at the Shintomi-za in March 1878. According to Brandon and Leiter, "The scenes of modern warfare, with exploding artillery shells (simulated by fireworks) and gunfire, were a great success" and were "an extremely important step toward contemporary realism." Source: Kabuki Plays on Stage: Restoration and Reform, 1872-1905, ed., James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 91.

In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

media.caption: Autumn Moon at Takanawa, No. 35 (高輪秋月 三十五 Takanawa shūgetsu)

text.headline: Autumn Moon at Takanawa, No. 35 (高輪秋月 三十五 Takanawa shūgetsu)
text.text:
A view of Edo Bay at Takanawa with wild geese flying under an autumn moon. Takanawa at Shiba bordered Edo and the evening travelers going about their business would have to pass through a checkpoint at the town gate (machikido) into Edo. The town gate would close at about 10 PM and re-open at daybreak.
As with many of Hiroshige II's prints, the prints comprising the series Forty-Eight Famous Views of Edo borrowed from the designs of his teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I.

media.caption: Sumida River, No. 17  (すみ田川 Sumidagawa)

text.headline: Sumida River, No. 17  (すみ田川 Sumidagawa)
text.text:
A view of cherry trees in bloom along the Sumida River, with strollers taking in their beauty and small boats plying the river.
As with many of Hiroshige II's prints, the prints comprising the series Forty-Eight Famous Views of Edo borrowed from the designs of his teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I.

media.caption: Hollyhock Slope, No. 41 (葵坂 四十一 Aoi-zaka)

text.headline: Hollyhock Slope, No. 41 (葵坂 四十一 Aoi-zaka)
text.text:
A view of the dam along the Hollyhock Slope in Minoato-ku. According to Edo Meisho Zue, a gazetteer of Edo published in the 1810s, "Beside the dam on the other side of the corner checkpoint, which is on the north side of the reservoir, is an area which has been planted with aoi, hollyhocks. This area is called Hollyhock Hill, and the slope that runs downwards to the east from here is called Aoizaka, Hollyhock Slope." The tiled hut in the foreground and the other tiled hut on the hill to the left seem to be the corner checkpoints, or tsujibansho, mentioned in the gazetteer. These checkpoints were set up in this area where samurai and noblemen resided to maintain surveillance and keep order. The road sloping to the left is probably Aoizaka; the reservoir and the dam are on the right.
As with many of Hiroshige II's prints, the prints comprising the series Forty-Eight Famous Views of Edo borrowed from the designs of his teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I.

media.caption: End of Summer (夏の終り)

text.headline: End of Summer (夏の終り)
text.text:
One of Rei's semi-abstract landscapes created from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. "The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades. The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches. It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.
"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate. The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Francis Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.

media.caption: Brocade Portfolio, Scenic Views of Sapporo, Hand-printed Woodblock Collection, Volume 1

text.headline: Iyo Tangerine Mountain (伊予のみかん山 Iyo no mikanyama)
text.text: Kitaoka is likely depicting the citrus plantations in the mountains around Arida City in Wakayama province. If so, the blue patch of water depicted in the print must be the Arida River. This area is famous for its mikan or Japanese mandarins.

media.caption: Kintai Bridge (錦帯橋)

text.headline: Kintai Bridge (錦帯橋)
text.text:
Kitaoka's rendering of Kintai-bashi with Iwakuni Castle atop Mt. Yokoyama in the background.
“Kintaibashi is located on the foot of Mt.Yokoyama, at the top of which lies Iwakuni Castle. After Iwakuni Castle was completed in 1608 by Kikkawa Hiroie, the first lord of Iwakuni Domain, a series of wooden bridges were built. However, most of them were destroyed by floods several times before the construction of the iconic Kintaibashi in 1673. New stone piers replaced the old wooden ones.
"Though thought to be flood-proof; the bridge was destroyed by a flood the next year. As a result, the stone piers were redesigned for greater strength, and a special tax was created to maintain the bridge. This maintenance involved periodic rebuilding of the bridge: every 20 years for 3 spans in the middle, every 40 years for 2 spans connecting to the riverside.
"Consequently, the bridge remained undestroyed for 276 years, until washed away again by flooding from typhoon ‘Kijia’ in 1950. It had been in a weakened state at the time, due to the fact that the Japanese had stopped maintaining the bridge during World War II, and that the year before the typhoon, a large amount of gravel was taken by the US military forces from the river around the bridge to expand the US Marine Corps Air Station in Iwakuni, strengthening the flow of the river.
"In 1953, the bridge was reconstructed similarly to the original, using metal nails made from the same tatara iron as the Katana to increase its durability. Between 2001 and 2004, all five bridge girders were restored for the first time in 50 years." Source: website of oldtokyo.com http://www.oldtokyo.com/kintaibashi-iwakuni-c-1910/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Sukiya Bridge (数寄屋橋 Sukiyabashi)

text.headline: Sukiya Bridge (数寄屋橋 Sukiyabashi)
text.text:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Last Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print was made from recut blocks. It is one of two designs that Hiratsuka contributed to Scenes of Last Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955).
The building in the centre is the main office of Asahi Shimbun, one of Japan's biggest newspapers, completed in 1927. The bridge was demolished in 1957, and the canal filled in.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Spinning Wheel ( 紡車 Itoguruma)

text.headline: Spinning Wheel ( 紡車 Itoguruma)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design, which carries a date of 1920 below Yumeji's signature, appeared on the 1924 cover of the musical score for the song "Spinning Wheel" by the Japanese composer Kiyomi Fujii 藤井清水 (1889-1944) published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."- Source: Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: Day In, Day Out, at a Bay (浦のあけくれ Ura no akekure)

text.headline: Day In, Day Out, at a Bay (浦のあけくれ Ura no akekure)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally created for the 1926 cover of the musical score for Joseph Mazzinghi's "Ye Shepherds Tell Me" (The Wreath. A Pastoral Glee for Three Voices), published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"The prints in Yumeji Masterpieces highlight Yumeji's skillful treatment of the landscape genre. Tranquil, bucolic scenes such as this print, illustrating a hamlet nestled along a bay, were a frequent theme in Yumeji's art, and it could be conjectured that it conveyed a sense of nostalgia for his native Okayama or the port city of Kobe where he briefly spent time during his childhood."[1]
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."[2]
For another impression of this print see IHL.#1621 iwhich s printed on a heavier paper and appears to be an earlier printing.

[1]Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 14.
[2]Ibid., 2015, p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: Tiger (寅)

text.headline: Tiger (寅)
text.text:
Picturing a tiger with his prey, a parrot, in his mouth, and representing the third sign of the zodiac, this print was published on January 1, 1903, as dated in its left margin. Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, the series which this print is a part of, was originally issued c. 1901, again in 1903 and then reissued by Unsōdō Publishing several times into the early 1940s. As this print has a centerfold, it may have been issued as part of a folding album with the other eleven prints representing the animals in the zodiac, or it may have been issued as a stand-alone print.
Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

media.caption: Blue and White Space

text.headline: Blue and White Space
text.text: This print was included in the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, published in 1973.  Using woodblock for the irregular shapes defining the trapezoid, silkscreen for the yellow and the blue patterns and some type of hole punch to create a grid pattern of 5/16" circular holes Funasaka gives us another eye-pleasing print in his long-running series Blue and White Space.

media.caption: Birth of Shakyamuni Buddha (untitled)

text.headline: Birth of Shakyamuni Buddha (untitled)
text.text: In this print by an unidentified artist, Shakyamuni receives his first bath, the water of which is said to have been poured down from the heavens. He is pointing to the heavens with his right hand and to the earth with his left. He is naked apart from a cloth wrapped around his waist, which makes it clear that this is as a depiction of the baby Buddha. - Source: Global Nepali Museum, from a description of a sculpture depicting the birth of the founder of Buddhism, Shakyamuni.

media.caption: Four image harimaze-e: Old Story (昔咄 Mukashi banashi), Rape Blossoms and Crane (菜の花に鶴 Nanohana ni tsuru), Sumida River (すみた川 Sumidagawa), Okina (翁)

text.headline: Four image harimaze-e: Old Story (昔咄 Mukashi banashi), Rape Blossoms and Crane (菜の花に鶴 Nanohana ni tsuru), Sumida River (すみた川 Sumidagawa), Okina (翁)
text.text:
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III, a disciple of the great Utagawa Hiroshige I (1797-1858), created these sketches (manga) in 1879, which were arranged three, four or five to a single sheet as a harimaze-e. Titled "Sketches by Ryūsai," Ryūsai being an artist name (gō) of Hiroshige III, they were very much in the tradition of his master Hiroshige I, who is sometimes credited as the inventor of the print genre harimaze, which can be literally translated as "paste and mix pictures" and is commonly translated as "cut-out pictures."
The height of their popularity was in the mid-1800s and these inexpensive prints were purchased and then often cut-apart and pasted onto Japanese screens or into scrapbooks. Harimazi-e could include the work of multiple artists or just a single artist, as in the case of these harimaze-e. For other examples of harimazi-e in this collection see Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889) and his works from the series Kyōsai Manga.
The Four Panels:
top right: Old Story 昔咄 (The illustration appears to relate to the folktale the Tongue-Cut Sparrow 舌切り雀.)
top left: Chrysanthemum Flower and Crane 菊の花に鶴
bottom left: Sumida River すみた川
bottom right: Okina 翁

media.caption: Three image harimaze-e: Ōsumi Sakurashima・Iris and Kingfisher・Saigō Nanshū no zō (大隅さくらしま・菖蒲に翡翠・西郷南洲之像)

text.headline: Three image harimaze-e: Ōsumi Sakurashima・Iris and Kingfisher・Saigō Nanshū no zō (大隅さくらしま・菖蒲に翡翠・西郷南洲之像)
text.text:
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III, a disciple of the great Utagawa Hiroshige I (1797-1858), created these sketches (manga) in 1879, which were arranged three, four or five to a single sheet as a harimaze-e. Titled "Sketches by Ryūsai," Ryūsai being an artist name (gō) of Hiroshige III, they were very much in the tradition of his master Hiroshige I, who is sometimes credited as the inventor of the print genre harimaze, which can be literally translated as "paste and mix pictures" and is commonly translated as "cut-out pictures."
The height of their popularity was in the mid-1800s and these inexpensive prints were purchased and then often cut-apart and pasted onto Japanese screens or into scrapbooks. Harimazi-e could include the work of multiple artists or just a single artist, as in the case of these harimaze-e. For other examples of harimazi-e in this collection see Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889) and his works from the series Kyōsai Manga.
The Three Panels:
top right: Ōsumi Sakurashima 大隅さくらしま (おおすみ さくらしま) - picturing the volcano Sakurajima at Ōsumi on Sakura Island with sailing ships in Kagoshima Bay. Hiroshige III's image is quite similar to that of Hiroshige I's print of Sakurajima at Ōsumi from his 1854 series Famous Views in the Sixty-Odd Provinces.
top left: Iris and Kingfisher 菖蒲に翡翠 (しょうぶ にかわせみ)
bottom: Saigō Nanshū no zō 西郷南洲之像 (さいごうなんしゅうのぞう) - a portrait of one of the great heroes, and later betrayer, of the Meiji Reformation, Saigō Takamori 西郷隆盛 (1828-1877). Saigō is pictured brush in hand having just completed one of his many instructive verses. Saigō adopted the pen name Nanshū, meaning "south," during his five years in exile on the island of Oshima.

media.caption: The Maiden at Dōjō Temple  (京鹿子娘道成寺 Kyōkanoko Musume Dōjōji)

text.headline: The Maiden at Dōjō Temple  (京鹿子娘道成寺 Kyōkanoko Musume Dōjōji)
text.text:
This print advertises the March 1890 performance at the Kabuki-za of one of the greatest works of dance in Kabuki, Kyōkanoko Musume Dōjōji, starring Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Hanako the shirabyōshi dancer, as seen in the center sheet. In this scene, Hanako, wearing a tall eboshi hat, dances for three priests at the temple. The temple bell, that figures prominently in the story, can be seen in the upper right hand corner and the signboard on the left sheet reads "Women forbidden at the present time" (‘Nyonin kinsei toji’, 女人禁制 当時).
The actors and their roles depicted in the print are, from right to left, Ichikawa Sumizō 市川寿美蔵 as the priest Kurokumobō 黒雲坊, Ichikawa Shinzō 市川新蔵 as the priest Shirakumobō 白雲坊, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 as the shirabyōshi dancer Hanako 白拍子花子 and Ichikawa Gonjūrō 市川権十郎 as the priest Jōeibō 浄永坊.

media.caption: Raising a banner (untitled)

text.headline: Raising a banner (untitled)
text.text:
A rough looking man appears to be raising a banner on tall tree. Likely an illustration for a book.
The designer of this woodblock print, Igawa Sengai, is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

media.caption: Tomorrow! (あした Ashita)

text.headline: Tomorrow! (あした Ashita)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design appeared on the 1925 cover of the musical score for the song "Morgen!" [Opus 27, Number 4] by the German composer Richard Strauss (1864-1949) published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."- Source: Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: Flying Cloud Around Mt. Fuji・E (飛雲富士・E Hiun Fuji・E)

text.headline: Flying Cloud Around Mt. Fuji・E (飛雲富士・E Hiun Fuji・E)
text.text: One of at least three different prints by Sasajima bearing the same title of Hiun Fuji [Flying Cloud(s) Around Mt. Fuji]. Sasajima has used a heavier paper for this print and it bears a much lighter embossing than other prints in this collection printed using his "takuzuri" process, whereby damp paper is forced into the grooves of a carved woodblock with a press, to give a print a dynamic three-dimensional effect. He has hand-applied black ink directly on the raised areas of the print.

media.caption: Sound of the Wind (風のひびき Kaze no hibiki )

text.headline: Sound of the Wind (風のひびき Kaze no hibiki )
text.text:
Rei continued to pursue in this 1991 work an earlier style described by Francis Blakemore in 1975 as follows:
"The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades. The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches. It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.
"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate. The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Francis Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.

media.caption: Bijin holding battledore (untitled)

text.headline: Bijin holding battledore (untitled)
text.text: A bijin holding a battledore while delicately smelling a flower, this painting on silk is one of two in the nihonga style (Japanese-style painting) in this collection. Painted by Igawa Sengai (1876-1961) when he was seventy-four years old according to his signature which reads 七十四叟洗厓, "old man of 74 years, Sengai."

media.caption: Shakkyō 石橋 (Stone Bridge)

text.headline: Shakkyō 石橋 (Stone Bridge)
text.text:
From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Shakkyō: "A priest [the Monk Jakushō] goes to China to visit famous Buddhist places. One day he is about to cross a stone bridge across a ravine when child appears. He hears from the child that since the land on the other side of the bridge is the Paradise of the deity Monju Bosatsu [Manjusri Bodhisattva], even famous priests in olden times could only cross it after long and severe religious training. Telling the priest that if he waits by the bridge he will see something wonderful, the child disappears. After a while, a lion emerges and gambols and dances among the peony flowers - the king of beast enjoying the most majestic of flowers." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 158-159.

media.caption: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)

text.headline: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)
text.text:
From volume three of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Kumasaka: "A travelling priest stops at Akasaka in Mino Province and meets another priest who, after talking with him, gives him lodging for the night. This second priest is in reality the ghost of Kumasaka no Chōhan, a robber, and in the dream of the real priest that night the spirit appears and describers how he was killed by the young Ushikawa." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 89.

media.caption: Funa Benkei 船弁慶 (Benkei in the Boat)

text.headline: Funa Benkei 船弁慶 (Benkei in the Boat)
text.text:
From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Funa Benkei: "Benkei explains that in an attempt to clear himself of the suspicion which Yoritomo has about his younger brother's intentions, Yoshitsune has left the capital and come down to Daimotsu Bay. There Shizuka Gozen joins her lover Yoshitsune, but as Benkei insists that she must return to the capital, they have a farewell party at which Shizuka dances, and then she goes off alone. Yoshitsune and his men then put out to sea in a boat, but suddenly black clouds form, the seas rise, and the ghost of Taira no Tomomori comes upon them. It tries to seize Yoshitsune and carry him down into the sea to suffer the same fate as Tomomori himself, but is eventually driven off by the priestly poser of Benkei." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 35-36.

media.caption: Kamo 加茂

text.headline: Kamo 加茂
text.text:
From volume three of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Kamo: "A priest from the shrine in Muro in Harima province makes a pilgrimage to the sister shrine of Kamo Myōjin and there sees a white-feathered arrow set up beside the river. He learns from a woman who, with a companion, comes there to draw water, that when long ago a woman of the Hata family picked up such an arrow floating in the river and carried it home, she miraculously conceived and gave birth to a son. The child was the god Wake-ikazuchi and he, his mother and the arrow are now revered as the three gods of the Kamo Shrine. Telling the priest that she is one of these gods, the woman disappears with her companion. Later the goddess and her son Wake-ikazuchi come forth to dance and promise to protect the land and its people."- A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 67-68.

media.caption: Yoroboshi 弱法師 (The Priest with the Faltering Tread)

text.headline: Yoroboshi 弱法師 (The Priest with the Faltering Tread)
text.text:
From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Yoroboshi: "Believing some gossip he heard about his son Shuntoku, Michitoshi turned him out of his house. Deeply regretting his cruelty now, he goes on a pilgrimage to the Tennō-ji temple and there sees his son again - but he has become a beggar and having lost his sight as well, is known as 'the priest with the faltering tread.' He sings a song about the temple and then, when the other people go and leave the two of them alone, Michitoshi tells his son who he is and, full of happiness at having found him again, takes him by the arm to lead him home." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 217-218.

media.caption: Hanagatami 花筐 (The Flower Basket)

text.headline: Hanagatami 花筐 (The Flower Basket)
text.text:
From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Hanagatami : "The Crown Prince Ōatobe having suddenly left his country retreat to go to the capital to succeed his father, a servant gives Teruhi-no-mai, the lady who has been the Prince's constant companion, a letter and a flower basket which he has left for her. Some time later Ōatobe, now the Emperor Keitai, is viewing the maples in autumn when a mad woman comes along carrying a flower basket. This is Teruhi who, distracted by her love for the Prince, has come to try to see him. Happy now that she has met him again, Teruhi is once more taken into the Emperor's favour and returns with him to the capital." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 49-50.

media.caption: Semimaru 蝉丸

text.headline: Semimaru 蝉丸
text.text:
From volume five of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Semimaru: "On the order of the Emperor Daigo, a Court official takes Prince Semimaru, who has been blind since he was a child, to Ōsaka-yama and leaves him there with only his lute to comfort him. The Prince accepts his lot with resignation, feeling that his blindness is the result of some failure of his in a previous existence, and that the present apparent cruelty of his father is only due to a desire to help him gain a happier fate in a future life. Meanwhile, his sister Princess Sakagami has gone out of her mind and is now a wild-haired figure, wandering aimlessly from place to place. She comes one day to Ōsaka-yama and, attracted by the sound of Semimaru's lute, finds her brother again. For a while they forget their loneliness as they talk together and comfort each other, but then the Princess leaves him and continues her sad wanderings." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 154-155.

media.caption: Sumidagawa (隅田川)

text.headline: Sumidagawa (隅田川)
text.text:
From volume five of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934. The woodblock prints were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963), the photographs by Genzō Kitazumi (1898-1982), the album's text was written by Kanze Sakon (1895-1939), the 24th head (sōke) of the Kanze School and Nō actor, and the preface was written by Sasakawa Rinfu (active 1920s-1930s).
Synopsis of Play Sumidagawa: "A ferryman on the Sumida-gawa is told by a traveller about to cross the river that following close behind is a woman whose mind has been unbalanced ever since her son was taken from her. He therefore waits for her to arrive, and then begins to cross the river. On the way, the traveller asks the reason for the crowd of people on the other bank. The boatman tells him that they are there to perform a mass for a boy of about eleven years of age, the son of one Yoshida from the capital, who died there a year ago after being taken from his home. At this, the woman weeps bitterly, and reveals that the boy was the son she is seeking. The ferryman takes her to the grave and when they recite prayers there, the boy's voice is heard. The mother prays again and her son appears to her. But when she reaches out for him he is no longer there, and with the coming of dawn he disappears again forever." - source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 173-174.

media.caption: Shōjō 猩々 (The Tippling Elf)

text.headline: Shōjō 猩々 (The Tippling Elf)
text.text:
From volume five of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.
Summary of the play Shōjō: "A man named Kō-fū, living in ancient China, explains that by following a dream which he had in reward for his filial piety and which told him to sell wine in the market, he has become a prosperous man. At the market, there is one particular person who always comes to him to buy wine, and since he told the dealer that he is an elf living in the sea, the man has come down to the estuary to wait for him to appear. When he does so, red-faced from his drinking, the man serves him with wine and watches him dance. The elf, in return, gives him a well of wine which never runs dry." - A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 163-164.

media.caption: Art Exhibition (展覧会 terankai)

text.headline: Art Exhibition (展覧会 terankai)
text.text:
One of three prints in this collection that appear to be crayon lithographs by Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), who had learned lithography at a young age from his father. The images have the feel of period illustrations for stories appearing in magazines and the paper also appears to be of the type used in popular magazines of the period. Hakutei edited and participated in a number of literary and art magazines, and it is possible the three prints originated in one of those magazines.
This print has a hand written notation verso with the name of the artist 石井柏亭 (Ishii Hakutei) and a print title reading 展覧会 (Art exhibition.) (tenrankai).

media.caption: Moss Garden (苔寺新緑 Koke-dera shinryoku)

text.headline: Moss Garden (苔寺新緑 Koke-dera shinryoku)
text.text:
Kitaoka depicts the lower level gardens and Ogonchi Pond at Kokedera (Moss Temple), also known as Saihoji.
Saihoji Temple belongs to the Rinzai school of Japanese Buddhism. In 1994 the site was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The gardens built by Muso Soseki (a nationally designated scenic and historic site) consist of an upper level of dry karesansui-style rock arrangements and a lower level built around Ogonchi Pond, which is shaped like the Chinese character meaning "heart." Blanketed by more than 120 species of moss, the temple is popularly and affectionately known as Kokedera ("Moss Temple").

media.caption: Work 28 (作品 sakuhin 28)

text.headline: Work 28 (作品 sakuhin 28)
text.text:
A small, postcard size, print by Kusaka from his continuing series of prints carrying the title Work [作品 (sakuhin)] begun in the early 1960s. This series began with some reference to identifiable objects but quickly became more abstract and dynamic with use of intense primary colors.
Starting around 1967 Kusaka introduced the circle form which subsequently morphed into an oblong egg shape. This egg shape counterbalanced his straight lines and angular corners as we see in this print.

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 6 (日清戦闘畫 第六編 (Nisshin Sentō Gahō, dairoku hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 6 (日清戦闘畫 第六編 (Nisshin Sentō Gahō, dairoku hen)
text.text: Volume 6 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

media.caption: Treasure of Saruwaka (猿若の宝物 Saruwaka no Takaramono)

text.headline: Treasure of Saruwaka (猿若の宝物 Saruwaka no Takaramono)
text.text: This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print)  picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō explaining the origins of the gold military baton given to Saruwaka Kanzaburō (1597?-1658, the founder of Edo-style kabuki and its first licensed kabuki theater in 1624.)  The baton was one of the rewards given to Kanzaburō by the Shogun as a reward for entertaining the Shogun while he was on his pleasure boat Atakmaru in Edo bay in 1633. This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Listening to Rumors (風聞きゝFūbunkiki)

text.headline: Listening to Rumors (風聞きゝFūbunkiki)
text.text:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts a soba (buckwheat noodle) stand in front of the Ichimuraza Theater, one of the three officially recognized Kabuki theaters of Edo. The word "nihachi" (二八, literally 'two-eight'), written on the noodle stand, came from the noodles that cost sixteen (two times eight) mon a bowl and also from the proportion of 20 parts udon flour to 80 parts soba flour.
"With the excitement of the experience still in the air, fellow theatre aficionados might pass time after the performance exchanging opinions about what they had seen, as depicted in this print of men standing around talking in front of the theatre while slurping noodles from a food cart. Collecting this gossip was useful to the theatres. Spies would be sent out to listen in, and according to what they heard, acts might be replaced or play content might otherwise be modified. This print depicts a time before the three licensed Edo theatres (Edo sanza) were forced to move to Saruwaka-chō in Asakusa as a result of the Tenpō Reforms (1841-1843)." Source: Art Research Center, Ritsumeikan University https://www.arc.ritsumei.ac.jp/lib/vm/kabuki2015_e/2015/11/post-17.html [accessed 8-17-23]
This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Auspicious Plays (ワキ狂言 Waki kyōgen)

text.headline: Auspicious Plays (ワキ狂言 Waki kyōgen)
text.text:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts an annual waki kyogen performance starting at dawn, announced by the banging of the large drum, consisting of auspicious dances such as the Dance of the Seven Lucky Gods and the Sanboso dance. Reference is made in the scroll to both the Ichimura-za and Nakamura-za theaters in Edo.
This print is a later undated edition of IHL.0673. This later edition is characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Curtain-Raiser Performance (序開きJobiraki)

text.headline: Curtain-Raiser Performance (序開きJobiraki)
text.text:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts the opening performance of the theater season.
This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Praying to the Ōtsu Inari Shrine in 3rd Floor Dressing Room (大津稲荷 Ōtsu Inari)

text.headline: Praying to the Ōtsu Inari Shrine in 3rd Floor Dressing Room (大津稲荷 Ōtsu Inari)
text.text:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts an actor praying at an Inari shrine in the third floor dressing room of a Kabuki theater. Chief of the pantheon of gods worshiped under the name Inari, Ame-no-uzume-no-mikoto (the heaven-alarming-female whose dance for the Sun Goddess, Amaterasu, helped restore light to the world) is the "patron deity of all professional actors, for, as she does, they lighten the hearts of men, comfort them in distress, and make the sun shine again. An Inari shrine, large or small, is installed in every Kabuki theatre . . . ." - Source: The Kabuki Theatre, Earle Ernst, University Press of Hawaii, 1974, p. 164.
This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Front Entrance Ticket Sellers (木戸羽織 Kido haori)

text.headline: Front Entrance Ticket Sellers (木戸羽織 Kido haori)
text.text:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts kidoban, employed by the theater, at the front entrance encouraging passerby to purchase tickets. Sometimes kidoban would imitate actors to entice people to buy tickets. "Their attire included a small towel (tenugui) wrapped around the face and a long outer garment (haori), which was a gift from the troupe's top female-role actor and was therefore marked with that actor's crest. The small towel and folding fan were provided by the troupe leader (the top male-role actor) and carried his crest, so passersby would know right away who the troupe's top stars were." - Source: Art Research Center, Ritsumeikan University http://www.arc.ritsumei.ac.jp/lib/vm/kabuki2015_e/2015/11/b09.html [accessed 8-17-23]
This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

media.caption: Bijin in brown kimono (untitled)

text.headline: Bijin in brown kimono (untitled)
text.text:
Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).
This untitled offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) with its characteristic tri-fold, appeared in an unknown magazine.

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

media.caption: Kanadehon Chūshingura, Act VI (仮名手本忠臣蔵、六段目)

text.headline: Kanadehon Chūshingura, Act VI (仮名手本忠臣蔵、六段目)
text.text:
One of a series of twelve prints portraying a Kabuki version of the play Kanadehon Chūshingura. This particular print was likely part of an album as it bears a vertical centerfold and has remnants of being mounted along the left edge verso. Prints in this series are dated either 1896 or 1897.
In this scene two of the rōnin, Gōemon and Yagorō, visit Kanpei (seated with his head bowed) to return the money he contributed to erect a monument to their dead master, saying: "It would not please his spirit if we paid for the monument with money taken from a man who had proved disloyal and faithless to his lordship." In the background on the left we see Okaru (Kanpei's lover) being carried by a palanquin to a brothel and behind Kanpei sits Okaru's mother weeping.

media.caption: Kanadehon Chūshingura, Act X (仮名手本忠臣蔵、十段目)

text.headline: Kanadehon Chūshingura, Act X (仮名手本忠臣蔵、十段目)
text.text:
One of a series of twelve prints portraying a Kabuki version of the play Kanadehon Chūshingura. This particular print was likely part of an album as it bears a vertical centerfold and has remnants of being mounted along the left edge verso. Prints in the series are dated either 1896 or 1897.
In this scene we see Gihei's four year old son Yoshimatsu playing with Igo "a round-faced boy of nineteen" who holds a puppet. In the back room, Gihei is seen writing a letter of divorce to his wife while his father-in-law Ryōchiku waits. On the orange curtain we see, in reverse, the name of Gihei's shop 天川屋 (Amakawa-ya).

media.caption: Picture of Higashi Okumi 15th Ward Elementary School (東大組十五区小学校之図)

text.headline: Picture of Higashi Okumi 15th Ward Elementary School (東大組十五区小学校之図)
text.text: One of several western-style school buildings built in the Naniwa area of Osaka in the early/mid-1870s. In this print we see an appreciative crowd looking around the school. Perhaps it's opening day at the school and parents are bringing their children for the first day of classes.

media.caption: Peaches (桃)

text.headline: Peaches (桃)
text.text: The artist reworked and reprinted this still life of peaches numerous times. This impression likely being the original or early state. See IHL.1662 for what is likely a later state of this print.

media.caption: Day In, Day Out, at a Bay (浦のあけくれ Ura no akekure)

text.headline: Day In, Day Out, at a Bay (浦のあけくれ Ura no akekure)
text.text:
One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally created for the 1926 cover of the musical score for Joseph Mazzinghi's "Ye Shepherds Tell Me" (The Wreath. A Pastoral Glee for Three Voices), published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"The prints in Yumeji Masterpieces highlight Yumeji's skillful treatment of the landscape genre. Tranquil, bucolic scenes such as this print, illustrating a hamlet nestled along a bay, were a frequent theme in Yumeji's art, and it could be conjectured that it conveyed a sense of nostalgia for his native Okayama or the port city of Kobe where he briefly spent time during his childhood."[1]
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."[2]
For another impression of this print see IHL.1575 printed on a lighter weight paper that appears to be a later edition than this impression.

[1]Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 14.
[2]Ibid., 2015, p. 133, p. 135.

media.caption: Bird and Animal Drawings by Seihō (栖鳳習畫帖 Seihō shūgachō)

text.headline: Bird and Animal Drawings by Seihō (栖鳳習畫帖 Seihō shūgachō)
text.text: This book is a re-print by Shima Art Company of twenty woodblock prints, of original drawings, by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō. The woodblock prints originally appeared in the four volumes of Seihō's Guide to Drawing (栖鳳 習畫帖 Seihō shūgachō), published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1901. (See Seiho's Guide to Drawing V. 1-4, IHL.0783, IHL.0784, IHL.2225, IHL.0785.)

media.caption: Morning Mist, Burning Fields  (三十六富士朝霧野焼  Asagiri noyaki)

text.headline: Morning Mist, Burning Fields  (三十六富士朝霧野焼  Asagiri noyaki)
text.text: Hagiwara’s Thirty-Six Fujis series is the artist’s only excursion into landscape. It is his homage to the sacred mountain and to past ukiyo-e artists, such as Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1848) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858). Living near Mount Fuji, Hagiwara gathered his impressions of the mountain for over fifteen years before beginning work on this series. Toward the end of the project he wrote: “Just when I think I have grasped [Fuji], it slips through my hands. Let's pick up this ‘slippery Fuji’ and keep on going.” Hagiwara captures a view of Fuji from the town of Ōhara on a spring morning, during the annual burning of grasslands (noyaki) on the northern foot of the mountain.

media.caption: Remains of Flowers (三十六富士名残の花 Nagori no hana)

text.headline: Remains of Flowers (三十六富士名残の花 Nagori no hana)
text.text: Hagiwara’s Thirty-Six Fujis series is the artist’s only excursion into landscape. It is his homage to the sacred mountain and to past ukiyo-e artists, such as Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1848) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858). Living near Mount Fuji, Hagiwara gathered his impressions of the mountain for over fifteen years before beginning work on this series. Toward the end of the project he wrote: “Just when I think I have grasped [Fuji], it slips through my hands. Let's pick up this ‘slippery Fuji’ and keep on going.”  In this print Hagiwara pictures the remnants of the moss phlox (shibazakura) that surrounds Mount Fuji in spring.  The flowers begin to bloom at the end of April with most of them dying at the end of May.  Hagiwara masterfully employs his unique color overlay technique to intensify his abstract coloration and a subtle dusting of ground mica highlights the colors.

media.caption: Early Winter in Gotemba (三十六富士御殿場初冬 Gotemba shotō)

text.headline: Early Winter in Gotemba (三十六富士御殿場初冬 Gotemba shotō)
text.text: Hagiwara’s Thirty-Six Fujis series is the artist’s only excursion into landscape. It is his homage to the sacred mountain and to past ukiyo-e artists, such as Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1848) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858). Let's pick up this ‘slippery Fuji’ and keep on going.”  In this print Hagiwara pictures storm clouds rolling in, about to obscure an early winter clear view of Fuji from Gotemba on the southeastern flank of Mount Fuji. Hagiwara masterfully employs his unique color overlay technique to intensify his abstract coloration and a subtle dusting of ground mica highlights the colors.

media.caption: Suruga-chō, No. 30 (するか町・三十)

text.headline: Suruga-chō, No. 30 (するか町・三十)
text.text: This view of Suruga-chō (Suruga Street) with the Mitsui Echigoya store (present day Mitsukoshi department store) occupying both sides of the street in the foreground, with Edo Castle in the mid-ground and Mt. Fuji dominating the background, borrows heavily from the more famous print by Utagawa Hiroshige I issued in 1857 by the same publisher as part of the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei).

text.headline: Woman with letter (untitled)

media.caption: Sanuki masu, frontispiece from the magazine Omoshiro Club, Volume 4, Number 3 (面白倶楽部　第4巻3号・口絵 讃岐桝)

text.headline: Sanuki masu, frontispiece from the magazine Omoshiro Club, Volume 4, Number 3 (面白倶楽部　第4巻3号・口絵 讃岐桝)
text.text:
Little appears to be known about Noguchi Kōgai the designer of this print and similar prints, which served as frontispieces for popular magazines. His most encountered works are the two designs he contributed to the woodblock printed 1926 series Taishō Shinsai Gashū 大正震災画集 (Taishō Earthquake Disaster Print Collection.)
This print titled "Sanuki masu" served as a frontispiece for the magazine Omoshiro Club, Volume 4, Number 3 and pertained to the second installment of serialized historical novel by Shozan Maeda 前田曙山 (1872-1941) about an Edo period uprising by farmers led by the farmer Toya Shin'emon to protest the use of a larger than normal measure of rice to collect an increased tax. Although the protests were successful, Shin'emon would be put to death for his role in the uprising.

text.headline: Woman in brown kimono (untitled)
text.text:
One of many chromolithograph bijin kuchi-e created for popular magazines by Morita, a yōga-trained (western style) artist who worked as a reporter, illustrator and art director. He contributed illustrations to numerous popular magazines in the late Meiji and Taishō era. His illustrations were primarily of the bijinga genre and they appeared in mass culture magazines such as Kōdan Kurabo, Kōdan zasshi, Fujokai, Jogaku sekai and in serialized novels. It is reported that his illustrations for a serialized novel appearing in the Yomiuri shinbun in 1921 were the first such illustrations to actually identify the illustrator by name.

text.headline: Woman in blue kimono (untitled)
text.text:
This chromolithograph bijin kuchi-e served as an illustration for the story Life's Fallen Leaves appearing in an unknown magazine. It is one of many bijin kuchi-e created for popular magazines by Morita, a yōga-trained (western style) artist, who worked as a reporter, illustrator and art director. He contributed illustrations to numerous popular magazines in the late Meiji and Taishō era. His illustrations were primarily of the bijin-ga genre and they appeared in mass culture magazines such as Kōdan Kurabo, Kōdan zasshi, Fujokai, Jogaku sekai and in serialized novels. It is reported that his illustrations for a serialized novel appearing in the Yomiuri shinbun in 1921 were the first such illustrations to actually identify the illustrator by name.

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

media.caption: Sayama Motosuke from the novel The Gold Demon  (狭山元輔・金色夜叉)

text.headline: Sayama Motosuke from the novel The Gold Demon  (狭山元輔・金色夜叉)
text.text:
One of eight prints, seven of which are woodblock prints, appearing in the 1920 "pocket edition" (shukusatsu 縮刷), published by Shunyōdō 春葉堂, of The Gold Demon 金色夜叉 by the popular novelist and poet Ozaki Kōyō 尾崎紅葉 (1868-1903).
Sengai's illustration is that of the character Sayama Motosuke, the true love of O’Shizu (really Aiko of the Kashiwaya geisha house), who makes a suicide pact with her. Pictured are the rings they exchanged the night of their planned suicide, which was interrupted by the novel's main character, Kan’ichi.
For other prints appearing in the novel see IHL.1642, IHL. 1643 and IHL.1644.
Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to such popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) A Pair of Pines (Hiyoku no matsu), Lady Shizuka (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and The Gold Demon (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

media.caption: Kamata Tetsuya from the novel The Gold Demon (金色夜叉・蒲田鉄弥)

text.headline: Kamata Tetsuya from the novel The Gold Demon (金色夜叉・蒲田鉄弥)
text.text:
One of eight prints, seven of which are woodblock prints, appearing in the 1920 pocket edition (shukusatsu 縮刷), published by Shun'yōdō, of The Gold Demon (Konjiki yasha) by the popular novelist and poet Ozaki Kōyō 尾崎紅葉 (1868-1903). The eight prints illustrate characters appearing in the novel.
Shunsen's illustration is that of the character Kamata Tetsuya, a high school friend of the main character Hazama Kan'ichi. Kamata has become a successful attaché in the Diplomatic Service and Hazama a usurer. Kamata pays off a debt owed to Hazama by one of their mutual friends, but hard feelings result.
For other prints appearing in the novel see IHL.1641, IHL. 1643 and IHL.1644.
Ozaki Kōyō, born in Tokyo, became a novelist at an early age, publishing his first novel Love Confessions of Two Nuns (Ninin bikuni irozange) in 1889. His subsequent novels were all serialized by the newspaper Yomiuri shinbun which Ozaki was the literary editor for. When he died in 1903, his most successful novel The Gold Demon was not yet complete, although already in serialization.

The Gold Demon tells the story of the tragic love affair between Omiya and Kanichi who plan to marry. In this print, Yamanaka depicts the wealthy businessman Tadatsugu Tomiyama who wins the approval of Omiya's parents to propose to her, presenting her with an expensive ring, which Omiya is obligated to accept. She then must tell Kanichi of their misfortune.
For other prints appearing in the novel see IHL.1641, IHL. 1642 and IHL.1643.

media.caption: Oshio 小塩

text.headline: Oshio 小塩
text.text:
The print depicts the ghost of the poet Narihira at Ōhara viewing the cherry blossoms, in a scene from the play Oshio by the playwright Komparu Zenchiku (1405-c. 1470).
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 81, cat. 26.) - A man (waki) and his two companions (wakizure) view the famous cherry blossoms at Ōhara, also known as Oshio, a hill to the southwest of Kyoto. They meet an old man (shite), who is obviously a person of elegant taste. He tells them stories about the place and recites poems written by the famous Heian courtier Ariwara no Narihira when he visited the spot. In the second part of the play, the old man now reappears as Narihira, riding in a vehicle from which to view the flowers. He recites some of his poems, dances in the moonlight, and then vanishes at dawn.
In the print, Narihira stands in a flower-viewing vehicle and observes the cherry blossoms.
The square inset in the upper right-hand corner includes part of a famous waka poem on the vicissitudes of love written by Narihira, which the shite delivers:
Is not the moon the same?
The spring
Not the spring of old?
Only this body of mine
Is the same body. . .


Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Mochizuki 望月

text.headline: Mochizuki 望月
text.text:
The print depicts the climatic scene in the play Mochizuki sometimes attributed to the playwright Sa-ami (15th c.). "Thirteen years ago, the evil Mochizuki no Akinaga had killed Yasuda no Tomoharu. Now Mochizuki is staying at an inn, having just returned from Kyoto where he claimed Yasuda’s property. Unbeknownst to the murderer, the innkeeper Kozawa had been a retainer of Yasuda. Also at the inn are Yasuda’s widow and son. The three plot revenge: they offer to entertain Mochizuki. While the widow sings, her son plays a drum and then dances. Kozawa appears dressed as a lion dancer and is able to approach and stab Mochizuki to death." - Source: Ruth Chandler Williamson Gallery, Scripps College http://web-kiosk.scrippscollege.edu/Obj21710?sid=83782&x=1666787 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Kashihara Shrine, Yamato  (大和橿原神宮 Yamato Kashihara jingū)

text.headline: Kashihara Shrine, Yamato  (大和橿原神宮 Yamato Kashihara jingū)
text.text:
Print number thirteen (十三, as printed in the right margin) in the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi shiseki meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting the large plaza in which sits the shrine's first gate (Kashihara jingū daiichi torii). The obelisk to the right is engraved with the shrine's name 橿原神宮.
Kashihara jingū is a Shinto shrine located in the city of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture, Japan. The shrine's vast precincts cover an area of roughly 500,000 square meters. It was built in 1889 at the site of the Kashihara-gū where Japan's mythical first emperor, Emperor Jimmu, is said to have acceded to the throne on February 11, 660 BC.
The use of the word Yamato 大和 in the print's title references the national foundation story embodied by Emperor Jimmu and the Kigen 2600 celebrations, starting in 1940, that marked the mythical 2,600th anniversary of Japan's founding. These celebrations which were years in the planning, were used to build popular support for Japan's territorial ambitions. More than 12,000 events were held to commemorate the anniversary including the publishing of this print series. Commenting on the series the artist writes that his devotion to the sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the "dignity of the national polity," going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, or the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.

In his commentary on the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

media.caption: Usa Shrine 宇佐神宮 (Usa jingū]

text.headline: Usa Shrine 宇佐神宮 (Usa jingū]
text.text:
Print number nineteen (十九, as printed in the right margin) in the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941. Tokuriki gives us a view of the sacred bridge [神橋 shinkyō], leading to the main entrance of the shrine, on a moonlit evening.
The shrine was founded in Kyūshū during the Nara period. Ancient records place the foundation of Usa jingū in the Wadō era (708-714). A temple called Miroku-ji was built next to it in 779, making it what is believed to be the first shrine-temple (jingū-ji) ever. From 1871 through 1946, Usa was officially designated one of the Kanpei-taisha (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. The shrine is the main sanctum of over 40,000 hachiman shrine locations. The Emperor Ojin, who was deified as Hachiman-shin (the god of military power) and worshiped as the protective deity of the Imperial City, is enshrined in these shrines.

text.headline: Kawarazaki Gonjūrō, Nakamura Ganpachi, Arashi Kangorō, Seki Sanjūrō, Sawamura Tanosuke, Nakamura Ichō and Bandō Hikosaburō in the play Imayō Shuten Dōji (河原崎権十郎、中村鴈八、嵐冠五郎、関三十郎、沢村田之助、中村いてう、坂東彦三郎・ 當世酒呑童子)
text.text:
Picturing the actors (from right to left) Kawarazaki Gonjūrō as Minamoto no Yorimitsu, Nakamura Ganpachi as the demon Shiyatsuki, Arashi Kangorō as the demon Metsuki, Seki Sanjūrō III as Shuten Dōji, Sawamura Tanosuke III as Jijo (lady attendant) Keiko, Nakamura Ichō as Hanazono Hime and Bandō Hikosaburō V as Hirai no Yasumasa (a retainer of Minamoto no Yorimitsu) in the play A Modern Shuten Dōji (Imayō Shuten Dōji), performed at the Nakamura-za in February 1863.
"One of Japan's most popular stories was the legend of the destruction by Minamoto no Yorimitsu (who actually lived AD 948-1021) of the ogre called the Shuten Doji ('The Drunken Boy'). This flesh-eating, drunken giant lived in the mountains, where he kept young women captive, some of whom he ate. Yorimitsu and his four companions gained access to his lair disguised as travelling priests, got the monster intoxicated, and cut off his head. The real Yorimitsu was a warrior who helped the court rid Japan of bandits and pirates, hence the attachment of this legend to him." - Source: website of The British Museum https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_1881-1210-0-383-416-a [accessed 8-27-23]

media.caption: Electrical Linesman (電線工)

text.headline: Electrical Linesman (電線工)
text.text:
Linesmen installing electrical lines and transformers during the era when electrical power, its generation, transmission and distribution, were under state control. This print is number twenty-one in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures.
A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "Looking down from a high place upon the crowds of a busy city, the profession of the electrical linesman, always wearing blue and working beneath the blue sky, is a happy one. The work that from our earthbound perspective looks like it is no trouble at all, is in reality truly nerve-racking, because their life depends on how they handle the so-called 'lifeline' and 'death line.' The difference between them is whether electricity runs through them or not.
"Tokyo is gradually becoming more distinguished, but I will not go into detail here about how it fills me with pride when I see the above ground utility poles standing closely together, which major cities in the west do not have."[1]

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: River Boatman, Number 6 (川船頭 其六)

text.headline: River Boatman, Number 6 (川船頭 其六)
text.text:
A helmsman and his wife ply their boat through a fast moving river, while their two children lounge on a plank in the boat. A more modern boat chugs along in the background. This first edition of the print uses a lovely embossing to enhance the movement of the river and the smoke from the boat in the background. Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The vast majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.
The commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "This is a scene still to be found on the Sumida River. Among the busy steam and motor boats, weaving up and down the stream, slowly move the man-propelled barges. The occupation of the river boatman, sharing his work with his wife, living day in and day out on the water, making one corner of his narrow boat his world and enjoying his family life there, is a rich possession, alleviating the bewilderment of dizzy modern life."

text.headline: Sukedakaya Takasuke, Ichikawa Danjūrō and Nakamura Shikan in the play Kongen Kusazuribiki at the Shintomiza (助高屋高助, 市川団十郎, 中村芝翫, 根元草摺引新富座)
text.text:
Picturing, from right to left, the actors Sukedakaya Takasuke IV as the courtesan Kewaizaka no Shōshō, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Soga Gorō and Nakamura Shikan IV as Asahina Saburō in the dance drama Kongen kusazuribiki (The Armor Pulling), based on the legend of the Soga brothers' vendetta.
Soga no Gorō, to save his brother Jurō from danger, grapples with Kobayashi no Asahina over the treasured suit of armor stolen by Asahina. The courtesan Kewaizaka no Shōshō will attempt to calm the hot-tempered Gorō.
Asahina's costume bears the crest of a crane in a circle while Gorō's bears the Soga butterfly crest.

media.caption: Bunraku Puppets Hisamatsu and Kyūsaku in The New Scandalous Ballad of Osome and Hisamatsu (文楽人形 形新版歌祭文 久松 久作 Bunraku ningyō Hisamatsu Kyūsaku, Shinpan Utazaimon)

text.headline: Bunraku Puppets Hisamatsu and Kyūsaku in The New Scandalous Ballad of Osome and Hisamatsu (文楽人形 形新版歌祭文 久松 久作 Bunraku ningyō Hisamatsu Kyūsaku, Shinpan Utazaimon)
text.text:
Picturing the puppets Hisamatsu 久松 and his elderly foster father Kyūsaku 久作 in the play Shinpan Utazaimon (The New Scandalous Ballad of Osome and Hisamatsu) written by Chikamatsu Hanji (1725-1783) and first staged in 1780. In this famous scene, Hisamatsu is rubbing Kyūsaku's shoulders just before Hisamatsu and Osome will decide to commit suicide if they cannot marry.
A later edition, post-WWII, print by Uchida Publishing issued without the tissue overlay present in the original edition.
The Illustrated Collection of Famous Japanese Puppets of the Osaka Bunrakuza consists of twelve sets of prints each set depicting a specific play in the bunraku repertory. Each set contains a stage set for the specific play along with three prints of puppet characters appearing in the play and an explanatory sheet, for a total of forty-eight color woodblock prints and twelve monochrome explanatory sheets. All of the plays pictured were performed at the Bunraku Theater (Bunraku-za) located within the Goryō Shrine compound in Osaka. The Goryō Bunraku-za burned down in November 1926 after what has been described as "an extremely difficult managerial era" and "lost interest" by the public in the late Taishō era. It is unknown what role, if any, the management of the Goryō Bunraku-za may have played in the formulation and issuance of this print series in their efforts to revitalize the theater.

text.text:
Illustration of the stage set for Act V “The Yamazaki Highway” of the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) attributed to the playwrights Takeda Izumo II (1691-1756), Miyoshi Shōraku (1696-1772) and Namiki Senryū (1695-1751) and first performed in 1748.
This set presents us with a moonlit night along the Yamazaki highway running between Kyoto and Osaka. Robbery and murder will ensue!
The play is one of the “Three Masterpieces” of the puppet theater along with Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura and Sugawara Denju Tenarai Kagami.
