media.caption: Yumi yawata 弓八幡 (The Bow at the Hachiman Shrine)

text.headline: Yumi yawata 弓八幡 (The Bow at the Hachiman Shrine)
text.text:
Play synopsis - Yumi Yawata is a two act play centering on a warrior’s bow wrapped in a brocade bag. The maejite, an old man, appears with the bow at the Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine in Kyoto and presents it to the waki, a retainer of the Ex-Emperor Gouda (1267-1324), to be offered up to His Majesty. As the shite explains: “Among the historical precedents of the land of China, brought to peaceful rule under the Zhou, one finds the precedent of wrapping one’s bow and arrows in a bag and shutting away one’s lance and shield. Accordingly, I have stuffed this bow into a bag and put my sword away in a box; these very actions are a sign of our lord’s age of great peace.” According to the recorded words of Zeami, the author of the play, the play was written “in honor of the inaugural celebration for the reign of the present shogun."

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Kamo Monogurui 加茂 物狂 (Madness at Kamo)

text.headline: Kamo Monogurui 加茂 物狂 (Madness at Kamo)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 68-69) - A man from the capital who has been away in the eastern provinces for more than three years returns to the capital on the day of the Kamo Festival and there sees his wife. She, however, has lost her reason and although they talk together and she dances for him, she does not realize who he is. She tells how, unable to bear her husband's absence any longer, she set off to the east on a fruitless search for him, and how loneliness and disappointment have made her mad. They then recognize and acknowledge each other, but because of the curiosity of the onlookers they pretend to be strangers and leave separately, to be reunited in their home.

media.caption: Peaches (桃)

text.headline: Peaches (桃)
text.text: The artist reworked and reprinted this still life of peaches numerous times. This impression likely a later state. See IHL.1620 for what is likely a first or early state of this print.

media.caption: Hakkō Ichiu Tower in Miyazaki (宮崎八紘一宇基柱 Hakkō ichiu kijū)

text.headline: Hakkō Ichiu Tower in Miyazaki (宮崎八紘一宇基柱 Hakkō ichiu kijū)
text.text:
Print number fifty (五十, as printed in the right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941. It is perhaps the ultimate nationalist print in the series, depicting Hakkō Ichiu Tower in Miyazaki erected in 1940 to commemorate the 2,600th anniversary of the mythical ascension of Japan's first emperor, Jimmu, on 11 February 660 BC.

SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, or the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.
In his commentary on this series, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

media.caption: Kyoto Kinkakuji (京都金閣寺)

text.headline: Kyoto Kinkakuji (京都金閣寺)
text.text:
A postcard size, unsigned print, of Kinkakuji 金閣寺 (the Golden Pavilion) in snow, after a design by the artist Kawase Hasui. (See IHL.0653 and IHL.1424 for similar views of Kinkakuji in snow and see IHL.1538 for the original design by Hasui. Reference Hp-45 in "Kawase Hasui, The Complete Woodblock Prints, Volume 1" Hotei Publishing, 2003, p. 143.) The publisher of this print was Yokohama-based Hideo Takemura (H. Takemura & Co.) who targeted his work at a Western audience, specializing in, as printed on his business card, Christmas Cards, Japanese Old Colour Prints, Famous Modern Colour Prints and Water Colors.
The publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō became so upset by these copies of original designs by Hasui and several other artists he published that he included the following warning in his 1936 catalogue titled, "Catalogue of Wood-Cut Colour Prints of S. Watanabe, S. Watanabe, 1936" :
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.”
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints).

media.caption: Benten Island, Lake Hamana and Mount Fuji (濱名湖辨天嶋と富士)

text.headline: Benten Island, Lake Hamana and Mount Fuji (濱名湖辨天嶋と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji is barely visible from the rice planting area around Bentenjima. Three bi-planes along with four birds fly through the sky, while a traditionally dressed rice-farmer and old-fashioned fishing boats go about their business. Again, the artist juxtaposing the traditional with the modern.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: Taira no Tadanori (平忠度)

text.headline: Taira no Tadanori (平忠度)
text.text:
Standing impatiently outside the house of his lover, the courtier Taira no Tadanori rustles his fan to get her attention. At the age of forty, Tadanori was killed in the Battle of Ichinotani, where he showed great courage. He was mourned as a peerless warrior, artist, and poet, even by his enemies, and a chapter of the Heike monogatari is devoted to his death.

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

media.caption: Bon Festival Moon (つき百姿 Bon no tsuki)

text.headline: Bon Festival Moon (つき百姿 Bon no tsuki)
text.text:
Bon, a Buddhist festival, is the most important summertime festival in Japan, still celebrated today. It is held in the middle of the seventh lunar month when the moon is full. During the festival, the spirits of the dead are believed to visit their descendants in the world of the living.[1]

media.caption: Momijigari 紅葉狩 (Maple Viewing)

text.headline: Momijigari 紅葉狩 (Maple Viewing)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Momijigari, written by Kojirō, in which a lady of rank who has entertained Taira no Koremochi, shown arising and about to draw his sword, reveals herself as a demon.
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 126.) - In the piece, the Taira warrior Koremochi (waki) is hunting in the sacred Togakushi mountains when he comes across a beautiful woman (shite) and her lovely companions (tsure) banqueting under the maple leaves. They give him wine, and he falls asleep watching them dance. Soon the woman returns to her true form of a demon. Meanwhile, however, the god from a nearby shrine has come to Koremochi and warned him of this danger. He awakens in time to vanquish the demon with a sword the god has brought to him.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Kanawa 鉄輪 (The Iron Crown)

text.headline: Kanawa 鉄輪 (The Iron Crown)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Kanawa by an unknown author, sometimes attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), in which "the avenging wife, portrayed as a devil, lurks behind a stand used in Shinto ceremonies as a type of prayer shelf. On the shelf are a samurai hat and a wig - representing the husband and wife - as well as Shinto paper offerings." (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 80, cat. 25.)

Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 80) - An official (kyōgen) of the Kibune Shrine in Kyoto speaks with a woman (shite) whose husband has abandoned her for another woman. She has come to the shrine to pray for assistance in exacting revenge against him. An oracle instructs here that if she places an iron crown with three burning tapers on her head and dons a red kimono, she will turn into a devil and will then succeed with her plan. Later, her former husband (wakizure) seeks advice from the diviner Abe no Seimei (waki) about nightmares he has been experiencing. The seer explains that these dreams emanate from his former wife and that his life is in danger. Abe then promises to pray in an attempt to save the man. When the spirit of the deserted wife tries to carry out her revenge, she is overcome by the efforts of the diviner.

media.caption: Lake Towada (十和田湖)

text.headline: Lake Towada (十和田湖)
text.text: Tōjirō was a watercolorist known for his landscapes. In this small print he presents Lake Towada in its autumn colors.

media.caption: Russo-Japanese War: Great Japan Red Cross Battlefield Hospital Treating Injured (日露戰爭・大日本赤十字野戰病院負傷者救療の圖 Nichiro sensō・dai Nihon Sekijūji yasenbyōin fushōsha kyūryō no zu)

text.headline: Russo-Japanese War: Great Japan Red Cross Battlefield Hospital Treating Injured (日露戰爭・大日本赤十字野戰病院負傷者救療の圖 Nichiro sensō・dai Nihon Sekijūji yasenbyōin fushōsha kyūryō no zu)
text.text:
As part of Japan's efforts to emulate Western institutions, the Japanese Red Cross was established in 1877 during the Seinan War (a.k.a. Satsuma Rebellion). By the time of the Sino-Japanese War [1894-1895], images of the Red Cross tending to fallen soldiers had become part of the standard iconography of the battlefield; the Japanese were to be seen as not only mighty but also magnanimous, as befitted an "enlightened" nation. Such descriptions would only proliferate during the Russo-Japanese War, with the Japanese Red Cross shown selflessly caring for Japanese and Russian wounded alike.[1]
In this print the magnanimity of the Japanese is driven home by the inset in the top of the center sheet showing "brutal Russian soldiers" 露國野蠻兵 tearing a child away from its mother. (For another print depicting the Japanese Red Cross in action on the battlefield see IHL.0104, The Humane Ambulance Corps of the Japanese Red Cross.)
A later state of this print added an English transcription, written in cursive, to the upper left hand corner of the left sheet reading "Japan Red Society Hospital treating the wounded in the Russo-Japanese war."

[1] A Much Recorded War: The Russo-Japanese War in History and Imagery, Fredrick A. Sharf, Anne Nishimura Morse, Sebastian Dobson, MFA Publications, 2005, p. 44.

media.caption: Funasaka Yoshisuke One Man Print Show at the Parco Gallery (舩坂芳助版画個展 Parco Gallery)

text.headline: Funasaka Yoshisuke One Man Print Show at the Parco Gallery (舩坂芳助版画個展 Parco Gallery)
text.text: A poster promoting Funasaka's "one man print show" at the now defunct Parco Gallery in Chiba City.  As with much of his work, the poster combines silkscreen and woodblock. Funasaka has used mica impregnated ink for the blue silkscreened background with silver metallic ink for the lettering. He employs the large grid pattern and the irregularly shaped, along one side, vertical forms created from reusable woodblock cutouts that are often seen in his work from the mid/late 1970s till the end of the 1980s.

text.headline: Buddhist Temple Winter (來寺 冬)

media.caption: Hidaka (日高)

text.headline: Hidaka (日高)
text.text: Sekino's depiction of Hidaka Kogen Ranch in the Saru District on Hokkaido. While the print itself bears the title 日高 (Hidaka), the longer title 日高高原牧場 (Hidaka Kogen Ranch) is printed on the portfolio cover the print was originally placed in.

media.caption: Illustration of the Main Gate at Aoyama During the Imperial Funeral Ceremony (青山御大葬式場総門前の図 Aoyama Gotaisō shikijōsōmonzen no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Main Gate at Aoyama During the Imperial Funeral Ceremony (青山御大葬式場総門前の図 Aoyama Gotaisō shikijōsōmonzen no zu)
text.text:
Bordered in black, this is one of two prints (the other being the hexaptych Illustration of His Imperial Majesty's Funeral Outside Nijūbashi, IHL.2214) created by the artist picturing the September 13, 1912 evening funeral procession for Emperor Meiji from the Imperial Palace to the Aoyama military parade grounds. While this print depicts the procession entering the parade grounds, the hexaptych pictures the procession just after its departure from the Imperial Palace and passage over Nijūbashi.
While not completely accurate in its detail, the print captures the solemnity of the funeral procession illuminated by lanterns and torches.
A song of mourning appears in the pink cartouche in the upper left hand corner of the triptych.
For a print announcing the funeral for the Empress Dowager Eishō, the arrangements for which served as precedent for the Emperor's funeral, see IHL.1809, Empress Dowager Eishō’s Imperial Funeral, 1897.

media.caption: Korean Market Town

text.headline: Korean Market Town
text.text: One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life, this print depicting a crowded street market. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945.

media.caption: Washing Clothes

text.headline: Washing Clothes
text.text:
One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945. In this idyllic scene, women are washing or carrying laundry. Isabella Bird, in writing about her visit to Korea at the end of the 19th century, painted a less idyllic picture, at least of clothes washing in Seoul, as follows:
"She washes in this foul river, in the pond of the Mulberry Palace, in every wet ditch, and outside the walls in the few streams which exist. Clothes are partially unpicked, boiled with lye three times, rolled into hard bundles, and pounded with heavy sticks on stones. After being dried they are beaten with wooden sticks on cylinders, till they attain a polish resembling dull satin. The women are slaves to the laundry, and the only sound which breaks the stillness of a Seoul night is the regular beat of their laundry sticks."

media.caption: A Set of Three Nōsatsu Kōkanfuda: Fūjin the Wind God, Raijin the Thunder God, Calligraphic Cover Sheet

text.headline: A Set of Three Nōsatsu Kōkanfuda: Fūjin the Wind God, Raijin the Thunder God, Calligraphic Cover Sheet
text.text: Pictured in this set of woodblock prints are the Buddhist and Shinto gods of wind, Fūjin 風神, and thunder, Raijin 雷神, whose names are written in calligraphic form on the cover print. All three prints were placed in an envelope with a label adhered to it noting that they were “not for sale.” These prints, designed by an unknown artist who signed his name 守拙 (Shusetsu?), were commissioned by a nōsatsukai (an association of nōsatsu, Japanese votive slips, devotees) and meant for distribution to members, hence they were“not for sale.” The names of the members of the nōsatsukai appear as small votive strips in the bottom portion of each print, 75 slips on each of the three prints. While the prints are undated, they are most likely a post-1950 production.

media.caption: Sanomura and Mount Fuji (佐野村と富士)

text.headline: Sanomura and Mount Fuji (佐野村と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji looms large behind the rice field and farmers in the foreground at work irrigating the rice field.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: Lake Tōya and Mount Usu (洞爺湖と有珠岳 Tōyako to Usuzan)

text.headline: Lake Tōya and Mount Usu (洞爺湖と有珠岳 Tōyako to Usuzan)
text.text:
Miyata depicts a very spare Lake Tōya with its islands in pink light (a sunrise or a sunset?) and the active volcano Mount Usu looming ominously in the background in solid black. This print is from one of the volume of prints, likely a volume of scenes of Hokkaidō where Lake Tōya is located, from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.

Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

media.caption: Glass Festival (ガラスの祭 典  garasu no saiten)

text.headline: Glass Festival (ガラスの祭 典  garasu no saiten)
text.text: Bits and pieces of colored glass float above a speckled background - perhaps glass fragments washed up on the beach.

media.caption: The Bloodstained Document of the Hosokawa's (細川家大火忠死誉 Hosokawa no chi-daruma)

text.headline: The Bloodstained Document of the Hosokawa's (細川家大火忠死誉 Hosokawa no chi-daruma)
text.text: The actor Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 in the role of Okawa Tomoemon in the sensational act IV, Tsuta moyō chizome no goshuin, of the play Hosokawa no chi-daruma. In this scene the hero Tomoemon, his clothes on fire, has just rescued the title deed to his master's, the daimyo Hosokawa, fiefdom from the treasury room in Hosokawa's burning palace. Hemmed in by the fire and having no escape he is about to slit-open his belly and place the document inside to save it. The final scene will show Tomoemon's burnt corpse being carried before Hosokawa and the discovery that the deed, and therefore his master's fortune, has been saved, as the blood-stained document is drawn from Tomoemon's bosom. The title deed clutched in Tomoemon's mouth in the print bears the characters 御朱印, goshuin, a letter bearing the shogun’s scarlet seal.

media.caption: Artist's Son (画家の息子)

text.headline: Artist's Son (画家の息子)
text.text:
Sekino's son Yowsaku (b. 1944) at about 8 years of age. Yowsaku, a print artist in his own right, is represented in this collection by prints IHL.2146, IHL.2415, IHL.2097 and IHL.2096.
This print exists in many different editions and states. An oil painting using the same pose was created by Sekino in 1952, likely prior to the first edition of this print.
Sekino's children have often appeared in his prints and Oliver Statler notes: "Ingenuous and friendly, he consistently manages to give the impression of fresh pleasure with the world, but nothing makes him light up like consideration of his three extraordinarily handsome and winning children, two boys and a girl . . . ." - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn, Oliver Statler, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1956, p. 65-56.

media.caption: Horse (馬 Uma)

text.headline: Horse (馬 Uma)
text.text:
This print of a horse in a barn, simply titled Horse, was one of a set of two woodblock reproductions of paintings by the artist issued by Okamoto Studio in 1983, as supervised by the Sakamoto Hanjirō Institute (坂本繁二郎研究所). Hanjirō began painting horses at about the time he moved to the city of Yame in 1931. "He would head out to Aso, Unzen, and other parts of Kyushu in search of a horse that appealed to him, sketch it, and then work on the painting back in his studio in Yame. He was enthralled by the forms of horses, bathed in the sunlight, dappled with so many colors." - Source: website of the Bridgestone Museum.
The colophon for the folio this print was originally issued in notes that the print underwent 35 color woodblock printings on Kizuki hōsho, a handmade paper from Echizen.

media.caption: Doll Shop in Fushimi - Indian Summer Day, Kyoto (伏見人形店・小春、京都 Fushimi ningyōten・koharu、Kyoto)

text.headline: Doll Shop in Fushimi - Indian Summer Day, Kyoto (伏見人形店・小春、京都 Fushimi ningyōten・koharu、Kyoto)
text.text: A sign proclaiming 伏見人形 (Fushimi ningyō) sits outside a Kyoto store  displaying traditional clay dolls made in Fushimi. It is nighttime and the display table next to the sign is empty. This collection's print is an “épreuve d'artiste," or "artist's proof."

media.caption: Spring Water from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 15, No. 5  (春水・文芸倶楽部 第十五巻, 第五号)

text.headline: Spring Water from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 15, No. 5  (春水・文芸倶楽部 第十五巻, 第五号)
text.text:
As noted by the National Library of Australia, "The [woodblock] print was produced as a kuchie frontispiece in a literary magazine titled Bungei kurabu, dai 15-kan, dai 5-gō. Not created to accompany a particular literary piece in the issue." It has also been suggested that the print was an illustration for a serialized novel titled "春水" (Shunsui), "Spring Water."

THE LITERARY MAGAZINE BUNGEI KURABU
Bungei Kurabu 文芸倶楽部 was a very popular literary magazine published from 1895-1933 by Hakubunkan. It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan. In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

media.caption: Four Bridges, frontispiece appearing in the magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 2, No. 10 (文芸倶楽部, 第二巻, 第 十編・井字橋 Bungei kurabu, dai 2-kan, dai 10-hen・Ijibashi)

text.headline: Four Bridges, frontispiece appearing in the magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 2, No. 10 (文芸倶楽部, 第二巻, 第 十編・井字橋 Bungei kurabu, dai 2-kan, dai 10-hen・Ijibashi)
text.text:
Although he studied with the Kanō school painter Kobayashi Eitaku (1843-1890), Tomioka Eisen was primarily an illustrator creating frontispieces and illustrations for serialized novels published by various newspapers and magazines, such as this print for the literary magazine Bungei Kurabu illustrating the story "Four Bridges" by the writer of popular fiction Takeda Gyōtenshi 武田仰天子 (1854-1926).
In this print Oshun, in the circular opening, the love of Genshichi, has just read a letter held by Genshichi from her malicious sister-in-law who wants her to marry her nephew rather than Genshichi. In the tragic ending, Genshichi and Oshun will commit suicide.

media.caption: Brief History of Japan Pictorial Gameboard, top left sheet (皇国史畧雙録 Kōkoku shiryaku sugoroku)

text.headline: Brief History of Japan Pictorial Gameboard, top left sheet (皇国史畧雙録 Kōkoku shiryaku sugoroku)
text.text:
The top left sheet of an e-sugoroku (pictorial game board) with its top panel depicting Nintoku Tennō, who is considered to have reigned from 313 to 399. This top panel is the goal or finish of the game. Each of the four sheets comprising the game, depicts three or four scenes of famous stories and historical figures demonstrating moral actions to be emulated. Brief explanatory texts appear in the scrolls on each panel. Note that one of the sheets making up the complete game is missing from this collection, but is shown with a red border in the image to the left for reference.

E-SUGOROKU
The earliest surviving examples of e-sugoroku date from the 17th century. Starting as Buddhist teaching tools, by the end of the 17th century they had become popular entertainment for the common people. The increasing popularity of e-sukoroku is tied to the development of woodblock printing, with the "game-boards" being composed of multiple standard oban size sheets after the advent of multicolor woodblock print technique towards the end of the 1700s. "Game-boards were often assembled from two, four or nine sheets joined together, so that the sizes of the finished products vary, up to a size of about 90 x 70 cm. They were sold in folded form (rather like modern maps), in envelopes or wrappers into which they could be easily inserted again after use."[1]
"In order to play, players needed a die and markers or figures with which to play. . . All sugoroku games have a starting square usually called furidashi and a goal called agari."[2] In this collection's e-sugoroku, a tobi sugoroku or "jumping sukoroku," "[e]ach field or square in the game gives instructions as to which square players must proceed to, when a given number is thrown. Sometimes, fewer than 6 numbers are given; in this case, players who fail to come up with one of the stipulated numbers have to wait for the next round in order to make a move."[3]

[1] "Playing with Filial Piety – Some Remarks on a 19th-Century Variety of Japanese Pictorial Sugoroku Games," by Susanne Formanek and Sepp Linhart appearing in the magazine Board Game Studies, Volume 5, International Journal for the Study of Board Games, CNWS Publications, 2002, p. 40.
Ibid. p. 41.
Ibid. p. 43.

media.caption: Brief History of Japan Pictorial Gameboard, top right sheet (皇国史畧雙録 Kōkoku shiryaku sugoroku)

text.headline: Brief History of Japan Pictorial Gameboard, top right sheet (皇国史畧雙録 Kōkoku shiryaku sugoroku)
text.text:
The bottom right sheet of an e-sugoroku (pictorial board game) with its four panels showing incidents in the lives of (clockwise starting in the upper right), Komatsu Daifu Shigemori 小松内府重盛 (Taira no Shigemori 平重盛, 1138-1179), Kusunoki Masashige 楠正成八河内 (1294-1336), Ōta Dōkan 太田道灌持資 (1432-1486) and, in top left panel, Hachimantarō 八幡太郎 (Minamoto no Yoshiie 源義家, 1041-1108). Each of the four sheets comprising the game, depicts three or four scenes of famous stories and historical figures demonstrating moral actions to be emulated. Brief explanatory texts appear in the scrolls on each panel. Note that one of the sheets making up the complete game is missing from this collection, but is shown with a red border in the image to the left for reference.

E-SUGOROKU
The earliest surviving examples of e-sugoroku date from the 17th century. Starting as Buddhist teaching tools, by the end of the 17th century they had become popular entertainment for the common people. The increasing popularity of e-sukoroku is tied to the development of woodblock printing, with the "game-boards" being composed of multiple standard oban size sheets after the advent of multicolor woodblock print technique towards the end of the 1700s. "Game-boards were often assembled from two, four or nine sheets joined together, so that the sizes of the finished products vary, up to a size of about 90 x 70 cm. They were sold in folded form (rather like modern maps), in envelopes or wrappers into which they could be easily inserted again after use."[1]
"In order to play, players needed a die and markers or figures with which to play. . . All sugoroku games have a starting square usually called furidashi and a goal called agari."[2] In this collection's e-sugoroku, a tobi sugoroku or "jumping sukoroku," "[e]ach field or square in the game gives instructions as to which square players must proceed to, when a given number is thrown. Sometimes, fewer than 6 numbers are given; in this case, players who fail to come up with one of the stipulated numbers have to wait for the next round in order to make a move."[3]

[1] "Playing with Filial Piety – Some Remarks on a 19th-Century Variety of Japanese Pictorial Sugoroku Games," by Susanne Formanek and Sepp Linhart appearing in the magazine Board Game Studies, Volume 5, International Journal for the Study of Board Games, CNWS Publications, 2002, p. 40.

media.caption: The Great Virtue and Influence of the Inspiring Tenjin Sutra (大威徳天神感應經 Dai Itoku Tenjin kannō kyō)

text.headline: The Great Virtue and Influence of the Inspiring Tenjin Sutra (大威徳天神感應經 Dai Itoku Tenjin kannō kyō)
text.text:
This vertical diptych depicts Sugawara no Michizane 菅原道真 (845–903), who after his death in exile was elevated to "Tenjin" (a god who was originally mortal), sitting in the Tenman Shrine. Behind him is a painting of a plum tree (ume), alluding to his famous poem written in exile in which he laments the absence of a particular plum tree he had loved in the capital. Beneath him, on the bottom sheet, are his guardian attendants and two komainu (guardian dogs) on pedestals, each pedestal bearing the characters 奉納 (hōnō) "votive offering."
Known as the patron of scholarship, Tenjin shrines are visited by multitudes of students each year as entrance exams approach. Votive offerings are made requesting academic success and admission to the college of their choice. In commenting on this yearly student pilgrimage, Professor Emeritus Robert Borgan writes, "They give the impression that Japan's largely secular youth is experiencing a religious revival."[1]
The scroll at the top of the print is the Tenjinkyō (Tenjin sutra). Likely composed in the early Edo era, the Tenjinkyō, which incorporates elements of the Tenjin cult and Buddhism, is a short apocryphal sutra invoking the name of Sugawara no Michizane (Tenjin) read before classes in the Tokugawa period terakoya (temple schools) which contributed greatly to the spread of literacy during the Tempō era (1830-1844) into the Meiji period.[2]

[1] Sugawara No Michizane and the Early Heian Court, Robert Borgen, University of Hawaii Press, 1994, p. 1.
[2] Terakoya (temple schools) were public educational institutions that provided children with an education of reading and writing and in some places taught the use of the abacus. They existed not only in Edo but also in other towns and villages throughout Japan. The number of terakoya at the end of the Tokugawa Shogunate seems to have reached some thirty or forty thousand and it was these institutions that contributed to the high levels of literacy among ordinary people.

media.caption: Frontispiece for the novel Kuroda Kenji, Vol. 2 (黒田健次 後篇)

text.headline: Frontispiece for the novel Kuroda Kenji, Vol. 2 (黒田健次 後篇)
text.text:
The frontispiece for the revised first edition of volume two of the novel "Kuroda Kenji" 黒田健次 by Murakami Namiroku 村上浪六 (1865-1944).
The designer of this print Mizuno Toshikata, a student of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892), frequently found work illustrating for the publishers Hakubunkan, Shun'yōdō and others, designing kuchi-e (frontispieces) for many novels by well-known authors of the time.

media.caption: Fireflies (untitled)

text.headline: Fireflies (untitled)
text.text: Fireflies (hotaru) dart among the reeds in this kachō-ga (bird and flower print) by Kōgyo, one of about fifty in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by the artist whose publishing is attributed to Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) in the early 1900s.

media.caption: Quails and Full Moon (untitled)

text.headline: Quails and Full Moon (untitled)
text.text:
One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) around the turn of the 20th century and attributed to the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi).
"A silver moon dominates this striking nocturnal scene, which shows seven quails among autumn grasses. In Japanese art, the subject is common in the Tosa painting school.
"As fighting birds, the quail (uzura) is a traditional symbol of courage and victory in battle." - source: The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 149.

media.caption: Ships at Night (untitled)

text.headline: Ships at Night (untitled)
text.text:
An unusual subject for the artist. The print exists in several color variations, two of which are in this collection. Print IHL. 1193 is the darkest of the color variations. It carries the "Toshihisa" seal of the artist, while other impressions of this print, including this collection's IHL.1716, do not.
"In this composition, a fire in the distance illuminates the sky and creates an effective backdrop to the three moored boats." - Source: The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 151.

media.caption: 71-1 (Haniwa)

text.headline: 71-1 (Haniwa)
text.text:
One of at least a half-dozen prints of haniwa (ancient Japanese funerary clay figures) created by Maki. It is assumed that this print's title "71-1" would make it the first print that Maki created in 1971.
Maki made his own printing blocks by carving a motif onto a piece of plywood, filling the carved-out areas with cement paste, and passing the print several times through a press to achieve various textures. Calligraphy is central to his works; he sometimes manipulates calligraphy to defy reading, thereby drawing attention to the form of Chinese characters.

media.caption: Poem 71-5 (仁)

text.headline: Poem 71-5 (仁)
text.text:
Maki presents us with the Chinese character for ren, "仁", the Confucian concept of benevolence. Maki's "poem" prints may be a tribute to his teacher, the pioneering abstract print master Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), who used "poem" as a title for a number of his prints and was often inspired by poetry. While he had no formal art training, Maki studied for two years with Onchi, attending meetings of the Modern Print Study Society (Gendai Hanga Kenkyūkai 現代版画研究会), founded in 1950 by Onchi and Kitaoka Fumio (1918-2007) under the auspices of the Nippon Hanga Kyōkai.

media.caption: Mount Myōgi (妙義山 Myōgisan)

text.headline: Mount Myōgi (妙義山 Myōgisan)
text.text:
A view of Mount Myōgi, one of the "Three Mounts of Jōmō," in the fall. This print is one of twelve prints from the series "Here and There in Jōshin'etsu."
Mount Myōgi (妙義山 Myōgi-san) is one of the major mountains in the Gunma Prefecture, Japan. Well known for its rocks weathered into fantastic forms, this famous peak is ranked among Japan's three most noted places of rugged beauty. There are many hiking courses, and when the foliage changes color there are splendid views to be seen. Mount Myōgi, along with Mount Akagi and Mount Haruna, is one of the "Three Mountains of Jōmō". (Jōmō is an old name for Gunma.) Source: Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_My%C5%8Dgi [accessed 8-17-23]
Jōshin'etsu, is a kanji acronym consisting of three characters which represent the former names of provinces of the area: Kōzuke Province (上野国) in present-day Gunma Prefecture, Shinano Province (信濃国) in present-day Nagano Prefecture, and Echigo Province (越後国) in present-day Niigata Prefecture.

media.caption: Mount Asama (浅間山 Asamayama)

text.headline: Mount Asama (浅間山 Asamayama)
text.text: A view of a very gentle Mount Asama, an active volcano, from the southeast. Beyond the town, the remnants of an old lava flow are depicted. This print is one of twelve prints from the series "Here and There in Jōshin'etsu."

media.caption: Sōmon (相聞)

text.headline: Sōmon (相聞)
text.text:
This abstract small print was included in the second of two portfolios, each consisting of twelve prints, published by Hanga kanshōkai, titled Hanga kanshōkai sakuhin-shū.

COLLECTION OF WORKS BY THE WOODBLOCK PRINT APPRECIATION SOCIETY
The two volumes of Hanga kanshōkai sakuhin-shū (Collection of Works by the Woodblock Print Appreciation Society), were published by Hanga kanshōkai, a creation of the Yokohama publisher and gallery Chikuhōdō (竹芳洞 or 竹芳堂). The two portfolios were initially issued in 1959 or 1960 in an edition of 700 for volume 1 (上) and 500 copies for volume 2 (下) and reissued at least once in 1980 in an edition of 200. This collection's print is likely from the 1980 edition.

media.caption: Fukagawa Kiba (深川木場)

text.headline: Fukagawa Kiba (深川木場)
text.text:
A view of the lumber district in the Fukagawa Kiba ("kiba" meaning "place of wood") area that operated as a log gathering and lumber distribution point for the greater Edo/Tokyo area until the early 1970s when it was moved to Shin-kiba 新木場. The old Kiba was then turned into Kiba Kōen 木場公園 (Kiba Park).
Originally published in 1929, at least two editions (two separate printings) of this print were made.

media.caption: Spring Glance, Women's Illustrated Calendar of the Twelve Months from the magazine The Ladies' Graphic, Volume 1, No. 6 (春の眼、婦人絵暦十二ヶ月・婦人グラフ 第1巻 第6号)

text.headline: Spring Glance, Women's Illustrated Calendar of the Twelve Months from the magazine The Ladies' Graphic, Volume 1, No. 6 (春の眼、婦人絵暦十二ヶ月・婦人グラフ 第1巻 第6号)
text.text:
This print appeared in the October 1924 issue of "The Ladies' Graphic" (Fujin gurafu), a magazine targeted to women covering "international news, matters relating to the lifestyle of the 'contemporary' woman as well as information about cuisine and current styles in clothing, hair and make-up." - Source: Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 108.
Yumeji contributed illustrations to the magazine starting with its first issue in May 1924. Yumeji's designs were printed separately by woodblock and tipped onto a page in the magazine.

media.caption: Actors' New Year’s Party (俳優新年筵会 Haiyū shinnen enkai)

text.headline: Actors' New Year’s Party (俳優新年筵会 Haiyū shinnen enkai)
text.text: Twenty-six kabuki actors at a New Year's party. The actor Bandō Kichiroku I, "a low-ranking travelling actor" is costumed as a turtle (a symbol of longevity) in the center panel, paired with the actor Nakamura Tsuruzō II, a supporting tachiyaku actor, in a dance. They are being watched with critical eyes by their more famous colleagues such as Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the plaid-patterned kimono in the center of the right sheet, Ichikawa Sadanji I sitting over the brazier to Danjūrō's right and Onōe Kikugorō V in the left sheet holding the red fan.

media.caption: Asakusa, Tenth Month (浅草・十月)

text.headline: Asakusa, Tenth Month (浅草・十月)
text.text:
In this print we see what appear to be vendors selling sake, fish and other delectables on Azuma bridge, while a strange looking gentlemen in a red coat performs. In the background we see Asakusa and its Buddhist temple Sensō-ji and the five-story pagoda Asakusa Shinto shrine. The yellow title cartouche of this print remains largely unread, except for the first two characters 十月, 10th month, and the characters 浅草, Asakusa.
Each print in this twelve print series is a comic riff on famous places or sites in Tokyo. Twelve Months at Famous Places in Tokyo was created during the same year that the artist created his more famous comic series Thirty-Six Famous Views of Tokyo: A Comic Selection. In discussing this larger comic series of prints, a parody of Hiroshige's famous 1856/1859 series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, Johnathan Solomon notes that Shōsai "found comic expression a suitable response to the chaos and uncertainty" of the early Meiji Era. - Source: "Bridging Edo and Meiji, Shōsai Ikkei's Comic Views of Early Tokyo" appearing in Impressions: The Journal of the Ukiyo-e Society of American, Inc., Number 21, 1999, p. 45.

media.caption: Sanemori 實盛 (The Warrior Sanemori)

text.headline: Sanemori 實盛 (The Warrior Sanemori)
text.text:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 148-149 and http://www.noh-kyogen.com/story/english/Sanemori.pdf [not accessible 8-17-23]) - Summary: Sanemori was of the Genji Clan but sided with the losing Heike in 12th century Genji-Heike battles, dying at Shinowara at the age of 72. To hide his age, he dyed his white hair black and also obtained the privilege of wearing brocade robe in battle. The ghost of Sanemori appears before a traveling priest two centuries later, tells how he met his death, and asks to be saved.

Details: After a local person of Shinowara explains in a short prologue that the priest Ta-ami preaches there every day, apparently to himself, the priest begins his sermon. An old man, visible to Ta-ami but to no one else, then comes to listen as he has on every previous day. When asked about himself, he reveals that he is the ghost of the warrior Sanemori who was killed in battle there more than two hundred years ago, and then he vanishes beside the pond in which his head was washed after his death. When the priest prays there through the night for the repose of Sanemori's spirit, the ghost appears and tells the story of his last battle before which, being already an old man at the time, he died his white hair to hide his age.
This collection's print is unusual in that it is in its original state after printing. It has not been bound into book form, as were most of the prints from this series, nor trimmed in any fashion. The title 實盛 and number of the print 七, which would normally have been trimmed off, appear in the right hand margin.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Yuya 熊野

text.headline: Yuya 熊野
text.text:
Play synopsis (the-NOH.com http://www.the-noh.com/en/plays/data/program_016.html and A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 224-225) - Yuya, the mistress of an inn in Ikeda in Tōtoumi (present-day Shizuoka Prefecture) serves the power-holder Taira no Munemori of the Heike clan, in the capital. Because she has heard that her mother at her home is seriously ill, she asks Munemori to allow her leave to return home. However, Munemori does not grant her request, because he wants to enjoy the cherry blossoms with Yuya. Around that time, Asagao, a woman serving Yuya’s family, visits her with a letter from her mother. In the letter, her mother pours out her desperate desire to see Yuya before leaving this world as she has been seriously ill. Yuya, who does not want to waste even a second where she is, reads her mother’s letter to Munemori, and asks his permission to let her go home. But contrary to her hope, he orders her to accompany his entourage to enjoy cherry blossoms at Kiyomizu-dera Temple.

Even as she looks at the people who are enjoying the full spring beauty, Yuya’s heart is filled with concern for her mother and home. When she reluctantly dances at a party, a sudden drizzle causes the cherry blossom to fall. Yuya, who observes the falling blossom, reads a poem to express her feelings of love for her mother. Yuya’s love expressed in her poem thaws Munemori’s stubborn heart, and Munemori finally allows her to return home. Yuya quickly departs to home before he changes his mind.
This collection's print is unusual in that it is in its original state after printing. It has not been bound into book form, as were most of the prints from this series, nor trimmed in any fashion. The title 熊野 and number of the print 一三, which would normally have been trimmed off, appear in the right hand margin.

media.caption: The Heroine Osai in Gonza the Lancer (鑓の権三重帷子のおさい Yari no Gonza kasane katabira no Osai)

text.headline: The Heroine Osai in Gonza the Lancer (鑓の権三重帷子のおさい Yari no Gonza kasane katabira no Osai)
text.text:
In this print Osai, the wife of a tea ceremony teacher, who secretly longs for Sasano Gonza, her intended son-in-law, holds the sash she has just torn from Gonza after a struggle. The sash displays his crest and a reverse chrysanthemum joined in a lover's knot. After tearing off the sash she cries "Are you so devoted to that sash? Here, I know you won't like it, but wear my sash instead. It will become a vengeful snake, wrap itself around you waste, and never let you go." While jealous, she smiles sweetly, looking over her shoulder with a tender expression of affection. When Gonza throws her sash into the garden it is taken by the samurai Bannojō, hiding there, as proof of their adultery, the penalty for which is death. - Source: The Major Plays of Chikamatsu, translated by Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 1961, p. 291.

One of 18 prints published from 1922 to c. 1925 as part of the celebration of the two-hundredth anniversary of the death of Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1623-1724), perhaps the greatest dramatist in the history of the Japanese theater. Each design illustrates a scene or character from one of Chikamatsu’s famous works which were compiled into 16 volumes by Chikamatsu researcher Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950). The prints were inserted into the volume containing the story they illustrated and were also separately sold.

media.caption: Dancing Ladies (fan design sample)

text.headline: Dancing Ladies (fan design sample)
text.text: A fan design sample created as a marketing tool for deluxe fan makers. While this fan design was likely created during the Taishō or early Shōwa eras (c. 1912-1940), fan design samples date back to the Meiji era. They showed the season's available designs, commissioned from some of the most eminent artists of the day. Once the season was over, the sample fans and books of fans were sold. Most samples in this collection do not carry a signature or seal and the artists will be forever unknown, but some famous names do appear on several of the prints. The designs range from Art Deco to traditional genre scenes. The shape of these prints indicate they were designs for folding fans (sensu 扇子, or ōgi 扇 as they are also known.) While often described as "woodblock prints", most of these sample designs appear to be hand painted or inked rather than printed.

media.caption: Monster Reforms Mayor, No. 8 appearing in the Ōsaka Nichinichi Shinbunshi (大阪日々新聞紙・第八号)

text.headline: Monster Reforms Mayor, No. 8 appearing in the Ōsaka Nichinichi Shinbunshi (大阪日々新聞紙・第八号)
text.text:
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability. Following their introduction in Tokyo, nishiki-e shinbun made their appearance in Osaka. The Osaka issued prints differed from their Tokyo counterparts in being half-size (chūban rather than ōban size).
In this print, "the fearful-looking monster was in fact a good spirit. It made its appearance before a [Mr.] Nakayama, who was so captivated by a certain widow' s charms that he neglected his duties as the chief of a certain district in what is now Hyogo prefecture. The monster is shown trying to reform the man." The text is signed Bun Sanjin 文山人記, certainly a pseudonym of an unknown writer. - source: website of Waseda University Library http://www.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kosho/bunko10/b10_8068_6/index.html [accessed 8-17-23]
The red cartouche in the upper left hand corner provides the name of the paper 大阪日々新聞紙 (Ōsaka Nichinichi Shinbunshi) and the print number 第八号 (8).

media.caption: Evening Cherry Blossoms at Gion (祇園夜桜)

text.headline: Evening Cherry Blossoms at Gion (祇園夜桜)
text.text:
A chuban size print depicting illuminated cherry trees in bloom in Kyoto's Gion district in the evening. A large crowd of admirers are silhouetted along the bottom of the print. The cherry trees start to bloom sometime in mid- to late April in Gion. The beauty of yozakura (night time cherry blossoms) is exceptional and popular places for cherry blossom viewing are illuminated at night.
This print is part of a set of five prints by the artist created for the famous soba shop Owariya 尾張屋 in Kyoto, which has been in business since 1465. Four of the prints depict scenic views in and around Kyoto and the fifth depicts the Owariya. Originally published in the 1930s, this set was reprinted for the celebration of the 15th generation household head of Owariya during the 1980s. The Owariya name in kana をはりや or kanji 尾張屋, within a rectangular cartouche, appears on each of the prints.

media.caption: Autumn in Ohara (大原の秋)

text.headline: Autumn in Ohara (大原の秋)
text.text:
A chuban size print depicting two woman in traditional dress in the town of Ohara (Oharame - maidens of Ohara) in present day Sakyo-ku, Kyoto. Oharame (maidens of Ohara) were once a frequent sight, carrying flowers or other merchandise on their towel-wrapped heads and wearing traditional dress.
There is an annual Oharame Festival in Ohara, in late April and early May, during which time the Oharame experience, dressing in costume, can be had for about 1,000 yen.

media.caption: Illustration of the Owariya Denzaemon Shop at Kyo[to] Kurumayacho Nijo (京車や街二条尾張屋伝右エ門見世先ノ図)

text.headline: Illustration of the Owariya Denzaemon Shop at Kyo[to] Kurumayacho Nijo (京車や街二条尾張屋伝右エ門見世先ノ図)
text.text: The famous Owariya soba shop in Kyoto is pictured under a half moon on a quiet evening. The original shop (honke Owariya), founded in 1465 to sell confectionery, still operates near the Old Imperial Palace. The Owariya name 尾張屋 can be seen on the lantern and the shop's noren (entrance curtain) advertises their specialty of fresh soba 大名物 生蕎麦 (dai-meibutsu nama soba).

media.caption: Miidera 三井寺 (The Miidera Temple)

text.headline: Miidera 三井寺 (The Miidera Temple)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Miidera, often attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 108.) - A mother whose child has disappeared makes a long pilgrimage to the Kyōmizu-dera in Kyoto and asks the goddess Kannon to help her find him again. She has a dream which is interpreted by a fortune-teller to mean that she must go to the temple called Mii-dera [in Ōmi Province] to meet her son again. Arriving there on the night of the full moon quite unbalanced through anxiety and grief, she rings the temple bell. The priests of the temple, who are looking after her son Semmitsu and have been viewing the moon with him, come up to reproach her. But as they talk, it is found that she is the boy's mother and the two are happily reunited.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Saigyō Zakura 西行桜 (Saigyō and the Cherry Tree)

text.headline: Saigyō Zakura 西行桜 (Saigyō and the Cherry Tree)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Saigyō Zakura in which the spirit of the cherry tree near the poet Saigyō’s retreat dances to show its delight in spring blossoms while Saigyō watches.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 145.) - An old cherry tree beside Saigyō's retreat comes into full bloom, but just when the poet resolves to enjoy the beauty of it quietly on his own, a group of people come there on a flower-viewing trip. Saigyō composes a poem in which he blames the cherry itself for the noisy intrusion, but while he is resting beneath the tree later, the spirit of the cherry comes to him and denies that it is to blame. It then dances to express the delight to be found in the spring blossom. The dream then fades, and Saigyō awakens.

text.text:
A fan design print by the nihonga painter Dōmoto Inshō who was made an Imperial Household Artist in 1944 and received the Order of Culture in 1961.
Fan design samples were created as a marketing tool for deluxe fan makers. While this fan design was likely created during the Taishō or early Shōwa eras (c. 1912-1940), fan design samples date back to the Meiji era. They showed the season's available designs, commissioned from some of the most eminent artists of the day. Once the season was over, the sample fans and books of fans were sold. Most samples in this collection do not carry a signature or seal and the artists will be forever unknown, but some famous names do appear on several of the prints. The designs range from Art Deco to traditional genre scenes. The shape of these prints indicate they were designs for folding fans (sensu 扇子, or ōgi 扇 as they are also known.) While often described as "woodblock prints", most of these sample designs appear to be hand painted or inked rather than printed.
Some of the prints carry inventory numbers; some bear a cartouche with the word nambu (literally, "southern region" and possibly the name of a company) written in kanji 南部 or kana なんぶ, and some bear a fan-shaped cartouche with the kanji character 業 ("karma" or simply the character for "industry" or "business") inside it, possibly the trademark of another fan company.
This print bears the kanji character 業, has what appears to be a handwritten inventory number of "187" and an inscription (that loosely says that the sample should be handled with care and then returned.

media.caption: A Man in Armor 17 (鎧へる人 17 Yoroeru hito)

text.headline: A Man in Armor 17 (鎧へる人 17 Yoroeru hito)
text.text: One of Hagiwara’s 1962-1964 twenty print homage to the samurai, through abstract renderings of samurai armor. "The Man in Armor prints are either metallic in appearance or possess the luster of leather, like medieval breastplates.  They are visually heavy but far from being dull.  Hagiwara's sense of proportion prevents the prints from falling under their own weight." - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973 p. 112.

media.caption: Mallards in Coastal Scene

text.headline: Mallards in Coastal Scene
text.text:
Originally issued in 1931, this collection's print is a later edition c. 1946-1957.
"Less successful are Koson's attempts at integrated landscape compositions such as "Mallards in a coastal scene," one of the few dated prints by the artist (1931), in which the groupings of ducks appear wooden and stolid in an equally lackluster landscape setting. The forms of the diving and swimming ducks in this print are clearly borrowed from other prints like "Mallards and lotus" or visa versa. In Japanese art, the reuse of motifs and the reworking of compositions by painters and print designers is not unusual . . . ." - Source: Crows, Cranes & Camellias: The Natural World of Ohara Koson 1877-1945, Amy Reigle Newland, Jan Perrée, Robert Schaap, Hotei Publishing, 2003, plate 146 caption.

media.caption: Bijin in brown haori over green kimono (untitled)

text.headline: Bijin in brown haori over green kimono (untitled)
text.text:
Ikeda Terukata, primarily known as a bijinga artist, began his career as an illustrator and would go on to win prizes as a nihonga (modern Japanese-style) artist at the Bunten, the annual Ministry of Education art exhibition.
This bijin kuchi-e, reproduced using a color offset lithographic process, displays the characteristic tri-fold of prints inserted into popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi).

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

media.caption: Hometown of the Sea (ふるさとの海 Furusato no umi)

text.headline: Hometown of the Sea (ふるさとの海 Furusato no umi)
text.text:
Nozomi Naoi finds this print reminiscent of Yumeji's native Okayama with his childhood home "nestled at the foot of a small hill overlooking the main road leading to Ushimado port." - Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 141.
"The publisher Katō Jungi drew from Yumeji's book illustrations, paintings and magazine cover designs to produce this set, which contains ten woodblock prints accompanied by poetry originally composed by Yumeji." - Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 141.

media.caption: Woman of the Wind (風の女)

text.headline: Woman of the Wind (風の女)
text.text: One of twenty prints in a collection of Yumeji's small works published posthumously by the Katō Printmaking Institute.

media.caption: Act XII [The Treasury of Loyal Retainers] (十二段目 [假名手本忠臣蔵])

text.headline: Act XII [The Treasury of Loyal Retainers] (十二段目 [假名手本忠臣蔵])
text.text:
Act XII: The deed has been done, revenge achieved, Moronao (the historical figure protocol officer Kira Kōzuke-no-suke Yoshinaka) has been slain, and his head, washed and wrapped with a purple cloth, is being presented by forty-six of the "loyal forty-seven rōnin" at the grave of their master, Enya Hangan (the historical figure Asano Takumi-no-kami Naganori, the daimyō of Akō [Lord Asano]) in Segakuji temple. The dirk by which Lord Asano disembowled himself is held aloft by Hazama Jūjirō, one of the rōnin who discovered where Moronao was hiding.
The gravestone seen in the print contains the following inscriptions:
源長矩朝臣 (Lord Asano Naganori) 吹く毛玄利大居士 (Asano's posthumous Buddhist name, alluding to his passing in the spring of life)
元禄十四年三月十四日 (Genroku 14th year, 3rd month, 14th day - April 21, 1701, the day when Asano Naganori drew his sword in a corridor of Edo Castle and slashed at the senior bakufu protocol official, Kira Yoshinaka.)
The names of sixteen of the loyal ronin are shown in the red cartouches, including the names of Hazama Jūjirō 間十次郎, who is seen holding the dirk before the grave of his lord; Ōishi Kuranosuke 大石内蔵助 (the leader of the loyal forty-seven rōnin), seen holding the manuscript laid upon the tomb of their master and Takebayashi Tadashichi 竹林唯七, offering incense.

media.caption: Bijin looking askance, (untitled)

text.headline: Bijin looking askance, (untitled)
text.text:
Kitano Tsunetomi 北野恒富 (1880-1947) was considered an innovator in the modern (Taishō era) bijinga genre, as can be seen in this magazine illustration of a young woman with a worried or askance gaze. An Osaka-based "nihonga" (modern Japanese-style) painter who mentored many Osaka-based painters including the "young rebel" woman painter Shima Seien, his early career was as a newspaper illustrator.

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

text.text:
Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).
This offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) with its characteristic tri-fold, appeared in an unknown magazine. The print's untranslated title, 阿艶殿, appears in the upper left corner of the print.
