media.caption: Nostalgia 7

text.headline: Nostalgia 7
text.text: A largely self-taught artist, Amano first exhibited his work in 1955 and his work would later appear in numerous international exhibitions. His prints range from the representational to the abstract and he is best known for his abstract and semi-abstract works, such as Nostalgia 7. At least 20 of the artist's prints carry the word "Nostalgia" in their title followed by their number (likely chronological) in the series. In the words of Gaston Petit, a great fan and promoter of post-war avant-garde woodblock print artists in Japan, "Amano works in a series, though not in the sense of repeating the same image in a loosely realted manner . . . but in a more systematic permutational sense." - Source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha, 1973, p. 56.

media.caption: Taiwan War: Illustration of the Battle of Baguashan (臺灣戰争・八卦山激戰占領圖)

text.headline: Taiwan War: Illustration of the Battle of Baguashan (臺灣戰争・八卦山激戰占領圖)
text.text:
A fabricated scene by the artist of the Battle of Baguashan fought in late August 1895 against Taiwanese resistance forces. Taiwan was awarded to the Japanese under the Treaty of Shimonoseki ending the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) and remained a colony of Japan until 1945.
"After landing in Taiwan and encountering much local resistance, the Japanese army reached the northern banks of the Dadu River (大肚溪), on what is today’s border between Taichung and Changhua County, on Aug. 25, 1895. They did not cross the river immediately, as the enemy had regrouped on the south banks in the city of Changhua and on the nearby battery on Baguashan (八卦山). After a few days of scouting and minor skirmishes, the Japanese army of about 15,000 men split into two wings, with the left wing crossing the river in the dark on Aug. 27. They attacked the battery in the morning, and thus began the Battle of Baguashan (八卦山之役), the largest clash between the two sides." - Source: Taipei Times, "Taiwan in Time: Defending the Homeland to the Death," Han Cheung, August 28, 2016.
By the third week in October the armed resistance had been crushed and for the next fifty years Taiwan would be occupied by the Japanese.

media.caption: The Moon: A Modern Meiji Beauty, a supplement to the magazine Shufu no tomo (The Housewife's Friend), Volume 19, Number 1 (主婦之友、附録・月 明治風俗美人、第十九巻 第一號)

text.headline: The Moon: A Modern Meiji Beauty, a supplement to the magazine Shufu no tomo (The Housewife's Friend), Volume 19, Number 1 (主婦之友、附録・月 明治風俗美人、第十九巻 第一號)
text.text:
This chromolithograph was one of three long pillar-format bijin prints titled Snow, Moon and Flower issued as special supplements to the January 1935 issue of the magazine The Housewife's Friend (Shufu no tomo). The other two artists contributing designs were Yamakawa Shūhō (1898-1944), "Flower: A Modern Meiji Beauty," (IHL.2103) and Itō Shinsui (1898-1972), "Snow: A Modern Meiji Beauty," (IHL.2104).
Shufu no tomo began publishing in 1918 using the slogan "Once you're married, it's Shufu no tomo." Print runs for the magazine were in the tens of thousands, hitting over 300,000 in some months.
Printed on the top margin is this paean to Kiyokata (as translated by art historian Lynn Katsumoto): "No one but a great artist like Kiyokata could have captured the lyrical mystery of an exceptional beauty, one whose countenance evokes the mysterious luminosity of a misty moonlit night. This work exceeds even the superb artwork that Kiyokata had previously submitted (perhaps the reader knows that the jury awarded it a top prize) to the Imperial Art Exhibition."
Kaburaki Kiyokata, a successful illustrator for newspapers and novels, turned to nihonga (Japanese-style) painting in his early twenties becoming one of its 20th-century luminaries.

media.caption: Woman Combing Her Hair

text.headline: Woman Combing Her Hair
text.text: This collection contains two impressions from the same edition of Tokuriki's portrait of his wife combing her hair.  (See IHL.0098.) This is one of Tokuriki's iconic sōsaku hanga prints. While a number of sources, including the Honolulu Academy of Arts, date the original publication of this print to 1935, Statler dates it to 1947, as do the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston and The British Museum. In commenting on Tokuriki's technique Statler writes "the best of his creative prints, like Woman Combing Her Hair . . ., show a resolute effort to design with the knife. 'I want to break away from the brush,' says Tokuriki," referring to moving away from his Japanese-style painting (nihonga) background. - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn, Oliver Statler, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1956, p. 122.

media.caption: Ukiyo-e World, Volume 5, No. 1 (浮世絵界 第五卷 第一号 Ukiyo-e kai, dai go-kan, dai ichi gō)

text.headline: Ukiyo-e World, Volume 5, No. 1 (浮世絵界 第五卷 第一号 Ukiyo-e kai, dai go-kan, dai ichi gō)
text.text: Sixty-seven issues of the magazine Ukiyo-e kai were published from March 1936 through June 1941. Each issue featured a woodblock printed cover. Initially, the magazine, a successor to the magazine Ukiyo-e geijutsu, both edited by the print scholar Muneshige Narazaki, sometimes featured modern designs, such as the February 1937 issue with a work by the sōsaku hanga artist Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960) as a frontispiece, but subsequent to that issue the focus was on traditional ukiyo-e design, such as this issue's woodblock print cover by the shin hanga artist Yamakawa Shūhō 山川秀峰 (1898-1944), in keeping with the mission of the Society for Ukiyo-e Enthusiasts (ukiyo-e dōkōkai).

media.caption: Idaten (韋駄天)

text.headline: Idaten (韋駄天)
text.text:
In this print Sasajima depicts the Buddhist deity Idaten (the Indian deity Skanda) who is "faster than the wind."
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with Sasajima's original printing of the work, Yoneda has used the technique of "back coloring" 裏彩色 in his reproduction.

media.caption: Guardian of the South (増長天 Zōjōten)

text.headline: Guardian of the South (増長天 Zōjōten)
text.text:
Picturing Zōjōten the Guardian of the South, one of Four Heavenly Kings who protect the four cardinal directions (shintennō), adapted by Japanese Buddhism from Hindu deities. Shintennō exist between the heavenly and the earthly panes in which mankind and bōhisattvas live. Zōjōten's companion guardians are Jikokuten, Guardian of the East who links heaven and earth; Kōmokuten, Guardian of the West; and Tamonten, Guardian of the North.

This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with the original printing by Sasajima, Yoneda has colored this print from the verso, a technique known as "back coloring" 裏彩色.

media.caption: Thunder God (雷神 Raijin)

text.headline: Thunder God (雷神 Raijin)
text.text:
Picturing the Shinto god of thunder Raijin who holds a circle of hand drums over his shoulder to produce thunder. Most often pictured as a pair with Fūjin, the wind god, Raijin and Fūjin are portrayed as oni (demons), though in Buddhism both are attendants of Kanno, the Goddess of Mercy, and neither are inherently good or evil, capable of displaying both characteristics.
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with the original printing by Sasajima, Yoneda, in his reproduction, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance.

media.caption: Empress Dowager Eishō’s Imperial Funeral from the Kyoto Ōmiya Palace to the Imperial Tomb (京都大宮御所ヨリ陵月縄新御陵ヘ御送柩心圖)

text.headline: Empress Dowager Eishō’s Imperial Funeral from the Kyoto Ōmiya Palace to the Imperial Tomb (京都大宮御所ヨリ陵月縄新御陵ヘ御送柩心圖)
text.text:
The Empress Dowager Eishō (consort of Emperor Kōmei, 1831-1867), who was suffering with catarrhal pneumonia, died at on the evening of January 11, 1897 after a visit earlier in the day from Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken. Her funeral was held on February 7. This print published on February 5, two days before the funeral, is an announcement of that event. The illustration was likely created from details provided by the Imperial Household Ministry. The black bordered inscription on the top of the center sheet starts with the words "Imperial Funeral Bulletin" 御大葬彙報.
The funeral arrangements for the Empress Dowager were to be the model for those of Emperor Meiji when he died in 1912. (See IHL.1683, Illustration of the Main Gate at Aoyama During the Imperial Funeral Ceremony, 1912.)

media.caption: The Occupation of the Fortress at Niuzhuang: The Battle of Lieutenant Colonel Imada (牛荘城占領今田中作戰闘之圖 Gyūsōjōsenryō: Imada chūsa sentōno zu)

text.headline: The Occupation of the Fortress at Niuzhuang: The Battle of Lieutenant Colonel Imada (牛荘城占領今田中作戰闘之圖 Gyūsōjōsenryō: Imada chūsa sentōno zu)
text.text: Depicting Japanese troops taking a Chinese battery above the strategic town of Newchwang (Niuzhuang), the battle was fought in brutally cold weather during the first week of March 1895.  Frostbite claimed more casualties than the actual fighting, although before the town was taken by the Japanese they would encounter fierce resistance and house-to-house fighting.  Involved in the fighting for the Japanese were their 3rd and 5th Divisions attacking from different directions.  Japanese losses were 70 killed and 319 wounded, while the Chinese lost over 2,000 men with 635 soldiers taken prisoner.

media.caption: Captain Higuchi, in the Midst of the Attack, Personally Holds a Lost Chinese Child (樋口大尉進撃之途次自抱持清民遺兒之圖 Higuchi taii shingeki no toji mizukara Seishi no ishi o hōji suru no zu)

text.headline: Captain Higuchi, in the Midst of the Attack, Personally Holds a Lost Chinese Child (樋口大尉進撃之途次自抱持清民遺兒之圖 Higuchi taii shingeki no toji mizukara Seishi no ishi o hōji suru no zu)
text.text:
"One of the most celebrated Japanese heroes of the Sino-Japanese War was Captain Higuchi, who reportedly rescued a Chinese infant in a crucial battle near Weihaiwei. As the story was told, Captain Higuchi heard the abandoned child crying on the battlefield, scooped him up in his left arm, and led his forces to victory flourishing his sword with his right arm. After the battle, Higuchi returned the child to his parents." Source: MIT Visualizing Cultures https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/throwing_off_asia_02/visnav_ii_d.html [accessed 8-17-23]
This print was one of a number of Sino-Japanese war prints on display in the "posters" section at the 1895 Nineteenth Triennial Exhibition of the Massachusetts Charitable Mechanic Association. They were contributed by the famous importer and purveyor of Japanese goods Bunkio Matsuki.1 In the report of the judges for foreign and American posters they note, "Your jury further wish to highly recommend the artistic and graphic nature of the Japanese War series of bulletins."2
For other depictions of Captain Higuchi rescue of a Chinese infant see IHL.1343 "Captain Higuchi" by Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) and IHL.2163 "The Attack on Weihaiwei: The Taking of the Hundred Foot Cliff [Captain Higuchi saves a child]" by Watanabe Nobukazu (c.1872-1944).

text.headline: Young Sea Bream from the book Gekkō's Artwork  (かすこ鯛 月耕画圃 kasugo tai Gekkō gaho)
text.text: The last of twelve prints picturing two sea bream appearing in the book titled Gekkō Gaho.

media.caption: December, Ukifune, the Ten Chapters of Uji  (十二月　浮舟, 宇治十帖内 Jūnigatsu, Ukifune, Ujijūjō no uchi)

text.headline: December, Ukifune, the Ten Chapters of Uji  (十二月　浮舟, 宇治十帖内 Jūnigatsu, Ukifune, Ujijūjō no uchi)
text.text:
This print from a series of twelve prints titled Twelve Months of the Floating World, said to be Ogata's first complete series of prints, depicts perhaps the most famous scene from The Tale of Genji. In this scene, from Chapter 51, A Boat Upon the Waters, Prince Niou has carried Ukifune away to a boat on the Uji River and is taking her to the Islet of Oranges, Tachibana-no-kojima. It is a mid-winter eve, the moon is full, and a heavy snow has fallen.
Written in the eleventh century by Murasaki Shikibu, an aristocratic lady of the late Heian court, the Genji monogatari (The Tale of Genji) is considered one of the world's great literary works. It became a source not only for poets but also for artists, who illustrated scenes from the story in many mediums — including books, handscrolls, and screens — from the twelfth century into modern times. The final ten chapters are often distinguished from the rest of the narrative as the "Uji jūjō" (The Ten Chapters at Uji).

media.caption: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum from Heaven)

text.headline: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum from Heaven)
text.text:
This print depicts a scene from the play Tenko, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 188-189.) - A boy name Tenko has a wonderful drum which had come down from Heaven, but when this was taken from him to be presented to the Emperor he drowned himself. An Imperial envoy tells this story and explains that as no one has been able to make any sound come from the drum since it was taken to the Palace, he has been sent to fetch the father of Tenko. Together they go to the Palace, and when the father strikes the drum it gives out such a miraculous sound that he is promised a rich reward and a musical performance is arranged to placate the soul of his son. When this is done, the ghost of Tenko comes and dances before them.

media.caption: Dormitory in Spring Rain (春雨の寮)

text.headline: Dormitory in Spring Rain (春雨の寮)
text.text: From an album of twelve small prints of bijinga by Kaburaki issued in 1914.  This print, one of four woodblock prints in the album, depicts a young maiko, identified by her red collar, walking in the rain. Each of the four woodblock prints in the album is likely an original design by Kiyokata for the album.

media.caption: Deep Blue Sky (靑き星)

text.headline: Deep Blue Sky (靑き星)

Each of the four woodblock prints in the album is likely an original design by Kiyokata for the album.

media.caption: Illustration of Mitsui Group's Western-style Three Story House at Surugachō, Tokyo (東京駿河町三井組 三階家西洋形之圖 東京名所之内駿河町之圖)

text.headline: Illustration of Mitsui Group's Western-style Three Story House at Surugachō, Tokyo (東京駿河町三井組 三階家西洋形之圖 東京名所之内駿河町之圖)

media.caption: Shōjō 猩々(The Tippling Elf)

text.headline: Shōjō 猩々(The Tippling Elf)
text.text:
In this scene Shōjō, an elf-like creature, dances for Kōfū, a Chinese wine dealer, in front of a vat of wine that never empties. A monkey, in myth the elf-like creature, is seen on the left.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 163-164.) - A man named Kō-fū, living in ancient China, explains that by following a dream which he had in reward for his filial piety and which told him to sell wine in the market, he has become a prosperous man. At the market, there is one particular person who always comes to him to buy wine, and since he told the dealer that he is an elf living in the sea, the man has come down to the estuary to wait for him to appear. When he does so, red-faced from his drinking, the man serves him with wine and watches him dance. The elf, in return, gives him a well of wine which never runs dry.

Illustrations of Noh is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints issued between 1897 and 1904. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Nozaki Village (野崎村 Nozakimura)

text.headline: Nozaki Village (野崎村 Nozakimura)
text.text: This print, one of eight collotype prints in the album, depicts a scene from Nozakimura, a frequently staged section of the play Shinpan utazaimon written by Chikamatsu Hanji (1725-1783), et. al. for the puppet theater in 1780 and later staged for kabuki. The play's theme is that of a love triangle involving Osome, the daughter of the owner of an aburaya (oil store); Hisamatsu, an apprentice working in the aburaya, and Omitsu, the daughter of the farmer Kyūsaku living in Nozakimura.

media.caption: Early Summer Rain (五月雨)

text.headline: Early Summer Rain (五月雨)

This print, one of eight collotype prints in the album, all of which are reproductions of paintings by Kiyokata, depicts two women with umbrellas on a stroll through a peaceful rain while a flower seller pulls his cart in the background.

media.caption: Shimadakuzushi (島田くづし)

text.headline: Shimadakuzushi (島田くづし)
text.text: From an album of twelve small prints of bijinga by Kaburaki issued in 1914. This print is one of eight collotype prints in the album, all of which are reproductions of paintings by Kiyokata. The title of this work, Shimadakuzushi, references the bijin's hairstyle.

media.caption: Green Crow and White Boat (緑の鳥と白い船)

text.headline: Green Crow and White Boat (緑の鳥と白い船)
text.text: A loan fishing boat sits on stilts. Black crows wander on the beach in the background, while a green crow (perhaps the angle of the sun or a truly peculiar bird) sits on the boat's bow. Done largely in shades of gray, the print comes alive with Kitaoka's reserved splashes of red, brown, green and yellow.

media.caption: Cape Tachimachi (立待岬 Tachimachi Misaki)

text.headline: Cape Tachimachi (立待岬 Tachimachi Misaki)
text.text: The artist's rendering of Tachimachi Cape in Hakodate, Hokkaido. The cape sits at the southeastern end of Mount Hakodate and overlooks the Tsugaru channel. Late in the eighteenth century the shogunate built a fort there which is now only noted with a marker. It is known for its wildflowers and its views. This print is one of the three different states of this landscape created by the artist.

media.caption: Soga no Gorō Tokimune and Gosho no Gorōmaru (曽我五郎時宗 五所五郎丸)

text.headline: Soga no Gorō Tokimune and Gosho no Gorōmaru (曽我五郎時宗 五所五郎丸)
text.text:
In this print we see Soga no Gorō Tokimune being grabbed by Gosho no Gorōmaru, as Gorō bursts into shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo's room seeking revenge for his brother's death.
Yoshitoshi designed this series of thirty-three prints towards the end of his career when he was about forty-four, just before his most famous series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon was issued. "The [Courageous Warriors] compositions depict famous warriors from Japan’s past with an intensity and detailed care that demonstrate Yoshitoshi’s reverence for the role long played by warriors in the formation of Japan."- source: website of the Brooklyn Museum https://www.brooklynmuseum.org/opencollection/objects/173661 [8-25-23]
Also seen translated as Yoshitoshi's Warriors Trembling with Courage, this series was another extremely popular series designed by Yoshitoshi, as at least five versions of each print in the series were issued. The series was originally published by Kobayashi Tetsujirō 小林銕次郎 (Maruya Tetsujirō 丸屋銕次郎) from December 1883 through October 1886, and was later republished by Tsunajima Kamekichi 綱島亀吉 (Tsujiokaya Kamekichi 辻岡屋亀吉) in 1886.

media.caption: Kurō Hōgan Minamoto Yoshitsune and Notonokami Noritsune (九郎判官源義經 能登守教経經)

text.headline: Kurō Hōgan Minamoto Yoshitsune and Notonokami Noritsune (九郎判官源義經 能登守教経經)
text.text:
In this print we see the great Taira warrior Notonokami Noritsune in his final battle at Yashima. Fending off the arrows of Kurō Hōgan Minamoto Yoshitsune (Japan's foremost tragic hero), he goes to grab his foe only to see Yoshitsune make his legendary leap to another boat and then mock him from a safe distance.
Yoshitoshi designed this thirty-three print series towards the end of his career when he was about forty-four, just before his most famous series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon was issued. media.caption: Hino Kumawakamaru (日野隈若丸)

text.headline: Hino Kumawakamaru (日野隈若丸)
text.text:
In this print we see the the priest Daizenbo and the young Hino Kumawakamaru summoning back a ship to rescue the boy who has just avenged his father's death on Sado Island.
Yoshitoshi designed this series of thirty-three prints towards the end of his career when he was about forty-four, just before his most famous series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon was issued. media.caption: Portrait of Shiga Nayoa  (肖像画　滋賀直哉)

text.headline: Portrait of Shiga Nayoa  (肖像画　滋賀直哉)
text.text:
The fourth state of this print, originally created by Sekino in 1968. Sekino has captured the novelist Shiga Nayoa (1883-1971) from rough sketches, his own photograph and impressions of his meeting with the novelist, who would not agree to sit for his own portrait.
Sekino comments: "One who is famous for disliking to sit for his portrait was the novelist Shiga Naoya. I asked him if I could sketch him, but the request was turned down. I heard that another painter tried to sketch him too, but he apparently ended up fighting with Mr. Shiga. When I visited Mr. Shiga, I was at least allowed to take his photograph; but I am only an amateur photographer, and unfortunately the picture did not turn out well. Later I made his portrait using my rough sketch, photo, and my impression of him."

media.caption: W-396 (Wandering Heart) (漂白 (さすらひ) のハート)

text.headline: W-396 (Wandering Heart) (漂白 (さすらひ) のハート)
text.text: While Kurosaki has written "W - 396", "W" followed by a number (a type of inventory number he gave to almost every print), he has omitted, intentionally or otherwise, the descriptive title "Wandering Heart" appearing on other impressions and listed in his catalog raisonné.

media.caption: Illustration of the Disastrous Flood (大洪水之図)

text.headline: Illustration of the Disastrous Flood (大洪水之図)
text.text:
In September 1896, devastating floods hit the Tokyo area after several weeks of heavy rain. Multiple rivers in the Tokyo area, including the Arakawa, Tone, Tama, Naka, Edogawa and Sumida overflowed their banks causing severe flooding. Water levels rose over 24 feet in some places leading to the collapse of a number of embankments and dams. The flooding, which continued for several weeks, effected a broad area of Tokyo.
As the print's inset in the right sheet explains, the flooding was the worst in fifty years. The embankment of the Nakagawa collapsed and the entire area of Mukojima became a lake that could only be navigated by boat. Officials and police officers rescued people and did what they could to mitigate the disaster.
The scene depicted in this print includes the area around the Mimeguri Shrine along the Sumida River, whose torii is pictured at the top of the center and right sheets of the print.
Only the left and right sheets of this triptych are part of this collection and the left sheet of this collection's print has the information in the publisher's seal blacked out, for an unknown reason, as do other impressions of this print, leaving it only partially readable.

media.caption: Nurse and patient (untitled)

text.headline: Nurse and patient (untitled)
text.text: Likely an illustration appearing in a book or magazine, this photo offset print of a nurse and sleeping patient may have been designed by the Western-style artist Nakamura Tsune 中村彝 (1887-1924). The signature in the bottom left of the print appears to read "T Sune."

media.caption: The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, memorial print

text.headline: The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, memorial print
text.text: This memorial print (shini-e) issued upon the death of the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII on August 8, 1854 by an unknown artist shows the actor in a death robe (kamishimo) holding a scroll on which he has, perhaps, written his death poem.  A lacquer box with pen and ink stone lie before him. The bold script in the center column of theater signboard in the upper right of the print shows us the name 市川白猿 (Ichikawa Hakuen), another stage name for Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII.  As with many shini-e, neither the artist's signature or seal or the publisher's mark are present. In addition, government censor seals were not required on memorial prints.

media.caption: The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, memorial print

text.headline: The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, memorial print
text.text: This memorial print (shini-e) issued upon the death of the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII on August 8, 1854 shows the actor in a death robe (kamishimo) holding Buddhist prayer beads in his right hand and a sprig of Japanese anise (shikimi) in his left.  As with many shini-e neither the artist's signature or seal or the publisher's mark are present.  In addition, government censor seals were not required on memorial prints. Danjūrō VIII, whose career was cut short by his suicide in Osaka, was given the posthumous Buddhist name (hōmyō) Enhaku-in Jõsei Nichida Shinji 猿白院成清日田信士, as inscribed on the print.

media.caption: Two headed palanquin bearer fighting off samurai, untitled frontispiece illustration from an unidentified book or magazine

text.headline: Two headed palanquin bearer fighting off samurai, untitled frontispiece illustration from an unidentified book or magazine
text.text: Trained as a nanga-style artist, Suzuki Kinsen is best known for his work as a designer of woodblock printed illustrations (kuchi-e) for novels and magazines. In this frontispiece for an unknown magazine or book, a two-headed palenquin bearer prepares to fight off multiple attackers.

media.caption: Sesshū Watanabe bashi kuyō (摂州渡辺橋供養)

text.headline: Sesshū Watanabe bashi kuyō (摂州渡辺橋供養)
text.text:
The right sheet of a triptych depicting the actors, from right to left, Arashi Rikitsumaru I 嵐璃橘丸 as Kumawakamaru くま若丸 and Fujikawa Tomokichi III 三代 藤川友吉 as as Hondatsuma Shizuhata 本田妻賤機 in Sesshū Watanabe bashi kuyō, playing at the Kado no Shibai ("corner theater") located on the Dōtonbori canal in Osaka.
Written in 1748 for the Osaka bunraku (puppet theater) by Toyotake Chikujennō Shozō (1700-1783) and Asada Itchō (?-c. 1763), the plot falls within the genre called Mongaku Shōnin mono based on selected tales from the Heike monogatari (Tale of the Heike), involving the epic struggle between the Minamoto (Genji) and Taira (Heike) clans for control of Japan at the end of the 12th century, and the Genpei seisuiki (History of the Rise and Fall of the Genji and Heike) covering the Genpei wars (1160-1185). - Source: website of Osaka Prints http://www.osakaprints.com/content/artists/info_pp/yoshitaki_info/yoshitaki_19.htm [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Monkey Bridge (猿橋 Saruhashi)

text.headline: Monkey Bridge (猿橋 Saruhashi)
text.text:
Depicting Monkey Bridge (saruhashi), this print, as marked in the lower left margin, is number 2 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
Saruhashi is one of "Japan's Three Odd Bridges." It is 33 meters high, 3.3 meters wide and 31 meters long. The bridge is built over a narrow ravine, with four stacked haneki, or cantilevered members, embedded to the rock wall of both banks. The structural support is similar to architectural roofing. The construction year is unknown, but there are records of this bridge style existing in 1676. The oldest estimation is that it was completed over 500 years ago. The bridge was restored in 1984.

media.caption: Yokosuka Shipyard (横須賀造船所 Yokosuka zōsenjo)

text.headline: Yokosuka Shipyard (横須賀造船所 Yokosuka zōsenjo)
text.text:
Depicting the shipyards at Yokosuka on Tokyo Bay, this print, as marked in the lower left margin, is number 13 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
The Yokosuka shipyards were located at Yokosuka, Kanagawa prefecture on Tokyo Bay, south of Yokohama. In 1866, the Tokugawa shogunate government established the Yokosuka Seisakusho, a military arsenal and naval base, with the help of foreign engineers, including the French naval architect Léonce Verny. The new facility was intended to produce modern, western-style warships and equipment for the Tokugawa navy. The construction of the arsenal was an important first step for the modernization of Japan's industry. Modern buildings, an aqueduct, foundry, brick factories, technical schools to train Japanese technicians were established.
After the Boshin War and the Meiji Restoration, the new Meiji government took over control of the facility in 1871, renaming it the Yokosuka Zōsenjo (Yokosuka Shipyards). The first dry dock was opened in 1871, and is still in operation today. Japan's first domestically produced warship, Saiki, was completed the same year.
The Yokosuka Naval District was established at Yokosuka, Kanagawa in 1884, as the first of the naval districts responsible for the defense of the Japanese home islands, and the Yokosuka Shipyards was renamed the Yokosuka Naval Arsenal in 1903.

media.caption: Narita-san Shinshōji Temple (成田山新勝寺)

text.headline: Narita-san Shinshōji Temple (成田山新勝寺)
text.text:
Depicting the Niomon Gate entrance to Narita-san Shinshōji Temple in Narita, outside of Tokyo. This print, as marked in the lower left margin, is number 16 of 28 prints in the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
"Naritasan is a time-honored temple with a history of over 1000 years since its foundation. On the temple grounds, there are five buildings designated as important cultural properties. Komyodo, the oldest building among them, was built in 1701, when Naritasan became popular along with Kabuki and one of the temples representative of the Japanese style. The next oldest building is a three-story pagoda, which was built in 1712, and in 1830, a Deva gate was constructed. An elaborately carved Shakado (a hall where a statue of Shakyamuni is enshrined) was built in 1858 and Gakudo, which houses a number of votive picture tablets dedicated by celebrities of the Edo period, was completed in 1861, when Sakamoto Ryoma played a key role as a leader of the movement to overthrow the Tokugawa Shogunate. Thanks to carpenters specialized in temples and shrines in the Edo period, these buildings, some of which are over 300 years old, still exist and are appreciated by visitors. We hope you come and appreciate the temple history of over 1000 years and fully enjoy the atmosphere reminiscent of the Edo period on the vast grounds of Naritasan. - Source: website of Naritasan Shinshoji Temple http://www.naritasan.or.jp/english/about.html

media.caption: Inner Valley at Tsukigase (月ヶ瀬奥の谷 Tsukigase Okunotani)

text.headline: Inner Valley at Tsukigase (月ヶ瀬奥の谷 Tsukigase Okunotani)
text.text:
Number 19 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.
"This print depicts one of the most remote places featured in the series and a location that Kiyochika may have been unable to visit in person.
"This location is a secluded mountain valley whose fame for scenic beauty was relatively recent. . . . The plum trees at Tsukigase were made famous in Travels in Plum Valley (Baikei yuki) of 1830 by the Confucian scholar Saito Setsudo.
"The vast plum orchard that Kiyochika shows in Inner Valley at Tsukigase is located along both banks of the Naban River, the name for the Kizu River in its upper reaches in the mountains of the Kii Peninsula. Tsukigase (known locally as Tsukinose) is about ten miles due east of Nara along a stretch of the river running from east to west. Some ten thousand plum trees line both sides of the V-shaped valley for over two miles. The trees were planted in the precincts of a nearby temple in the late thirteenth century, and later propagated in great numbers as the source of a dye extracted from the plum fruits.
"The sight of the thousands of plum trees blooming in February and March is spectacular, and the white blossoms fill the valley with a heady fragrance, noted in the haiku concluding the text:
Spring in Tsukigase:
Bush warblers
Drunk with fragrance.

"Kiyochika’s print is remarkable for the coloring-or rather the absence of it. It is rendered almost completely in black sumi ink, which serves to heighten the sense of the whiteness of the blossoms; only the rushing waters of the Nabari River are shown in color, as streaks of subtle blue." - Source: Kiyochika Artist of Meiji Japan, Henry D. Smith II, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, 1988, p. 108-109.
See IHL.0340 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Willow Tree Along Misogi River (御祓川渕の柳 Misogi-gawa fuchi no yanagi)

text.headline: Willow Tree Along Misogi River (御祓川渕の柳 Misogi-gawa fuchi no yanagi)
text.text:
The large old willow near the bridge over the Misogi river in the city of Nanao, on the Noto peninsula.
Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) artist and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own landscapes such as this print and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

media.caption: Deer and bat 鹿蝙蝠 (untitled)

text.headline: Deer and bat 鹿蝙蝠 (untitled)
text.text: A woodblock print, reproducing two 19th century ink paintings of a deer and a bat, both asupicious animals. The painting of a bat was done by the Edo period nanga artist Chikoku who studied under the literati painter Tani Bunchō 谷 文晁 (1763-1841) and the painting of the deer was done by the obscure nanga painter Bunshin. The story is told that Chikoku was expelled from Bunchō's school for impersonating the artist.

media.caption: Mountain hut

text.headline: Mountain hut
text.text: Although well-known in his day, no information appears to be available on the life of Kyoto artist Ki Chikudō a nanga (literati) artist. This woodblock print is likely a later, c. 1900, woodblock reproduction of the original print that appeared in volume 2 of Chikudō Picture Album containing twenty-two prints of works by the artist.

media.caption: Battle on the Roof from the Tale of the Eight Dog Warriors, to assemble  (八犬傳芳流閣組上 Hakkenden Hōryūkaku kumiage)

text.headline: Battle on the Roof from the Tale of the Eight Dog Warriors, to assemble  (八犬傳芳流閣組上 Hakkenden Hōryūkaku kumiage)
text.text: Possibly the most famous scene from the novel The Eight Dog Warriors. Written by Kyokutei Bakin 曲亭馬琴 (1767-1848), it was published in 96 volumes between 1814 and 1842. The story recounts how its protagonists strive to restore the fictional Satomi clan to power. This collection's print is the second sheet of a toy print depicting the famous fight scene on the roof of the Horyukaku in Koga Castle, between the samurai Inuzuka Shino 犬飼信乃 and Inukai Genpachi 犬飼現八. The print was designed to be cut out and assembled, if desired, by the owner. A finished picture 出来上り圖 of the assembled scene is shown in the upper left of the print.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Fancy-Free Type, from the series Ten Physiognomic Types of Women  (複製：婦人相學十躰・浮気之相 Fujin sōgaku juttai・Uwaki no sō)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Fancy-Free Type, from the series Ten Physiognomic Types of Women  (複製：婦人相學十躰・浮気之相 Fujin sōgaku juttai・Uwaki no sō)
text.text:
A modern reproduction by Adachi Hanga, which specializes in fine reproductions of ukiyo-e masterworks, of a 1792-1793 print by Kitagawa Utamaro, protraying the fancy-free type from the series Ten Physiognomic Types of Women.
"The idea of the project was apparently that Utamaro observed women's faces, and produced ten depictions as explanations of the different types. A beautiful woman in yukata (summer kimono) just after a bath is turning her head and drying her hands with the towel hung on her shoulder. Her just-washed hair is tied around an ornate hairpin, the hair style called bai-mage (spiral-shell chignon)." - Source: Translated comments by the Tokyo National Museum

media.caption: Reproduction of: Ichikawa Monnosuke II as Osome (複製：二代目 市川門之助のお染)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Ichikawa Monnosuke II as Osome (複製：二代目 市川門之助のお染)
text.text: A modern reproduction of a 1789 "large-head" (ōkubi-e) print of the actor Ichikawa Monnosuke II in the role of Osome, possibly in the play Osome and Hisamatsu by Katsukawa Shunkō 勝川 春好 (1743-1812). The artist is credited with designing the first ōkubi-e actor protraits.

media.caption: Two Travelers (untitled)

text.headline: Two Travelers (untitled)
text.text: A drawing, ink on paper. Possibly a hanshita for a print. Signed "Sōri ga," the artist may be Hishikawa Sōri III 三代目 菱川宗理 (active c. 1798-1840), an early student of Hokusai whose work closely resembles that of his teacher who used to artist name Sōri II for a period. Sōri III produced designs for commercially printed woodblock prints, surimono, book illustrations and calendars.

media.caption: Soap Bubbles

text.headline: Soap Bubbles

media.caption: Big Octopus

text.headline: Big Octopus
text.text: A drawing picturing a big octopus turning the tables on a fishmonger, perhaps to exact revenge. After a 1788 toba-e titled "Big Octopus" by Takehara Shunshōsa i竹原春朝斎 (active 1772-1801)

media.caption: Meiji Shrine (明治神宮 Meiji jingū)

text.headline: Meiji Shrine (明治神宮 Meiji jingū)
text.text:
Yamaguchi pictures the torii at the entrance to the Meiji Shrine, a Shinto shrine in Shibuya, Tokyo, that is dedicated to the deified spirits of Emperor Meiji and his wife, Empress Shōken. It is identified by Laurence Smith as one of the six prints in this series depicting "places with serious imperial resonances."
For another impression of this print see IHL.0121.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: Nakayama-dera - temple 24 (中山寺 二十四)

text.headline: Nakayama-dera - temple 24 (中山寺 二十四)
text.text:
Nakazawa depicts a line of Jizō bodhisattvas, protector of children, within the Nakayama-dera grounds, with small offerings on the ledge beneath them. The temple is the 24th along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage route encompassing 33 Buddhist temples in Western Japan (Kansai region) dedicated to Kannon (bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara), the Bodhisattva of Compassion, who hears the cries of the world and assists anyone in distress.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1946 second edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.2243 and IHL.2413.32 for the first edition published in 1925 of the same print.

text.headline: Kami Daigōji - temple 11 (上醍醐寺 十一)
text.text:
Kami Daigō-ji, a complex of some of the oldest temple buildings in Japan, is the upper precinct of Daigō-ji and is the 11th temple on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. Off to the right we see a bluish stone marker leading the way to Iwama-dera 岩間寺, the 12th temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage.

media.caption: Onshi no musume (恩師の娘)

text.headline: Onshi no musume (恩師の娘)
text.text:
Having just read the card on the table, she clutches her handkerchief in this illustration for a story titled "Onshi no musume" (My Teacher's Daughter), as printed in red kanji charachters below the artist's signature and seal. This offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) displays the characteristic tri-fold resulting from its insertion into a popular culture magazine (taishū zasshi).
Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

text.headline: Bijin adjusting her hair (untitled)
text.text:
The artist Terashima Shimei was a Japanese-style (nihonga) painter who studied under the famous Kyoto nihonga artist Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972). He was considered one of Kiyokata's best disciples and had an important influence on the bijin-ga genre. Terashima designed a small number of woodblock prints, all in the bijin genre, along with designing illustrations of bijin serving as frontispieces for the popular magazines of the time.

text.text:

It is not known if this illustration was created for Tsubouchi Shōyō's 坪內逍遙 (1859-1935) 1914 reworking of this 17th-century story by Ihara Saikaku 井原西鶴 (1642-1693) for the kabuki stage or for a Taishō era serialized version of the original story.
While the artist Oda Tomiya turned to painting in his later life, he is best remembered for his illustrations, both in color and black and white, for popular novels during the Taishō era.

text.text:
This offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) with its characteristic tri-fold, resulting from its insertion into a popular culture magazine (taishū zasshi), served as an illustration for the story "Life's Fallen Leaves" appearing in an unknown magazine.

media.caption: Fūzoku gahō, Issue 359 (風俗画報・参百五十九號)

text.headline: Fūzoku gahō, Issue 359 (風俗画報・参百五十九號)
text.text:
The cover illustration, titled Gentle Spring Rain 春雨, for this March 1907 issue of the magazine Fūzoku gahō (Illustrated Customs), was designed by Kūrosaki Shusai 黒崎修齋 (1877-?), a painter and illustrator who was a frequent contributor to the magazine. The two other artists contributing color illustrations to this issue were Yamamoto Shōun 山本松谷 (1870-1955) whose color lithograph double-page frontispiece, titled "Ashio Copper Mine Miners' Violence" 足尾銅山坑夫の暴擧, depicts the miners' attack on mine officials while buildings burn and Sakamaki Kōgyo 坂巻耕漁 (1869-1927), better known as Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁, whose print depicts a scene in the Noh play Utaura (Poem Divination).

Fūzoku gahō was a Meiji-early Taishō period illustrated magazine, published from 1889-1916 covering a variety of topics related to folk customs. The magazine described itself as relating "customs of the nation-state, both old and new." - Source: Splendid Monarchy: Power and Pageantry in Modern Japan, Takashi Fujitani, University of California Press, 1996, p. 184.
And, from the Tuesday, July 17, 1900 issue of the Paris, Kentucky "The Bourbon News," the article "A Japanese Magazine," relates the following:
"The Fuzoku Gaho is profusely illustrated in various ways - double-paged pictures confined to single subjects, or made up of many sketches, as we find them in weekly numbers of the Graphic etc. This system is most frequently resorted to where several classes of the community are engaged in the same occupation or when the old and new version of existing things are set off against each other by way of contrast. Single-paged pictures in black and white or colors, and also small sketches interspersed in the text are comprised within the covers of this monthly. The Fuzoku Gaho embraces a variety of subjects of historic worth and present interest - ancient manners and customs that are rapidly disappearing, such as the secret forging of swords, the cutting of stone implements, the celebration of old established festivals, down to the latest incidents in Corea and Formosa, thus insuring many readers by the wide range of subjects it embraces. Occasionally, advertisements of English goods appear in a cloud of Chinese ideographs, for instance the figure of an English watch printed on colored paper to arrest attention and Japanese articles of manufacture are recommended in the same European method."

text.headline: Spring - Toshogu Shrine at Ueno (春・上野東照宮)
text.text: The cherry trees are in spring bloom as visitors of all ages enter Toshogu Shrine, passing under the tori and walking along a path flanked by 256 stone-and-bronze lanterns. Built in remembrance of Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1627, it is the historical pride of Ueno Park.

Autumn - The Night-Scene of Sukiya Bridge
(秋・数寄屋橋夜景)

text.headline:
Autumn - The Night-Scene of Sukiya Bridge
(秋・数寄屋橋夜景)
text.text: Autumn in Tokyo and the moon shines over Sukiyabashi, originally built in 1629 to cross the outer moat of Edo Castle. Re-constructed as a double-arched stone bridge in 1929, it quickly became a popular tourist attraction, surviving until 1958, when the moat was filled in for the construction of a highway through the heart of Tokyo.

media.caption: Yoroboshi (弱法師)

text.headline: Yoroboshi (弱法師)
text.text:
In this print for the month of February, the young man Shuntokumaru arrives at Tennoji Temple in the Noh play "Yoroboshi." Years of living in depravity has left him sick and blinded and he comes to the temple in search of alms and salvation.

The Play - Yoroboshi (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 217-218.)
"Believing some gossip he heard about his son Shuntoku, Michitoshi turned him out of his house. Deeply regretting his cruelty now, he goes on a pilgrimage to the Tennō-ji temple and there sees his son again - but he has become a beggar and having lost his sight as well, is known as 'the priest with the faltering tread.' He sings a song about the temple and then, when the other people go and leave the two of them alone, Michitoshi tells his son who he is and, full of happiness at having found him again, takes him by the arm to lead him home."
Twelve Months of Noh Pictures
From a series of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1970. Six of the prints (for the months of January, February, June, September, November and December) were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963) and the other six (for the months of March, April, May, July, August and October) were created by his son Matsuno Hideyo (1936-2002). As Sōfū died in 1963, his prints must have been created from existing designs.
As originally issued, the prints were sold as a set with each print placed inside its own mat, which was overlaid with a commentary sheet on the play in Japanese and English. The matted print and commentary were then placed inside an envelope and all twelve envelopes were then placed into a cloth folio.
Interestingly, the artist seals appearing on the prints, each one being different, relate to the play being pictured, such as in the square red seal on this print whose characters, according to the commentary sheet accompanying the print, read "The Whole View of Green Hills in the Mind's Eye."

text.headline: Hanagatami, katami-no-den (花筐 筐之伝)
text.text:
In this print for the month of November, the Lady Teruhi kneels by the flower basket given to her by the emperor in the Noh play Hanagatami by the playwright Zeami.
The Play - Hanagatami (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 49-50.)
"The Crown Prince Ōatobe having suddenly left his country retreat to go to the capital to succeed his father, a servant gives Teruhi-no-mai, the lady who has been the Prince's constant companion, a letter and a flower basket which he has left for her. Some time later Ōatobe, now the Emperor Keitei, is viewing the maples in autumn when a mad woman comes along carrying a flower basket. This is Teruhi who, distracted by her love for the Prince, has come to try to see him. Happy now that she has met him again, Teruhi is once more taken into the Emperor's favour and returns with him to the capital."

text.headline: Miidera, sasa-no-den (三井寺 笹之伝)
text.text:
In the play Miidera, for the month of September, a mother finds herself by the famed belfry of the Mii Temple during the harvest moon festival. Though the belfry is closed to female visitors, she strikes the bell, crazed with grief and searching for her lost son.

The Play - Miidera (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 108.)
"A mother whose child has disappeared makes a long pilgrimage to the Kyōmizu-dera in Kyoto and asks the goddess Kannon to help her find him again. She has a dream which is interpreted by a fortune-teller to mean that she must go to the temple called Mii-dera to meet her son again. Arriving there on the night of the full moon quite unbalanced through anxiety and grief, she rings the temple bell. The priests of the temple, who are looking after her son Semmitsu and have been viewing the moon with him, come up to reproach her. But as they talk, it is found that she is the boy's mother and the two are happily reunited."

text.headline: Kakitsubata, koi-no-mai (杜若 恋の舞)
text.text:
In the play Kakitsubata, for the month of June, the main character, the spirit of the iris flower, kneels and unfolds her fan after completing her dance and observes that the unfolded fan is like the unfurled hear of enlightenment.
The Play - Kakitsubata (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 66-67.)
"In the early Japanese work called the Ise Monogatari is a story telling how Ariwara no Narihara stopped at Yatsuhashi while on his way to the eastern provinces and, being stuck by the beauty of the irises blooming there, composed an anagrammatic poem by beginning each of the five lines with one of the syllables in the name of the flower, kakitsubata. In the play a wandering priest comes to Yatsuhashi and lodges in the house of a woman living there. When she appears in a magnificent robe he asks who she is. She replies that she is the spirit of the irises, immortalized by Narihira's poem, and after telling him the story, dances for him."

media.caption: Dōjōji, akagashira (道成寺 赤頭)

text.headline: Dōjōji, akagashira (道成寺 赤頭)
text.text:
In this print for the month of April, a young woman dances to insinuate herself into the Dōjōji temple. She will shortly undergo a transition to a serpent.
The Play - Dōjōji (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 21-22.)
"On the day of a ceremony held in the Dōjō-ji temple to celebrate the installation of a new bell, a woman dancer comes there. Although women are forbidden to enter the compound, she persuades a servant to let her in by saying that she wants to perform a dance in honour of the occasion. She dances and then seizes the opportunity to move beneath the bell and pull it down on top of her. The noise of the falling bell throws the servants into great alarm, and when the priests are told what has happened, one of the realises who the woman is. When a young yamabushi priest went on his yearly pilgrimage to Kumano, he explains, he used to stay in the house of an old man who lived with his daughter. In joke, the old man told her that the priest was to be her husband, and the girl grew up believing this. When, eventually, the priest refused her, she followed him to the Dōjō-ji where he had been hidden under the bell. Having changed into a serpent on the way to cross a river in her pursuit, she coiled herself round the bell and took her revenge on the priest by reducing it to a flaming, molten mass. Convinced that it is this woman who has returned, the priests approach the bell rubbing their rosaries and murmuring prayers. The bell is lifted and reveals the serpent, but this time the priests drive it away into the river by means of their holy power."

text.headline: Matsukaze, tawamure-no-mai (松風 戯之舞)
text.text:
In this print for the month of July, Matsukaze journeys home with the moon’s reflection. She has just filled her pail with sea water and loaded in her cart as can be partially seen at the lower left.
The Play - Matsukaze (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 101-102.)
"A traveling priest comes to Suma Bay and prays for the souls of the two fishergirls Matsukaze and Murasame who were loved by the poet Yukihira when he was exiled there long ago. At dusk he begs shelter from two girls who appear, carrying brine to fill the salt-pans. They weep when he quotes a poem by Yukihira and tells them of his prayers, and when he questions them, reveal that they are the spirits of Matsukaze and Murasame. After they tell him of their happiness with Yukihira, Matsukaze, who is particularly affected by the memory, puts on the poet's cap and robe and dances. Morning comes, the priest awakes, and nothing is to be heard but the murmur of the wind in the pine trees."

media.caption: Sōshi Arai Komachi, saishiki (草子洗小町 彩色)

text.headline: Sōshi Arai Komachi, saishiki (草子洗小町 彩色)
text.text:
In this print for the month of May, the poetess Ono no Komachi reads her poem at a poetry contest for the emperor in the Noh play "Sōshi Arai Komachi."
The Play - Sōshi Arai Komachi (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 170-171.)
"At a poetry competition in the presence of the Emperor, Ōtomo no Kuronushi's opponent is to be the poetess Ono no Komachi. Fearing that he will be defeated, Kuronushi plans to avoid this and to discomfit his rival at the same time. He and his servant manage to overhear the poem Komachi has written for the competition, and this he writes into a leaf from a copy of the Manyōshū anthology. When the poetess later recites this in the contest, he challenges it on that grounds that it is an old poem and produces the copy of the Manyōshū as proof. Komachi is overcome with humiliation at this, but with the help of Ki no Tsurayuki she obtains the permission of the Emperor to test the leaf in question by rinsing it with water. When she does so, the freshly written poem is washed away. Having had his trickery thus exposed, Kuronushi feels that the only course left for him is suicide, but the persuasion and forgiveness of Komachi and an order from the Emperor bring him back. To dispel any lingering awkwardness, Komachi entertains the company by performing a dance in honour of the Emperor and his reign."
Twelve Months of Noh Pictures
From a series of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1970. Six of the prints (for the months of January, February, June, September, November and December) were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963) and the other six (for the months of March, April, May, July, August and October) were created by his son Matsuno Hideyo (1936-2002). As Sōfū died in 1963, his prints must have been created from existing designs.
As originally issued, the prints were sold as a set with each print placed inside its own mat, which was overlaid with a commentary sheet on the play in Japanese and English. The matted print and commentary were then placed inside an envelope and all twelve envelopes were then placed into a cloth folio.
Interestingly, the artist seals appearing on the prints, each one being different, relate to the play being pictured, such as in the square red seal on this print whose characters, according to the commentary sheet accompanying the print, read "The Waterside Grass," a reference to the poem written by the poetess Ono no Komachi that she was maliciously accused of plagiarizing.

media.caption: Hanjo, sasa noden (班女笹之伝)

text.headline: Hanjo, sasa noden (班女笹之伝)
text.text:
In this print for the month of August, we see the forlorn Hanago searching for her lost love Yoshida no Shōshō in the Noh play "Hanjo."
The Play - Hanjo (Scripps College Ruth Chandler Williamson Gallery website http://web-kiosk.scrippscollege.edu/Obj20860)
"In this play, two lovers are forced to part. They exchange fans, representing the promise of their future reunion. Hanago soon becomes heart-stricken and can do nothing more but look longingly at the fan that her lover has left behind. Thus she is nicknamed Hanjo, a name taken from the Chinese story about Han Shoyo. According to the Chinese story, when Han Shoyo was replaced by another woman as the emperor’s favorite, she wrote a poem comparing herself to a fan: once treasured during summer, the fan is quickly abandoned in autumn. This print depicts Hanjo’s lonely, passionate, and even obsessive search for her lost love. At the end of the play, Hanjo’s lover identifies her by the fan that she has placed inside her robe and over her heart. They are once again united."

media.caption: Portrait of Yoshida Shōin, sensei (吉田松陰 先生之像)

text.headline: Portrait of Yoshida Shōin, sensei (吉田松陰 先生之像)
text.text:
In this woodblock print titled "Portrait of Yoshida Shōin," Okuyama has copied a well-known photo of Yoshida Shōin (1830-1859), a samurai from the Chōshū domain who was executed in 1859 for the attempted assassination of Ii Naosuke, the shogunate Tairō (prime minister). Yoshida had a profound impact on a number of key figures in the Meiji Restoration, including Hirobumi Ito and Aritomo Yamagata.
Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) maker and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own woodblock prints, such as IHL.1844, and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.
When this print was produced in 1943, Okuyama was one of many print artists who had joined the wartime nationalist print organization Nihon Hanga Hōkōkai. This portrait of Yoshida Shōin (1830-1850), whose Tokugawa-era writings were used as justification by nationalist supporters of Japan's military and colonization of Asia was created to bolster Japan's war effort.
For another impression of this print see IHL.2187.

media.caption: Woman with parasol from the magazine The Ladies' Graphic, Vol. 3, No. 5 (婦人グラフ 第3巻 第5号 Fujin gurafu dai3shū dai5gō)

text.headline: Woman with parasol from the magazine The Ladies' Graphic, Vol. 3, No. 5 (婦人グラフ 第3巻 第5号 Fujin gurafu dai3shū dai5gō)
text.text: An illustration appearing in the May 1926 issue of The Ladies' Graphic (婦人グラフ Fujin gurafu), a magazine targeted to women covering "international news, matters relating to the lifestyle of the 'contemporary' woman as well as information about cuisine and current styles in clothing, hair and makeup," which began publishing in May 1924 and ceased publishing in 1928.  A big selling point for the magazine were tipped-in color woodblock  illustrations by leading artists, the most prominent of whom was  ‎Takehisa Yumeji (1884-1934)‎.

media.caption: Imperial Palace and Mount Fuji (宮城と富士)

text.headline: Imperial Palace and Mount Fuji (宮城と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print we see the Imperial Palace grounds in the foreground (with the palace's outer moat in the immediate foreground), the National Diet Building, which would have been under construction at the time behind the palace grounds on the left and a very white Mount Fuji standing as a beacon in the background. Cars and people dot the scene and hazy clouds, reddened by the setting sun, streak the sky.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: Yashima 八島

text.headline: Yashima 八島
text.text:
Play synopsis (the-NOH.com http://www.noh-kyogen.com/story/english/Yashima.pdf [not accessible 8-17-23]) - Several priests come to Yashima Bay, the sight of a famous Genpei battle in which the Minamoto, led by general Yoshitsune, routed the Taira. Two fishermen appear and tell the priests in detail of that battle. When asked their names, the fishermen promise to return in the priest’s dream. Later the ghost of Yoshitsune appears and tells of the battle, in particular how he retrieved his dropped bow from among the enemy ships. He mimes the battles between asuras in warrior hell, and then disappears.
This collection's print is unusual in that it is in its original state after printing. It has not been bound into book form, as were most of the prints from this series, nor trimmed in any fashion. The title 八島 and number of the print 二七 (27), which would normally have been trimmed off, appear in the right hand margin.

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: The Fushimi Earthquake Night Chat (伏見街地震夜話 Fushimichō Jishin no Yobanashi)

text.headline: The Fushimi Earthquake Night Chat (伏見街地震夜話 Fushimichō Jishin no Yobanashi)
text.text: A scene from the play Fushimichō Jishin no Yobanashi by Takeshiba Kinsaku (Kawatake Shinshichi III, 1842-1901). Fires burn in the night in the aftermath of the 1596 Fushimi Earthquake that destroyed Toyotomi Hideyoshi's (1536-1598) Fushimi Castle and much of the surrounding area. Hideyoshi, played by Nakamura Jusaburō III (1839-1896), is seen seated in the right panel.

media.caption: Kusu no tsuyu 楠露 (Camphor Tree in Dew)

text.headline: Kusu no tsuyu 楠露 (Camphor Tree in Dew)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Kusu no tsuyu in which Masashige, fearing his imminent death, has his retainer read his last words of advice to his son, Masatsura. For two other impressions of this print see IHL.1149 and IHL.1923.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 95-96.) - Feeling that he will die in the coming battle with Ashikaga Takauji, Masashige calls his son Masatsura to him in the town of Sakurai and gives him his last words of advice. At the farewell party Onchi Mitsukazu dances to entertain them. Masashige then sends his faithful retainer away with his son to take him back to their home, while he himself prepares for battle.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Sakahoko 逆矛 or 逆鉾 (The Spear of the Gods)

text.headline: Sakahoko 逆矛 or 逆鉾 (The Spear of the Gods)
text.text:
Depicting the god Matsuri-no-Kami holding the sacred spear of Izanagi and Izanami, the heavenly creators of Japan in a scene from the play Sakahoko attributed to the playwright Miyamasu (1482-1556).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 148-149 and http://www.noh-kyogen.com/story/english/Sanemori.pdf [no access 8-17-23]) - A Court official on his way to the shrine of Tatsuta Myōjin falls in with an old man who guides him to the hill on which the shrine stands. When asked, he tells the official that here is enshrined the sacred spear which was carried by the gods Izanai and Izanami when they descended from Heaven and created the islands of Japan. He adds that he himself is Taki-matsuri no Kami, the protective god of the shrine, and then disappears. That night, while the official is resting, a goddess comes to the place and dances, and then the god himself appears, carrying the spear. He tells of its marvels and rejoices at the peace enjoyed under the present reign.

media.caption: Tropical Fish

text.headline: Tropical Fish
text.text: A small print depicting a semi-abstract tropical fish similar to Hagiwara's 1957 much larger print of a tropical fish, titled Tropical Fish 熱帯魚.

media.caption: Tokyo, Konishiki Yasokichi (東京 小錦八十吉)

text.headline: Tokyo, Konishiki Yasokichi (東京 小錦八十吉)
text.text:
Yasokichi I 小錦八十吉 (1866-1914) was a sumo wrestler from Musha District, Kazusa Province. Konishiki made his professional debut in May 1883 and reached the top makuuchi division in May 1888. He won 39 bouts in a row after his makuuchi debut. Konishiki was promoted to ōzeki in May 1890, and awarded a yokozuna licence by the house of Yoshida Tsukasa in March 1896. He was the sport's 17th yokozuna.
As we see in this print an impressive part of sumō-e are their depictions of the kesho-mawashi (ceremonial brocaded aprons) worn by wrestlers. These aprons, originally bestowed by daimyō upon the professional wrestlers they retained as a "badge of accomplishment," became increasingly splendid in appearance as daimyō competed with each other in this display of ornamental finery used in classical sumō ritual in the ring.

media.caption: Iyo, Asashio Tarō (伊豫 朝汐太郎)

text.headline: Iyo, Asashio Tarō (伊豫 朝汐太郎)
text.text:
Asashio Tarō I (November 28, 1864 – August 26, 1920) was a sumō wrestler from Ehime Prefecture (formerly Iyo Province). He wrestled professionally from 1890 until his retirement in January 1908. The highest rank he obtained was ōzeki.
As we see in this print an impressive part of sumō-e are their depictions of the kesho-mawashi (ceremonial brocaded aprons) worn by wrestlers. These aprons, originally bestowed by daimyō upon the professional wrestlers they retained as a "badge of accomplishment," became increasingly splendid in appearance as daimyō competed with each other in this display of ornamental finery used in classical sumō ritual in the ring.

media.caption: Aconitum japonicum (やまとりかぶと[山鳥兜] )

text.headline: Aconitum japonicum (やまとりかぶと[山鳥兜] )
text.text:
Hisui Sugiura (1876-1965), one of Japan’s most gifted graphic designers, was heavily influenced by Art Nouveau and Art Deco. He is best remembered as the artistic brain behind the Mitsukoshi Department Store. He started work at the luxury goods purveyor in 1908. After two years, he became the first head of the design department. His career at Mitsukoshi spanned 27 years.
"Hisui's Album of One Hundred Flowers," originally issued in 20 volumes by the publisher Shun'yōdō from 1920 to 1922 was republished multiple times after the destruction of the original woodblocks during the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. In subsequent printings, from newly carved blocks from Hisui's original drawings, the number of volumes and the way the prints were arranged were sometimes changed. The second edition of the Album was issued by Shun'yōdō between June 1929 and January 1934. As originally packaged, each print was accompanied by a "projection sketch" (silhouette), a photograph of the actual flower taken by Hisui himself, and a botanical commentary.
This second edition print, originally print number 82, in volume 17 of the first edition, is a rendering of Japanese Monkshood (Aconitum japonicum), a deciduous perennial with dark blue flowers and rounded, deeply lobed, dark green leaves.

media.caption: Allium fistulosum (葱)

text.headline: Allium fistulosum (葱)
text.text:
Hisui Sugiura (1876-1965), one of Japan’s most gifted graphic designers, was heavily influenced by Art Nouveau and Art Deco. He is best remembered as the artistic brain behind the Mitsukoshi Department Store. He started work at the luxury goods purveyor in 1908. After two years, he became the first head of the design department. His career at Mitsukoshi spanned 27 years.

In subsequent printings, from newly carved blocks from Hisui's original drawings, the number of volumes and the way the prints were arranged were sometimes changed.
