media.caption: [Illustrations] No. 24 and No. 25 appearing in the Illustrated News No. 9 [of the Yomiuri Shinbun]  ([読売新聞] ,  絵入新聞 九号 第卄四号 第卄四五号)

text.headline: [Illustrations] No. 24 and No. 25 appearing in the Illustrated News No. 9 [of the Yomiuri Shinbun]  ([読売新聞] ,  絵入新聞 九号 第卄四号 第卄四五号)
text.text:
Two illustrations for a story, with likely lurid content, published by the "Yomiuri shinbun" in August 1875 under a banner held aloft by two cherubs reading "Illustrated Newspaper." A transcript of the text on illustration no. 25 can be found at https://www.lib.iii.u-tokyo.ac.jp/collection/ono_sn/17.html#N015 [accessed 8-17-23]
Brief Overview of Nishiki-e Shinbun
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written (using furigana and katakana to enhance readability), by popular writers of light novels and the pictures were drawn by woodblock print artists of the day.
While the "Tokyo nichinichi shinbun" was the first paper to publish news nishiki-e, many other print publishers in Tokyo and Osaka jumped into the news nishiki-e market adopting a similar masthead design, featuring the name of their news nishiki-e on an unfurled banner held in the air by a pair of fat cherubs.
At their brief height, around forty nishiki-e shinbun were in publication. While nishiki-e shinbun were largely gone by the late 1870s, challenged by the rise of faster and cheaper letterpress newspapers, they played an important role during their short life in spurring the growth of the Japanese press during its formative years.

media.caption: Hibiya Park Concert Hall: Tokyo Famous Sights (日比谷公園音樂堂・東京名勝 Hibiya Kōen Ongaku-dō・Tokyo meishō)

text.headline: Hibiya Park Concert Hall: Tokyo Famous Sights (日比谷公園音樂堂・東京名勝 Hibiya Kōen Ongaku-dō・Tokyo meishō)
text.text:
This souvenir woodblock print with its saturated colors was likely created shortly after the opening of Hibiya Park in 1903. This Western-style park is located in Chiyoda Ward, Tokyo, next to the Imperial Palace. An electric tram is shown in the center of the print, with the park being a major stop along its route, and the park's bandstand is prominently shown in the circular inset.
The first concert in the bandstand took place on August 1, 1905 with fifty Army Band musicians performing. European classical music was introduced to many Japanese through these concerts.
Five weeks after this first concert, on September 5, the park was the scene of the "Hibiya Riots" in which protesters rallying against the disappointing terms of the Treaty of Portsmouth ending the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) clashed with police and later destroyed more than 300 buildings in central Tokyo. Some 450 policemen were injured and seventeen died during the three days of riots. Martial law was declared to quell the riots.

media.caption: The Unbreakable (不破伴左衛門 Fuwa Banzaemon)

text.headline: The Unbreakable (不破伴左衛門 Fuwa Banzaemon)
text.text:
A preparatory watercolor painting (left, top image) used in the creation of the woodblock print Fuwa Banzaemon 不破伴左衛門 (The Unbreakable) (left, bottom image) from the 1916 series Kabuki Jūhachiban 歌舞伎十八番 by the artist Torii Kiyotada VII. See IHL.2256 for details of the print.

Traditional Woodblock Printmaking
Traditional woodblock printmaking was a "project" brought to fruition by a team consisting of publisher, artist, carver and printer. The publisher was the project leader who commissioned the artist to create a design which was then turned into a print by carvers and printers in the publisher's employ. The publisher marketed the print and had ownership of the "intellectual property," the carved woodblocks.

media.caption: Sake Brewing at Itami in Settsu Province (摂津国伊丹酒造之図)

text.headline: Sake Brewing at Itami in Settsu Province (摂津国伊丹酒造之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the brewing of refined sake at Itami in Settsu Province (摂津国, Settsu no kuni) which is now part of Hyōgo Prefecture.
Settsu Province (摂津国 Settsu no kuni) was a province of Japan, which today comprises the southeastern part of Hyōgo Prefecture and the northern part of Osaka Prefecture. It was also referred to as Tsu Province (津国 Tsu no kuni) or Sesshū (摂州). Osaka and Osaka Castle were the main center of the province. Most of Settsu's area comprises the modern day cities of Osaka and Kōbe.

media.caption: Viewing the Cherry Blossoms on the Sumida River at Night (隅田川夜櫻)

text.headline: Viewing the Cherry Blossoms on the Sumida River at Night (隅田川夜櫻)
text.text: A mounted folding fan print picturing courtesans on a pleasure boat during an evening viewing of the cherry blossoms along Tokyo's Sumida River, still billed as the "ultimate spring experience" while in Tokyo.

media.caption: Pagoda at Yanaka Tennōji Temple at Shitaya,View 78 (下谷・谷中天皇寺之塔 ・七十八景)

text.headline: Pagoda at Yanaka Tennōji Temple at Shitaya,View 78 (下谷・谷中天皇寺之塔 ・七十八景)
text.text:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view of the main road leading into the Yanaka cemetery and the five-story Tennōji pagoda that once stood there. A woman with baby and young child, a peddler and a figure dressed in a light blue kimono walk along a path.
The pagoda which survived the 1923 earthquake and the allied bombing was burnt down in 1957. The artist comments, “In the middle of the Yanaka cemetery stands a five-story pagoda made of plain, unpainted wood.”

Print number seventy-eight in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort . . . .” - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

media.caption: Pagoda

text.headline: Pagoda
text.text: An untitled scene of a pagoda within a temple grounds. Several states of this print are known.

media.caption: Mitsuke: Stone Embankment Along the River (見附 川石垣)

text.headline: Mitsuke: Stone Embankment Along the River (見附 川石垣)
text.text:
Sekino's rendition of station number 29, Mitsuke, along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. The print is the 12th, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekino created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858).
"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching for a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

media.caption: White Herons and Willow (柳に白鷺 Yanagi ni shira-sagi)

text.headline: White Herons and Willow (柳に白鷺 Yanagi ni shira-sagi)
text.text:
Two little egrets (Egretta garzetta) are depicted in flight past a green willow. Later printings, such as this collection's print, utilize a brighter green and lack the subtle grey shading of the background of the first edition.
Ohara Koson was one of the most important and prolific kachō-ga (bird and flower) woodblock prints artists of the early 20th century shin-hanga (new print) movement.

media.caption: Moulin de la Galette: Paris (ムーラン･ド･ギャレット･ パリ)

text.headline: Moulin de la Galette: Paris (ムーラン･ド･ギャレット･ パリ)
text.text:
This small print of a street leading to the windmill in the Moulin de la Galette was included in the second of two portfolios of twelve prints each by twelve artists published by Hanga kanshōkai, titled Hanga kanshōkai sakuhin-shū.
The Moulin de la Galette is a windmill and the associated businesses situated near the top of the district of Montmartre in Paris. Sekino made at least two trips to France, in 1958 and again in 1976.

COLLECTION OF WORKS BY THE WOODBLOCK PRINT APPRECIATION SOCIETY
The two volumes of Hanga kanshōkai sakuhin-shū (Collection of Works by the Woodblock Print Appreciation Society), were published by Hanga kanshōkai, a creation of the Yokohama publisher and gallery Chikuhōdō (竹芳洞 or 竹芳堂). The two portfolios were initially issued in 1959 or 1960 in an edition of 700 for volume 1 (上) and 500 copies for volume 2 (下) and reissued at least once in 1980 in an edition of 200. This collection's print is likely from the 1980 edition.

media.caption: Old Elementary School Building in Komono (菰野小学校旧校舎)

text.headline: Old Elementary School Building in Komono (菰野小学校旧校舎)
text.text:
In 1973, on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Komono Elementary School in the small city of Komono about 90 miles due east of Kyoto in Mie Prefecture, Tokuriki issued two prints to mark the occasion. This collection's print depicts the old administrative building built in 1934. The second print, not part of this collection, depicts the site of the castle ruins located next to the school.
Today, this beautiful building is gone, as are the other early structures, replaced by unattractive and blocky white buildings.

media.caption: Hiragata Harbor (平潟港 Hiragatakō)

text.headline: Hiragata Harbor (平潟港 Hiragatakō)
text.text:
Miyata depicts Hiragata harbor in the city of Kitaibaraki, Ibaraki Prefecture. As with so many of his prints, all is calm, serene and quiet, and no people can be seen. This print is from one of the volume of prints, likely a volume of scenes of Hokkaidō where Lake Tōya is located, from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.

Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

media.caption: Pasture Scene (牧場の風景 Bokujō no fūkei)

text.headline: Pasture Scene (牧場の風景 Bokujō no fūkei)
text.text: This pastoral scene of horses in a field is one of a number of similar themed prints by Takagi, a mostly self-taught artist whose work became more representational as he aged.

media.caption: Pulling Up a Whale (同 [壱岐] 神楽桟にて引揚図)

text.headline: Pulling Up a Whale (同 [壱岐] 神楽桟にて引揚図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. This crêped print version depicts the hauling onto shore of a whale for processing. The whale has been taken close to shore by a hunting party in fast chase boats (seko-bune 勢子船).
When this print was issued in 1877 near-shore whaling had given way to offshore, or open sea, whaling. By 1877 Japanese whaling was undergoing a transformation from traditional to modern practices forced upon them by declining near-shore whale populations. In traditional active whaling, whalers belonged to a specific whaling group (ōnaya) based out of a coastal village that had space on the beach for processing whales taken near shore (shore-based whaling). As inshore whale populations declined, larger open sea whaling ships were used to haul whales back to processing plants on shore and ownership of whaling operations passed to larger business groups, such as the massive Masutomi group, able to provide the bigger ships and on-shore facilities. By the 1920s factory ship whaling had begun in which harpooned whales taken on the open seas were towed to a centralized factory ship for processing.

media.caption: Mandarin Orange Plantation in Kii Province (紀伊国蜜柑山畑之図)

text.headline: Mandarin Orange Plantation in Kii Province (紀伊国蜜柑山畑之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. This crêped version of the print depicts workers harvesting mandarin oranges in a terraced grove in Kii province. Kii Province (紀伊国, Kii no Kuni), or Kishū (紀州), was a province of Japan in the part of Honshū that is today Wakayama Prefecture, as well as the southern part of Mie Prefecture. Kishū has been a major orange growing area for centuries. Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan describes a scene much as depicted in this print. "We are now in the district of Arida [in Kishū province], notable as the greatest orange-producing centre in Japan; and as we proceed, we find all the lower slopes of the wide sheltered valleys covered with orange-groves."
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print. See IHL.0540 for the non-crêped version of the print.

media.caption: Planting Rush in Bingo Province (備後国 藺を植ル図)

text.headline: Planting Rush in Bingo Province (備後国 藺を植ル図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the planting of rush (igusa) in Bingo Province (備後国, Bingo no kuni) which is now part of Hiroshima Prefecture.
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print.

media.caption: Mat Making in Bingo Province (備後國 疊表ヲ製圖)

text.headline: Mat Making in Bingo Province (備後國 疊表ヲ製圖)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of tatami mats 畳表 in Bingo Province (備後国, Bingo no kuni) which is now part of Hiroshima Prefecture.
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print. See IHL.0540 for the non-crêped version of the print. See IHL.0461 for the non-crêped version of the print.

media.caption: Haniwa [4] (埴輪 [四])

text.headline: Haniwa [4] (埴輪 [四])
text.text:
One of at least fifteen prints by Saitō picturing one or more haniwa, ancient clay funeral sculptures from the Kofun era (approximately 200-552CE). Saitō's rendering of a haniwa warrior in this collection's print makes the figure look monumental, but comical, with its lopsided face.
Writing in 1957, Oliver Statler called the artist's haniwa prints "adventures with straight lines and curves, stimulated by his study of the nude" and "an exercise in deformation." - Source: Saitō Kiyoshi hangashū, Oliver Statler and Chisaburō Yamada, Kodansha International, 1957.

media.caption: Kusu no tsuyu 楠露 (Camphor Tree in Dew)

text.headline: Kusu no tsuyu 楠露 (Camphor Tree in Dew)
text.text:
The print depicts a scene from the play Kusu no tsuyu in which Masashige, fearing his imminent death, has his retainer read his last words of advice to his son, Masatsura. For two other impressions of this print see IHL.1149 and IHL.1896.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 95-96.) - Feeling that he will die in the coming battle with Ashikaga Takauji, Masashige calls his son Masatsura to him in the town of Sakurai and gives him his last words of advice. At the farewell party Onchi Mitsukazu dances to entertain them. Masashige then sends his faithful retainer away with his son to take him back to their home, while he himself prepares for battle.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Unoha 鵜羽 (The Cormorant Plumes)

text.headline: Unoha 鵜羽 (The Cormorant Plumes)
text.text:
Depicting the birthing hut of the sea goddess Unoha and its partially thatched roof hut from the play Unoha, written by Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis ( Developing Zeami: The Noh Actor's Attunement in Practice, Shelley Fenno Quinn, University of Hawaii Press, 2005, p. 405.) - The play is set on the shoreline in Hyūga Province and retells the myth of the birth there of the Shintō deity Unoha fuki awasezu no mikoto (deity of the hut partially thatched with cormorant feathers.) His father was the Shintō deity Hiko hohodemi no mikoto, and his mother the dragon princess Toyotamahime (princess of abundant jewels) from the dragon palace under the sea. Through this union, Hiko hohodemi no mikoto came into possession of the precious jewels that controlled the waxing and waning of the tides. The couple came to earth when she became pregnant, and Hiko hohodem no mikoto managed to thatch only part of the parturition hut before the birth occurred, which is how the child received his name.
Toyotamahime is the shite of the second act of Unoha. The play is set on the birthday of the child. The shite of the first act appears as a young woman who makes her living from the sea; she appears with a young female cohort (tsure). They encounter the waki, a retainer of the emperor, and his attendant (waktsure), who are there to pay their respects at this famous spot. The women retell the myth of the birth and go through the motions of thatching the hut. In the second act. Toyotamahime reappears to reveal her identity and to dance. The play ends with the intertwining of the jewel imagery of the Shintō myth and the Buddhist parable "The jewels of ebb and flow (raises fan and circles stage) are wondrous treasures and yet, my heart desires the true jewel of enlightenment."

media.caption: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum From Heaven)

text.headline: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum From Heaven)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Tenko, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), in which Tenko's father appears before an Emperor's official to play his son's drum. For another impression of this print see IHL.0946.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 188-189.) - A boy named Tenko has a wonderful drum which had come down from Heaven, but when this was taken from him to be presented to the Emperor he drowned himself. An Imperial envoy tells this story and explains that as no one has been able to make any sound come from the drum since it was taken to the Palace, he has been sent to fetch the father of Tenko. Together they go to the Palace, and when the father strikes the drum it gives out such a miraculous sound that he is promised a rich reward and a musical performance is arranged to placate the soul of his son. When this is done, the ghost of Tenko comes and dances before them.

media.caption: Ikuta Atsumori 生田敦盛

text.headline: Ikuta Atsumori 生田敦盛
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Ikuta Atsumori, written by Konparu Zempō (1454-1520?), in which the son of Atsumori, accompanied by a priest, meets his father's ghost.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.61-62.) - The young orphan child of the warrior Atsumori who is being cared for by priests, goes with one of them to pray at the Kamo shrine that he may see the father he has never known. As the result of a dream he has there they go down to the forest of Ikuta and there he meets his father's ghost.

media.caption: Yōkihi 楊貴妃 (The Chinese Beauty Yang Guifei)

text.headline: Yōkihi 楊貴妃 (The Chinese Beauty Yang Guifei)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Yōkihi, written by Komparu Zenchiku (1405-1470?), in which the Chinese tang dynasty emperor Genshō (Hsüan-tsung in Chinese) grieves over his favorite mistress Yōhiki (Yang Guifei or Yang Kuei-fei in Chinese.)
Play synopsis ( A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 214-215.) - The Emperor Gensō (Hsuan Tsung) of T'ang, grief stricken at the death of his beloved Yōhiki (Yang Kuei-fei), has commissioned a magician to find out where she is. Hearing at last that she is in the palace on the magic island of Hōrai, he gains an audience with her there and asks for something to take back to the Emperor as proof of their meeting. She gives him a bejewelled hair ornament but when pressed for some more certain identification, discloses that she and Gensō promised each other that 'In Heaven, we shall become birds flying ever wing to wing; on earth, we shall become trees with branches entwined.' Yōhiki dances for the visitor and then sadly watches him return to her lover with her memento and secret words.

media.caption: Morihisa 盛久

text.headline: Morihisa 盛久
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Morihisa, written by Kanze Motomasa ( d. 1432)), in which Morihisa holds a sutra while his executioner prepares to cut off his head.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 163-164.) - After his capture by the Minamoto, Morihisa is sent to Kamakura in the charge of Tsuchiya no Saburō, but continues to pray faithfully to the goddess Kannon throughout the journey. Even after arriving at Kamakura, Morihisa talks with Tsuchiya about the power of the sutras. In the course of a short nap he then has a wonderful dream, but immediately afterwards is led off to the execution ground. There, just when the executioner lift his sword to strike off Morihisa's head, he is so dazzled by the light from the sutra in the prisoner's hand that he drops the sword and sees it shatter into fragments. In the second act Morihisa appears before the Shōgun Yoritomo (not represented on the stage) and tells of his dream. Having had a similar dream, Yoritomo takes it as an omen and spares Morihisa's life. He then orders wine to be brought and has Morihisa perform a dance for him.

media.caption: Kayoi Komachi 通小町 (The Courtship of Komachi)

text.headline: Kayoi Komachi 通小町 (The Courtship of Komachi)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Kayoi Komachi, written by Kanami (1333-1384), in which the ghost Komachi asks a priest to pray for her soul while being held back by her former suitor's (Shōshō's) ghost.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.75-76.) - A priest who is spending the summer in the mountain village of Yase is brought wood and fruit every day by an unknown woman. When he asks who she is, he realizes from her reply that she is the ghost of Ono no Komachi, the poetess of old who was so famed for her beauty. He therefore goes to her grave and prays. At this, her spirit and that of her most ardent suitor, Fukakusa no Shōshō, appear and tell the priest of the trial Komachi set him. She promised herself to him if he came to her house every night for a hundred nights, but after braving all manner of obstacles to fulfill his task, he failed on the hundredth night.

media.caption: Asō 麻生 (Asō has His Hair Fixed)

text.headline: Asō 麻生 (Asō has His Hair Fixed)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the kyōgen play Asō, in which the two servants Tōroku and Geroku dance for their master.
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 23-24) - A Daimyō from Shinano named Asō calls his servants Tōroku and Geroku and informs them that he has finished his business in the capital and that they will all go home today. Since they haven't been home for a long time, they are very happy. Tōroku suggests that since it has been a long time, the Daimyō should dress in the best ceremonial style for his return trip. The Daimyō agrees, but says he has not made such preparations. Tōroku and Geroku reply that they have made the necessary preparations, that the proper clothes are ready and the eboshi (a ceremonial lacquered hat) has been ordered. The Daimyō says the hair style is very difficult to do and Tōroku replies that he has learned how to do it. The Daimyō, very happy at the efficiency of his servants, sends Geroku after the hat and orders Tōroku to fix his hair. The hair takes a long time during which the Daimyō asks about various things, such as the pattern and color of the new clothes, etc. Geroku has still not returned when Tōroku has finished fixing the Daimyō's hair, so he goes out in search of him.
Geroku has received the hat on a stick because the lacquer was not yet dry. On the way home he loses his way. Tōroku runs into him and scolds him for forgetting the way to his own master's house. They enter a house and find it is the wrong one. Thus it turns out that Tōroku has also forgotten which house is their master's. This time Geroku does the scolding. They decide to put their problem in a song and in this way search for their master's house. The Daimyō hears them and rewards them with rice cakes for their cleverness.

media.caption: Shōjō (猩々)

text.headline: Shōjō (猩々)
text.text:
In this print for the month of December, Shōjō, the ocean dweller, dances drunkenly for his friend Kōfū, the liquor seller, in the Noh play "Shōjō."
The Play - Shōjō (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 163-164.)
"A man named Kō-fū, living in ancient China, explains that by following a dream which he had in reward for his filial piety and which told him to sell wine in the market, he has become a prosperous man. At the market, there is one particular person who always comes to him to buy wine, and since he told the dealer that he is an elf living in the sea, the man has come down to the estuary to wait for him to appear. When he does so, red-faced from his drinking, the man serves him with wine and watches him dance. The elf, in return, gives him a well of wine which never runs dry."
Twelve Months of Noh Pictures
From a series of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1970. Six of the prints (for the months of January, February, June, September, November and December) were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963) and the other six (for the months of March, April, May, July, August and October) were created by his son Matsuno Hideyo (1936-2002). As Sōfū died in 1963, his prints must have been created from existing designs.
As originally issued, the prints were sold as a set with each print placed inside its own mat, which was overlaid with a commentary sheet on the play in Japanese and English. The matted print and commentary were then placed inside an envelope and all twelve envelopes were then placed into a cloth folio.
Interestingly, the artist seals appearing on the prints, each one being different, relate to the play being pictured, such as in the square red seal on this print whose characters, according to the commentary sheet accompanying the print, read "The Well That Contains Water in Endless Supply."

media.caption: Actor Onoe Tamizō Playing the Role of Nakanori [Kaminari] at the Age of Eighty from the magazine Bijutsu Sekai Vol. 16 (俳優尾上多見蔵頽齢八十にして中乗を演ずる図 美術世界 巻十六)

text.headline: Actor Onoe Tamizō Playing the Role of Nakanori [Kaminari] at the Age of Eighty from the magazine Bijutsu Sekai Vol. 16 (俳優尾上多見蔵頽齢八十にして中乗を演ずる図 美術世界 巻十六)
text.text:
Adoring fans watch Onoe Tamizō II 尾上多見蔵 二代目 (1800-1886) at the age of 80, playing the thunder god, raijin, [Nakanori Kaminari], in the play Hatsuharu no kotobuki iwau kokonobake, in this double-bookplate by Kyōsai appearing in the 16th volume of the arts magazine Bijutsu Sekai (World of Art), published in February 1892, three years after Kyōsai's death in 1889. Note the candles at the end of bamboo rods that the kurogo (black-clad stage assistants) would have held to illuminate the actor at critical times in the play.
It is one of four prints designed by Kyōsai appearing in volume 16, all of which feature older characters - the kabuki actor Onoe Tamizō II at the age of 80; the warrior Ōkubo Hikozaemon 大久保 彦左衛門 (1560-1639) at the age of 82; the Confucian scholar Kō Gentai 高玄岱 (1649-1722) at the age of 78; and a prostitute at the age of 89.

media.caption: Takachiho (高千穂)

text.headline: Takachiho (高千穂)
text.text:
Kuroki captures the colors of terraced rice fields and a blazing sunset in this semi-abstract rendering of the town of Takachiho in the Nishiusuki District of Miyazaki Prefecture located about 40 km west from his birthplace of Nobeoka. Surrounded by the Kyūshū Mountains, Takachiho is located in a forest-enclosed environment where flat land is rare.

Takachiho has been known since ancient times as a sacred ground where the gods descended to earth. The area is also famous for yokagura, sacred dance rituals reenacting the legends, which are performed in the fall and early winter.

media.caption: New Year at the Lakeshore and Mount Fuji (湖畔の正月と富士)

text.headline: New Year at the Lakeshore and Mount Fuji (湖畔の正月と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji is blanketed with snow as villagers prepare for a New Year's festival which includes paying honor to the goddess of Mount Fuji, Sakuyahime (traditional name: Sengen). Her name 咲耶姫 appears on the white banner which has been brought to the festival by parishioners from a local shrine. A taiko drum is in the center of the print which will herald in the New Year and a pole festooned with prayer slips and colorful decorations dominates the right side.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: Imperial Japanese Army Emperor Banzai Tank Death Squad

text.headline: Imperial Japanese Army Emperor Banzai Tank Death Squad
text.text:
A color lithograph patriotic fan sample print, likely dating from the early years of the Asia-Pacific War (1931-1945), extolling the brave warriors of the suicide tank squads. The print carries the sample catalog number そ印 參百五拾參號 So jirushi (or in) 353 Sanbyaku go jū san gō. (Also see IHL.1936.)
These numbered fan prints (uchiwa-e 団扇絵), were used as samples to show wholesale customers the range of available designs. The sample prints were gathered into a sample book (uchiwa mihonchō 団扇見本帳, or uchiwa gachō 団扇画帖.)
The first two columns of text on the print read, 戰車ヲマモル勇士 | 決死隊ノ勇士夕テハ extolling the "warrior who guards the tank" and the "brave soldier of the suicide squad."

media.caption: Japanese National Defense Women Association (大日本國防婦人会)

text.headline: Japanese National Defense Women Association (大日本國防婦人会)
text.text:
A color lithograph patriotic fan sample print, likely dating from the early years of the Asia-Pacific War (1931-1945), promoting the Japanese National Defense Women Association which, at its height, boasted over 9 million members. The two women wear white aprons over kimono, with a sash bearing the association's name 大日本國防婦人会. The red text to the left of the women reads, 興亞長期建設, a reference to the government's long-term national policy on East Asia, whose stated purpose was to unite Asian nations and solidify and create a continental identity to defeat the designs of the Western nations to perpetuate hegemony.

The print carries the sample catalog number そ印 參百五拾貳號 So jirushi (or in) 352 Sanbyaku go jū ni gō. (Also see IHL.1935.)
These numbered fan prints (uchiwa-e 団扇絵), were used as samples to show wholesale customers the range of available designs. The sample prints were gathered into a sample book (uchiwa mihonchō 団扇見本帳, or uchiwa gachō 団扇画帖.)

media.caption: Around Ueno (上野附近)

text.headline: Around Ueno (上野附近)
text.text:
One of two prints contributed by the artist Takashima Unpō (1894-1987) to the series Pictures of Taishō Earthquake, issued in 1926 three years after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. This print pictures the Ueno district ablaze in the aftermath of the earthquake. Takashima has captured a cross-section of Tokyo-ites running for their lives as the fires swirl around them.
The series consists of 25 prints by nine, mostly lesser-known, artists, a number of whom, including this print's creator, were students of the Nihonga artist Tomioka Eisen (1864-1905). The nine artists are Katayama Shunhan (fl. c. 1901–1926); Hakuhan Yawata (1893–1957); Noguchi Kōgai (born c. 1899, active c. 1919-1930s); Igawa Sengai (1876-1961); Kirigaya (Kiriya) Senrin (1877–1932); Shibata Kōyō (fl c. 1920s); Hamada Josen (1875-1928); Kondō Shiun (fl. c. 1915–1940) and Takashima Unpō (1894-1987).
In his recollections of the fires, playwright and theater historian Kawatake Shigetoshi describes "scenes of frenzied panic and terror." Fleeing his home in Honjo in eastern Tokyo, he recalls looking north to a "blazing inferno." He writes, "I was speechless, watching the whirlpools of fire and the undulating waves of flames. It was utterly beyond description." Kawatake's son perished in the disaster. - Source: website of Smithsonian.com https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-great-japan-earthquake-of-1923-1764539/ [accessed 8-29-23]
"The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 stands in memory as one of the most terrifying calamities in Japanese history. Registering at a magnitude of 7.9, the quake struck on September 1, with its epicenter some 50 miles southwest of Tokyo, in Sagami Bay. The hour was 11:58A.M., just when households everywhere were lighting small charcoal stoves to prepare lunch. Fires broke out instantly in the densely populated cities of Tokyo and Yokohama and were spread by high winds. Since the earthquake had broken the water lines, both cities were reduced to smoldering ruins within a few hours. . . . The earthquake and its aftermath caused well over 140,000 deaths and left nearly 700,000 people homeless." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 273.

media.caption: Yugyō Yanagi 遊行柳 (The Priest and the Willow)

text.headline: Yugyō Yanagi 遊行柳 (The Priest and the Willow)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Yugyō Yanagi by the playwright Kanze Nobumitsu (mid-1400s-1516).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.222.) - The priest Yugyō passes the barriers at Shirakawa and meets an old man who guides him to an aged and withered willow tree standing on a mound. The man explains that this is the tree made famous by Saigyō who rested in its shade, and then vanishes from sight. That night, after praying at the spot, the priest sees the spirit of the willow tree, which rejoices at his prayers and tells him stories connected with other willows. It then dances for him, but fades from sight again with the coming of dawn.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Sanemori 實盛 (The Warrior Sanemori)

text.headline: Sanemori 實盛 (The Warrior Sanemori)
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Sanemori attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 148-149) - After a local person of Shinowara explains in a short prologue that the priest Ta-ami preaches there every day, apparently to himself, the priest begins his sermon. An old man, visible to Ta-ami but to no one else, then comes to listen as he has on every previous day. When asked about himself, he reveals that he is the ghost of the warrior Sanemori who was killed in battle there more than two hundred years ago, and then he vanishes beside the pond in which his head was washed after his death. When the priest prays there through the night for the repose of Sanemori's spirit, the ghost appears and tells the story of his last battle before which, being already an old man at the time, he died his white hair to hide his age.

media.caption: Yōkihi 楊貴妃 (The Chinese Beauty Yang Guifei)

text.headline: Yōkihi 楊貴妃 (The Chinese Beauty Yang Guifei)
text.text:
The print depicts Yōkihi (Yang Guifei or Yang Kuei-fei in Chinese) the favorite concubine of the Chinese emperor Hsüan-tsung holding a hair ornament of gold and coral in the play Yōkihi written by Komparu Zenchiku (1405-1470?).
PLAY SYNOPSIS
The Emperor Gen-sō (Hsuan Tsung) of T'ang, grief stricken at the death of his beloved Yō-kihi (Yang Kuei-fei), has commissioned a magician to find out where she is. Hearing at last that she is in the palace on the magic island of Hōrai, he gains an audience with her there and asks for something to take back to the Emperor as proof of their meeting. She gives him a bejewelled hair ornament but when pressed for some more certain identification, discloses that she and Gen-sō promised each other that 'In Heaven, we shall become birds flying ever wing to wing; on earth, we shall become trees with branches entwined.' Yō-kihi dances for the visitor and then sadly watches him return to her lover with her memento and secret words.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.214.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Higaki 桧垣 (Cypress Fence)

text.headline: Higaki 桧垣 (Cypress Fence)
text.text:
The print depicts the old woman Higaki performing a dance she once did for Fujiwara no Okinori in the play Higaki written by Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
PLAY SYNOPSIS
A priest living in the mountains sees a very old woman come every day to draw water. Questioning her, he learns that she is the woman Higaki who long ago composed a poem on being asked for water by Fujiwara no Okinori. After asking for his prayers, the woman disappears. When she returns later, she tells the priest of her early life and performs a dance as she recalls the time when she danced for Okinori.[1]

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[2]

[1] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 54.
[2] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007

media.caption: Evening Shore (夕浜 Yūhama)

text.headline: Evening Shore (夕浜 Yūhama)
text.text:
An evocative night time scene of seaside village.
To realize his dark atmospheric prints, Tadashige uses a water-based-pigment technique called inkoku tashoku-zuri mokuhan (color negative woodblock printing) that he developed in 1948. This process involves first dying the paper with black bokujū, made from dissolving and grinding sumi in water, then printing a thick opaque white gouache beneath the areas to be colored to keep the black from absorbing the colors.

media.caption: The Glory of the Imperial Flowers (花の都御代乃榮 Hana no miyako goyo no sakae)

text.headline: The Glory of the Imperial Flowers (花の都御代乃榮 Hana no miyako goyo no sakae)
text.text:
This scene of courtly ladies and imperial regalia first appears as if it’s out of the Heian era (794-1185), when court ladies painted eyebrows high up on their foreheads after shaving their real eyebrows. But, these lady’s eyebrows are not shaved, suggesting an elaborate dress-up, and who is the man sitting high-up in the left panel? Could it be Emperor Meiji? Donald Keene tell us that in June of 1880 the emperor embarked on a journey to understand the local conditions of his subjects. Included in his journey was a stop in Kyoto in July, when this print was issued. While in Kyoto he visited his aunt, Princess Sumiko, who had arranged a program of plays for his entertainment. “The performance was attended also by members of the nobility still living in the old capital, a momentary revival of their former glory.”
While the artist would certainly not have attended the performance, details of the emperor’s journey were widely reported allowing Nakashima to construct this scene using his artistic license.

media.caption: Index to Thirty Subjects of Kyoto

text.headline: Index to Thirty Subjects of Kyoto
text.text: This print, mounted on its original stiff board, serves as the index to the portfolio of thirty prints titled Thirty Subjects of Kyoto published by the Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936.

media.caption: Shipping New Brew Sake in Settsu Province (同 [摂津国] 新酒荷出之図)

text.headline: Shipping New Brew Sake in Settsu Province (同 [摂津国] 新酒荷出之図)
text.text:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts laborers moving vats of sake in preparation for loading onto boats in Osaka Bay. The Cambridge History of Japan notes in discussing the governments 1874 survey of physical production in Japan that "The value of sake produced was astonishingly large, more than the value of all silk and cotton textiles and three times value of raw silk output."
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print. See IHL.0540 for the non-crêped version of the print.

media.caption: Illustration of Military Review Outside [Osaka] Castle (城外観兵式之圖)

text.headline: Illustration of Military Review Outside [Osaka] Castle (城外観兵式之圖)
text.text:
The Emperor reviews troops as they parade outside of Osaka Castle in this color lithograph, part of a twenty print portfolio published in April 1895 to coincide with the opening of the Fourth National Industrial Exhibition in Kyoto.
This portfolio of color lithographs 色石版画, issued by the Osaka publisher Furushima Takejirō in 1895, consists of ten well-known scenes in Kyoto and ten scenes in Osaka. The portfolio is likely the earliest use of color lithography, most likely using zinc plates, for the production of meisho-e, or pictures of famous places. The portfolio was sold in shops in the exposition hall and in souvenir/gift shops around Kyoto. The selling price and number of total copies is unknown, but it appears that at least two editions of this portfolio were produced. As over 1.3 million people attended the exposition, the print runs must have been quite large.

media.caption: View of the West Gate of Shitennō-ji Temple (四天王寺西門の景)

text.headline: View of the West Gate of Shitennō-ji Temple (四天王寺西門の景)
text.text:
Visitors in traditional and Western dress near the stone torii leading to the West Gate (Gokuraku mon) of Shitennnōji, Japan's first Buddhist temple, located in Osaka. The five-storied pagoda (Gojūnotō) can be seen in the background. The yellow sign pillar to the right of the torii reads 従是東公園地 大阪府, telling us that we are at the affiliated East Park area in Osaka prefecture.
This portfolio of color lithographs 色石版画, issued by the Osaka publisher Furushima Takejirō in 1895, consists of ten well-known scenes in Kyoto and ten scenes in Osaka. The portfolio is likely the earliest use of color lithography, most likely using zinc plates, for the production of meisho-e, or pictures of famous places. The portfolio was sold in shops in the exposition hall and in souvenir/gift shops around Kyoto. The selling price and number of total copies is unknown, but it appears that at least two editions of this portfolio were produced. As over 1.3 million people attended the exposition, the print runs must have been quite large.

media.caption: Valiant Battle at Jiuliancheng (九連城勇戦図 Kyūrenjō yūsen zu)

text.headline: Valiant Battle at Jiuliancheng (九連城勇戦図 Kyūrenjō yūsen zu)
text.text: On October 26, 1894 the Japanese army, having crossed the Yalu River into Chinese territory on the morning of the previous day, engaged the Chinese forces at Hushan and on the banks of the Ai River. The Japanese then marched west, surrounded Jiuliancheng, a fortified town guarding the Yalu and a gateway to Manchuria, and launched a full-scale offensive.  The Chinese forces, rather than defend this strategic town which served as their headquarters, retreated to defensive positions leaving the Japanese to enter the town without opposition.

media.caption: Illustration of The Sino-Japanese War, Ansong Crossing, Korea (朝鮮安城渡日清戦争ノ図)

text.headline: Illustration of The Sino-Japanese War, Ansong Crossing, Korea (朝鮮安城渡日清戦争ノ図)
text.text:
The legendary Captain Matsuzaki (松崎大尉 as printed in the small red cartouche), front and center with sword drawn, leads his men in the Advanced Column across the Ansong (Anjō in Japanese) River in Korea attacking the enemy. The captain was felled by several bullets and died. Lieutenant Colonel Fukushima (福嶋中佐 as printed in the small red cartouche) on his white horse with his troops attacks.
The large scroll in the print begins, "On the night of July 29th, 1894, at half-past twelve, our army crossed the Ansong." The crossing of the Ansong was the beginning of the battle to take the Chinese stronghold of Songhwan, Korea, which the Japanese would take later that day.

media.caption: Illustration of a Scouting Patrol in a Skirmish in the Vicinity of Port Arthur (旅順口附近我斥候進撃之図 Ryojunkō fukin waga sekkō shingeki no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of a Scouting Patrol in a Skirmish in the Vicinity of Port Arthur (旅順口附近我斥候進撃之図 Ryojunkō fukin waga sekkō shingeki no zu)
text.text:
Port Arthur fell on November 21, 1894. Prior to its capture there were major engagements on the Liaotung (Chinchou) Peninsula where the Port Arthur forts were located. This print, from the artist's imagination, depicts a skirmish between a Japanese Army scouting party (likely a part of the Second Army) and Chinese troops. As usual, the casualties are all Chinese.
The print is a wonderful composition of movement. Kokunimasa was one of the more talented artists of the later years of the Meiji Era.

media.caption: A Courtly Mirror of Ashiya Dōman (蘆屋道満大内鑑 Ashiya Dōman Ōuchi Kagami)

text.headline: A Courtly Mirror of Ashiya Dōman (蘆屋道満大内鑑 Ashiya Dōman Ōuchi Kagami)
text.text:
This print depicts the child separation scene, act four, in the play Ashiya Dōman Ōuchi Kagami in which the two Kuzunoha, one a princess (far right) and the other a transformed fox (far left), meet. Meeting the real Kuzunoha, the fox Kuzunoha realizes she must leave and return to her former state, telling her son she must treat the real Kuzunoha as his mother. Before she leaves she writes a waka poem, pen in mouth, on a sliding screen which reads, "If you love me, you will seek me Izumi's Shinoda Forest."
The print was created for the March 1891 performance of the play at the Kabuki-za theater.
The actors (names in red cartouches) and their roles (in adjoining smaller cartouches) are from right to left:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 as Kuzunoha [hime] 葛の葉[姫
Ichikawa Botan 市川ぼたん as [Abe no] Dōji 安倍の]童子
Ichikawa Gonjūrō 市川權十郎 as Abe no Yasuna 安倍の保名
Ichikawa Yaozō VII 市川八百蔵 as Yohei Kanpei 與勘平
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 as the "fox lady" Kuzunoha くずのは
Note that Ichikawa Danjūrō IX is playing both Kuzunohas.

media.caption: Nikko Senjōgahara from the book Nihon no sansui (日本の山水・日光戰場原)

text.headline: Nikko Senjōgahara from the book Nihon no sansui (日本の山水・日光戰場原)
text.text: Picturing the Senjōgahara marshlands in Nikko National Park, this print was originally published as part of the 1946 book titled Nihon no sansui (Mountains and Waters of Japan.) This collection's print was either issued separately from the book or removed from the book, designed and compiled by Onchi Kōshirō 恩地考四郎 (1891-1955). The book contains poetry by twenty-one poets, three color woodblock prints by the artists Yamaguchi Susumu 山口進 (1897–1983), Azechi Umetarō 畦地梅太郎 (1902-1999) and Maekawa Senpan, and a cover print presumably designed by Onchi.

media.caption: Akasaka Palace (赤坂離宮  Akasaka gosho)

text.headline: Akasaka Palace (赤坂離宮  Akasaka gosho)
text.text:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Last Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print, made from recut blocks, is one of two designs that Hiratsuka contributed to Scenes of Lost Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955).
Hiratsuka's view of Akasaka Palace is rather bleak - trees without leaves, absent of people, an ochre hued sky, foreground and palace itself. The palace was lightly damaged during the allied bombings of Tokyo on the night of April 13-14, 1945.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

media.caption: View of Ikejiri, Setagaya (世田谷 池尻 風景)

text.headline: View of Ikejiri, Setagaya (世田谷 池尻 風景)
text.text: A view, seemingly of a formal garden, possibly leading to a temple, in Ikejiri, Setagaya. This print was issued in 1922, a year before the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. Today, Setagaya has the largest population and second largest area (after Ōta) of Tokyo's special wards.

media.caption: Aridōshi 蟻通

text.headline: Aridōshi 蟻通
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Aridōshi attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 134) - In the play, the poet Ki no Tsurayuki (waki) annoys the groundskeeper (shite) by riding his horse within the precincts of the Aridōshi Shrine. Tsurayuki soothes the feelings of the shrine deity by reciting a poem he has composed, after which, at the poet’s request, the god recites some Shinto prayers.
Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Hakurakuten 白楽天

text.headline: Hakurakuten 白楽天
text.text:
Depicting a scene from the play Hakurakuten (Chinese: Bai Juyi or Po Chu-i) attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443). The print shows a split scene. One the left, three men in Edo-period dress place the costume on the shite (primary actor) as he prepares for his dance in the second part of the play. On the right, Bai Juyi stands before the three fishermen from the first part of the play.
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 148-149) - The Chinese poet Haku Rakuten (Po Chu-i) comes over to Japan to test the wisdom of the Japanese, but while still offshore he meets two fishermen near Matsura in the province of Hizen. Surprised to find that they address him by name, he talks to them of poetry and composes a Chinese poem - only to have it capped immediately by a similar Japanese poem. After promising to return and dance for the poet, the fishermen disappear. Later the god Sumiyoshi Myōjin emerges from the waves and dances as promised. He then declares that he will not suffer Haku Rakuten to stay any longer and, with the help of other gods, summons up a wind which blows his boat back to China.

In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

media.caption: Picture of the Famous Kōbe Steam Train (神戸名所鉄道蒸気車之図 Kōbe meisho tetsudō jōkisha no zu)

text.headline: Picture of the Famous Kōbe Steam Train (神戸名所鉄道蒸気車之図 Kōbe meisho tetsudō jōkisha no zu)
text.text:
One of fifteen prints originally created by Hasegawa Sadanobu II in the early to mid 1870s that were re-carved and reprinted as part of a 1936 collection of prints of famous sights in Kobe issued by an organization called the Kobe Old Print Association.
The railroad connection between Kobe and Osaka was opened in May 1874 (Meiji 7). It took 70 minutes to travel the 32.7 kilometer route. The first Osaka Station, popularly known as Umeda Teishajo (梅田停車場), was located in Umeda, Osaka and was opened on May 11, 1874 (Meiji 7).
Two English-made steam locomotives were imported by the Imperial Government Railway of Japan for use on the Kobe-Osaka Line and Hasegawa's rendition of the engine is a fair rendering of the actual locomotives.

media.caption: Vive La (ヴィヴ・ラ)

text.headline: Vive La (ヴィヴ・ラ)
text.text: This print is marked 見本 "sample print" in the upper left margin. The black ink marks (printer marks) in the lower left of the image area and the absence of  "ひで" (Hide in kana) in the circular area of the artist seal in the lower right corner of the image are consistent with a trial print not meant to be sold. This design was originally issued in a different color scheme in 1957 and then reissued for the second volume of the Kawanishi Hide Print Collection containing five "original" woodblock prints issued in 1980 by Keishōsha and edited by Hide's son Kawanishi Yuzaburō 川西祐三郎 (1923-2014).

media.caption: Wang Xiang, No. 7 [Catching Fish for His Stepmother in Winter]  (第七號王祥)

text.headline: Wang Xiang, No. 7 [Catching Fish for His Stepmother in Winter]  (第七號王祥)
text.text:
"Among the legends represented in the 24 Paragons of Filial Piety is the story of Wang Xiang (Osho), a third-century court official who, to fulfill his ill stepmother's craving for fresh fish in midwinter, caught some carp by lying on the ice until it melted. Wang Xiang is represented in the upper panel: his robe hangs from the branch of pine while a carp peeks through the hole he has made in the ice. This scene is reflected in the lower panel where a woman and a girl watch a fisherman wading in a lake beside a boat while a large carp leaps in front of him. The flowering cherry tree above them places this in the spring, rather than the winter. Print no. 7 of series." - Source: Claremont Colleges Digital Library https://ccdl.claremont.edu/digital/collection/cyw/id/278/rec/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

"[I]n the 1890s, Chikanobu began to show increasing concern for teaching moral values to the new generations, especially to women. Increasingly, women were seen as the protectors of Japanese customs and virtues, while men were expected to cope with Western influences and the modernization process taking place. Beginning in 1890-1891 with Juxtaposed Pictures of Twenty-four Paragons of Filial Piety [Nijūshi ko mitate awase) . . . , Chikanobu created a series of didactic images that encouraged traditional values found in filial piety, social hierarchies and restrained behavior." - Source: Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p.46.

media.caption: Tanzi, No. 10 [He Fed His Parent's Doe's Milk] (第十號剡子)

text.headline: Tanzi, No. 10 [He Fed His Parent's Doe's Milk] (第十號剡子)
text.text:
"These two pictures seem to be only tangentially related. At top Tanzi is dressed in deer hide so he could sneak into a herd of deer to get milk for his ailing parents. However, when a hunter was about to shoot the deer, Tanzi revealed his identity, shouting, “Don’t shoot!’ The larger image shows a boy being scolded by his mother for having upset the desk items, including brushes, books and a paper weight. What connects the two scenes is that both boys are wrapped in fur, but from the mother’s gestures and the little boy’s expression, the Japanese narrative seems unrelated to proper behavior."[1]
"[I]n the 1890s, Chikanobu began to show increasing concern for teaching moral values to the new generations, especially to women. Increasingly, women were seen as the protectors of Japanese customs and virtues, while men were expected to cope with Western influences and the modernization process taking place. Beginning in 1890-1891 with Juxtaposed Pictures of Twenty-four Paragons of Filial Piety [Nijūshi ko mitate awase) . . . Chikanobu created a series of didactic images that encouraged traditional values found in filial piety, social hierarchies and restrained behavior."[2]

[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p.156.
[2] Ibid., p. 46.

media.caption: Hotei from the book Kaiga kōshū roku (布袋・繪画講習録 第六回 第十二号)

text.headline: Hotei from the book Kaiga kōshū roku (布袋・繪画講習録 第六回 第十二号)
text.text:
The god of good fortune, happiness and laughter, Hotei, one of the seven shichifukujin (gods of good fortune), resting in his sack filled with toys and treasures for the flocks of children who swarm around him everywhere.
This print was included in the 6th book of the 12th volume of Kaiga kōshūroku (Painting training book), a series of correspondence training books teaching subscribers how to paint. Each issue contained five examples of paintings reproduced as woodblock prints, along with an explanation of each painting. The books were issued on a quarterly basis by Dai Nihon Kaiga Kōshūkai 大日本絵画講習会.

media.caption: Miyajima in Rain (雨の宮島)

text.headline: Miyajima in Rain (雨の宮島)
text.text: The artist's rendering of Itsukushima on Miyajima with Gojunoto (the Five-storied Pagoda) in the background and the famous Sika deer in the foreground during a gentle rain. The print was included in a portfolio titled 瀬戸内三題 (Three Subjects of Setouchi), issued by Watanabe Publishing in 1935, which included three woodblock prints designed by Ogyū.

media.caption: In Praise of the Harmonious Soga at Mount Fuji (和合曽我誉富士 Wagō Soga Homare no Fuji)

text.headline: In Praise of the Harmonious Soga at Mount Fuji (和合曽我誉富士 Wagō Soga Homare no Fuji)
text.text:
Three sheets of a possible pentatych portraying the actors, from right to left, Nakamura Fukusuke III 三代目中村福助 (1846-1888) as Minamoto no Yorimasa 源ノより朝, Onoe Tamizō II 二代目 尾上多見蔵 (1799-1886) as Kudō Saemon Suketsune 工藤左衛門祐経 and Jitsukawa Enjaku 実川延若 as Soga no Jūrō Sukenari 曽我十郎助成 in the play Wagō Soga Homare no Fuji, a variation of the epic tale of the revenge of the Soga Brothers, staged at Osaka's Kado-za in April 1875.

Osaka Region Prints - Kamigata-e (Osaka-e)
While Edo/Tokyo was the dominant center of woodblock print production, Osaka was an important regional production center focusing on the Osaka theater. Osaka actor prints (kamigata-e) took on a different, smaller (chūban-size) and less spectacular, appearance than those produced in Edo/Tokyo. While Edo audiences demanded their fire and brimstone, Osaka kabuki patrons craved intricate, heartrending plots.
Kawasaki Kyosen (1841-1899) the son of Yoshitaki and a print designer himself, provides a glimpse into the start of the design process in his account of the Osaka printmaking process, as follows:
"In those days, certain Osaka publishers set out to the theaters on opening day with the artists who drew actors’ likenesses. The dividers were removed from four or five boxes right in the middle of the floor section of the theater and spread with rugs. Tables were set up with brushes and paper, and all was made ready to sketch the happenings on stage. The artist sat in the middle, with the proprietor of the publishing house and his clerks alongside. Besides them, some first-class female entertainers managed the food and drink, so things were quite lively. This was a form of promotion, as much as to say that actor prints were being designed for this performance." – an account by the artist’s son, Kawasaki Kyosen (1841-1899) as translated in The Theatrical World of Osaka Prints, Roger S. Keyes and Keiko Mizushima, David R. Godine in association with Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1973 p. 318.

media.caption: Kikugorō in the role of Jūjirō (菊五郎 十次郎)

text.headline: Kikugorō in the role of Jūjirō (菊五郎 十次郎)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō VI in the role of Jūjirō in the play Ehon Taikōki 絵本大功記, staged at the Ichimura-za, Tokyo in June 1915. One of twelve prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Utaemon in the role of Agemak (歌右衛門の揚巻 Utaemon no Agemaki)

text.headline: Utaemon in the role of Agemak (歌右衛門の揚巻 Utaemon no Agemaki)
text.text:
The actor Nakamura Utaemon V in the role of of the courtesan Agemaki in the play Sukeroku performed in April 1915 at the Kabuki-za. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

media.caption: Terukuni (照國)

text.headline: Terukuni (照國)
text.text:
The sumo Terukuni Manzō 照國万藏 (1919-1977) from an untitled series of sumo portraits by the prolific and stylistically varied artist Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981), whose work bridged the sōsaku hanga and shin hanga movements. The wrestler pictured in this print, Terukuni Manzō, was promoted to the highest rank of yokozuna in 1942 and retired in 1953.
While this impression is not signed or sealed by the artist, other impressions carry both Gihachirō's signature and seal.

media.caption: Gamō Kunpei (蒲生君平)

text.headline: Gamō Kunpei (蒲生君平)
text.text:
Isoda constructs this fictional scene showing the writer and imperialist Gamō Kunpei (1768-1813) castigating the shogun, Tokugawa Ienari (1773-1841), on the poor state of the Imperial Tombs he surveyed in the late 18th century. Gamō subsequently published the "Sanryō shi" (Record of the Imperial Tombs) in 1808. His work prompted "members of the Sonnō Movement at the end of the Edo period to pressure the bakufu for better treatment of the tombs." - Source: "Contested Access: The Imperial Tombs in the Postwar Period" by Walter Edwards appearing in the Journal of Japanese Studies, Vol. 26, No. 2 (Summer, 2000), p. 377.

The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

media.caption: Hashimoto Sanai (橋本左内)

text.headline: Hashimoto Sanai (橋本左内)
text.text:
Shimada depicts the samurai philosopher Hashimoto Sanai (1834-1859) shortly before his execution at the age of 25. He sits at his desk reading his treatise Keihatsuroku 啓發録 (A Book of Resolutions or Treatise on Enlightenment) which he wrote at the age of 15 in 1848. Written on the panel against his bookcase in the upper right is 急流中底之柱、即是大丈夫之心 , a saying that Hashimoto treasured.

media.caption: Rai San'yō (頼山陽)

text.headline: Rai San'yō (頼山陽)
text.text:
Ōta portrays the Confucian scholar, historian and calligrapher Rai San'yō (1781-1832) with his widowed mother Baishi viewing the cherry blossoms at Mount Yoshino in Yamato in 1827. This fulfilled her desire to once more see the cherry blossoms before her death. While there, he pointed out to his mother Emperor Go-Daigo's (1288-1339) tomb, lamenting Go Daigo's failed attempt tin 1331 to overthrow the Kamakura Shogunate (1185-1333) and restore Imperial rule.

media.caption: Thomas Carlyle (カーライル)

text.headline: Thomas Carlyle (カーライル)
text.text:
One of fourteen prints in the series of color woodblock educational prints titled Legends of Great Westerners issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print depicts a distraught Thomas Carlyle, the English writer, historian and philosopher, rushing towards his burning manuscript, the first volume of his history of the French Revolution, while his dog looks on.
While the text on the print blames the burning of the manuscript on his dog knocking over a candle, it was in fact John Stuart Mill's maid who thought the manuscript, given to Mill by Carlyle, was scrap and burned it for kindling. Carlyle would go on to rewrite the first volume and complete two more volumes, publishing the three-volume work The French Revolution: A History in 1837, and establishing his reputation and one of the great intellectuals of the time.
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued full-color woodblock prints for childhood education between 1873 and 1885. The Ministry advertised these prints "As an aid to the education of the young child (yōdō) 幼童) within the home… use these pictures as a toy when the child is sitting or lying down. And when the child reaches the age to enter elementary school, the effect will be no small matter.” - Source: "Raising Subjects: The Representation of Children and Childhood in Meiji Japan," Rhiannon Paget an article from New Voices: A Journal for Emerging Scholars of Japanese Studies in Australia and New Zealand, Volume 4, 2011.

media.caption: Richard Arkwright (アークライト)

text.headline: Richard Arkwright (アークライト)
text.text:
One of fourteen prints in the series of color woodblock educational prints titled Legends of Great Westerners issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print depicts an angry Richard Arkwright (1732-1792), British inventor and industrialist, casting his wife out of house for destroying his model of the spinning frame.
Arkwright's 1768 spinning frame was the first textile machine designed to be water powered. There are various versions and embellishments to the story of Arkwright's wife smashing his model. Some have his wife, in fact his second wife Margaret Biggins, smashing many of his models, but they all mention that she was angered by the time and money he was spending on his models and wanted him to return to his earlier profession as a barber and wig-maker.
The newly formed Ministry of Education issued full-color woodblock prints for childhood education between 1873 and 1885. The Ministry advertised these prints "As an aid to the education of the young child (yōdō) 幼童) within the home… use these pictures as a toy when the child is sitting or lying down. And when the child reaches the age to enter elementary school, the effect will be no small matter.” - Source: "Raising Subjects: The Representation of Children and Childhood in Meiji Japan," Rhiannon Paget an article from New Voices: A Journal for Emerging Scholars of Japanese Studies in Australia and New Zealand, Volume 4, 2011.

media.caption: Kagoshima Shinbun: Illustration of the Battle of Yamagaguchi (鹿兒嶋新聞 山鹿口戰之圖 Kagoshima Shinbun・Yamagaguchi sensō no zu)

text.headline: Kagoshima Shinbun: Illustration of the Battle of Yamagaguchi (鹿兒嶋新聞 山鹿口戰之圖 Kagoshima Shinbun・Yamagaguchi sensō no zu)
text.text:
At least a dozen woodblock triptychs depicting various battles during the Satsuma Rebellion, issued by various publishers using the drawings of various artists, carry a cartouche reading "Kagoshima shinbun" (Kagoshima Newspaper) accompanied by the title of the battle being depicted and a descriptive scroll. While an actual newspaper called the Kagoshima shinbun would come into existence in the late 1880s, it had no relationship to these earlier prints and their publishers.
In this print by Adachi, one of several prints of the rebellion he designed, the battle of Yamagaguchi is depicted. The engagement being referenced is most likely the March 12 battle in the Nabeta-Yamaga area, about 30 km due north of Kagoshima Castle.
Translation of text on print: "As the Western insurgents made a name for themselves they stood momentarily poised to make good on their rebellion by resisting the Government forces. One of their fiercest commanders was no doubt Maehara Issei, a brigand chieftain and traitor to the nation who brought many a disturbance to the realm. This Issei’s youngest brother was Maehara Ikkaku. In the retreat from Hagi, he hid himself, and when the time came he joined the Kagoshima rioters. Wearing a white cloth over one shoulder with his name written on it, he rode at their head, attacking at Yamagaguchi. Perhaps the brigands’ luck had yet to run out, for he was unharmed even as he galloped around alone amid the vortex of Government soldiers, going back and forth under a rain of bullets. It was a ferocious battle truly Ikkaku may be called a mighty warrior. - Ōta Jō, editor"
Note: Maehara Ikkaku is the figure on horseback in the center of the composition. Hagi, in Yamaguchi Prefecture, was the site of a failed samurai rebellion in late 1876, a precursor to the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, of which the fighting at Yamagaguchi described here was a minor part. Despite the rebel heroics depicted in this print, the Government forces prevailed here as elsewhere. - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon)

media.caption: Ichiriki Teahouse (一力茶屋 Ichiriki chaya)

text.headline: Ichiriki Teahouse (一力茶屋 Ichiriki chaya)
text.text:
Three maiko in conversation outside the Ichiriki Chaya in Kyoto. The most famous teahouse in Japan, it figures prominently in the great early 18th century tale of revenge and honor, The Revenge of the Forty-Seven Rōnin.
At today's Ichiriki Chaya, only established guests are admitted and an evening's entertainment costs many thousands of dollars.
The series Life of Kyoto consists of six chuban-sized prints depicting activities and places in and around Kyoto. The series was published by an unknown publisher identified as 宮脇美風扇版 in the rectangular cartouche in the lower right margin of each print.

media.caption: Untitled abstract print

text.headline: Untitled abstract print
text.text: An abstract composiion by an unkown artist, employing woodblock technique with the addition of various objects to the blocks such as plant forms. The grain of the woodblock is put to effective use as the "eye" of the composition.

media.caption: Glaring Contest  (睨シ子)

text.headline: Glaring Contest  (睨シ子)
text.text:
Two figures square off against each other in a glaring contest ( 睨ッ子)* accompanied by a verbal battle recorded in the upper left of the print between the "man on the right" (人ノ右) and the "man on the left" (人ノ左), perhaps a reference to their political positions. The print is neither signed or sealed and is not dated. It appears to be a ponchi-e (political cartoon).

* 睨ッ子 is a slang term originating from the Kansai dialect. It is typically read as "niramikko" and refers to the act of glaring at someone to intimidate or express anger. It is used to describe the action of furrowing one's brow or narrowing their eyes while staring.

media.caption: Illustration of [The Emperor’s Carriage] Departing the Imperial Palace [over] Nijūbashi (宮城御出門貳重橋圖)

text.headline: Illustration of [The Emperor’s Carriage] Departing the Imperial Palace [over] Nijūbashi (宮城御出門貳重橋圖)
text.text: While the red sky may seem glaring, red became the color of modernity during the early years of the Meiji era, and this print's red sky heralds the departure of the Emperor and Empress from the Imperial Palace after the promulgation of the constitution ceremony in the main hall of the Meiji Palace on February 11, 1889. The Emperor and Empress are headed for the military parade at the Aoyama Drill Hall. In the center of the print is Nijūbashi Bridge and in the upper right is the Imperial Palace.

media.caption: Nizaemon in the role of Gonpachi (仁左衛門 権八)

text.headline: Nizaemon in the role of Gonpachi (仁左衛門 権八)
text.text:
The actor Kataoka Nizaemon XI in the role of Shirai Gonpachi 白井権八 likely in the play Kamiko Jitate Ryōmen Kagami. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.
