media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Sendo Tonbei in the play Miracle and Yaguchi Ferry (市川団十郎・ 船頭頓兵衛・ 神霊矢口渡)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Sendo Tonbei in the play Miracle and Yaguchi Ferry (市川団十郎・ 船頭頓兵衛・ 神霊矢口渡)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as the evil ferryman Tonbei in the play Shinrei Yaguchi no watashi (Miracle and Yaguchi Ferry). In keeping with the rest of the series, extensive embossing is employed in the background and mica was applied to the upper black background and Tonbei's hair and beard.
In the play's most famous scene, Yoshimine Nitta, who was escaping from pursuers sent by his enemy, and his lover, Utena, visited the house of Tonbee [Tonbei], a ferryman, for a one night stay. Tonbee had betrayed the Nitta family, which he used to serve, and killed one of Yoshimine’s older brothers, Yoshioki. Now Tonbee saw his chance to also kill the younger brother. But, despite Tonbee’s scheme, his daughter, Ofune, fell in love with Yoshimine at first sight. She betrayed her father and let Yoshimine and Utena get away in order to protect the one she loved. Her outraged father than killed her.

One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits. A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

media.caption: Rough Tales of the Floating World told on Eastern Brocades:  Araki Mataemon Yoshimura, Sekiguchi Yatarō,, Kimura Matazō, Musashibō Benkei (東錦浮世稿談・荒木又右エ門吉村・関口弥太郎・木村又藏・武蔵坊辨慶)

text.headline: Rough Tales of the Floating World told on Eastern Brocades:  Araki Mataemon Yoshimura, Sekiguchi Yatarō,, Kimura Matazō, Musashibō Benkei (東錦浮世稿談・荒木又右エ門吉村・関口弥太郎・木村又藏・武蔵坊辨慶)
text.text:
Four small prints depicting four heroic and fierce figures from Japanese history printed on a single ōban-size sheet, intended to be cut apart. Toshikata's four small prints model his teacher's, Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), earlier full ōban-size designs published as part of a 50 print series bearing the same title Azuma nishiki ukiyo kōdan ("Rough Tales of the Floating World told on Eastern Brocades") as do these four small prints.
The four figures pictured are, as follows:
top right: Mataemon Araki Yoshimura 荒木又右エ門吉村 (1599-1638), a master of the art of the sword, with the head Kawai Matagorō at his feet.
top left: Sekiguchi Yatarō 関口弥太郎 (1640-1729) staring down a pack of wolves in the Hakone Mountains.
bottom right: Kimura Matazō 木村又藏 (lived c. 1600) holding a yari (straight-headed spear), looking at distant fighting.
bottom left: Musashibō Benkei 武蔵坊辨慶 (1155-1189) pretending to read the contents of an empty scroll to be allowed safe passage through the Ataka barrier.

media.caption: Zen-2

text.headline: Zen-2
text.text:
A beautiful composition consisting of the characters 放下 (hōge, a Zen term for casting off one's attachments) above a separately printed irregularly shaped overturned black bowl with two splotches of gold. The overturned black bowl was separately printed and then laminated to a heavy sheet of fine cream-colored paper. The bowl stands out in relief, looking to be deeply embossed, but there is no sign of embossing on the verso.
In regards to these separately printed objects, Daniel Tretiak in his book "The Life and Works of Haku Maki" quotes a friend of Maki's as saying "Once Maki sensei told me that he had difficulties in making prints without any black ink dots in the white space, and he found this new technique - cutting the printed bowl and pasting it on the paper. He said it was a very happy way for him to make clean prints successfully. So, I think he made blocks, printed each image, cut each image and pasted it on the clean paper with his unique technique. As to the characters, I believe them to be stenciled on the print."
In the early 1960s Maki developed his own process of relief printmaking using woodblocks and cement. He first carved a conventional woodblock and then placed a cement mixture around the areas raised in relief on the block. Before the cement was set, Maki would texture it and after it dried he carved and chiseled the cement into the desired shape. After the cement completely dried, the entire surface of the plate was shellacked.

media.caption: Soba Deliveryman (蕎麦の出前もち Soba no demae-mochi)

text.headline: Soba Deliveryman (蕎麦の出前もち Soba no demae-mochi)
text.text:
In this second edition of the print Soba Deliveryman from Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Series 2, a soba deliveryman, his delicious hot and cold soba dishes stacked to the sky, peddles down the street on his way to his customers.
The English language commentary accompanying this post-war edition reads, "A Delivery Boy (Demai-mochi). The Japanese like 'Soba' and 'Udon' which are something like spaghetti and macaroni [sic]. The udon shop delivers the dishes when ordered, and several kinds of containers are used. You see a delivery boy on his bicycle, holding a stack of bowls or trays, cases, sauce-bottles and cups with his left hand, and steering the bicycle with a single hand, just like trick-riding seen in the circus. Depicted by Sanzo Wada. Printed by KYOTO-HANGA-IN."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

media.caption: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 2 (日清戦闘畫報 第四編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daini hen)

text.headline: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 2 (日清戦闘畫報 第四編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daini hen)
text.text: Volume 2 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

media.caption: Spring (untitled)

text.headline: Spring (untitled)
text.text: This collection contains two almost identical prints by the artist using the same woodblocks, with minor modifications, IHL.1091, titled Spring, and this untitled print IHL.1985. In these prints Chizuko presents two tilting city landscapes. In this untitled print (IHL.1985), Chizuko has shifted the position of the chain of heart-shaped objects to the right and darkened the background.  Additional marks, most noticeable in the lower left of the image have also been made. Known for her later prints featuring myriads of butterflies, there may be one flitting about in the upper left quadrant of both these prints.

media.caption: Kamigata shumi (Kamigata Taste), 1921, Autumn Issue  (上方趣味 大正十年 秋の巻 Kamigata shumi, Taishō jūnen, aki no maki)

text.headline: Kamigata shumi (Kamigata Taste), 1921, Autumn Issue  (上方趣味 大正十年 秋の巻 Kamigata shumi, Taishō jūnen, aki no maki)
text.text:
Featured in this October 1921 issue of the magazine "Kamigata shumi" (Kamigata taste) were works of the Ōsaka artist Ogami Nanryō 小上南嶺 (1893-1966) and the long dead Kyōto bijinga painter Gion Seitoku 祇園井特 (active 1789-1830). Ogami designed the magazine's woodblock printed cover of an ant crawling on an andon (Japanese paper lamp) titled "Autumn Night" (秋の夜) along with an inserted woodblock print titled "Otsuta" (お蔦). Gion was represented by an inserted woodblock reproduction of what must have been his original painting, simply titled "Kyōto Bijin" (京美人).

KAMIGATA SHUMI (source: website of the Osaka Prefectural Library https://www.library.pref.osaka.jp/nakato/shotenji/24_shumi.html [accessed 8-17-23]
"Kamigata shumi," edited and published by Watanabe Ryō (渡邊亮), was a long running (146 volumes) small magazine filled with "content related to customs, legends, traditions, specialties, travelogues, and performing arts from various places in Kamigata [the Kyōto-Ōsaka area]."
Setting out the intent of the magazine in its first issue in April 1915, Watanabe wrote, "We intend to publish this magazine with the aim of igniting the passion of Kamigata taste against Edo taste . . . ." The magazine's small size made it easy to carry and read, and to make it easier on the reader the main text was annotated with furigana.
A diverse group of authors including Watanabe himself, writing under the name Watanabe Shisen 渡辺紫染 (birth and death dates unknown), Udagawa Bunkai 宇田川文海 (1848-1930), Ema Tsutomu 江馬務 (1884-1979), Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950), Takaya Shin 高谷伸 (1896-1966) and Takayasu Gekkō 高安月郊 (1869-1944), contributed stories and articles.

media.caption: Matsushima (松島)

text.headline: Matsushima (松島)
text.text:
Okuyama's rendering of Matsushima's Godaidō Temple 五大堂 (temple of Five Great Wisdom Kings) in snow. This small temple sits on a small island in Matsushima Bay, attached to the mainland by Sukashibashi bridge. It has been named an Important Cultural Property. As written in the right margin of the print, the printer of this image was the artist's son Okuyama Gijin 奥山義人 (1934-2020), who took over management of his father's studio in 1973.

Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) artist and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own landscapes such as this print and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

media.caption: Eight Phases of the Life of Shakyamuni, a Japanese Library, v. 32, 2nd part (釈迦八相倭文庫 三拾二編 下 Shaka hassō Yamato bunko dai 3 hen 2)

text.headline: Eight Phases of the Life of Shakyamuni, a Japanese Library, v. 32, 2nd part (釈迦八相倭文庫 三拾二編 下 Shaka hassō Yamato bunko dai 3 hen 2)
text.text: "Eight Phases of the Life of Shakyamuni, a Japanese Library (Shaka hassō Yamato bunko) was published as a serialized novel in fifty-eight installments from 1845 to 1871. While the author of the series, Mantei Ōga (born 1819 and died 1890 in Edo/Tokyo), loosely based the story on the biography of the Buddha in India, he presented episodes from the life of the Buddha (Shakyamuni in Sanskrit) and his disciples as dramatic scenes recast mostly from images of popular entertainment culture of the day. Critical reviews of the time complained about how distant the tales were from Buddhist canonical traditions." - Source: Sherry Fowler, Kansas State University, Beach Museum of Art

media.caption: A Brief Description of World Geography (Compiled by Uchida Masao),  Africa, first of three, vol. 8 ([內田正雄纂輯]・輿地誌略 三篇上 巻八 亜非利加州 Yochi shiryaku・Uchida Masao sanshū, 3-shū, jō, kan 8, Afurica shū)

text.headline: A Brief Description of World Geography (Compiled by Uchida Masao),  Africa, first of three, vol. 8 ([內田正雄纂輯]・輿地誌略 三篇上 巻八 亜非利加州 Yochi shiryaku・Uchida Masao sanshū, 3-shū, jō, kan 8, Afurica shū)
text.text:
Volume 8 of an eventual 13 volumes of the geography textbook Yochi shiryaku (1870-1880). Volume 8 covers Africa.

Yochi shiryaku was the most widely used world geography textbook in the early Meiji era, compiled by former Edo Government officer, Uchida Masao. Uchida was sent to Europe from 1862 to 1866 by the Tokugawa government, to gather information to compile these lavishly illustrated textbooks. He returned to Japan with oil paintings, photographic albums, and hundreds of pictorial natural history images. Based upon the sources he collected on his travels, Uchida began to compile the Yochi Shiryaku in 1870, a thirteen-volume of encyclopedia of world geography. Its success was primarily due to the huge number of illustrations that Uchida called "shashin (photography)," the images copied from the Western photographic albums and traveling magazines by the artist Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827/1828-1881/1882) who turned them into copperplate illustrations. Yochi shiryaku was published in various editions over ten years and used in schools all over Japan, as well as being widely read as the book of "enlightenment." After Uchida's death, volumes 10 through 13 were compiled by the educator Nishimura Shigeki 西村 茂樹 (1828-1902), a colleague at the Ministry of Education, based on Uchida’s draft.
A premise of Yochi shiryaku was the existence of "a finely ordered hierarchy of peoples and states," with racial differences [the physical features and geographical dissemination of the "five human races" being described] being an "important factor underlying this hierarchical arrangement." - Source: "The Race and Racism Discourses in Modern Korea, 1890s—1910s," Vladimir Tikhonov, appearing in "Korean Studies, 2012, Vol. 36," University of Hawai'i Press, 2012, p. 41.

media.caption: Maru-maru chinbun 團團珍聞, No. 937 (Blue Pencil News of the Weird)

text.headline: Maru-maru chinbun 團團珍聞, No. 937 (Blue Pencil News of the Weird)
text.text:
Maru-maru chinbun was a popular satirical journal published weekly from 1877 to 1907. It was founded by Nomura Fumio 野村文夫 (1836-91), a former official of the Meiji government and journalist, in the style of the British weekly magazine of satire and humour, Punch. Maru-maru chinbun satirised the government with its editorial articles, comic tanka and haiku poems, and caricatures and promoted the Movement for Civil Rights and Freedom in the 1880s.
Like Tokyo Puck and Jiji manga, Maru-maru chinbun was a landmark in the history of manga. Published weekly from 1877 to 1907, it was patterned after the British Punch in its mixture of satirical essays, poems, and cartoons. The famous cover design, too, was reminiscent of Punch, but with Japanese twists everywhere. The horse and deer, for example, were meant to suggest the word baka – written with the characters for “horse” and “deer” but meaning “idiot.”
The title itself involves several puns. Maru-maru literally means “circle-circle,” and refers to the empty circles often printed in lieu of words deemed offensive by censors. Chinbun puns on shinbun or “newspaper,” with “outlandish” substituted for “new.” Thus the title may be thought of as “[censored] News of the Weird.” (“Blue Pencil News” is scholar W. Puck Brecher’s solution.) The magazine was subtitled Odoke-e or “clownish pictures,” but written with characters that mean “Pictures of Tokyo,” a reference to the new capital’s status as the center of the nation’s political life and the magazine’s mission to lampoon it.
source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon)

source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon)

media.caption: Maru-maru chinbun 團團珍聞, No. 946 (Blue Pencil News of the Weird)

text.headline: Maru-maru chinbun 團團珍聞, No. 946 (Blue Pencil News of the Weird)
text.text:
Maru-maru chinbun was a popular satirical journal published weekly from 1877 to 1907. It was founded by Nomura Fumio 野村文夫 (1836-91), a former official of the Meiji government and journalist, in the style of the British weekly magazine of satire and humour, Punch. Maru-maru chinbun satirised the government with its editorial articles, comic tanka and haiku poems, and caricatures and promoted the Movement for Civil Rights and Freedom in the 1880s.
Like Tokyo Puck and Jiji manga, Maru-maru chinbun was a landmark in the history of manga. Published weekly from 1877 to 1907, it was patterned after the British Punch in its mixture of satirical essays, poems, and cartoons. The famous cover design, too, was reminiscent of Punch, but with Japanese twists everywhere. The horse and deer, for example, were meant to suggest the word baka – written with the characters for “horse” and “deer” but meaning “idiot.”
The title itself involves several puns. Maru-maru literally means “circle-circle,” and refers to the empty circles often printed in lieu of words deemed offensive by censors. Chinbun puns on shinbun or “newspaper,” with “outlandish” substituted for “new.” Thus the title may be thought of as “[censored] News of the Weird.” (“Blue Pencil News” is scholar W. Puck Brecher’s solution.) The magazine was subtitled Odoke-e or “clownish pictures,” but written with characters that mean “Pictures of Tokyo,” a reference to the new capital’s status as the center of the nation’s political life and the magazine’s mission to lampoon it.
source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon)

media.caption: Stone Pagodas (石塔)

text.headline: Stone Pagodas (石塔)
text.text: The series title Eight Views of the Land of the Morning Calm is a reference to the famous Eight Views of Korea, consisting of areas of scenic beauty or historical importance. Kurosaki takes a different tack with his eight views, providing us with "views" encompassing traditional Korean dress to pagodas.

media.caption: Shichimenzan and Mount Fuji (七面山と富士)

text.headline: Shichimenzan and Mount Fuji (七面山と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print the sun rises above Fuji as a family who has made the climb up Mount Shichimen looks on. During the equinoxes, it appears as though the sun is rising out of Fuji's crater and this view may be set during the autumn equinox. Two pilgrims can be seen in the bottom left heading down the mountain. The signboard on the right reads 日天子 遙拝所 月天子 七面山 and there is a round directional finder to the left of the family indicating the four cardinal directions.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: Spring Field A (春の野 A)

text.headline: Spring Field A (春の野 A)
text.text: A combining of abstract organic forms, discernible as a freshly plowed field, and a grouping of trees, make for a lovely composition.

media.caption: The Rural Cottages in Onuma and Mount Fuji (小沼の田家と富士)

text.headline: The Rural Cottages in Onuma and Mount Fuji (小沼の田家と富士)
text.text:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. When this print was published, cottages such as the one depicted in this print, with its small shrine and waterwheel, were common. Today the area around Onuma, located in Nishikatsura, Minamitsuru-gun (Yamanashi) about 49 mi (or 78 km) west of Tokyo, is a bustling suburb.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

media.caption: Asakusa Battledore Fair (浅草羽子板市 Asakusa hagoita ichi)

text.headline: Asakusa Battledore Fair (浅草羽子板市 Asakusa hagoita ichi)
text.text:
The artist's rendering of the annual three-day Battledore Fair that takes place each year in Asakusa starting on December 17. Koga gives us a view of the bottom tiers of the Five Story Pagoda of Sensoji, the stalls selling hagoita 羽子板 and the crowds.
This print was one of twenty five included in a portfolio of woodblock prints titled Lyricism of Shitamachi 下町抒情 published by Han no kai, the print society formed by Tadashige Ono (1909-1990) to encourage and support young artists. Tadashige contributed three prints to the portfolio and twenty-one other little-known artists contributed prints.
Shitamachi was the name used to designate Tokyo's "low city," an area associated with the common people before the war. In post-war terminology it designates everything east of the Imperial Palace. It is also used more generically to refer to those areas of modern Tokyo that maintain the flavor of the old city.

media.caption: Village Blacksmith

text.headline: Village Blacksmith
text.text: A kappizuri-e (stencil prints) depicting a village blacksmith or farrier at work while a horse looks on.

media.caption: The Wheel of Causation, Volumes 21 and 22 (編童謡妙々車 21編, 22編 Warabeuta myōmyō guruma)

text.headline: The Wheel of Causation, Volumes 21 and 22 (編童謡妙々車 21編, 22編 Warabeuta myōmyō guruma)
text.text: Volumes 21 and 22 of the 25 volume illustrated novel (kusazōshi 草双紙) Warabeuta myōmyō guruma, originally published between 1855 and 1871 by the Edo/Tokyo publisher Tsutaya Kichizō of the firm Kōeidō. While volumes 21 and 22 were originally issued in 1867 this collection's edition was issued in 1874. Commonly translated as The Wheel of Causation, the story revolves around the romantic adventures of Princess Uzuki and the hero Shidoroku. While written for the masses, the heavily illustrated kusazōshi have been called "a crucial element in the production of modern literary idiom" and "a unique form of verbal-visual art" deserving "to be treated as a national cultural heritage." - Source: "Eyes of the Heart: Illustration and the Visual Imagination in Modern Japanese Literature" [a dissertation], Pedro Thiago Ramos Bassoe, University of California, Berkeley, 2018, p. 1.

media.caption: Scenic View of Tokyo, Ueno Park Tōshō-gū Shrine (東京名所上野公園地東照宮 Tōkyō meisho Ueno kōenchi Tōshō gū)

text.headline: Scenic View of Tokyo, Ueno Park Tōshō-gū Shrine (東京名所上野公園地東照宮 Tōkyō meisho Ueno kōenchi Tōshō gū)
text.text: It is spring and the cherry trees are in bloom as two women and a child all dressed in Western fashion are  strolling through Tokyo's Tōshō-gū Shrine. The shrine dedicated to shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616) and founded  in 1627, has been spared the many natural and man-caused disasters that have visited Tokyo and today remains largely unchanged from its renovation in 1651. The trio likely entered the grounds through Karamon gate, seen in the left sheet. Five small figures, three priests and two groundskeepers, can also be seen. While the print is a "scenic view" of this Tokyo landmark, the real scenic view is the high-fashion Western dress of the women and child.

media.caption: Sarusawa Pond (猿沢池)

text.headline: Sarusawa Pond (猿沢池)
text.text: Sarusawa Pond in Nara on a rainy day. One of the most popular subjects for shin hanga print artists. "This pond is located within Nara Park, and has a circumference of 360 meters. The five-storied pagoda of Kofuku-ji Temple, as well as the willow trees surrounding the pond reflect beautifully in its surface, and are recognized as one of the Eight Views of Nara."- website of Nara Travelers Guide https://narashikanko.or.jp/en/spot/nature/sarusawaike/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Play A Board Game of the Road to Iga Pass, Act IX  (伊賀越道中双六, 九 Igagoe dōchū sugoroku, kyū)

text.headline: Play A Board Game of the Road to Iga Pass, Act IX  (伊賀越道中双六, 九 Igagoe dōchū sugoroku, kyū)
text.text:
This print depicts Act IX of Igagoe dōchū sugoroku, one of the three great revenge plays, along with Kanadehon Chūshingura and Soga no Taimen, in Japanese literature. In this scene we see Otani おたに, ill and clutching her baby, outside of her husband's (Karake Masaemon 唐木政右衛門 - the real life Araki Mataemon) house in Okazaki. Seated beside Masaemon is the wife of samurai Sawai Matagorō, who is the object of revenge. The orange rectangular cartouche in the upper left reads 岡崎の浪宅に政右衛門不計妻お谷に廻逢図, describing the scene being illustrated.
This play was originally written for the bunraku theater in 1783 by Chikamatsu Hanji (1725-1783) and is often seen titled as Numazu after its often performed Act VI. The sugoroku in the title references a board game that incorporated the stations along the Tōkaidō highway running from Edo to Kyoto. Samuel Leiter in his "New Kabuki Encyclopedia: A Revised Adaptation of Kabuki Jiten" provides the following commentary on the play:
"Igagoe deals with the vengeance wrought by Araki Mataemon. The original play’s most distinctive feature was that each of its ten acts represented another stage on the journey along the Tokaido Highway from Edo to Kyoto. Only Act VI’s “Numazu” scene and the VIII’s “Okazaki” scene are still regularly performed.
"The actual vendetta was carried out in 1634 at Iga Ueno, located between Nagoya and Nara, on Kawai Matagorō by Watanabe Kazuma and his master swordsman brother-in-law, Araki Mataemon. The deed occurred four years after Kazuma’s father, Watanabe Yukie of the house of Lord Tadao Ikeda of Okayama, was killed by Matagorō, a retainer of lord of Koremori. The dramatists, as usual, have taken liberties with names, places, and events. The play is a complexly woven tragedy in which numerous loyalties and obligations crisscross with one another among a host of characters." - Source: New Kabuki Encyclopedia: A Revised Adaptation of Kabuki Jiten, Samuel Leiter, Greenwood Press, 1997, p. 211-212

media.caption: Oirasegawa (奥入瀬川)

text.headline: Oirasegawa (奥入瀬川)
text.text:
In the summer 1932 Yasui, considered one of Japan’s most respected Western-style (yōga) painters from the1930s through his death in 1955, stayed at Lake Towada and produced several works under the auspices of the Kokuritsu Kōen Kyōkai (National Park Association.) On his way back home he created a number of sketches of the Oirase River which drains Lake Towada.
This woodblock print is likely a reproduction of one of the sketches of the river he created on this trip.

media.caption: Karuizawa Station (軽井沢駅)

text.headline: Karuizawa Station (軽井沢駅)
text.text: The artist's rendering of the old Karuizawa Station built in 1910 and closed c. 1999 to make way for the new station handling high speed shinkansen services from Tokyo. The old building was relocated and turned into a museum. Recently, there has been discussion of using the building for new station facilities.

media.caption: Former Mikasa House (旧三笠ハウス)

text.headline: Former Mikasa House (旧三笠ハウス)
text.text: The artist's rendering of the 1905 Mikasa Hotel in Karuizawa in Nagano, now a museum.

media.caption: Karuizawa Kōgen Church (軽井沢高原教会)

text.headline: Karuizawa Kōgen Church (軽井沢高原教会)
text.text: The artist's rendering of Karuizawa Kōgen Church built in 1921.

media.caption: Saruwaka Performance by the Descendants of Nakamura Kanzaburō (猿若狂言 Saruwaka kyōgen)

text.headline: Saruwaka Performance by the Descendants of Nakamura Kanzaburō (猿若狂言 Saruwaka kyōgen)
text.text:
One of two prints designed by Torii Kiyosada for this twenty-five print series (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater. This print depicts the comic dance pantomime known as saruwaka kyōgen.
Saruwaka kyōgen is a dance in the style of the kyōgen of the No theatre that found its way into Kabuki. The earliest kabuki saruwaka involved the actor’s participation in chaya asahi (“visit to a teahouse”) scenes, in which a dashing fellow (played by Okuni) went to a teahouse accompanied by his servant, the saruwaka, who wore a tenugui kerchief covering his cheeks; a rough, wide-sleeved, single layer kimon (hitoe), and leggings (kyahan). The plot involved the star’s encounter with the teahouse proprietress (kaka), played by a kyōgen actor (the kyōgenshi). There was a banquet and the characters sang and danced a kouta.
Kiyosada copied this design from one of the earlier Torii masters, Torii Kiyonaga (1752-1815).

media.caption: Bird (鳥)

text.headline: Bird (鳥)
text.text: The first of ten prints in the first of five sets of prints comprising the series Outdoor Sketches created by the artist between 1928 and 1935.  In this print a man relaxes on a hillside as a flock of birds flies by. Maekawa created this series of five sets (ten prints each set) of black and white linoleum cuts as, in the artist's words, prints of affection (shin'ai ban).  Each small print, its image area measuring approximately 5 x 5 in. (12.7 x 12.7 cm), depicts a figure engaged in outdoor work or recreation.

media.caption: Parasol (パラソル)

text.headline: Parasol (パラソル)
text.text: The sixth of ten prints in the first of five sets of prints comprising the series Outdoor Sketches created by the artist between 1928 and 1935.  In this print a woman in a bobbed haircut leans against a railing on what might be a boardwalk with a parasol resting lightly on her shoulder. Maekawa created this series of five sets (ten prints each set) of black and white linoleum cuts as, in the artist's words, prints of affection (shin'ai ban).  Each small print, its image area measuring approximately 5 x 5 in. (12.7 x 12.7 cm), depicts a figure engaged in outdoor work or recreation.

media.caption: Music at Winter Garden in New York

text.headline: Music at Winter Garden in New York
text.text: An Art Deco style portrayal of a lively singing performance, accompanied by a live orchestra, at New York's Winter Garden, the iconic venue for musical reviews and theater in the Broadway theater district. Dispatched on a three year around-the-world print fact finding mission in 1926, New York certainly would have been on Yamagishi's itinerary. While the date 1930 is written in pencil on this print's verso, Yamagishi presents us with a scene, imagined or real, prior to 1928, before the theater was brought under the management of Warner Bros. (1928-1933) and used exclusively for cinema.

media.caption: February (二月) calendar page from the 1941 Japan Print Association Calendar

text.headline: February (二月) calendar page from the 1941 Japan Print Association Calendar
text.text:
Fujimori, a founding member of the Nihon Hanga Kyōkai (Japan Print Association) in 1931, contributed this print of a cricket on a branch to the 2601 calendar issued by the JPA. 2601, counting since the mythical beginning of Japan in 660 BCE, translates to 1941, a year that would find Japan attacking Pearl Harbor in December.
The JPA calendars were issued from Showa 11 (1936) through Showa 19 (1944).

media.caption: Shinjuku Imperial Gardens (新宿御苑 Shinjuku Gyoen)

text.headline: Shinjuku Imperial Gardens (新宿御苑 Shinjuku Gyoen)
text.text:
Kitaoka presents us with one of the many tree-lined promenades in this now public garden that contains over 10,000 trees. This undated artist's proof, signed in pencil by Kitaoka, likely dates from 1950 and was released as part of the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio (each portfolio containing five prints), titled The Face of Tokyo 東京の顔.
This artist proof appears identical to the print in the collection of The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo. However, it is printed on different paper than the other four prints from The Face of Tokyo in this collection which are printed on a distinctive mica-impregnated paper.
This beautifully designed and, unfortunately, overlooked series portrays post-war Tokyo in the social-realist style that Kitaoka embraced after the war and later rejected. For other prints in this series see IHL.0626 "Around Ochanomizu (Kanda River)", IHL.0640 "Playing Bingo", IHL.0641 "Outside Shinjuku Station, the West Exit" and IHL.0642 "Behind the Stage".

media.caption: Work '66 (作品 '66)

text.headline: Work '66 (作品 '66)
text.text: A tiny print with an image area measuring 2 1/4 x 2 5/8 in. (5.7 x 6.7 cm). Takahashi's compositions work well at this small size, inviting even closer scrutiny than his better known large works.

media.caption: B3

text.headline: B3
text.text: A tiny print with an image area measuring 2 1/4 x 2 5/8 in. It's amazing that Takahashi's compositions work so well as this small size, inviting even closer scrutiny than his better known large works.

media.caption: Portrait of a Woman (watercolor on paper)

text.headline: Portrait of a Woman (watercolor on paper)
text.text: While most famous for his prints, Hagiwara trained as a painter and continued to produce paintings, both small (as in this painting) and large, in both oil and watercolor (as in this work) throughout his printmaking career.

media.caption: Nanban Dining (untitled) an Ex-Libris for S. Kagayama

text.headline: Nanban Dining (untitled) an Ex-Libris for S. Kagayama
text.text: Like a number of other sōsaku hanga artists, Kawakami created numerous bookplates for collectors. In this ex libris 蔵書票 created for the collector S. Kagayama, we see five Nanban gentlemen seated around a table eating and drinking, as they're being waited upon.  Kawakami was fascinated by Nanban (southern barbarians, i.e., Portuguese) culture, producing many woodblock prints on the subject.

media.caption: Woman with Apples (untitled) an Ex-Libris made for  S. Kagayama

text.headline: Woman with Apples (untitled) an Ex-Libris made for  S. Kagayama

Three of the bookplates show the collector's name in kanji characters, either 加賀山 (Kagayama) or 加賀山 蔵書 (Kagayama library) and the other two provide the collector's name in English, either Kagayama or S. media.caption: Triangular Hood (三角頭巾 Sankaku zukin)

text.headline: Triangular Hood (三角頭巾 Sankaku zukin)
text.text: Maekawa produced a number of prints of Japanese country women in similar poses.

media.caption: Hello, Ms Mao (毛さん今日は)

text.headline: Hello, Ms Mao (毛さん今日は)
text.text: "This series is like a report on China. Woodblock printing originated in China, and I had wanted to visit there for a long time, but due to the unstable political situation I was unable to do so. In these prints, I could make good use of video and photographic print techniques while also using Chinese history, culture, written characters, seals, and traditional Chinese composition to establish a new style and changes in my work." - the artist Kurosaki Akira

media.caption: Roof Landscape (屋根の風景 Yane no fūkei)

text.headline: Roof Landscape (屋根の風景 Yane no fūkei)
text.text: Rooftops of one of the stately neighborhoods in Kyoto. If we need a hint that this view is of Kyoto roofs, the copula on the left carries the characters 西陣, telling us these roofs are in Kyoto's famous Nishijin district, known for its townhouses, machiya, and traditional weaving and textiles.

media.caption: Scenes of the Inner Provinces, Yamato (Nara), Volume 2 (畿内見物 大和の卷 Kinai kenbutsu Yamato no maki)

text.headline: Scenes of the Inner Provinces, Yamato (Nara), Volume 2 (畿内見物 大和の卷 Kinai kenbutsu Yamato no maki)
text.text: Volume two of the three volume set of "sketch tour" books titled Kinai kenbutsu (Scenes of the Inner Provinces), published by Kanao Tanejirō (1879-1947) (the publishing house Bunendō) in 1911 and 1912.1 Volume 1, subtitled Kyōto, and volume 2, subtitled Yamato (Nara), were issued in 1911 and the third volume, subtitled Ōsaka, in 1912. The three volumes contain 57 stitched-in woodblock prints, as well as woodblock printed covers, end papers and slipcases, all but one of the woodblock designs by the Western-style artist Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964). While photogravure, and halftone and heliotype (collotype) reproductions of paintings and sketches by Hiromitsu, and a single heliotype of a painting by Asai Chū (1856-1907), far outnumber the woodblock prints, the quality of these reproductions varies and the true highlight of these volumes are the woodblock prints. See IHL.2398 for volume 1.

media.caption: I Love You B

text.headline: I Love You B
text.text: Ay-O derived I Love You B from his own silkscreen work of 1974 titled I Love You (Love Letters) (see IHL.1472), and Marcel Duchamp's Étant donnés (1946-1966), an assemblage containing a headless woman mannequin. The Artist Comments, "I love you B combines the Mexican fellow's garments, a nude and a gas lamp said to be made of pig hide held in the hands of a headless woman's torso suggested by Duchamp's last work [Etant donnés] owned by the Philadelphia Art Museum, repeated in a pattern along with parallel lines. A part of this work I titled Portrait of Yoshiaki Tono [art critic]." - Source: AY-O’s Rainbow Prints Catalogue Raisonne 1954-1979, Sadajirō Kubo, Sohbun-sha, p. 160.

media.caption: Shade of a Tree

text.headline: Shade of a Tree
text.text: This color lithograph was issued at the same time as Measure and Pig (IHL.2037), picturing a pig, possibly prior to a trip to slaughter house. The yellow pig in this print, standing among the foliage, seems quite unaware of what fate may hold in store.

media.caption: Measure and Pig

text.headline: Measure and Pig
text.text: Issued at the same time as Shade of a Tree (IHL.2036), which pictures a seemingly contented pig under green foliage, one wonders if Ida is presenting us with that pig's fate, being measured for the slaughter.

media.caption: Battleship Island (軍艦島 Gunkanjima)

text.headline: Battleship Island (軍艦島 Gunkanjima)
text.text:
The caption on the inside of this New Year's greeting card, signed S. Takagi, Mitsubishi Mining Co., Ltd., President, reads:
"A view of the 'Battleship Island.' 500,000 tons of best coking coal annually are produced here from the working faces 2,400 feet below the sea. The island [Hashima] is a part of the Mitsubishi's Takashima Coal Mine, one of the oldest coal mines in Japan and yet being developed on the most modern lines."
Left unmentioned is the use of forced labor during wartime by Mitsubishi, including the use of forced Korean labor during World War II to extract coal. At least 800 Koreans were sent to Hashima during the war, 134 of whom reportedly died while working there.
Even for the Japanese who worked at the mine it was a harsh environment and by the end of the war in August 1945 about 1,300 laborers had died on the island, some in underground accidents, others of illnesses related to exhaustion and malnutrition and some drowning while trying to escape from the island which lies in the East China Sea some fifteen kilometers from Nagasaki.

media.caption: New Skin (新膚 Shin hada)

text.headline: New Skin (新膚 Shin hada)
text.text: This print was originally created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) Han geijutsu (Print Art), Volume 1, No. 5 published in August 1932 in Tokyo by Shiro to Kurosha, the company of the artist Ryōji Chōmei (Kumata) (1899-1982). This collection's print was re-printed in 1933 for Ryōji Kumata's compilation of prints from Han geijutsu, titled simply 版畫 (Hanga). All the prints were re-printed for this volume from the original blocks created by the artists by the master printer Takahashi Kobo 高橋春正.

media.caption: Bamboo (untitled)

text.headline: Bamboo (untitled)
text.text:
A stand of bamboo done in black and grey, evokes winter. Perfect for the custom holiday card in the name of Walter and Edith Simmons on which the publisher S. Watanabe has mounted this print.
In regards to custom Christmas Cards, Watanabe's 1962 Catalog of Woodcut Color Prints notes, "These Christmas Cards made by S. Watanabe Color Print Co. are the finest quality in Tokyo and are made of genuine Japanese paper with Woodcut prints attached. We will gladly accept your order to make Christmas Cards in any design you wish."
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints).

media.caption: Pine branches and poem (surimono)

text.headline: Pine branches and poem (surimono)
text.text:
Being a painter of the Shijō school, Zeshin's surimono have been referred to as "Shijō surimono." Robert Schapp writes, "Shijō surimono seemed to have flourished mainly after the gradual disappearance of their ukiyo-e counterparts in the 1830s. And based on his sound Shijō education the talented Zeshin soon became one of the leading designers for Shijō surimono in Edo." He notes that while the total number of surimono designed by Zeshin is unknown, it may run into the thousands.[1]
In this print, auspicious pine branches and the edge of a stream are pictured. Ten haikai (seventeen syllable poems) are written to the left of the image with the names of their composers.
The Art Institute Chicago notes, "Many examples of large-scale [and smaller] surimono by Shibata Zeshin exist; he must have set up a large establishment in order to cater to orders from poets and intellectuals. Since Zeshin was engaged in many official commissions in other media and had a large group of apprentices, he probably left most of the details of surimono production to his apprentices."[2]

[1] "Zeshin's Shijō surimono and his later shikishiban prints," by Robert Schapp, Andon 102, Journal of the Society of Japanese Arts, October 2016, p. 55-67.
[2] Art Institute Chicago https://www.artic.edu/artworks/43726/the-cup-of-long-life [access 8-17-23]

media.caption: Illustration of Komatsu-hiki (小松引図)

text.headline: Illustration of Komatsu-hiki (小松引図)
text.text:
Zeshin's drawing of a samurai and courtier out for a day of "pulling pines," the popular custom in which Heian period nobles took pines home during the fondly-held event called the Komatsu-hiki (pulling out small pine trees on the first day of the Rat), using them to pray for longevity.
This woodblock print appearing in the 12th issue of the magazine Bijutsu Sekai 美術世界 (World of Art) was published three months after Zeshin's death.

media.caption: Illustration for Chapter 13 Akashi (明石)

text.headline: Illustration for Chapter 13 Akashi (明石)
text.text:
A color woodblock illustration from the first volume of Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari, Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), written by Murasaki Shikibu 紫式部著 in the early 11th century.
The color woodblock illustrations for the four books comprising Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari were stitched into the books and it is likely, though no definitive proof exists, that the publisher Kanao Tanejirō printed additional copies of the woodblock illustrations to be sold as single sheet prints. This collection's three stand-alone prints (IHL.2046, IHL.2101 an IHL.2270) would be examples of this, as they do not display any evidence of having been removed from a bound volume nor do they display any of the toning present on many of prints bound into the books due to contact with their acidic translucent protective sheets also bound into the original volumes.

media.caption: Birds from the book Simplified Forms of Drawing Birds and Animals (鳥獸略画式 Chōjū ryakugashiki)

text.headline: Birds from the book Simplified Forms of Drawing Birds and Animals (鳥獸略画式 Chōjū ryakugashiki)
text.text: A single page from Kitao Masayoshi's drawing manual. Kitao was a pioneer of a new style of drawing manual called ryakugashiki, which marked an important point in the development of this style of illustration and he strove, in his work, to simplify forms and capture the spirit of the animals he was depicting. The drawing manuals were reprinted many times and it is not known which edition this single page is from.

media.caption: Work・73-112 (Snow)

text.headline: Work・73-112 (Snow)
text.text:
The character for snow 雪, balanced with a pink teardrop, a white circle and Maki's seal, which he always handles as a design element of his print.
In the early 1960s Maki developed his own process of relief printmaking using woodblocks and cement. He first carved a conventional woodblock and then placed a cement mixture around the areas raised in relief on the block. Before the cement was set, Maki would texture it and after it dried he carved and chiseled the cement into the desired shape. After the cement completely dried, the entire surface of the plate was shellacked.

media.caption: The Fight between Hideyoshi and Ito Hyuganokami (秀吉伊東日向守を打取る図)

text.headline: The Fight between Hideyoshi and Ito Hyuganokami (秀吉伊東日向守を打取る図)
text.text:
This diptych print is from a series of 31 diptych prints plus a table of contents commemorating the rise to power of Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537-1598), one of the three great unifiers of Japan who rose from humble origins to become the second unifier of Japan who, after 100 years of war, brought stability and peace. This print depicts Toyotomi, when he was known as Kinoshita Tokichirō, arriving at Fujikawa for his first battle. Arriving when the battle is almost over, he hides in the reeds along the river and ambushes the commander of the enemy forces, Ito Hyuga no Kami, with a spear. Mt. Fuji rises in the distance.
Born in 1538, as the son of a peasant foot soldier from a village in Owari province, Toyotomi Hideyoshi was the loyal vassal of Oda Nobunaga. By consistently showing political cunning and strategic skills during military campaigns Hideyoshi eventually assumed the mantle of Nobunaga and became a powerful warlord. By 1591 he had brought order to the country, becoming the second of "the three unifiers," the others being Oda Nobunaga (1534-1582) and Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616).
Multiple publishers were involved with this series.

media.caption: Symbol No. 2 (象徴 Shōchō)

text.headline: Symbol No. 2 (象徴 Shōchō)
text.text: "Maki Haku is known for using the established tradition of calligraphy and abstracting kanji characters—the Chinese ideographs that are used in Japanese writing—into quirky images. At first glance, the top portion of this print seems ambiguous; some may see a twirling figure holding round bells. In fact, the figure is the character for gaku/raku (樂), meaning “music” and “enjoyment.” The etymology of gaku comes from the word for a hand instrument with bells and ornamental strings that was shaken to make music for the enjoyment of the gods. When the bells were not in use, they were hung on wooden stands (as represented by the 木 character, meaning “tree,” which appears at the bottom of the gaku/raku character)." -  Source: Yale University Art Gallery website https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/110323 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Frontispiece, Robinson hyōkō kiryaku 魯敏孫漂行紀略 (An Abridged Account of Robinson’s Shipwreck)

text.headline: Frontispiece, Robinson hyōkō kiryaku 魯敏孫漂行紀略 (An Abridged Account of Robinson’s Shipwreck)
text.text:
This print displays woodblock reproductions of the three woodblock illustrations appearing in the first translation of Robinson Crusoe into Japanese, the 1857 work titled Robinson hyōkō kiryaku 魯敏孫漂行紀略 (An Abridged Account of Robinson’s Shipwreck.) (For another reproduction of these illustration see IHL.2125.)
The first published Japanese translation of Daniel Defoe's (1661-1731) 1719 work Robinson Crusoe was made in 1857 by the polyglot Yokoyama Yoshikiyo 橫山由清 (1826–1879), translated not from Defoe's English language original but from the c. 1850 Dutch work, targeted to children, titled Beknopte levensgeschiedenis van Robinson Crusoe (Brief Life History Of Robinson Crusoe Containing His Major Adventures And Encounters.)[1] The three woodblock illustrations accompanying the Japanese work were drawn by the pioneering Western-style artist Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1828-1881) and were copied from the Dutch work.[2]
Kawakami's frontispiece set below the original Dutch title, is signed with his real name 冬崖川寛, rather than his artist name 川上冬崖, with an appended character 摹 indicating that his drawings are copies. The notation to the left of the two illustrations (transcribed below), tells us that the original Dutch version, a "historical novel," has twenty-six illustrations, one appearing in each chapter, but this version only uses two, namely the fifth and seventh illustration.[1]

Transcription of Notation
「原本一章ごとに挿絵ありて所謂（いわゆる）出像の稗史（はいし：小説）なり。　今その一・　二をこゝに出して其（その）他を略す。　即（すなわち）第五章と第七章のとなり」[2]

[1] "The Study of Illustrations of Robinson Crusoe in Early Modern East Asia," Li Yun, appearing in Asia and The World, Volume 2, Social Sciences Academic Press (China).
[2] transcription taken from the blog of Sumi Haruo http://haruuo.blogspot.com/2009/04/blog-post_03.html [accessed 8-17-23]

Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1828-1881) A painter, first in the literati style and later in the Western-style, translator, scholar he was "in charge of the painting collection at the Bureau for the Investigation of Barbarian Books (Bansho Shirabesho 蕃書調所) and successor institutions in the late 1850s and 1860s."[1] While considered to be a "moderately skilled artist" in the literati style, he was a driving force in the early Meiji years "to develop and popularize Western art."[2] Employed by the Ministry of Education to develop public school curriculum, he instituted "realistic drawing with pencils, rather than painting with the traditional Japanese ink-brush," a most useful tool for the creation of drawings for science.[3]

[1] Modern Asian Art, John Clark, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 137.
[2] Japanese Culture, Paul Varley, University of Hawaii Press, 4th ed., 2000, p. 265.
[3] Ibid.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as Yashio and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Masaoka in the play The Precious Flowers and Autumn Incense of Sendai (八汐尾上菊五郎・政岡 市川団十郎・伽羅先代萩)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Yashio and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Masaoka in the play The Precious Flowers and Autumn Incense of Sendai (八汐尾上菊五郎・政岡 市川団十郎・伽羅先代萩)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) in the role of Yashio and, in the top inset, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Masaoka in the play Meiboku sendaihagi (The Precious Flowers and Autumn Incense of Sendai).

In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as Washi no Chōki and Kawarazaki Kunitarō as Tōgokuya musume (鷲の長吉尾上菊五郎・東国屋娘およし 故初代河原崎国太郎)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Washi no Chōki and Kawarazaki Kunitarō as Tōgokuya musume (鷲の長吉尾上菊五郎・東国屋娘およし 故初代河原崎国太郎)
text.text:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) in the role of Washi no Chōkichi and, in the top inset, Kawarazaki Kunitarō I (1849-1867) as Tōgokuya musume Oyoshi, possibly in Kawatake Shinshichi II's play Yagura Daiko Otomo Yoshiwara.
