media.caption: World of Art, Issue 21 (美術世界 巻廿一 Bijutsu Sekai maki nijūichi)

text.headline: World of Art, Issue 21 (美術世界 巻廿一 Bijutsu Sekai maki nijūichi)
text.text:
The twenty-first issue of the art magazine Bijutsu Sekai, containing 18 woodblock prints consisting of 9 color double plates, 8 color single plates and 1 black and white plate. Artists represented in this issue include Ganku 岸駒 (1749-1839), Kikuchi Yōsai 菊池容斎 (1788-1878), Watanabe Kazan 渡辺崋山 (1793-1841), Kubota Beisen 久保田 米僊 (1852-1906), Kakizaki Hakyō 蛎崎波響 (1764-1826), Nishikawa Sukenobu 西川友信 (1671-1750), 英一蝶 Hanabusa Itchō (1652-1724), Kubota Kinsen 久保田金僊 (1875-1954), Imao Keinen 今尾景年 (1845-1924), Iwasa Matabei 岩佐又兵衛 (1578-1650), Oishi Matora 大石真虎 (1792-1833) and Kumagai Naohiko 熊谷直彦 (1829-1913). For another issue of Bijutsu Sekai see IHL.2144.

Twenty-five issues of Bijutsu Sekai 美術世界 (World of Art) were published from December 22, 1890 until the final issue on January 2, 1894. The magazine presented fifteen or more works of well-known contemporary and past master artists to the public in woodblock form in each issue. The woodblocks were either reproductions of paintings in reduced-size or original woodblocks. Published by Wada Tokutarō 和田篤太郎 of Shun'yōdō 春陽堂, a Tokyo publishing firm best known for publishing illustrated novels, each issue was edited by the nihonga artist and designer of woodblock prints Watanabe Seitei 渡辺省亭 (1851-1918), who specialized in kachōga (bird and flower paintings).
Artists' works appearing in the magazine included those of Seitei himself, Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889), Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), Kōno Bairei (1844-1895), Kobayashi Eitaku (1843-1890), Imao Keinen (1845-1923), Shibata Zeshin (1807-1891), Kitagawa Utamaro (1753-1806), Maruyama Ōkyo (1733-1795), Yosa Buson (1716-1784) and Katsushika Hokusai (1760-1849). The final issue, volume 25, consisted of works only by Seitei.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Ichikawa Danjūrō and Yamanaka Heikurō (複製：婦人相學十躰・浮気之相)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Ichikawa Danjūrō and Yamanaka Heikurō (複製：婦人相學十躰・浮気之相)
text.text:
A reproduction published by Nihon fūzoku zue kankōkai 日本風俗図絵刊行会 and the artist and ukiyo-e scholar Hashiguchi Goyō 橋口 五葉 (1880-1921). In 1916-1917, Hashiguchi Goyō supervised the twelve-volume Ukiyo fūzoku Yamato nishiki-e (Japanese Color Prints in Ukiyo Style), containing 240 woodblock-printed reproductions. This collection's print designed by Torii Kiyonobu in 1714 is contained in volume 1 covering the early Edo period.
"Goyo's interest in ukiyo-e. . . blossomed during the last decade of his life. He studied the large ukiyo-e collection of a relative, Mihara Shigekichi. He also put together his own collection of prints.
"Goyo's interest extended to selecting and overseeing the reproduction of prints by ukiyo-e masters. [H]e intended these recuts, not as forgeries, but as means of preserving a great native art form that over the previous generation had been collected and prized primarily by Westerners. In November 1917, together with Kiyokata [Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)], Goyo selected (and wrote commentaries for) a variety of masterpieces in the twelve-volume 'Ukiyo fuzoku yamato nishiki-e' (Ukiyo customs and Japanese color prints), published by the Nihon fūzoku zue kankokai (Association for publication of pictures of Japanese scenery)." - source: Shin-Hanga: New Prints in Modern Japan, Kendall Brown, Hollis Goodall-Cristante, Los Angeles County Museum of Art, 1996, p. 47.

media.caption: Reproduction of: Illustration of a Dutch Man and Woman (複製：阿蘭陀人男女図 Orandajin dan jo zu)

text.headline: Reproduction of: Illustration of a Dutch Man and Woman (複製：阿蘭陀人男女図 Orandajin dan jo zu)
text.text:
One of ten prints included in a portfolio of woodblock reproductions of Nagasaki-e 長崎絵, woodblock prints, paintings, and illustrated woodblock-printed books made in the port of Nagasaki. "Often serving as miyage hanga (souvenir prints: 土産版画), nagasaki-e were inexpensive mementos for merchants or scholars who traveled to Nagasaki on business. Moreover, the market for such images was large and profitable, as the Japanese were themselves endlessly curious about foreign visitors whom they were typically forbidden to meet. Nagasaki-e were sold not only in Nagasaki, but also in Edo and Osaka, and no doubt in the provinces." - Source: website of John Fiorillo's Viewing Japanese Prints https://www.viewingjapaneseprints.net/texts/topics_faq/nagasakie.html [accessed 8-25-23]
The prints in this portfolio of reproductions were done under the auspices of the Nagasaki Municipal Museum (長崎市立博物館 Nagasaki Shiritsu Hakubutsukan).

media.caption: Bakeitei Zakki 馬薊亭雑記 (with woodblock reproductions of illustrations for Robinson hyōkō kiryaku 魯敏遜溧行纪略)

text.headline: Bakeitei Zakki 馬薊亭雑記 (with woodblock reproductions of illustrations for Robinson hyōkō kiryaku 魯敏遜溧行纪略)
text.text:
In 1942 the artist, author and bibliophile Masuda Gorō 増田五良 (1895-?) compiled a series of essays ("miscellaneous notes") on various topics under the title Bakeitei zakki 馬薊亭雑記, published by the Kōbe publisher Goten Shoin 五典書院. The characters 馬薊 in the book's title are a reference to the "horse thistle," lightly silhouetted on each page of text. Woodblock print reproductions of Kawakami Tōgai’s three original 1857 woodblock illustrations for Robinson hyōkō kiryaku were presented in the front of the book. In addition to the woodblock prints placed in the beginning, Masuda provided his personal observations on Robinson hyōkō kiryaku in an essay of the same title, providing the history of Robinson hyōkō kiryaku and noting that it should be valued not only as the first translation of Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, but also for the woodblock prints by Kawakami and the joy of simply looking at and handling the book.
For additional detail on woodblock illustrations by Kawakami Tōgai, see IHL.2051.

media.caption: Splendid View of Hibiya Park: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 日比谷公園之光景)

text.headline: Splendid View of Hibiya Park: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 日比谷公園之光景)
text.text:
A color lithograph of Hibiya Park which opened in 1903 (Meiji 36) as Tokyo’s first Western-style park. The bandstand (Music Hall in the Park [公園内音楽堂]), the forerunner of today’s small concert hall, was completed in 1904 (Meiji 37) and is pictured in the inset. Front and center, as it is in a similar color lithograph of this area of the park (see IHL.2130), is the bronze crane fountain (鶴之噴水) in Kumogata-ike Pond.
In September 1905, at the conclusion of the Treaty of Portsmouth ending the Russo-Japanese War, over 30,000 people would gather outside the park to protest the treaty and then when denied permission to enter the park and hold their rally, riot in what became known as the Hibiya Incendiary Incident or the Hibiya Riots.
Hibiya Park "served as a bridge between the 'western' and 'eastern' aspects of the redefined city. After a very lengthy debate over the specific contents of the park, it was decided that one quarter of the park would be a traditional Japanese water and mountain garden while the rest of the park would consist of an open space with trees, grass, and wide, winding carriage paths. The park also featured a place for sports and recreation, which was the result of distinctly western influenced ideas as in the Edo period recreation was thought of as simply venturing out into nature. When the park opened it also hosted a small zoo, a public restroom, and a bandstand for public performances, all hallmarks of western style public park." - Source: Japan's Samurai Revolution (Harvard University, Fall 2014) https://samurairevolution.omeka.net/exhibits/show/bev/page1 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Famous Places of Tokyo: Hibiya Park, Music Hall, Nijubashi, Kudan Yasukuni, Asakusa Kannon Main Hall, Nihonbashi, Statue of Kusunoki Masashige, Statue of Ōmura Masujirō (東京名所: 日比谷公園, 音楽堂, 宮城二重橋, 九段靖國神社, 淺草觀世音本堂楠, 日本橋, 楠公銅像, 大村銅像)

text.headline: Famous Places of Tokyo: Hibiya Park, Music Hall, Nijubashi, Kudan Yasukuni, Asakusa Kannon Main Hall, Nihonbashi, Statue of Kusunoki Masashige, Statue of Ōmura Masujirō (東京名所: 日比谷公園, 音楽堂, 宮城二重橋, 九段靖國神社, 淺草觀世音本堂楠, 日本橋, 楠公銅像, 大村銅像)
text.text: A color lithograph of famous places in Tokyo issued in 1926, three years after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, highlighting places that had been rebuilt subsequent to the quake. In 1926, Tokyo was only three years into the rebuilding plan that would continue into the early 1930s.

media.caption: True View of Nihonbashi: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 日本橋之真景)

text.headline: True View of Nihonbashi: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 日本橋之真景)
text.text:
A color lithograph of Nihonbashi and its surrounds, looking from the northeast corner to the southwest corner of the bridge. The artist, printer and publisher Kuroki Hannosuke, specializing in lithographs, has crammed a trolley, an auto, a bicycle, a horse drawn carriage, a river barge, a porter carrying fresh fish to or from the fish market that sat near the bridge until relocated to Tsukiji after the 1923 earthquake, buildings such as the Ōkura Shoten 大倉書店 building, publisher of woodblock prints and books, on the far side of the bridge and Tokyoites in all manner of dress. (The building in the inset remains unidentified.) Of course, a snow covered Mount Fuji towers over the scene as the sun begins to set.
This same scene was published numerous times, sometimes under a slightly changed title, until 1923 when the Great Kanto Earthquake destroyed much of Tokyo and its surrounds.

media.caption: True View of Asakusa Park Around Twelve-Story Tower: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所  淺草公園十二階附近之真景)

text.headline: True View of Asakusa Park Around Twelve-Story Tower: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所  淺草公園十二階附近之真景)
text.text:
This color lithograph brings us a "true view" of the area near the twelve-story Ryōunkaku (Cloud Surpassing Pavilion), designed by the Scottish engineer W. K. Burton, in Asakusa's sixth district. Strolling along the Gourd Pond in Asakusa Park is a family dressed in their Sunday best. A soldier and sailor in uniform gaze out oacross the pond. From the carp in the pond, to the spring cherry blossoms, to the airship and two planes overhead, all signs are auspicious.
Two years later, on September 1, 1923, the Great Kantō Earthquake would devastate not only the 12-story Ryōunkaku but much of the city.
See IHL.2063 for another color lithograph of this same area.

media.caption: Splendid View of the Crane Fountain at Hibiya Park: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 日比谷公園鶴噴水之光景)

text.headline: Splendid View of the Crane Fountain at Hibiya Park: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 日比谷公園鶴噴水之光景)
text.text:
A view of Tokyo's Hibiya Park, known as Japan's first Western-style park, which opened in 1903. The bronze crane fountain erected in 1905 in Kumogata-ike Pond dominates the scene. The park's "new music hall" 新音楽堂 (an open-air bandstand), which opened in 1904, is pictured in the inset in the upper right. For a similar view of the fountain and park see IHL.2116.
In September 1905, at the conclusion of the Treaty of Portsmouth ending the Russo-Japanese War, over 30,000 people would gather outside the park to protest the treaty and then when denied permission to enter the park and hold their rally, riot in what became known as the Hibiya Incendiary Incident or the Hibiya Riots.
Hibiya Park "served as a bridge between the 'western' and 'eastern' aspects of the redefined city. After a very lengthy debate over the specific contents of the park, it was decided that one quarter of the park would be a traditional Japanese water and mountain garden while the rest of the park would consist of an open space with trees, grass, and wide, winding carriage paths. The park also featured a place for sports and recreation, which was the result of distinctly western influenced ideas as in the Edo period recreation was thought of as simply venturing out into nature. When the park opened it also hosted a small zoo, a public restroom, and a bandstand for public performances, all hallmarks of western style public park." - Source: Japan's Samurai Revolution (Harvard University, Fall 2014) https://samurairevolution.omeka.net/exhibits/show/bev/page1 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: His Royal Highness the Crown Prince of Great Britain (近く御來朝の英國皇太子殿下)

text.headline: His Royal Highness the Crown Prince of Great Britain (近く御來朝の英國皇太子殿下)
text.text:
A lithograph from a photographic portrait of Edward Prince of Wales, later King Edward VIII (1894-1972), appearing in the Tokyo Asahi Graphic (東京朝日グラフィック). The caption beneath the portrait reads, "His Royal Highness, the Crown Prince of the United Kingdom, who is visiting soon."
"By the time the Prince of Wales arrived in Japan [in April 1922], the Emperor Taishō (1879-1926) had retired from his royal duties due to ill health. Thus, the prince was mainly entertained by the Empress Teimei and the Prince Regent [Crown Prince Hirohito]. Many press images of the visit . . . demonstrate the warm hospitality he received. However, the Prince of Wales could communicate with the empress only through an interpreter, and even then their conversations were limited to subjects such as the weather and the cherry blossom." - Source: website of the Royal Collection Trust https://www.rct.uk/collection/themes/publications/japan-courts-and-culture/visit-of-edward-prince-of-wales-later-king [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: View of Nihonbashi Dori Mitsukoshi Gofukuten (kimono store): Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 帝都日本橋ヨリ三越呉服店ヲ望ム)

text.headline: View of Nihonbashi Dori Mitsukoshi Gofukuten (kimono store): Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 帝都日本橋ヨリ三越呉服店ヲ望ム)
text.text:
At least five editions of this chromolithograph depicting Tokyo's bustling Nihonbashi were created with the first being issued in April 1925 and the last being issued in 1932. Editions issued subsequent to this collection's 1928 print carry the title "Scenes of Bustling Nihonbashi," eliminating the Mitsukoshi name. All of the editions celebrate the resurgence of this area after the devastating 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake.
There are many ukiyo-e prints depicting Nihonbashi, but it is rare to see it from the south to the north direction. The red brick building with a greenish-blue dome is the former Imperial Hemp Company Headquarters. The white building behind it is the Mitsukoshi Nihonbashi Main Store.

media.caption: Illustration of Large-Scale Maneuvers of the Army Under the Supervision of His Majesty (陸軍特別大演習大帥陛下御統監之圖)

text.headline: Illustration of Large-Scale Maneuvers of the Army Under the Supervision of His Majesty (陸軍特別大演習大帥陛下御統監之圖)
text.text: Picturing military maneuvers with Emperor Taishō standing over a map supervising. This largely black and white lithograph emphasized the emperor's role as head of the military under the constitution, although his actual role was ceremonial. Plagued by physical and mental problems that progressively incapacited him, Emperor Taishō would increasingly withdraw from even ceremonial military appearances.

media.caption: A True Illustration of the Army Transport Command Marching (陸軍輜重隊行軍之真圖)

text.headline: A True Illustration of the Army Transport Command Marching (陸軍輜重隊行軍之真圖)
text.text:
This large color lithograph depicts the transport of supplies by the Army Transport Command. The two insets in the print picture the bivouacking of horses and the rapid movement of both horses and men. The Saint Louis Art Museum has an earlier version of this lithograph, printed using only orange and black inks and dated two years earlier.
Little information is available on the designer of this print, Kuroki Hannosuke, who was associated with the publishing house Hakugakan, likely his own business. He was active from c. 1904 until the early Taishō era, designing, printing and publishing lithographs of scenic spots in Tokyo, various military and war related scenes and various maps. Works by this illustrator can be found in the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston and the Stanford University Libraries, among others.

media.caption: No. 4 (四), One Hundred Beauties in Takasago Dyed Yukata

text.headline: No. 4 (四), One Hundred Beauties in Takasago Dyed Yukata
text.text: One of an intended one hundred designs, of which twenty appear to have been completed, for an advertising campaign to help revive flagging demand for the traditional Takasago dyeing process. The designer of the prints, Itō Shinsui 伊東深水 (1898-1972), was the best-known bijin-ga designer of the time, working to create designs to be reproduced through traditional woodblock technique or through new technologies employing photo-offset technology, such as in the prints in this series. It appears that all the designs for the series were newly drawn by Shinsui. It is unknown who financed these prints (possibly a trade association) and while the name of the publisher, Kisendō 喜扇堂, located at the time in Suitengu-mae, Tokyo, appears on all the prints no information is readily available on this publisher.

media.caption: Butterfly Dance - Winter (蝶舞う・冬)

text.headline: Butterfly Dance - Winter (蝶舞う・冬)
text.text:
One of many hybrid process prints, using zinc plate (letterpress) and woodblock, of butterflies in various configurations and colors created by Chizuko from the early 1970s into the early 2000s. This collection's print Butterfly Dance - Winter is one of four the artist created with the title "Butterfly Dance" - one for each of the seasons.
In discussing her butterfly prints the artist acknowledged the difficulty of escaping one’s own success, admitting that she continued to make butterfly prints long after she had grown tired of the subject simply because they sold so well. - Source: A Japanese Legacy: Four Generations of Yoshida Family Artists, Laura W. Allen, Kendall H. Brown, Eugene M. Skibbe, et. al., The Minneapolis Institute of Arts, 2002, p. 181.

media.caption: Strawmat Flags and Neighing Horses of Gunma, first volume, first book (蓆簱群馬嘶初編 上  Mushirobata Gunma no inanaki)

text.headline: Strawmat Flags and Neighing Horses of Gunma, first volume, first book (蓆簱群馬嘶初編 上  Mushirobata Gunma no inanaki)
text.text:
The first book of volume 1 of the 3 volume set (a total of 9 books) comprising the illustrated novel Mushirobata gunma no inanaki by the gesaku writer Saikaen Ryūkō (1857-1902) and illustrated by Utagawa Kunimasa IV (1848-1920), under his gō (art name) Baidō Kunimasa.
This 1881 work of popular fiction was based on the 1871 uprising by some 150 villages, in what was then Nakano and Gunma prefectures, against high taxes, rising prices and the collapse of the local silk trade, attributed to a local official. The three day uprising saw widespread destruction in the prefectural capital, attacks on property of rich commoners and the murder of two government officials. Government troops were quickly sent in to restore order and twenty-eight participants were executed and many more imprisoned.
Mushirobata in the title is a reference to the strawmat banners used to display demands during peasant uprisings and inanaki is a reference to the common grounds used for horse fodder, which were being taxed by the new government. The novel opens with the hero Mashio Monya (真塩紋弥) presenting the peasant demands in the form of a letter of grievance (歎願書) to the Chief Cabinet Secretary of the prefecture, as Mashio's wife looks on along with Gunma's chief of police.

media.caption: Strawmat Flags and Neighing Horses of Gunma, first volume, third and last book (蓆簱群馬嘶初編 下 Mushirobata Gunma no inanaki)

text.headline: Strawmat Flags and Neighing Horses of Gunma, first volume, third and last book (蓆簱群馬嘶初編 下 Mushirobata Gunma no inanaki)
text.text:
The last book of volume 1 of the 3 volume set (a total of 9 books) comprising the illustrated novel Mushirobata gunma no inanaki by the gesaku writer Saikaen Ryūkō (1857-1902) and illustrated by Utagawa Kunimasa IV (1848-1920), under his gō (art name) Baidō Kunimasa.

Mushirobata in the title is a reference to the strawmat banners used to display demands during peasant uprisings and inanaki is a reference to the common grounds used for horse fodder, which were being taxed by the new government. The novel opens with the hero Mashio Monya (真塩紋弥) presenting the peasant demands in the form of a letter of grievance (歎願書) to the Chief Cabinet Secretary of the prefecture, as Mashio's wife looks on along with Gunma's chief of police.

media.caption: The Violets of Edo: Great Man, Gallant Woman (江戸紫・傑士侠女 Edo murasaki・kesshi kyōjo)

text.headline: The Violets of Edo: Great Man, Gallant Woman (江戸紫・傑士侠女 Edo murasaki・kesshi kyōjo)
text.text: The author and art critic Kuroda Tengai was a native of Hikone who was active in the latter half of the Meiji era as a reporter for the Kyoto Hinode Shimbun. The novel The Violets of Edo: Great Man, Gallant Woman was first published in 1901, with this collection's novel being a second edition published the following year. The woodblock frontispiece (kuchi-e) for this 1902 edition of the novel does not carry a signature or seal.

media.caption: Rainy Day

text.headline: Rainy Day
text.text: Filled with energy, motion and music. By 1954, Chizuko had set aside her painting career to focus on creating woodblock prints. Her international travel inspired many of her early prints including this print, which is part of her jazz themed prints.

media.caption: Rat and Radish (untitled)

text.headline: Rat and Radish (untitled)
text.text: A small rat (nezumi) nibbles on a bright red radish. One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of last century. Multiple editions of this print exist. See IHL.1516 for another impression of this print.

media.caption: Op. 28

text.headline: Op. 28
text.text:
The twenty-eighth in a group of over fifty prints carrying the title "Op." (opus or "work"), followed by a number, created by Nonaka in the mid-1970s. This body of work employs curvilinear forms and pastel colors.

The artist notes, "I have been interested in color surfaces since I was a child, and my basic attitude is to create my own world with my own sensibility, which is different from minimal art and American abstract expressionism."

media.caption: Road (道 michi)

text.headline: Road (道 michi)
text.text:
In this color engraving, Ōuchi appropriates two images, the Wind God, Fūjin, and what appears to be one of the characters in Tales of the Water Margin from undetermined ukiyo-e artists of the past. The character 道 michi appears to the left of the cube and an unread character appears on the cube's top surface.

In discussing Ōuchi's appropriation of images from famous ukiyo-e artists, the Tolmans wrote the following in 1982: "Ōuchi uses them to evoke the past, but it is his originality that makes them contemporary. First of all, they are not photographs but are completely redrawn by the artist, as he sees them. Secondly, he is not using a woodblock, but portrays them through the etching process in warm, soft colors - rusts, browns, gold - that give them an added poignancy." - Source: People Who Make Japanese Prints, A Personal Glimpse, Mary S. and Norman H. Tolman, Sobunsha, 1982, p. 116-117.

media.caption: World of Art, Issue 16 (美術世界 巻十六 Bijutsu Sekai maki jūroku)

text.headline: World of Art, Issue 16 (美術世界 巻十六 Bijutsu Sekai maki jūroku)
text.text:
The sixteenth issue of the art magazine Bijutsu Sekai, containing 17 woodblock prints consisting of 9 color double plates, 7 color single plates and 1 black and white plate. Artists represented in this issue include Kikuchi Yōsai 菊池容斎 (1788-1878), Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889) and Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1808-1891). For another issue of Bijutsu Sekai see IHL.2122.

Twenty-five issues of Bijutsu Sekai 美術世界 (World of Art) were published from December 22, 1890 until the final issue on January 2, 1894. The magazine presented fifteen or more works of well-known contemporary and past master artists to the public in woodblock form in each issue. The woodblocks were either reproductions of paintings in reduced-size or original woodblocks. Published by Wada Tokutarō 和田篤太郎 of Shun'yōdō 春陽堂, a Tokyo publishing firm best known for publishing illustrated novels, each issue was edited by the nihonga artist and designer of woodblock prints Watanabe Seitei 渡辺省亭 (1851-1918), who specialized in kachōga (bird and flower paintings).
Artists' works appearing in the magazine included those of Seitei himself, Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889), Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), Kōno Bairei (1844-1895), Kobayashi Eitaku (1843-1890), Imao Keinen (1845-1923), Shibata Zeshin (1807-1891), Kitagawa Utamaro (1753-1806), Maruyama Ōkyo (1733-1795), Yosa Buson (1716-1784) and Katsushika Hokusai (1760-1849). The final issue, volume 25, consisted of works only by Seitei.

media.caption: Varieties of the Japanese Print, Volume 1

text.headline: Varieties of the Japanese Print, Volume 1
text.text:
Volume 1 of a planned two volume instructional book illustrating various stages and techniques of Japanese woodblock print creation. For the book, Yoshida carved twenty woodblocks to illustrate, as he states in the books foreword, most traditional and some modern techniques of woodblock print production.
While the afterword mentions a future volume that will "cover some other important varieties of the Japanese print" and requests the "interested reader to inform his address to the author in person" the second volume was never issued.

media.caption: White Cattleya Orchid (白いカトレヤ Shiroi Katoreya)

text.headline: White Cattleya Orchid (白いカトレヤ Shiroi Katoreya)
text.text: A red-lipped white orchid in a Rothkoesque vase floats in its ethereal earth-toned surroundings.

media.caption: Near Shinjuku Station Neighborhood (新宿駅付近 Shinjuku-eki fukin)

text.headline: Near Shinjuku Station Neighborhood (新宿駅付近 Shinjuku-eki fukin)
text.text: The bustling area near Shinjuku Station a few years after the end of the occupation by American forces in 1952. Sasajima produced this print with traditional woodblock technique rather than his takuzuri technique of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press which he did not begin using until 1959.

media.caption: Composition F (作品F Sakuhin F)

text.headline: Composition F (作品F Sakuhin F)
text.text: Thickly applied and layered pigments give this abstract composition depth. Composition F is one of Hagiwara's most widely held works in American museums, with at least six museums listing this work in their collection. From 1958 to 1960, Hagiwara produced a number of abstract works titled "Composition" followed by a letter, including Composition B, Composition L, Composition M, Composition P, Composition Q, Composition Z . All of these works were "produced from roughly carved blocks printed to reveal the wood's uneven texture." - Source: website of  Asian Art Museum Chong-Moon Lee Center for Asian Art and Culture.

media.caption: Tourists Arriving on the Pier in Kobe

text.headline: Tourists Arriving on the Pier in Kobe
text.text: Western tourists arriving in Kobe. The pier would have been lined with rickshaw drivers awaiting fares. In commenting on this print Osaka Prints notes, "This design is one of a handful that, in 1951, Hide carved but then allowed the Tokyo-based Katō Hanga Kenkyusho (a publishing firm founded 1930 by Katō Junji specializing in contemporary artists) to print and publish for him. The image of foreigners arriving at Kobe port and hiring rickshaws is a very different re-working in a far larger and vertical format of a similar theme among his smaller mid-1930s '100 Views of Kobe' scenes. Although one might be tempted to read some 'spoiled rich Westerners' social commentary into the scene, Kawanishi is known to have pitied the tourists for how badly the rickshaw men cheated them!" - Source: website of Osaka Prints https://www.osakaprints.com/content/artists/info_pp/kawanishi_hide_info/kawanishi_hide_09.htm

media.caption: Woman Sitting on a Chair (椅子に坐る女性)

text.headline: Woman Sitting on a Chair (椅子に坐る女性)
text.text: Nakagawa designed very few woodblock prints. This collection's untitled print known as Woman Sitting on a Chair, is perhaps unique in that it attempts to duplicate his painting style, possibly replicating an existing painting (although a similar painting cannot be found online), rather than being a print whose design was done by the artist specifically for reproduction by woodblock, as in the case of his book design work.

media.caption: The Best Bridge in Japan:  True View of Azumabashi Bridge in Tokyo (日本第一之名橋 東京吾妻橋之真図)

text.headline: The Best Bridge in Japan:  True View of Azumabashi Bridge in Tokyo (日本第一之名橋 東京吾妻橋之真図)
text.text:
A lithograph with hand-coloring by the publisher, artist and lithographer Watanabe Tadahisa of Azumabashi, the first metal bridge spanning Tokyo's Sumida River. "It was officially dedicated and opened to the public on December 9, 1887. It served the bustling pleasure quarter of Asakusa on one side and a beer factory on the other. Japanese woodblock artists drew its vertical posts and diagonal eyebars in Western perspective and for good measure populated the walkway with ladies in bustles and the deck with top-hatted gentlemen in carriages."[1] It was damaged and repaired in the Great Kanto Earthquake, but was replaced with a new bridge in 1964.
Note the man in Western dress riding a penny-farthing (high wheel) bicycle. This collection's print has had the faces of the two figures on the right cut out and replaced, although the figures are the same as in other impressions of this print.
For other prints depicting Azumabashi see IHL.0269, IHL.0446 and IHL.2435.

[1] - Meiji Revisited The Sites of Victorian Japan, Dallas Finn, Weather Hill, Inc. 1995 p. 145.

media.caption: Complete Map of Naritasan, Taishō Revision (成田山全圖 大正年度改正)

text.headline: Complete Map of Naritasan, Taishō Revision (成田山全圖 大正年度改正)
text.text:
A 1927 color lithograph map by an unknown artist, published by a little-known publisher, of Narita-san Shinshō Temple 成田山新勝寺 in Narita Japan. Naritasan Park (成田山公園) can be seen in the upper left of the print and major buildings inside the temple grounds are named in the vertical red cartouches. A small white rectangular horizontal cartouche in the right side of the bottom of the print references the Narita electric streetcar (Seisō Denki Kidō) which opened in 1910 to bring more pilgrims to the site.
About Naritasan
"Naritasan Shinsho-ji Temple is a Buddhist temple located in Narita, Chiba Prefecture. The temple deity is Fudo Myo-o and has long been known as “Narita Fudo”. This place is major center of Fudoson belief. About 3 million people visit the temple from January 1st to January 3rd for the first prayer worship of the year. It is also known that sumo wrestlers and popular actors scatter beans during the Setsubun Festival in February at this temple.
"The temple is closely related to the famous Kabuki Ichikawa family. This well-known Kabuki family, the name of "Naritaya" Ichikawa Danjuro is originated in Naritasan.
Since opening, we have been carrying out a continuous Ogoma prayer. We have been praying for world peace and the fulfillment of each visitor's request." - Source: https://www.naritasan.or.jp/english/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Camellia (椿 tsubaki)

text.headline: Camellia (椿 tsubaki)
text.text:
One of three prints in the fifth of ten envelopes containing the prints comprising set one of Seihō's Masterpieces.

SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century."
Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.
While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

media.caption: Evil Warrior (武惡)

text.headline: Evil Warrior (武惡)
text.text:
One of three prints in the fifth of ten envelopes containing the prints comprising set one.

media.caption: Outside Plymouth Bay, Great Britain (英国 プリマウス港外)

text.headline: Outside Plymouth Bay, Great Britain (英国 プリマウス港外)
text.text:
Yamagishi traveled the world on behalf of the Japanese government from 1926 to 1929 studying print techniques and giving demonstrations of Japanese print techniques in the fifteen countries he visited, including Great Britain. Here he presents us with a view of the military battery on Drake's Island in Plymouth Sound lying 500 meters off the Plymouth coast. Drake's Island was originally fortified in the mid-sixteenth century as a defensive measure against France. It has not been in use as a military installation since the end of WWII. Plans are in place to develop it as a resort.
This collection's print carries the date September 10, 1928 within the image next to the artist's signature. A notation in the margin, in the artist's hand, indicates this print was printed almost eight years later in March 1936.

media.caption: Index Sheet (梅幸百種目録 Baikō hyakushu mokuroku)

text.headline: Index Sheet (梅幸百種目録 Baikō hyakushu mokuroku)
text.text:
The index sheet for the entire series of 100 prints. While this print is usually attributed to Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900), the designer of all the prints in the series, it was actually designed by the artist Sekine Takejirō 関根竹二郎, active 1887-1896, whose signature and seal are found in the bottom left margin. While he used the character 書 (sho) to indicate he was the writer/calligrapher for the titles displayed on the print, it is most likely he also designed the background.

In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to the actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). The series One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

media.caption: Onoe Kikugorō V as Seishin and Iwai Hanshirō VIII as the geisha Izayoi in the play Kosode Soga Azami no Ironui (せいしん魚屋宗五郎・十六夜 岩井半四郎・小袖曽我薊色縫)

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Seishin and Iwai Hanshirō VIII as the geisha Izayoi in the play Kosode Soga Azami no Ironui (せいしん魚屋宗五郎・十六夜 岩井半四郎・小袖曽我薊色縫)
text.text:
The actors Onoe Kikugorō V as the priest Seishin and, in the inset, Iwai Hanshirō VIII as the geisha Izayoi, in the play Kosode Soga Azami no Ironui. The most performed act of the play Kosode Soga Azami no Ironui, also known as Izayoi Seishin, tells the story of the young priest, Seishin and his love affair with the geisha, Izayoi, their unsuccessful suicide and the robbery murder of the young page Motome by Seishin.

In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Hayano Kanpei and Iwai Hanshirō as Okaru in the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (早野勘平魚屋宗五郎・おかる 故岩井半四郎・仮名手本忠臣)
text.text:
The actors Onoe Kikugorō V as Hayano Kanpei, and, in the top inset, Iwai Hanshirō VIII (1829-1882) as Okaru, Kanpei's lover then wife, in the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers).
The play is based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. Hayano Kanpei is the fictitious name in the play for the real-life Kayano Sanpei, a young retainer of Asano's, who was caught in the dilemma of agreeing to be part of the revenge plot against Kira and then being offered into the service of another lord by his parents. Trapped in a situation where he will either disgrace his family by not fulfilling their offer of his service or disgracing himself by not fulfilling his pledge of revenge, he commits suicide.

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Igami no Gonta and Bandō Kakitsu as Kajiwara in the play Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees, (いかみの権太魚屋宗五郎・梶原坂東家橘・義経千本桜)
text.text:
The actors Onoe Kikugorō V as the villainous Igami no Gonta, the son of a sushi shop owner, and, in the top inset, Bandō Kakitsu as the Genji general and retainer of Yoritomo, Kajiwara, in the play Yoshitsune senbon zakura (Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees).
Originally written for the puppet theater in 1747, Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees is set in the aftermath of the twelfth-century Genji–Heike wars. The play follows the adventures of the military commander Minamoto no Yoshitsune as he tries to avoid capture by his jealous older brother, Minamoto no Yoritomo, and his loyal henchmen.

media.caption: Sōnosuke in the role of Sawaichi (宗之助 澤市)

text.headline: Sōnosuke in the role of Sawaichi (宗之助 澤市)
text.text:
The actress Murata Kakuko 村田嘉久子 (1893-1969) in the role of the beautiful Osato and the actor Sawamura Sōnosuke 澤村宗之助 (1886-1924) in the role of the blind masseur Sawaichi in the play The Miracle at Tsubosaka Temple (壺坂霊験記 Tsubosaka Reigenki) performed in May at the Imperial Theatre (帝国劇場 Teikoku Gekijō). One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.

SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: The Attack on Weihaiwei: The Taking of the Hundred Foot Cliff 威海衛攻撃・百尺崖所占領之圖 Ikaiei kōgeki・Hyakuseki gaisho senryōno zu)

text.headline: The Attack on Weihaiwei: The Taking of the Hundred Foot Cliff 威海衛攻撃・百尺崖所占領之圖 Ikaiei kōgeki・Hyakuseki gaisho senryōno zu)
text.text:
The brave Captain Higuchi was celebrated in prints, in song and in writing. In this print he leads a cavalry charge while holding a Chinese infant during the Battle of Weihaiwei (January 20 - February 15, 1895), an offensive by Japanese naval and land forces which resulted in the destruction of the Chinese forts and much of the Chinese fleet located there. For other prints celebrating the captain see IHL.1343 and IHL.1811.
In commenting on this incident historian John W. Dower notes, "Captain Higuchi became a symbol of the bravery and benevolence of the Japanese forces and . . . was celebrated in a number of woodblock prints (often with enemy bullets streaking around him). At a deeper symbolic level, he exemplified the whole notion of a righteous war against China. The implication was that the child had been left in peril by its own irresponsible parents and caretakers. Thus, even as they were depicted overthrowing the Chinese, the propaganda message of such prints to Japanese viewers was that their fighting men not only were strong and resolute, but also were protecting and preserving China’s future." - Source: website MIT Visualizing Culture: Throwing Off Asia II Woodblock Prints of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) by John W. Dower https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/throwing_off_asia_02/visnav_ii_d.html [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Sanjō Sanetomi (三條実美)

text.headline: Sanjō Sanetomi (三條実美)
text.text:
Sanjō, a central figure in the Sonnōjōi Movement ("revere the Emperor and expel the barbarians"), is shown fleeing to Chōshū along with six other noblemen (known as the "Seven nobles of decline," shichikyō-ochi) in 1863 in the aftermath of a coup d’etat at the imperial court which expelled members of the Sonnōjōi Movement and forced the emperor to stop his efforts to reassert authority over the shōgunate. Sanjō took shelter in the more sympathetic Chōshū domain in western Honshū.

The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

media.caption: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Fox Tadanobu in the play Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees (市川団十郎・ 狐忠信・ 義経千本桜)

text.headline: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Fox Tadanobu in the play Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees (市川団十郎・ 狐忠信・ 義経千本桜)
text.text:
The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as Kitsune (Fox) Tadanobu in the play Yoshitsune Sanbon-zakura ("Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees"). The Honolulu Museum of Art notes, “The vibrant red on the drum and subject's lips and the flash of deep purple in the robe lining are hallmarks of his [Kunichika’s] careful but exquisite use of color.” In keeping with the rest of the series, extensive embossing is employed in creating the hair-like texture on the fox robe worn by Tadanobu.

One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits. A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

text.headline: Onoe Kikugorō V as Sakanaya Sōgorō and Bandō Kakitsu as Urato Jūzemon in the play Sōgorō the Fishmonger (魚屋宗五郎 尾上菊五郎・十左衛門 故坂東家橘・新皿屋舗月雨暈)
text.text:
The actors Onoe Kikugorō V as Sakanaya Sōgorō and, in the top inset, Bandō Kakitsu as Urato Jūzemon, in the play Sōgorō the Fishmonger.
The play, also known as Shin Sarayashiki Tsuki no Amagasa, was written for Kikugorō V by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893). "The highlight of this piece is the process by which the honest townsman (fishmonger) Sōgorō breaks his abstinence and starts to drink in vexation after his younger sister Otsuta was unjustly punished and killed by her master, and then gradually loses himself to alcohol to become a vicious drinker." - Source: website of the Japan Arts Council

media.caption: Commemoration of the Grand Ceremony: Domestic Production Promotion - Panorama of the Tokyo Expo Held at Tokyo Ueno Park ((大礼記念国産振興 東京博覧会全景 東京上野公園に於て開催)

text.headline: Commemoration of the Grand Ceremony: Domestic Production Promotion - Panorama of the Tokyo Expo Held at Tokyo Ueno Park ((大礼記念国産振興 東京博覧会全景 東京上野公園に於て開催)
text.text:
The lettering on the dominating tower flying the Japanese flag tells us that this color lithograph depicts the site of the "Commemoration of the Enthronement Ceremony: Domestic Products Promotion Tokyo Exhibition" held in Ueno Park in 1928. The enthronement pavilion (大礼記念館) itself can be seen rising in the background and the Korean Pavilion (朝鮮館) juts out into Shinobazu Pond. The large building behind the Korean Pavilion is the Hyokeikwan (Imperial Museum) housing the Machinery Pavilion (機械館).
The Domestic Products Promotion Exhibition organizer was the Tokyo Chamber of Commerce and Industry. It was held to commemorate the Emperor Showa's accession to the throne and to promote and popularize domestic products. The exhibition was held from March 24 to May 27, 1928, and attracted approximately 2.23 million visitors. It was the last major exhibition to be held in Ueno Park.

media.caption: Violence in Kagoshima Prefecture, No. 1 appearing in Kagoshima-ken ari no sonomama (鹿児島県有のそのまま・初号・鹿児島県下暴)

text.headline: Violence in Kagoshima Prefecture, No. 1 appearing in Kagoshima-ken ari no sonomama (鹿児島県有のそのまま・初号・鹿児島県下暴)
text.text:
The first print in a series of twenty prints describing and depicting the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion published under the newspaper-like banner Kagoshima ken ari no sonomama, loosely translated as "Kagoshima Prefecture As It Is Now." Published in Osaka by Kanai Tokubei 金井徳兵衛, the prints, classified as nishiki-e shinbun (newspaper prints), provided short articles with accompanying simplified graphics of the Rebellion's progress, or lack thereof. All twenty prints in the series show a publication month of March or April, so the life of this "newspaper" was even shorter than the nine month rebellion. For another print published under this banner see IHL.0567
The text begins by relating that on January 31 a large number of people unexpectedly broke into the ammunition storehouses and did so again on February 2nd and 3rd. It goes on to tell of the dispatch of Hayashi Tomoyuki, an official with the Home Ministry with Admiral Kawamura Sumiyoshi in the warship Takao to investigate the situation. There is hope, by the author of the text that "They [the rebels] will see the evidence of the evil they have done and will return to their homes."
No artist's signature or seal appears on any of the twenty prints, and neither Waseda University or Kagawa University Library list the artist, but two sources, Andreas Marks on p. 190 of his book "Japanese Woodblock Prints: Artists, Publishers and Masterworks 1680-1900" and Kansai University Library attribute the prints to Hasegawa Sadanobu II (Konobu I) (1848-1940).
The entire series of twenty prints may be seen on the Waseda University Library website at http://archive.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kosho/bunko10/bunko10_08061/ [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: A Boy Who Likes to Fight (争闘を好む童男 Sōtō wo konomu warabe)

text.headline: A Boy Who Likes to Fight (争闘を好む童男 Sōtō wo konomu warabe)
text.text:
From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) showing examples of children's good (moral) and bad behavior. In this print a boy who has bloodied the head of another boy is taken in hand by a policeman. In the window above the bad boy sits a reading lamp and books, an indication of how he should better use his time.
In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

media.caption: Murakami Yoshiteru (村上義光)

text.headline: Murakami Yoshiteru (村上義光)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Murakami Hikoshirō Yoshiteru (村上 彦四郎 義光), a retainer of Prince Morinaga's (1308-1335), taking back his prince's Imperial banner from imperious villagers. He wears the cap of a yamabushi (fighting monk) which the Prince's party used as disguises during their flight from Kyoto to Yoshino in Yamata where the Prince intended to build a new castle outside the reach of the Regent, Hōjō Takatoki (1303-1333.) For the original issue of this print see Murakami Yoshiteru from the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition IHL.1032.
The 1902 reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

media.caption: Chōdensu (兆殿司)

text.headline: Chōdensu (兆殿司)
text.text:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Chōdensu (1352-1431), also known as Mincho 明兆, the famous 14th century ink painter and Zen priest sternly looking at his disciple Kikuchi Myōtaku (釋氏妙澤) painting a picture of the deity Fudō Myō-ō. Initially opposed to Kikuchi Myōtaku's painting, he relented when he realized Myōtaku's talent. For the original issue of this print see Chōdensu from the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition see IHL.0952.
The 1902 reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

media.caption: Op. 10

text.headline: Op. 10
text.text:
The tenth in a group of over fifty prints carrying the title "Op." (opus or "work"), followed by a number, created by Nonaka in the mid-1970s. This body of work employs curvilinear forms and pastel colors.
The artist notes, "I have been interested in color surfaces since I was a child, and my basic attitude is to create my own world with my own sensibility, which is different from minimal art and American abstract expressionism."

media.caption: Night Encounter on the Ichihara Moor scene from An Eastern Capital Brocade Picture of Willow Cherry (柳桜東錦絵｜市原野のだんまり)

text.headline: Night Encounter on the Ichihara Moor scene from An Eastern Capital Brocade Picture of Willow Cherry (柳桜東錦絵｜市原野のだんまり)
text.text:
Starring Onoe Taganojō II (R), Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (C) and Nakamura Shikan IV (L)
Depicted here is a short pantomime [one of ten pieces on the playbill at the Shintomi-za during April 1883] that recounted the famous tale of Fujiwara Yasumasa (center), an 11th-century courtier renowned for his flute playing, and the bandit (left) who stalks him beneath a full moon. Intending to rob the noblemen of his valuable attire, the bandit plans the attack in the presence of the mysterious Kidōmaru, appearing as a beauty disguised beneath the carcass of a cow. But instead of the theft, the bandit becomes entranced by the music, and finds himself unable to wage the assault.
The cartouches that appear near the top of each sheet in the triptych identify the actors and the roles that they played. Play titles, scene titles, and sometimes names of the theaters are provided in some cases, usually appearing on the right-most sheet. In this case, there is no inscription giving the play title, leaving it to theater aficionados to recall (or researchers to discover). - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

media.caption: Ukai 鵜飼 (The Cormorant Fisher)

text.headline: Ukai 鵜飼 (The Cormorant Fisher)
text.text:
Print number 30 in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts Raiden, the god of thunder, the spirit of the former Michizane, planning to take revenge upon his enemies in the imperial palace who sent him into exile. The god is finally quelled by an imperial decree that he, Michizane, is to be worshiped as the Heavenly God (Tenjin) of Tenma.
Play Synopsis, Ukai (The Cormorant Fisher) from A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 139-140: "When two travelling priests meet an old cormorant fisher one of them recognizes him as the man who gave him shelter two or three years ago. The old man then tells them that as he broke the strict prohibition against taking life in the nearby river by fishing there nightly with his cormorants, he has been drowned in the river as punishment. In return for the priests' promise to pray for his soul he shows them how the fishing is done and then disappears. Nichiren takes up some stones and after writing part of the Lotus Sutra on them, throws them into the river. Emma, the King of Hell, then appears and tells them that although the fisherman deserves to suffer for his sins, he will send him to Paradise because of the kindness he showed the priest."
For other depictions of the play see the prints IHL.0162 and IHL.1147.
Each print in this series depicts a main character from a Noh play and is tipped to the top edge of a solid-colored woodblock-printed backing sheet featuring the three small pines appearing along the higashigakari 橋掛 (bridgeway) stretching from the main stage to the kagami-no-ma (mirror room) where the performers gather before going on stage. The trees are printed with a dark gold metallic pigment, a deluxe printing technique.

media.caption: Shunkan 俊寛

text.headline: Shunkan 俊寛
text.text:
Print number 12 in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts the priest Shunkan listening to the ever fainter voices of his companions as their boat sails back to the capital while he remains in exile.
Play Synopsis, Shunkan: "Before the story of the play unfolds, three men - the priest Shunkan (shite) and the officials Fujiwara no Naritsune (tsure), and Taira no Yasuyori (tsure) - have been exiled to the remote island of Kigaigashima beyond the southern tip of Kyushu. The men were sent away because of their plot to overthrow Taira no Kiyomori. At the beginning of the play, Naritsune and Yasuyori have returned from a mock pilgrimage around the island. Shunkan has remained behind in their miserable dwelling. Then, Kiyomori's emissary (waki) arrives by boat, bringing a pardon for two of the three men. Shunkan's joy soon turns to despair when he learns that he is the only one who will not be permitted to return to the capital. His two companions set off with heavy hearts, leaving him alone to watch their departure." - Source: The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 114.
For another depiction of this play see IHL.0999.

media.caption: Naniwa 難波

text.headline: Naniwa 難波
text.text:
Print number 31 in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts the Emperor Ōnin with a drum stand on his left.
Play Synopsis, Naniwa: "On his way back to the capital from Kumano, a Court official stops at Naniwa and there meets two men. When one of them begins to tidy the ground beneath a plum tree, the official asks if it is a particularly famous one. He is then told that plum blossom in general is superior to any other flower, and an old poem in praise of it by Ōnin is also quoted. The old man reveals that he is Ōnin and the younger man the spirit of the plum blossom, and then they both disappear after promising to come again that night and dance. This they do, each this time in their true form."
Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 121-122.

media.caption: Tamakazura 玉葛 (The Jeweled Chaplet)

text.headline: Tamakazura 玉葛 (The Jeweled Chaplet)
text.text:
Print number 43 in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts Lady Tamakazura performing a dance that conveys her feelings about marrying a man she detested.
Play Synopsis, Tamakazura: "The servant Kochō comes bringing prescribed medicine to Minamoto no Raikō, who is ill in bed. However, his illness becomes more and more serious.
"Deep in the night after Kochō leaves, an unknown monk visits the bedridden Raikō and inquires about his condition. Suspicious, Raikō asks the name of the monk, and the monk approaches Raikō reciting a poem in the Kokin-shū, 'my love will visit me tonight, because a spider…' Looking closely, Raikō finds that it is a monstrous spider. Although the spider spins out thousands of silk threads to tie Raikō up, from his pillow side Raikō takes the great sword Hiza-maru, which has been passed down within the Genji clan. When he draws the sword and cuts the monster, the spider monk disappears instantly.
"Hitorimusha, a warrior who serves Raikō, hears the commotion and rushes to Raikō's room with many of his followers. Raikō tells about the event and announces that he will change the name of the great hereditary sword from Hiza-maru to Kumokiri (Spider Slasher). Then Raikō tells Hitorimusha to exterminate the monstrous spider as he could not give it a death blow.
"Hitorimusha and other servants follow the blood spots of the monstrous ground spider to an old mound, which seems to be the nest of the spider. The ground spider appears when they demolish the mound. The ground spider gives them trouble with its silk threads. However, Hitorimusha's entourage encircle it in strength and finally slay it." - Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 183.

media.caption: Tsuchigumo 土蜘蛛 (Earth Spider)

text.headline: Tsuchigumo 土蜘蛛 (Earth Spider)
text.text:
Print number 45 in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts Tsuchigumo, a monstrous ground spider, stepping out of his nest to cast his silk treads.
Play Synopsis, Tsuchigumo: "A priest on his way to pray at the Hade-dera comes to the Hatsuse-gawa and there meets a woman who lands from a small boat. She leads him up to two cryptomeria trees and tells him that this was where Tama-kazura met the maid of her mother Yūgao when she fled from Kyūshū after refusing the attentions of a powerful warrior there. She is the spirit of Tamakazura, she adds, and then vanishes. The priest prays, and in his dream the spirit reappears to tell of her unhappiness." - Source: The Noh.com website http://www.the-noh.com/en/plays/data/program_002.html [accessed 8-17-2023]
For other depictions of the play see the prints IHL.0153 and IHL.1144.

media.caption: Women Warriors, No. 6 from the newspaper Kagoshima Prefecture, A Full and True Report (鹿児島県 まことの電知  六号 Kagoshima-ken makoto no shirase)

text.headline: Women Warriors, No. 6 from the newspaper Kagoshima Prefecture, A Full and True Report (鹿児島県 まことの電知  六号 Kagoshima-ken makoto no shirase)
text.text:
Print number 6 in a series of woodblock prints issued in Osaka carrying the latest news of the Satsuma Rebellion. This series of news prints, consisting of fifteen prints, was published for three months and then ceased publishing for an unknown reason. The series was one of a handful that sprung up to fulfill public demand for information on the short-lived rebellion.

KAGOSHIMA PREFECTURE, VOL. 6 A FULL AND TRUE REPORT (translation of text)
"A certain person in the service of Kumamoto joined the Government forces and died spectacularly in battle. When his wife heard of this she thought that, rather than live out her remaining years in vain upon the largesse of the province, she would instead go forth and dispel her husband’s frustration. She tightened her sash and smoothed down her hems as she ran after the bandit-soldiers, determined not to let them escape. Wait for us, said the women who had served her for years, for we too would join our lord. They ventured forth onto the battlefield and gazed upon the bandit gang. Nimbly they brandished their swords, cutting into their foes, charging them, taking their heads, until it was a right bloodbath. They smiled as they strode onto the field of battle. Theirs was a virtue rare these days.
"Among the rebels were women whose fathers or husbands had died in battle, and who yearned to send them off properly, even if it meant becoming corpses themselves, rather than fading in the world crying helpless tears. A women’s brigade numbering over one thousand thus gathered unto the bandits’ encampment, it is said. Carrying halberds the older women wore long white robes, while the younger wore gaiters of crimson cotton, and all wore headbands. &c, &c; to be continued in the next volume." - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon

media.caption: Headgear and Demon Stick Stage Props from the play Ryōko

text.headline: Headgear and Demon Stick Stage Props from the play Ryōko
text.text: This composition shows two stage properties (kodōgo) of the Nō theater: a kaburimono (headgear) with the figure of a running tiger and an uchizue ("demon stick"). The headgear is topped with the figure of a tiger and the inscription on the print indicates that this work is associated with the play Ryōko. The story centers on a fight between a tiger living in a bamboo grove and a dragon from a nearby mountain.

media.caption: The Manrin Restaurant, Shinagawa-chō (品川町 万林)

text.headline: The Manrin Restaurant, Shinagawa-chō (品川町 万林)
text.text:
One of thirty-six prints in the series Thirty-Six Modern Restaurants issued in 1878. The print's composition, which has been described as "a jarring juxtaposition" of the traditional and modern, captures, in my view, the changing reality that was Tokyo in the early Meiji period, where tension between tradition and modernity was ever present and life was becoming a "jarring juxtaposition" of the traditional and the Western.
The two red cartouches above the courtesans read 本石三泉屋 さん and 本石町小三代. It would be appropriate if the Westerners pictured were Dutch, as the Dutch introduced single point perspective (which Kunichika employs in this print) to Japan in the 17th century.

media.caption: Portrait of Yoshida Shōin, sensei (吉田松陰 先生之像)

text.headline: Portrait of Yoshida Shōin, sensei (吉田松陰 先生之像)
text.text:
In this woodblock print titled "Portrait of Yoshida Shōin," Okuyama has copied a well-known photo of Yoshida Shōin (1830-1859), a samurai from the Chōshū domain who was executed in 1859 for the attempted assassination of Ii Naosuke, the shogunate Tairō (prime minister). Yoshida had a profound impact on a number of key figures in the Meiji Restoration, including Hirobumi Ito and Aritomo Yamagata.
Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) maker and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own woodblock prints, such as IHL.1844, and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.
When this print was produced in 1943, Okuyama was one of many print artists who had joined the wartime nationalist print organization Nihon Hanga Hōkōkai. This portrait of Yoshida Shōin (1830-1850), whose Tokugawa-era writings were used as justification by nationalist supporters of Japan's military and colonization of Asia was created to bolster Japan's war effort.
For another impression of this print see IHL.1889.

media.caption: Ehon Chūshingura, Volume 5 (繪本忠臣藏 之五巻)

text.headline: Ehon Chūshingura, Volume 5 (繪本忠臣藏 之五巻)
text.text: Volume five of ten bound volumes comprising a novel loosely based on the real life 1701 Akō Incident (with names changed) that gave rise to the tale of Chūshingura, popularized in the kabuki theater and the written word.

text.headline: White Woods A (白い林 A)

media.caption: Shimabara District After the Rain (しまばらくるわ雨後 Shimabara kuruwa ugo)

text.headline: Shimabara District After the Rain (しまばらくるわ雨後 Shimabara kuruwa ugo)
text.text:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), using the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.
This print depicts the main gate entrance to Shimabara, Kyoto's former red-light district, after a night rain. When this print was made Shimabara was still a licensed entertainment area. Japanese art historian Lynn Katsumoto notes: "The sign on the stand to left says 'tako' - the 'yaki' is left off, but I think that's what most people assume. Tako yaki are little bready balls with bits of octopus inside, popular street fare." A crude drawing of an octopus appears to the right on the stand's curtain. For another impression of this print see IHL.1126.

media.caption: Plum Tree at Kitano Tenmangū Shrine (北野の梅 Kitano no ume)

text.headline: Plum Tree at Kitano Tenmangū Shrine (北野の梅 Kitano no ume)
text.text:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), using the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.
In this print, a woman, pushing her young son in a stroller, passes by one of the many statues of reclining cows at Kyoto's Kitano Tenmangū Shrine, dedicated to the spirit of the exiled scholar and poet Sugawara no Michizane. The young boy is pointing to the cow, which visitors seeking good fortune in their scholarly pursuits often stroke as they pass by. The temple is known for its famous plum trees that bloom from late February throughout March.

media.caption: Oharame (大原女)

text.headline: Oharame (大原女)
text.text: From a never completed series portraying fifty traditional dances, this print depicts an Oharame (woman of Ohara) dancing in a comical mask with a woman's snub-nosed face, bulging cheeks and a happy grin, known as an Otafuku or Okame mask.

media.caption: Nagasaki Confucian Temple (長崎孔子廟 Nagasaki kōshi-byō)

text.headline: Nagasaki Confucian Temple (長崎孔子廟 Nagasaki kōshi-byō)
text.text:
Always in love with rooftops, Sekino presents us with a tantalizing view of the rooftop of Kōshi-byō, the Chinese Confucian temple in Nagasaki.
Nagasaki Confucian Temple (Kōshi-byō 孔子廟) is a Confucian temple in Nagasaki, Japan. Today the land on which it stands is owned by the Chinese Embassy in Tokyo. First built in 1893 by Chinese residents of Nagasaki with the support of the Qing Dynasty government, the shrine was designed to serve as a place of worship and learning for the Chinese community, and housed a Confucian sanctuary and primary school. The buildings were severely damaged by the atomic bomb explosion on August 9, 1945 and were not restored and opened to the public until September 1967. The shrine was extensively renovated in 1982. Standing outside the shrine are 72 statues representing the 72 followers of Confucius. - Source: Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius_Shrine,_Nagasaki [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Famous Courtesan Jiro of Hamadaya in Sumi-yoshichō (住よし町名妓 濵田屋じらう)

text.headline: Famous Courtesan Jiro of Hamadaya in Sumi-yoshichō (住よし町名妓 濵田屋じらう)
text.text:
From a set of hand-colored lithographs of famous courtesans by Kumazawa Kitarō, whose name is shown on the margin of the prints as the artist, printer and publisher, based in Tokyo. Kumazawa produced a broad range of lithographs covering subject matter including maps, scenic views, children, the military, the Sino-Japanese (1894-1895) and Russo-Japanese (1904-1905) wars, proper etiquette for women and an 1895 portrait of Emperor Meiji and Empress Haruko.
Little is known about Kumazawa other than he was active during the period that saw a decline in the woodblock print publishing industry as the realism achievable by new technical developments in color lithography became popular and publishers realized its efficiency over woodblock printing of illustrations.

media.caption: Table of Contents, Twelve Aspects of Kyoto (京洛十二趣 目録)

text.headline: Table of Contents, Twelve Aspects of Kyoto (京洛十二趣 目録)
text.text:
The table of contents for the series Twelve Aspects of Kyoto. In the background are various auspicious items including daruma dolls, a red torii gate and a treasure ship for the seven gods of good luck.
The Series - Twelve Aspects of Kyoto
This series consisting of twelve ko-tanzaku format prints and this table of contents print, was originally published in November 1943. Each of the twelve prints corresponded with a month of the year. As originally released, the prints were mounted onto a stiff backing, as was this print, and placed in a folding portfolio by the publisher or placed into a decorative wooden box. At an unknown later date the prints were sold unmounted without the stiff backing.

media.caption: View of the Mint Bureau (造幣局を望む)

text.headline: View of the Mint Bureau (造幣局を望む)
text.text:
One of twelve woodblock-printed postcards designed by Tokuriki that make up the three part series Famous Places of Osaka, issued in the 1930s by Unsōdō Publishing.
This postcard features a sidewheel steamer on the Okawa River passing by the Japan Mint built in 1871 in the Western-style. The Japan Mint was established in Osaka by the Meiji government to modernize the coinage system. As built, it included factories to make the necessary equipment for the mint. A power plant was added in 1911 and it was this building that was renovated into the Mint Museum in 1969.

media.caption: Allegiance of the Entire Nation (万民きふく banmin kifuku)

text.headline: Allegiance of the Entire Nation (万民きふく banmin kifuku)
text.text:
One of thirty prints in the series Azuma fūzoku, fukuzukushi (Eastern Customs, Enumerated Blessings), issued between 1887 and 1890. In the background of this print we see Emperor Meiji's Phoenix Carriage leaving the Imperial Palace grounds, having just passed over Nijubashi. The two women revelers in the foreground are festively dressed and a celebration is taking place. Given the print's date of 1889, the activities depicted must relate to the February 11, 1889 promulgation of the constitution.
Japanese art historian Lynn Katsumoto comments that the fan being held open by the woman with the parasol bears an inscription that might read 宝作万来 hōsaku banrai which could be taken to mean ”abundant harvests for all time to come” and that behind the title inscription in the upper right corner you can see an observation stand with purple bunting and a signboard with the partially obscured characters 万歳 banzai, the cheer that means "May His Reign Last Ten Thousand Years" (that is, forever). Both inscriptions befit a celebration for the new constitution.

EASTERN CUSTOMS, ENUMERATED BLESSINGS
"Some of these single sheet designs are among Chikanobu's finest renderings of Meiji period life, with elegant modern ladies dressed in the latest French fashions and handsome government officials donning their European style uniforms. He also created vignettes of daily life at home in Tokyo, with a baby learning to crawl, children playing games, young girls reading in the afternoon, and two young women enjoying flute music at dusk in an iris garden.
"These images have a proud sense of well being, that Japan has successfully transitioned into the modern era but still retained the best aspects of its traditional culture. The Roman alphabet has been used in titles to give a contemporary global outlook to the prints, even though the letters spell Japanese words. These works were published at a time when discussions were taking place in Tokyo about whether Chinese characters (kanji) should be abandoned as too old fashioned and cumbersome, and how English should become more widespread in Japan as a way of making the Japanese more internationally conscious and competitive."[1]
Each print carries one of the many meanings of the word "fuku" (or "huku" as it appears in each print's multi-colored title cartouche, written in a hybrid form of Western fonts.)
Many of the prints in the series, if not the entire series, were issued more than once, as color variants of many of the prints exist and varying dates of publication can be found on several prints. In addition, many of the prints in the series can be found both with and without printed dates in the publisher's rectangular cartouche.

[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p.46.

media.caption: Spraying Water (霧ふくkiri fuku)

text.headline: Spraying Water (霧ふくkiri fuku)
text.text:

media.caption: Blessed with Many Children (子福者 kofuku sha)

text.headline: Blessed with Many Children (子福者 kofuku sha)
text.text:
One of thirty prints in the series Azuma fūzoku, fukuzukushi (Eastern Customs, Enumerated Blessings), issued between 1887 and 1890. In this print, a tired mother looks over her seven children.
"Seven children are shown amidst toys, games and books. Two girls play ayatori ("string pulling") or cat's cradle, while a young lad looks at pictures of samurai ("warriors"). An inu haiku (papier mache dog) is at right, next to a fan, drum and drumsticks. In the foreground is a miniature sake (rice wine) set for pretend parties. The whole group looks well-fed and happy, although the mother seems rather tired from managing such a crew." - Source: Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 142.

media.caption: Blessings Inside (子福者 fuku wauchi)

text.headline: Blessings Inside (子福者 fuku wauchi)
text.text:
One of thirty prints in the series Azuma fūzoku, fukuzukushi (Eastern Customs, Enumerated Blessings), issued between 1887 and 1890. In this print, children gather up beans thrown by a toshi-otoko (Man of the Year), as further explained below.
"During the Setsubun ('Change of Season') festival held at the end of winter by the lunar calendar, mame-maki ('bean throwing') is accompanied by shouts of 'Fuku wa uchi, oni wa soto' ('Good fortune in, demons out!'). The beans are usually thrown out by a toshi-otoko, a man whose zodiac sign matches that of the new year, and in this print he is the shadowy figure beyond the shoji screen. Children are gathering up the scattered beans to use in cooking the first rice pot on risshun ('the first day of spring') hoping this will bring them good health and good luck. Setsubun decorations hang above the door to the sliding door panel, and a plum tree blooms in the garden."[1]
