media.caption: Chikako (ちか子)

text.headline: Chikako (ちか子)
text.text:
Print number 43 (四十三), one of two designs contributed by Chikanobu, to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Chikako, the daughter of the once wealthy, later disgraced, businessman Zeniya Gohei, just before she commits suicide by jumping into the Asano River to demonstrate her sincerity.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Biographies of Brave and Loyal Retainers, Act 1 (忠雄義臣傳 [忠雄義臣伝] 巻之一 Chūyū gishin den, maki no ichi)

text.headline: Biographies of Brave and Loyal Retainers, Act 1 (忠雄義臣傳 [忠雄義臣伝] 巻之一 Chūyū gishin den, maki no ichi)
text.text:
Depicting a scene in Act 1, "Examining the Helmet," from the play Biographies of Brave and Loyal Retainers, a version of the vendetta tale commonly referred to as Chūshingura or Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of the Loyal Retainers). In this scene, we see Lady Kaoyo, the wife of Lord En'ya, identifying the helmet of the dead Nitta Yoshisada, an enemy of shōgun Ashikaga Takauji, which is to be enshrined in Kamakura's Hachiman shrine. The four other figures in the print are Lord En'ya, Lord Wakanosuke, Lord Moronō and Naoyoshi Ashikaga, the younger brother of the shogun.
At least two editions of this print exist, published by different publishers. This print is considered a first edition and was published by Yamadaya Shōbei. This first edition by Yamadaya Shōbei is framed with the saw-tooth pattern associated with Chūshingura. The second edition by Izumiya Ichibei is framed by a solid blue border inset with circles containing bats. It is assumed that Izumiya Ichibei purchased the woodblocks from Yamadaya Shōbei. (See IHL.2081 for the second edition print.)

media.caption: Illustration of His Imperial Majesty's Funeral Outside Nijūbashi (二重橋外御大葬之圖 Nijūbashi-gai gotaisō no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of His Imperial Majesty's Funeral Outside Nijūbashi (二重橋外御大葬之圖 Nijūbashi-gai gotaisō no zu)
text.text:
Bordered in black, this is one of two prints (the other being the triptych Illustration of the Main Gate at Aoyama During the Imperial Funeral Ceremony, IHL.1683) created by the artist picturing the September 13, 1912 evening funeral procession for Emperor Meiji from the Imperial Palace to the Aoyama military parade grounds. While this print depicts the procession just after its departure from the Imperial Palace and passage over Nijūbashi, the triptych depicts the procession as it enters the Aoyama military parade grounds, where it ends.
"The funeral session was enormous in scale, involving more than 20,000 people. It began at 8:00 p.m. with the departure from the palace grounds through the main gate at Nijūbashi (Double Bridge). It is this first stage of the procession that is represented in this hexaptych, the format of which certainly lent itself to such an occasion.
At the center of the procession was the hearse, which was pulled by five oxen and accompanied by some three hundred individuals carrying torches, drums, gongs, banners, bows, shields, and lances. Among those closest to the hearse were imperial prices, senior members of the aristocracy and peerage, and high-level military personnel of the army and navy in full dress uniform. The contrast between those wearing ancient court dress and those resplendent in Western-style uniforms, with black armbands was a vivid one, and well captured by the artist." - Source: Conflicts of Interest: Art and War in Modern Japan, Philip K. Hu, et. al., Saint Louis Museum of Art, 2016, p. 276-277.

media.caption: Kinsatsu 金札 (The Golden Tablet)

text.headline: Kinsatsu 金札 (The Golden Tablet)
text.text:
Depicting the god Amatsu Futodama carrying a bow and arrow with which to subdue demons and ensure the peace of the land. The pyre in the background "suggests that this is an outdoor performance called takigi nō. The custom has its origins in the practice of burning sacred firewood (takigi), a special ceremony held at the Kofuku Temple (Kōfukuji), one of the most ancient Buddhist temples in Nara."[1]
PLAY SYNOPSIS
An Imperial envoy goes to the village of Fushimi in Yamashiro Province in connection with a new shrine being built there by the Emperor Kammu. While talking with an old man whom he meets there, a tablet with gold writing on it falls from the sky. Taking it up, the envoy read that the god to whom it belongs promises constant protection to the land. The old man then takes the tablet and disappears, revealing as he does so that he is the god, Amatsu Futodama. He then appears in his true form, carrying a bow and arrow with which to subdue demons and ensure the peace of the land.

ONE HUNDRED PRINTS OF NOH
Kōgyo's second series of prints, One Hundred Prints of Noh, consists of 120 prints derived from 100 Noh plays. Fourteen diptych and three triptych prints were included. These prints are quite different from those in Kōgyo's first series, The Illustrations of Noh. The principal actor is nearly always the focus of the composition and all the prints are in vertical rather than horizontal oban format. "The backgrounds often contain rich gradations of color, or dramatic, painterly suggestions of a setting. The monumentality of the figure creates a powerful, authoritative tone."[3]

[1] The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 93.
[2] A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 77-78.
[3] The Prints of Tsukioka Kōgyo, a brochure from the exhibition of the same name held at the Frick Art Museum February 3 - April 7, 2007.

media.caption: Phalaenopsis and Haniwa (胡蝶蘭と埴輪)

text.headline: Phalaenopsis and Haniwa (胡蝶蘭と埴輪)
text.text:
Picturing a a vase, an ancient funerary haniwa figure and a stem of a Phalaenopsis orchid (commonly referred to as a "moth orchid"), this 1985 print was previously issued, using a different color scheme, in an edition of 120 in 1980.
This print carries the notation 家蔵, in the artist's hand, indicating the print was part of his collection, possibly a proof print never put into production.

media.caption: Lily (ゆり)

text.headline: Lily (ゆり)
text.text:
A still-life of a single lily in three phases of budding, set in front of what appears to be a black vase with a sake cup or bowl on the left.
This print carries the notation 家蔵, in the artist's hand, indicating the print was part of his collection, possibly a proof print never put into production.

media.caption: Barley at Sunrise

text.headline: Barley at Sunrise
text.text:
One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) around the turn of the 20th century and attributed to the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi).
Titling this print "Rice Stalks" the authors of "The Beauty of Silence Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927)" comment, "Green rice stalks in the foreground contrast a brilliant orange sky at sunset." Other sources use the title "Barley at Sunrise", a more accurate descriptive title I believe.

media.caption: New Translation of The Tale of Genji, 3rd volume, part 2 (新訳源氏物語 下巻の二 Shin'yaku Genji monogatari, gekan no ni)

text.headline: New Translation of The Tale of Genji, 3rd volume, part 2 (新訳源氏物語 下巻の二 Shin'yaku Genji monogatari, gekan no ni)
text.text:
The fourth and last book (part two of the third volume), containing chapters 50 through 54, of Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of Lady Murasaki Shikibu's 紫式部著 (973-1025?), The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), an account of court life in Heian period Japan, written in the early 11th century. Her translation, originally published in 1912 (the first two volumes) and 1913 (the last two volumes) by Kanao Tanejirō (1879-1947), through his publishing house Kanao Bun'endō, was illustrated with sixty-one woodblock prints (including four frontispieces) designed by the Western-style (yōga) artist Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964).
Yosano, in writing Shin'yaku Genji monogatari, is credited with transforming "Genji [perhaps the world's first novel] into a modern novel, thus making it part of modern Japanese literature." - Source: Envisioning The Tale of Genji Media, Gender, and Cultural Production, ed. Haruo Shirane, Columbia University Press, p. 7.
For the other volumes see IHL.2288 (vol. 1), IHL.2289 (vol. 2), IHL.2290 (vol. 3, part 1), IHL.2219 (vol. 3, part 2)

media.caption: New Translation of The Tales of the Heike, first volume (新訳平家物語 上巻  Shin'yaku Heike monogatari, jōkan)

text.headline: New Translation of The Tales of the Heike, first volume (新訳平家物語 上巻  Shin'yaku Heike monogatari, jōkan)
text.text:
The first volume of a two volume "new translation" into modern colloquial Japanese by journalist, author and poet Shibukawa Genji, of The Tale of the Heike (Heike monogatari, 平家物語), an epic account of the struggle between the Heike (Taira) and Minamoto (Genji) clans for control of Japan at the end of the twelfth century in the Gempei War (1180-1185). Published by Kanao Tanejirō through his publishing house Kanao Bun'endō in 1914 in two volumes, it was illustrated with woodblock prints designed by the Western-style artist Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964). This first volume contains the first seven chapters with each chapter having multiple sections.
The Tale of the Heike (Heike monogatari, 平家物語) was compiled in 1240 by an unknown author from a collection of oral stories composed and recited by traveling monks, who chanted them to the accompaniment of the biwa (lute). The most widely read version of the Heike monogatari was compiled by the blind monk Kakuichi in 1371, and includes later revisions glorifying military valor. The story is intended to be told in a series of nightly installments. Written in the genre of gunki monogatari (military tales), the story illustrates themes of samurai ethics and glorifies the military values of loyalty, bravery, and strong leadership. It also promulgates Buddhist teachings; the theme of the impermanence of the material world appears throughout the story, and the fates of the characters are preordained by the good or evil deeds of prior existences. Often characters seek enlightenment, or atone for their sins, by entering religious life. The Tale of the Heike is considered one of the great classics of medieval Japanese literature and has provided material for many later artistic works ranging from Noh plays to woodblock prints.
In the words of Helen Craig McCullough, it is the story "of a proud and mighty man, Taira no Kiyomori, of his contumacy, 'freakish caprices,' and selfishness, and of the destruction visited on his descendants in accordance with the law of karmic retribution." - Source: The Tale of the Heike, Helen Craig McCullough, Stanford University Press, 1988, p. 456.
Clicking on the thumbnail will bring you to a pdf. displaying the woodblock illustrations in this volume. Please allow time for the file to download.

media.caption: New Translation of The Tales of the Heike, last volume (新訳平家物語 下巻  Shin'yaku Heike monogatari, gekan)

text.headline: New Translation of The Tales of the Heike, last volume (新訳平家物語 下巻  Shin'yaku Heike monogatari, gekan)
text.text:

media.caption: Sōshi Arai Komachi, saishiki (草子洗小町 彩色)

text.headline: Sōshi Arai Komachi, saishiki (草子洗小町 彩色)
text.text:
In this print for the month of May, the poetess Ono no Komachi reads her poem at a poetry contest for the emperor in the Noh play "Sōshi Arai Komachi." The print and the print with its commentary overlay, as explained below, is pictured to the left.

The Play - Sōshi Arai Komachi (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 170-171.)
"At a poetry competition in the presence of the Emperor, Ōtomo no Kuronushi's opponent is to be the poetess Ono no Komachi. Fearing that he will be defeated, Kuronushi plans to avoid this and to discomfit his rival at the same time. He and his servant manage to overhear the poem Komachi has written for the competition, and this he writes into a leaf from a copy of the Manyōshū anthology. When the poetess later recites this in the contest, he challenges it on that grounds that it is an old poem and produces the copy of the Manyōshū as proof. Komachi is overcome with humiliation at this, but with the help of Ki no Tsurayuki she obtains the permission of the Emperor to test the leaf in question by rinsing it with water. When she does so, the freshly written poem is washed away. Having had his trickery thus exposed, Kuronushi feels that the only course left for him is suicide, but the persuasion and forgiveness of Komachi and an order from the Emperor bring him back. To dispel any lingering awkwardness, Komachi entertains the company by performing a dance in honour of the Emperor and his reign."
Twelve Months of Noh Pictures
From a series of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1970. Six of the prints (for the months of January, February, June, September, November and December) were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963) and the other six (for the months of March, April, May, July, August and October) were created by his son Matsuno Hideyo (1936-2002). As Sōfū died in 1963, his prints must have been created from existing designs.
As originally issued, the prints were sold as a set with each print placed inside its own mat, which was overlaid with a commentary sheet on the play in Japanese and English. The matted print and commentary were then placed inside an envelope and all twelve envelopes were then placed into a cloth folio.
Interestingly, the artist seals appearing on the prints, each one being different, relate to the play being pictured, such as in the square red seal on this print whose characters, according to the commentary sheet accompanying the print, read "The Waterside Grass," a reference to the poem written by the poetess Ono no Komachi that she was maliciously accused of plagiarizing.

media.caption: Hagoromo, wagō (羽衣 和合)

text.headline: Hagoromo, wagō (羽衣 和合)
text.text:
In this print for the month of March, the celestial maiden dances in order to retrieve her “feathered robe” (hagoromo). She sings of the beauty of spring breezes in the pines at Miho Bay, and then flies off to the misty peak of Mt. Fuji, seen in the hazy background shape, in the Noh play "Hagoromo."

The Play - Hagoromo (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 46-47.)
"Some fishermen are walking at Matsubara on Mio Bay when one of them finds a beautiful robe hanging from the branch of a pine tree. He is about to take this home when an angel comes to claim it, explaining that it is a feather robe from Heaven. This makes the fisherman determined to keep it as a national treasure, but when the angel tells him that without it she can never again ascend to Heaven he is so moved by her distress that he agrees to return it if she will dance for him. He at first refused to give it back before she dances for fear that she will fly away as soon as the robe is hers again, but when the angel tells him that such behaviour is only to be found in the ways of men, he shamefacedly gives up the robe. Overjoyed now, the angel puts it on and dances. Then, calling down blessings without number on the land, she disappears up to Heaven among the mists and clouds."
Twelve Months of Noh Pictures
From a series of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1970. Six of the prints (for the months of January, February, June, September, November and December) were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963) and the other six (for the months of March, April, May, July, August and October) were created by his son Matsuno Hideyo (1936-2002). As Sōfū died in 1963, his prints must have been created from existing designs.
As originally issued, the prints were sold as a set with each print placed inside its own mat, which was overlaid with a commentary sheet on the play in Japanese and English. The matted print and commentary were then placed inside an envelope and all twelve envelopes were then placed into a cloth folio.
Interestingly, the artist seals appearing on the prints, each one being different, relate to the play being pictured, such as in the square red seal on this print whose characters, according to the commentary sheet accompanying the print, read "The Sleeve of White Clouds."

media.caption: Rainy Antwerp (雨のアントワープ)

text.headline: Rainy Antwerp (雨のアントワープ)
text.text: Looking so much like the zinc rooftops of Paris, the title on a label accompanying the print tells us it is "Rainy Antwerp."  Sekino traveled extensively through Europe, leading to a number of atmospheric prints of the cities he visited. A wonderful marbling technique (perhaps the grain of the wood?) is used on the walls of the houses.

media.caption: Seiho's Guide to Drawing, Vol. 3 (栖鳳 習畫帖 第三 Seihō shūgachō)

text.headline: Seiho's Guide to Drawing, Vol. 3 (栖鳳 習畫帖 第三 Seihō shūgachō)
text.text:
Published just after Seihō's return from Europe, Seihō's Guide to Drawing was exhibited at the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition, held in St. Louis, Missouri, as part of the Japanese government's display of Books and Publications.
"Printed on deluxe paper with specially designed covers and bindings, Seihō’s Painting Instruction Album is more of a luxury object than a tool for the would-be self-taught painter. Nevertheless, the designs progress from the simplest monochrome ink sketches, in volumes 1 and 2, to more complex motifs with color, in volumes 3 and 4." - source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 248.
See IHL.0783 for Volume 1, IHL.0784 for Volume 2, IHL.2225 for Volume 3 and IHL.0785 for Volume 4.

media.caption: Bird Resting On a Bamboo Carrying Device

text.headline: Bird Resting On a Bamboo Carrying Device
text.text: A master of everyday things, Zeshin depicts a sparrow sitting on a bamboo carrying pole tenbinbō 天秤棒 with two roped trays at either end. This print was designed as one of twenty prints for the two volume illustrated book Ehon Yamato Nishiki: Shibata Zeshin sensei gafu 繪本大和錦: 柴田是真先生畫譜 , commonly referred to as Shibata Zeshin Gafu 柴田是真画譜.

media.caption: Two Stacks of Bamboo Baskets and a Spray of Purple Iris

text.headline: Two Stacks of Bamboo Baskets and a Spray of Purple Iris
text.text: A master of everyday things, Zeshin depicts two stacks of baskets with what appears to be water splashing out of a few of them forming rivulets and a bouquet of purple irises. This print was designed as one of twenty prints for the two volume illustrated book Ehon Yamato Nishiki: Shibata Zeshin sensei gafu 繪本大和錦: 柴田是真先生畫譜 , commonly referred to as Shibata Zeshin Gafu 柴田是真画譜.

media.caption: Wooden Rice Tub and Nori

text.headline: Wooden Rice Tub and Nori
text.text: A master of everyday things, Zeshin depicts a wooden bench, a hangari (bamboo rice tub) and sheets of nori (dried seaweed) for one of twenty prints in the two volume illustrated book Ehon Yamato Nishiki: Shibata Zeshin sensei gafu 繪本大和錦: 柴田是真先生畫譜 , commonly referred to as Shibata Zeshin Gafu 柴田是真画譜.

media.caption: Picture Card Show, Behind Meritorious Deeds (紙芝居 殊勲の蔭に Kamishibai Shukun no kage ni)

text.headline: Picture Card Show, Behind Meritorious Deeds (紙芝居 殊勲の蔭に Kamishibai Shukun no kage ni)
text.text:
A twenty print (all color lithographs) kamishibai (picture card show) authorized and sponsored during the Pacific War by the Nihon Kyōiku Kamishibai Kyōkai (Japanese Association for Educational Kamishibai), "a quasi-governmental organization charged with producing plays in support of Japanese government policies, to be performed domestically and throughout the Japanese Empire and conquered territories." - Source: https://networks.h-net.org/node/20904/discussions/10774246/kamishibai-database [accessed 8-17-23]
During a picture card show, the presenter would show each image while reciting, sometimes ad-libbing, the accompanying text on each card's verso. For wartime propaganda picture card shows the presenter was required to carefully follow the script and not ad-lib.
While a picture card show associated with children's street entertainment, may seem innocent enough, picture card shows used for war propaganda purposes were targeted not only at children but also at "adults, particularly those of lower classes: factory workers, farmers and other agricultural workers, inhabitants of poor urban neighborhoods, and small business owners, among others." - Source: Propaganda Performed, Kamishibai in Japan's Fifteen Year War, Sharalyn Orbaugh, Brill, 2015, p. 2.
Post-war, wartime kamishibai were the subject of an investigation by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East (IMTFE), better known as the Tokyo War Crimes trial. During this investigation into Japanese wartime propaganda, Akio Saki, President of the Nihon Kamishibai Association, was called as a prosecution witness. The investigation briefly traced the development of educational kamishibai 教育紙芝居 which were originally used, according to Akio, "to make children be honest, kind and to study their lessons," but would later be used as war propaganda (a wartime kamishibai titled "Japan Is Now Fighting" was referenced) "made on direct orders from various branches of the government and many others also by orders from Imperial Rule Assistance Association." Source: website of the University of Virginia School of Law The International Military Tribunal For The Far East Digital Collection, Transcript of proceeding of June 21, 1946 p. 1129- 1187 http://imtfe.law.virginia.edu/collections/morgan/4/1/trial-transcript-june-21-1946 [accessed 8-17-23]

media.caption: Yanagi Bathhouse (柳湯 Yanagi-yu)

text.headline: Yanagi Bathhouse (柳湯 Yanagi-yu)
text.text: A modern large-format woodblock reproduction by the publisher Yūyūdō of a design originally appearing in Takehisa Yumeji's 1915 book of poetry titled Samisen-kusa (Shamisen Leaves), published by the Tokyo publisher Shinchōsha.

media.caption: Fishing Village (漁村)

text.headline: Fishing Village (漁村)
text.text: In keeping with the artist's focus on traditional fishing along the Japanese coast, he portrays a street, absent of villagers, in a small fishing village. Compare Okubo's print with that of his contemporary, Kitaoka Fumio's (1918-2007) print titled Fishing Village in the Afternoon (IHL.0194).

media.caption: Tokyo Asakusa Park: Picture of the Ryōunkaku Building (東京浅草公園凌雲閣之図)

text.headline: Tokyo Asakusa Park: Picture of the Ryōunkaku Building (東京浅草公園凌雲閣之図)
text.text:
As Tokyo's, and Japan's, first Western-style skyscraper, Ryōunkaku 凌雲閣 ("Cloud-Surpassing Pavillion") was subject of a number of depictions in woodblock and lithograph prints, posters and postcards. The colors of modernity, red and purple, dominate, as is befitting this architectural marvel which opened in late 1890.
This twelve-story 170' tower stood in the Asakusa district of Tokyo from 1890 until its demolition following the Great Kantō Earthquake on September 21, 1923. Designed by Scottish engineer W. K. Burton, the Asakusa Jūnikai 浅草十二階 (Asakusa Twelve-Stories), as it was affectionately called by Tokyoites, was the most popular attraction in Tokyo, and a showcase for new technologies, housing Japan's first electric elevator.

media.caption: Highland Flowers (高原の花)

text.headline: Highland Flowers (高原の花)
text.text:
In this print, Kitaoka showcases a "skunk cabbage" on the high moors and peatlands in Hokkaidō's Sarobetsu wilderness. Through the rain we see Mount Rishiri, a stratovolcano on Rishiri Island off the coast of Hokkaidō in the Sea of Japan.
This print's image was turned into a large porcelain mural titled 春のサロベツ原野, 1990 (Spring Sarobetsu Wilderness) by the ceramics manufacturer Iwao Jiki Kogyo Co., Ltd. in 1990 and hangs in the Town Hall of Horonobe, Hokkaidō.

media.caption: Mochizuri Stone (信夫文字摺石 Shinobu Mojizuriishi)

text.headline: Mochizuri Stone (信夫文字摺石 Shinobu Mojizuriishi)
text.text:
Autumn and the maple trees are aflame in this depiction of the Mochizuri Stone (the "dyeing stone" or "pattern-pressing stone") and a small temple in the Mochizuri Kannon temple grounds in Mojizuri (formerly Shinobu Village) on the outskirts of Fukushima City.
The stone was visited by the haiku poet and traveler Matsuo Bashō during his Narrow Road of Oku journey, which he began in 1689, and appears in a famous poem titled Kawara no Sadijin by Minamoto no Toru (822-295) about unrequited love.

media.caption: Hattachi no kai (波立の海)

text.headline: Hattachi no kai (波立の海)
text.text: A view of Bentenjima and its torii from the Hattachi coast in Iwaki City, the southernmost city along the Fukushima coast. The island was inundated when the tsunami hit on March 11, 2011 but recovered, as has Iwaki City.

media.caption: Aso noyaki (阿蘇野焼き)

text.headline: Aso noyaki (阿蘇野焼き)
text.text: Sekino has captured the many colors of grassland burning on the meadows of Aso, the largest active volcano in Japan. Noyaki 野焼き is the name given to the process of the controlled burning of the grasslands of Aso. Grassland burning has been documented for over a 1000 years in and around the Aso caldera. The burning prevents shrubs and trees from taking over the land and so preserves the grasslands not only for the cattle and horses that graze there but also as a unique landscape for Aso’s visitors.

media.caption: Pokhara (ポカラ)

text.headline: Pokhara (ポカラ)
text.text: A drypoint and aquatint by the artist Noriko Saitō whose work has been described as "playful," "whimsical" and "expressive."  This print titled Pokhara pays homage to this Nepalese city on Phewa Lake, in central Nepal. Noriko's husband is Nepalese.

media.caption: Eagle Perched on Cliff (untitled)

text.headline: Eagle Perched on Cliff (untitled)
text.text: This untitled print of an eagle perched on a cliff on a gray wind-swept day in winter, is attributed to Koson by the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art and is stamped as such on the presentation folder for this print, as sold by Robert Muller's Robert Lee Gallery. The print is also seen attributed to the shin hanga artist Shoda Kōhō (1870-1946), but I think this unlikely. It does not appear in Crows, Cranes & Camellias: The Natural World of Ohara Koson 1877-1945, the closest we have to a catalog raisonné for the artist. This print has a small MADE IN JAPAN ink stamp on verso.

media.caption: Musician Greenwich Village (グリニッジビレッジの音楽家)

text.headline: Musician Greenwich Village (グリニッジビレッジの音楽家)
text.text:
It is always fascinating to look at an artist's proof print (IHL. 2240) and the final edition of the print (IHL.0238). While the editioned version is of very poor quality with severe toning and horizontal and vertical "burn" marks on the paper, we can see that the biggest change from the artist proof to the editioned print was the addition of the orange markings in the lower right of the print.
Created the year following Takahashi's 1963 visit to the United States, this print captures the feel of the Greenwich Village jazz scene in the early 60s.

media.caption: Tale of the Wind, W376 (風のメルヘン)

text.headline: Tale of the Wind, W376 (風のメルヘン)
text.text:
Kurosaki's squiggles bring three-dimensionality to this print, wrapping around a granite-like cone. A scarlet and black spearhead stands guard over these dream shapes of the artist.
Though traditional in technique, Kurosaki set his goal "to re-animate their [traditional woodblock prints] style in modern form through strong color contrasts and radical compositions."[1] In the artist's words, "I combine shapes and aspects to create a world reminiscent to that found in ukiyo-e prints" and his favorite shapes originated from his own imagination.[2]

[1] Akira Kurosaki Woodblock Prints, 1965-1983, Hideo Tomiyama and Akira Kurosaki, Shirota Gallery November, 1984, p. 16.
[2] The Complete Works of Akira Kurosaki: Catalogue Raisonne: Woodcuts & Paper Works 1965-2006 黒崎彰の全仕事. Tokyo, Abe Shuppan, 2006.

media.caption: Sumidagawa (隅田川)

text.headline: Sumidagawa (隅田川)
text.text:
In this undated painting of an actor in the role of the mother of Umewaka-maru in the Noh play Sumidagawa, the actor wears a fukai (middle-aged woman’s mask) and carries a sasa (bamboo) branch to suggest her madness at the loss of her son Umewaka-maru. In the last scene "the boy appears (or seems to appear) twice before the mother. She tries to touch him but he slips away back into the grave. What seemed to be her child is but the wild grasses of the tomb. With only sorrow remaining, the woman weeps." - Source: website of noh-kyogen.com http://www.noh-kyogen.com/story/english/Sumidagawa.pdf [web page not active 8-17-23]
One of six siblings and son of the print artist and painter of the Noh theatre Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963), Hideyo followed in his father's footsteps. He is best known for his paintings of stage backdrops (kagami-ita) for the Kanze Noh Theater in Tokyo, the Nagoya Noh Theater (名古屋能楽堂 Nōgaku-dō) and the Noh theater at the MOA Museum of Art, Atami, Shizuoka and a series of wall paintings at Itsukushima Shinto shrine.

media.caption: Nakayamadera - temple 24 (中山寺 二十四)

text.headline: Nakayamadera - temple 24 (中山寺 二十四)
text.text:
Nakazawa depicts a line of Jizō bodhisattvas, protector of children, within the Nakayama-dera grounds, with small offerings on the ledge beneath them. The temple is the 24th along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage route encompassing 33 Buddhist temples in Western Japan (Kansai region) dedicated to Kannon (bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara), the Bodhisattva of Compassion, who hears the cries of the world and assists anyone in distress.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1925 first edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.1855 for the second edition print published in 1946.

media.caption: Imakumano Kannonji - temple 15 (今熊野 観音寺 十五)

text.headline: Imakumano Kannonji - temple 15 (今熊野 観音寺 十五)
text.text:
Nakazawa's view may either be the long entrance path to the temple grounds of Imakumano Kannon-ji in the Higashiyama-ku district of Kyoto, or the path leading to its two-story pagoda, Isei-dō Tahōtō. This Buddhist temple is the fifteenth along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1925 first edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.1858 for the second edition print published in 1946.

media.caption: Matsunoodera - temple 29 (松尾寺 二十九)

text.headline: Matsunoodera - temple 29 (松尾寺 二十九)
text.text:
In this print, Nakazawa depicts the temple gate Niōmon at the entrance to Matsunoo-dera, a Shingon sect Buddhist temple and the 29th temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1925 first edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.1860 for the second edition print published in 1946.

media.caption: Testing a New Sword on a Central Pillar (中柱の試斬)

text.headline: Testing a New Sword on a Central Pillar (中柱の試斬)
text.text:
The fifteenth print appearing in Volume 3 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
Pictured is Muramatsu Sandayū Takanao 村松三太夫高直 (1677-1703), one of the Righteous Samurai, sword in hand, with fellow avenger Mimura Jirozaemon 三村次郎左衛門 (1666-1703), testing the sharpness of his sword against a pillar at the sword sharpener's shop in Yanagihara, Kanda in Edo. According to legend, Sandayū brought his beloved sword to be sharpened before the raid on Kira's mansion. In section 180 of Fukumoto's Genroku Kaikyoroku, he notes in the appendix to that section that this story does not appear in Issekiwa 一夕話 [Akō gishi den issekiwa 赤穂 義士 傳 一夕話, written in 1854], a source he often references, but that "some of the stories that happened in Edo are often recognized as true, so I have included them here for the time being."

GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

media.caption: Mother's Short-Sleeved Kimono (母の小袖)

text.headline: Mother's Short-Sleeved Kimono (母の小袖)
text.text:
The twentieth print appearing in Volume 3 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
On the first day of the twelfth month in 1702, Tominomori Suke’emon Masakata 富森助右衛門正因, one of the Righteous Samurai, accepted his mother's kosode to wear under his clothing to protect him from the cold after death, as was done by warriors in days gone by to protect themselves from arrows on the battlefield. On December 14, the night of the revenge attack on Lord Kira Yoshinaka, he was one of the first gishi to enter Kira's mansion through the main door. After the deed was done, he was ordered by Ōishi Yoshio to go with Yoshida Chūzaemon 吉田忠左衛門 to report their actions to the bakufu's Inspector General Sengoku Hisanao and surrender. They would be joined by their fellow gishi to await the verdict of the shogunate.

GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

media.caption: Official Opening of Sumida River Cherry Blossom Sightseeing (開仕之花隅田ノ遊覧)

text.headline: Official Opening of Sumida River Cherry Blossom Sightseeing (開仕之花隅田ノ遊覧)
text.text: This print depicts Emperor Meiji in his military uniform and an entourage of court ladies on the phoenix boat viewing the cherry trees along Tokyo's Sumida River. It's unclear whether this print was commemorating an actual event that the emperor took part in the spring of 1883, or was just displaying a popular theme to sell prints. It is known, however, that in April 1883, the month before this print was published, the emperor and his entourage paid a visit to Suzuki-shinden to view the cherry blossoms, about which he later composed several haiku. - Source: Native and Newcomer: Making and Remaking a Japanese City, Jennifer Robertson, University of California Press, 1991, p. 176-177.

media.caption: Inscribed Poem set above Landscape of either Kyoto or Nara

text.headline: Inscribed Poem set above Landscape of either Kyoto or Nara
text.text: This poem by the poet Kawai Suimei 河井 酔茗 (1874-1965) set above a landscape, possibly designed by Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964), was added to the second edition of Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces published in 1946 by Kanao Tanejirō. The original 1925 edition, also published by Kanao Tanejirō, included this landscape, without a poem, as one of two end pieces in the album. (See this collection's print IHL.2413.59 Landscape from the Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces.)

media.caption: Tanigumisan Kegonji - temple 33 (谷汲山華厳寺 三十三)

text.headline: Tanigumisan Kegonji - temple 33 (谷汲山華厳寺 三十三)
text.text:
Nakazawa presents us with a view of a small building on the temple grounds of Tanigumi-san Kegon-ji, the thirty-third and last temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, which displays a circular sign, blue with a yellow frame, proclaiming "votive offering" 奉納. Pilgrim's have attached prayer slips and prayer boards to its walls.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1946 second edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.2413.41 for the first edition print published in 1925.

media.caption: Yoshiminedera - temple 20 (善峯寺 二十)

text.headline: Yoshiminedera - temple 20 (善峯寺 二十)
text.text:
Nakazawa presents us with a view of a thick horizontal branch of the 600-year-old Yōryu no matsu pine tree behind a low wooden fence at Yoshimine-dera, the 20th temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. The roof of a temple building is seen in the midground and the hills of Nishiyama stretch across the print's background.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1946 second edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.2413.28 for the first edition print published in 1925.

media.caption: Chikubushima Hōgonji - temple 30 (竹生岛 宝厳寺 三十)

text.headline: Chikubushima Hōgonji - temple 30 (竹生岛 宝厳寺 三十)
text.text:
It is unclear which temple building Nakazawa depicts in this print. It may be the main temple building with a view of Lake Biwa off to the right. Hōgon-ji, the thirtieth temple on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage sits on Chikubu Island in the north of Lake Biwa, Japan's largest freshwater lake.
In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.
This print is from the 1946 second edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.2413.38 for the first edition print published in 1925.

media.caption: Meine Liebe ist Grün  (我が恋は緑なり)

text.headline: Meine Liebe ist Grün  (我が恋は緑なり)
text.text:
This song sheet (Senow song sheet No. 341) for Johannes Brahms' (ブラームス) Opus 63, No. 5, "Meine Liebe ist Grün" (My Love is Green), with lyrics by the poet Felix Schumann (1854-1879), was issued in 1924 by the music publisher Senow Ongaku Shuppansha. The lyrics were translated into Japanese from the German by the composer and lyricist Keizō Horiuchi 堀内敬三 (1897-1983). The cover illustration (a color lithograph) was designed by Takehisa Yumeji (1884-1934), a leading figure in the Taishō Romanticism movement.

In 1910 the music publisher Senoo (Senow) Ongaku Shuppansha, headed by Senoo Kōjirō 妹尾幸次郎 (1891-1961), also known as Senoo Kōyō 妹尾幸陽, began issuing musical scores, the majority of them by Western composers. Over 1000 scores for classical and popular music, including children’s music, were issued, many under the titles “Senoo Gakufu” (セノオ楽譜) and “Senoo Shin-kouta" (セノオ新小唄). From 1916 until 1929, Yumeji designed over 280 covers for Senoo’s published scores and contributed the lyrics for 24 songs of his own, the most famous of which is “Evening Primrose” (Yoimachigusa), published in 1918. The scores became very popular although few people could read or play the scores. They were bought because of their cover art.

media.caption: Tomochidori (友千鳥)

text.headline: Tomochidori (友千鳥)
text.text:
Print number 四十 (40) in the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the famous rikishi (sumo) Tanikaze Kajinosuke (1750-1795) outside the home of the younger, and less accomplished, wrestler Tomochidori (b. 1756). Tomochidori, who is struggling financially, is seen feeding delicacies to his sick father, who is only seen in silhouette. His sacrifices to buy food and medicine for his father and forego his own well-being is a demonstration of shikō, or supreme filial piety. Tanikaze is reaching into the sleeve of his robe, perhaps to retrieve money to give to Tomochidori.
Kuniaki contributed a single print to this series and it is fitting that it involves sumo, as Kuniaki's most famous print is that of a sumo and he is best known for his sumo prints.
To see another edition of this print go to IHL.1036.

INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

media.caption: Kiyokawa Hachirō (清河八郎)

text.headline: Kiyokawa Hachirō (清河八郎)
text.text:
Kiyokawa sits, ink brush in hand, before a fuzukue on which lies a fan he is inscribing. Known as a scholar and an exceptional writer, he wanted to "turn the realm upside down" and restore power to the emperor.

The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

media.caption: The Unbreakable (不破伴左衛門 Fuwa Banzaemon)

text.headline: The Unbreakable (不破伴左衛門 Fuwa Banzaemon)
text.text:
One of the eighteen prints in Kiyotada's second series of prints picturing the eighteen plays that make up Ichikawa Danjūrō VII's "Kabuki Jūhachiban" (The Kabuki Eighteen). In this print we see an actor in the Danjūrō line in the role of Fuwa Banzaemon in the thunder bolt pattern kimono in the play "Fuwa." The tale of the rivalry between Nagoya Sanzaburō and Fuwa Banzaemon for the love of Katsuragi, a courtesan of the Shimabara quarter in Kyoto (as told in the "Nagoya Sanzaburō monogatari"), is one of the oldest themes in popular theater in the Edo period and is known to have been performed in versions for the puppet theater as early as the Kambun era (1661-1673).
Kiyotada's better known first series of the eighteen plays in "Kabuki Jūhachiban" was published in 1896. (See IHL.1272, IHL.0805, IHL.0991, IHL.0723, IHL.1510, IHL.0722, IHL.0724, IHL.0990, IHL.0471, IHL.0992, IHL.1255.)
For the preparatory painting used as a guide to create this print see IHL.1906.

media.caption: View of Uji Bridge, 4 (宇治橋之景・四)

text.headline: View of Uji Bridge, 4 (宇治橋之景・四)
text.text:
The fourth print in a set of twelve color lithographs depicting famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print pictures Uji Bridge, leading to Naikū shrine, the inner sanctum of Ise Jingū. Crossing over the bridge takes you from the secular to the sacred world. The inset in the upper left, titled 内宮神苑正面ノ景, depicts the entrance to Naikū, the main sanctuary of Ise Grand Shrine (Isejingū), in evening. A lone figure is seen and a signpost on the right has the characters 下馬 (geba), a prohibition against entering on horseback.
This collection contains two copies (IHL.2257 and IHL.2343) of this print, issued two weeks apart. The impressions for these two prints show significant differences in coloration, with IHL.2343 using softer, a little less saturated, colors. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2343 and February 25, 1897 for IHL.2257.

media.caption: View of Magatama Pond, 5 (曲玉池之景・五)

text.headline: View of Magatama Pond, 5 (曲玉池之景・五)
text.text:
The fifth print in a set of twelve color lithographs depicting famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print pictures Magatama Pond 曲玉池 on the grounds of Gekū, the outer sanctum of Ise Jingū. The print shows both Japanese visitors in Western and traditional dress, and a single figure dressed in the traditional garb of a pilgrim, around the pond with cherry trees blooming and dusk approaching. The round inset in the upper right of the print is a nighttime scene of a small bridge and pathway leading through an Ise (jingū) torii on the grounds of Gekū.
This collection contains two copies of this print (IHL.2258 and IHL.2344) , issued two weeks apart. The impressions for these two prints show significant differences in how the evening scene in the inset is handled and in overall coloration, with IHL.2344 using less saturated colors. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2344 and February 25, 1897 for this print IHL.2258. The artist seals are also different on the two prints.

media.caption: View of Futamigaura, 6 (二見浦之景・六)

text.headline: View of Futamigaura, 6 (二見浦之景・六)
text.text:
One of two copies (see IHL.2345) of print number six (the two prints being issued two weeks apart) in a set of twelve color lithographs of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print depicts pilgrims and visitors viewing the sunrise between the Wedded Rocks (meoto iwa), a natural torii, offshore of Futamigaura in Mie Prefecture. Mt. Fuji is visible in the distance. The buildings on the right are Futami Okitama Shrine, dedicated to the deities Sarutahiko Ōkami and Ukanomitama. Pilgrims often visit this shrine and purify themselves before proceeding to Ise Shrine.
The inset in the upper right presents us with a "View of Hinjitsukan" 賓日館及海水景 at night. The famous Hinjitsukan was built as a luxury inn which hosted Emperor Meiji's mother-in-law in March 1887, followed by other royals and the well-healed.
The printer has used his discretion, perhaps at the behest of the publisher, in how he printed the insets on the two prints, changing both the coloration and the dappling on the ground. While the dates of printing for these two prints are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2345 and February 25, 1897 for this print IHL.2259. The artist's seal is also different on the two prints and other small differences in the use of color can be seen.

media.caption: A Young Boy Studying (勉強する童男 Benkyō suru warabe)

text.headline: A Young Boy Studying (勉強する童男 Benkyō suru warabe)
text.text:
From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) which show examples of children's good and bad behavior. In this print a young boy is dutifully studying in his parents' open-air store which advertises rice crackers with salt 塩せんべい while other young boys are playing. A gentleman walking by notes the boy's good behavior.
In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

media.caption: Day Laborers (日雇労働者 nikoyon)

text.headline: Day Laborers (日雇労働者 nikoyon)
text.text:
Day laborers, known as Nikoyon after the paltry wages they were paid after the war of 240 yen per day (less than a U.S. dollar a day) are either awaiting work in the foreground or at work with shovels and pushcart in the background. This print is number thirteen in the twenty-four print post-WWII series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Continued (3rd series).
The English language commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "The day-labourers are generally called 'Nikoyou' in Japan. This slang expression was originated from the fact that they earn two hundred forty yen (or Nikoyon) for one day's labour. They go to the labour-offices each day early in the morning in hopes of getting a job. [There are quite a few people who return home without purpose, who only 'work and eat' because they are unable to obtain a proper livelihood.] Most of them are engaged in sweeping and cleaning parks or roads. Recently, their wages are said to have been elevated to a little more than two hundred forty yen; however, it is still very trying for them to live on such a low wage-scale established by the government during that chaotic time after the war. All the labourers who go to the labour offices, do not always get jobs. Most of these people who have no other particular ability have no other way to sustain themselves but to sell their labour. Consequently they work without spirit and this represents one of today's biggest social problems."


OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

media.caption: Nuns (シスター shisutā)

text.headline: Nuns (シスター shisutā)
text.text:
Sisters and children at work preparing food at one of the Catholic social institutions in Japan. This print is the last print in the twenty-four print post-WWII series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Continued (3rd series).
The English language commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "These nuns belong to a world-wile [sic] religious organization which has done much beneficial social work in Japan. Their self-sacrificing sincerity is appreciated by everyone. [Since ancient times, Roman Catholic nuns have formed communities in the nunneries attached to Catholic churches where they have created a solemn world and lead lives of abstinence.] They run the kindergardens, orphanages, hospitals and even universities. [After the war, the nuns became especially popular in this country, and they have enthusiastically bought half of Japan's social education. I think that there is no one who is not sincerely grateful for this.] The history of these nuns goes back to the 6th century when Saint Benedict established convent in Europe. The Japanese school girls adors [sic] the nuns and are especially teken [sic] by their simple and neat clothing. [It seems only natural that the prim and proper nuns appear in many a girl's dream and that they are a source of admiration for them.]"

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

media.caption: Dollmakers (人形師 Ningyōshi)

text.headline: Dollmakers (人形師 Ningyōshi)
text.text:
A small workshop creating the famous Fushimi dolls.
The English language commentary for this print reads, "Many kinds of distinctive dolls, representative of their own local colour, are made here and there in Japan. 'Dollmakers' depicts a workshop of Fushimi dolls, true examples of a primitive craft. It is said that Fushimi dolls were first made by Koemon Ikaruga during the Genna Era (1615)."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

media.caption: Kintai Bridge (錦帯橋 Kintai bashi)

text.headline: Kintai Bridge (錦帯橋 Kintai bashi)
text.text:
Miyata depicts, using black ink only, 500 year old Kintai-bashi, a wooden arch bridge below Iwakuni Castle in Yamaguchi Prefecture. This print is from an unknown volume from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.

Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

media.caption: Illustration of the Record of the Rise and Fall [of the Heike and Genji clans] in Renga (盛衰記連歌之圖 Seisuiki renga no zu)

text.headline: Illustration of the Record of the Rise and Fall [of the Heike and Genji clans] in Renga (盛衰記連歌之圖 Seisuiki renga no zu)
text.text: While the Tokyo Metropolitan Library references the kabuki play Hiragana Seisakuiki ひらがな盛衰記, all of the print's cartouches reference historical figures rather than  character names in the play. Of course this is an imaginary scene, but renga (linked verse) in the title suggests a poetry session among these important Kamakura era personages.

media.caption: Three Crows Flying at Sunset

text.headline: Three Crows Flying at Sunset
text.text:
Three crows are passing through the frame of this design as the sun sets (some say, as the sun rises) in gradations of red, achieved through the printing technique known as bokashi. Zeshin's best known, and perhaps best loved, woodblock print design. Originally designed for an 1887 surimono, the design was edited and re-purposed after the artist's death for a shikishiban (square format) version sometime around 1900, and possibly as early as 1888, and subsequently issued numerous times at least through the 1930s and possibly continuing after WWII.
In his article dedicated to this print appearing in the journal Andon 95, Robert Schaap notes, "One of the highlights of Meiji period (1868-1912) printmaking is without doubt Zeshin's print of crows flying across the sky in the red glow of a rising sun."
Crows were a common subject of Japanese prints and they figured prominently in Shibata's oeuvre, the crow being generally associated with auspicious things, most importantly as part of the official mythology of the nation, in which the three-legged sun-crow Yatagarasu served as a messenger of the sun goddess, assisting the first (legendary) Emperor Jimmu (Jinmu tennō 神武天皇) in pacifying Japan.

media.caption: Illustration of Depth of the Sea (海中高低之図)

text.headline: Illustration of Depth of the Sea (海中高低之図)
text.text:
The top print in a three scene harimaze-e from a series of prints based on the 13 volume encyclopedia titled A Compilation of Geographical Knowledge (Yochi shiryaku 輿地誌略) by the multi-talented scholar of the West, Uchida Masao 内田正雄 (1839-1876), who traveled throughout the world to compile this encyclopedia. This top portion of the harimaze-e depicts a ship doing a sounding of the ocean bottom using a lead-line to determine depth. Various topographical formations are called out on the print and the red vertical cartouche on the right explains how ocean depth is measured as explained by "Uchida Sensei" (Uchida Masao) in Yochi shiryaku.
In the case of this collection's image, Sadanobu has largely copied the image from Volume 1, Asia of Uchida's encyclopedia, first published in 1870.

media.caption: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Deluxe Edition Book, 2 Volumes, and Portfolio, "The Original Prints," containing five original prints

text.headline: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Deluxe Edition Book, 2 Volumes, and Portfolio, "The Original Prints," containing five original prints
text.text:
Two volumes bound in the publisher's original cloth over boards (volume one in green cloth with yellow stamping on the spine, volume two in purple cloth red stamping on the spine). Illustrated throughout with 90 plates printed in 4-color and 268 in double-tone offset. Includes a descriptive list of plates. All housed in a matching slipcase. The five artists contributing prints were Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939) (see IHL.2269b), Fukita Fumiaki 吹田文明 (b. 1926) (see IHL.2269a), Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (b. 1937) (see IHL.2269c), Tamura Fumio 田村文雄 (b. 1941) (see IHL.2269d), Yoshida Hodaka 吉田穂高 (1926-1995) (see IHL.2269e).
The author Gaston Petit is a French Canadian Dominican priest who went to Japan as a missionary; painter, printmaker and collector and continues to reside there and create art, including prints, stained glass and paintings, in his Atelier Petit in Tokyo. "He experiments with different styles and incorporates Christian, Shintoist, and Buddhist beliefs in his works." - Source: "The Varsitarian," Student Publication of the University of Santo Tomas, by Tomas U. Santos -Number 8, November 30, 2010, Vol. LXXXII

media.caption: Sun and Water (太陽と水) from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"

text.headline: Sun and Water (太陽と水) from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"
text.text:
This print is part of the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, published in 1973. Many of Fukita's works are described as ethereal and this brilliant red sun setting into water is no exception.
Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 1 block of rawan-faced plywood; 5 printing stages using both baren and press; paper: torinoko; pigment: Japanese water-based color; oil-base ink.

media.caption: Blue and White Space from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"

text.headline: Blue and White Space from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"
text.text:
This print is part of the print portfolio, "The Original Prints," accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's "44 Modern Japanese Print Artists," published in 1973. Using woodblock for the irregular shapes defining the trapezoid, silkscreen for the yellow and the blue patterns and a hole punch to create a grid pattern of 5/16" circular holes Funasaka gives us another eye-pleasing print in his long-running series Blue and White Space. The print contains a centerfold as issued, allowing it to fit into the portfolio. (See IHL.1579 for another copy of this print.)
Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 1 screen frame; 15 blocks of shina-faced plywood; paper: torinoko hanga yōshi; pigment: vinyl-base screen-print ink, Japanese water-base color.

media.caption: An Omen from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists

text.headline: An Omen from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists
text.text:
This print is part of the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's "44 Modern Japanese Print Artists," published in 1973. (See IHL.2269.)
An Omen was one of five original prints included in the 1973 print portfolio "The Original Prints," which accompanied 300 numbered copies of the two volume work "44 Modern Japanese Print Artists," authored and compiled by Dominican priest, print artist and supporter/promoter of modern Japanese prints, Gaston Petit. This print was retitled "Secret Codes A: Omen" and reprinted in an edition of 350, apparently in the same year as "An Omen."
While human body parts became part of Akira's work early on, the ear awaited its debut until 1973, the year this print was issued. The bright and saturated color we see in this print is typical of Akira's work through the 1980s and is explained by curator Hideo Tomiyama in his essay "Traces of the Woodblock Print, Artist Akira Kurosaki," as follows: "Because he did not use a key-block method which outlines each form, he began to use pigments whose value and chroma were intended to give strong contrasts in order to distinguish the borders between colors and clarify forms."
Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 6 blocks of shina-faced plywood; paper: torinoko; pigment: watercolor, oil paint.

media.caption:
Confined in Blue (青にこもる)
from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"

text.headline:
Confined in Blue (青にこもる)
from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"
text.text:
This print is part of the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, published in 1973.
Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 4 aluminum plates, lithographic process; 5 printing stages; paper: torinoko; pigment: Toyo lithographic ink.
In commenting on Tamura's work, Petit states that Tamura's "human forms are creatures of a different world, the world of the dream. . . . Uninterested in eroticism per se, Tamura's work alludes indirectly to various aspects of sexual activity. However, the sensuous appeal of the forms is primary. . . ."

media.caption: Paradise from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"

text.headline: Paradise from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"
text.text:
This print is part of the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's "44 Modern Japanese Print Artists," published in 1973. This print was created when Hodaka was working on a series of fabricated landscape prints during, what the collector Eugene Skibbe has called, the artist's Mythology and Landscape phase (1966-74), which he describes as follows: "Hodaka began his landscape prints in 1970, and they partly paralleled and partly replaced his mythology series. As in the mythology prints, he drew inspiration from Pop art and continued to use collage techniques for his compositions. But in the landscapes, he portrayed the devastating effects of pollution on the environment . . . . For these prints, Hodaka again cut pictures out of magazines: men and women, clothed or unclothed, pieces of fabric, junked cars, wristwatches, portable radios, paper currency, whiskey bottles, and the like. He then cut each image into a collage, with the whole appearing a bit like a landscape . . . . He then photographed the collage. A photoetched zinc plate inked with black supplied the details for the final image, while woodblocks provided the colors."
Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 4 blocks of shina-faced plywood; 1 zinc plate, photoengraving; 12 printing stages; paper: torinoko; pigment: Talens WN poster color, Hobein watercolor, oil-base ink.
See IHL.0397 for another copy of this print.

media.caption: Illustration for Chapter 2 The Broom Tree (Hahakiji 帚木)

text.headline: Illustration for Chapter 2 The Broom Tree (Hahakiji 帚木)
text.text:
A color woodblock illustration from the first volume of Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari, Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), written by Murasaki Shikibu 紫式部著 in the early 11th century.
The color woodblock illustrations for the four books comprising Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari were stitched into the books and it is likely, though no definitive proof exists, that the publisher Kanao Tanejirō printed additional copies of the woodblock illustrations to be sold as single sheet prints. This collection's three stand-alone prints (IHL.2046, IHL.2101 an IHL.2270) would be examples of this, as they do not display any evidence of having been removed from a bound volume nor do they display any of the toning present on many of prints bound into the books due to contact with their acidic translucent protective sheets also bound into the original volumes.

media.caption: No. 2 Bad Example (悪・二)

text.headline: No. 2 Bad Example (悪・二)
text.text:
Print number 9 (二) from the series Moral Lessons for Daughters About the Two Sides of Life, consisting of twelve ōban-size sheets, each sheet consisting of two-chūban size images, the top image displaying an example of bad behavior and the bottom half displaying good behavior. It is not unusual for the sheets to have been separated into two chūban-size prints.
In this chūban-size print (the top half of the ōban-size sheet) a woman plays a shamisen while a mother, a friend and her daughter talk, being inattentive to the music. Seven akudama 悪 urge them on in their inattentiveness.
The bottom print (not part of this collection) also shows a shamisen player, but this time her audience is attentive. Four good souls (zendama) dressed in white urge on this good behavior, as compared with seven bad souls (akidama 悪) fostering bad behavior in the top print. It usually takes more akudama to foster bad behavior than zendama to encourage good behavior.

media.caption: Saigō Takamori (西郷隆盛)

text.headline: Saigō Takamori (西郷隆盛)
text.text:
Portraying Saigō Takamori, the leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. Above the seated Saigō is a white banner reading "Shinsei kotoku" (New Government rich in virtue), a slogan attributed to the Rebellion but likely concocted by the press.
Saigō was a revered figure to many Japanese. Physically he was imposing, standing six feet tall and weighing 200 pounds. He was a key player in the formation of the Meiji government, both as a military leader against the Tokugawa shogunate and as a politician shaping foreign and domestic policies. After leaving service with the Meiji government, largely over differences on Japan’s Korea policy, he returned to his home province of Satsuma. While not actively engaged in politics he remained politically involved through the Shigakkō (private samurai schools), where he was celebrated as the spiritual leader. After a raid on the government arsenal by Shigakkō students, his hand was forced and on February 7, 1877 he announced his decision to “confront the central government.” Nine months later the rebellion was over, Saigō was dead and his outmanned and out-gunned rebels decimated.
This print is one of six in the series titled "Kagoshima eimei kurabe," loosely translated as "Kagoshima Competition for Glory." Each of the six prints portrays an important rebel figure in the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. For other prints in the series see IHL.2273 and IHL.2274.

media.caption: Murata Shinpachi (村田新八)

text.headline: Murata Shinpachi (村田新八)
text.text:
Portraying Saigō's close friend Murata Shinpachi who committed suicide after witnessing Saigō's death in the aftermath of the Battle of Shiroyama on September 24, 1877. Murata had served in the Imperial Household and been part of the 1871-1873 Iwakura Mission to Europe and the United States. He resigned from the government along with Saigō after his return and went on to head the shigakkō artillery school, part of a system of private schools in Kagoshima supported by Saigō and set up "as a way to inculcate samurai values [in] the last generation of birthright samurai."[1] Murata was to command Saigō's 3rd division. He is buried along with Saigō at the Nanshū Cemetery in Kagoshima.
This print is one of six in the series titled "Kagoshima eimei kurabe," loosely translated as "Kagoshima Competition for Glory." Each of the six prints portrays an important rebel figure in the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. For other prints in the series see IHL.2272 and IHL.2274.

[1][1] "Saigō Takamori in the Emergence of Meiji Japan", Charles L. Yates appearing in Modern Asian Studies, Vol. 28, No. 3 (Jul., 1994), Cambridge University Press, p. 467.

media.caption: Shinohara Kunimoto (篠原国幹)

text.headline: Shinohara Kunimoto (篠原国幹)
text.text:
Portraying Shinohara Kunimoto, a long-time friend of Saigō Takamori and a former major general and commander of the Imperial Guards who resigned after Saigō left the Imperial government. He accompanied Saigō on his return to Kagoshima and was later to head the shigakkō infantry school, part of a system of private schools in Kagoshima supported by Saigō and set up "as a way to inculcate samurai values [in] the last generation of birthright samurai."[1] Shinohara was to command Saigō's 2nd division and died at the Battle of Tabaruzaka on March 3, 1877. He is buried along with Saigō at the Nanshū Cemetery in Kagoshima.
This print is one of six in the series titled "Kagoshima eimei kurabe," loosely translated as "Kagoshima Competition for Glory." Each of the six prints portrays an important rebel figure in the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. For other prints in the series see IHL.2272 and IHL.2273.

[1] "Saigō Takamori in the Emergence of Meiji Japan", Charles L. Yates appearing in Modern Asian Studies, Vol. 28, No. 3 (Jul., 1994), Cambridge University Press, p. 467.

media.caption: WAN_16B

text.headline: WAN_16B
text.text:
One of Maki's heavily textured ceramic tea bowl (chawan) prints from a series of prints that use the characters 禅味 zenmi (taste of Zen) in a cartouche within the plate. Above the beautiful black tea bowl is the Zen circular form ensō.
In the early 1960s Maki developed his own process of relief printmaking using woodblocks and cement. He first carved a conventional woodblock and then placed a cement mixture around the areas raised in relief on the block. Before the cement was set, Maki would texture it and after it dried he carved and chiseled the cement into the desired shape. After the cement completely dried, the entire surface of the plate was shellacked.

media.caption: Sawamura Tosshi in the role of Matsudaira Yoshimine (澤村訥子 松平吉峯)

text.headline: Sawamura Tosshi in the role of Matsudaira Yoshimine (澤村訥子 松平吉峯)
text.text:
This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō is one of six he created for the twelve print series Sketches from the Stage, conceived by Yamamoto Kanae (1882-1946) who also contributed six prints. In this print we see the actor Sawamura Tosshi VII (1860-1926) in the role of 松平吉峯, which can be read Matsudaira Yoshimine. All of the prints in the series were of actors appearing at the Imperial Theater (Teikoku Gekijō) which had opened in March 1911.
Yamamoto Kanae, the artist who conceived of this series, is credited with creating the seminal work launching the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement, a self-carved and self-printed woodcut portrait known as Fisherman (Gyofu 漁夫) in 1904.
In an attempt to revitalize Japanese prints he formed the Tokyo Print Club in 1911 along with Sakamoto. To create this series of actor portraits, consisting of three sets, each set made up of two prints by Yamamoto and two by Sakamoto, Kanae first photographed actors in performance. He and Sakamoto then drew actors from life at the new Imperial Theater which had recently opened on the moat opposite the Imperial Palace. Kanae hoped this series would be a money maker by "appealing to the stylish audience" that would be attending the modern plays at the Imperial Theater. He intended to issue actor portraits from thirty-four new plays, but only twelve prints were produced of the June, July and September performance at the Imperial Theater before the project was abandoned. - Source: Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 123.

media.caption: Kyūshū  Mamehon, vol. 7 (九州 まめほん 第七集)

text.headline: Kyūshū  Mamehon, vol. 7 (九州 まめほん 第七集)
text.text:
The cover engraving for this issue of Kyūshū Mamehon was designed by Sekino Jun’ichirō (1914-1988) whose model, according to his son Junpei, was "undoubtedly my sister who was only 8 at the time." (Also see IHL.2278.) Contributing artists in addition to Sekino were Kawakami Sumio (1895-1972), Takei Takeo (1894-1983) and Mutō Kan'ichi (1892-1982) with articles by Takei Takeo, Suiyōsō Shujin 水曜荘主人 (1897-1973) (the pen name of Sakai Tokuo), Oikawa Fujio (?-?), Hattori Shizuo (1902-1970), Yamanaka Rin (?-?), Ōuchi Kakunosuke (?-?) and Seigen Toko? (?-?).
Mamehon "Bean Book"
Literally "bean book", the term mamehon "is used by Japanese bibliophiles for a book smaller than an ordinary pocket book, which has been artistically printed and bound, issued in a limited edition, and made exclusively to appeal to the refined taste of a collector."[1] Although miniature books have a history going back to the Edo period, modern mamehon date from the post-War period, with the first books issued in 1953. Modern mamehon are roughly 4 x 3 in. (10 x 8 cm) and contain graphic art, essays, poems and stories. The art generally takes the form of line drawings. etchings and prints, woodblock and even potato prints tipped into pages. The books were generally string bound, knotted or stitched.
Kyūshū Mamehon 九州 まめほん, was first published in March 1953. and sold exclusively to members of Kyūshū mamehon no kai (Kyūshū Miniature Book Association.) Kyūshū Mamehon was discontinued after twenty-four issues (plus a supplemental volume) due to the illness of its publisher Mizutani Mamoru 水谷護.[2]
Contributing artists to Kyūshū Mamehon included Takei Takeo 武井武雄 (1894-1983), illustrator of children's books, poet, print maker and driving force behind the post-War resurgence of of mamehon; Serizawa Keisuke 芹沢 銈介 (1895-1984), a leading member of the mingei movement, stencil dyer and Living National Treasure; Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960), self-taught artist who became a major figure in the sōsaku hanga movement; Sekino Juni'chirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988), a leader of the post-War sōsaku hanga movement who worked in both etching and woodblock; Hatsuyama Shigeru 初山滋 (1897-1973), children's book illustrator and sōsaku hanga artist; Mutō Kan'ichi 武藤完一 (1892-1982), woodblock and etching artist; Kagawa Tokio 香川軍男 (1915-2002) known for his book of "potato prints" (薯版 ) of Ainu culture and Kawakami Sumio 川上澄生 (1895-1972), self-taught sōsaku hanga print artist fascinated with the intersection of foreign cultures with Japanese culture.

[1] UCLA Librarian Volume 15, Number 16, June 8, 1962, p. 113-114.
